### A POEM OF THREE PARTS FOR VOLUME II.
<note>original: "Tristychon in Tomum II." While "tristychon" usually refers to a three-line stanza, Kircher uses it here for a six-line poem composed of three couplets.</note>

The World plays like a vocal organ with its ten registers;
As many beings as exist within it, so many are its musical rhythms.
GOD is the Harmonizer, <note>original: "Harmostes," a term derived from Greek meaning one who fits things together or a master of harmony.</note> in whom the Wisdom of the Father,
Which has ordered all things well, is united by the Spirit as Love.
This love is harmony; the world is bound together by this love;
O mortal, <note>original: "ψαῦτ’" (psaut'). This likely refers to the reader or "one who touches/perceives" the physical world.</note> do you deny that this world belongs to the Divinity?

# BOOK EIGHT OF THE GREAT ART OF CONSONANCE AND DISSONANCE

## ON MIRACULOUS <term>MUSURGY</term> <note>original: "Musurgia Mirifica"; Kircher uses this term to describe the systematic or mechanical production of music.</note>

->that is<-

### THE NEW MUSARITHMIC ART, RECENTLY INVENTED,

*by which anyone, no matter how unskilled in Music, can reach a perfect knowledge of composing in a short time.*

## PREFACE.

<note>An ornamental woodcut drop cap letter 'I' decorated with detailed leaf and vine patterns.</note>
In all arts and sciences, Practice and Theory seek such a union that if one should fail the other, both would deservedly fail; for practice does not maintain its reputation without theory, nor does theory alone maintain its own without practice. These principles apply in other fields, but most especially in the faculty of Music. For although the theory of music—content with the love of truth alone—might be said to have achieved its goal in some manner (that is, its own intellectual delight), it is nonetheless impossible for a musician, if they are entirely destitute of practice, to produce anything of worth regarding said faculty. Hence, from my early youth, I decided that I must apply myself equally to both—

<summary>This page introduces Book Eight of Kircher's work, detailing his "Musarithmic Art," a system intended to allow even non-musicians to compose music by combining theory and practice.</summary>
<keywords>Musurgia Universalis, Musarithmic Art, Music Theory, Musical Practice, Composition, Athanasius Kircher, Baroque Music</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to Book Eight, following from the author's resolution to unite musical theory and practice. The text explains the motivation behind his invention of a mechanical composition system.</meta>

...so that one whose mind was set on searching more deeply into the innermost secrets of Music would find that, in the intent of execution, theory did not fail practice, nor practice theory. The arrogant reproach of purely practical musicians added a stimulus to carry out this proposal; for they think it impossible for a theorist to compose a melody with the skill, elegance, and grace that modern music rightly requires. Indeed, asserting the contrary with laughter and derision, I sought to show that this reproach of theirs was false and unjust. For many years now I have applied myself seriously to this task, leaving nothing untried by which I might discover some Art through which anyone, however unskilled in Music, could achieve in a short space of time and without labor that which practical composers hardly achieve in many years.

Therefore, having learned through frequent musical experience and noting the great power of combinations hidden beneath musical intervals and the diversity of tones, I approached the principles of the whole musurgical combination by the aid of analytical art. I reduced the more excellent and necessary <term>metatheses</term> <note>Original: "metatheses"; here referring to the rearrangement or transposition of musical elements.</note> of harmonic relations into tables with truly great labor, using such a disposition of secret skill that, in whatever position the <term>Melotactic</term> column <note>A term coined by Kircher for his "arrangement of melody" system.</note> was ordered, a new harmony would always emerge. While this truly wonderful Melotactic combination—still wailing, as it were, in its first cradle in simple counterpoint—obtained its own successful results, I was immediately carried away by an intellectual fervor. Not content with these, I applied my mind to bringing forth a universal method of <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of composing melodies or setting text to music.</note>. In this, I seem indeed to have succeeded so well as to exhibit all harmonic beauty and grace together with the appropriate artifice of words. 

Though these things seemed at first paradoxical <note>original Greek: "παράδοξα"</note> and truly miraculous to musicians, they nonetheless learned to have faith in this Art—whose principles they did not yet understand—once the experiment was performed by various illustrious men. Now, this new <term>Musurgy</term> of ours consists chiefly in the ingenious combination of Melotactic Tables; by which, however they are arranged, a new harmony must necessarily emerge. Thus, since compositions of this kind are nearly infinite, an infinite diversity of harmonic concert is also born. Therefore, whoever knows how to adapt our Melotactic Tables according to the rules to be prescribed by us shortly, and knows how to rightly transfer the harmonic numbers into the melotactic scale, will also know that they will compose with the same ease—in whatever tone and with whatever texts of words are given—any ingenious songs: simple, composite, florid, diminished, syncopated, interwoven with ingenious <term>ligatures</term> <note>Notes tied together, indicating they should be sung to a single syllable or played smoothly.</note>, and following one another in the manner of fugues. 

For just as in Algebra a <term>Logista</term> <note>A practitioner of logistical calculation or algebra.</note>, by following the course of a rule, completes the explanations of paradoxical questions with such ease that the operator himself does not know how he has done it—and thus an unexpected effect comes forth while the calculator is scarcely thinking—so here, for those composers following the course of the prescribed rules, the desired harmony will come forth, whether performed by those skilled in music or those ignorant of it, even children and women. Certainly, the vows and effective prayers of our Fathers migrating to the most remote Indies were able to do much to make this secret public. Since the attraction of unlearned people consists in the frequent practice of music and divine praises, and neither printed books nor composers are always present, they believed this Musurgy would be of the greatest use to them. For with this, they will produce not only the desired songs in the Latin language, but also in any proposed language—even Indian and however "barbarian" an idiom—as will be discussed at length later.

His <note>Catchword: "To these..." or "With these..."</note>

<summary>Kircher explains that he developed his "Musurgical Art" to prove that a theorist could compose as well as a practitioner. He compares his system of Melotactic tables to algebra, claiming it allows anyone—including children, women, and missionaries in the Indies—to compose complex music mechanically.</summary>

Book VIII. On the Miraculous Art of Music-Making.
Signature: A 2
<meta>The catchword at the bottom right is "4 Si".</meta>

Therefore, led by these considerations, I wished to make this miraculous art of music-making <note>Original: "Musurgia Mirifica," Kircher’s term for his system of automated musical composition.</note> available to the public, lest I should seem to have omitted anything that might contribute to the propagation of divine worship and honor in this endeavor. But truly, lest we keep the reader's eager mind in suspense any longer, let us approach the task with favorable omens. However, so that we do not proceed in this new and unheard-of art without method <note>Original: ἀμεθόδως (amethódōs)</note>, we shall proceed with that order and method which this miraculous art of music-making rightly claims for itself.

# OF THE MIRACULOUS ART OF MUSIC-MAKING
## PART ONE.
### COMBINATORIAL MUSIC-MAKING
### MUSURGICAL LEMMA I.
<note>A "Lemma" is a preliminary proposition or a "stepping stone" theorem used to prove a larger point later on.</note>

Whenever a ratio—for example, A to B—is said to be "composite" (as if made from the ratios A, E, and I), I say that this ratio is composed from those same parts regardless of the order in which they are placed. That is, between two terms A and B, it is permissible to continue these ratios as many times as they can change places among themselves. For example: let as many numbers be taken in a natural series as there are proposed things. When these numbers are multiplied by each other, they produce the total sum of mutations <note>In this context, "mutations" refers to what modern mathematics calls permutations—the different ways a set of items can be arranged.</note>; thus, for two things, two mutations result; for three things, six; for four, 24; for five, 120.

->Paradigm.<-

<margin>A B 1 & B A 2</margin>
1. Let there be, for example, two proposed things, A and B. I say they can be changed twice and no more, for each will occupy the first place only once, as is clear in the margin; for these numbers multiplied together (1 x 2) produce two.

2. But three things can be varied in six ways. For these numbers—1, 2, and 3—multiplied in order, produce six. That is to say, 1 times 2 makes 2, and 2 times 3 makes 6, etc. The reason for this is that each thing will hold the first place once, and the remaining two can be changed twice among themselves, as is clear in the following example.

->Example.<-

| | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | O R A | 3 | R O A | 5 | A O R |
| 2 | O A R | 4 | R A O | 6 | A R O |

3. Suppose there are four things to be changed among themselves; therefore, multiply four by the number produced from the previous multiplication—namely, by 6—and 24 mutations will be produced. This is because these numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4, multiplied in order, produce 24. For each thing will hold the first place only once, and the remaining three can be varied six times among themselves. Indeed, inspect the present example.

->Example.<-

| A 1. | M 2. | E 3. | N 4. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 AMEN | 7 MAEN | 13 EAMN | 19 NAME |
| 2 AMNE | 8 MANE | 14 EANM | 20 NAEM |
| 3 AEMN | 9 MEAN | 15 EMAN | 21 NMAE |
| 4 AENM | 10 MENA | 16 EMNA | 22 NMEA |
| 5 ANEM | 11 MNAE | 17 ENAM | 23 NEMA |
| 6 ANME | 12 MNEA | 18 ENMA | 24 NEAM |

If, however, you wish to change 5 things, place the numbers in their natural order <note>The "natural order" refers to the sequence of counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.</note>, as follows: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. ->Permutations, and so on into infinity.<-

You see, therefore, how for any number of things placed in their natural order, the number of permutations <note>original: "mutationum"</note> suitable to those things is produced from the multiplication of the numbers performed in sequence among them. Thus, 10 things can be combined among themselves 3,628,800 times, and 20 things 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 times. These figures can scarcely be believed, unless a mathematical demonstration convinced our intellect.

### PROPOSITION II <note>original: "Lemma II"</note>.

<margin>Permutations of a five-letter name <note>original: "pentagrammati"</note> in which two letters are the same.</margin>
Whenever similar things occur—or, what is the same thing, the same items are placed several times among the things to be combined—the combination of the whole divided by the number of combinations of the similar items (as proposed in the preceding table) will give the required number of combinations.

Suppose the name **MARIA** is proposed. Since it has two similar letters—or, what is the same thing, the letter **A** is placed twice—we ask how many times it can be combined. Since the name is a <term>pentagrammaton</term> <note>A word consisting of five letters.</note> or five-letter word, if all the letters were different, they would have 120 combinations as shown in the preceding table. Let this number be divided by the number of combinations for two items <note>The factorial of 2, which is 2.</note>, as the table shows; it will give a quotient of 60. And that is how many times any 5-letter name can be combined if it has two letters that are similar or the same, as in the present name with the two **As**.

<margin>Of a three-letter name <note>original: "trigrammati"</note>.</margin>
Again, let a <term>trigrammaton</term> <note>A word consisting of three letters.</note> or three-letter name be given in which two letters are placed twice, as in the name **ALA**, and someone wishes to know how many times it can be combined. He will achieve his wish if he divides the combination of the whole (namely the combination of three things, which is 6) by the number of combinations for two items (which is 2). The result will be 3, which is the required combination of the proposed name.

You see, therefore, in this example, that this name <note>Kircher uses "name" or "voice" to refer to a string of letters.</note> does not allow more than three changes because the letter **A** is placed twice. For if you place the two **AA**s at the beginning once; then one at the beginning and the other at the end; and thirdly, both at the end; the entire combination will be exhausted. Likewise, if you wish to know the combinations of a four-letter name <term>tetragrammaton<gloss>a word consisting of four letters</gloss></term> with two similar letters, you divide 24 by 2; the resulting 12 will be the sought-after combination of said name.

<note>The table shows permutations of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (Y-H-V-H). In this name, the letter *He* (ה) appears twice. In the permutations shown, Kircher explores the 12 possible arrangements of these four characters.</note>

You see in this example that this name is not combinable except twelve times, as the example teaches. There you see the letter *He* (ה) placed six times at the beginning, *Vav* (ו) three times, and *Yod* (י) three times, which joined together constitute the sought number of 12 for the combinations of this four-letter name. The same is to be said of any other four-letter name. If, however, some four-letter name had three similar letters—that is, the same ones—24 divided by 6 will give the sought change of combination, as is clear in the second example. There you see it is impossible for it to admit more than 4 changes.

<note>This table is a seventeenth-century guide for calculating permutations of a multiset (arrangements of objects where some are identical). While the logic is sound, the printed numbers in columns 5 and 10 contain some calculation errors typical of the era's typesetting; for instance, the permutation of 8 items with 4 similar should be 1,680, but is printed here as 1,663.</note>

---

## USE OF THE TABLE.

<margin>
Use of the 
Table.
</margin>
This table has 10 columns, decreasing in order proportionally. In the first column, 10 numbers are contained signifying the combinable things, or the series of things to be combined. The second column contains combinations of things where every single item differs from the others. Thus, 5 <note>The Latin text mistakenly says "IV" (4), but refers to the row for 120, which corresponds to V (5).</note> things can be changed 120 times; whereas 7 things can be changed 5040 times. The third column contains combinations of things in which two items are the same. The fourth column contains combinations of things in which three are the same, and so on for the other columns in order up to the tenth column, in which combinations of things where nine items are the same are contained.

The use of this table, therefore, is this: if someone desires to know how many times a name of, for example, 8 letters can be changed, which nevertheless has 4 of the same letters—as this invented name **MARABANA** <note>In the name M-A-R-A-B-A-N-A, the letter 'A' appears four times.</note> shows—since there are 4 identical letters, one asks how many times it can be combined. Therefore, look in the first column for VIII (for the proposed name has that many letters); then look for the column of the combination of things in which four are the same, and the intersecting angle will give 1663; <note>Modern calculation ($8! / 4!$) yields 1,680.</note> and that is how many times the proposed name of 8 letters, of which 4 are the same, can be combined. Likewise, a name of six letters in which three are the same is changeable in 120 ways; you will find this number at the intersecting angle if you move across from the number VI in the first column and ascend from the third column <note>Kircher counts the "similar" columns starting after the "all diverse" column.</note> upward.

Thus you see that six things, all different, can be rearranged 720 times. If, however, two of them were the same, there are 360 variations; if 3 are the same, 120; if 4 are the same, 25 <note>original: "25". Mathematically, the permutation of 6 items where 4 are identical should be 30 (720 ÷ 24), but the author is following the values printed in Table II on the previous page, which contains several calculation errors.</note>; if 5 are the same, they can be changed six times; and if all 6 things are the same, there is 0 <note>In modern combinatorics, we would say there is only 1 way to arrange identical items, but the author likely means there are zero *additional* variations possible.</note> variation. You will proceed no differently regarding any other number of things contained within ten. We have composed this table according to the rules delivered a little before, so that it would not be difficult to extend it to any number whatsoever. # CHAPTER I.
## On the Combinations of Notes.

**T**hrough several Problems, we will teach here the method and reasoning by which one may determine how, and how many times, any number of musical notes <term>Notes (Notæ): The individual symbols representing musical pitches on a staff.</term> may be varied and combined among themselves.

### Combinatorial Problem I.

->*Given a melody of any number of notes, to find how many times it can be rearranged within a certain musical interval.*<-

**L**et there first be a melody <term>Melody (Vox): Literally "voice," but in this context referring to a specific sequence of musical notes.</term> of three notes which ascends through a third, from C through D to E. The question is how many times it can be rearranged within this interval so that no note is placed twice on the same degree of the scale, but each is unique within that same interval? I answer that this can be done six times and no more; for since, according to Lemma I, three diverse things can be changed six times, and here there are three notes placed on three different degrees, it follows necessarily that they can also be changed six times within the interval of a single third. Indeed, for a further demonstration of this, nothing else seems to be required except a visual proof, which follows:

<note>The illustration displays musical notation on a five-line staff with a C-clef. It shows six variations of a three-note melody (the notes C, D, and E) using square and diamond-shaped notes typical of the period. Each variation is numbered 1 through 6 beneath the staff to show the different possible permutations of the three pitches.</note>

You see, therefore, in the example, how the proposed melody is changed six times so that no note is placed twice on any one degree, but each is different within the same interval; we have therefore achieved what was proposed.
No differently, a melody of four notes ascending step-by-step from C to F through the interval of a fourth can be changed 24 times according to Lemma I. For since the 4 places in the interval of a fourth are all different, the melody can be changed six times starting from the note <term>Note (Chorda): Literally "string," a term used here to refer to a specific pitch or "chord" in the sense of a scale degree.</term> C; and six times starting from note D; six times starting from note E; and finally six times starting the melodic permutations from note F. Moreover, four multiplied by six gives the total number of the proposed combination [24]. As is evident in the following example.

### Combinatorial Problem II.

->*Given a melody of any number of notes, of which any number of notes sit upon the same pitch, to find the number of combinations for the proposed melody.*<-

**T**his problem is solved without any difficulty by using the preceding Combinatorial Table II. Let there be, first, a melody <term>Melody (vox): Kircher uses the word "voice" to mean a musical phrase or sequence of notes.</term> of six notes, two of which are the same—that is, they sit upon the same pitch <term>Pitch (chorda): Literally "string," referring to the specific line or space on the staff representing a tone.</term> F. What is the combination of this melody? Divide the combination of a set of six <note>original: "senarij". A senary is a group or set of six.</note> (namely, 720) by the combination of a set of two (the binary), and the quotient, 360, will give the sought-after combination; for the proposed melody can be rearranged that many times. Alternatively, using the preceding table: look for VI in the first column, and the shared corner in the second column will give 360, the sought combination, as before.

<note>Musical notation displays a staff with six notes. Two of these notes are placed on the same line, which is labeled with the letter F to indicate their shared pitch.</note>

Again, let there be a melody of four notes, of which two are the same. The combination is sought; therefore, divide the combination of a set of four <note>original: "quaternarij". A quaternary is a group of four.</note> (namely, 24) by the combination of a set of two (2), and the quotient will give 12 as the sought combination, as is clear in the example.

### Combinatorial Problem III.

> Given a melody of any number of notes, including any number of doubles, triples, or quadruples of notes existing upon the same or different pitches, to find the permutations of the melody.

By this divisor, the total combination of five things (namely, 120) when divided leaves 30 as the sought-after combination or permutation of the proposed melody <note>Mathematically, Kircher is calculating 5! / (2! * 2!). 120 divided by 4 equals 30.</note>. ## Problem IV. Combinatorics.

->Given a melody <term>Melody (vox): A sequence of notes.</term> of any number of notes, of which two are the same on one pitch <term>Pitch (chorda): Literally "string," referring to the specific line or space on the musical staff.</term> and three are the same on another pitch; to find the combination, that is, the number of permutations of the melodies.<-

Let there be a certain melody of nine notes, of which two are the same on pitch A, three are the same on pitch C, and two others are again on pitch A, as is evident in the present example; what is the permutation of the proposed melody? Proceed thus: multiply the combination of three (which is 6) by the square of the combination of two things (which is 4). You will have a divisor of 24. Divide the combination of nine <note>9 factorial (9!).</note>, namely 362,880, by this, and 15,120 will result, which are the sought permutations in the given melody.
<margin>
<note>A short musical staff displays nine notes on five lines using a C-clef on the third line. The notes are grouped to illustrate the math: two notes on the second line (labeled A), three notes on the second space (labeled C), then two more on C and two more on A. The letters A A C C C C C A A appear below to guide the reader.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
The combination of 4 <note>4 factorial (4!).</note> is 24, the square of which is 576.
</margin>
If a melody of 22 notes should occur, of which two notes are repeated twice, and one note is repeated thrice, and two others are repeated four times, it is asked how many times the melody can be changed? The process is as follows: you will square the combination of 2 and you will have 4; you will multiply this by 6 (the combination of three) so that you have 24; then you will multiply this again by the square of the combination of 4, which is 576; and the product, 13,824, will give the divisor. By this, the combination of 22—that is, 1,124,000,727,777,607,680,000 <note>This is the value of 22 factorial (22!).</note>—when divided, will give 8,130,792,301,632,000, which is the number of permutations of the sought song.

## Various Examples.

->*In a melody of nine notes.*<-

<columns>2</columns>

Whenever all notes are in different positions, the melody will have 362,880 permutations, as shown.

Whenever two notes out of the nine have the same position, the melody will have 181,440 permutations.

Whenever three out of the nine are on the same pitch, the melody will have 60,480 permutations.

Whenever seven out of the nine occupy the same pitch, the melody will have 72 permutations.

Whenever 2 and 2 out of the nine are the same, the melody will have 90,720 permutations.

But when 2, 2, and 2 out of the nine are of the same position, the melody will be changed 45,360 times.

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<columns>2</columns>

...permutations, the total of which is so great that if someone were to write down only a thousand of these same changes every day, he would labor in describing them for 22,260,896,143 years. This is a thing altogether incredible to those who do not know the power of numbers and the nature of combination, which are nevertheless easily demonstrated from the preceding arguments. From this it is also clear how an inconceivable multitude of permutations can emanate from any motet <term>Motet (Motecta): A polyphonic musical composition, usually on a sacred text.</term> consisting thereafter of 50, 100, or 200 notes. Certainly, if the entire machine of the world were filled with paper, it would not suffice to contain all the permutations even in a combination of 30 notes.

## Problem V. Universal.

->*Given in any voice <note>original: "voce"; here meaning a musical sequence or melody line.</note> however many notes, whether differing or not differing, to find how many times any other number of notes, chosen from this assumed and determined number, can be changed.*<-

This proposition has something wonderful about it, from which it seemed best to begin more deeply; and so that we may more easily explain our meaning, we shall begin from the very example of the proposition. Let someone from among the Music-makers <term>Music-makers (Musurgis): A term Kircher uses for composers or scholars of the musical arts.</term> propose this combinatoric riddle: having set in order 22 notes, first all different, ascending through a triple octave <term>Triple Octave (trisdiapason): A musical interval spanning three full octaves.</term>, exactly as many as there are notes in the musical scale of Guido <note>The "Guidonian Scale" refers to the system of hexachords and the "Guidonian Hand" developed by Guido of Arezzo, which formed the basis of Western music theory in Kircher's time.</note>, as appears in this present diagram.

It is asked first, how many times those notes can be simply changed, and we shall immediately satisfy this question through Lemma I and Problem I. Since all are different, they will admit the customary combination of the number 22, as Table I shows, namely: 1,124,000,042,171,709,440,000. <note>This massive number represents 22 factorial (22!), the total possible arrangements of 22 unique notes.</note>

It is asked therefore secondly, how many times 2 notes can be changed within the space of a triple octave, and how many times again 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and so on up to the number 22 exclusive—how many times, I say, within a determined triple octave interval a voice of however many notes assumed from the 22 notes is changeable? In order that this may be known, do thus: Since 22 notes have been assumed, multiply 22 by 21 (that is, by the next smaller number), and 462 will be produced. And so many times can two notes be arranged within a triple octave interval, always differing. The reason for this is that since all 22 notes are different and ascending by degrees, it follows consequently that the order can change twenty-one times. For the first change occurs through 21 degrees. The second change will occur when the notes are arranged thus, or ascend through a third. The third change of notes will occur through a fourth. The fourth through a fifth. The fifth change through a sixth, and so on for the others up to 22, which is the triple octave. Since, therefore, in 22 notes there are 21 different changes, these consequently multiplied by 22 will produce the proposed number 462. So many times, therefore, can two notes be changed within a triple octave, and no more, as the proposition requires.

All of which things must be understood regarding the 462 different permutations of two notes variously arranged within the interval of a triple octave, as is clear in the attached examples. From this, if you desire to know how many times three notes within the interval...

In like manner, you see that an interval of 5, or 5 numbers, can be changed 4,683,336,365,740,320,000 times. And so it is for the rest. But since these things may seem incredible to one unskilled in <term>Arithmetic (Arithmetices): The study of numbers and their properties, here applied to the "science of music."</term>, and because this combination could not be exhausted by 10,000 writers even if they labored for 1,000 years, it seemed appropriate to provide examples here in smaller numbers, so that the truth of the matter may be recognized through expanded mutations of combinations; for the method of proceeding is the same in small numbers as in large ones.

### Examples in smaller numbers.

Suppose, therefore, someone wishes to know how many times, out of five proposed notes, only two notes can be changed so that they are always different, and the melody always produces different intervals; proceed as follows: let the numbers be placed in their natural order, as is evident in the example, in which the first number shows five notes, or the whole set. The second column, using Roman numerals, signifies the parts of the whole—namely, how many times the parts of the five notes can be changed within the interval of a fifth. The third column signifies the mutations themselves. Thus you see that a single note can be changed only five times, two notes twenty times, three notes sixty times, and four notes one hundred and twenty times. Finally, five notes can be changed as many times as the ordinary combination of the first table prescribes. This table is made very easily in this way: multiply 4 by 5, and the product 20 will give the mutation of two notes. Again, multiply 3 by 20 and you will have 60 mutations of 3 notes. Again, 2 times 60 will produce 120 mutations of four notes, and 1 times 120 will give the ordinary combination of the matter as stated, but let us show the matter with examples.

## Mutations of two notes out of five—that is, within the interval of a fifth—such that they are never found twice upon the same pitch.

For if, out of 5, you establish two notes twice on the same degree, as is evident in the last 5 mutations of this diagram, these added to the previous 20 will give exactly 25 mutations of 2 notes out of 5. The reasoning is clearly evident from the positioning of the notes.

## Problem VI. A most universal combinatory rule.

> *Given any number of notes, how many mutations can be made from any number of notes chosen from them, whether those notes are different, the same, or similar, or a mixture of similar and different.*

In the preceding section, we showed the method by which, given any number of notes, we can derive different mutations from any chosen number of those notes. Now it must also be shown how mutations of notes can be made from any number assumed within a certain interval, whether those notes be different, similar, or partly similar and partly different.

Proceed in this way. Let the <term>Great System (Systema maximum): The full range of the musical scale used in this period, typically spanning three octaves or 22 notes.</term> of the musical scale consist of 22 notes, for example. Suppose someone desires to know how many times each musical interval assumed within it allows for precise mutations. For example, I desire to see how many 3 notes, variously arranged within the musical scale, undergo mutations. Act thus: multiply 22 notes by itself, and 484 will be produced; these are the mutations that 2 notes, variously arranged within the whole system, can undergo. Furthermore, multiply this number 484 again by 22, and you will have 10,648, the sought-after mutations of three notes within the said scale.

In this manner, 22 multiplied by 10,648 will produce 234,256, the number of mutations of four notes variously arranged within the scale. Thus, 22 multiplied by the recently found number 234,256 will give the mutations of [five] notes variously placed within the given System. By always multiplying the last product by the notes of the entire scale (that is, by 22), the number of all mutations for that number of notes which follows next in natural order will be produced. If you truly wish to know the number of notes that are partly similar and partly different, subtract the numbers of the preceding table from the numbers of this table, and the remainder will give the desired result.

### Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making <note>original: *Musurgia Mirifica*</note>.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the combination of the value of notes.

We have spoken in the preceding problems about the combinations and permutations of notes, or how many times given notes can change their position among themselves to constitute different voices <note>meaning different melodic lines or sequences</note>. Now we shall also show by what method we can know how many times notes of different value <note>original: *valoris*; referring to the rhythmic duration of the notes</note> can be changed, even when arranged on a single pitch. This is as follows:

### Problem I.

> *To find, given a melody of any number of notes that are all of different value, how many times those notes of different value can be changed among themselves.*

We do not demonstrate here how many times the proposed notes can change their location <note>referring to their pitch on the staff</note>, but only how many times notes of different values, even when arranged on one and the same pitch, can be changed and variously arranged among themselves. To begin, therefore, with small examples: let three notes of different value be proposed, and you wish to know how many times they can be changed among themselves.

<margin>
3 3 3
  9
 27.
</margin>
You will cube the number three <note>original: *ternarium*</note> placed three times, as is evident in the margin, by multiplying 3 by 3 to make 9; then, you will multiply 3 by 9, and you will have 27. That is how many times three notes of different value can be changed among themselves, as is clear in the subjoined example.

### Permutation <note>original: *mutatio*</note> of 3 notes of different value.

<note>A musical diagram consisting of three musical staves, each starting with the number 9. Each staff contains nine numbered groups of three notes positioned on a single line. The notes represent three different rhythmic durations: a hollow diamond (semibreve), a hollow diamond with a stem (minim), and a filled diamond with a stem (semiminim or crotchet). Together, the three staves visually demonstrate all 27 mathematical permutations of these three rhythmic values, numbered sequentially from 1 to 27.</note>

And from this example, the method of proceeding is clear enough, where you see the semibreve placed nine times in the first series; in the second series the minim is placed nine times; and nine times in the third series...

## Problem II.

*Given a voice of any number of notes differing in both position and value, to find how many times the given voice can be changed under this double variety.*

In the preceding problem we showed how many times a voice of any number of notes of different value can be changed, with no respect given to the change of place <note>original: *loci*; meaning pitch position</note>. In this problem, however, we intend to demonstrate how many times a voice of any number of notes, differing in both position and value, can be changed and transposed.

<note>Four small musical staff segments are arranged horizontally to the right of the text, labeled I, II, III, and IV above, and 1, 2, 3, and 4 below. Each staff displays a pair of notes—one white whole note and one black half note—arranged in different combinations of pitch (one higher or lower than the other) and rhythm (the long note appearing before or after the short note) to illustrate the concept of "position" and "value" mutations.</note>

Let this therefore be the universal rule: Whenever notes in some voice differ in both position and value, the combination of notes differing in position must first be multiplied <note>original: *ducenda est*; literally "must be led," a common Latin term for multiplication</note> by the combination of notes differing in value, and the product will give the result sought. Let us show the matter in the smallest numbers. If, therefore, someone wishes to know how many times a voice of two notes differing in position and value can be changed: he will multiply the combination of notes differing in position only, namely 2, as the first column shows, by the combination of notes differing in value, namely the number 2, as the second column shows; the product will give the result sought, namely 4, as is evident. If, however, you desire to know the mutations of 3 notes differing in both position and value, you will multiply the combination of the number three, namely 6 in the first column, by the combination of the number three in the second column, namely 27, and 162 sought mutations will be produced.

But the preceding table teaches everything exactly. If, however, in three notes one differs from the other two which are similar, the cube of three multiplied twice into itself, as appears at the side, namely 27, will give the sought number of mutation for three notes in which one differs and the rest are similar, as the subjoined example teaches.

## L E M M A.
<note>A lemma is a preliminary proposition used to prove a larger theorem.</note>

If any chosen number is repeated in order—twice, three times, four times, five times, and so on to infinity—the numbers repeated in that order, when multiplied by themselves in sequence, will produce the algebraic <note>original: *cossicum*; from *cosa* (the "thing"), an early term for an unknown variable or power in algebra</note> number of that order, which is indicated by the character of the number continued in natural order, or by what the numerical exponents demonstrate.

<margin>The wonderful affinity of Music to Algebra.</margin>
Let the number three be repeated several times, as is evident in this example. Then, if 3 is multiplied by itself <note>original: *33 in se*; meaning $3 \times 3$</note>, it will result in a Square <note>original: *Q.* for *Quadratus*</note>. If 3 is multiplied by itself four times <note>original: *3333 in se*</note>, the result will be a biquadrate <note>the fourth power, or $x^4$</note>, and so on for the rest, as the table shows. In this table, you see that the number 3, when placed twice and multiplied by itself, produces a square, which the algebraic symbol **Q** placed before the number 2 indicates. However, the numbers continued in a natural series are called "exponents," because they set forth how many times the chosen number should be placed and how many times it should be multiplied by itself to produce the desired algebraic power <note>original: *dignitas*</note> indicated by the symbol prefixed to the exponents. Thus, the exponent 4 shows that three should be placed four times and then multiplied, to produce 81, the biquadrate of the number three, indicated by the symbol **QQ**. The exponent 6, however, shows that 3 should be placed six times and multiplied in order to generate 729, the squared-cube <note>the sixth power, or $x^6$</note> of the number three, which the symbol **QC** indicates. Therefore, having established this Lemma, we shall apply it to the following problems.

| Symbol | Exponent | Sequence | Result | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R. | 1 | 3 | 3 | Root. |
| Q. | 2 | 33 | 9 | Square. |
| C. | 3 | 333 | 27 | Cube. |
| QQ. | 4 | 3333 | 81 | Biquadrate. |
| SS. | 5 | 33333 | 243 | Sursolid. |
| QC. | 6 | 333333 | 729 | Squared-cube. |

Thus, this six, placed twice and multiplied by itself, will produce the Square, 36, which shows the variations of 2 voices: where each voice has 3 notes, it can be varied 36 times. For while the first voice can be changed 6 times by singing one of its six variations, the second voice can meanwhile sing all 6 of its variations at the same time; and while the first voice sings the second of its 6 variations, the second voice will meanwhile sing another 6; and so on until the first singer completes six variations and the other completes 36. This is the reason why two voices can be varied 36 times. For the same reason, three voices can be varied 216 times, because just as 6 placed three times and multiplied in order produces a cube, so three voices, each of which is changeable six times, when multiplied by each other produce what we might call a harmonic cube, namely the 216 sought-after variations of three voices. By this reasoning, 6 placed four times in order and multiplied by itself produces the harmonic <term>biquadrate</term><note>The fourth power ($x^4$).</note>, which is 1,296 variations of 4 voices, and so on for the rest, as the following table shows. ->*On the mutations resulting from the 12 different modes or Tones.*<-

# THE MIRACULOUS MAKING OF MUSIC
## PART II.
## RHYTHMIC OR POETIC MUSIC-MAKING.
### CHAPTER I.
### On the power and efficacy of the Rhythmic art.

<margin>The human voice provokes imitation.</margin>
I truly do not know what hidden and hitherto unpenetrated power of nature dwells within motion, by which we see that one is able to effect in another what he does himself. This is seen not only in the outward movement of the body, but also and most especially in that motion which, through the service of the tongue, breaks forth into words and song. For we see that even one person singing excites others to do the same by a certain hidden force (whether it happens through fear, as in those struck by a panic terror, or by the instinct of joy, as occurs in those dancing). While this happens in other movements, it certainly holds the greatest place in human voices. For since the human voice is nothing other than a certain skillful movement of the tongue formed according to the intention of a person to signify something, we see it accomplish in others exactly what it performs itself. Experience has taught that one person humming, or wailing, or whistling, or even yawning, excites others to do the same. Since this is true in sounds and voices that are even rough and unpolished, it will certainly be verified much more so in the harmonious arrangement of words and voices. 

The Masters of primeval wisdom noted this hidden power of nature from the beginning; hence they did not compose the praises of the immortal Gods with just any haphazard arrangement of words. Instead, as if casting chains, they constrained their speeches with a certain harmonic measure, so that the measure of the words would precisely correspond to the internal passions of the soul. From this, you may recognize the first rudiments of sacred poetry, which—just as it did then—has at all times maintained a certain divine quality among posterity in the minds of men. For they believed that by this sympathetic alteration, they could not only cause Spirits and Gods to stand near them as neighbors, but could also change the minds of men into whatever state they wished. All these things that famous <term>polymath</term> <note>original: "πολυΐστωρ" (polyistōr), a person of great and varied learning.</note> Horace teaches so excellently that it seems nothing else can be added to his words.

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>In what sense the Poets of old were said to have drawn wild beasts and stones.</margin>
> *Poets wish either to be useful or to please,*
> *Or to speak things both delightful and fit for life.*
> *Orpheus, the wood-dwelling men’s priest and interpreter of the Gods,*
> *Deterred them from slaughter and a foul way of living;*
> *Because of this, he was said to soothe tigers and fierce lions.*
> *Amphion, too, the founder of the Theban citadel, was said*
> *To move stones by the sound of his lyre, and by persuasive prayer*
> *To lead them where he wished. This was wisdom in former times:*
> *To distinguish public from private things, sacred from profane;*
> *To forbid wandering lust; to give laws to the married;*
> *To build towns, and to carve laws into wood.*
> *Thus honor and name came to divine prophets and their*
> *Songs. After these, the illustrious Homer*
> *And Tyrtaeus sharpened courageous souls for grim wars*
> *With their verses; oracles were spoken through song,*
> *And the way of life was shown; the favor of Kings*
> *Was sought in Pierian measures, and leisure was discovered.*
<note>This is a famous passage from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* (The Art of Poetry), lines 333–334 and 391–407. It explains the civilizing power of music and poetry through the myths of Orpheus and Amphion.</note>

Certainly, we have elsewhere declared at length that this divine and impenetrable power (to speak with Plato) has no origin except from harmonic motion; especially if it responds in a way that is measured to the internal affections of the soul. Moreover, it will correspond in a measured way if the speech is drawn together through the brevity or length of syllables into fitting and harmonious periods. Or—which is the same thing—if a swift and rapid measure follows the swift motions of the mind, and a slow measure follows the slow. And although this possesses a marvelous power in the art of Metrics or Rhythmics, it is certain that it has much greater energy in Musical poetry or Rhythm; for history’s nearly infinite monuments testify that when rhythm is joined to music, as if completed in all its parts, it obtains truly prodigious effects in the souls of men. For as I said a little earlier, there is a certain sympathetic bond between our soul and the motions of harmony and rhythm, so that as soon as metrical harmony is presented to the ears, the mind—driven by various affections—now shows signs of joy, now of love, now of sorrow, compassion, anger, groans, and other disturbances. These signs sometimes increase so much that the mind, unable to be contained within the internal cloisters of the soul, excites the external limbs to acts corresponding to the emotion. But since we have shown these things extensively in our *Magnetic Art*, Book III, concerning the "Magnetism of Music" and "Tarantism," we refer the reader there.
<note>Kircher refers to his own theory that music acts like a magnet on the human soul. "Tarantism" refers to the historical phenomenon in Italy where the bite of a tarantula was believed to be cured by a specific, frantic style of dancing and music called the Tarantella.</note>

Therefore, so that even those unskilled in music might know how to join rhythms to harmonic numbers aptly and without any error, it seemed best to provide here the Rhythmic music or Poetic harmony, so that directed by it, they might achieve their intended effect. Under this metrical art of ours, we include not only poetry, but also Rhetoric; that is, the creation of graceful periods in free-flowing prose and the application of music to the proper pronunciation of syllables. Since this is the case, let us begin the matter from its very cradle.

### CHAPTER II.
### On Accents.

<margin>What is an acute accent.</margin>
An accent is nothing other than the method of raising or lowering a syllable in regard to its pitch. Among the Greeks, it is threefold: Acute, Grave, and Circumflex. The Latins enjoy only the acute and circumflex, neglecting the grave as has been said. Moreover, the acute accent is that by which a syllable is lifted up, the effect of which is <term>arsis</term> <note>original: "ἄρσις". A Greek term meaning "elevation" or the upbeat in a musical measure.</note>, that is, elevation; the grave accent, by which a syllable is lowered, loves <term>thesis</term> <note>original: "θέσις". A Greek term meaning "placing" or the downbeat.</note>. They are called "accents" from the word for "singing along" (*accinendo*), because they accompany the song or reci—

<meta>The word "recita-" is a catchword, indicating the first word of the next page will be "recitation."</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the moral and civilizing power of poetry and rhythm, citing classical myths and Horace. Kircher transitions from mathematical music theory to the practical study of accents and meter in both poetry and prose.</summary>

# Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making

...they moderate rhythmic recitation; hence everywhere tones, tenors, vocalizations, and the "heights" of voices are mentioned. On these, see Cicero's *On the Orator*, Book 3; then Quintilian, Book 1, Chapter 5; Gellius, Book 13, Chapter 6; and Martianus Capella, who calls accent the "soul of voices" and the "nursery of music." Furthermore, just as an accent placed on a syllable does not show that the syllable over which it is placed is short or long, so too harmonic times—or notes—do not indicate the length or brevity of that syllable to which they are applied. Instead, only the precise elevation or expression of the voice through fast or slow time, as indicated, is observed.

<margin>Triple quantity in the pronunciation of a syllable.</margin>
From this, a triple quantity in the pronunciation of a syllable can be considered. The first is of time, by which we linger in the utterance of a syllable before we cease its prolation; this is what authors mean when they say a syllable is "short" or "long." For they used one "time" <term>tempus: the basic unit of duration in ancient prosody</term> to utter a short syllable, and two "times" for a long one, as is clear in the musical notes placed here.

<note>A musical staff shows mensural notation above the words "Maater", "deemit", "pijpit", "poonit", and "puunit." This illustrates the ancient practice of using double vowels (like 'aa' or 'ee') to demonstrate how a long syllable requires a doubled duration in musical time.</note>

Hence the ancients, as Quintilian teaches in Book 1, Chapter 7, pronounced long syllables with a double vowel, such as *Maater* for *Mater* <note>original: "Mother"</note>, *deemit* for *demit* <note>original: "takes away"</note>, *pijpit* for *pipit* <note>original: "chirps"</note>, *poonit* for *ponit* <note>original: "places"</note>, and *puunit* for *punit* <note>original: "punishes"</note>. The second quantity is the intensive "tenor" <term>tenor: here meaning pitch or vocal tension</term>, by which the tone of the voice is raised more intensely or lowered more mildly; this is perceived in the steps of the musical scale. Therefore, whether a syllable is long or short, if it is "acute" <note>the high-pitched accent</note>, it requires a note one step—and at least a semitone—higher than if it were "grave" <note>the low-pitched accent</note>, as is clear in example A. If, however, it is "circumflex," it requires two notes, one on a higher step and the other on a lower one, as seen in B.

<note>A musical diagram shows two examples. Example A displays a single note on a staff, representing an acute accent (high pitch). Example B shows two notes in descending order, representing a circumflex accent, which in ancient grammar involved a rise and fall in pitch on a single syllable.</note>

<margin>The nature of pronunciation.</margin>
The third quantity, arising from the accent, is the *mora* <term>mora: a delay or lingering of sound</term>, by which not so much the syllable itself, but its image propagated through the air, endures in the air and the space it encounters. For an acute or circumflex syllable penetrates a longer interval and propagates more "images" of itself in the air; therefore, its audible image lives longer, is better perceived from a distance, and is repeated at a greater interval by an Echo than a grave syllable or one uttered softly with a syllabic accent. It is no different from what happens with a string drawn more intensely versus one drawn more loosely. From this, it is surely the case that an acute syllable always seems longer than a grave one; this is regarding its *mora*—not because one lingers on it while it is in the mouth of the speaker, but because its "species" <note>In 17th-century physics, the "species" was the sensible form of a sound or sight traveling through a medium like air.</note> lives on in the air.

You see, therefore, how Music gradually grew out of the nature of the accent. For the accent directs the entire business of human speech; indeed, eloquence is more elegant the more distinct it is in its accents. Hence all races and nations have their own accents peculiar to their people, by which they are distinguished from other nations. But since we have reserved all these matters for other treatises, we do not wish to be too lengthy here. Just as the accent gives birth to syllabic pronunciation, so the musical accent gives birth to harmonic pronunciation. And just as rhythm is born from syllabic pronunciation, moving now with fast and now with slow "feet" <note>referring to poetic meters like dactyls or iambs</note>, so too is harmonic rhythm born. Having seen the nature of the accent, it now remains to inquire what Rhythm is.

# CHAPTER III.
### Of Rhythm and its accent.

**R**hythm, therefore, as it regards time and motion, is common to both Poets and Orators as well as Musicians, since both groups distinguish voices and the periods of voices by certain times. They differ, however, in this: among Poets, all short syllables are of the exact same brevity, and all long syllables of the same length and extension. Conversely, among Musicians, the shortening and lengthening of syllables is not taken so precisely according to their natural [poetic] quantity. Instead, in three-syllable words, only the middle one is considered long or short; in four-syllable words, the second-to-last is observed. They measure this brevity and length with various note values, as will be shown shortly. Thus, the order of various times and measures...

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...rhythm is defined by Plato in Book 2 of the *Laws* as <gloss>original Greek: tēs kinēseōs taxin</gloss> "the order of motion," while Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle, considered the most important music theorist of antiquity.</note> defines it as <gloss>original Greek: tōn chronōn taxin</gloss> "the order of times." This suggests that a single "minimum time" in Rhythm is what a sound is in Music, a point in Geometry, or unity in Arithmetic. For Rhythm arises from a specific order of motions or times—whether slow or fast—which is perceived in tones, dances, strings, and even the pulse of the arteries. Because this Rhythm establishes the slowness and speed of time and motion, shining forth through the length and brevity of harmonic voices, it is called **Rhythmic Music**. While Harmony focuses on the movement of the voice from high to low pitch, tending from place to place, its only goal is to arrange sounds aptly through the proper dimensions of intervals. However, unless Rhythm is added as its soul, Harmony is rightly judged to be crippled and imperfect.

It is clear how much Rhythm differs from the low and high pitch of sounds by the simple pronunciation of verses, which is neither raised nor lowered but maintains the same tenor from start to finish. This is also evident in the noise of a drum <note>Latin: *tympani strepitu*</note>. While the drummer signals various messages for various circumstances of war, he certainly maintains Rhythm, but the drums can exhibit no gravity or acuteness of sound <note>meaning the drum skin cannot change its musical pitch</note>. No matter how intensely you strike the hide, the same sound is always perceived; nevertheless, it possesses remarkable power in stirring the spirits of soldiers, especially if the Rhythm is precisely observed. This occurs because of a certain analogy which the first strike has with those following, or which all strikes collected together produce. For the first strike immediately equals the length of the next two, and the last immediately corresponds to the two preceding, and so on for others, whether they are performed in a double, hemiolic, or epitrite ratio <term>proportions of 2:1, 3:2, and 4:3 respectively</term>. <margin>Definition of Rhythm</margin> Thus, Rhythm in its broad sense is nothing other than a certain proportioned sound composed of slow and fast motions, or—which is the same thing—composed of various degrees of height and depth. More strictly defined, it is a certain conformation and, as it were, a character of the voice's quality, by which a voice shaped in this or that way completes the Rhythm. Aristotle also asserts that in rhythms, motion possesses an imitation of the order of low and high sounds, and that all rhythms enjoy song and symphonies; so much so that all motions that are ordered and bound by a certain law can be called Rhythms.

If, therefore, the Music-maker <note>Kircher uses the term *Musurgus* to mean a composer or one who crafts music.</note> joins harmonic rhythms—that is, musical numbers—to poetic Rhythm, he will surely be able to seize his listeners with wonder. For what can a "numerous" melody <note>a melody governed by metrical numbers</note> not achieve? The more elegant and appropriate the Rhythm, the more easily it will move the listeners, running through their minds by *arsis* and *thesis* <term>the "lifting" and "setting down" of a foot in meter, or upbeat and downbeat</term> like feet, wandering with harmonious motions. Thus, grave affects are expressed by long feet such as spondees, molossi, and epitrites; while cheerful ones are expressed by short feet like pyrrhics, chorees, tribrachs, and paeons. But these must be treated a little more extensively.

---

## CHAPTER IV.
### On the Feet of Rhythms or Meters.

<margin>The difference between a metric and a harmonic foot.</margin> A Metrical Foot is nothing other than a part of a verse, meter, or rhythm, defined by a specific number and order of syllables. Just as a physical pace is measured by feet, so meter is measured by long and short vocal sounds as if by feet.

However, there is a great difference between the feet used by Music-makers and those used by Poets. Poets preserve the quantity of syllables in the feet owed to a meter more exactly. Music-makers, however—as was mentioned shortly before—do not look to the shortening or lengthening of *all* syllables, but preserve the quantity only of the middle or penultimate syllables in relation to the first; they do not care for the remaining syllable quantities, whether they be long or short. Thus, Music-makers accept the feet of two syllables indiscriminately for the spondee, choree, iamb, or pyrrhic, since to the ear, in two-syllable units, the brevity or slowness of motion is made

# Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music

...becomes imperceptible? For who can distinguish by ear these two feet <note>original Latin: *Ponit & polit*, meaning "he places and he polishes"</note> where one is a trochee <note>a long syllable followed by a short one</note> and the other a pyrrhic <note>two short syllables</note>, since both are performed in equal time in Music?

In three-syllable words, however, music-makers only pay attention to the middle or penultimate syllable. Thus, the Molossus, Bacchius, Antibacchius, and Amphibrachys are considered as the same foot if their penultimate syllable is long. In the same way, the dactyl, tribrach, anapest, and amphimacer are taken as one foot if the penultimate or middle syllable is short. Examples of these are:
<gloss>long-short-short</gloss> Breast, <gloss>short-short-short</gloss> to read, <gloss>short-short-long</gloss> they give birth, <gloss>long-short-long</gloss> they season.

By the same reasoning, in four-syllable words, music-makers only attend to the quantity of the penultimate syllable. Thus, the dispondee, dichoree, antispast, ionic a minore, third paeon, and the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th epitrites—such as *Orators*, *to compare*, *to celebrate*, and so on—are everywhere taken as a single four-syllable harmonic foot whose penultimate syllable is long. However, the proceleusmatic, first paeon, second paeon, choriamb, and similar ones where the penultimate syllable is shortened—as is clear in these examples: <gloss>short-short-short-short</gloss> to repeat, <gloss>short-long-short-short</gloss> to conceive, <gloss>long-short-short-short</gloss> misery, <gloss>short-short-long-short</gloss> they bring forth, etc.—are likewise taken for one and the same foot.

For who could perceive by ear the different quantity of the first syllable in these two feet, *Orators* and *honored*? Therefore, I wonder at those who think that the quantity of metric feet should be used too superstitiously in music to stir the emotions. Certainly, anyone who considers this more deeply will see that in harmonic feet, nothing but the penultimate syllable needs to be observed. Everything else is superfluous; for to explain myself by example, if in a Sapphic verse <note>A poetic form consisting of specific patterns of long and short syllables, famously used by the Greek poet Sappho.</note> I place a trochee, an iamb, a pyrrhic, or a spondee, it will always sound the same in music. As is clear in this Sapphic example:

->*This sacred Confessor of the Lord*<-
->*Pious Confessor, pray to God*<-
->*The holy Confessor hears the Orators.*<-

In these, only the first verse, which consists of its proper poetic feet, is truly poetic; the other two are musical, not observing the strict quantity of the feet, but only maintaining the rhythmic "leaps" <note>likely referring to the musical beat or stress</note> adapted to the verses. The specific length of the other syllables is set aside, except for the penultimate, which always requires an acute accent in this meter.

All these things are said concerning words or polysyllables bound by no laws of meter; as happens when we compose melodies over some passage from Holy Scripture or any other text in prose <term>soluta oratio: literally 'loosened speech,' meaning prose as opposed to verse</term>. For as I said a little while ago, rhythmic and measured prose belongs no less to Rhythm than does the "bound" language of poetic meters.

If anyone applies harmony to verses and meters composed according to the laws of prosody <note>the patterns of stress and intonation in a language</note>, just as we will professedly teach in what follows, he will create a work that is more perfect the more the song or meter is skillfully crafted and exact in its rhythmic beats.

But so that you may see how you can reduce metric feet to harmonic ones, we will show you the individual poetic feet in harmonic notes, after we have first set down a few things for the better clarification of the matter.

It should be noted, therefore, that just as with the Poets only one kind of syllable brevity and length is considered, so with Musicians there are many, according to the variety of value and the lessening of the notes. For example, *pains* <note>original: "pænæ"</note> is a spondee <note>two long syllables</note>, and among Poets it is of one kind. But among Musicians it can be manifold, since all these following notes are able to express a spondee.

### And these are the harmonic feet which correspond to metric feet, in which these things especially must be observed.

**F**irst, that not all feet of this kind are suited to metric feet, nor can all be presented to all. For if anyone were to apply this pyrrhic (<gloss>short-short</gloss>) to the harmonic feet contained in the fourth or fifth column <note>where the beat is divided into many small, fast notes</note>, he would cause a pronunciation that is altogether difficult and unpleasant, not without a grating of the ears; which ordinarily occurs in two-syllable words in which consonants are frequent. Or in these two-syllable words: *constant, full, viceroy, they carry* <note>original Latin: *constans, plenus, prorex, portant*</note>; and similar words which, as they love slowness in pronouncing, so too they must correspond to longer feet; of which kind the first column contains. On the contrary, in two-syllable words which abound in vowels, just as they love speed, so too they must consist of more extended harmonic feet <note>i.e., those with more notes dividing the beat</note>, as in these: *read, flee, evils* <note>original Latin: *lege, fuge, mala*</note>, and infinite words of this genre.

Second, it should be noted that these two-syllable words expressed with harmonic notes, as they are slower, love the spondaic gait more; thus the faster ones love the pyrrhic more. The trochee <note>original: *Choræus*</note>, however, will be expressed better and more easily by two notes struck with a dot <note>referring to dotted rhythms</note>, or even with a syncopation preceded by a rest, as is clear in the following example.

<note>A musical score illustrating rhythmic settings of Latin phrases. The first example sets "Lift up your hearts" (*Sursum corda*) and "Lawful" (*Licitus*) to a slow, steady rhythm. Subsequent examples show syncopated and more florid rhythmic divisions using eighth and sixteenth notes for "Hail of the Sea" (*Ave Maris*), "Unlawful" (*Illicitus*), and "Lawful" (*Licitus*).</note>

The iamb, however, can hardly be tolerated in an ascending passage <term>anabasis: a musical phrase where the pitch rises</term> because of the grave accent which it attaches to the last syllable in the ascent, than which nothing more foolish can be heard. For who would not laugh if someone made these two iambs *Hail of the sea* <note>original: *Ave maris*</note> low-sounding <term>barysona: words or syllables accented with a low pitch</term>? In which, however, I often find our musicians stumbling—the worst accent in music, and absurd beyond what can be said.

Book VIII. Wondrous Music-making.

## §. I.
### On three-syllable harmonic feet.

**F**irst, a triple progression can be considered in three-syllable harmonic feet: **ascending**, **level**, and **descending** <note>original Greek: *anabatos*, *isobatos*, and *katabatos*</note>. An ascending progression occurs when the foot moves upward, whether by steps or by leaps. A level progression is when the foot moves forward on the same step at an equal level. A descending progression occurs when the foot moves downward, either by steps or by leaps. This triple classification of progression is of such great importance in rhythmic music that without it, nothing can be correctly established in Music-making <note>original: *Musurgia*</note>, as will be seen in the following sections.

Second, the greatest consideration in three-syllable feet must be given to the <term>upbeat and downbeat<gloss>arsis and thesis</gloss></term>. For anyone who began a **Molossus** <note>a foot of three long syllables</note> **on the downbeat** <note>original Greek: *kata tēn thesin*</note> would create a ridiculous pronunciation; it would be quite different if he performed it **on the upbeat** <note>original Greek: *kata tēn arsin*</note>.

Third, certain three-syllable feet are better suited to <term>perfect time<gloss>triple meter</gloss></term>, others to <term>imperfect time<gloss>duple or quadruple meter</gloss></term>; which ones these are will be seen shortly.

Fourth, dotted notes <note>original: *Notas puncto elisas*</note> do much to assist in the shortening of syllables. But let us look at the matter more closely. In order to proceed more solidly in our Music-making, we shall adapt poetic feet to various harmonic feet in different ways; once these have been seen and examined, we shall then decide which is better and more suited to musical melodies.

First, therefore, the middle syllable must be considered above all in three-syllable feet; it is either short or long. Among those feet that have a short middle syllable are the **Dactyl**, the **Tribrach**, the **Anapest**, and the **Cretic**, which for that reason are called **middle-shorts** <note>original: *mesobrachos*</note>. Those that have a long middle syllable are these: the **Molossus**, the **Bacchius**, the **Antibacchius**, and the **Amphibrach**; these we call **middle-longs** <note>original: *mesomacros*</note>. In the first method, some adapt these to harmonic feet so that the notes perfectly correspond to these signs of quantity: — $\cup$ —; as follows:

<note>Musical notation on a five-line staff with diamond-shaped notes and various rhythmic markings above. Below the notes are the words: "Gaudia posteris gaudia posteris" [Joys for posterity, joys for posterity]. Following the text are symbols for repetition.</note>

For who does not see that in this dactylic pronunciation, the middle syllable is almost always produced as long, to the greatest torment of the ears? Their harshness increases all the more as the notes are of longer duration or involve a greater leap. The same inconvenience occurs in the example of an Anapestic song; in which, if someone were to keep several anapests in order according to the notes placed there, he would make the syllabic pronunciation of the song utterly ridiculous; for even if he pronounced the second syllable somewhat short, he would nevertheless sharpen the last more than is proper, and would attach a grave accent to the end of each Anapest, not without laughter from the listeners. As appears in the example, where the first and second progression is uttered with a grave accent, useless for Latin pronunciation; but in the third example, although the last syllable is not <term>low-pitched<gloss>barytona</gloss></term>, the middle one is nonetheless lengthened because of the leap.

<margin>
<note>Musical notation on a five-line staff with diamond-shaped notes and rhythmic symbols above (long, short, long). The word "pariant" [they bring forth] is printed below.</note>
they bring forth
</margin>

From these things, if I am not mistaken, it is most clearly evident that musical melodies can in no way correspond to metrical feet by this method, since when taken this way, they bring forth infinite <term>errors in speech<gloss>solecisms</gloss></term> in pronunciation. Those, however, who wish to proceed successfully in this business will attain their goal by the following method.

---

->A certain and most fit method, by which harmonic metrical feet can be accommodated exactly and<-
->naturally, without danger and without a solecism of syllabic pronunciation.<-

---

**F**irst, therefore, it must be noted that in three-syllable words <note>original: *trisyllabis*</note>, we take no account of the first and last syllables, but only of the middle one, whether it be shortened or lengthened, since musical progression in three-syllable words regards only the quantity of the middle syllable. Therefore, for one and the same foot, those first four feet can be taken which are <term>short in the middle<gloss>mesobrachi</gloss></term>, or what is the same thing, having a short middle syllable. For these three notes are indifferent to the four said feet; for whether you adapt to them these words *facere* [to do], *parcere* [to spare], or *pariunt* [they bring forth], *competunt* [they are suitable], the pronunciation will always fit. The same must be said of the four <term>long-in-the-middle<gloss>mesomacris</gloss></term> feet, or those having a long middle syllable. For whether you adapt to these three notes these "long-in-the-middle" words *commendans* [commending], *laborans* [laboring], or these, *parata* [prepared], *Regina* [Queen], the same harmonic accent will always be perceived.

# Book VIII. The Wondrous Art of Music.

Secondly, it must be noted that for the natural accent of individual poetic feet to be preserved, great regard must be had for the ascent and descent of notes. For if in three-syllable feet that are <term>mesobrachic</term> <note>feet with a short middle syllable, such as the dactyl (long-short-short)</note> there is an <term>anobatus</term> <note>original: "anobatus," meaning an ascending or upward-climbing melodic line</note> or ascending movement—whether by steps or by leaps—the pronunciation will not be without a <term>solecism</term> <note>a grammatical or structural error; here, a musical mistake</note>. Indeed, in such a progression, the middle short syllable will cause I know not what kind of violent lengthening, which will be all the more absurd as the leap is greater, as was shown in the preceding example. Conversely, a <term>catobatos</term> <note>a descending or downward-moving melodic line</note> or descending progression will, for whatever reason, produce the natural accent of these same feet.

### Unlawful progression of Mesobrachic feet. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Lawful progression of Mesobrachic feet.

<note>Two musical examples are placed side-by-side. The left example, labeled "unlawful," features several bars of music on a five-line staff with diamond-shaped notes ascending in pitch. Above the staff are rhythmic notations (long and short signs). Below the first bar is the word "facere" [to do/make]. The right example, labeled "lawful," shows similar staves where the melodic line is descending or maintaining the same pitch—a movement called "isobatus." Rhythmic markings are also present above the notes.</note>

Where you see the <term>Isobatus</term> <note>a level progression where the pitch stays the same</note> moving evenly, it holds a kind of middle ground of equality; the further you recede from this, the more imperfect you make the pronunciation. Thus, the best progression of all is the level one, then that which proceeds by steps; thereafter, the larger the intervals of the leaps, the greater the violence it will inflict upon the ears.
In three-syllable feet that are <term>mesomacric</term> <note>original: "Mesomacris," feet with a long middle syllable, such as the amphimacer (long-short-long)</note>, however, the progression behaves in the opposite manner. For an ascending progression preserves the natural accent however it is placed; but a descending one destroys it, affecting I know not what kind of forced lengthening in the middle syllable, as is clearly seen in the following example.

### 4. Unlawful progression of Mesomacric feet. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Lawful progression of the same.

<note>Musical notation examples. The left section (unlawful) displays musical phrases with the text "Defunctum plangebat Arator Arator" [The plowman lamented the deceased] beneath the notes. The right section (lawful) displays a short musical phrase with the word "Orator" [Orator] beneath it. Both use diamond-shaped notes on five-line staves with quantitative rhythmic markers above.</note>

Thirdly, it must be noted that just as the quantity of <term>mesobrachic</term> feet does not suit <term>breves</term> and <term>semibreves</term> <note>longer note values in the notation of the time</note>, so the quantity of <term>mesomacric</term> feet does not suit <term>semiminims</term> well, and suits <term>fusas</term> and <term>semifusas</term> <note>shorter, faster notes like eighth and sixteenth notes</note> worst of all, due to a certain natural <term>asymmetry</term> <note>original: "ἀμετρίαν" (ametrian), a lack of proportion or irregularity</note>. But having noted these things, we shall now hand down some rules by which we can give a perfect accent to harmonic melodies.
*Rule I.* Mesobrachic feet are descending or level; mesomacric feet, on the contrary, are ascending or level. Mesobrachic feet are conveniently applied to all notes of lesser value than <term>minims</term>, because of the similarity of their inherent speed. Mesomacric feet, however, can be applied to all notes of greater value preceding <term>semiminims</term>, whether in an ascending or descending progression, because of the natural slowness which exists in both the notes and the syllables.
*Rule II.* Mesobrachic feet acquire a perfect and natural accent if the middle is elided by a dot; this dot has such power that in an ascending progression it saves the shortening of the middle syllable. The same will happen if the first note of the Mesobrachs is <term>syncopated</term> by placing a rest before it. It will have a better effect, however, in descent than in ascent. Mesomacric feet will acquire a perfect accent if a <term>semiminim</term> rest precedes the first note. But let us give examples of each.
