Behold, these are the feet that all poets use in composing meters, which some people apply to the value of notes with an excessive, almost superstitious devotion. For some apply long feet to the smallest notes and short feet to <term>semiminims</term> <note>a shorter note value, equivalent to a modern quarter note</note>, but in harmonic pronunciation, these would more likely provoke laughter than any real emotion. Hence I wonder again why <term>Mersenne</term> <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a famous French polymath and rival music theorist</note>, who is otherwise so perceptive, thinks in his *Harmonie Universelle* that this comparison of notes with metric feet is something remarkable. For who would not laugh at such a style of harmonic pronunciation, when he thinks that four <term>minim</term> notes <note>white diamond-shaped notes</note> should be applied to a Major Ionic foot?

<note>A musical score on a five-line staff featuring diamond-shaped notes. The melody begins with a descending leap and then moves in a varied melodic line. The lyrics below are: "You shall perform miracles" <note>original: "Miracula patrabitis"</note>.</note>

It is clear, therefore, that in harmonic pronunciation, no account should be taken of the length or brevity of syllables, except for the <term>penultimate</term> <note>second-to-last</note> syllable alone. Thus, all eight feet listed just above that have a long penultimate can be treated as one and same harmonic foot. Likewise, the eight feet that have a short penultimate can be accepted as another harmonic foot. Consequently, there are only two tetrasyllabic harmonic feet: one that has a short penultimate and another that has a long one. How these feet are to be applied to notes remains to be investigated.

Feet with a long penultimate support harmonic pronunciation whether the melody moves in an <term>anabatic</term> <note>ascending</note>, <term>catabatic</term> <note>descending</note>, or <term>isobatic</term> <note>level/staying on one pitch</note> progression, as is clear in the following example.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the Variety of Meters.

<margin>Which feet are <term>catalectic</term> <note>a line of verse that is syllable-deficient in the last foot</note> and <term>acatalectic</term> <note>a line of verse that has the complete number of syllables</note>.</margin>
Meter or verse is speech bound by a certain kind, number, and order of feet, not without harmony <note>original: "concentu," implying a musical or melodic agreement</note>. For verse without harmony would not be distinguished from prose, since prose cannot exist without some degree of rhythm and order of feet. And just as a line arises from the flow of a point, and a surface from the motion of a line, and a solid body from the extension of a surface, so also is a foot formed from a syllable, and meter from feet. Since these feet have an infinite breadth, they can also constitute an infinite variety of meters. Some of these take their name from the number of feet. Certain ones from the excess or lack of syllables; some from the feet themselves, others from the number of stanzas <note>original: "stropharum"</note> and limbs <note>original: "membrorum," referring to the segments of a verse</note>, concerning each of which I shall speak in order. 

Verses established by the number of feet are mostly Iambic and Trochaic, of which the first is a <term>dipody</term> <note>a pair of poetic feet</note> or two feet; for no meter can have less than two feet, otherwise it would not be a meter but a single foot. Therefore, one meter is a dipody, but two meters consist of four feet, of which kind are the verses they call <term>dimeters</term>. If, however, a verse consists of six feet, it is called a <term>trimeter</term> by the Poets, and if eight, a <term>tetrameter</term>. 

Since some also name verses by the number of syllables, such as those with 11 syllables called <term>hendecasyllabic</term> verses. But since meters are not always measured so precisely by a fixed number of feet that a syllable is never missing at the end or one is never extra, hence Poets call verses that lack a syllable at the end **catalectic**. Those which lack nothing they call **acatalectic**; those where a syllable is extra at the end they call **hypercatalectic** verses. If, however, an entire foot is missing at the end, they are called **brachycatalectic** <note>original: "bibrachi catalecti"</note>. And this is the first and simple dimension of verses.

<margin>What <term>distrophic</term> and <term>dicolous</term> are.</margin>
The second dimension considers the multitude of meters, which they call odes. If an ode lacks stanzas, it is called **monostrophic**, that is, one whose stanza is completed in a single verse. If, however, the stanza is completed in two verses, it is called **distrophic**; if in three, **tristrophic**; if in four, **tetrastrophic**. 

Or the division of meters can be considered by the variety of the meters themselves; for if a stanza is completed by two heterogeneous <note>different kinds</note> meters, it is called **dicolon** <note>original: "δίκωλον," meaning two-limbed</note>, if by three, **tricolon**, if four, **tetracolon**. It is possible, therefore, for a tetrastrophic poem to be dicolous, as in **Sapphic** stanzas, which consist of three similar verses and one dissimilar verse, namely an **Adonic**.

And from these things it is clearly evident that there are innumerable kinds of verses, all of which I would show in this place, if I had not reserved this poetic art for our <term>combinatoric art</term> <note>Kircher refers to his "Ars Combinatoria," a mathematical system for generating all possible combinations of elements, which he applied to music and language</note>; for there these will be treated extensively. Therefore, let us return to the specifics of our purpose.

### On Meters consisting of an unchangeable quantity of feet.

There are besides some meters which admit various feet, that is, which do not have a certain and fixed placement of feet, such as **Hexameters**, **Pentameters**, **Anapestic**, **Hendecasyllabic**, **Alcaic**, **Choriambic**, and others of this sort; concerning these, consult the writers of prosody. On the other hand, there are others which maintain a certain and unchangeable placement of feet. And they are the following.

<sig>I</sig>
<meta>catchword: Ado- (This leads into "Adonic" on the next page)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the classification of poetic meters from Chapter V and transitions into Chapter VI, where the author discusses the practical application of these meters to musical composition. It focuses on which meters are most stable for harmonic setting.</meta>

<header>Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

1. **Adonic**, which always consists of a dactyl and a spondee at the beginning.
2. **Glyconic**, in the first place always consisting of a spondee and a choree <note>original: "choræo," also known as a trochee, consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one</note>, then of two dactyls, as in *Stars of heaven* <note>original: "Sidera cæli"</note>.
3. **Dactylic Alcaic**, which consists of a spondee, an iamb, and a long caesura <note>a rhythmic break or pause in a line of verse</note>, then two dactyls. [*You see how the high mountain stands white with deep snow.*] <note>original: "Vides vt alta stet niue candidum," a famous line from Horace</note>.
4. **Choriambic Asclepiadean**, consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, a long caesura, and two dactyls. [*Maecenas, descended from royal ancestors.*] <note>original: "Mecænas Atauis edite regibus," the opening of Horace's Odes</note>.
5. **Euripidean Iambic** consists of three iambs; however, it can also admit a spondee and a pyrrhic <note>a foot of two short syllables</note> in the third place, as in [*Hail, Star of the sea.*] <note>original: "Aue maris Stella," a famous medieval hymn</note>.
6. **Anacreontic** consists of three iambs and a syllable, as in [*When you have drunk enough dew, O sweet cicada, you fill the pleasant fields with song.*] <note>original: "Roris vt sat bibisti dulci cicada cantu campos reples amænos"</note>.
7. Finally, **Archilochian Iambic**, both <term>catalectic</term> <note>a line lacking a final syllable</note> and <term>hypercatalectic</term> <note>a line having an extra syllable at the end</note>. [*God powerfully moves the stars as the ancient race of mortals.*] <note>original: "Deus potenter astra vt prisca gens mortalium"</note>.

To these are added the Phalaecian, the hendecasyllable, and the Sapphic.
And these meters are the most suitable of all for harmonic melodies, since the numbers contained in these <term>musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical rules used to map poetic rhythm to melody</note> can be applied to them perpetually and without error. As we shall see later.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the Application of Poetic Meter, or Rhythms, to Harmonic Poetry.

In the preceding sections, it has been explained at length that in poetic harmony, the quantity of syllables is not precisely observed, but rather attention is paid to the accent, which shines forth most strongly in the middle or penultimate syllable of the words. But so that even one who is unskilled in music may nevertheless be able to animate all kinds of meters into harmonic concerts, here first must be declared the meters most suitable and fit for this task. For as was also said above, not all poems are suitable for harmonic melodies, but only those which maintain a certain and unchangeable position of feet; such as the Adonic, Glyconic, certain Iambics, Phalaecian, Sapphic, and others of this kind. For Hexameters and Pentameters, and Anapaestics, since they receive a varied mixture of feet—and if you except the dactyl with the spondee at the end of a hexameter, they have a fixed foot nowhere else—it happens that they cannot be so easily accommodated to harmonic melodies, unless someone were to preserve the same tenor of feet perpetually, which would however be a difficult task. Therefore, we judge that Hexameters, Pentameters, and similar meters of unstable feet are to be ascribed not to harmonic prosody, but to the rhythms of Rhetoric or prose; how these are to be accommodated to musical melodies will appear shortly after.

# § I.
## On the Five-Syllable Adonic Verse.

Although, strictly speaking, a word composed of two Iambs, Chorees, Pyrrhics, or Spondees could be called a meter (inasmuch as it consists of more than one foot), because a four-syllable number easily vanishes from the ears due to the shortness of the time and does not sufficiently exhibit the proportion of motion, it is therefore rejected by poets as unsuitable for meter. No four-syllable unit, therefore, should properly be called a meter. Thus, the first of the meters is deservedly five-syllabled; for this five-syllable unit exhibits the first and a somehow pleasing proportion of motion to the ears. Such are the five-syllable verses called Adonics, and they consist of two feet, a dactyl and a spondee, as follows.

We have already shown the quality and condition of the Adonic meter <note>A short meter consisting of a dactyl (long-short-short) followed by a spondee (long-long)</note>; now it is our duty to explain the system of the Adonic <term>metrometer</term> <note>Kircher’s term for a standardized rhythmic unit used to set poetic meters to music</note>. For in the future, we shall call these not merely poetic feet, but "musical measures" of every kind, by which we may distinguish musical meters from those of the poets. Therefore, when we speak of a "Musical Adonic," a "Musical Glyconic," a "Musical Iambic," and so on, we refer to the specific rhythmic patterns that correspond to the accents of poetic meters or those which measure the song itself. These signs, when applied to the words of a particular meter, will measure it perfectly both in terms of its duration and its accent, such as we have placed here. We have provided twelve Musical Adonics expressed in rhythmic notation, which can be beautifully applied to each and every Adonic poem according to the subject matter and the flow of the words; from this, the Reader may learn the admirable variety possible in harmonics. 

If you were to combine one of these five-note Adonics in various ways according to their different rhythmic values, 256 variations would result. These can be precisely calculated even if you do not change the sequence of the notes, as was demonstrated at length above in the section on <term>Combinatorial Music</term> <note>The mathematical study of how many musical variations can be produced from a set of notes</note>. Thus, a single poetic Adonic can be expressed by 256 different Musical Adonics. However, we have selected only the twelve most suitable examples from those 256, which will be more than enough for the composer to express any poetic Adonics. We have included eight Musical Adonics in <term>imperfect time</term> <note>common or duple meter</note> and four in <term>perfect time</term> <note>triple meter, considered "perfect" because of its association with the Holy Trinity</note>, so the composer may use them as he pleases. A fuller explanation of these follows.

First, the Aristophanic Iambics can be categorized under the Adonics. Although they consist of two iambs and an extra syllable at the end, the first three syllables express a musical dactyl, and thus they can be used for Musical Adonics, as seen in the following verses:

# §. II.
## Concerning the Six-Syllable Meter: That is, the Dactylic Adonic and the Euripidean Iambic.

That which follows the Adonic in order is the "Dactylic Adonic," a six-syllable meter. It is called dactylic because it consists of two dactyls. It is so closely related to the Adonic that its name was derived from it. For if you change the final <term>spondee</term> <note>two long syllables</note> of an Adonic into a <term>dactyl</term> <note>one long and two short syllables</note>, you will have a dactylic meter. In musical settings, if you double the second-to-last note, you will create Musical Dactylics, as shown in the following example:

->Lift up your eyes<-
->To the wandering stars<-
->Behold the Divinity's<-
->Shining gifts.<-

### §. III.

### Concerning the Anacreontic Iambic, a seven-syllable meter.

The Anacreontic iambic is a seven-syllable meter <note>original: "heptasyllabon"</note>, and it consists of three iambs and one extra syllable. It is twofold: the first type always enjoys an iamb at the beginning, while the latter always enjoys an anapest <note>A foot consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one</note>. Behold an example of both in the accompanying figure.

<margin>
Rhythmic signs for the Anacreontic verse.
<note>Twelve rows of rhythmic notation symbols corresponding to the seven-syllable Anacreontic meter.</note>
</margin>

I
O thrice and four times happy
Cicada, who in the green
Heights of the trees,
Having drunk a little dew,
Rejoice to sing sweetly. <note>This is a Latin translation of a famous poem attributed to the Greek poet Anacreon.</note>
The anapestic ones follow:

<column-break/>

II
Every pleasure has this:
It drives those who are raging with stings,
And like a swarm of flying bees,
Once it has poured out its pleasing honey,
It flees and strikes those hearts
With a too-persistent bite, etc. <note>These lines are from Boethius's "The Consolation of Philosophy," Book III, Metrum 7.</note>

<column-break/>

From these twelve harmonic Anacreontics, any one can be accommodated to individual stanzas. However, since the latter type has an anapest at the beginning of the stanzas, you will have Anapestic Anacreontic musical settings if you divide the first notes in each of the five-syllable units into two notes equal to the original first note. This is evident in the accompanying example, where you see the individual first notes divided into two equivalent ones, so that you may have an Anapestic Anacreontic; and although the anapestic is eight syllables <note>original: "octofyllabum"</note>, it is nevertheless the same as the seven-syllable Anacreontic, whether you look at the accent or the duration of time.

### §. IV.

### Concerning the Eight-Syllable Archilochian Iambic Meter.

<margin>
Note on the Iambic Archilochian Metrometer <note>Kircher's term for a musical template that dictates rhythm for specific poetic meters.</note>
<note>Twelve rows of mensural notation symbols (circles with stems, dots, and squares) representing rhythmic patterns for the octosyllabic Archilochian iambic meter.</note>
</margin>

After the seven-syllable meter follows the eight-syllable <note>original: "octosyllabon"</note>, which is the most widely sung of all types of verse. Indeed, there is hardly a hymn found in the *Roman Breviary* <note>The liturgical book containing the public prayers of the Catholic Church</note> that does not consist of this kind of poem, for it is uniquely suited to musical settings. Of this type are the hymns:

> The banners of the King go forth. <note>original: "Vexilla regis prodeunt," a famous 6th-century hymn by Venantius Fortunatus.</note>
> Come, Creator Spirit. <note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus"</note> And that other:
> Enough for death, enough for tears,
> Enough is given to sorrows. <note>original: "Sat funeri sat lachrymis / Sat est datum doloribus"</note>

The musical notes to be adapted to these verses are placed here; and since this kind of meter is most often a four-line stanza <term>tetrastrophon</term>, one of these 12 musical metrometers may be applied to each stanza.

### §. V.

### Concerning the Enneasyllabic Meter, or Nine Syllables.

<margin>
Note on the Iambic Archilochian Metrometer
<note>Twelve rows of rhythmic notation symbols (circles, dots, and stems) arranged for the enneasyllabic (nine-syllable) meter.</note>
</margin>

The Archilochian Iambic dimeter <term>hypercatalectic</term> <note>A line of verse that has an extra syllable at the end beyond the regular meter.</note> is a nine-syllable meter, of which every third line in the stanzas of Horace <note>A famous Roman lyric poet</note> is composed, namely:

> The laboring woods and the frost. <note>original: "Syluæ laborantes geluque"</note>

However, when it consists of only four iambs along with one extra syllable, it is an Alcaic Iambic dimeter, such as:

> The murderers love poisons. <note>original: "Amant Venena parricidæ"</note>

The meter of both is measured by the same musical metrometers, as is evident in the accompanying example.

### §. VI.

### Concerning the Ten-Syllable Meter.

The Alcmanian Iambic trimeter <term>catalectic</term> <note>A line of verse missing a syllable at the end to complete the final foot.</note> is a ten-syllable meter, an example of which is the following verse:

> You spurn the maiden’s lovely marriage-beds. <note>original: "Spernis decoros Virginis thoros"</note>

However, since this kind of poem is characterized by a varied mixture of rhythms and has a foot that is more "mobile" than is proper, we reject it as being less suitable for harmonic poetry. If, however, someone wished to use them, they would have to maintain the measure of the verse placed a little before this with a perpetual and unchanging pace. If this were done, then one could without any trouble apply the preceding metrometer notes to the syllables of that kind of meter, provided one divides the second-to-last note into two equivalent notes.

### §. VII.

### Concerning the eleven-syllable meter: the Phalaecian, the Sapphic, and the dactylic Alcaic, commonly called Horatian.

The eleven-syllable <note>original: "Hendecasyllabum"</note> meter is varied; from many types, we have selected three that are more suited to harmony, the first of which is the Phalaecian. Because of its frequent trochees <note>original: "choreos"; a metrical foot consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one</note>, it is extremely well-suited to harmony. Indeed, the Italians hardly use any other kind of verse more frequently in their poetry; as there is none more suited to harmonic melodies, they are generally accustomed to adding the seven-syllable <term>Anacreontic</term> meter to it to establish a perfect harmony, as will be seen in the following pages.

Whoever, therefore, desires to adapt musical poetry to this kind of meter should first take care, as much as possible, that the Phalaecian verses are pure and consist of frequent trochees, rejecting dactyls, anapests, and tribrachs; in this way, he will easily achieve his purpose. The metrometric notes <note>Kircher's term for rhythmic templates</note> are placed in the margin, any one of which you may apply to any of the Phalaecian verses.

->The Sapphic Meter.<-

<margin>
Metrometers of the Sapphic Poem
<note>Twelve rows of musical rhythmic notation symbols (circles, stems, dots, and square notes) specifically arranged for the Sapphic meter, which consists of three long lines and one short "Adonic" line.</note>
</margin>

The second eleven-syllable meter is the Sapphic, a very common form of verse, usually a three-stanza, two-limbed structure <note>original: "tristrophon dicolon"</note>. This means it consists of three stanzas <note>lines</note> to which an Adonic verse <note>a short five-syllable line</note> is attached at the end; it is called "two-limbed" because it is composed of two different species of meter. This form is not at all inferior to the preceding one in its fitness for forming excellent harmonies. Indeed, this kind of meter possesses a certain hidden, effective harmony within itself, such that beginners in poetry are hardly able to scan it except by singing; this is a clear sign of its great kinship and affinity with Music. It differs from the previous Phalaecian eleven-syllable meter because that one consists of pure trochees and iambs, while this one also consists of dactyls and anapests. Of this kind is the hymn in the *Roman Breviary*:

> This Confessor of the Lord, whom the people worship, etc. <note>original: "Iste Confessor Domini colentes"</note>

Also the hymn usually recited on the feast of St. John the Baptist:

> So that your servants may be able to sing 
> the wonders of your deeds with loosened vocal cords, 
> wash away the guilt from our polluted lips, 
> ->O Saint John.<- 
> <note>original: "Ut queant laxis resonare fibris / Mira gestorum famuli tuorum / Solve polluti labii reatum / Sancte Ioannes."</note>

This is a most famous meter indeed, by occasion of which Guido of Arezzo <note>The 11th-century monk regarded as the inventor of modern musical notation</note> discovered figured music <note>polyphony or mensural notation</note>, as was shown extensively in the preceding books. The metrometric notes are placed here.

Note in this place that the metrometric notes of the preceding Phalaecian meter can be adapted to Sapphics, and likewise Sapphic notes to Phalaecian verses without any hesitation. For the Adonic verse that must be attached to the three stanzas, you shall take the metrometric notes from Section I of this chapter.

To the explained eleven-syllable meters, the Hipponactean Iambic may rightly be added, such as this:

> Three measures of old Falernian wine 
> the bold ruler and arbiter of Kings, 
> the descendant of powerful Romulus, has drained, etc. 
> <note>original: "Ternos vetusti Congios falerni / Hausit potentum Romuli nepotum / Regnator audax arbiterque Regum"</note>

<margin>
Metrometers of the Horatian eleven-syllable meter.
<note>Twelve rows of musical rhythmic and mensural notation symbols—including circles, stems, dots, and square notes—are specifically arranged to provide a rhythmic template for the Horatian hendecasyllabic (eleven-syllable) meter.</note>

The third eleven-syllable meter <note>original: "Hendecasyllabum"</note> is the dactylic Alcaic, commonly called the "Horatian," because Horace used no other kind of verse more frequently. An example follows:

> See how Mount Soracte stands white with deep snow,
> and the woods can no longer bear the burden.
> <note>original Latin: "Vides vt alta stet niue candidum / Soracte, nec iam sustineant onus." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

But since this type of meter has a short penultimate syllable, the metrometric notes of the preceding eleven-syllable meters cannot be applied to them. Instead, the metrometric notes of both the Adonic <note>A meter consisting of a dactyl and a spondee or trochee</note> and the dactylic joined together will provide the metrometric notes for the Horatian poem, as appears here in the margin.

### §. VIII.

### Concerning the twelve-syllable meter.

<margin>
<note>A continuation of musical rhythmic notation rows in the margin. The first set of twelve rows corresponds to the Asclepiadean meter, followed by several rows illustrating different rhythmic combinations including simple circular notes and more complex arrangements of stems and dots.</note>
</margin>

The twelve-syllable <note>original: "Dodecasyllabum"</note> Asclepiadean Choriambic meter proceeds with frequent choriambs <note>a metrical foot of four syllables: long, short, short, long</note>, such as the following from Horace:

> Maecenas, descended from royal ancestors...
> But if you insert me among the lyric bards,
> I shall strike the stars with my exalted head.
> <note>original Latin: "Mecœnas Atauis edite regibus... Quod si me Lyricis vatibus inseris / Sublimi feriam vertice sidera." From Horace, Odes 1.1.</note>

The metrometric notes for this are the same as the previous eleven-syllable metrometers; however, to make it a twelve-syllable line, the fourth note in all the preceding metrometers must be divided into two equal parts. You will then have the required metrometric notes for the Asclepiadean choriambic, as is clear in the example.

Furthermore, whatever meters exceed 12 syllables are entirely composed of the preceding ones, or they possess such a variety of feet that they can only serve musical poetry with difficulty—such as Hexameters, pentameters, and many others of the Lyric genre, which we intentionally omit. If anyone should nonetheless desire to compose them, he ought, as has been said, to always maintain a single tenor of feet. Truly, having seen the nature of verses suitable for music, nothing remains but for us to establish here some combination for composing them.

If, therefore, you prefix a <term>Spondee</term> <note>a foot of two long syllables</note> to an Adonic, you will have a Pherecratic poem.
If you again prefix a spondee to a dactylic Adonic, you will have a Glyconic meter.
If you prefix to this same spondee <note>an Anacreontic</note>, an Anacreontic Iambic will be born.
If you join two Adonics together, an Anapestic will be born.
If you join two dactylic Adonics together, you will have the Asclepiadean choriambic.
If you add a dactylic Adonic to an Adonic, you will have the dactylic Alcmanic, otherwise known as Horatian.
If, however, you prefix a spondee to an Anacreontic, you will have the third meter, that is, the Horatian or Archilochian Iambic.
A Spondee prefixed to an Anacreontic generates the Alcmanic Iambic.
The same prefixed to an Archilochian Iambic generates the Phalaecian eleven-syllable meter.

You see, therefore, that just as foot added to foot, so poem added to poem always generates another. Since this business involves nearly infinite combinations, I have decided it should not be extended further, but left to the consideration of the curious reader. Whatever we have said here, however, should be understood only regarding the metrometric notes. We shall speak more diffusely of these in the practical composition itself.

# OF THE MIRACULOUS MAKING OF MUSIC

## PART III.

-> EXHIBITING THE PRACTICE OF MELOTHETIC MUSARITHMS. <-
<note>The term "Melothetic" refers to the art of composing melodies; "Musarithms" are Kircher's unique invention of musical-mathematical tables.</note>

### C H A P T E R  I.

### Concerning the goal and purpose of the Author.

<note>A large decorative drop-cap 'C' depicts a figure, likely a scholar or musician, framed within an ornate architectural structure.</note> Since in the preceding sections we promised to provide a method by which anyone, even if unskilled in music, could arrive at a perfect knowledge of composition, we wished to fulfill those promises in this place—once we have first explained in what our invention consists.

<margin>In all sciences, there is one principal foundation.</margin> Since I have become more learned through frequent experiment, I observed that one thing is contained in all, and all in one, by a certain admirable reason. That is, I more sagaciously perceived that in all sciences and faculties there is some single principle to which all other things may be referred back according to a certain analogy. Truly, these things could not be handled without a perfect knowledge of combinations. Thus, I established the *Combinatory Art* <note>original: "Artem combinatoriam"; a mathematical approach to logic and discovery</note> in which, exhibiting the thoughts of my mind, I represented the principles of all sciences to the eyes through various orchestrated means, so that nothing could seem easier than to reach an exact knowledge of all things in a short time by their help. Since, however, I found such a wonderful power of the combination of things in music, just as in all other subjects, nothing else seemed to be lacking except that the principles of music—explained more fully in the preceding sections—should here be reduced into methodical tables. We have entitled these "Musarithms," or "harmonic numbers," and as it was conceived in the mind, so was it immediately put into execution.

Lest anything in music remain hidden even from the <term>unmusical</term> <note>original Greek: ἄμουσον; refers to one who is uninitiated or unskilled in the arts of the Muses</note>—that is, those unskilled in music—we have established three collections of tables in which we have arranged, by many composition charts <note>original: "Pinaces melotheticos"</note>, whatever might be rare and excellent in the entire universe of the music of melody or composition, in the order and method which follows.

<margin>The order of the tables constructed for the composition of songs.</margin> *The First Collection* contains ten charts or tables in which we exhibit the whole of poetic or metrical music-making <note>original: "Musurgiam poeticam siue metricam"</note>, so that given any kind of verse, you may be able to compose a melody upon it for whatever purpose you seek.

*Chart I* <note>original: "Pinax I."</note> shows us the Musarithms of multi-syllable poetic feet, from two-syllable up to seven-syllable feet. We include in this chart only the multi-syllable feet whose second-to-last syllable is long, as the very front of the table demonstrates; at the bottom of the columns are placed the "metrometric" notes that measure the given feet.

*Chart II* shows us the Musarithms of multi-syllable feet whose second-to-last syllable is short, along with the metrometric notes corresponding to each.

*Chart III* shows us the Musarithms for Adonic and Dactylic meters <note>Classical poetic meters based on patterns of long and short syllables</note>, the forms of which are: *The joys of the world* <note>original: "Gaudia mundi"</note> and *Lift up your eyes* <note>original: "Tollite lumina"</note>.

*Chart IV* shows the Musarithms for Euripidean Iambics and Dactylics, the form of which is that most celebrated hymn *Hail, Star of the Sea* <note>original: "Ave maris stella"</note>; for such a verse, therefore, you will complete the desired melody with no trouble by the help of this table. Other smaller details of the table will be explained in their proper places.

*Chart V* shows the Musarithms for Anacreontic meters, whose form is *O thrice and four times happy* <note>original: "O ter quaterque felix"</note>, together with the metrometric notes corresponding to each, added at the bottom of the columns.

*Chart VI* shows the Musarithms for eight-syllable Archilochian Iambics; of which...

*Table I.* contains Musical Algorithms of polysyllabic feet, to nearly each of which we have attached metrometric notes.

*Table II.* contains Musical Algorithms of the aforementioned feet.

*Table IV.* contains Musical Algorithms of ingenious fugues <note>musical "fugas": imitative compositions where one voice follows another</note> with which the beginning of any song can be ingeniously established.

*Table VI.* contains melody-making algorithms adapted for both the recitative style and the comic and theatrical styles; furthermore, they contain the method for composing music in the chromatic and enharmonic styles <note>advanced and complex harmonic systems used to evoke specific moods</note>.

And within these three sections, we have deservedly encompassed whatever is rare, elegant, beautiful, and emotive in the whole of music, as the Reader will see with wonder in the progress of this work.

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>In what this new method of composing consists.</margin>
Our new *Musurgia* <term>Kircher’s term for his "musical workings" or the art of composition</term> consists chiefly in the skillful arrangement of melody-setting columns. From these, regardless of how they are used, a new harmony will necessarily result. Since these types of compositions are infinite, an infinite diversity of harmonic variations is born. For example, the combinations of the first table (*pinax*) are so numerous that the entire world, from the earth to the highest heavens, could more easily be filled with grains of sand than the diversity of resulting harmonies could be exhausted. Indeed, if all the writers in the world since the creation had spent their time describing these harmonic combinations, they would not yet have exhausted them. However, since these things are known only to those steeped in the mysteries of numbers, I do not wish to pursue them further, especially as I have demonstrated this extensively in the first part of this book. I have chosen to add these points here to restrain the slander of certain practical musicians who, upon seeing these tables, immediately object that the music produced is always the same. We do not dwell on their ignorance; experience itself will teach the truth. Therefore, whoever knows how to skillfully adapt these columns into movable tiles according to the rules prescribed in the fourth part of this work, and knows how to properly transfer the harmonic numbers into a melody-setting scale, will find himself able to compose skillful melodies for any given tone and any given words. Just as an algebraist, by following the path of a rule, completes the clarification of paradoxical questions with such ease that the operator himself may not fully grasp what he has done—producing an unexpected effect while the mathematician's mind is barely taxed—so too will a desired harmony emerge for composers following the path of these rules, even for those who are *unskilled in music* <note>original Greek: "ἀμούσοις" (amousois); referring to those without formal musical training</note>. But lest we keep the eager reader in suspense any longer, let us now approach the secrets of our musical-making art more closely.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the Requirements for our Musarithmic Musical Composition.

We define a *Musarithm* <term>Kircher's term for a musical algorithm; a mathematical set of numbers representing musical intervals</term>, as stated in the definitions, as nothing other than a specific collection of harmonic numbers through which, by applying rhythmic notes to the Musarithm, perfect harmony is drawn out. To perform this with excellence, the following things are required.

->Requirement I.<-
->The Sound-Arranging Palimpsest.<-

<margin>What a Palimpsest is.</margin>
Since all mathematical science consists in demonstration to find the truth, rather than in a vague and obscure style of disputation, it was necessary to represent these demonstrations with sensible signs so they might be better perceived. For this reason, the first masters of wisdom discovered points, surfaces, solids, numbers, and infinite other characters; by depicting these on paper, they could reveal the thoughts of the mind and the meaning of the things they conceived. In a very similar way, the Musical-Makers (*Musurgi*), in order to bring their speculations into action and present their demonstrations to the senses, discovered certain signs by which sounds—which are otherwise imperceptible—might become known through the placement of visible marks. Following their example, to bring our own speculations into practice, we first ordain the *Palimpsestus phonotacticus* <term>The Sound-Arranging Palimpsest; a reusable writing surface for mapping out musical settings</term>. A palimpsest is nothing other than that leathery membrane made of donkey skin from which notebooks or writing tablets are commonly made, and which modern musicians usually prefer to use above all others for this task. On this surface, writing is easy, and what is written is just as easily erased.

### Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music.

We use the term **Phonotactic** <term>Kircher’s term for the arrangement of sounds, from the Greek 'phono' (sound) and 'taktikos' (ordering)</term> for the method by which individual voices are adapted to their own **staves** <note>original: "pentagramma"; literally "five-lines," the standard musical staff</note> through the scales and clefs appropriate to each voice.

-> Hard or natural song <- -> Soft or fictive song <-

<note>Four rows of musical staves (five-line grids) are divided into two columns. The left column represents "hard" or natural song and the right represents "soft" or "fictitious" song (music using flats). Each row contains variations of clef placements on the five-line staff for different vocal ranges.</note>

-> Marking of the Bass Staff <-

<note>A series of musical staves showing the Bass part with F-clefs positioned on various lines to indicate different vocal depths.</note>

-> Marking of the Tenor Staff <-

<note>A series of musical staves showing the Tenor part with C-clefs positioned on various lines.</note>

-> Marking of the Alto Staff <-

<note>A series of musical staves showing the Alto part with C-clefs positioned on various lines.</note>

-> Marking of the Soprano Staff <-

<note>A series of musical staves showing the Soprano (Cantus) part with G-clefs positioned on various lines.</note>

The staves are marked primarily with three signs, which are called the "principles of the musical scale"; these are **F**, **C**, and **G**. The **F sign**, or the starting point of the scale, is placed on the Bass staff either on the middle line, the fourth line, or the fifth line. In transposing songs, it is most often placed on the middle line, and in that case, the bass sounds higher. If it is placed on the fourth line, it indicates a medium pitch, which is most natural for the voices, a **minor third** <note>original: "semiditono"</note> lower in pitch. Finally, if placed on the fifth line—which happens rarely—it denotes the deepest pitch, a minor third lower than the previous one. The markings for the remaining voices follow this bass arrangement, as was shown just above. This is the first way of marking, which they call "hard" or "natural." The other is "soft," which they also call "fictitious," and it differs from the previous one in no other way except that a **♭** <note>the flat symbol</note> is placed in the appropriate space for each voice, as is shown in the second column.

Note in this place that wherever you find this sign **𝄢** placed on the bass staff, know that it is the **F clef**. From this point, by counting up or down, we arrive at the knowledge of the positions of the seven principal letters or characters **A B C D E F G**, which, like keys <note>a play on the Latin 'clavis', meaning both 'clef' and 'key'</note>, open the door to all melody.

In the Tenor, wherever this sign **𝄡** is found, know that it is the **C clef**; from there, by counting up or down, you will arrive at the knowledge of any other clef position you seek. These same rules are to be observed in the Alto (or Counter-Tenor) and the Soprano. In the Soprano <note>original: "Cantus"</note>, or the upper voice, you will begin to find the positions of the remaining notes from the line on which you see the **G clef** placed. These things are said for the sake of those unskilled in practical music, for whose benefit we have decided to join the entire system of the **phonotactic palimpsest** <term>A reusable musical slate or grid used in Kircher's mechanical composition system</term> here.

Having explained the **phonotactic system** <term>the arrangement of sounds and notation</term>, let us now proceed to the second Requirement.

### Requirement II.
## The Tonographic Table.

Just as the preceding phonotactic system is a certain material principle for ordering melodies, so we may not undeservedly call this the formal principle of those same melodies. It is nothing other than a representation of the 12 Tones according to the 7 species of the **octave** <term>original: "diapason"</term> in columns proper to each tone, according to their harmonic numbers. However, instead of using more profuse words, we here set the whole system before your eyes: so that we are not forced to repeat here what we treated at length in previous books concerning the nature and condition of the tones.

<margin>Notes concerning the Tonographic Table.</margin>

We have woven together this Tonographic Table by a certain secret ingenuity, so that we have encompassed entirely infinite combinations of harmonic modulations within very few columns; so much so, that this Tonographic Table may not undeservedly be called the base and foundation of our entire miraculous **Musurgy** <term>Kircher's term for the process of musical composition</term>. And indeed, we have set down twelve Tones <term>modes</term> commonly used in the Church—which we therefore call Ecclesiastical Tones—so that nothing might be lacking for the curious composer <note>original: "melothetae"</note> regarding the immense variety of modulations. Although, in strict terms, there are only six Tones that undergo perfect mutations; for the other Tones either fall into the same intervals, or take their difference from another logic of changing from "hard" to "soft" <term>referring to the use of B-natural vs. B-flat in the hexachord system</term>, which Musicians call transposition, as will be said later. 

We have not preserved the natural order of the tones in the table, so that the order of the numbers, as well as the difference of the intervals, might be more clearly evident. And so that you might be able to name each one with a suitable title, we have attached the designations of the Ancients to each, together with the nature of each one. Thus, according to the logic of the theme which you desire to animate with harmony, you may find the corresponding **affects** <term>emotional states intended to be evoked in the listener</term> within the tones themselves. We have assigned to each tone whether it is "hard" or "soft," so that if any tone is hard, you use the characterization appropriate for hard song; if soft, the soft. 

Furthermore, we added the ancient names to each one, along with their nature, so that for the logic of the theme you wish to bring to life with harmonic melodies, you might find the corresponding affects: namely of joy, love, compassion, pain, mourning, dissolution, religion, vanity, ferocity, indignation, and similar things appropriate for stirring the souls of men. For just as modulation according to the first [mode] is intended to incite a divine character, so on the contrary it is the property of the sixth mode to excite the sparks of military affection, ferocity, and magnanimity. In the first column, we have placed the keys indicated by the seven letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G in order, as if they were a certain soul and guide of our entire Musurgical work; for this column, running horizontally across the columns of the modes, reveals the correspondence of the individual intervals in any tone with the keys, as will be seen later in practice.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### Requirement III.
### Concerning the value of notes and the measure of time.

To ensure that those unskilled in music find no obstacle in this, our musical work, we have decided to include here the value of musical notes (which we call <term>metrometric notes</term><note>original: "notas metrometras"; literally "meter-measuring" notes, a term Kircher uses to describe notes as units of mathematical time.</note> in our tables of musical patterns).

Since there is a great variety of harmonic movements (which all come together in one multi-voice composition), such that some proceed at a fast, some at a slow, and others at a moderate pace, it seemed best to musicians to establish a certain sign to avoid confusion, according to which singers might direct their voices. Since this sign is a kind of rule or precise measure of harmonic motions, it was not appropriate for it to be immobile. Therefore, they established a moving sign—the lifting or lowering of the hand or any other object held in the hand—which they called <term>arsis</term><note>From the Greek ἄρσιν, meaning "lifting" or the upbeat.</note> and <term>thesis</term><note>From the Greek θέσιν, meaning "placing" or the downbeat.</note>. The Italians call it <margin>Things to be noted concerning the Beat.</margin> *the beat* (la battuta), <term>Boethius</term><note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> calls it *clapping* (plausum), others call it *the touch and measure* (tactum & mensuram); we entitle it the *Chronometron* (time-measurer). This measure consists of two parts: one in the falling of the hand, which the ancients called *thesis*, and the other in the lifting of the hand, which they called *arsis*. These correspond to the movement of blood in the body, which <term>Galen</term><note>A famous physician of antiquity who compared the rhythm of the pulse to musical intervals.</note> calls *diastole* (expansion) and *systole* (contraction). Just as one pulse of the veins is formed from diastole and systole, so one complete time or measure is completed from an arsis and a thesis. The characters of the *Chronometron* are those musical notes commonly used, the values of which we set before your eyes here in a single glance.

### Table I.
->Of the Value of Notes.<-

<note><image-desc>A musical notation chart displaying notes on a five-line staff with their relative values indicated by numbers or fractions above each. From left to right:
- A square Breve note with '2' above it.
- A diamond-shaped Semibreve with '1' above it.
- A Minim (hollow diamond with stem) with '1/2' above it.
- A Semiminim (solid diamond with stem) with '1/4' above it.
- A Fusa (solid diamond with stem and one flag) with '1/8' above it.
- A Semifusa (solid diamond with stem and two flags) with '1/16' above it.
The names of the notes are printed directly below the staff: Breve, Semibreve, Minim, Semiminim, Fusa, Semifusa.</image-desc> A chart illustrating the hierarchical duration of notes. In modern terms, the Semibreve corresponds to a whole note, the Minim to a half note, the Semiminim to a quarter note, the Fusa to an eighth note, and the Semifusa to a sixteenth note.</note>

The first note denotes two measures; the second, one; the third, half a measure; the fourth, one-fourth part of a measure; the fifth, one-eighth; and the last denotes one-sixteenth part of a measure, each decreasing in a double proportion from the note immediately preceding it. Thus, a semibreve taken twice constitutes a breve; a minim taken twice constitutes a semibreve; a semiminim taken twice, a minim; a fusa taken twice, a semiminim; and finally, a semifusa taken twice, a fusa. Again, sixteen semifusas, 8 fusas, 4 semiminims, and two minims are always equivalent to one semibreve. Indeed, these things are clear in the following illustration.

<note><image-desc>A hierarchical diagram illustrating the subdivision of musical notes. The diagram uses symbols connected by vertical and slanted lines to show how each note type divides into two of the next smaller value.
- At the top: 32 Semifusa symbols (labeled "Semi fusae").
- Second row: 16 Fusa symbols (labeled "Fusae").
- Third row: 8 Semiminima symbols (labeled "Semi minimae").
- Fourth row: 4 Minima symbols (labeled "Minimae").

# Book VIII. The Miraculous Making of Music.

However, so that these things may be better understood, something must first be indicated here regarding time. Musical time, therefore, is nothing other than a certain and determined quantity of either smaller notes or figures contained within one *brevis* or *semibrevis*, as is clear in the preceding diagram. It is two-fold: perfect and imperfect. Perfect time is found at the beginning of a melody marked with this character <note>original: "hoc charactere", referring to the circle symbol</note> by which it is indicated that the *brevis* is perfect—that is, it is equivalent to three *semibreves*, as shown here at the side; but when a half-circle is placed at the beginning of a song, as appears here at the side, it is indicated by this character that the *brevis* is imperfect—that is, it is equivalent to two *semibreves*. Indeed, since these matters have been discussed at length in the preceding sections, we only wished to recall these sayings to memory.

->Perfect Time<-
<note>A musical staff with five lines. The time signature is a circle with a dot in the center, representing "perfect" or triple time. The staff contains one square brevis note followed by three diamond-shaped semibrevis notes, demonstrating that in perfect time, a single long note is divided into three smaller parts, symbolizing the Holy Trinity.</note>

->Imperfect<-
<note>A musical staff with five lines. The time signature is a broken circle, shaped like the letter C, which is the origin of the modern "common time" symbol. The staff contains one square brevis note followed by two diamond-shaped semibrevis notes, demonstrating the binary division of an imperfect brevis into two equal parts.</note>

### On Rests.

**F**inally, since all voices are not always in motion, it happens that they must occasionally be still. For this reason, notes were devised by which singers <note>original: "phonascis"; a Greek-derived term Kircher uses for vocalists or those trained in the art of the voice.</note> are shown how much time they ought to remain silent. The Greeks call these notes <term>pausis</term> <note>original: "παύσις"; meaning a pause or cessation.</note>, and the Latins, changing the name, call them rests <note>original: "pausas".</note>. Truly, for the understanding of these, nothing else seems necessary except a synopsis of rests, which I present to you here.

### Table II.
->A Model of Rests.<-

<note>A musical notation chart showing sixteen different rest symbols (pausae) on a staff. Above each rest is a number or fraction indicating its value in beats (tactibus). From left to right, the values decrease: 8, 7, 6, 5 1/2, 5, 4 1/2, 4, 3 1/2, 3, 2 1/2, 2, 1 1/2, 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8. The rests are represented by vertical bars of varying lengths that span different numbers of staff lines or portions of the spaces between them, providing a visual guide for silence in a composition.</note>

The lines inserted into the staff <note>original: "pentogrammo"; literally the five-lined graph.</note> signify rests in this diagram; the numbers placed above denote the value of the rests—that is, for how many beats <note>original: "tactibus".</note> the singers must remain silent. For example: the first rest marking shows a silence of eight beats; the second, seven; the third, six; the fourth, five and a half; and so on until the last. For the last shows a silence of 1/8 of a time; the second to last, 1/4 of a time; and the third to last, 1/2 of a time or half a beat. But as these things are very easy and known even to the youngest students, I did not think they needed to be explained further; I have only placed them here to provide an introduction for those who are entirely ignorant of music.

### Requirement IV.
### Knowledge of Musarithms.

**W**e call a Musarithm in this context nothing other than a collection of harmonic numbers corresponding to certain metrical feet and reduced into methodical "pinaces" or tables. It seemed fitting to honor this new art with this new and most appropriate title. For a Musarithm is the same as a <term>musical number</term> <note>original: "μελικός ἀριθμός" (melikos arithmos); meaning a number pertaining to melody or song.</note>, that is, a heap of sounding numbers most fit for expressing harmonic periods, as you will see after...

# CHAPTER III.
## Concerning simple counterpoint, and how it can be composed from the Musarithms of the first Collection by anyone, even those unskilled in music.

The first Collection <note>original: *Syntagma*</note> contains, besides ten others, two tables of polysyllabic Musarithms <note>Kircher's "Musarithmi" are mathematical-musical building blocks—pre-calculated sets of notes that correspond to the rhythm of words.</note>. The first table contains polysyllabic words with a long penultimate syllable; the second contains polysyllabic words with a short penultimate. With their help, anyone—even one who is <term>unskilled in music<note>original Greek: ἄμουσος (*amousos*), meaning one without the Muses or lacking musical training.</note></term>—may easily complete any simple counterpoint using the practice to be explained shortly. We have placed this collection of Musarithms before the others as it is simpler than the rest, so that by beginning with the easier and simpler elements, we might encounter less difficulty in those that follow. Furthermore, so that we do not proceed <term>without method<note>original Greek: ἀmethedōs (*ἀμεθόδως*).</note></term> in this educational task, we have followed the style of mathematicians and decided to demonstrate the craftsmanship of our entire *Musurgia* <note>The "Art of Making Music," referring to Kircher's monumental work.</note> through practical propositions or certain "problems." Let us therefore begin the matter with God's blessing.

# Problem I.
### *Given any theme of words and any tone, to compose the desired song in simple counterpoint using the first table.*

<margin>A new way of composing.</margin>
If, therefore, anyone desires to test our art in simple counterpoint, he must first have prepared a <term>phonotactic slate<note>original: *Palimpsestum phonotacticum*, a reusable writing surface or "palimpsest" Kircher designed for arranging musical notes according to his system.</note></term> according to the requirements of the second chapter of this part. Second, he must have the <term>Tonographic table<note>A chart Kircher provided to map musical tones to specific moods or scales.</note></term>. Third, he should keep the theme of the words written down separately, choosing a tone for himself that is appropriate to the "energy" or emotional character of those words. 

For example, to implore the grace of the Divine Power, let the theme of words be: *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original Latin: "Veni Creator Spiritus," a famous medieval hymn to the Holy Spirit.</note>. Since these words denote hope and trust in divine mercy, the sixth tone—also known as the <term>Hypolydian<note>One of the traditional church modes, often associated in the Baroque era with a gentle or "soft" character.</note></term>—will suit them best. Since this tone is characterized by "softness" (as the title of the tone in the tonographic table demonstrates), you will mark the <term>Pentagramma<note>The five-line musical staff.</note></term> of voices on the phonotactic slate with the symbols for "soft" song <note>original: *mollis cantus*, indicating the use of a B-flat.</note>. Then, from the Tonographic table, you will apply the column for the Sixth Tone, which is taken from the column of keys. The arrangement <note>original: *schema*</note> will appear as follows.

### Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music

...it is established, it will necessarily have as many notes as there are points marked in the spaces of the staves <note>original: *pentagrammorum*; literally "five-lines," the standard musical staff.</note>. You shall place these notes above the points of the **Bass** <note>original: *Basis*</note> in order; then you shall write these same notes on the points of the **Tenor**, the same on the points of the **Alto**, and finally the same on the points of the **Soprano** <note>original: *Cantus*</note>. You will then have the first period or strophe of your theme, complete in all its measures. You must, however, carefully observe that the notes are placed precisely in the spaces indicated by the points. Look at the paradigm shown previously, which will teach you every part exactly. By this very same reasoning and method, you will bring the remaining strophes or periods to life in harmony through their own **Musarithms** <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical algorithms or "building blocks" used in his system.</note>. In all the rest, the exact same practice is to be followed. Given, therefore, a theme of words and a certain tone, we have completed the simple counterpoint, as was to be done. <term>Melotheſia<note>From the Greek *melothesia*, meaning the art of composing or setting a melody to text.</note></term> follows.

<note>A musical notation diagram for four voices (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass). Each voice is represented on a five-line staff containing a series of points with numbers above them, representing Kircher's mechanical composition system. -> Come, Creator Spirit, visit the minds of Thy people; fill with heavenly grace the hearts which Thou hast created. <-
<note>original: *Veni Creator Spiritus mentes tuorum visita imple superna gratię qui tu creasti pectora*</note>

<margin>
This new method of composing is capable of infinite variation.
</margin>
But at this point, practical musicians will object, saying that by this method the same harmony will always be produced, and consequently, the variety of harmonies which the Author claims will not result. We shall easily shut their mouths when we demonstrate the wonderful diversity even in this single example. The objection is therefore false. For it will then be clear that this theme is capable of infinite variation, once we have first put forward certain points.

I say, therefore, that this aforementioned theme can be varied in four ways. First, by means of the transposition of the Musarithms; second, by means of the tones; third, by means of the notes to be applied; and fourth, by means of the columns, which admit infinite combinations through the different "feet" <note>Metrical feet or poetic rhythms.</note> that even a single strophe possesses. Let us examine each one separately.

<margin>
Variation by means of the transposition of the Musarithm.
</margin>
First, since this four-strophe theme is composed of four polyphonic Musarithms, it is certain—as was demonstrated at length in the first part of this *Musurgia*, Problem 1—that by the nature of the number four, it is twenty-four times variable; that is, it admits 24 combinations so that a new harmony, different from the previous one, always emerges. For any of the said four Musarithms can occupy the first place six times, with the remaining ones always being variable. Since all these things were demonstrated in the place cited, we refer the reader there. Therefore, this four-strophe theme can first be changed twenty-four times so that the harmony is never the same.

Second, by means of the Tones <note>Referring to the 12 musical modes or keys.</note>, it is again changeable twelve times. For the movable scale of keys, when applied to the individual columns of the Tones, will always produce essentially different harmonies according to the different nature of the tones. If, therefore, you multiply 24 by 12, we already have 288 mutations by which this mentioned four-strophe theme is variable.

Third, it can be changed by means of different notes; and according to the 12 series of notes placed at the bottom of the column, first according to simple placement, there are 3,456 variations. But according to the combinations of notes made among themselves in any way you please (there will arise 16,554,298,160,800 mutations), and in so many possible ways is this single four-strophe theme strictly variable.

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s explanation of the "Musurgia Mirifica," moving from basic note placement to more advanced methods of rhythmic and metric variation. # Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Since all these things were demonstrated in the first book, I have deemed it superfluous to explain them further here; for we have demonstrated all these matters in the cited place so clearly that anyone, even if ignorant of these things, should not and cannot doubt them hereafter.

Fourthly, a change can be made that is almost infinitely variable if, for instance, the columns are arranged according to the distinct metric feet of a period. I have decided to clarify this matter with an example; let it be, therefore:

# Problem II.
## ANOTHER METHOD.
### By animating the assumed theme into musical measures through distinct members or syllables.

The other method is through distinct members of a period <note>original: *periodi mēbra*; a "period" in rhetoric and music refers to a complete thought or sentence.</note>, or according to a collection of columns adapted to metric feet. Thus, once the **phonotactic palimpsest** <note>Kircher's term for a reusable writing surface or grid used for arranging musical "algorithms."</note> has been prepared, and the spaces divided according to the syllables of the assumed theme, you will begin to arrange the columns in this manner: Since the assumed theme is *Come, Holy Spirit, Creator* <note>original: *Veni Creator Spiritus*</note>, and the first word of the theme, *Veni*, is two syllables, you will place a column of two-syllable units; but since the second word, *Creator*, is three syllables with a long penultimate syllable, you will take a column of three-syllable units with long penultimates from the first **table** <note>original: *pinace*; from the Greek *pinax*, meaning a table, chart, or plate.</note> and add it to the column of two-syllable units. Since the last word, *Spiritus*, is three syllables with a short penultimate syllable, you will take a column of three-syllable units with short penultimates from the second table and arrange it after the preceding column. You will then have three columns arranged according to the three feet of the poetic strophe.

Note, however, that in this place it is not necessary to always take entire words for individual feet; instead, you may add one or two syllables (or as many as you wish) to one word from the word immediately following. Even two words joined into one can represent a single polysyllabic vocabulary. This matter is, again, almost infinitely variable. But so that these things may be better understood, it seemed appropriate to provide an example here, so that from it you might understand our meaning in the remaining cases.

<margin>Infinite variation here</margin>
-> 1 Come Holy Spirit Creator <- <note>original: *Veni Creator Spiritus*</note>
-> 2 Come | Holy Spirit | Creator <-
-> 3 Come | Holy Spirit Creator <-
-> 4 Come Holy Spirit | Creator <-
-> 5 Come Ho | ly Spirit Creator <-
-> 6 Come Holy | Spirit Creator <-
-> 7 Come | Holy Spirit Cre | ator. <-

<margin>Variation by reason of changing the feet</margin>
Behold the schema of the variation of the theme regarding the feet: The first behaves as an eight-syllable meter <note>original: *octofyllabi*</note>, as was shown in the preceding example. The second is by way of three feet. The third is by way of two feet, of which the first is two-syllable, namely *Veni*, and the other is six-syllable <note>original: *hectasyllabus*</note>, namely *Creator Spiritus*, treated as a single word. The fourth has a five-syllable foot at the beginning and a three-syllable foot with a short penult at the end. The fifth, with the words broken and cut, has a three-syllable **metric foot** <note>original: *metriam*</note> at the beginning, namely *Veni Cre*; then the two-syllable *ator*; thirdly, the three-syllable *Spiritus*. The sixth, by taking two syllables from the following word and joining them to the first, creates a four-syllable foot, leaving another four-syllable unit, *tor Spiritus*. The seventh, so that the middle may be four syllables, borrows a syllable from the last word.

You see, therefore, how mutations occur by reason of the diversity of the feet which can be considered in an assumed theme. Having seen these mutations, let us now return to the proposed paradigm.

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of Kircher's musical "computer," the Musurgia Mirifica. Having established the poetic feet of the hymn "Veni Creator Spiritus" on the previous page, Kircher now demonstrates how to map these syllables to numerical sequences (Musarithms) and then translate those numbers into musical notation using his phonotactic tables.</meta>

### Book VIII. The Wondrous Making of Music.

Let the proposed theme be, therefore, as above: *Come, Holy Spirit, Creator* <note>original: *Veni Creator Spiritus*</note>; you are to join the columns of the individual poetic feet, as has been said. Once this is completed, in whatever way you arrange these columns—provided that the **Musarithms** <note>Kircher's term for musical algorithms or sequences of numbers representing intervals</note> always correspond to the **Musarithms**—a new harmony must necessarily come forth. For example, in the three columns placed just before; for the proposed **melothesia** <note>the composition of a melody</note>, let us take the first three **tables** <note>original: *pinaces*; reference to the charts in Kircher's system</note> in the columns of the Musarithms, to which the following scheme corresponds:

| Bisyllabic II | Trisyllabic long III | Trisyllabic short III |
|-----------|----------------|----------------|
| 2 3       | 6 7 8          | 2 2 3          |
| 7 8       | 8 7 6          | 7 7 8          |
| 5 5       | 4 2 1          | 5 5 5          |
| 5 1       | 4 5 6          | 5 5 1          |
| Come      | Creator        | Spirit.      |

Once this is done, place before you the **phonotactic palimpsest** <note>a reusable grid or sliding scale used for mechanical composition</note> together with the column of keys for the sixth tone, as previously applied. See the numbers 2 3 6 7 8 2 2 3 pertaining to the **Cantus** <note>the highest voice part, or Soprano</note>; you will find which letters they correspond to in the column of keys: soon you will find that 2 corresponds to G; 3 to A; 6 to D; 7 to E; 5 to C; 4 to B; and 2 to G; 3 to A. Thus, having marked the points on the **musical staff** <note>original: *pentagrammo*</note> of the Cantus, see these numbers 7 8 8 7 6 7 7 8: see which letters they correspond to in the column of keys, and you will find 7 corresponds to E, 8 to F, 7 to E, 6 to D, and finally 7 to E. Therefore, having marked the points in the designated spaces for these letters on the staff of the **Altus**, you will have the locations of the notes. You shall proceed no differently in transferring the Musarithms of the **Tenor** and **Bass** onto their own staves. When these steps are finished, you shall add to each poetic foot the corresponding notes from the bottom of the columns (selecting any from the 12 for each voice), and you will have a perfect harmony. Truly, the example will teach you better than I could declare even with many words.

-> Example of the operation <-

<note>A detailed musical composition diagram. On the far left is a table titled "Column of the 6th Tone" with columns "Key" and "Tone" mapping letters F, E, D, C, B, A, G, F to numbers 8 through 1. To the right of this table is a column of numbers (3, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3) serving as a guide. The central part shows four musical staves with lettered notation (a through g) indicating positions. Below the staves are four rows of numbers corresponding to the musical parts: 2 3 6 7 8 2 2 3 (Cantus/Soprano), 7 8 8 7 6 7 7 8 (Altus/Alto), 5 5 4 2 1 5 5 5 (Tenor), and 5 1 4 5 6 5 5 1 (Bassus/Bass).</note>

And by this same reasoning, you will dispatch the remaining stanzas in order. Whoever, therefore, has well understood the examples given thus far, will find absolutely no difficulty in the remaining ones to follow.

You see, therefore, with what great ease any musical compositions are dispatched by this practice. And lest a musician ignorant of our art might object to us that the same song always comes forth, those things which we demonstrated concerning the almost infinite mutations of the preceding paradigm will easily convince him. For it is certain that in the transposition and various application of these three columns, a much greater variety of combinations occurs than in the preceding one: the mutations of these are so great that they can by no means be comprehended by the human mind. If, therefore, from the various application of only three columns such an inconceivable variety of mutations should be born, how great a variety do we believe will emanate from the transposition of 10, 20, or even 30 columns? But since these things are commonly seen as paradoxes, we have decided they should be wrapped in silence rather than declared at greater length. We will give only a certain specimen in this place of the way in which this same stanza undergoes an essential mutation by reason of different Tones; and first indeed in all 12 tones except the 4th, which, on account of the intervening false fifth <note>the tritone, traditionally avoided in Renaissance counterpoint</note>, does not sustain this cadence, unless it is corrected by a sharp <note>original: the symbol for a diesis or sharp</note>.

<header>Of the Consonant and Dissonant Great Art.</header>
<meta>catchword: Diagram-</meta>

# The First Diagram.
### The transformation of a composed theme from the sixth tone into the first tone of the keys.

<margin>
The method of changing a song from one Tone into another Tone.
</margin>
If, therefore, anyone should desire to change this subject into the first tone, let him apply the column of keys to the column of the first Tone. Then, on the musical slate <note>original: *palimpsesto phonostatico*, a reusable writing surface Kircher designed for musical calculation</note>, let him first change the character of the "soft" melody into the "hard" <note>original: *mollis cantus in durum*. In this context, it refers to changing a scale with a B-flat to one with a B-natural</note>, which is done by removing the ♭ symbol. Next, he must carefully observe which letters in the column of keys correspond to the same numbers of the four <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the numerical sequences used to represent musical intervals</note> excerpted from the three columns. For we wish the same Musarithms to always remain, so that a greater variety of these may be revealed. If indeed you mark the points in the staff spaces <note>original: *pentagrammis*, meaning five-line staves</note> for the letters indicated by the numbers, and add the <term>metrometers</term> <note>rhythmic notations or signs that measure the time of the notes</note> to each according to the previous model, as has been said, you will have a harmony composed in the first tone, essentially different from the sixth tone, as appears in the first example of the following universal diagram.

Where you should first note that in the column of the first tone, a ♭ is always placed next to the number 6. Since this number corresponds to the letter B in the column of keys, wherever and in whichever voice’s staff it is found, know that a ♭ <note>original: *b molle*, a flat sign</note> must be prefixed to the note occurring in that place. This appears in the B note of the Bass <note>original: *basis*</note> in the following diagram in the first column of the first tone, and in the fifth note of the Alto, and in the third note of the Tenor; all of which must be noted most carefully. For whatever we say in this place must be strictly followed hereafter.

Note secondly that in the aforementioned column of the first tone, the number 7 is marked with the ⁜ sign of the <term>semitone</term>. This denotes that wherever the letter C is found in any voice’s staff—which the number 7 of the First Tone column indicates in the column of keys—the ⁜ sign <note>this symbol is used here to indicate a sharp (♯) to raise the note to a leading tone</note> must always be prefixed to the note occurring in that place. This is required if the immediately following note ascends, or if it is the final note, or if a rest follows immediately; however, it should be omitted if the melody descends, except in rare cases which are discussed elsewhere. Know that this should also be understood regarding the columns of other tones in which 7 or any other number is found marked with this sign. You have an example in the Alto voice, where you will find the first and sixth notes marked with this ⁜ sign, followed by an immediately ascending note. In the Soprano voice <note>original: *Cantus*</note>, you will find the last note marked with this sign because it is the final note.

---

# The Second Diagram.
### Of the transformation of a composed theme from the sixth tone into the second "soft" tone.

If anyone should desire to compose this thematic arrangement in a pleasant, gentle, and flattering style, let him choose the second tone. This is done by applying the column of keys to the column of the second <term>Hypodorian</term> tone. For if he marks the letters in the four-voice staves indicated by the four Musarithms in the column of keys, using dots and notes with their rhythms as mentioned, a new kind of harmony will emerge. It will be composed in a pleasant, gentle, and flattering style, such as the second tone contains, as shown in the second column of the following universal system. Meanwhile, observe carefully that wherever a note occurs on the E key in the four-voice staves, you must prefix a ♭ <note>flat sign</note>, as indicated by the number 6 in the second tone column (where you find ♭ attached), following the first instruction above. And wherever a letter indicated by ⁜ 7 occurs, always prefix the ⁜ sign in the same way to this note, provided (as I said) the following note ascends or is the final note. You have an example of the B-flat <note>original: *B. mollis*</note> in the fifth note of the Bass, and in the third note of the Tenor; an example of the ⁜ semitone is found in the first and sixth notes of the Alto in the example for the second tone.

<header>Book VIII. The Miraculous Making of Music.</header>

# The Third Diagram.
### On the transformation of a composed theme from the sixth tone into the third "hard" tone.

Furthermore, if anyone should wish to transform the first composed theme from the sixth tone into the third tone—which is mournful and suited for somber subjects—he will achieve his aim by applying the column of keys to the column of the third, or <term>Phrygian</term> <note>The Phrygian mode was traditionally associated with intense, sometimes volatile or mournful emotions in Baroque music theory.</note>, tone. For if he marks the locations on the <term>musical staves</term> <note>original: *pentagrammis*, referring to the five-line staff</note> of the letters denoted by the <term>Musarithm</term> <note>Kircher's term for numerical sequences that represent musical intervals</note> numbers in the column of keys—first with points, and then, as has been said, with the <term>metrometers</term> <note>Signs used to indicate the rhythmic duration or "measure" of the notes.</note>—a new kind of song will emerge, sought according to its nature. This is beautifully demonstrated in the third column of the following system. However, one must observe with all diligence the locations of the ⁜ <note>original: *semitoniorum*, meaning sharps or semitones</note>, or also the ♮ and ♭ symbols, according to the rules indicated previously.

# The Fourth Diagram.
### On the transformation of a theme from the sixth into the fourth tone.

You will change the chosen theme into the fourth tone if you apply the column of keys to the column of the fourth tone. For if you mark the locations of the letters on the staves as indicated by the Musarithm numbers—first with points, and then with the appropriate rhythmic notes—the result will be a tone suited for weeping and lamentation. See the diagram for Tone IV in the following System. Therefore, whoever correctly understands this method of changing the said melody from one tone into any other among these four tones will encounter no difficulty in forming the remaining ones. Thus, nothing remains but for us to place the general system for the transformation of a chosen theme according to the twelve tones before the eyes of the curious Reader in a single synopsis; for from this, the procedure for the rest will be clearly evident.

### The universal system by which a chosen theme is essentially changed through the XII tones.

<note>A musical diagram contains three vertical sections of musical notation on four-stave systems. Each section represents the same theme transposed into a different musical mode or "tone."
1. The first section is titled "I. Dorian Tone" <note>original: *I. Tonij ſiue dorij*</note>.
2. The second section is titled "II. Hypodorian Tone" <note>original: *II. Toni hypodorij*</note>.
3. The third section is titled "III. Phrygian Tone" <note>original: *III. Toni phrygij*</note>.
The music is written in mensural notation with diamond-shaped notes. C-clefs and F-clefs are used, along with various accidental signs such as sharps and flats.</note>
