# Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making.

You have here, Reader, the transformation of a single theme into all tones demonstrated in a single system, so that from this you may see the immense variety even of a single <term>Musarithm</term> <note>Kircher's term for the numerical combinations or "musical algorithms" used in his system to generate harmony.</note>; if to these are added different note values, an altogether inconceivable variety of changes of that same theme will emerge. I wished to show all of these things here more extensively so that the <note>original: "καθολικισμὸς" (katholikismos)</note> universality of our art might be more clearly evident. But now, let us say something about the value of the notes, or the change of time.

## Table V.
### On the transformation of metrical notes.

Anyone who has correctly weighed the eighth chapter of the first part of this book will easily see that there is scarcely any end to the variations of a theme according to different time signatures. There is, moreover, a twofold <term>time, perfect and imperfect</term> <note>In Renaissance and Baroque music theory, "perfect time" refers to triple meter (associated with the Holy Trinity), while "imperfect time" refers to duple or quadruple meter.</note>, about which, since enough was said in the third Requirement, I do not wish to be longer here; but at last, I will explain how that can be applied in various ways to our theme. We have subjoined the notes of perfect time to the individual columns of the Musarithms, which we also call <term>metrical notes</term>, because they correspond perfectly to the numbers of the Musarithms in terms of count and time. Those notes without a marked proportion number signify <term>imperfect time</term>; those, however, which have a prefixed number of time proportion are called notes of <term>perfect time</term>, and are commonly called <term>tripla</term> <note>Triple meter or proportions.</note>.

And although, as I said above, an altogether infinite variety emanates from the mutual combination of the eight notes explained in the third Requirement, we have nevertheless chosen twelve from all of them to facilitate our <term>Musurgy</term> <note>The "work of music" or the craft of composition.</note>, as it were; these will suffice abundantly for the said variety of modulations to be established. Our theme, therefore, first assumed in the preceding system, is replicated twelve times; for it can be replicated that many times by applying one series out of any of the twelve notes to each of the four voices. So that you may understand this, it must be noted that since in this place we are teaching simple counterpoint that is <note>original: "ἰσόχρονον" (isochronon)</note> <term>isochronous</term>—that is, proceeding in equal time—in which the same notes are applied to each of the four voices, one series of notes to be applied to the four voices suffices. For if anyone were to apply different series to different voices, the entire harmony would be destroyed, as it would have a time least consistent with the Musarithms.

This having been noted beforehand, so that you may see the method of application and so it may be more perfectly clear here, we wished to present only the <term>basis</term> <note>The bass line or fundamental part.</note> of the assumed theme, marked with a different value of notes. For anyone will easily be able to mark the remaining corresponding voices with the same series and order of notes. Therefore, in a single synopsis, we place the artifice before your eyes; for this variety of different time will serve to excite various <term>affects</term> <note>Emotional states or "passions" intended to be stirred in the listener by specific musical devices.</note> in the modulation. For just as the affects of sadness, languor, and mourning require slow times, so the affects of joy, cheerfulness, dissolution, and indignation require fast times.

## Diagram of perfect time, either Minor Triple or Hemiola.

If anyone, therefore, wishes to change a melody from <term>imperfect time</term> <note>In the music theory of Kircher’s day, "imperfect time" referred to duple or quadruple meters (like modern 2/4 or 4/4), symbolized by a broken circle.</note> into <term>perfect time</term> <note>"Perfect time" refers to triple meter (like 3/4), which was traditionally associated with the Holy Trinity and symbolized by a full circle.</note>, they will mark the voices and notes using the method set down here. They will then have a variation distinct from all others. You will find this kind of time at the bottom of the tables under these titles: <term>major triple</term> and <term>minor triple</term>. You may choose either one, though I would have it noted that in metrical verse (poetry), the triple time should be continued through every stanza and not mixed with imperfect time; however, in non-metrical words (prose), we leave the use of triple time to the composer's judgment.

From these few examples, unless I am mistaken, the wondrous power of our craft is sufficiently clear: from the same unchanging numbers of the three <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for his "musical algorithms"—pre-calculated sets of numbers that allow a user to generate four-part harmony automatically.</note>, such a huge and admirable variety is born. Therefore, whatever has been said so far regarding the <term>melothesia</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning the "composition" or "setting" of a melody.</note> of the chosen theme is common to all the operations that follow. For the method of operation is the same in all of them; thus, it seemed best to treat the method of the art fully here, so that we would not be forced to repeat the same thing so many times in the following sections. We will always refer the reader back to this point.

These things having been so performed, nothing remains except that, before we proceed further, we should here set down certain precautions, which we rightly call the Canons of the whole art. By following these, we may overcome all occurring difficulties and arrive at a perfect knowledge of composition.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the Musarithmic Canons, or the Cautions to be 
## Applied in the Operations of Music-Making <note>Original: *Melotheticis*; referring to the art of composing melodies.</note>.

Lest musicians be able to object to us that something within the entire scope of practical music lies hidden—something we either did not foresee or could not remedy when other difficulties arose—we have seen fit to set down here the Canons <note>In this context, "Canons" refers to fundamental rules or laws of the art.</note> that direct the whole art. If these are observed with singular care, no difficulty will ever arise so great that even an <term>unmusical</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἄμουσος* (amousos), meaning someone without the Muses or lacking musical training.</note> novice will not easily overcome it.

## CANON I.
### On the Characteristics of the Staves, or the Method of Marking
### the Voices on the Phonotactic Palimpsest <note>Original: *palimpſeſto phonotactico*. Kircher’s "phonotactic palimpsest" was a physical device or slate used for his mechanical composition system.</note>.

The harmonic keys <note>Clefs and signatures.</note>, which others call the scale, occupy various positions on the staves <note>Original: *pentagrammis*, meaning the five-line musical staff.</note>; therefore, that marking must be used with caution. So that the novice of this art does not wander into uncertainty, he shall operate in this way when about to compose any piece of music: first, he shall select for himself a certain tone <note>A musical mode.</note> from the twelve prescribed above, one suited to the meaning of the words, as was said before. Once this is done, let him look in the system of mutation for the characteristics of the staves for the twelve tones—that is, what the arrangement of the keys or scale is in the column of the tone he has chosen. He shall mark his staves, drawn on the palimpsest, with this same characteristic. If the characteristic is "hard," <note>Original: *durus*; referring to the *hexachordum durum* (using B-natural).</note> he shall mark it as hard; if "soft," <note>Original: *mollis*; referring to the *hexachordum molle* (using B-flat).</note> as soft. I would, however, advise novices to always accept that signature of the scale which those tones immediately following obtain in the universal system of six orders. For this renders the song more natural and more suitable for the individual voices. If anyone uses that type of scale found in the first and the last three tones, it will render the voices higher than is proper and unsuitable for the voices of the singers. Nevertheless, in those tones where such a signature is encountered, it must be left as it is. You should also know that we have placed the twelve tones here that are commonly used in the Church, and which I have judged best for our purpose, not being ignorant of the great controversy regarding the quality of the tones, which we have sufficiently discussed in the preceding books.

## CANON II.
### On Musarithms and Their Arrangement.

We have declared in the preceding sections what a Musarithm <note>Kircher's term for a numerical code representing a musical phrase or harmony.</note> is: for it is a certain aggregate of harmonic numbers, such as are contained in the individual cells or areas of the columns, distributed into four series of numbers. The first of these represents the melody or the first voice <note>The Soprano.</note>; the second, the second voice, which is the Alto; the third, the third voice, which is the Tenor; and the fourth, the fourth voice, which is the Bass. And the Bass series is unchangeable; it can never take the place of another voice, just as the series of any other voice cannot take the place of the Bass. However, the three series besides the Bass can be permuted among themselves at will, if necessity compels it. I say "if necessity compels it"; for it happens occasionally in certain tones that a certain voice from the Musarithms turns out now higher, now deeper; so that you may remedy this, the voices must be swapped. For example, if the Soprano or Tenor were too high, either voice would have to be changed into the Alto, and the voice of the Alto into the Soprano or Tenor—namely, to either one...

# Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music-Making

We have placed eight columns here; the first column shows the excess of voices that rise beyond their natural constitution. The second column shows the change of those voices when reduced to moderation <note>Original: *mediocritatem*; referring to the comfortable middle range or "tessitura" of a voice.</note>. Thus, you see that for the Alto voice to be reduced to moderation, it must take the place of the Soprano <note>Original: *Cantus*</note>, and for the Soprano to have moderation, it must yield to the place of the Alto. The Tenor, however, if it does not have moderation, must proceed an octave lower. If you follow this rule strictly, you will find no further difficulty in proportioning the voices; for voices are so prepared by nature that when one exceeds moderation, its change into another necessarily brings that excess back to moderation. This mutual transformation takes place most often in the Alto; for whether the Soprano has exceeded its range, either voice moving into the Alto will be considered restored to moderation. Nevertheless, migration into the Tenor's octave is better suited to the Tenor than to the Soprano; yet if it should descend so deeply as to move below the notes of the Bass, as happens in the Tenor, then the Soprano and Tenor can swap their seats.

<margin>How the transmutation of voices is to be carried out.</margin>
Furthermore, these things must be explained more fully. If the four voices had the constitution shown in the third column—that is, each descending more than is right—then they would have to be changed into the voices in the fourth column corresponding to the first. Namely, the Soprano into the Alto, the Alto into the Soprano, and the Tenor and Bass should move an octave higher, as the fourth column shows. In the same way, if the voices moved higher than is right, as the fifth column demonstrates, then they would have to be changed into the voices shown in the sixth column. Specifically, the Soprano into the Alto, the Alto into the Soprano, and the Tenor must be changed either into the Alto or, like the Bass, into the octave below. But since these things are clear from the examples, we shall not dwell on them. Only one doubt might occur here to the student <note>Original: *Tyroni*; a beginner or apprentice.</note>: by what method can those voices be changed immediately?

I respond that nothing is easier to do. For if you mark the locations of the keys <note>Original: *clauium*; referring to the musical clefs or the letter-names of the notes.</note> or letters on the Soprano staff <note>Original: *pentagrammo*</note> with the same dots and notes on the staff of the Alto or any other voice, you will have what you seek. For the locations of the keys are common to all four voices, and it is exactly the same whether you place the locations of the Alto keys in the Soprano, or those of the Soprano or Tenor in the Alto. From this it follows that in any <term>Musarithm</term> <note>A "Musarithm" is Kircher's term for a set of numbers representing a musical phrase or harmonic progression in his system.</note>, the series of three numbers belonging to the three voices remaining after the Bass are indifferent <note>Interchangeable.</note>. Thus, the first series fits both the Alto and the Tenor, and the second and third fit the Soprano as well as the Alto and Tenor. The "indifference" consists only in this: that in one voice they may occasionally move higher or deeper than is right, and in this case, the voices are to be swapped in the manner described. But to give the student some satisfaction here: let the Soprano voice in the preceding example be reduced from its excess to moderation—that is, let it be changed into the Alto. You will work it thus: since the first two notes of the Soprano consist of F, the third in E, the fourth in C, the fifth in B, the sixth and seventh in C, and the eighth in D, you will see where the locations of said keys are on the Alto staff. Notes placed in these positions will give the Soprano part reduced to moderation in the Alto voice. You will work in this way for all others. Here you will also note that the Tenor and Soprano are so similar that one can be taken for the other without any hesitation at all, since they differ by only a single interval on the staves. Therefore, the only transformation that must be made is from either one into the Alto, which is distant from the said voices for the most part by a <term>Major Third</term> <note>Original: *ditono*</note> or a <term>Perfect Fourth</term> <note>Original: *diatessaron*</note>.

## RULE III. <note>Original: *CANON III.*</note>

### Concerning the signs ♭, ♮, and # occurring within the columns of Tones.

In the columns of Tones, these signs ♭ and # occasionally occur in certain tones. By this we show that those letters indicated by the number to which this letter ♭ is assigned—wherever they are found on the staves—must always have a flat [♭] prefixed to them. The same must be said of the natural sign <note>Original: *b quadrato*; the "square b," ancestor of the modern natural sign ♮.</note> and the sign for the major semitone [#]. This latter sign is almost always attached to the number 7. Therefore, the letter which is marked by this number seven in the scale of keys requires a note affected by this sign—not always, indeed, but then when the following note ascends.

### CANON IV.
->On the choice of Tones.<-

All <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Mathematical sequences or "musical algorithms" used in Kircher's mechanical composition method.</note> neither should nor can be adapted to each of the twelve tones <note>Refers to the twelve musical modes.</note> at will or indiscriminately, since there are many Musarithms which cannot be applied to certain tones because of the occurrence of "forbidden intervals" (about which we shall say more later). Hence, so that we might look to the convenience and ease of the tones in the operation, we have assigned to each column the tones appropriate to the Musarithms of said columns; if these are followed, all errors will undoubtedly be easily avoided. The fourth and fifth tones are rarely in use and are adapted only to a few Musarithms because of the aforementioned occurrence of forbidden intervals. All the others can easily come into use. Hence, I advise that the Beginner should first exercise himself especially in six tones: namely, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8. For these, since they are the principal ones and agree with almost all the six others, will be abundantly sufficient for all harmonic modulation; indeed, hardly any song <note>Original: *cantilena*</note> can be assigned that is not composed according to one of these six tones. If, however, anyone wishes to use the other six tones as well for greater variety, we do not oppose him, provided he proceeds with the caution already mentioned. The Beginner will also do better to exercise himself first in the 2nd and 6th tones.

# CANON V.
## On avoiding illicit intervals.

It happens from time to time that by changing the tone <note>Original: *tonus*. In this context, it refers to the musical mode or key being used in the composition.</note>, the pitch-letters fall into illicit intervals. I would wish for you to avoid these with all possible diligence. For they are the greatest absurdity in Music and lash the ears in a marvelous <note>Meaning "extraordinary" in a negative sense; Kircher often uses "marvellous" to describe extreme effects.</note> way. They are as follows:

->**Illicit intervals.**<-

<note>Musical notation systems showing twelve numbered examples of "illicit intervals" on five-line staves. Examples 1 and 2 show the "mi contra fa" tritone (F-B and B-F). Subsequent examples (3-12) demonstrate other prohibited melodic and harmonic intervals using square and diamond-shaped mensural notes with various sharps and flats.</note>

->**The reduction of illicit intervals to licit ones.**<-

<note>Musical notation systems showing twelve numbered examples corresponding to the "Illicit intervals" above. These staves demonstrate the "reduction" or correction of those prohibited intervals into acceptable consonant ones through altered accidentals or changed pitch relationships.</note>

The first series of intervals shows the illicit intervals; the second shows the reduced <note>That is, corrected or resolved.</note> intervals. In the first and second columns, you see <term>mi contra fa</term> <note>A classic rule in medieval and Renaissance counterpoint prohibiting the "tritone"—an interval of three whole steps (like F to B-natural) often called "the devil in music" for its harsh dissonance.</note> and *fa contra mi*, a most absurd interval, being reduced by changing the <term>Hard Song</term> <note>Original: *Cantus durus*. This refers to music using B-natural (the "square B").</note> into the <term>Soft Song</term> <note>Original: *Cantus mollis*. This refers to music using B-flat (the "round B").</note>. In the third and fourth columns, you see *mi contra fa* in the first tone being reduced by changing the Hard Song into B-flat <note>Original: *b. mollem*.</note>. In the fifth and sixth columns, you see illicit intervals in the Soft Song being reduced by changing the Soft Song into the Hard by omitting both flats, or from the Hard into the Soft by admitting both; and so on for the rest.

You see, therefore, by what method the prohibited intervals ought to be reduced. Whenever you fall into one of these, either the <term>clausula</term> <note>A musical phrase or cadence.</note> must be changed from hard to soft, or from soft to hard; or, what I would judge more advisable, the <term>Musarithm</term> <note>Kircher's term for the specific sets of numbers used in his tables to generate musical harmonies mathematically.</note> must be changed. This is done if you seek another Musarithm whose last two numbers in the bass <note>Original: *basis*.</note> are different from the previous one, and you will have the whole business finished without such a great change. From this, we form the rule [canon] thus:

Whenever the numbers of the Musarithms fall into prohibited intervals, then the Musarithm must be changed. This is done if you take another one whose last two numbers in the bass are different. Let this be the example:

Suppose the two last numbers of the Musarithm for the bass are 5 and 1. In the column for the 5th tone, these will fall on the notes F and B. If the song is "hard" <note>Using B-natural.</note>, the notes will have a cadence like that shown in the second column—namely, a prohibited one. Search, therefore, for another Musarithm for the bass whose numbers are not 5 and 1, but, for example <note>Original: *v. g.* (verbi gratia).</note>, 6 and 2. If you apply these to the same column of keys, two letters <note>Pitch names.</note> will be produced...

# CANON VI.
## On the change of Tones in one and the same song, or on the mixture of Tones.

**Lest** any musician be able to object to us that we have no variety in our <term>Musarithms</term>, we have wished to hand down the method for the mixture of Tones here. However, so that <term>Tyrones</term> <note>A Latin term for beginners or apprentices.</note> may understand this mixture of tones, it must be known that Music is so fond of variety that if, in one and the same song (whatever it may be), the constant character of the chosen tone and the same intervals are always maintained, it can neither please nor provide any sweetness to the ears; rather, it would bring annoyance and boredom. Hence more skilled <term>Musurgi</term> <note>Kircher's word for composers or masters of the musical art.</note> are accustomed to display their melodies with great delight for the listeners by using the cadences of different tones, just like so many different colors. Therefore, lest the said composers think our "Musurgical" art is deprived of this way of ingeniously interweaving tones, I will show by this canon by what method we can adorn our <term>Melothesias</term> <note>The process of composing or setting a melody.</note> with similar textures, so that we do not seem to have omitted anything in this, our <term>Musurgia</term> <note>The total art of musical composition or the system Kircher is teaching.</note>.

You see, therefore, with what easy effort a mixture of tones may be made. In songs composed upon a tone of <term>soft song</term> <note>original: "mollis cantus"; refers to the hexachord system using B-flat (B-moll), often associated with flatter keys and a more somber or "soft" character.</note>, the greatest care must be taken that the application or movement of the number-column does not land on a step which properly belongs to <term>hard song</term> <note>original: "duro cantui"; refers to the hexachord system using B-natural (B-durum), associated with sharper keys and a "harder" or brighter character.</note>. If a song has been made in "soft song," the tones belonging to "hard song" cannot and should not be mixed by any means, except in certain very rare cases—namely, when we wish to skillfully suggest a massive change from joy to sadness. To recognize the tones that are properly mixable, observe these two Canons, but let us give another example.

Whenever you select the 2nd tone for completing any composition, know that the same <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the numeric sequences representing musical intervals or phrases.</note> of the second tone can be changed three or four times by means of <term>transposition rods</term> <note>original: "bacillos transpositorios"; sliding mechanical aids Kircher designed for his organum mathematicum to help non-musicians compose.</note>. But the matter will shine more clearly in an example. Let a Musarithm of this kind be proposed in the notes of the second tone. If you wish this to be changed, apply the column of Musarithm numbers to the column of keys or musical letters, so that 1 corresponds to the first note of the Musarithm—namely, on G. In this way, the first cadence of the second tone for the first verse of any meter will come forth. If, however, you move the column number to B, so that 1 corresponds to B, and then resolve the Musarithm numbers into notes, you will have the first "mutation" of the previous cadence, as appears here. If you apply the said column of numbers with its number 1 to the letter C in the column of keys, and then resolve the Musarithm numbers into notes according to this application, the second mutation of the cadence will come forth, as appears here. If you apply the column of numbers with its radical number to D, and resolve the numbers into notes according to this application, the third mutation will come forth, as appears here. The fourth cadence, however, will be the same as the first.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### CANON VII.
### Concerning the avoidance of prohibited intervals.

<margin>I.</margin> Whenever a piece of music is marked with the character of <term>soft song</term> <note>original: "cantus mollis"; the musical system or hexachord that uses B-flat, usually sounding more somber or "mellow."</note>, the number 1 or 8 from the previously mentioned columns should never be applied above the letters A and E. Since these intervals properly belong to <term>hard song</term> <note>original: "cantus duri"; the musical system that uses B-natural, sounding "sharper" or brighter.</note>, not only would they be inserted into tones of a different nature, but they would also result in illicit <note>prohibited or dissonant</note> intervals. However, the aforementioned number 1 or 8 can be applied to all the remaining letters.

<margin>II.</margin> If the song is marked with the character of <term>hard song</term>, then the number 1 or 8 should never be placed above B and above E—and this applies even when the signs ♭ <note>flats</note> are used—except very rarely. If you observe these two rules correctly, you will proceed without any danger in the mixing of tones.

### CANON VIII.
### Concerning the placement of chromatic signs ♭ ♮ ♯.

In both parts of the sliding application columns, you will find chromatic signs <note>accidentals</note> attached to both letters and numbers. By these, we indicate that whenever both a number and a letter appear with the same signs, then that sign must be placed before the note. However, if either cell in the column lacks them, the sign must be omitted. Thus, in the first column, you will find the letter C marked with the ♯ sign. However, the corresponding number 5 lacks the same sign; we use this to indicate that C should not be marked with this sign, but it should be omitted entirely. Again, in the same column, you will find the seventh number likewise marked with the ♯ sign, to which the letter E responds with a prefixed ♭. Because the letter lacks the ♯ and the number 7 lacks the ♭, it serves as a sign to you that both the ♭ and the ♯ should be omitted in this tone. All these things must be noted diligently.

But when the column of numbers is moved forward by one step—for example, from F to G—you will find the number 6 marked with a ♭, and the number 7 marked with a ♯. Since the letters E and F that respond to these numbers are marked with those same signs, it indicates to you that just as ♭ must be prefixed to E, so ♯ must be prefixed to F. Thus, this can be a universal rule: whenever both the letters and the corresponding numbers are marked with the same signs, then the letters require those signs; but if only one or the other—either the letter or the number—is marked with these signs, the letter should by no means be marked with that sign. Note also that the ♯ sign should not always be placed as we advised in the third Canon, but only when the following note ascends, or when a rest immediately follows, or if it is the final note. But all these things will be treated more extensively in the following part, for which reason we refer the reader there.

To show greater variety in our <term>Musurgia</term> <note>The art of making or composing music.</note>, we have arranged this Canon. With these notes, you will be able to accommodate any hymns of words, and finally any psalms whatsoever. ### CANON X.

->On the fitting of words to notes<-

In the first <term>Pinax</term> <note>original: "Pinace"; from the Greek for "table" or "chart."</note> we have placed polysyllabic words whose second-to-last syllable is long; in the second Pinax, conversely, we have placed polysyllabic words with a short second-to-last syllable. Therefore, whenever any word of any number of syllables occurs where the second-to-last syllable is long, you shall use the polysyllables of the first table. If, however, the second-to-last syllable is short, you shall use the <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical units of music used in his system.</note> of the second table, just as the title demonstrates. At the bottom of each table—that is, at the foot of each column—are placed notes called <term>metrical indicators</term> <note>original: "Metrometræ"</note>, so named because they perfectly measure any given polysyllable in many ways. For example: if a composition is to be made upon these words, *My soul doth magnify the Lord* <note>original: "Magnificat anima mea Dominum"; the opening of the Canticle of Mary.</note>, take any Musarithm from the second table in the column for four-syllable words with a short second-to-last syllable for the word *Magnificat*; the metrical notes at the bottom correspond to it. For the words *Anima mea* <note>my soul</note>, you will take any Musarithm from the first table in the column for five-syllable words, to which any series of metrical notes at the bottom corresponds. For these five-syllable words, although they may have a naturally short second-to-last syllable, they nonetheless have a long one in terms of sound. Or, as you please, you may use a three-syllable word for *Anima* and a two-syllable word for *mea*, all of which has already been explained above.

## CHAPTER V.

->On Poetic, Metrical, and Rhythmic Music-making, which is to be constructed<-
->by common simple counterpoint or by an equal<-
->progression of voices.<-

The second collection of <term>melothetic</term> <note>relating to the composition of melody.</note> tables contains Musarithms applied to meters of every kind. Thus, in this place, we shall treat the whole of poetic music, as far as possible, <term>universally</term> <note>original Greek: "καθ' ὅλα"</note>; so that there may be no nation in the world that cannot construct harmonies of every kind (even if they are unskilled in music) over any verses constructed in their native language. I do this all the more gladly because, not long ago, this was urgently requested of me by the Syrians and Arabs, as well as by our Fathers in India and others from various provinces; additionally, I know of no one who has provided this until now. For since masters who know the melothetic art are not always found in every place, yet songs are frequently necessary—whether to stir the devotion of men, for theatrical uses, or even for private recreation—I judged that I would be doing something worthwhile if I handed down in this place a method by which all peoples could compose for themselves any harmonies, adorned with any level of artifice, over any verses constructed in their native language. This could be brought to effect by no better means than through "poetic music-making," which, since it [concerns] a speech or a certain arrangement of words...

<meta>The word "con-" at the end of the page is a catchword for "contextum" (context/arrangement) on the following page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for Book VIII of Athanasius Kircher’s "Musurgia Universalis," specifically the "Miraculous Art of Music-Making" (Musurgia Mirifica). # Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music-Making.

The text should not be composed in a wandering or loose style, but should be bound and constrained by a certain metrical rule under a fixed number of syllables and feet. These meters can be applied to all languages; certainly, this provides us with a great shortcut to reaching our goal. But, leaving aside wordy diversions, let us proceed to the matter itself, beginning with Latin verses.

Just as a body arises from various limbs, a painting from various colors, and harmony from diverse voices, so too are verses, meters, or rhythms born from various feet. Thus, a verse is nothing other than speech bound by a certain type and order of feet. Some have categorized these into nine species; some twenty-four; others more or fewer. Each of these is discussed at length in the second part of this book. We, leaving aside these quarrels of the "poetasters" <note>A dismissive term for inferior or pedantic poets.</note>, will adopt those types of meters that seem to have more energy for exciting the affections of the soul and more fitness for musical numbers. Proceeding in a natural order, we shall apply "Musarithms" <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical units of music used in his system.</note> appropriate to each through tables, ranging from the smallest verses to the largest. In this way, given any verse, the <term>Pinax</term> <note>original: "pinax"; a Greek-derived word for a table or chart.</note> containing the Musarithms for that verse can be found immediately. However, since usually not just one verse or stanza is used, but many are piled together, we shall divide all types of verses into <term>tetrastrophs</term> <note>original: "tetrastropha"; a set of four poetic lines or stanzas.</note> so that the novice may proceed with greater ease in the art of <term>Musurgia</term> <note>The "art of making music."</note>.

## Proposition I.

->*Given Adonic meters and a specific tone, to compose a musical setting in any of an infinite variety.*<-

Let the given four-line Adonic meter be as follows:

### Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music

**Eighthly**, take for the **Bass** the fourth numerical series of the first Musarithm, **87651**, and see to which letters in the column of keys it responds; you will find **FEDCF**. Therefore, mark as many points in the distinct spaces and locations that correspond to the keys on the Bass staff; and you will have the determined locations for the bass, as is evident in the preceding diagram.

**Ninthly**, once the points are placed, you will set the notes above them according to the following method: take any series of notes at the bottom of the column and apply individual notes to individual points, so that all notes in each of the four staves corresponding to a single syllable are of the same value; and the first harmonic strophe <note>A "strophe" here refers to a poetic stanza or a musical section corresponding to a verse.</note> will appear, as is evident in the diagram above.

**Tenthly**, you will complete the remaining strophes by exactly the same reasoning and method by which we completed the first. For no different way of working can occur in them. Thus, given an **Adonic tetrastrophic** meter <note>A poetic meter consisting of four-line stanzas of Adonic verse (typically a dactyl followed by a spondee).</note> and a specific tone, we have assigned a musical setting, which was what was to be done. <note>original: "quod erat faciendum"; a common phrase in logic and mathematics signifying the completion of a prescribed task.</note>

## *Notes on the completed procedure.*

Note **firstly**, that in metric compositions of this kind, exactly the same cautions and rules must be observed as those we handed down in the preceding ten canons. You ought to master these perfectly so that you may progress more successfully in the business; thus, if any difficulty should occur, you may be able to deliberate on what should be done. For in those ten canons, we have resolved whatever difficulty can occur in the whole of <term>Musurgia</term> <note>Kircher's term for the entire practice and theory of music-making.</note>. However, in the following proposition, we will assign some particular rules by which whatever has been omitted here will be abundantly compensated.

Note **secondly**, that Musarithms of this kind can be accommodated to any tones, except those which do not admit them because of a <term>tritone</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones, historically avoided as dissonant.</note> or a <term>semidiapente</term> <note>A diminished fifth.</note>.

Note **thirdly**, that the positions of accidental signs must be observed; for without these, an error could easily happen.

Note **fourthly**, that either through the application of a single Musarithm to various tones, the same effect is produced as through four different Musarithms accommodated to different strophes.

Note **fifthly**, that to introduce mixtures of tones more skillfully in the second and third strophe, the natural order of the columns must be kept; so that the first column corresponds to the first strophe, the second to the second, the third to the third, and the fourth to the fourth. In this way, every error in the mixing of tones will be avoided, and the song, constituted by a natural progression, will strike the ears more sweetly. All of these things must be observed with the greatest zeal.

# Of the Great Art of the Consonant and Dissonant
<meta>translator's note: PINAX refers to an engraved plate or table</meta>

Having prepared the musical grid <term>phonotactico systemate: Kircher’s term for a system of musical notation where numbers are mapped onto a staff</term> and having marked off as many spaces as there are syllables for each, you shall begin the composition as follows:

First, you will work out the <term>Musarithm: a set of numbers representing musical intervals</term> for the first stanza, then the others in order. Look, therefore, to which letters in the column of keys the first series of numbers of the first Musarithm—123423—corresponds, and you will find GABCAB. Find the locations of these letters on the five-line staff <note>original: "pentagrammo"</note> for the Cantus <note>the Soprano or highest voice</note>, and mark the points there. Next, see which letters in the column of keys the second series of numbers in the first Musarithm—578878—corresponds to, and you will find DFG GFG. Find the locations of these letters on the staff for the Altus, and mark the points there. Third, see which letters the third series of numbers—321155—corresponds to in the same Musarithm, and you will find it corresponds to BAGGDD. Find the locations of these letters on the staff for the Tenor, and mark the points there. Fourth, see which letters in the column of keys the Musarithm for the Bass—876458—corresponds to; you will find GFECDG. Diligently note the locations of these letters on the staff for the Bass, and mark the points there. Once these are marked, take any series of rhythmic values <note>original: "notarum metrometrarum," referring to the note lengths or meters</note> (which you will find at the bottom of the columns) and apply that one and the same series to each of the four voices—specifically, above the points marked on each staff. For these points show the spaces in which the notes corresponding to the numbers and points ought to be placed, and you will have the first stanza composed. You will work out the remaining stanzas in order by exactly the same method. Thus, given a four-stanza Euripidean Iambic and given the requested tone, we have composed the given melody, which was the task to be done.

---

## Six Notes on Table IV.

I. To ensure the melody of the stanzas is held more purely, the Musarithms should be selected from the columns of stanzas arranged in their natural order. We advise this so that Musarithms extracted from here and there without any selection do not provide certain sequences that might flow with a less sweet melody. For this reason, we have provided that Musarithms drawn in their natural order always exhibit a perfect harmony, which consists in an exact mixing of tones. We have advised this above, and it is to be observed in all the tables <note>original: "pinacibus"</note> that follow. I would not want this said as if no harmony results from Musarithms drawn promiscuously; for harmony will always emerge in whatever order you draw them. Rather, it is because those results do not show an effect equal to those drawn from the columns in their natural order. However, if anyone is more practiced in this business, he will also easily achieve his intended effect by drawing them from here and there through the arrangement of the numbers.

II. The locations of sharps (♯) and flats (♭) must be observed with the greatest zeal, according to the precepts handed down in the preceding sections.

III. Even a single Musarithm will suffice for the perfect harmony of four stanzas if, as was said previously, it is applied to different tones—or what is the same thing, to different letters in the column of keys—by means of the transposition rods <note>original: "bacillos transpositorios," likely referring to the physical wooden slats in Kircher's musical composing machine</note>. This must be observed in the meantime: that the last stanza always corresponds to the first in terms of the tone.

IV. You will be able to apply these four aforementioned Musarithms of the stanzas to all the tones described at the head of the columns; this must be observed, however: if in any voice the part becomes too high or too low, you should swap it with another voice, as has been said in the rules <note>original: "canonibus"</note>.

The notation uses square and diamond-shaped notes typical of the 17th century. The melody and harmonies correspond to the numerical Musarithms described in the instructional text above.</note>

## Proposition III.

->Given a four-line stanza of a single meter in Anacreontic verse, to compose any desired harmony upon it.<-

**L**et there be given a double four-line stanza as follows, one in Anacreontic meter properly so-called, and one in Boethian meter.

<margin>Anacreontic <note>A Greek poetic meter often used for light, celebratory verses.</note></margin>
> O three and four times happy
> Cicada, who in the highest
> Greenery of the trees
> Delights to sing so sweetly.
<note>original: "O ter quaterque felix / Cicada, quæ supremis / In arborum viretis / Cantare dulce gaudes"</note>

<margin>Boethian <note>Referring to the meter used by the philosopher Boethius in his "Consolation of Philosophy."</note></margin>
> Every pleasure has this:
> It drives the frantic with stings,
> And like a flight of bees,
> It strikes the heart with its bite.
<note>original: "Habet omnis hoc voluptas / Stimulis agit furentes / Apiumque per volantum / Ferit acta corda morsu."</note>

Whoever desires to compose a harmony upon this meter should proceed as follows. Let the 8th Tone <note>One of the ecclesiastical modes, traditionally known as the Hypomixolydian mode.</note> be given as the form for the song.

II. Let the five-line staves of the <term>phonotactic palimpsest</term> <note>A reusable writing surface or "musical slate" Kircher designed for mechanical composition.</note> be marked with the signature of "hard" song <note>original: "cantus duri," indicating the use of B-natural in the scale.</note> as the eighth tone requires.
III. <term>Musarithms</term>: Mathematical-musical sequences of numbers that represent specific musical intervals or steps within a scale.
<term>Anacreontic</term>: A light, rhythmic poetic meter named after the Greek poet Anacreon.
<term>Musurgia</term>: The art or science of composing music.
<term>Stanza</term>: A grouping of lines in poetry; in this context, it corresponds to a section of the musical composition.
<term>Tone</term>: Also known as a "Mode," referring to the specific scale (such as Dorian or Phrygian) used for the harmony.
<term>Rhythmic Notations</term>: The specific durations assigned to the notes (longs, shorts, etc.).
<term>Tetraphonium / Quadricinium</term>: A musical composition written for four distinct voices or parts.

## Proposition IV.
### Given a four-line stanza <note>original: "Tetrastropho"</note> of a single-meter <note>original: "monocolo"</note> Archilochian Iambic verse, and given a tone, to compose the requested harmony.

Let the following four-line stanza be given, namely a hymn very frequently sung in the Church.

->The banners of the King go forth <note>original: "Vexilla Regis prodeunt"</note><-
->The mystery of the cross shines forth <note>original: "Fulget crucis mysterium"</note><-
->Where life endured death<-
->And by death brought forth life.<-

And let the first tone be given, upon which someone will desire to compose a harmony; he shall proceed as follows.

<margin>
| Of the 1st Tone | |
| :--- | :--- |
| F | 3 |
| E | 2 |
| D | 8 |
| C | ♮ 7 |
| B | ♭ 6 |
| A | 5 |
| G | 4 |
| F | 3 |
</margin>

I. Apply the column of keys <note>the musical pitches</note> to the column of the first tone. Then you will mark the staves for four voices on the compositional slate <term>palimpsesto phonotactico: a reusable surface used with Kircher's music-composing box</term> according to the first tone, which is of a hard character <note>original: "characterismi duri," referring to the "Cantus Durus" system which typically uses B-natural</note>.

II. Take any 4 Musarithms <term>Musarithmos: Kircher’s term for numerical sequences that represent musical intervals or chords</term> from the following Table <note>original: "Pinace"</note>, from which we have selected 4 equal musarithms corresponding to the 4 lines of the stanza.

| I. | II. | III. | IV. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 33334223 | 33282222 | 33287777 | 33388778 |

<note>Four systems of musical notation are set for four voices—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass—using white mensural notation on five-line staves. The music provides a polyphonic setting for the hymn "Vexilla regis prodeunt." ->The banners of the King go forth, The mystery shines forth, etc.<-

Then proceed by marking points on the staff, as was described in the preceding sections; then apply the series of whatever note-values to the points at the base of the columns. We have chosen the triple meter <note>original: "triplam"</note> here, and it produces the sought-after four-line harmony, as appears here; diligently observing that the placement of chromatic signs ♮ and ♭ must be made in appropriate places. How indeed compositions of this kind of song can be varied in infinite ways, we have explained in the rules <note>original: "canonibus"</note>, which you should consult, and in the first proposition of the first table. Meanwhile, I would want you to note with the greatest care what we also advised above in Rule II: if the voices in any tone should descend or rise more than is proper, they must be exchanged among themselves <note>a technique known as voice-crossing</note>, as we have taught extensively in the cited place.

# T A B L E VI.
## Archilochian Iambics of eight syllables with a short penultimate syllable.

<margin>Form of the meter: Come, Holy Ghost, Creator Blest <note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus"</note></margin>

<header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

## Proposition V.
### Given a four-line stanza <term>Tetrastrophon: a poem consisting of four-line stanzas</term> of nine-syllable meter, to complete a musical setting <term>Melothesia: the art or method of composing a melody</term> over it.

Let there be given a four-line stanza of a single type of nine-syllable verse, as follows:

->*Hail, Queen of Angels* <note>original: "Aue Regina Angelorum"</note><-
->*Hail, healing of the peoples* <note>original: "Aue medela populorum"</note><-
->*Greetings, fountain of life, greetings, gate* <note>original: "Salue fons vitæ salue porta"</note><-
->*From whom the light of the world has risen for us.* <note>original: "Ex qua lux mundi nobis orta."</note><-

Now, a harmony is to be composed upon this type of meter, and let the Seventh Tone <note>Tone VII: In the 17th century, this usually refers to the Mixolydian mode</note> be given. Therefore, once the staves of the musical slate <note>palimpsesti: here referring to a reusable writing surface or a template for notation</note> have been set out and marked according to the given tone, select any four-line musical algorithm <term>Musarithm: a set of numbers used to automatically generate musical counterpoint</term> from Table VII <note>original: "Pinace VII"</note>.

| | | I. | II. | III. | IV. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G | 8 | 354365355 | 552354322 | 321234545 | 554315355 |
| F | ♯7 | 886887678 | 882876867 | 8,6486567 | 886887678 |
| E | 6 | 534542123 | 334622545 | 331432522 | 334562123 |

Having selected the musical algorithms, you will apply the column of keys to the column of the Seventh Tone. Then, proceed as we taught in the preceding sections by marking each staff with its points, which you will then "clothe" with notes as before. Since we have used notes of the minor triple time <term>tripla minor: a rhythmic proportion in Baroque music where three notes are played in the time usually allotted to two</term> here, the desired four-voice harmony will result as requested, and it follows below.

<note>The illustration shows four systems of musical notation in white mensural style for four voices (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass). The music is written in triple time, indicated by the numeral '3' at the start of each staff. Each system corresponds to one line of the poetic text. The notes are diamond-shaped, representing semibreves and minims, typical of 17th-century liturgical or academic music printing.</note>

Hail Queen of Angels, Hail healing of the peoples, Greetings, etc.

And you will be able to vary this model again in infinite other ways according to what was said previously; but so that we are not forced to repeat the same things constantly, we refer the Reader to the rules and diagrams. Thus, given the four-line stanza and the tone, we have completed the requested harmony.

# Proposition VI.
## Given a ten-syllable verse, whether Iambic or Dactylic, to construct the requested harmony.

The following Table <note>original: "Pinax"</note> VIII is organized for Alcmanian Iambic trimeter brachycatalectic meters <note>A specific form of Greek and Latin lyric poetry</note>, such as the following verse:

->You despise the maiden’s graceful bridal beds. <note>original: "Spernis decoros Virginis thoros."</note><-

If anyone, therefore, wishes to weave a multifaceted harmony upon such a theme, let them first choose the Musical Algorithms <term>Musarithmos: Kircher's term for the numerical sets representing musical intervals and rhythms</term> according to the nature of the subject; then let them proceed as was stated in the preceding sections, and they will achieve their intent. We shall present here only a single stanza as a model, thus composing upon this theme, for example:

->Great creator of all things. <note>original: "Magnæ creator rerum omnium."</note><-

Then, having applied the column of keys <note>the musical pitches</note> to the column of the sixth tone, proceed according to the rules provided; and the following harmony will emerge.

You may then continue this model through its subsequent stanzas, meanwhile observing the precepts and rules set forth at length in the preceding pages. Given, therefore, etc. Which was to be done.

# Proposition VII.
## Given a three-stanza hendecasyllabic meter, to construct the requested harmony for it.

Let there be given a three-stanza hendecasyllabic verse <note>A verse line consisting of eleven syllables.</note> from Horace, as follows:

> Three measures of aged Falernian wine <note>original: "Ternos vetusti congios falerni"</note>
> The bold ruler and arbiter of Kings <note>original: "Hausit potentum Romuli nepotum"</note>
> Drained, for the powerful descendants of Romulus. <note>original: "Regnator audax, arbiterque Regum." This is a quote from Horace's Odes, 3.19.13-15.</note>

Prepare the musical tablet <term>phonotacticum palimpsestum: a physical device or grid used for mechanical composition</term> and the five-line staff <note>original: "pentagráma"</note> with its clefs, and adapt it to the scale according to the given mode (which, for example, shall be the second mode). Apply column to the column of the mode, and then extract any <term>Musarithmos: numerical sequences that represent musical intervals and rhythms</term> in order from the following Table 3. Then operate according to the rules already given, and the sought-after harmony will emerge.

| I. | I I. | I I I. |

The musical lines correspond directly to the numerical "musical numbers" provided in the table above, demonstrating how the numbers are translated into melody and harmony.</note>

->Three measures of aged Falernian, etc.<-

By what method this paradigm can be varied infinitely, you will perceive from the rules handed down in the preceding sections; likewise, you will see how, given one set of musical numbers, you may vary it through a mixture of modes. You will also perceive when and where the sharp signs [♯] are to be placed. You see, therefore, how from a given hendecasyllabic meter, the desired harmony results. The same follows if given a four-stanza hendecasyllabic verse, etc. Which was the thing to be done.

## Proposition VIII.
### Given a Sapphic poem of three stanzas and two meters, to animate it into harmony.

**I**n the following Table [Pinax], we have arranged Sapphic Musical-Numbers [Musarithms]. The first three columns contain the three-stanza structure. In the fourth column, the Adonic Musical-Numbers are contained, because Adonic lines <note>An Adonic line is a short poetic line consisting of five syllables, traditionally used to conclude a Sapphic stanza.</note> are always usually added after three Sapphic lines.

If, therefore, anyone should wish to compose in this genre of meter—which of all is the most suitable for musicians—he will work no differently than has been done up to now. But let us clarify the matter with a single example.

Let the theme of the musical composition <term>Melothesia: The art of setting text to music</term> be that most famous and celebrated Sapphic triple-stanza, double-meter hymn, usually sung on the feast of Saint John the Baptist:

| Tone II <note>The Second Mode, a specific scale or "key" in early music theory.</note> | |
|---|---|
| G | 8 |
| F | ♯ 7 |
| E | ♭ 6 |
| D | 5 |
| C | 4 |
| B | 3 |
| A | 2 |
| G | 1 |

> So that your servants may resonate with loosened vocal cords <note>original: "fibris" (fibers). This refers to the throat or vocal cords.</note>
> the wonders of your deeds,
> wash away the guilt from our polluted lips,
> Saint John. <note>original: "Ut queant laxis resonare fibris / Mira gestorum famuli tuorum / Solve polluti labii reatum / Sancte Ioannes." This hymn is historically significant because the starting note of each phrase provided the names for the musical notes: Ut (Do), Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</note>

Therefore, once the parchment <note>original: "palimpsesto," meaning a writing surface.</note> has been prepared and the five-line staves <note>original: "pentagrammis."</note> for the voices have been marked, select from the following table any three Musical-Numbers along with an Adonic number. You will then animate these into harmony by applying the column of keys to the column of the chosen tone (which here is the second tone), working according to the precepts and rules handed down. The following harmony of voices will come forth:

| I. | II. | III. | Adonic. |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 55122222171 | 313171125445 | 54323117123 | 34123 |
| 88877777555 | 887655577877 | 77555665355 | 55455 |
| 33355444323 | 565423343323 | 32177442171 | 32171 |
| 88655777851 | 863458875673 | 37853445651 | 86651 |

<note>A four-voice musical score for Canto (Soprano), Alto, Tenore, and Basso is set to the text "Iste Confessor Domini sacratus" (This confessor of the Lord, consecrated). The music is written in rhombic choral notation—diamond-shaped notes common in the Renaissance and Baroque periods—on four separate five-line staves. Vertical bar lines mark the phrases of the hymn.</note>

->This confessor of the Lord, consecrated<-

With similar industry, you will be able to vary this single example in infinite ways; but concerning these, read the Canons and rules handed down above. However, I would have you note in this place that the preceding table and this one can be used interchangeably for Sapphic verses; for the Musical-Numbers of both can be adapted to either Sapphic or Phaleucian meters. Given therefore, etc., which was to be done.

Each cell contains four rows of rhythmic indicators for four musical voices—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass. <header>Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.</header>

# Proposition IX.

->Given any Asclepiadean strophe, to construct a skillful<-
->harmony upon it.<-

Let the theme of the meter be that well-known Asclepiadean verse of Horace:
->*Maecenas, descended from ancient kings, etc.*<- <note>original: "Mecænas atauis edite Regibus &c."; the opening line of Horace’s Odes, Book 1, Ode 1.</note>
Should you wish to adorn it with harmonic melodies, proceed as follows: Extract from any of the following tables <note>original: "pinace," from the Greek word for a board or tablet</note> the musarithms for the strophes. Then, having applied the column of keys to the column of the tone which you have assumed for your theme, work according to the precepts and rules already handed down; and you will have achieved your goal. We provide an example here; the rest we leave to the industry and practice of the novice <term>melothete</term> <note>Melothete: A term used by Kircher for a composer or "melody-setter."</note>.

And these are the things which I thought should be briefly explained concerning the practice of the musical charts or tables. In these, once the industrious novice has exercised himself a little, I do not doubt that he will complete any compositions assigned to him with the greatest ease and almost no effort; for nothing else is required here but continuous practice. I advise, however, that he most diligently weigh those things which we handed down at length in the beginning concerning the requirements for this art. Let him also first make himself familiar with the canons as well as the rules of poetic music. Instructed in these, nothing in simple counterpoint will be so hidden that, as I said, he will not penetrate it with easy effort.

Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

# Rules for Poetic Music-making.

Lest we be forced to repeat the same things constantly, we shall set down here certain rules to guide us in <term>melothetic<note>The art of setting words to melody or the practice of musical composition.</note></term> operations, so that we may more easily avoid the "rocky shoals" of difficulties that may arise.

**Rule One.** Since poetic music-making proceeds through <term>polystrophic periods<note>Musical structures consisting of multiple stanzas or strophes.</note></term>, it must first be noted that these harmonic numbers of the bass, 5. 1. or 5. 8., whenever they occur applied to the same tone, always produce the same result. For example: in the sixth tone, they always signify a cadence from C to F; in the second tone, a cadence from D to G; and so on for the rest. Therefore, so that the same sound and tone are not always perceived, the <term>Novice Melotheta<note>A beginner composer using Kircher's system.</note></term> should seek other harmonic numbers among the <term>musarithms<note>original: "Musarithmos"; these are the numerical sequences in Kircher's tables that represent musical intervals and rhythms.</note></term> of the bass besides those mentioned—such as 2. 5., or 7. 3., or 6. 5., or whatever others occur. He can always use these for the second or third strophe. The first and last strophe, however, must always maintain the tone assumed at the beginning, so that a much greater variety may be perceived in the harmonic modulations. We gave an example of this in the preceding composition, where you see that in the 2nd and 3rd musarithms of the bass, the final notes are different from the notes of the first and last musarithm. From this, a harmony of a different tone is consequently born, as was said. For the first strophe has the form of the second tone, the second strophe has the form of the ninth tone, the third strophe the form of the fifth tone, and finally, the fourth strophe reflects back to the second tone assumed at the beginning.

<margin>A quick method for changing tones.</margin>
This rule must therefore be observed most diligently. If one were to always take the same harmonic numbers for the second tone, he would always produce the same tone; although this is permitted, it is not as pleasing to the ears as when a mixture of various tones intervenes, as we also taught above in the sixth canon. If, however, one cannot find different numbers, he should use the easiest practice of all, indicated in the sixth canon: namely, by moving the column of the assumed tone (placed next to the **column of keys**) one degree, or two, or four, or five degrees higher. The musarithms will immediately transition into the form of another tone. This is the most efficient method of all for mixing tones. It is so apt and convenient for establishing any variety that even a single fixed musarithm—through the application of the four-fold column of numbers to different degrees of the moved column of keys—will always emerge as four different harmonic strophes.

For example, let the musarithm of the bass brought forward a little earlier be 8 7 6 4 5 1. To show this same musarithm in four strophes through a varied mixture of tones, proceed as follows: apply the last number of the musarithm, 1 or 8, above the assumed tone (the second tone, or what is the same thing, above G), and the harmonic composition of the first strophe of the second tone will result. Again, apply the first or eighth number (the last of the first bass musarithm) above D in the column of keys, and the second strophe composed upon the ninth tone will result. Then, let the same number be applied above B from the composition of numbers made; the third strophe composed upon the fifth tone will result. Finally, let the first or eighth number in the column of numbers be applied above G as in the beginning, and the final strophe of the second tone will result again—all while most diligently observing these two rules.

**Rule Two.** Whenever the song is <term>durus<note>Literally "hard"; in this context, music using the "natural" or "hexachordum durum" (often associated with B-naturals or a lack of flats).</note></term>, the first or eighth number should never be placed above B or above F, and only rarely above E, and then only with great skill. You may, however, move them above all other letters.

**Rule Three.** Whenever the song is <term>mollis<note>Literally "soft"; music using the "hexachordum molle" (associated with B-flats).</note></term>, the first or eighth number should never be applied to the letters A or E; they may be applied to all others with impunity.

**Rule Four.** Regarding the placement of chromatic signs (flat, natural, sharp), see what we have said at length in the ninth Canon, the rule of the preceding chapter, and above in section IV concerning the placement of these same figures. But so that you are not always forced to consult the said rules, we will place others here that are much shorter.

Whenever the numbers 5. 1. (or what is the same, 5. 8.) correspond in the column of keys...

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "uium," which completes the word "clauium" (keys) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Kircher explains how to create musical variety using his numerical system by shifting "musarithms" across different musical modes (tones) for different stanzas of a poem. He provides specific constraints on which notes can serve as the foundation for a composition depending on whether the music is in a "hard" or "soft" key signature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for using the musarithm tables, focusing on the application of accidentals (sharps and flats) and how to adapt musical patterns to different poetic meters.</meta>

Book VIII. The Wondrous Music-making.

...letters C, F, or G, C, or F, B, whether it be in the <term>hard song<note>Latin: "cantus durus"; music using B-natural, typically associated with the hexachord starting on G.</note></term> or <term>soft song<note>Latin: "cantus mollis"; music using B-flat, typically associated with the hexachord starting on F.</note></term>, then the key or letter that corresponds to the seventh number in the column of numbers should never be marked with a sharp (#).

Whenever, however, the numbers 5, 1, or 5, 8 of the <term>musarithm<note>The numerical sequences in Kircher's tables that represent musical intervals and rhythms.</note></term> bass correspond to the letters D-G, E-A, or A-D in the column of keys, then the letter corresponding to the seventh number rightfully requires the sharp sign (#). This applies if the note following the one marked with this sign rises immediately, or if it is the final note; however, if the note immediately following descends, the sharp is to be omitted. We have demonstrated the reasoning for all of these rules at length in the preceding book.

Furthermore, whenever in a soft song the numbers 5, 1 fall on D-G, then the letter corresponding to the 6th number will almost always be <term>B-flat<note>original: "b molle"</note></term>; that is, a flat (b) must always be placed before the notes on the B string. If, however, it is a hard song and the numbers 5, 1 fall on A-D, then likewise the letter corresponding to the 6th will ordinarily be B, or rather, the notes to be placed on the B string must be marked with a flat (b), namely in the 2nd and 1st tones. If you observe these rules, you will produce a harmony subject to no defect whatsoever.

<margin>Corollary I.</margin>
From these points it follows, first: that individual four-voiced musarithms, varied four times through the mixing of tones according to the rules provided, produce a harmony for four stanzas that is perfect in every respect. For although the intervals of the notes remain the same in each stanza, they are essentially changed by the diversity of the tones, presenting a most pleasing harmony to the ears. This would not happen if musarithms of different intervals were applied to only one tone. Such is the power in the diversity of tones.

**The fifth rule, concerning the change from one meter to another.** It also follows by what method an <term>Euripidean Iambic Catalectic<note>A type of verse meter that is "catalectic," meaning it lacks a final syllable or is incomplete in its last foot.</note></term> may become <term>Hypercatalectic<note>A verse that has an extra syllable at the end beyond the regular meter.</note></term>.
An Euripidean Iambic hypercatalectic is that which has one redundant syllable at the end, as appears in the following four-line stanza.

->Hail, Virgin of Virgins<-
->Hail, Life of the heavenly ones<-
->Hail, Light of the celestial ones<-
->One Hope of the earthly ones<-
<note>original Latin: "Aue Virgo Virginum / Aue vita cælitum / Aue lux cælestium / Vna spes terrestrium"</note>

Whoever, therefore, desires to transfer the musarithms of this meter into a particular table, shall perform nothing else but double the penultimate number in all the musarithms of Table IV adapted for Euripidean Iambics; that is, he should place the given number twice. He will then have a particular table of musarithms adapted for the hypercatalectic iambic. For example, let the musarithm of the first stanza of Table IV be as follows:

| Type | Text/Instruction | Musarithm |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Catalectic** | Hail, star of the sea | 5 5 5 5 5 5 |
| | <note>Six musical notes (specifically quarter notes or crotchets) are shown here to illustrate the rhythmic values.</note> | 3 3 3 2 2 3 |
| | Hail, Virgin of Virgins | 8 8 8 5 5 1 |
| **Hypercatalectic** | From the catalectic comes the hypercatalectic by doubling the penultimate numbers at the end of each Musarithm as follows: | 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 |
| | | 3 3 3 2 2 2 3 |
| | | 8 8 8 5 5 5 1 |

In the same way, you will either double the penultimate of the metrical notes in each series, or split the penultimate into two equivalent notes. You will then have metrical notes also adapted to the hypercatalectic iambic, as can be seen in the preceding example of notes.

<margin>Corollary II.</margin>
From this, it is also clear that a catalectic iambic composition composed a little earlier can be changed entirely into a hypercatalectic one with very little effort; if the penultimate note of each stanza is divided into two notes which, taken together, are equivalent to the said penultimate.

<margin>Corollary III.</margin>
Finally, it is clear from this how one and the same musarithm can be adapted to different meters with very little effort, solely by the division of the initial or final note into two similar equivalent divisions. And I have thought these things especially worth noting before I proceed further, so that the <term>Novice Melotheta<note>A beginner in the art of setting words to melody.</note></term>, being instructed, might more readily prepare himself for practice in all things. Many things were to be said in this place concerning the multiplication of musarithms and the nearly infinite variety of combinations; but because we have handed all these down at length in the ten canons of the preceding chapter, we therefore refer the reader to them. For whatever we said there can also be adapted to this poetic music-making. Therefore, let us move to other matters.

# A P P E N D I X

## On Poetic or Rhythmic Music-making

Hitherto we have treated "monocolon" poetic music-making—that is, the method by which we can animate any single, uniform type of meter with musical melodies through diligent effort. Now, however, we must demonstrate the method and industry by which "heterogeneous" meters of different kinds joined together (which writers of prosody call <term>dicolon<note>A stanza consisting of two types of meter.</note></term> from the mixture of two different verses; <term>tricolon<note>A stanza of three types of meter.</note></term> from three; or <term>tetracolon<note>A stanza of four types of meter.</note></term> from a mixture of four different verses) may be converted for the sake of establishing a greater variety of musical operations. We shall settle the entire business with a few syntheses.

**Synthesis I.** If, therefore, you apply the <term>musarithms<note>Kircher's term for the numerical sequences representing musical intervals and rhythms.</note></term> from column I of <term>Table<note>Latin: "Pinax"; Kircher uses this term for the large charts or grids of numbers used in his combinatorial music system.</note></term> I to the musarithms of column I of Table III, you will have the musarithms for the Pherecratic meter, such as the following:

> Under a pleasant grotto, Pyrrha
> The seas with black winds
> He hopes for, ignorant of the breeze.
> <note>original: "Grato Pyrrha sub antro / Nigris æquora ventis / Sperat nescius auræ." These are snippets from Horace's Odes.</note>

**Synthesis II.** If you place Column I (the Adonic column) of Table III twice, you will have the musarithms for Anapestic meters, as follows:

> Gird the brows of poets with laurel.
> <note>original: "Cingite vates tempora lauro."</note>

**Synthesis III.** If you duplicate the second Dactylic Column of Table III—that is, if you place it twice—you will have the musarithms for the Choriambic Asclepiadean meter, as follows:

> But if you insert me among the lyric bards,
> I shall strike the stars with my sublime head.
> <note>original: "Quod si me Lyricis vatibus inseris / Sublimi feriam sydera vertice." From Horace, Odes 1.1.</note>

**Synthesis IV.** If you join the first column of Table I to the second Dactylic column of Table III, you will have the musarithms for the Glyconic meter, as follows:

> Breathing the heavens with voices,
> Pegasus takes on wings.
> <note>original: "Spirans Æthera vocibus / Alas pegasus induit."</note>

**Synthesis V.** If you join the first and second columns of Table III together, you will have the Dactylic Alcmanic or Horatian meter, as follows:

> You see how Soracte stands white with deep snow,
> and the woods no longer sustain the burden.
> <note>original: "Vides vt alta stet niue candidum / Soracte, nec iam sustineant onus." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

**Synthesis VI.** If you prefix the first column of Table I to one of the columns of Table V, you will have the musarithms for that Iambic meter, specifically for the third verse of a Horatian Ode:

> The woods laboring with frost.
> <note>original: "Syluæ laborantes geluque." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

**Synthesis VII.** If you prefix the first column of Table I to one of the columns of Table VI, the musarithms for the Alcmanic Iambic meter will be produced, as follows:

> You scorn the honorable marriage bed of the Virgin.
> <note>original: "Spernis decoros Virginis thoros."</note>

**Synthesis VIII.** If you place a column from Table V after one of the trisyllabic columns of Table I, you will have the musarithms for Sapphic and Phaleucian hendecasyllables, as follows:

> Slower than lethargy and resin.
> <note>original: "Veterno resinaque pigriores."</note>

**Synthesis IX.** If you prefix the fourth column of pentasyllables from Table I to the column of Dactylics from Table III, you will have the musarithms for Horatian meters such as those that follow:

> I hate the uninitiated crowd and keep them away.
> <note>original: "Odi profanum vulgus & arceo." From Horace, Odes 3.1.</note>

**Synthesis X.** If you place two columns of Table V, or two columns of heptasyllables from Table II together, you will have the musarithms for a dactylic pentameter.

> Dreadful with its gushing mouth, Avernus boils with waters.
> <note>original: "Horridus ore scatens feruet Auernus aquis."</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for Kircher’s "Musurgia Mirifica" (Wondrous Music-making), specifically focusing on how to use his combinatorial tables (Pinaces) to set complex, multi-metered classical poetry to music.
