Book VIII. The Wondrous Art of Music-making.

And by this practice of joining columns to columns, more and more diverse types of meters will be born. For example, from the first and second <term>tables<note>Kircher uses the Greek-derived word "Pinax" for his large grids of musical data.</note></term>, in which we described polysyllabic <term>musarithms<note>Musarithms are the core of Kircher's system: sequences of numbers that represent specific musical intervals and rhythms, allowing a non-composer to "calculate" a melody.</note></term>, every kind of meter will arise through various combinations. Just as this combination expands almost into infinity, so it also looks toward an infinite variety of meters. Indeed, the columns of the first and second tables, when combined with the columns of poetic metrics, will again give birth to an innumerable offspring of harmonic variety. From this, the reader may understand the immense vastness of our craft.

You will have <term>polycola<note>From the Greek for "many limbs"; poems where the individual lines follow different rhythmic patterns.</note></term>, whether meters of different members or heterogeneous Odes, if you join different columns from different tables. For example, if someone wanted to compose a harmony for that famous Ode of Horace:

->You see how Mount Soracte stands white with deep snow;<-
->nor can the laboring woods now bear the burden;<-
->and the rivers have stood still<-
->with sharp frost.<-
<note>original: "Vides ut alta stet nive candidum / Soracte; nec iam sustineant onus / Sylvæ laborantes; geluque / Flumina constiterint acuto." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

He will work in this way: join the first and second columns of Table III twice; to these, add one of the columns from Table VI; then one second column from Table II; and finally, one from the columns of Table V. You will then have the musarithms arranged for the given Ode.

In the same way, you will perform other syntheses. Moreover, "polycola" odes can be categorized as "pure" or "not pure." Pure odes are those which have every single verse heterogeneous (each line is a different meter). For example, if someone attached an Archilochian Iambic to an Iambic-Euripidean Anacreontic, and finally an Adonic to that, he would have a <term>tetrastrophon tetracolon<note>A four-line stanza where every line is a different type of meter.</note></term>. Odes are called "not pure" when meters of one kind are used twice, thrice, or four times, and then another meter of a different kind is added. This happens in the Horatian Odes, where the first two meters are of the same kind, but the following two are of a different kind; hence it is called a <term>tetrastrophon tricolon<note>A four-line stanza using three different types of meter.</note></term>, as is clear in the Ode cited just above. Similarly, in Sapphic verses, three verses of the same kind are followed by an Adonic of a different kind, which is why it is called a <term>tetrastrophon dicolon<note>A four-line stanza using two different types of meter.</note></term>.

The same principles apply to all parts of our Poetic Music; for if someone takes one of the four-line columns of Table IV, which contains the Euripidean musarithms, and to this adds another from Table V, and to this another from Table VI, and finally attaches the first column of Table III, he would have the musarithms for a "tetrastrophon tetracolon," arranged in order, where each individual meter is of a different kind. The first would be Euripidean Iambic, the second Anacreontic, the third Archilochian, and the fourth Adonic.

From all this, if I am not mistaken, it is very clear that an infinite power and force shine forth in the mutual combination of different columns. Truly, all these things will be demonstrated more fully both in the following pages and in our "Combinatorial Art," if God grants us life.

## On Hexameter and Pentameter Verses.

The Hexameter or Heroic meter consists of six "feet," of which the fifth is always a <term>dactyl<note>A metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones.</note></term>, and the rest are either dactyls or <term>spondees<note>A metrical foot consisting of two long syllables.</note></term>. The Pentameter, however, consists of five feet, all of which are dactyls, spondees, <term>trochees<note>Latin: "Choraei"; a foot with one long and one short syllable.</note></term>, or <term>pyrrhics<note>A foot with two short syllables.</note></term>. However, since this type of meter is inconsistent due to the great variety it allows, and does not hold the feet fixed in a certain place, we reject it as less suitable for music. Yet if someone wished to construct a <term>symphony<note>Here meaning a harmonious multi-part composition.</note></term> upon such types of meters, he will easily obtain his aim if he arranges the musarithms of the first and second Tables according to the feet of the meter. For example, if someone were laboring over this couplet:

->All human things hang by a slender thread<-
->And those which were strong fall by a sudden accident.<-
<note>original: "Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo / Et subito casu quæ valuere ruunt." A famous distich by Ovid.</note>

If, I say, he wanted to compose a four-part piece over these verses, he would extract the musarithms from the columns of Tables I and II according to the feet of each verse. For the foot [omnia], take Column II of Table II; for this has polysyllables with short penultimates; for the other foot [sunt...

[...are of men] take column III of the same <term>Table<note>original: "Pinacis". Kircher uses the Greek term "Pinax" for his large data grids.</note></term>. For the word [slight] take again column II of Table II. For [hanging] use column III of Table II. Finally, for [thread], use the first column of Table I or II. By coordinating the columns with this diligence, you will be able to select any transverse series of <term>Musarithms<note>Musarithms are Kircher's specific numerical sequences that represent musical intervals and rhythms, allowing a non-musician to calculate a melody.</note></term> for the desired <term>musical setting<note>original: "Melothesia"; the art of setting text to music.</note></term>; and then operate exactly as we prescribed in the preceding sections. A hexameter adorned with musical measures will emerge, just as you requested. By exactly the same reasoning, you will complete a Pentameter, for the method of operation is the same in all things.

### Corollary.

From these things it is clear that the columns of the first and second Tables can serve both prose and verse. Indeed, given any theme of words—whether in verse or prose—the poetic feet of the given theme will always be assigned within the polysyllabic columns.

# CHAPTER VI.

## Explanation of the second collection, or flowery and ingenious metric music-making.

What "florid counterpoint" is was sufficiently demonstrated at the beginning of the preceding sixth book. Since we have so far handed down the method of simple counterpoint in our metric music-making, in this Chapter we will show the way by which anyone—even one unskilled in Music—can complete a musical setting imposed upon them, not only with simple counterpoint, but also by what means they might adorn their songs with an ingenious and florid style. We do this so that professional Musicians cannot object that we have only handed down the most basic principles of the art of composition. 

We call this "florid and ingenious music-making" because in it, the flow of the voices does not proceed by "point against point" and "note against note" in equal steps, as has been shown until now. Rather, the harmony is depicted as if with certain colors by various "diminutions" <note>In the Baroque period, "diminution" refers to breaking a long note into many faster, decorative notes.</note> of different voices, and a specific concord of consonant and dissonant notes, which can soothe the ears of listeners with singular grace and pleasure. For this effect, we have provided six Musarithmetic Tables.

**The First Table** contains florid and ingenious Musarithms for Adonic and Dactylic six-syllable meters.

**The Second Table** contains Musarithms for Euripidean Iambics.

**The Third Table** contains florid and ingenious Musarithms for Anacreontic seven-syllable meters.

**The Fourth Table** contains florid and ingenious Musarithms for Archilochian Iambic meters.

**The Fifth Table** contains florid and ingenious Musarithms for nine-syllable and ten-syllable meters.

**The Sixth Table** contains florid and ingenious Musarithms for Sapphic and any eleven-syllable <note>original: "hendecasyllabis"</note> meters.

Behold, in these six Tables we present to you unique Musarithms, containing harmonious, clear, and most suitable symphonies for the Church.

The rhythmic notes <note>original: "Notę Metrometrę"; markers of time and duration.</note> are specific to each individual voice of the Musarithm. In this, they differ from the rhythmic notes handed down in the First Collection; there, out of twelve series of rhythmic notes, one set was sufficient as a common standard for all four voices. Here, however, the voice of each individual Musarithm claims for itself its own specific series of notes, which must not be changed. For they are so connected with the numbers that they neither can nor should be separated from one another. Hence, for however many numbers there are in any one Musarithm, it is necessary to find just as many notes in the corresponding series of notes. 

Otherwise, the method of operating—and of expressing the Musarithmetic numbers through harmonic measures—differs in no way at all from the method handed down in the preceding Collection. Indeed, I am confident that beginner composers will find the operation in these tables much easier than in the earlier ones. However, having briefly explained these things, let us now finally clarify the whole business with some examples.

# Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music.

### Proposition I.

#### Given an Euripidean Iambic meter <note>A marginal sign in the original manuscript marks the specific rhythmic structure of this meter.</note> in the first tone, to compose a musical setting <term>Melothesia<note>The art or process of composing a melody or a musical setting for a text.</note></term> for it in the florid style.

**Y**ou will carry out this proposition through double, simple, and mixed operations, just as was done in the preceding section. Indeed, you can establish a simple operation either by using a single <term>Musarithm<note>A numerical sequence used in Kircher's system to represent musical intervals and pitches, allowing even those without musical training to generate melodies.</note></term> corresponding to one strophe of the verse, which is then repeated through a change of tones to assign the musical setting, as we showed in the first operation previously. Alternatively, you may use several Musarithms, provided that the "base" Musarithm has its last two numbers different from 5 and 1, or 5 and 8, as has been stated; ensure the tone of the first and fourth strophe is the same, and you will achieve what is sought. However, let us provide a varied example, so that we are not always compelled to give an example of the double operation.

Therefore, let us suppose we must complete a musical setting in the florid style for an Euripidean Meter, such as the hymn *Ave Maris Stella* <note>original: "Ave Maris Stella"; a famous plainchant hymn to the Virgin Mary, "Hail, Star of the Sea."</note> and so on. Let Musarithms of various tones be selected, specifically those we mentioned whose final numbers in the base sequence are different from 5 1 or 5 8. If such sequences are not found, a single Musarithm may be repeated across different tones.

## Proposition II.

### To complete a musical setting <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note> imposed upon a given Anacreontic meter and the second tone in the florid style.

Table III <note>original: "Pinax III"</note> follows for arranging Anacreontic meters in the florid style; in this table, you must observe the exact same instructions as in the preceding one. Suppose, therefore, that a musical setting is to be established for some three-stanza verse <note>original: "tristrophon"</note> of this meter. Having extracted any Musarithms <note>Kircher's term for numerical sequences that represent musical motifs</note> as we have taught, together with the musical notes assigned to each Musarithm, you shall establish either a simple or a mixed operation. 

A mixed operation can be established through simple Musarithms extracted from Table IV of the Anacreontics in the preceding section <note>original: "syntagmatis"</note>, which are then aptly inserted among the florid Musarithms of this table. Finally, we advise you to diligently follow the rules handed down in the previous sections so that you may at last reach the proposed goal. But let us provide an example for a better clarification of the matter.

# Proposition III.

->Given an Iambic Archilochian meter and any tone, to provide a desired musical composition arranged in the Florid style.<- <note>"Melothesia" refers to the art of composing a melody or musical setting; the "Florid style" is a decorative, polyphonic style of composition.</note>

The following Table <note>original: "Pinax"</note> corresponds to Iambic Archilochian meters and contains Musarithms <note>Kircher's technical term for numerical sequences used to generate musical intervals and rhythms</note> adapted to the florid style. Therefore, anyone whose intention it is to compose songs for this genre of meter may here animate the extracted Musarithms into harmony according to the number of stanzas <note>original: "stropharum"</note>, using either a simple or mixed operation by applying the rules and canons prescribed in the preceding sections.

This genre of meter is most suitable for harmonic measures <note>original: "harmonicis modulis"</note> and is frequently encountered in the Roman Breviary <note>The liturgical book containing the daily prayers, psalms, and hymns of the Catholic Church</note>; indeed, nearly all hymns consist of this poetic meter. For example: *Already the star of light has risen* <note>original: "Iam Lucis orto sidere"</note>; *Christ, Redeemer of all* <note>original: "Christe Redemptor omnium"</note>; *Sweet Creator of the stars* <note>original: "Creator alme siderum"</note>; *The banners of the King go forth* <note>original: "Vexilla Regis prodeunt"</note>; and other similar examples. This meter differs from the preceding Anacreontic meter by only one syllable; thus, if anyone wishes to adapt the previous Musarithms to these, he need do nothing more than double the penultimate number of every voice in the Musarithm. As for the note corresponding to the number—that is, the penultimate note—let him divide it into two notes of equal value to the original, and he will have the desired Musarithms for the Iambic Archilochian meter. We provide an example so that the beginner <note>original: "Tyro"</note> may have something with which to practice.

# Proposition IV.

### *Given a nine-syllable meter and any musical tone, to arrange the desired musical composition in the Florid style.* <note>The "Florid style" (stylus floridus) refers to a decorative way of composing where one syllable of text might be stretched over several musical notes, as opposed to the "Simple style" where each syllable gets just one note.</note>

If anyone, therefore, has the desire to animate such meters into harmony, he shall work according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections. First, extract the Musarithms <note>Kircher's "Musarithms" are sequences of numbers where each digit represents a specific note in a scale, allowing even a non-composer to generate melodies mathematically.</note> appropriate to the meter; then, let him aptly distribute the notes attached to each Musarithm according to the points printed on the musical staves. When all these things have been duly performed, you will obtain the desired Musical Composition. <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note>

For ten-syllable meters <note>decasyllabic</note> where the second-to-last syllable is short, you will use the same Musarithms, provided you double the second-to-last note of each Musarithm in the following table and divide that note into two equal rhythmic parts.

Let the given form of the meter be: *Amant venena parricidæ* <note>Latin: "Parricides love poisons." This is an example of a nine-syllable line of poetry used to demonstrate the rhythm.</note>, and let the assigned Tone be the 2nd. <note>The "2nd Tone" refers to the Hypodorian mode, a specific musical scale used in the 17th century that was often associated with a serious or mournful character.</note> You will extract from the following table any musarithms along with the rhythmic notes proper to each, as follows:

<note>This table serves as a "cipher key." It maps the numbers 1 through 8 to specific notes on the scale of G (the 2nd Tone). For example, if a Musarithm asks for a '5', the composer writes a 'D'.</note>

You will first transfer these musarithms into the proper musical staves <note>original: "pentagramma"</note> for the voices; then, according to the keys which the numbers indicate, you will mark points in the spaces of the said staves, over which you will place the rhythmic notes corresponding to the individual musarithms. Thus, you will have what was sought. As was said above, each musarithm has as many corresponding notes in its row as it has numbers; therefore, if the points marked on the staves are either more or fewer than the numbers, let it be a clear sign to you that an error has been made somewhere. In such a case, repeat the operation until your results are satisfactory. We do not provide a finished example of the composition here, so that we might provide the young student of music <note>original: "Musico Tyroni"</note> an opportunity for some exercise.

<header>Book VIII. The Great Art of Concord and Discord</header>

# Proposition V.

->Given a Sapphic three-line stanza and any musical tone, to construct a harmony set upon it in the Florid style.<-

The Sapphic meter <note>original: "Sapphicum metrum"; a poetic form consisting of three long lines and one short line, named after the Greek poet Sappho</note> is the most suitable of all for musical settings, and is ideal for theatrical and festive harmonies. If anyone wishes to arrange this meter into musical melodies, let him know that he must constantly observe the course of rules prescribed in the preceding sections, and he will obtain his goal. Furthermore, since Sapphic verses are hendecasyllables <note>verses with eleven syllables</note>, the musical-rhythms described here can also be applied to Phalaecian hendecasyllables <note>another classical meter with the same syllable count</note> without any effort. If, therefore, one wishes to compose music over the following Sapphic poem by Horace:

> Enough already of snow and dire hail <note>original: "Iam satis Terris niuis atque diræ"</note> &emsp;&emsp;&emsp; He terrified the nations, lest there return <note>original: "Terruit gentes graue ne rediret"</note>
> The Father has sent upon the lands, and with his red &emsp;&emsp;&emsp; The age of Pyrrha, complaining of new monsters <note>original: "Seculum Pyrrhæ noua monstra questæ"</note>
> Right hand having struck the sacred citadels, <note>original: "Dextera sacras iaculatus arces"</note> &emsp;&emsp;&emsp; When Proteus drove all his herd to visit <note>original: "Omne cum Proteus pecus egit altos"</note>
> &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; He terrified the City. <note>original: "Terruit Vrbem"</note> &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; The high mountains. <note>original: "Visere montes"</note>

Let him choose any musical-rhythms from the following Table <note>original: "Pinace"</note>, and having applied them to any tone, let him arrange them into a harmony according to the rules handed down previously, and he will achieve his intent. For example: Let there be a musical-rhythm for the first strophe, applied to the column of the 3rd Tone <note>The 3rd Tone refers to the Phrygian mode</note>, as follows:

# The Harmony and Dissonance of the Great Art

The rules regarding the mixing of different types of meters, provided in the appendix of the fourth chapter, can also be applied to these tables. Thus, the Phalaecian <note>A hendecasyllabic meter often used in Greek and Latin lyric poetry.</note> combined with the Anacreontic <note>A light, rhythmic meter named after the Greek poet Anacreon.</note> is most suitable for musical melodies. However, see what we have discussed at length regarding this business of combination in the said appendix.

Having therefore finished the treatise on metric music and its adaptation to various verses, nothing remains but that we now show how the listed **Musarithms** <note>original: "Musarithmi"; Kircher's term for musical algorithms or sequences of numbers representing notes.</note> can be common to all languages, and indeed no language or idiom in the entire universe is so "barbaric" that it cannot use these **Musarithms** of ours to animate every kind of meter with harmonic melodies.

## Proposition VI.

### Given Adonic or Dactylic meters, to perform the requested composition <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note> upon them.

A double operation can be established by means of this kind of **Musarithm**: Simple or Mixed—or what is the same, homogeneous or heterogeneous. It is Simple or homogeneous when we use the **Musarithms** of only one table <note>original: "pinacis"</note>; it is Mixed or heterogeneous when we mix "florid" <note>Ornate or complex melodies with varying note lengths.</note> **Musarithms** with those of simple counterpoint excerpted from the tables of the preceding section. Let us explain both methods.

## First simple operation.

We have said that the simple method of operating is when we use the **Musarithms** of only one Table; but since the **Musarithms** in the tables almost all have the same termination from time to time—that is, they always provide the same cadences, whether of the sixth, second, or another tone <note>In this context, "tone" refers to the musical mode or key.</note>—which you will recognize from the last two numbers of the bass **Musarithm**, which will always be 1, 5, 1, or 5, 8, or 4, 8. We have shown in the preceding sections that this is unpleasant to the ears. Hence, to obtain the variety required in music, you will diligently observe the sixth Canon regarding the mixture of tones; but for the sake of the **novice** <note>original: "Tyronis"</note>, let us repeat it in this place.

## Example I.

Let there be, therefore, some Adonic **composition** <note>original: "Melothesia"</note> gathered together, to be performed in a certain florid style. And let the words be the following:
> The joys of the world, religious anxiety, sends back the charming [things].
<note>original: "Gaudia mundi, blanda remittit, sollicitudo, relligiofa." This is a series of Adonic verses, which follow a specific dactylic rhythm (long-short-short-long-long).</note>
To animate these words into a florid harmony, a single **Musarithm** can suffice in this manner. Let the following florid **Musarithm** (and the given Tone VI) be excerpted from the following table.

Then you see to which letters the **Musarithm** of the first voice (54321) responds, and you will find it responds to C, B, A, G, A. Therefore, you will mark the same number of points on the staff <note>original: "pentagrammo"</note> of the first voice or "Cantus"; to each of which, if you apply the notes placed in the region of the now-resolved **Musarithm**...

Whenever, therefore, a rest occurs between the meter-measuring notes, it must be placed most diligently. It matters little, however, on which line of the staff <note>original: "pentagrammorum"; referring to the five lines of musical notation.</note> you place it, for they can be situated on any of them; yet usage has prevailed that they be placed either in the middle of the lines, or at least within the space occupied by the note immediately following the rest. For the musical numbers, according to the letters to which they correspond...

### Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

transferred into the musical staff and marked by points, and finally distinguished with the corresponding notes, they will produce the second member of the harmonic Adonian <note>The Adonian refers to a specific poetic meter (a dactyl followed by a spondee) which Kircher here translates into a musical phrase or "clause."</note>, as is shown in the paradigm.

Again, if you move the number 1 or 8 above the character D in the column of keys, and then resolve the Musarithms into harmonic forms according to the aforementioned rules, the third harmonic clause of the Adonian member will be born.

If finally you either repeat the first Musarithm at the end, or take any other from the table <note>original: "pinace"; from the Greek *pinax*, referring to a list or mathematical table</note>, and having repeated the sixth tone you proceed according to the preceding rules, the sought-after fourth harmonic clause will come forth for the fourth Adonian, as is clear.

In this example it is most clearly evident how a gracious harmony emerges even from a single Musarithm, according to the diversity or mixture of tones. But lest any further doubt occur, nor any occasion for error <note>original: "hallucinationis"; literally "hallucination," but used here in the sense of a technical mistake or oversight</note> be possible for the novice, we have decided to fortify him here first with several rules.

| A | 8 | A | |

**Rule I.** In "soft" song <note>Latin: *cantu molli*; music using flats, primarily the F hexachord</note> the numbers 1 or 8 in the column of numbers can never and should not be applied to the letter B <note>B-flat</note> in the column of keys if the number 4 in the application column corresponds to a plain E without an added flat; nor can number 1 or 8 be applied to the letter A if the number 5 corresponds to the letter E with an added flat, thus: B-flat. For the composer <term>Melotheta</term> <note>original: "Melotheta"; a term Kircher uses for one who sets text to music</note> would commit a very great error if he employed this application during a change of tones. In all other intervals, however, he may apply them without penalty, and this rule is universal; see what we have handed down extensively regarding these matters in Canon V on prohibited intervals <note>This refers to avoiding the "tritone" or "diabolus in musica," an unstable interval of three whole steps.</note>.

**Rule II.** In song of the "hard" character <note>Latin: *cantu characterismi duri*; music using natural signs or sharps, primarily the G hexachord</note> the numbers 1 or 8 should never and cannot be applied to the B-natural <term>♮</term> <note>original: "b quadrato"; the "square b" or natural sign</note> in the column of keys such that the number 5 corresponds to F in the column of keys; nor can they be applied to B-flat if the number 4 corresponds to E. In all other keys, the application of said numbers can occur freely, so that these two rules are universal.

**Rule III.** Whenever, therefore, in "soft" song, for the sake of changing tones, the application of numbers 1 or 8 is made on B, then it requires the note E to be affected by a flat; and whenever the application is made on A, then E will necessarily lack the flat.

Again, when in "hard" song the application of numbers 1 or 8 is made on B, then this B necessarily requires a flat prefixed to it. If indeed the application of 1 or 8 is made over E, then B will necessarily lack the flat, for a reason entirely opposite to the previous ones, as is clear in the application columns.

**Rule IV.** To know truly when the chromatic sharp symbol <note>An image of a sharp symbol (#), used to raise a pitch by a semitone.</note> should be placed during a change of tones, consult Canon V, which we have explained sufficiently. For wherever in the two application columns—both the column of keys and of numbers—two sharps <note>A sharp symbol (#).</note> <note>A sharp symbol (#).</note> occur, then this sign <note>A sharp symbol (#).</note> must necessarily be added to that letter, provided however that the following note ascends; when, however, only one occurs in either column, then it should be omitted.

**Rule V.** The beginning and end of phrases <note>original: "clausularum"</note> must always be in the same tone; the middle may vary tones as desired, as has been said.

**Rule VI.** If in the context of the words the notes applied to the Musarithms do not correspond exactly to the syllables, in the case of a missing syllable, you may divide one note into two parts so that a place is given to the missing syllable; or if there is an excess syllable, two notes should be contracted into one. But singers can easily supply this deficiency.

**Rule VII.** If you reduce the notes of any phrase by half <note>A technique known as diminution, which increases the speed of the melody.</note>, you will have new variations of the melodies.

**Rule VIII.** Wherever there occurs in the Musarithms a base of numbers 5.1 or 5.8, it is a sign of phrases of one and the same tone; but where the bases 25, 65, or 73 are found in the Musarithms, it is a sign that phrases of different tones lie hidden there. You may use these for variety of harmony without further change of tone having to be made through the application column.

# Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music.

**Rule IX.** Wherever these last numbers, 4.1 or 4.8, occur in the base of the <term>Musarithm [a numerical code representing a musical phrase]</term>, you shall never use the musical phrases associated with these numbers at the beginning or in the middle, but always reserve them for the end.

**Rule X.** You shall diligently observe Rule IV <note>original: "Canonem IV"</note> so that when the voices ascend or descend more than is proper due to a change in tone, you may swap the Soprano <note>original: "Cantum"</note> or Tenor with the Alto, and the Alto with either of the others, as we have prescribed in the said Rule.

**Rule XI.** If, furthermore, it happens that the soprano descends more than is proper, you shall not interrupt the flow of its notes, but you shall begin the entire phrase an octave higher; this must also be observed if the soprano should ascend more than is proper, in which case you shall not interrupt the flow of the notes, but begin the entire phrase an octave lower.

And these rules are abundantly sufficient for the perfection of this art; therefore, let us return to our purpose. Having shown what a simple—or uniform—operation is, we shall now also show how we ought to establish a mixed—or varied—operation.

---

### Pattern II. Of the Mixed Operation.

Let the words of the chosen theme be the same, to be processed by a mixed or varied operation. To do this, for the beginning of the musical phrase, select any Adonian <note>The Adonian is a poetic meter consisting of a dactyl followed by a spondee; Kircher uses it here as a rhythmic template for a musical phrase.</note> Musarithm contained in the first column of Table III <note>original: "pinace III"</note> of the preceding section on simple counterpoint. For the second phrase, you shall select a "florid" Adonian Musarithm from the first table of the second section on Florid Counterpoint. Then, for the third phrase, choose a Musarithm of simple counterpoint again, and finally, for the fourth phrase, a florid Musarithm once more. The Musarithms will stand as you see here:

| Simple Musarithm | Florid Musarithm | Simple | Florid |
|---------------------|-----------------|---------|-----------|
| 66555 | 44321 | 55545 | 144565434565 |
| 88878 | 67867878 | 77867 | 45678888 |
| 44323 | 666655 | 22322 | 6654345654343 |
| 44151 | 44458 | 55125 | 444141 |
| **Gaudia mundi** | **blanda remittit** | **sollicitudo** | **religiosa** |
| (The joys of the world) | (charming, are set aside by) | (concern) | (religious) |

You see, therefore, in this single example how simple Musarithms ought to be mixed with florid ones. But who could adequately describe the immense multitude and variety of combinations resulting from this mixing of Musarithms? Certainly, the combinations of them in even a single table are so many that the entire Ocean could not hold more drops than the individual combinations of mixtures have diverse variations. For the number of these combinations far exceeds the number of grains of sand that the entire globe of the earth could contain. These things might truly be considered <note>original: "αδύνατα" (adynata)</note> impossible things, had we not long ago confirmed them by the irrefragable truth of mathematical scrutiny.

Thus, having selected the Musarithms in a mixed fashion from the appropriate tables, and having applied the columns according to the given tone, transfer the numbers together with the notes into the musical staff <note>original: "pentagramma"</note> for the voices, according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections, and the following musical setting <note>original: "Melothesia"</note> will come forth.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Musurgical Universal-Language, or concerning the Application of Musarithms <note>A "Musarithm" is Kircher's term for a numerical musical building block or formula used in his mechanical composition system.</note> to all other languages of the whole universe.

### §. I.

#### Concerning the verses and rhythms of the Hebrew language, addressed to the Professors of the Sacred Language of the Society of Jesus.

#### Concerning the feet of Hebrew Verses.

The Hebrew language, as the source and origin of all other languages, seemed appropriate to take the first principles of the Musurgical Art from it. And so that we may treat this Hebrew Musurgy more skillfully, we shall briefly put forward some things concerning the property of Hebrew meters. The poetry of the Hebrews is most ancient, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, and its meters consist of their own feet and syllables, just as in Latin. In their verses they use only two primary feet; the first they call <term>תנוע (Tenu’a)</term> <note>original: "Thema id est mutatio"</note>, which means "movement" or "change," and it consists of one long syllable. The other is called <term>יתד (Yathed)</term> <note>original: "iathed hoc est clavus"</note>, which means a "peg" or "nail," and it consists of two syllables—one short and one long—and it corresponds to our Iambic foot <note>An iamb is a metrical foot consisting of one short or unstressed syllable followed by one long or stressed syllable.</note>; for example, <term>לך (lecha)</term> "to you," or <term>מסור (mesor)</term> "hand over." From these feet, mixed in various ways, three others are created: namely the Spondee, the Bacchius, and the Cretic, as follows:

| Cretic | Bacchius | Spondee |
|----------|---------|----------|
| <term>כורמים</term> | <term>דברים</term> | <term>דבר</term> |
| *Coremim* | *Deuarim* | *Debar* |
| <note>A Cretic foot is long-short-long.</note> | <note>A Bacchius foot is short-long-long.</note> | <note>A Spondee foot is long-long.</note> |

By all of these, the Hebrews measure their songs.

The Hebrews call a poem a <term>baith</term> <note>original: "בית"; literally "house"</note>, and they generally join two verses together until the end of the poem, as is usually done in our elegies and distichs. They call the first verse a <term>daleth</term> <note>original: "דלת"; literally "door" or "gate"</note>; the second they call a <term>segor</term> <note>The OCR reads "legor," but the Hebrew "סגור" identifies it as *segor*, meaning "closure"</note>, because it closes the poem, as is evident in the following verse:

-><term>מרים שילדת לנו חן</term> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Mary, who bore grace for us* <note>original Latin: "Maria quæ peperiſti nobis gratiam"</note><-
-><term>שירנו אותך ירנן</term> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Our song shall praise you.* <note>original Latin: "Carmen noſtrum te laudabit."</note><-

Furthermore, if a poem does not exceed ten verses, it is called a <term>pasuk</term> <note>original: "פסוק"; a verse or sentence</note>. If indeed it exceeds ten, it is called a <term>schir</term> <note>original: "שיר"</note> or a song.

---

#### Concerning Hebrew Rhythms.

The **H**ebrews employ Rhythm in the composition of their poems as if it were salt; Rhythm is formed in roughly three ways. First, when only simple letters—whether one or many—agree, with no account taken of the vowel points. This is called <term>aber</term> <note>original: "עבר"; passing or common</note> rhythm; because it passes the ears so quickly that it is hardly perceived. A rhythm is called <term>Raui</term> <note>original: "ראוי"; worthy or proper</note>, or conspicuous and elegant, when the rhythmic members in both cases end similarly; as in *derekh* and *barukh* <note>original: "דרך" (way) and "ברך" (blessed); the OCR glosses this as "darech derech"</note>.
Thirdly, a rhythm is called <term>meshoubach</term> <note>original: "משובח"</note> or laudable, when two syllables end similarly; as in *oznaim* and *schamaiim* <note>original: "אזנים" (ears) and "שמים" (heavens)</note>.

-><term>אשא לבי גם כפים</term> *I will lift up my heart, and also my hands* <note>original Latin: "Leuabo cor meum, etiam manus"</note><-
<gloss>Asse libbi gam caphaim</gloss>
-><term>אל היושב בשמים</term> *To Him who sits in the heavens* <note>original Latin: "Ad ſedentem in cœlis"</note><-
<gloss>El haioscheu beschamaiim</gloss>

But truly, whoever desires to know more about the various forms of Hebrew verses, let them read Elias Levita <note>A 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian</note> and Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval biblical exegete and grammarian</note>, and others; lest we seem to overstep the limits of our Art, let us return to our purpose.

Note that since the Hebrews, like almost all Eastern peoples, read their letters from right to left—a manner contrary to others—it was necessary for the marking of the staves and the flow of the notes to have a reversed position. Hence, the musical setting must be sung in a **retrograde** <note>backward</note> order. In this, however, a wonderful thing occurs: that same piece, when sung in the forward order, produces another melody entirely different in character. Thus, whether you sing it in the forward or retrograde order, the composition will always maintain its perfection.

# § II.

## On Syriac or Chaldean Poetry, or on the Verses and Rhythms of the Syrians and Chaldeans.

->To the Fathers of the Society of Jesus in Syria, and especially the Maronite inhabitants of Mount Lebanon, for whom the Syriac language is their own.<-

### How to construct a requested <term>melothesia</term> <note>A musical composition or "text-setting" where music is applied to a specific set of words.</note> given a Syriac meter and any tone.

Although many and varied types of songs are found among the Syrians, especially in the books containing the divine offices, we shall not waste time unnecessarily enumerating them all, as they can easily be understood from what we will say here. We have chosen only two as the most noble, frequent, and necessary of all, and the most worthy of study. One was established by Saint James and the other by Saint Ephrem <note>Saint James of Serugh (c. 451–521) and Saint Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373) were two of the most influential theologians and hymnographers in the Syriac tradition.</note>, those most eloquent Doctors and the greatest lights of the whole Orient, and these meters bear their names. The first is called ܡܫܚܚܬܐ ܝܥܩܘܒܝܬܐ <note>original: *Mshuchtho Yaakuboitho*</note>, that is, the **Jacobite song**; the other is called ܐܦܪܝܡܝܬܐ <note>original: *Ephreimoitho*</note>, that is, the **Ephremite song**. The song of Saint James consists of three "pauses" <note>Kircher uses "pauses" to mean distinct rhythmic units or cola within a line of verse.</note>, as the Syrians say, each of which must consist of four syllables, as is evident in the following rhythm by Saint James:

->Because of them, look upon the sacrifices; look upon the sins.<-
->*Dachlopheihun Chur baalotho Cur bachtohe*<-
-><note>original Latin translation: *Quod pro illis Respice in sacrificia Respice in peccata*</note><-

But for the meter to be called perfect and complete, and for the poetic sense and song to be properly finished, it is customary for two such verses—comprising six "pauses"—to be composed and written, as seen in the cited passage. They will appear more elegant and beautiful if they end <term>ὁμοφώνως</term> <note>original Greek: "homophonously," meaning they rhyme or share similar phonetic endings.</note>, which is done in different ways. First, if the first pause of one verse corresponds to the first pause of the other, the second to the second, and the third to the third:

->How many are these ruins of his theft;<-
->How swift are these runners of his youth.<-
->*Cmo fagyn, holen thebre dognbututho*<-
->*Cmo kalilin Holen rehte Dobroiutho.*<-

You see how the individual pauses, or members of the verses, end **homophonously**. Sometimes only the third pause of one verse rhymes with the third of the other, or indeed all the pauses of both verses rhyme; or finally, none of them do, as one verse follows the other. But as I have said, the greater and more frequent the similarity of the endings, the more elegant and beautiful the songs are considered to be. There is scarcely any language that exhibits its rhythms with greater grace than the Syriac language, owing to the multitude of similarly ending terms. But let these things said in passing regarding the poetry of the Syrians suffice.

## §. III.

### Of Arabic Poetry.

->To the Fathers of the Society of JESUS dwelling in Egypt, Syria, and all<-
->of Asia.<-

Arabic poetry seems to yield to no other in the wit and elegance of its verses, nor is it particularly difficult; for indeed, I have found no nation to have greater license in the forging of verses than this people. I could declare all these things at length, were it not that the fear of overstepping my bounds restrained me from hand delivering them. Receive, therefore, its method briefly and in summary.

<margin>Of what the verses among the Arabs consist.</margin>
Just as among the Latins and Greeks, feet are born from syllables and meters from feet, so also among the Arabs, feet are born from syllables, and verses from feet. And there are indeed two feet among the Arabs, of which the first is called <term>سبب</term> *sabab* <note>original Arabic: *sabab*</note>, that is, a cord or string; the other <term>وتد</term> *vatad* <note>original Arabic: *watad*</note>, that is, a stake or peg. The similarity is taken from the structure of a house or tent, which they call the structure of a poem: <term>بيت الشعر</term> *beith al-shaar* <note>original: *bayt al-sha'r*, literally "house of hair," referring to a Bedouin tent.</note>. For the Arabs fashion tents for themselves from the hair and skins of animals; just as a house or tent is extended by the help of cords and pegs, so the structure of meters is perfected by the help of feet, which they themselves call cords and pegs. A "cord" consists of two consonant letters, of which the first always has a vowel, as is evident in these: <term>من</term> *men* (who) or <term>لم</term> *lam* (not). The second letter either has a vowel or it does not; if it does not, it is called <term>السبب الخفيف</term> *al-sabab al-khafif*, that is, the "light cord," as shown in the previous words; if, however, both are with a vowel, then it is called <term>السبب الثقيل</term> *al-sabab al-thaqil*, that is, the "heavy cord," as is evident in these: <term>ابو</term> *abo* (father) or <term>هذه</term> *hade* (this).

A "peg," however, consists of three consonants, of which two have a vowel and one is deprived of a vowel. If those having a vowel are immediate [adjacent], then they call it a "joined peg," like <term>هذه</term> *hade* (this); if, however, a resting [silent] letter is in the middle between each marked letter, as in <term>رجل</term> *raglo* (man), then it is called a "distinct peg." Thus there are four feet among the Arabs—neither more nor fewer—for constructing every kind of poem; and from these cords and pegs succeeding each other alternately, the patterns are composed.

### Of Rhythms or Particular Meters.

Even though there are many forms of verse types for the Arabs, they nevertheless seem to agree more with vernacular verses <note>Kircher refers to "vulgar" or modern European rhymed poetry as opposed to the unrhymed quantitative meters of Classical Latin and Greek.</note> than with Latin ones. Furthermore, they have greater license in composing verses than any other nations; and so as not to neglect some notable and sharp allusion in the verses, they do not always observe the integrity of the meter. To the Italians, however, the measure is always the same, and they mostly use hendecasyllables <note>Lines of eleven syllables.</note>, or twelve, such as those verses they call *sdruccioli* <note>Italian verses ending with an accent on the antepenultimate syllable, creating a "sliding" rhythm.</note>. Just as the Italians do, so the Arabs join verses in pairs so that the ends of both terminate in a <note>original Greek: ὁμοφωνίαν (*homophonian*)</note> "same-sounding" or similarly sounding feet. This the Latins call Rhyme, and the Arabs call <term>قافيه</term> *kaphieh* <note>original Arabic: *qafiyah*</note>. The end of the first verse is called <term>العروض</term> *al-aaruth* <note>original Arabic: *arud*</note>, that is, the "proposition"; while the end of the second verse, finishing similarly, is called <term>الضرب</term> *al-tarab* <note>original Arabic: *darb*, meaning a strike or beat</note>, that is, the "pulsation." Each of these is called <term>مصراع</term> *mesraa*—that is, a "door" <note>original Arabic: *misra'*, referring to one leaf of a double door, used metaphorically for a half-line of poetry.</note>.

Furthermore, they distinguish their verses into certain circles, so that one circle might be <term>مختلفة الدائرة</term> *the varied circle* <note>original: "mochtalefat al daiereth"</note>; another the composite circle, and another the similar circle, of which there are again three species.

## §. IV.
## On Samaritan Poetry.

The Samaritans <note>A group closely related to the Jews who follow the Samaritan Pentateuch</note> emulate the Hebrews in all things, although poetic books are scarcely found among them, if you except a few hymns that the Gazaeans <note>Likely referring to Samaritan communities in Gaza or a specific class of cantors</note> are accustomed to chant in their sacred rites. These hymns have a certain flavor of the Iambic meter; they indeed rhyme <term>homophonously</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμοφώνως (homophōnōs); meaning they end with similar sounds</note>, but they are not consistent in the identity of their syllables. Truly, this idiom, just like all others, could easily be adapted to meters if there were those who would labor in restoring this kind of poetry, as is evident in the following four-line verse, which we have composed according to the rule of rhyming <term>hendecasyllables</term> <note>eleven-syllable lines</note>.

### A Samaritan Rhythmic Four-line Verse.

<note><image-desc>Four lines of Samaritan script arranged horizontally.</image-desc> This script is a descendant of the ancient Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, distinct from the "square" Hebrew script used in modern Bibles.</note>

> *Schibbhu eloha col amme haarez*
> *Schibbhu talmez bearcha colma ſcharez*
> *Ki huhu malka colmabaſamaim*
> *Hu pooel colmabeauir vemaim.*

> Praise God, all peoples of the earth,
> Praise the Creator, everything that creeps upon the earth.
> For He is the King of all in heaven,
> And the Worker of all in the air and water.

## §. V.
## On Ethiopian Poetry.

->To the Fathers of the Society of Jesus in Ethiopia.<-

**A**mong the Ethiopians, I have found no other hymns except those they use in sacred rites. These are mostly homophonic <note>original: "homophonique"; where all voices move in the same rhythm</note> and rhythmic, though no account is taken of the quantity or number of syllables. From this, it is evident that no nation is so barbaric that it does not, by some innate instinct, strive for poetry and music in its hymns. But so that you may see a specimen of this language, we have composed for you the following Ethiopian four-line stanza, adapted to the Anacreontic <note>A style of short, light, lyrical verse named after the Greek poet Anacreon</note> form.

# Book VIII. The Wondrous Art of Music-making.

### §. VII.
### On Greek Music-making.

#### Given a Greek meter, to adapt a desired musical setting upon it.

**T**here is no reason for me to speak at length about the poetry of the Greeks, as both Latin and all other poetic forms have flowed from it. However, I will add an example so that we do not appear to have contemptuously bypassed this most excellent language—from which, as I have said, all sciences and skills, and especially Music, have flowed as if from a fountainhead.

->**Anacreon, Ode I: On the Lyre**<-

<margin>Greek Meter.</margin>
<columns>3</columns>
I wish to speak of the sons of Atreus,
I wish to sing of Cadmus,
But the strings of my lyre
Sound of Love alone.
<column-break/>
I changed the strings just now,
And the whole lyre as well,
And I sang the labors
Of Hercules; but the lyre
<column-break/>
Answered back of Love.
Farewell then, for us,
O Heroes; for the lyre
Sings of Love alone.

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### §. VIII.
### On the remaining Western languages.

**W**estern languages are properly those, and are called such, which Europe uses. These are primarily Spanish, French, Italian, and German, along with its "daughter" languages—such as Dutch <note>original: "Belgica"</note>, English, Scottish, and Illyrian <note>Kircher uses "Illyrian" to refer to the Slavic language family</note>, from which come Polish, Russian <note>original: "Ruthenica"</note>, and Bohemian. All these languages observe their own metrical laws in composing verses; however, it is usually the case that the given meters are similar to Iambics, both in seven-syllable and eleven-syllable forms. For they neglect the Hexameter, Pentameter, Sapphic, and all those meters consisting of dactyls and anapests <note>these are the quantitative meters of classical Latin and Greek poetry, which rely on vowel length rather than stress</note>. Furthermore, all these nations have this in common: they make their rhythms "homophonic"—that is, ending with similar sounds <note>rhyming</note>—either immediately or in alternating meters. Rhythmical poetry is thus innate to humans, as if from nature itself. But let us now see which meters best suit our Musarithms <term>Musarithm: Kircher’s term for a mathematical sequence of numbers that represent musical intervals and rhythms</term>. The Italians especially love the combination of the Anacreontic with the Phaleucian—that is, a seven-syllable meter paired with an eleven-syllable meter.

->**An Italian Anacreontic-Phaleucian Meter in six lines.**<-

<margin>Italian Rhythm.</margin>
>*Such sweet harmony,*
>*Such well-alternated melody,*
>*Are true images*
>*Of the revolving of the celestial spheres,*
>*Which, turning up there with their delights,*
>*Make human minds down here rejoice.*
<note>original Italian: "Così dolce harmonia / Così bene alternata melodia / Imagini son vere / Del raggirar delle celeste sfere / Che girando la sù co' suoi contenti / Fan che godan qua giù l'humane menti."</note>

To compose a Florid Musical Setting <note>original: "Melothesiam Floridam"</note> for the aforementioned meter, take three columns from Table II <note>original: "Pinace II"</note> of the *Florid Musurgy* and Book VI, Section II, according to the number and the progression of the meters which are applied to one another alternately; so that the first column is for the Anacreontics, the second for the eleven-syllable lines, the third for the Anacreontics, the fourth for the eleven-syllables, the fifth finally for the Anacreontics, and the last for the eleven-syllables. Once these are properly arranged, the Musarithms may be selected in any order—just as we have selected these in no particular order, but as they first occurred to us. Once the operation is completed according to the prescribed rules, the following musical setting is produced. Meanwhile, it must be observed with the greatest care that you place the time-keeping notes <note>rhythmic notation</note> corresponding to each point and number above them, with pauses placed if they occur anywhere. The notes corresponding to each Musarithm are as many as there are numbers in the Musarithm to which they correspond; from this, if an error has been made anywhere, a correction is easily given. And these things must be carried out with such diligence that unless everything is observed to the letter <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail"</note>, the desired goal of the composition cannot be achieved.

### §. IX.
### On Spanish meter.

**T**he Spanish are accustomed to construct their verses in exactly the same manner as the Italians; namely, through the grouping of Iambic verses, either of a single type <term>monocolon: a poem where every line follows the same meter</term> or of varying types <term>heterocolon: a poem where lines use different meters</term>, perfected by a certain rhythmical consonance or "homophony" <note>original Greek: ὁμοιοφώνως, meaning "with the same sound," referring here to rhyme</note>, as is clear in the following example.

*Laurel so justly crowned,*
<column-break/>
*No less is this dedicated work;*
*It girds with eternal and warlike honor*
*The Iberian, victorious in a thousand battles,*
*Equaling the pen with the sword.*

### §. XII.
### On Illyrian meter.

**T**he Illyrian language <note>Kircher uses "Illyrian" as a general term for the Slavic languages.</note>, enjoying a large family of offspring (for both Polish and Bohemian <note>Bohemian refers to the Czech language.</note>, among several others, recognize it as their mother), constructs its verses in a rhythmic way not unlike the others, or through meters ending with similar sounds. Therefore, nothing more is needed here except for a paradigm; once this is established, if anyone desires a musical composition <term>Melothesia: the art of composing a melody or full musical arrangement</term>, they may work according to the rules previously handed down and they will achieve their goal. These, then, are the principal languages of all Europe to which our Musurgic Art <note>original: "Ars nostra Musurgica," referring to his system of automated or assisted musical composition.</note> can be applied. If indeed there be any other languages, know that they are almost all dialects of one of the more recent languages; thus, you will have no difficulty in accommodating the Musarithms <term>Musarithmi: Kircher’s pre-calculated musical building blocks or algorithms</term> to the said dialects. I do not, however, include the American languages, as I have no knowledge of them. For this reason, I wished to include in this place only the principal and Oriental languages of Asia, Africa, and Europe, the understanding of which Divine Goodness has deigned to grant me. This I have done for the sake of our Fathers and other religious men laboring for the honor of God in various parts of the world; I earnestly vow that all these things may yield solely to the honor of God, the Virgin Mother, and the salvation of our neighbor.

# CHAPTER VIII.
# Rhetorical Music-making.

## PREFACE.

**A**lthough Rhetoric is very powerful in bending and stirring the minds of men in any direction, only someone who has not read the records of ancient writers could be ignorant of the fact that Music obtains a greater impression in moving those same minds. For we read that by the power of certain harmonic modulations arranged in different ways, the furious were made gentle, the lustful were made chaste, those with the most heavy infirmities were restored to full health, and finally, those possessed by demons were liberated. We have rarely heard of similar things regarding Rhetoric. Therefore, a greater force lies hidden within Music, a greater energy and efficacy in affecting the minds of mortals in various ways, than in Rhetoric. Since the explanation for this does not belong in this section, we shall treat it more extensively in *Physiological Musurgia* <note>Kircher refers to a different section of his work where he discusses the physical and biological effects of sound on the human body and spirit.</note>. Since we have until now treated "Poetic Music-making" in various ways and by an unseen method, order seemed to require that we follow up with "Rhetorical Music-making" using a similar method, delivering it with a new rationale desired by many until now. I trust that, with the assistance of the Divine Power, I shall achieve this in this part, and lest we be too long-winded, let us approach the matter itself.

### §. I.
### On the constituent parts of Rhetorical Music-making.

**J**ust as the noble edifice of a poetic composition rises from syllables into feet, from feet into meters, from meters into Odes, and finally from all of these; so too from words and names aptly arranged, various enunciations are born, from these periods, and from periods skillfully woven together through tropes or figures, an oration fit for persuasion is finally born. This can be established in three ways: through the judicial, deliberative, and encomiastic <note>Encomiastic: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.</note> genres. Our Music-making, proceeding by a certain parallel reasoning, and while it adapts Musarithms to words, produces various reasons according to their meaning, such as—

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 141 regarding the "Musurgic Art." Having established how music adapts to the meters of various languages, Kircher now moves into the rhetorical power of music—how it functions like speech to move the human heart and stir specific emotions.</meta>

->Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance<-

...just like certain statements; from the continuation of these, harmonic periods are born. Finally, from these periods—skillfully woven together through florid and colored Musarithms <term>Musarithmi: Kircher’s pre-calculated musical building blocks or algorithms</term> as if through certain figures and tropes—there results a song that is most effective for stirring up various passions of the soul according to the meaning of the chosen theme. Indeed, three types of musical modulation correspond aptly to the three types of oratory: the Deliberative corresponds to the Enharmonic, the Judicial to the Chromatic, and the Encomiastic <note>Encomiastic: a style of speech or writing intended to praise someone or something; a panegyric.</note> to the Diatonic. But these matters we have treated more extensively elsewhere.

### §. II.
### On the various passions of the soul to which music inclines.

**J**ust as Rhetoric, through various arguments and reasons and a varied weave of figures and tropes, now delights the soul, now saddens it, now provokes it to anger, now to compassion, now to indignation, revenge, violent impulses, and other affects, and finally, once the mind has been moved, inclines the listener to agree with what the Orator intends; so too does Music, through the various arrangement of periods and the different disposition of tones, agitate the soul in various ways. It moves our soul through three primary affects, from which, as if from a single root, others are later born. These three general affects are as follows:

The first is **Joy**, which contains within itself the affects of love, magnanimity, impulse, and desire, which find their origin in the blood. If, however, this joy becomes dissolute and intemperate, it generates properly "choleric" affects: anger, hatred, indignation, revenge, and fury.

The second is the general affect of **Remission** <note>Remissio: a state of relaxation, submission, or solemnity.</note>. Since it delights in slow movement, it generates affects of piety, love for God, as well as constancy, modesty, severity, chastity, religion, and contempt for human affairs; finally, it moves one toward the love of heavenly things.

The third is the affect of **Compassion**, under which fall all those affects that flow from phlegm and "black bile" <note>Original: "cholera nigra," referring to the humor associated with Melancholy.</note>, such as sadness, mourning, pity, languor, and similar things that can be recalled to this class.

How these sorts of affects are excited in the soul by the power of Music will be discussed in "Harmonic Physiology" <note>Kircher's term for the study of the physical and psychological effects of sound on the human body.</note>. For now, it must finally be shown which tones or tropical clauses and which figures are proper for stirring the said affects. First, we shall speak of the twelve tones; then, of as many tropes or harmonic figures, according to their aptitude for stirring the soul toward these or those affects.

### §. III.
### On the twelve tones, and their nature and properties.

**T**he tones and their arrangement have been dealt with extensively in the preceding books, so that nothing more is needed here except to declare the nature of each in a few words. Since there is great controversy among authors concerning the nature of the tones, we, "swearing by the words of no master," <note>original: "in nullius verba iurantes," a reference to Horace, implying Kircher is thinking independently rather than following a specific school.</note> determine the tones here according to our own opinion, yet in such a way that we leave to everyone their own judgment in this matter.

The **First Tone**, if it be more intense and loose, is by nature fit for dances, leaps, and festive processions. If it be subdued, it can also be suitable for piety, divine love, and the desire for heavenly things. The Antiphon *Sweet Mother of the Redeemer* <note>original: "Alma Redemptoris mater"</note> is composed in this tone.

The **Second Tone** is fit for tenderness and pertains to expressing the affects of mercy; if it be more intense, it can also serve the affects of joy.

The **Third Tone** inclines toward the third order of affects: it is fit for sorrow, tears, and compassion. The hymn *Hail, Holy Queen* <note>original: "Salve Regina"</note> is composed in this tone.

Book VIII. The Wondrous Art of Music. 143

The **fourth tone** is almost entirely similar to the preceding one; it belongs to the same class and stirs up the emotions of lamentation, anxiety, and calamity, being suitable for expressing all kinds of suffering <note>original: "pathemata"</note> to illustrate miseries.
   The **fifth tone** is Ecclesiastical; it shines with the greatest decorum, for it possesses a certain gravity and heroic majesty by which it seems to stir cheerful minds toward grave and arduous matters.
   The **sixth tone** invites the emotions contained in the first class; it can serve for military ferocity, or if used more dissolutely or more relaxedly, it can serve to stir up all kinds of passions.
   The **seventh tone** breathes modesty, pleasantness, and victory.
   The **eighth tone** serves to excite the emotions of the second class in the minds of men; it affects gravity and majesty.
   The **ninth tone** claims for itself lascivious, voluptuous, and threatening words; if it is more intense, it also rouses fury and disturbance.
   The **tenth tone** breathes modesty, gentleness, the meditation of celestial things, and divine love; it is most fit for expressing divine matters.
   The **eleventh tone** requires words that are sweet, suave, pleasant, and provide material for delight.
   The **twelfth tone** shares the same property as the sixth.
   And this is the character of the twelve tones according to my opinion; the reasons for all of these will be assigned, God willing, in the Musurgic Physiology.

### §. IV.
### On the Parts of Musurgic Rhetoric.

Just as Rhetoric consists of three parts—invention, arrangement, and delivery <note>original: "inuentione, dispositione & elocutione"</note>—so too does our Musurgic Rhetoric. **Invention** in Musurgic Rhetoric is nothing other than the suitable adaptation of Musarithms <term>Musarithmi: Kircher’s pre-calculated musical building blocks or algebraic formulas for composition</term> to congruent words. **Arrangement**, however, is a certain beautiful expression of these same things through the apt application of notes. Finally, **Delivery** is the exhibition through song of the Musical Composition <note>original: "Melothesia"</note> itself, perfected in every measure and adorned with tropes and figures. Indeed, the entire form of our Musarithmic art is made clear through these things.

### §. V.
### On the Opening of a Melody.

The opening <note>original: "Exordium"</note> of a melody is a modulation that renders the listener's mind suitable for what follows. It will be sound if it excites the listener and makes them eager for the rest. This will occur if the opening is grave, sweet, resonant, and full of harmonic weight, beginning its musical phrases with words congruent with the chosen tone. For it would be a fault if someone, having undertaken a musical composition in the sixth tone, were to begin from any other tone; likewise, he would create a faulty opening who began a song with excessive diminutions <note>diminutions: a technique where long notes are broken into many shorter, faster notes, often used for ornamentation</note> of the voices, unless perhaps the theme of the words suggested otherwise—as in that song by Monteverdi, *Flee, flee, my beloved* <note>original: "Fuge fuge dilecte mi"</note>, in which, while he expresses flight, he adorns the "flight" of the voices with the smallest, fastest notes. It would also be a fault if someone placed a closing phrase at the very beginning of the song.

### §. V I.
### On Ornamentation.

<margin>In what musical ornamentation consists.</margin>
The ornamentation of our <term>Musurgy</term> <note>Kircher's term for the art of musical composition</note> consists in this: that the arrangement of notes and intervals corresponds to the meaning of the words. Thus, if the words signify a swift movement of the mind, the composer should aptly express it with swift notes; if a slow movement, with slow notes. Furthermore, the melodic context should be elegant, with periods <note>musical phrases</note> cohering well with one another, and the excessive proximity of the same intervals should be avoided. Attention must be paid to the words themselves; since some are found to be more consonant than others, they will also produce a more consonant harmony. Thus, words such as *monstrous* <note>original: "immanes"</note>, *to celebrate together* <note>original: "concelebrare"</note>, *anxiety* <note>original: "sollicitudo"</note>, and *they shall be troubled* <note>original: "conturbabuntur"</note> will achieve a better effect in melodic disposition than words like *great* <note>original: "magnus"</note>, *to sing together* <note>original: "con cinere"</note>, *care* <note>original: "cura"</note>, and similar terms.

---

### §. V I I.
### On figures or tropes.

In this Musurgic art, we understand figures differently than the Rhetoricians do; for here, we take tropes and figures to mean the same thing. A Rhetorical figure consists of the various addition, doubling, multiplication, or repetition of the same word, in the manner of one speaking, questioning, rebuking, or proposing things that are great, high, admirable, vile, or unworthy. These cannot serve our purpose quite so conveniently, as they would become too scattered when harmonized by concordant voices—though this kind of figure suits the recitative style better, since a single voice has greater ease in expressing them.

Furthermore, Rhetoricians call a <term>Trope</term> a turning of speech from its proper significance to another with power. Since these can only be applied to our Musurgy with difficulty, we take tropes in another sense, saying they are nothing other than certain periods of <term>Melothesia</term> <note>the art of composing melody</note> denoting a specific affection of the soul. Following the diversity of the twelve tones, we constitute twelve such tropes; for this reason, even the ancients judged that the tones should be called nothing other than tropes. Since different tones denote different affections of the soul, they are the proper tools of Musicians, and they are as follows: of love, joy, exultation, dissolution, hatred, ferocity, impetus, gravity, modesty, temperance, religion, compassion, mourning, lamentation, and sadness.

<margin>The names of the tropes.</margin>
The Figures, however, which we properly use, are the following: the Pause, Repetition, the Climax, the Embrace <note>original: "Complexus"</note>, the Polysyndeton <note>use of many conjunctions</note>, the Symploce <note>interweaving</note>, the Omoioptoton <note>similar endings</note>, the Antithesis <note>opposition</note>, the Anabasis <note>ascending passage</note>, the Catabasis <note>descending passage</note>, the <term>Kyklosis</term> <note>original Greek: κύκλωσις; a circling or rounding</note>, and the Fugue.

---

### §. V I I I.
### Explanation of the figures.

<margin>The Rest <note>original Greek: Παῦσις</note>.</margin>
I. **The Rest** is the same thing as a silence. A Pause is conveniently employed when one person is not expected to speak much; it occurs opportunely when someone either asks a question or responds to things asked, as is found in the harmonic dialogues of Viadana <note>Lodovico da Viadana, a pioneer of the concerto style and basso continuo</note>. To this may be referred the **sigh** <note>original Greek: στεναγμὸς</note> or respiration, when through pauses of eighth or sixteenth notes—which are therefore called "sighs" <note>original: "suspiria"</note>—we express the affections of a groaning and sighing soul.

<margin>Repetition <note>original Greek: ἀναφορὰ</note>.</margin>
II. It is called **Anaphora** or repetition when, to express energy, one period is expressed several times; it is often used in the more vehement passions of the soul, such as ferocity or contempt, as can be seen in that well-known song: *To Arms, To Arms; etc.*

<meta>This page continues the catalog of musical-rhetorical figures from Section VII. Kircher is explaining how specific compositional techniques—borrowed from the art of oratory—can be used to evoke specific emotions or "affects" in the listener. This leads into "Syntagma III," where he introduces his "Musarithms" or musical tables designed to automate these rhetorical compositions.</meta>

<header>Book VIII. Wondrous Composition.</header>

<margin>Climax <note>original Greek: κλίμαξ, meaning "ladder"</note></margin>
III. It is called **Climax** or **Gradation**, and it is a musical phrase that ascends step by step. It is typically employed to express the affects of divine love and the longing for the heavenly homeland, such as in the work of Orlando <note>Orlande de Lassus (c. 1532–1594), a prolific Franco-Flemish composer</note>: *As the hart panteth after the water-brooks*. To this figure may also be referred the **stenasmus** <note>from the Greek for "sighing"</note>, which naturally expresses the sighs of a grieving soul through various pauses.

<margin>Symploke <note>original Greek: συμπλοκὴ, meaning "interweaving" or "embrace"</note></margin>
IV. **Symploke** or **Complexus** is a musical phrase in which the voices seem to breathe together as one. It is usually employed in the affects of machinations or plots, such as in that work of Clemens non Papa <note>Jacob Clemens non Papa (c. 1510–1555), a Renaissance composer</note>: *The kings of the earth stood up against the Lord, and against his Christ.*

<margin>Homoioptoton <note>original Greek: ὁμοιόπτωτον, meaning "with similar endings"</note></margin>
V. **Homoioptoton** or the **Similarly Ending figure** is a musical phrase that concludes with frequently repeated patterns. It is typically used in the serious affirmation, negation, or rebuke of a thing, as in the work of Palestrina <note>referred to here as Praenestini, from his birthplace Palestrina</note>: *We fools.*

<margin>Antitheton <note>original Greek: Ἀντίθετον, meaning "opposition"</note></margin>
VI. **Antitheton**, or the **Counter-position**, is a musical phrase by which we express opposing affects; such as that of Giacomo Carissimi, which he titled *The Laughter of Heraclitus and the Wailing of Democritus* <note>referring to the philosophical trope of the "weeping" and "laughing" philosophers</note>, and that of Leone Leoni: *I sleep, and my heart wakes.*

<margin>Anabasis <note>original Greek: ἀνάβασις, meaning "ascent"</note></margin>
VII. **Anabasis**, or **Ascension**, is a musical phrase by which we express exaltation, ascension, or high and eminent things, such as in the work of Morales <note>Cristóbal de Morales (c. 1500–1553), a Spanish composer</note>: *Christ ascending on high,* etc.

<margin>Katabasis <note>original Greek: κατάβασις, meaning "descent"</note></margin>
VIII. **Katabasis** or **Descension** is a musical phrase by which we pronounce affects opposite to the former: feelings of servitude, humility, depression, and for expressing the lowest things, as in the work of Massaino: *But I have been brought very low*, and that of Massentio: *they went down alive into hell.*

<margin>Kyklosis <note>original Greek: Κύκλωσις, meaning "wheeling"</note></margin>
IX. **Kyklosis** or **Circulation** is a musical phrase in which the voices seem to be driven as if in a circle. It serves words expressing circular action, such as in the work of Philippe de Monte: *I will rise and go about the city.*

<margin>Phuge <note>original Greek: Φυγὴ, meaning "flight"</note></margin>
X. **Phuge** or **Fuga** <note>Fugue</note> is a musical phrase suited to words indicating flight, of the sort: *Flee, my beloved;* it also serves to express successive actions, and indeed its use is the most frequent of all.

<margin>Homoiosis <note>original Greek: Ομοίωσις, meaning "likeness" or "imitation"</note></margin>
XI. **Homoiosis** or **Assimilation** is a musical phrase by which the actions of things are properly imitated, as when the phrases of individual voices represent different things. For example: *They play the drum, they play the lute, they strike for us, they shine in robes before the highest Trinity.* In this song, the Bass imitates a heavy drum, while the other voices represent all kinds of instruments.

XII. **Sudden Abruption** is a musical phrase by which we express a thing quickly finished; it most often takes place at the end, such as: *The desire of sinners shall perish.*

Behold, these are the tropes and figures which composers <note><term>Musurgi</term>: Kircher's term for those skilled in the art of musical composition</note> are most accustomed to use. Having explained these, let us now prepare ourselves for the practice.

---

# SYNTAGMA III.
## Presenting the Musarithms of Rhetorical Composition.

Having set forth those things which pertain to Rhetorical Musurgy, nothing remains but that we now also see how they may be applied to the aforementioned principles.
Therefore, just as in metric or poetic Musurgy we encompassed the whole art through 16 **Musarithmic Pinaces** <note>Mathematical tables or "boards" used for automated composition</note>; so also in this third Syntagma, we demonstrate the absolute reason and method of Rhetorical Musurgy. To make this more convenient, we have divided the entire Syntagma into 10 Pinaces. Of which:
I. The **Pinax** is two-membered, and contains the **Musarithms** of polysyllables; the first part for those with a long penultimate syllable, the second for those with a short penultimate. It is the same as the one we presented in the first Syntagma. It differs in this, however: that it has added notes drawn out in a more decorative <note>original: "pleonastice"</note> manner.
