Book VIII. Wondrous Music-making.

II. The Table contains <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for musical-mathematical formulas used for composition.</note> for Florid <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of composing a melody.</note> suited for exciting various emotions of the first class, adapted for polysyllabic words with a long penultimate syllable.

III. The Table contains Musarithms for florid composition, likewise suited for exciting various emotions of the second class, adapted for various polysyllabic words with a short penultimate syllable.

<margin>Tables of the Musurgical Ark reserved.</margin>
IV. The Table contains other florid Musarithms—syncopated, diminished, and artfully bound—suited for exciting various emotions of the third class, adapted for polysyllabic words with a long penultimate.

V. The Table contains Musarithms for the same emotions, but adapted for words with a short penultimate.

VI. The Table contains Musarithms adapted to the <term>Motet</term>, <term>Ecclesiastical</term>, and <term>Madrigal</term> styles.

VII. The Table containing Musarithms exhibits a framework of artful <term>fugues</term>. <note>In this context, "fugues" refers to imitative polyphony where one voice follows another.</note>

VIII. The Table exhibits Polyphonic Musarithms—that is, in 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, and 16 voices—for both simple and florid <term>Counterpoint</term>.

IX. It exhibits Musarithms in the <term>recitative style</term>. <note>A style of singing that imitates the rhythms and delivery of ordinary speech.</note>

X. It exhibits chromatic and enharmonic Musarithms.

And these are the Tables of which our <term>Musurgical Ark</term> <note>original: "Arca Musurgica." This was Kircher's famous mechanical invention, a wooden box filled with inscribed slats that allowed non-musicians to compose music by following mathematical rules.</note> consists, leading to a perfect knowledge of composing. However, we have deliberately omitted some of them in this book, partly so that we would not burden the work with an excessive multitude of things, and partly so that we would not reveal such a noble secret to just anyone.

-># EXPLANATION OF THE PLEONASTIC TABLE<-
->## Regarding Simple Counterpoint for Rhetorical Music.<-

This Table has four columns, each of which is divided into three parts. The first series of each column contains the Musarithms of simple counterpoint for words of two, three, four, and five syllables, as the series of each column shows. The second series contains the numbers for polysyllabic words with both long and short penultimates; we represent the short ones thus: IIĬ, which is a three-syllable word with a short penultimate; IV̆, a four-syllable word with a short penultimate; V̆, a five-syllable word with a short penultimate, and so on. We represent the long penultimate thus: IIĪ, a three-syllable word with a long penultimate; IV̄, a four-syllable word with a long penultimate; V̄, a five-syllable word with a long penultimate; VĪ, a six-syllable word with a long penultimate, and so on. The third series contains the notes corresponding to each polysyllable, which notes we call <term>pleonasms</term> <note>From the Greek for "excess." In music, Kircher uses this to mean adding ornamental notes to "fill out" a simple melody for rhetorical effect.</note>; this is nothing other than the multiplication of Musarithms represented in notes. We have extended the Musarithms in this Table from three-syllable to five-syllable words, because these four Musarithms are quite sufficient for expressing all possible word contexts in songs. Now, let us declare the wondrous use of this Table.

Note, therefore, that composers of melody do not always use the same cadences or intervals, but repeat the same clause in various ways according to the different mixture of tones, as was handed down above in the sixth rule. For if someone were to continuously pluck clauses from this and the following Musarithms according to the syllabic quantity of a given theme, he would indeed produce a composition complete in all its numbers and adorned with an artful and florid process; however, it would lack grace and brilliance. He would be doing the same as a <term>Rhetorical Novice</term> <note>original: "Tyro Rhetoricæ"</note> who, while piling up various flourishes and elegances, composes a speech that is indeed florid, but which lacks the soul of context and the decorum of harmony. For this reason, more skillful musicians with powerful judgment, in order to adorn a song or some motet with an ingenious connection of periods, are accustomed to mixing the clauses of simple counterpoint with florid and artful periods, repeating them through various intervals, and thus finally making the song perfect in its measures...

# Rule I.
## Regarding Musarithmic Pleonasm.

<margin>What joined and disjoined pleonasm is.</margin>
<term>Musarithmic Pleonasm</term> <note>From the Greek "pleonasmos" meaning "excess" or "redundancy"; here it refers to the technique of multiplying notes to fit more syllables than a basic musical formula provides.</note> is nothing other than the multiplication of any simple <term>Musarithm</term> <note>A mathematical-musical formula used in Kircher's system to generate melodies.</note> that has been proposed. This multiplication can be established in two ways, just as we previously taught in Canon 6. First, through "broken" or "disjoined" pleonasm—that is, when the notes of a <term>foot-measure</term> <note>original: "pedometræ"; the rhythmic units corresponding to poetic feet.</note> for a polysyllabic word are divided into different musical intervals. Second, through "whole" or "joined" pleonasm, where the notes of the foot-measure for a polysyllabic word are placed within the same interval. We have shown both in the columns, as the inscriptions demonstrate. Having proposed these things, let us now interpret the columns of Musarithms. The first column contains Musarithms for two-syllable words, which strictly speaking correspond only to two rhythmic notes, as was shown in the table of the first Section on simple Counterpoint. But now, so that <term>Rhetorical Musurgy</term> <note>Composition designed to mimic the persuasive power and variety of speech.</note>—which loves variety—might flourish with greater abundance, we have arranged this table so that the columns of Musarithms do not only precisely correspond to words of two, three, or four syllables. Instead, every single one of these can correspond to every imaginable polysyllabic word. Thus, the Musarithms of the first column can be adapted to words of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or however many syllables you wish, whether they have a long or short penultimate syllable, through either joined or disjoined Pleonasm. The same must be said for the Musarithms of the III and IV columns. However, the matter will become clearer by looking at the proposed examples.

Suppose, therefore, that this two-syllable Musarithm, "5. 1.", is represented in notes as follows; strictly speaking, this Musarithm only corresponds to two-syllable words. But we assert here that it can be applied to any given polysyllabic word, which we demonstrate thus: If you wish to apply it first to a three-syllable word, you can carry this out in multiple ways by doubling either the number or the note, in this manner:

->Example 1.<-
<note>A musical staff shows two voices. The upper voice consists of two notes (G and A) and the lower voice consists of two notes (C and D). Below the staff, the numbers 5 and 1 are aligned with these vertical pairs of notes, representing a basic two-syllable musical building block.</note>

->### Example II.<-
<note>A musical staff displays four different rhythmic applications of the word "Plaudite" (Applaud). 
1. Three notes with the numbers 5 5 1 below the word "Plaudite". 
2. Three notes with numbers 5 1 1, where the last two notes are grouped under a Roman numeral III, below "Plaudite". 
3. Three notes with numbers 5 5 1, with the last two grouped under a III, below "Plaudite". 
4. Three notes with numbers 5 1 1 below "Plaudite".</note>

You see in the second example that a three-syllable word with a short penultimate, shown in the word *Plaudite* <note>Latin: "Applaud" or "Clap."</note>, is expressed through the Musarithm 5. 1. if you double the first number of this Musarithm in this way: 5 5 1, and then apply whatever rhythmic notes correspond to this "foot." In this way, all the series of those <term>meter-measures</term> <note>original: "metrometrarum"; the values determining the length of the notes.</note> contained in Table II of the first Section at the end of the second column can be applied to this three-syllable word with a short penultimate. Again, let the Musarithm 5 1 be proposed, to be applied to a three-syllable word with a long penultimate; this will be done if you apply the rhythmic notes shown at the bottom of the second column of Table I in Section I, by multiplying the Musarithm as 5 5 1, as the third example here teaches.

Book VIII. Miraculous Musurgy.

## Example III.

<note>The illustration shows musical notation for two voices. Above the staves are the markers III, I, III, I. The lyrics below the staves are "Victori Victori" (To the victor, to the victor). To the right of the staves is the text: "The same Pleonasm under different notes."</note>

In the same way, if you double the last note of the proposed <term>Musarithm</term> <note>A numerical sequence in Kircher's system that dictates musical intervals.</note> 5 1 in this manner: 5 1 1, or 5 8 8, and then apply the notes to the Musarithmic numbers according to the quantity <note>The rhythmic duration of syllables (long or short) in Latin meter.</note> of the three-syllable word by the method shown a little earlier, as is clear in this example; you will have another variation.

## Example IV. Through Joined Pleonasm.

<note>The illustration shows musical notation for four voices in two sections. The first section is labeled "pen. br." (<term>penultima brevis</term> <note>original: "penultima brevis"; a word where the second-to-last syllable is short.</note>) with lyrics "Plaudite Plaudite" (Applaud, applaud). The second section is labeled "pen. lo." (<term>penultima longa</term> <note>original: "penultima longa"; a word where the second-to-last syllable is long.</note>) with lyrics "Victori Victori" (To the victor, to the victor).</note>

If, however, you wish to proceed through a whole or "joined" <term>Pleonasm</term> <note>The technique of repeating notes or intervals to expand a melody.</note>, you will double the entire three-syllable Musarithm 5 1, so that first the Musarithmic number is similarly tripled, in this way: 5 5 5 1 1 1. Then, you can add <term>metrometric</term> notes <note>Rhythmic templates found in the system's reference tables.</note> to these numbers at your pleasure, choosing from those contained in the cited columns according to the quantity of the three-syllable word, as shown in the example. This repetition must be multiplied in an equal proportion of numbers across the Musarithms of all the remaining voice parts, as is clear in the Musarithm we have taken up.

A <term>melothesia</term> <note>The art or process of musical composition.</note> will then emerge, either through joined intervals, as in the first example, or through discrete intervals, as is clear in the other.

You see, therefore, the replication of an eight-syllable phrase composed four times according to the four numbers of the Musarithm made in the first example; in the second, however, the same replication occurs, but separately. For the notes of the first Musarithm correspond to five notes <note>four musical notes with stems up</note> in the D of the bass. The notes of the second Musarithm correspond to three in G <note>three musical notes with stems up</note>. To the third correspond five others <note>five musical notes with stems up</note> in C and three others in F. Finally, the notes of the fourth Musarithm correspond. We have excerpted the last florid period from Column VI of the second <term>Syntagma</term> <note>A systematic collection or section of his musical tables.</note>, which contains florid Musarithms for eight-syllable words, to achieve a greater harmony in the song. This will always be done best if, after the Musarithms have been multiplied and repeated in a given ratio, we then insert a florid and artistic <term>clausula</term> <note>A musical cadence or concluding phrase.</note> responding to the multi-syllable word, as we shall now discuss.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...should occur, which does not abound in repetitions of this kind. So that musicians are not forced to repeat the entire context of words for every repetition, they are accustomed to place signs such as *ij.* or *iij.* <note>These are standard shorthand signs in 17th-century music notation indicating that the preceding text or musical phrase should be repeated.</note> We have also used these in the column of the first <term>pinax</term> <note>A "pinax" is a Greek term for a table or chart; here, it refers to the engraved data tables used in Kircher’s mechanical composing machine.</note> of this part. This is done especially in full <term>pleonasms</term> <note>Kircher uses "pleonasm" to mean the extension or repetition of musical notes to fit a poetic meter.</note> of notes; for instance, in the third series of the third column, this sign is placed twice (*ij. ij.*) for joined pleonasms, to signify that the preceding group of notes ought to be repeated twice. Where *ij. ij. ij.* is placed three times, the preceding group of notes is repeated thrice; and where *ij. ij. ij. ij.* is placed, it signifies it should be repeated four times. However, I would not want you to understand that this repetition is to be performed on the same chord (pitch), but rather upon those chords which the numbers of the <term>Musarithm</term> <note>The mathematical code Kircher used to represent musical intervals.</note> denote, as was shown in the preceding example.

Furthermore, in the notes of an interrupted pleonasm, you will see the notes divided in various ways, yet always according to the quantity of numbers the Musarithm contains. For example: in the 4th column of the 1st table, after the number VII (which marks a short seven-syllable verse), you will find these notes: <note>three minims, one minim, one minim, one minim, one minim</note> subdivided as you see. By this, we show that the first three <note>three minims</note> belong to the first number of the Musarithm; the fourth <note>one minim</note> belongs to the second; the fifth <note>one minim</note> to the third; the sixth <note>one minim</note> to the fourth; and finally, the seventh belongs to the last figure of the Musarithm. The distinctions between notes must be understood in this way. For you will always find as many distinctions as there are notes contained in the Musarithm, and the notes placed within each individual dividing space are to be considered as belonging to that note of the Musarithm indicated by the order. Thus, all notes contained in the first space are considered to belong to the first Musarithm note, all in the second space to the second, and so on for the rest.

## N O T E  I I.

### Regarding the common Ecclesiastical Pleonasm, which is popularly called [Fauxbourdon], but which we call Isobaton.

From these things, it is most clearly evident how <term>Fauxbourdons</term> <note>original: "falsi Bordones," a style of simplified, parallel harmony used in church music for singing psalms.</note> (to use the barbaric term) can be made with almost no effort. Indeed, the whole business can be managed with a single Musarithm of four, five, or any number of digits. Fauxbourdons are nothing other than certain musical cadences of fixed notes, the first note of which is expressed as a <term>long</term> or <term>maxima</term> <note>Musical note values of long duration.</note>, while the remaining following notes transition into a final cadence. This method of chanting is most commonly used in the psalms. Since the verses of psalms are usually in two parts, it follows that all Fauxbourdons are also in two parts—that is, they have two cadences. The first part corresponds to the first part of a psalm verse, and the second part to the second. Care must also be taken that the cadences in Fauxbourdons are not <term>similarly ending</term> <note>original: "ὁμοιόπτωτοι" (homoioptotoi), a Greek rhetorical term applied here to music to mean "having the same ending."</note>; rather, the first should always be assigned a different termination than the second. But let us teach the matter by example.

## NOTE IV.

### Providing an Explanation of Tablet II in the Musurgical Ark.

Tablet II contains florid and skillful <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Mathematical formulas or sets of numbers used in Kircher's system to represent specific musical intervals and rhythms.</note> for two-syllable, three-syllable, and four-syllable words, just as the heading of each column demonstrates. Note, however, that if anyone were to select various Musarithms from this tablet appropriate to the theme, he would indeed produce a skillful harmony; but because of the same and <term>equisonant</term> <note>original Greek: ἰσόφωνα (isophona); referring to intervals that sound identical, which can lead to a repetitive or "judgment-less" sound if not varied.</note> intervals, it would exhibit neither judgment nor would it be especially pleasing to the ears, unless one were to derive a single Musarithm—as was declared in the preceding sections—through various mixtures of tones. For then the harmony would retain its vigor and beauty. This tablet will serve most effectively for skillful and florid <term>clauses</term> <note>Musical cadences or concluding phrases.</note>, to be inserted into a <term>pleonastically</term> <note>In this context, an "expanded" or "repetitive" style used to stretch a short text over more music.</note> derived counterpoint, as is clear in the final period of the paradigm for the first proposition of this [section]. This florid clause beautifully closes a <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of musical composition or the setting of melody to words.</note> derived pleonastically from a single Musarithm; moreover, clauses of this kind can be interspersed everywhere, either at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. Use this caution, however: that the numbers of the base 4 8 and 5 1 should always be applied to the end; while 4 1 applies to the beginning, middle, and end; and the remaining numbers 6 5 and 2 1 are applied only to the beginning and the middle.

## NOTE V.

### Exhibiting the practice of Tablets III, IV, and V in the Musurgical Ark.

In this tablet are contained florid Musarithms most suitable for ecclesiastical chant and the motet style. If anyone, therefore, has the intention to produce a <term>Melothesia</term> in the ecclesiastical style, let him use this tablet especially. Moreover, this tablet has two columns, in each of which Musarithms are displayed along with their corresponding notes. Let it be as follows:

# I HAVE NOTED.

### Exhibiting the practice of Tablets VI, VII, and VIII, which contain the Musarithms of fugues.

This tablet contains the artifices of fugues; therefore, whoever has a mind to perfect a <term>Melothesia</term> <note>A term derived from Greek meaning the "composition or arrangement of melody."</note> with singular eloquence will be able to seek <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's specialized term for the mathematical-musical formulas used in his system.</note> for themselves from this tablet. ## Proposition IV.

In this way, you will hunt for fugues at the <term>ascending fifth</term> <note>original Latin: "hyperdiapente"; a fugue where the following voice enters a fifth higher than the first.</note> or by ascending to the fifth. In this manner, you will seek out fugues at the <term>ascending octave</term> <note>original: "hyperdiapason"</note> and the diatonic octave, as is presented here. If, indeed, the fugue descends, then it is expressed by the prefix *hypo-*; such is the <term>descending octave</term> <note>original: "hypodiapason"</note> fugue, which descends through a complete octave, whether composed of smaller intervals or not. If, however, the fugue ascends, then it is expressed by the particle *hyper-*; for example, an ascending octave fugue is one ascending through an octave, whether composite or simple. Truly, the columns explain the whole business clearly. However, we have intentionally decided to omit the patterns of each individual one, lest the work grow to an immense size.

# NOTE VII.

### Exhibiting the practice of Tablets VIII, IX, and X, which contain the Musarithms of polyphonic voices.

Tablet VIII contains Polyphony, that is, the method by which one can perfect the <term>musical settings</term> <note>original: "melothesias"</note> not only of four voices, but of many—indeed, of as many voices as you wish. We have done this so that our "miraculous music-making" might be perfect in every number, and so that musicians cannot object that we are <term>unmusical</term> <note>original Greek: Άμουσον (*Amouson*), meaning "without the Muses" or lacking in artistic skill.</note>—able to compose four-voice works but unable to reach beyond that. For that reason, we have organized this tablet of Polyphonic works so that one can compose a song of not just 4, but 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, or 16 voices, even if one is entirely unskilled in music, and with the same ease as four-voice works. 

Thus, if anyone has the mind to compose a five-voice song, he can select the appropriate <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical formulas used in his system to represent intervals and rhythms.</note> for himself from the column for five-voice pieces, animate them into matching notes, and he will have what he sought. Likewise, if he selects the same Musarithms from the columns for seven-voice and six-voice pieces, a musical setting for 6 and 7 voices will result. However, since these two polyphonic styles are not as frequently used as those for 4 and 5 voices, we have chosen to omit them and turn our pen to composing eight-voice songs. For an <term>eight-voice work</term> <note>original: "octicinium"</note> is nothing other than a kind of doubled <term>four-voice work</term> <note>original: "quadricinium"</note>, divided into two Choirs; similarly, a 12-voice work is nothing but a tripled four-voice work, distinguished into three choirs, as we demonstrated in the preceding books concerning the "Musical Knot." Truly, he who has well understood the manner of proceeding with eight voices will not be able to remain ignorant of the others, for the method of proceeding is exactly the same in all of them; but let us declare the matter with a single paradigm.

## Proposition V.

### Given a theme of words, to construct an eight-voice musical setting.

Before we proceed further: *Note First*. In this tablet, we could have used Musarithms for multiple voices partly in <term>simple counterpoint</term> <note>A style where all voices move in the same rhythm, note-against-note.</note> and partly in <term>florid</term> or composite counterpoint. Nor should anyone persuade themselves that an eight-voice composition consists in this: that the entire song is continued by the perpetual sounding of eight voices. Far from it! For this would be unpleasant to the ears. Rather, this artifice aims for the two Choirs, into which we distribute the four voices, to follow each other skillfully and with alternating choirs; and when they have followed each other for a little while, then, according to the requirement of the words, all eight sound together. This can be done either at the beginning or in the middle; however, at the end, all must always sound together. And what we have said about eight voices is also to be understood for 12 and 16 voices.

*Note Second*: The divided choirs—or what is the same thing, the four-voice works—can be in either simple or florid counterpoint. Consequently, all the tablets proposed up to this point can serve this polyphonic musical setting. The Musarithms, however, arranged in this present tablet, on-

## Rules to be Observed in Polyphony.

**T**he first: Total Musarithms for <term>Polyphony</term> <note>Music with multiple independent melodic lines.</note> are to be extracted from the appropriate columns; partial ones, however, are taken from the appropriate columns of this table, or from the preceding tables, yet with this caution: that the numbers of the Musarithms for the two basses, the first and the last, must always be the same.

For example, if the last number of the Musarithm of the bass of the first chorus was 8, the first number of the Musarithm of the bass of the second chorus must likewise be 8, or 1. If the last number of the first chorus was 5, the first of the following must similarly be 5. On the <term>musical staff</term> <note>original: "pentagrammio"</note> of the bass of the first chorus, the notes to which the Musarithms respond must be arranged so that the last note of the previous <term>clause</term> <note>A musical phrase or section.</note> is placed precisely beneath the first note of the following clause on the staff of the second chorus bass, in the same key, as is shown here.

# The Consonances and Dissonances of the Great Art
<meta>Header original: Artis Magnæ Consoni, & Dissoni</meta>

...must necessarily accord with the last note of the previous phrase, as has been stated. The bass of the first choir rests for three beats, and while the bass of the first choir sounds, the bass of the second choir likewise rests for three beats. Once these are completed, they intone the final clause <term>homophonously</term> <note>original: "ὁμοφώνως"; meaning in unison or with the same rhythmic movement</note>.

II. In total <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical sequences used in his system to generate harmonies</note>, the two basses must be placed so that they are carried by contrary motions from an octave into a unison, and vice versa, as the final clause demonstrates; nor does it matter if two octaves follow each other immediately, for that is permitted in this case, as was shown in the preceding book.

III. If anyone extracts such Musarithms from the tables (whether of simple or composite counterpoint) and resolves them in the <term>phonotactic system</term> <note>Kircher's term for the rules of arranging sounds</note> so that the last number of the first Musarithm is one and the same as the first number of the second Musarithm, the notes assigned to them will consequently be unisons. For these Musarithms, repeated by alternating choirs, will produce a perfect <term>octicinium</term> <note>A composition for eight voices</note>. Indeed, by variously changing these two Musarithms—now through a mixture of tones, now by a change of notes, and finally by deducing the clauses of both Basses in a <term>pleonastic</term> <note>In this context, referring to the rhythmic subdivision or extension of a musical phrase</note> manner—you will be able to produce even the longest song.

IV. In establishing <term>polyphonic Melothesia</term> <note>The art of composing multi-voiced music</note>, exactly the same rules and canons must be observed which we prescribed at the beginning of this part.

V. The signature of the <term>pentagrams</term> <note>Musical staves</note> in the first Choir is the same as the signature of the pentagrams in the second Choir. For it is nothing other than a replicated <term>quadricinium</term> <note>A four-voice composition</note>. However, if anyone wishes to set one Choir higher than the other, this shall be free to everyone. In that case, the two Choirs must be signed as we have described on the face of the following Musarithmic Ark.

VI. It should also be observed that in polyphonic Musarithms, the number 1 in the bass refers to an octave below, while 8 refers to an octave above. All these things must be noted diligently.

VII. A single Musarithm can serve any polysyllabic words through <term>Pleonasms</term>. For example, let the clause of the preceding paradigm be: *All peoples* <note>original: "Omnes gentes"</note>; this clause can be adapted to all polysyllables through pleonasm. For if you distribute the first and second notes into minims or semiminims while the two last notes remain unchanged, you will have all kinds of polysyllables with a long <term>penultimate</term> <note>The second-to-last syllable of a word</note>. But if you change the penultimate semibreve into these notes <note>Two musical notes are depicted, likely a minim and a semiminim, showing how to subdivide a single rhythmic value into two shorter ones.</note> and divide the remaining preceding notes according to the number of syllables in the occurring period, you will have all kinds of polysyllables with a short penultimate. Truly, you will better perceive our meaning in the following example.

### Corollary.

In this example, it is most clearly evident how even a single <term>Musarithm</term> <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical sequences used in his system to generate harmonies</note> can be <term>pleonastically</term> <note>In this context, referring to the rhythmic subdivision or extension of a musical phrase to fit more syllables</note> adapted to all polysyllabic words, even by one unskilled in Music; provided that he knows the value of the notes perfectly. It is also clear from this single example how all Musarithms of simple or metric counterpoint can be pleonastically derived into any periods of words.

VIII. Musarithms of <term>Florid counterpoint</term> <note>A more complex style of counterpoint involving varied rhythms and decorative notes against a fixed melody</note> can be adapted to any polysyllabic words in a not dissimilar manner. For if one wishes to set a polysyllable with a short <term>penultimate</term> <note>The second-to-last syllable of a word</note>, the penultimate note of any musical clause is to be divided into two equal parts. In other cases, you will be able to distribute simple notes according to the varying quantity of the syllables; meanwhile, observing diligently that you do not alter anything in the <term>syncopated</term> or tied notes. If, however, you wish to change short penultimates into polysyllables with a long penultimate, you will change these notes <note>A sequence of three diamond-shaped musical notes with stems.</note> into these <note>A sequence of two diamond-shaped musical notes with stems, the first of which is dotted.</note> and you will have what you seek.

IX. In Musarithms arranged for alternating Choirs, precisely the same thing must be observed as we prescribed in Rule VII. For they can be pleonastically adapted to any polysyllables; yet with this caution: that you also diligently observe what we prescribed in the first rule.

X. In 12 or 16 voices—or what is the same thing, in 3 or 4 Choirs—you shall proceed as follows: in 12 voices or 3 Choirs, a single Musarithm repeated three times can serve; as is clear in the example of Proposition V. There, the clause "Clap your hands" <note>original: "Plaudite manibus"</note> repeated in the second Choir will give an <term>octicinium</term> <note>A composition for eight voices</note>; if indeed the same were repeated on a <term>palimpsest</term> <note>Here referring to a reusable musical score or template</note> of 12 <term>pentagrams</term> <note>Five-line musical staves</note>, or 3 Choirs, you would have a completed 12-voice clause. But the following example will teach you all things, in which we have placed only the Basses of 4 Choirs.

# CHAPTER IX.

## Concerning the secret of completing a harmonic canon by means of Musarithms.

### PARADOX I.

I will add here another secret of these <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for his mathematical-musical building blocks or algorithms used to generate melodies</note>; although it is of such a nature that it ought not to be made common, being an exceptional and unique secret, I shall nevertheless bring it to light like all the rest, lest I seem to begrudge the public good. Divine goodness will provide even more abundant grace for the discovery of other things. It is as follows. You have seen up to this point how, from the various rearrangements and transpositions of the Musarithmic columns, innumerable types of different harmonies are born. Now I shall show how even in a single <term>quaternary Musarithm</term> <note>A set of four musical sequences</note>—that is, in the individual Musarithms (of which each column contains ten) divided into four voices—the same logic is present. Thus, any Musarithm in any column, which at first appeared to have a simple linear arrangement, possesses a certain circularity and infinity. We know with how much sweat and intense labor musicians have struggled until now, and how they are exhausted in the ingenious construction of <term>harmonic canons</term> <note>A musical piece where a melody is played and then imitated by another voice after a short delay, like a "round" or "row, row, row your boat"</note>. Indeed, a composer is rightly considered more talented than others if he knows how to make such canons harmonize most easily and cleverly. By our new Musarithmic art, we have removed all this labor and provided a way so that, hereafter, nothing is easier than composing canons of this kind. In fact, a single Musarithm can suffice to weave an entire hymn or even the longest song. This is how you shall work: let the four numbers of the Musarithms be extended into a continuum—either in one line or on a five-line staff—starting from the bass, and you will have it finished. It should suffice to have given a single example to grasp the secret. Therefore, let the following be the four series of a single Musarithm which you wish to arrange into a canon.

If you arrange these four series in a line in order, starting from the bass, you will have the canon arranged as follows:

<note>A vertical list displays four seven-digit numbers. To the right of each number is a short sequence of musical notes written in <term>mensural notation</term> <note>A historical system of notation where note values are determined by their diamond or square shapes</note>. To the far right of the middle two lines is the text: "The great secret in Music" <note>original: "Magnum secretum in Musica."</note>.
2314323 [notes]
7532171 [notes] The great secret in Music.
556655 [notes]
534451 [notes]</note>

If you resolve these numbers into the notes of a single voice and four of any kind, you will have the following circular canon, which can be sung without end with excellent and most beautiful harmony.

<note>A musical score is presented on a single five-line staff with a C-clef. The music is written in diamond-shaped mensural notation. Below the staff are the translated lyrics for the hymn: "Hail, star of the sea, God's dear mother and forever Virgin, happy gate of Heaven" <note>original: "Aue maris ſtella Dei mater alma atq; ſemper Virgo, felix Cœli porta."</note>.</note>

The second voice begins after the first following a pause of six beats; the third voice begins after the second following the same amount; the fourth begins the canon after the third with the same number of pauses. This hymn shall be sung in a certain cyclic progression into infinity. The same can be said of any other imaginable Musarithms contained in the tables; so much so that the members of the Musarithm can be swapped at will. I say no more; you have the secret revealed. The shrewd musician will see from this single specimen how he can arrange canons not only for four voices, but for 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, and as many voices as he wishes—a thing which I know not if it ever entered the mind of any musician. And these are the things which I thought should be communicated to musicians, a secret as miraculous as it is of great importance in the whole business of har—

harmonic significance. From this, the immense utility of these <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for his mathematical-musical algorithms</note> is apparent. Even a single Musarithm of simple counterpoint—in which note is simply placed against note without any complex fugal artifice—can nonetheless result in a fugue, and a perpetual one at that. This is rightly considered a musical paradox; to expert musicians, it seems <term>absurd</term> <note>original: ἄτοπον (atopos), meaning out of place or impossible</note>, even impossible, unless the reality itself clearly demonstrated the truth.

Note secondly: Since each individual Musarithm arranged in the preceding tables is capable of forming a <term>Canon</term> <note>A musical piece where a melody is played and then imitated by another voice after a delay</note>, an innumerable and inexhaustible multitude of Canons is born from this very fact. All of these strike the ears of listeners not with distorted harmony, as occurs in many other methods, but with the sweetest sounds.

<margin>2</margin>
### PARADOX II.

<margin>A specimen of artistic <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of musical composition</note> performed by the aid of the new Musarithmic art.</note></margin>

To compose excellently and exactly in any musical style is granted to few musicians, just as God grants this grace to few in any faculty, that they might be excellent in every part. We see that poets excel in either lyric or heroic verse; mathematicians in this or that part of mathematics; doctors in the cure of this or that limb. But to possess an intimate and universal knowledge of every single part of a faculty is granted, as I said, to very few. There are musicians who excel only in the <term>motet</term> <note>Sacred choral music</note> and ecclesiastical style; some in the <term>madrigal</term> <note>Secular vocal music for several voices</note> style; others in dance and orchestral music; and finally, there are those who are strong only in the <term>recitative style</term> <note>A style of singing that mimics the rhythms of speech</note>. 

We, however, in this Musarithmic art of ours, teach another artifice that is altogether admirable and <term>universal</term> <note>original: "Catholicum," meaning all-encompassing or universal</note>, by which anyone, even one unskilled in music, can complete their compositions in any imaginable style. Yet, at the urging of certain Princes and even of musicians themselves, I have decided to wrap this notable secret in deliberate silence, lest something that has been so highly prized by great men should become cheapened by being made public property. Let it suffice to have communicated it to well-deserving Princes either by word of mouth or in private writings. This artifice is entirely different from the preceding ones and requires a perceptive mind to operate well. 

However, lest anyone say that I boast of more than I can prove, I have decided to place here, as a specimen, an ingenious composition which the Illustrious and Reverend Lord Bernardinus Roccius performed with the help of my art. He is a <term>Referendary</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative official</note> to our Holy Lord Pope Innocent X, a man distinguished by his sharp wit and excellence. Although he was unskilled in practical music, he nonetheless completed compositions through the knowledge of our art which can rightly be compared with the works of the greatest masters. 

Among others is the one we place below, in which—so as to omit nothing of the styles, graces, and musical delights—he first wove a short composition in the form of a <term>dialogue</term>. In this, the recitative style responds, beautifully accommodated to the emotions; then follows a most pleasant <term>dyphonia</term> <note>a two-voice section</note>, then a <term>triphonia</term> <note>a three-voice section</note>, always interspersed with symphonies of the <term>hyporchematic</term> <note>dance-like</note> style. Finally, he wove together a harmony of six voices—arranged for four soprano/alto parts and two baritones—as a sort of complement to the whole harmony. In this, he omitted nothing that could be desired in the most polished composition. He saw to it that this was sung more than once in public before the assembly of the most Eminent Cardinals and in various churches, to the great admiration of all and with the applause that it seemed to demand as its right. 

And lest any malicious person might quibble that either my work or that of another was added to help the composer, I have decided to bring forward an eyewitness: Gino Angelo Capponi, a Knight most skilled in music and famous for the works he has published. He stood by the composer, and as soon as the pieces were finished, he reviewed and approved them. It seemed fitting to add all of this here to break the accusations of certain malevolent people. Indeed, the skilled reader will discover what has been achieved better through an inspection of the composition itself than I could explain even in many words.

...lest one ignorant of Music <note>original: "Musicæ"</note> commit an error in the placement of words; for indeed, notes are not assigned to individual syllables of the words as happens in <term>simple counterpoint</term> <note>original: "contrapuncto simplici"; a style where each note corresponds to exactly one syllable</note>. Instead, one syllable is occasionally sustained through various flows of notes, as occurs everywhere in <term>Florid counterpoint</term> <note>original: "contrapuncto Florido"; a decorative style where a single syllable is stretched over many notes, also known as a melisma</note>, finally leaping forward to the next syllable after several <term>measures</term> <note>original: "mensuras"; the basic units of musical time</note> have passed.

Hence, so that the Beginner <note>original: "Tyro"</note> might proceed more safely in this slippery business, you will find dots placed beneath the individual notes that are to be pronounced syllabically. However, where a continued flow of notes corresponds to a single syllable, we have omitted the dots. By this, we intended to indicate that after the last discontinuous dot, the pronunciation of the syllable must be continued until the next dot, to which the following syllable of the word [is assigned]...

**Rule II.** Singular industry must also be applied in selecting the <term>modes</term> <note>original: "tonis"; the specific scales or musical "keys" used in this period, such as Dorian or Phrygian</note>. Modes marked with a "soft" key <note>original: "Toni molli claue signati"; refers to keys or scales using B-flat</note> must be avoided in every way when combined with modes marked with a "hard" key <note>original: "Tonis dura signati"; refers to keys using B-natural or sharps</note>, unless the Composer <note>original: "Artifex"</note> knows how to mix them with the greatest skill on specific occasions. This mixture of Modes is achieved through the following industry: the column of keys must be applied to that specific column which provides a mode suitable for expressing the desired <term>affection</term> <note>original: "affectui"; the specific emotion or mood intended by the music</note>. Once this is done, you should proceed with the composition as before, and you will achieve your goal, provided you carefully note the positions of the semitones, which are indicated by this sign <term>#</term> <note>the sharp sign</note>, as well as by the <term>b</term> <note>the flat sign</note> of the "soft" modes. Because these signs are of great importance in expressing emotions, you must apply the same diligence to them that they demand by their own right. Furthermore, so that the Apprentice <note>original: "Tyro"</note> may know which musical phrases serve which emotions, we have almost always placed letters in the <term>Musarithm</term> columns <note>original: "Musarithmis"; Kircher's term for his mathematical tables used to generate musical compositions</note> that express the aforementioned affections.

**Rule III.** In polyphonic music <note>music consisting of several simultaneous melodies</note>, the Music-maker <term>Musurgus: Kircher's specific term for a composer or user of this musical system</term> should take diligent care regarding the distinction of voices on the composition tablet <term>palimpsesto: here referring to the grid-like musical slates or tables used in Kircher’s mechanical composition method</term>. Indeed, the heading of the columns will beautifully indicate the types of fugues suited to the intended purpose.

# OF MIRACULOUS MUSIC-MAKING

->PART V.<-

## ON MECHANICAL MUSIC-MAKING

->OR<-

### On the various arrangements or transpositions of the mobile Musarithmic <note>original: "Musarithmicarum"</note> columns.

Mechanical music-making <term>Musurgia mechanica; the art of composing music through automated or algorithmic means</term> is nothing other than a certain method invented by us, by which anyone—even an unmusical person <note>original: "ἄμουσος"</note>—can compose songs according to a desired level of craftsmanship through the various applications of song-making <note>original: "Melotheticorum"</note> instruments. We shall hand down this mechanical music-making with as much brevity as possible, and so as not to waste time with a preface, we shall begin with the construction of the Musarithmic Ark <term>Arca Musarithmica; a mechanical "computer" in a box used for generating musical counterpoint</term>.

---

->CHAPTER I.<-

### The Construction of the Musarithmic Ark. See Illustration XIV placed at the start of this book.

We call the "Musarithmic Ark" the container for the Musarithmic columns; we call "Musarithmic columns" the rods—made of wood or paper—upon which the musical ratios <note>original: "Musarithmis"</note> of the tables <note>original: "pinacum"</note> have been separately described. Therefore, you shall prepare the Ark with this diligence: Let a container be made whose length is equal to its height, specifically so that each is one full palm <note>A traditional unit of measure, roughly the width of a hand or about 3–4 inches</note> in size; the width, however, should be half a palm. You will divide this width into three other specific compartments using additional wooden partitions. Let the length of the Ark in the cited illustration <note>Referring to the diagram "Iconismus XIV" mentioned in the chapter heading</note> at AD be one palm; let the height AI or DV correspond to this. Let the width AB or DC be half a palm. The void within AB and DC should be further divided into 3 equal compartments by the partitions GE and FH passing through the middle. Furthermore, the first compartment HB FC is to be divided again into 12 equal parts by small partitions passing transversely through the hollow center, as the 12 cells marked with their own numbers clearly demonstrate. The second compartment GHEF is divided into 6 compartments by small partitions passing transversely through the middle, as the figure shows. The third compartment AGDE is divided into just as many parts or compartments as shown in the figure or Illustration XIV prefixed to this book, in the same order we handed down at the beginning of this part and as appears here. On the side DC, you will take care to make other compartments, as LM demonstrates; in these, you will place the Musarithmic columns of the tones according to the order described in the Tonal-Writing Table <note>original: "menfa Tonographica"</note>, as the illustration shows.

---

->CHAPTER II.<-

### Concerning the Musarithmic columns, and the arrangement of them in the compartments of the prepared chest.

First, take all the tables <note>original: "pinaces"</note> of simple counterpoint, 12 in number. On separate columns of these tables, on rods of paper or even wood, several times...

...you will transcribe these four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten times; however, we have described each column here only four times. For example, System I contains only twelve tables <note>original: "pinaces"</note>, each of which contains ten columns. The first table contains polysyllabic words with a long penultimate syllable; the second table contains polysyllables with a short penultimate syllable. <margin>The arrangement of the Tables in the Musurgic area.</margin> Therefore, you shall transcribe each column of these tables several times, together with the meter-measuring notes annexed at the bottom of the column. This must be done so that all columns have an absolutely equal division—that is, the cells in which the Musical Ratios <term>Musarithmi; numerical sequences representing musical intervals and rhythms</term> are to be written must all be equal. For if they were unequal, the application of the columns, however it was done, would not be free from errors. This equality must be observed not only in the columns of the first System, but also in the columns of the second and third Systems—in short, in every column whatsoever. 

But since the columns of different tables have an unequal number of cells—some have 9 transverse rows, while others have only 8—I would advise the Music-maker <note>original: "Musurgo"</note>, so that the device turns out more elegantly, to divide each column into ten cells. Then, in the empty spaces, he should write whatever Musical Ratios he wishes to be repeated in that same column (nothing is easier). In this way, all columns will obtain an equal number of cells, and the device will turn out more perfect in every respect. Once the small columns have been formed from thick paper or wood, and the Musical Ratios have been written upon them in the order described, you will insert them into their own specific receptacles. For example: in the first cell of the twelve-fold section <term>dodecamorion; a division of twelve parts</term> AC (for so we have chosen to name that part of the chest which is divided into 12 cells for Simple Counterpoint), in the first cell of this, I say, let the wooden rods <note>original: "bacilli vel taxilli"</note> or paper columns of the first table be placed. In the second cell, the columns of the second table. In the third, the columns of the third table, multiplied several times. In the fourth cell, the columns of the fourth table, also multiplied; and so on for the others in order, down to the last column of the table.

In the second six-fold section <term>Hectamorio; a division of six parts</term> or space marked GHEF, you will place in order the columns of the second System for poetic florid counterpoint, transcribed several times onto paper or wooden rods. The first cell will serve for Adonic and Dactylic meters; the second for Euripidean Iambics, and so on for the rest in order, as the description of the Ark teaches.

In the third six-fold section of the Ark, likewise divided into six parts for System III, you will insert all the columns in order. Inside the lid <note>original: "coöperculum"</note> which closes the Ark, you will store the Musical Ratio columns of the tones <note>The "tones" refer to the church modes or scales</note>, described separately, together with the summary two-part column <note>original: "columna dimera epitomica"</note>. You shall attach a specific lid to each receptacle, on the outermost surface of which the title of the columns hidden therein should be written, the use of which will become known shortly. And thus you will have an Ark perfect in all its parts; the use follows.

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

But so that you may better perceive our meaning, we shall give here a glimpse of various transpositions. ### Corollary I.

<margin>The multitude of combinations</margin>
From this arrangement, the infinite multitude of combinations is clear, which can result from the various dispositions of these five columns. These are certainly so great that if some Angel had begun to combine them from the beginning of the world, he would not yet have finished them today; this is shown most clearly from the demonstrations in the first part of this book. <note>Kircher often uses the metaphor of an "Angel" or a vast span of time to illustrate the combinatorial explosion of his mechanical systems, emphasizing that the possibilities are practically infinite.</note>

### Corollary II.

Therefore, from this single paradigm, it is clear how one should proceed in all other chosen themes, for the method of operating is no different in the rest.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Regarding the arrangement of columns belonging
### to Poetic Music.

<margin>The use and application of the tables contained within the Musurgical Ark.</margin>
Just as in the preceding example we arranged the columns of polysyllables <note>words of many syllables</note> in order to bring any context of words to life in harmony, so now we shall teach the method by which the metric columns inscribed in the "musurgia" <note>the composition machine</note> ought to be arranged. It must be noted first that if the chosen theme is a single-meter multi-stanza poem <term>polystrophon monocolon; a poem with many stanzas all using the same poetic meter</term>, all the columns are to be selected from the same compartment. For example, if someone were to take an Anacreontic six-stanza poem as a theme, he will join six columns taken from the fourth compartment of the twelve-part space <term>dodecamorium; a division of the Ark into twelve sections</term> according to the order of the six verses, combined in any way; and then one should proceed according to the rules handed down in the preceding part, and the desired musical setting for the Anacreontic six-stanza poem will come forth. In the same way, you will compose any kind of single-meter multi-stanza verse. If, however, the theme of words is multi-stanza with different meters <term>polystrophon; here meaning a poem composed of different types of verse</term>, then columns must be selected from the cells inscribed with the said meters. But the matter will become clearer by an example.

## CHAPTER V.

### Regarding florid poetic Musarithms.

<margin>The part of the Musarithmic Ark dedicated to elaborate music.</margin>
The sixth-part <term>hectamorium; a division of the ark representing one-sixth of the total space</term> space **GHFE** contains the poetic Musarithms <term>Musarithmi; the fundamental musical units or "musical numbers" used in Kircher's system to represent intervals and rhythms</term> of florid music. On each of the lids of these compartments is written the title or type of meter which the Musarithms serve. If anyone, for example, wished to compose a Sapphic verse <note>A classical poetic meter named after the Greek poet Sappho, typically consisting of three long lines and one short "Adonic" line.</note> in the florid style, let him first take from the last compartment of the sixth-part three columns corresponding to the three Sapphic single-meter lines; then, from the first compartment of the same sixth-part, take one column for the Adonic verses <note>original: *Adoniis*; short verses consisting of a dactyl and a spondee, used to conclude a Sapphic stanza.</note>. Once these are arranged in order, determine any transverse sequence of Musarithms in the columns, combined in whatever way you wish, and proceed according to the rules handed down, and you will have what you sought.

### Corollary I.

### On the Mixing of Poetic Musarithms.

If, however, you mix the columns of simple counterpoint <term>contrapunctum simplex; basic note-against-note harmony</term> contained in the twelve-part <term>dodecamorium; a division representing one-twelfth of the ark's space</term> space with the columns contained in the sixth-part space, a musical setting will be produced that is composed of the wandering florid, the elaborate, and the simple styles, provided you always most diligently observe the rules handed down in the preceding sections. The matter is clearer than it deserves to be declared at greater length.

### Corollary II.

From these things it is clearly evident in how many infinite ways even a single song can be changed. But I leave these things to be further weighed by the ingenious student <note>original: *Tyroni*; a beginner or recruit, here meaning a student of the musical art.</note>.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

(as was said in the preceding parts) wherefore we have extended the Musarithms <term>Musarithmi; the fundamental musical units or "musical numbers" used in this system</term> in the columns even up to five syllables. If you desire to proceed in the motet and ecclesiastical style, columns extracted from receptors II and III will give the result. Furthermore, if you wish to adorn a song with more than four voices, columns extracted from receptor V will provide your intent, provided you diligently observe the rules prescribed in the preceding sections concerning the composition of polyphony <term>polyphoniorum; multi-voiced musical works</term>.

But if you arrange columns extracted from the three spaces in a mixed fashion according to the logic of the theme, you will have a musical setting <term>Melothesia; the art of melody-making or composition</term> that is entirely varied and filled with infinite combinations. Truly, since these and similar matters have been discussed extensively in the preceding pages, I did not wish to be longer in recounting them here. Instead, we shall move forward to the description of other instruments.

# APPENDIX.
### Presenting new methods of composing.

## METHOD I.

### Musurgical Rabdology, or a description of the Musurgical Abacus.

<margin>Expanded Abacus. Contracted Abacus.</margin>
With any line divided into 8 equal spaces, let a square be drawn with all its small areas, of which you will have 64. In these, you shall inscribe the keys or musurgical letters in that order which you see done here, and the Musurgical Abacus <term>Abacus Musurgicus; a calculating grid for musical intervals</term> will be described; and this we call the **expanded Abacus**. You shall construct the **contracted Abacus** in this way: Let a certain parallelogram be made, whose long side equals 8 spaces; let the smaller side be divided into 4, and with lines drawn, there will be 32 cells or squares. In each column, let only those letters be placed which are marked with numbers; and you will have the sought-after contracted Abacus, which, like the expanded abacus, you will be able to multiply into various other columns. Indeed, examine the example.

# Proposition I.

->**Given a base in notes, to compose the remaining voices above it:**<-

<note>A musical stave contains seven notes. Above the notes are the numbers 1 through 7, indicating their order. Below the notes are the letter-names representing their pitches: F, B, G, D, B, C, F.</note>

You see, therefore, in this combination that the horizontal series **NO** contains the voice of the Tenor or the composed Soprano <term>Cantus; the highest voice in a polyphonic composition</term>, specifically in **C B B A B G F**. By the same method, you will extract the third voice through the repeated rearrangement <term>Metathesis; the mathematical transposition or reordering of elements</term> of the rods. Truly, although this artifice is by no means to be compared with the secret artifice of the *Musarithms* <note>Musarithms were Kircher's specific combinatorial units of music, which he considered more advanced than these mechanical rods</note>, I wished to attach it to these pages so that nothing might seem to have escaped us in this "Great Art."

We derive this artifice by means of a double Abacus <term>Abacus; here referring to a tabular calculating device for music</term>: the **Expanded Abacus** and the **Contracted Abacus**. ## Proposition II.
### Given a Bass voice, to build any number of voices above it.

<margin>The practice of composition from the counterpoint table.</margin>
If the musical phrase <term>clausula; a short melodic fragment or cadence</term> of the Bass voice is the same as the preceding one, you shall place it on the sound-arranging five-line staff <term>phonotactico pentagrammio; Kircher’s term for a musical staff designed for his mechanical system</term> for the Bass, marked with the same notes and clefs, just as was done in the previous operation. Once this is completed, since the first note is in **F**, look for the **F** column at the head of the Table. Then, in the Soprano <term>Cantus; the highest voice</term> staff, select any point along with its assigned number, and transfer this to the Soprano staff of your erasable slate <term>palimpsest; a reusable writing surface used for drafting the composition</term>. Next, from the Alto staff, simply transfer any point and its number to the Alto staff of the slate. Similarly, transfer any point and its corresponding number from the Tenor staff to the staff on the slate. Once these points are transferred, and since the second note of the phrase is **B**, take column **B** in the Table and proceed as before. Then take the column marked **G**, and proceed likewise with the remaining notes of the phrase until you have completed the whole piece. Always observe, in the meantime, that two **88s** <note>original: "duæ 88"; referring to the interval of an octave. In traditional music theory, moving two voices in parallel octaves was considered an error</note> or two **55s** <note>original: "duæ 55"; referring to the interval of a fifth. Like parallel octaves, parallel fifths were generally forbidden in counterpoint</note> do not immediately follow one another in different voices. When these points have been transferred, if you place the same notes of the Bass phrase above the points in each individual voice, the desired composition <term>Melothesia; the art of setting a melody or composing harmony</term> will result. It should also be noted that the intervals of the voices ought to be unified as much as possible, avoiding all discordant cadences.

Truly, these things are so easy that they may be grasped at first glance; therefore, let us proceed further.

### §. I.
### Preparation of the Erasable Slate.

<margin>The marking of the Scepters.</margin>
On the sound-arranging slate, 32 parallel lines should be drawn; let them be exactly equidistant in their spacing. Once this is done, mark the fifth line from the bottom with the character <note>An illustration shows the Treble or G-clef positioned on a segment of a two-line musical staff.</note>. Mark the thirteenth line with this character <note>An illustration shows the C-clef, used for middle voices like the Alto, on a two-line staff segment.</note>. Mark the twentieth line with the same character <note>An illustration shows another C-clef, likely for the Tenor part.</note>. Finally, mark the twenty-seventh line with this character <note>An illustration shows the Bass or F-clef on a two-line staff segment.</note>, or the twenty-ninth line with this character <note>An illustration shows the F-clef on a three-line staff segment.</note>. When this is also finished, you shall place the clefs for the individual voices on the sound-arranging slate; those lines that terminate the individual five-line staves for the voices should be drawn with thicker lines, as is clear in the paradigm shown below, and the slate will be prepared. Above this, the musical rods <term>plectra; here referring to the sliding wooden strips of the machine</term> will then be applied to complete the compositions, as we shall teach shortly.

### §. I. Designing the Scepters of the Muses.

Nine parallelograms should be made of wood or thick paper in the form of rods <note>original: "plectrorum," referring to the long, thin strips used as sliders in the machine</note>; you will apply these in order over the lines of the template <note>original: "palimpsesti," here referring to the ruled musical staff template described previously</note> prepared a little earlier. You shall draw lines on each rod in the same order and distance as was done on the template; they must correspond to the lines beneath them so that, however they are applied, they match perfectly. Furthermore, each scepter should be "serrated"—that is, they should have protruding points at the top. The tips of these points must have the exact same distance between them as the parallel lines have from each other, and you will then have what is required. 

We have named the first scepter the **Scepter of Thalia**, and it contains the musical phrases <note>original: "clausulas," the standard melodic endings or building blocks</note> for Adonic verses or Polysyllables. 
The second is the **Scepter of Terpsichore**, containing phrases for Euripidean Iambics, or six-syllable verses. 
The third is the **Scepter of Melpomene**, containing phrases for Anacreontic verses, also of six syllables. 
The fourth is the **Scepter of Clio**, containing phrases for Archilochian Iambics, or eight-syllable verses. 
The fifth is the **Scepter of Euterpe**, containing phrases for Alcmanic Iambics, or nine-syllable verses. 
The sixth is the **Scepter of Calliope**, containing phrases for Iambic Trimeters of ten syllables. 
The seventh is the **Scepter of Polyhymnia**, containing phrases for Phalaecian or eleven-syllable verses. 
The eighth is the **Scepter of Erato**, containing phrases for Sapphic verses. 
The ninth is the **Scepter of Urania**, containing phrases for Choriambic twelve-syllable verses.

<margin>
Arrangement and multiplication of the scepters.
</margin>

There are, therefore, nine "Musurgical" scepters, each of which you will multiply by ten. Thus, there will be ten scepters for Thalia, ten for Terpsichore, ten for Melpomene, and so on for the rest; in total, there will be ninety scepters, with which you can easily master the whole business of music through this industrious method. 

Let some learned and skilled composer <note>original: "Melotheta," a term Kircher uses for a creator of melodies</note> compose twenty highly ingenious musical phrases for the five-syllable Adonic meter. For the sake of brevity, we show only one of these here for each of the nine scepters: specifically, ten phrases for **simple counterpoint** and ten for **florid** and artistic counterpoint. The simple version will be placed on one side of the scepter, and the artistic version on the opposite side. 

Again, he shall compose twenty phrases for the six-syllable Euripidean meter, and so on for each polysyllabic meter in order, composing twenty harmonic phrases: ten for simple counterpoint and ten for artistic counterpoint. He shall compose all these phrases based on one determined tone <note>or musical mode</note>, and then inscribe each one on its respective scepter. Thus, he will write the Adonic phrases on one face of the ten scepters of Thalia, and the artistic phrases on the other face of the same scepters. 

In **simple counterpoint**, the phrases should be marked only by their points <note>simple dots indicating pitch without complex rhythmic notation</note>, as you see done here in the example of the nine rods. However, in **florid counterpoint**, you must inscribe the actual musical notes of the phrases onto their rods, as was done on the second scepter of Terpsichore. 

The reason why we show simple counterpoint only with dots is that in simple counterpoint—being <term>isochronous</term> <note>original: "ἰσοχρόνῳ," meaning "equal in time," where every note has the same duration</note> and always proceeding with equal movement of the voices—dots are suitable for representing any form of note. From the twelve series of "rhythm-measuring" notes <note>original: "notarum metrometrarum"</note> contained at the end of the tables in the first volume, you can apply any one of them here. Thus, in the column for Adonics in the cited place, twelve series of notes can each be applied to the said dots. This is not possible in florid counterpoint, however, because the voices proceed with unequal timing. Therefore, the complete phrases, along with their specific notes, must be inscribed on each rod. 

Once the phrases have been inscribed on the ninety rods, you will store them in a chest <note>the Ark</note>, constructed according to the standard of the "Musarithmic Ark," for the use which we shall now explain.

->The Use of the Scepter-Logic of the Muses.<-

<margin>
The use of the sliders <note>original: "plectrorum," referring here to the sliding rods of the machine</note> in changing musical Tones.
</margin>

First, it should be noted that this device is so constructed that the teeth or tips at the base of the scepter—no matter how or where they are applied to the key-spaces on the underlying template <note>original: "palimpsesto," referring to the reusable master grid or musical staff</note>—will always result in a new harmony of 4 voices. For example: if the last tooth of Thalia's rod is applied to the phonotactic template above F, all the remaining voices will produce a harmony in the sixth tone. If you apply the said tooth above the key of G on the template, you will have another musical arrangement <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note>, namely a four-part song in the second tone. If you apply the said tip again above A, you will have another four-part arrangement in the ninth tone, and so on for the rest. By changing the position of the base, all the other voices will change their positions proportionally.

Second, it should be noted that one side of the scepters holds the phrases <note>original: "clausulas"</note> of simple counterpoint, while the other side holds the phrases of florid <note>ornamented</note> counterpoint. We have displayed the phrases of simple counterpoint with dots alone for the reason handed down a little earlier; however, we have marked each of the florid phrases with their own specific notes, as appears on the slider of Terpsichore, the reason for which we likewise gave in the preceding sections. With these things observed, if anyone has the intention of creating a musical arrangement over a given theme, he will arrange the columns or sliders <note>original: "plectra"</note> of the Muses according to the order of the syllables with exactly the same industriousness as was done in the Musarithmic composition method. For example, let the theme be the following:

<margin>
The practice to be established.
</margin>

> *Serve God, all kings of the earth, for honor alone suits Him*; <note>original: "Servite Deo omnes Reges terræ, quia hunc solum decet honor"</note>

The first phrase, *Serve God* [*Servite Deo*], corresponds to the five-syllable Adonic meter on Thalia's slider; the second phrase, *All kings of the earth* [*Omnes Reges terræ*], corresponds to the six-syllable Euripidean meter on the second slider of Terpsichore; the third phrase, *for honor alone suits Him* [*hunc solum decet honor*], corresponds to the slider of Melpomene, namely the seven-syllable Anacreontic meters. We have chosen three sliders following one another in order so that we would not be forced to make another separate description.

Once the sliders are thus placed in order, you shall begin the composition in this manner: First, select whichever of the 12 tones you wish. We shall here select the sixth, which, since it ends in F (from what was demonstrated above when we explained the Tone-graphical Table), you will apply the last tooth of the base on Thalia’s slider above the lower F, and the other two sliders in this order, and you will have a perfect musical arrangement.

For if you press dots into the phonotactic template in those spaces that correspond and match with the points of the phrases described on the sliders, and then overlay the marked points with one of the twelve series of rhythmic notes <note>original: "notarum metrometrarum"</note> contained at the bottom of column I, table III, of the first section, the desired composition will emerge. And if you wish to mix an artistic phrase with the simple ones, turn the slider over, as was done with the second slider of Terpsichore. For if you then describe the notes of the individual voices in the corresponding spaces of the template without changing the position, you will have the artistically arranged phrase you were seeking. You shall proceed in no different a way for all other periods. Since we have shown in the preceding sections that it would be unpleasant to the ears if the phrases always had the same final cadence from C to F, you will easily avoid this if you observe what we have handed down extensively regarding the change or mixture of tones in the preceding part. For if, for example, you set the last tooth of the second slider for a florid phrase above G on the template, the phrase will immediately migrate from the 6th tone into the 2nd, and thus the desired variety will be born. For as I said a little before, the last tooth of the base applied above different notes in the base will always produce more and more new melodies. However, you must observe the rule handed down previously: namely, that the first and last phrases of the song must always be in the same tone, but you may vary the middle ones as you please. Once all these things are observed, the following melody will finally appear on the template.

You see from this varied paradigm how one must proceed in the rest of the cases. However, for a greater understanding of our invention, certain things must be studiously observed.

## §. IV.

->Cautions and observations to be applied.<-

I. **T**he sliders <note>original: "plectra," referring to the wooden rods used in Kircher's composing machine</note>, once applied, should be so firmly fixed upon the template <note>original: "palimpsestum," the underlying grid or musical staff</note> that they do not move even a hair's breadth from their place; otherwise, the entire business of the harmony would collapse.

II. For in the present paradigm, while the second phrase <note>original: "clausula"</note> moves from the sixth tone into the second, it encounters these ♯ and ♭ signs in certain places. To ensure everything is arranged properly, and so you may know exactly where such signs should be placed, proceed as follows.

<columns>2</columns>

Since none of these occur, you need not be concerned with placing such signs; for you will have this as a most certain sign that the tone is incapable of receiving them. # §. V.

->On the comparison between Musarithmic Musurgy and this plectrology.<-

<margin>The difference between Musarithmics and Plectrology.</margin>
These two musurgical inventions first devised by us relate to each other as that which exceeds and that which is exceeded. The Musarithmic invention taught in the preceding part is the most universal and filled with incredible variety; yet this current method <note>the plectrology or slider system</note> is much more splendid, ingenious, and finished. Although this plectrology is not as universal as the previous one, it has the advantage of being concise, easy, and—without any prior application of a tone-column to a key-column—it immediately shows the movement of any voice on its musical staves. However, it has this disadvantage: on one side of a slider, only a single musical phrase can be described, which corresponds to one of our four-voice Musarithms <note>mathematical musical units</note> arranged for four voices.

Hence, to make the invention more universal, more material would be supplied to the pious composer <term>Melothete: a composer of melodies or music</term>. If someone were to multiply the sliders to 300, they could reach the level of the previous Musarithmic art. It should also be noted that if someone were to have as many sliders made as there are Musarithms contained in the tables of the three Syntagmas <note>large collections or volumes of musical data</note>, and transferred each of the Musarithms from the tables onto corresponding sliders, they would possess a plectrology just as extensive as the Musarithmic invention. I have chosen to declare these things more fully here so that the reader might see how to bring this kind of plectrology to the highest perfection and make it completely universal. 

But let these things be reserved for those who have more leisure and who profess this skill. For us, distracted by an infinite variety of the most disparate occupations, it was no small feat to have invented these things, to have calculated each Musarithm through our own industry, and to have performed other things which posterity—unless I am mistaken—will admire, despite the smallness of my talent. These are seeds which I have no doubt will grow into most abundant sprouts through the continuous irrigation of others following me. And with these things, together with GOD, to whose goodness we ascribe all things, we bring an end to our Wonderful Musurgy.

## P R E F A C E.

Having put forth all those things which seemed to pertain in any way to speculative and practical Music, I thought it worth the effort if in this place I also gave a specimen of certain things which, by the help of Music, can be done in the secret science of sounds, which are altogether wonderful. But lest we proceed in so unusual a work in a disorderly fashion <note>original Greek: ἀτάκτως (ataktōs), meaning without order or discipline</note>, it seemed fit to divide this book into six parts; in which:

*The first part, the Physiology <note>the study of the natural properties</note> of Harmony and Dissonance, thoroughly investigates the secret power latent in Harmony and Dissonance.*

<margin>The study of wonders <note>original Greek: τερατολογία (teratologia)</note>.</margin>
