Book IX. The Magic of Harmony and Dissonance:

# PART I.
# THE PHYSIOLOGY OF HARMONY
# AND DISSONANCE
# CHAPTER I.

->On the Miraculous Power of Music.<-

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'M' is adorned with architectural and floral motifs.</note>

We say that the magic of harmony and dissonance is nothing other than that faculty which produces marvelous sounds, which surely holds no small place among the other species of natural magic. For there is in certain sounds such an admirable power both of altering and attracting that the human intellect seems scarcely able to reach a genuine understanding of their nature. No one is unaware of how much magnetism <note>In this context, "magnetism" refers to a natural force of attraction or "sympathy" between things, rather than just physical magnets.</note> exists in musical melodies, or how great the efficacy of their attractive power is; so that it was not without reason that the ancients presented Orpheus as a Musical Mage, drawing animals, forests, and even the very rocks by the magical sound of his lyre. Concerning this, Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a Latin poet.</note> writes quite elegantly in the preface of the second book of *The Rape of Proserpine* in these words:

> Then the bard, rejoicing in the festive time of his fatherland,
> Returned to the melodious strings of his long-neglected Lyre;
> And sitting down, having tuned the strings with a gentle quill,
> He guided the noble ivory with a festive thumb.
> Scarcely had he been heard, when the winds and waves were stilled;
> Rhodope <note>A mountain range in the Balkans.</note> extended her mountains, thirsting for his songs,
> And Ossa, more prone to shaking off its cold snows, grew still.
> The tall poplar descended from the bared Haemus,
> And the friendly Pine drew the oak along as a companion.
> Even though the laurel had despised the arts of the god of Phyrrhean <note>Referring to Apollo, the god of music.</note>,
> It came, suited to the voices of Orpheus.
> The flattering hounds saw the hare without harm,
> And the lamb offered its side to the neighboring wolf.
> Harmonious does play with the spotted tiger,
> And the stags did not fear the Massylian mane <note>A poetic reference to a lion's mane from North Africa.</note>.

<margin>What the attraction of stones performed by Orpheus signifies.</margin>
This prodigious attraction of animals, forests, and rocks is to be understood partly figuratively and partly allegorically. For the ancients noted that the greatest power of Music is upon the soul, and that the soul is changed according to its various sounds and harmonies, following them like wax, however you might mold it. Therefore, they called Music the "beginning of all things" <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴν πάντων (archēn pantōn)</note>, and as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar.</note> says in his *Music*: "The ancients held that music binds the whole universe together" <note>original Greek: τὴν μουσικὴν οἱ πάλαιοι συνέχειν ἅπαν τὸ πᾶν (tēn mousikēn hoi palaioi synechein hapan to pan)</note>. Furthermore, they saw that the same Music could compose and vary one's character; for nothing flows so easily into tender and soft souls as various musical sounds. It can hardly be said how great their power is in either direction: for it both incites the listless and makes the agitated grow calm; it now relaxes the mind, and then contracts it, as will be declared more fully hereafter. Therefore, he led the rocks, forests, and animals—that is, men who were utterly senseless, beastly, and monstrous in their cruelty—back to humanity and a civilized way of living, attracted by the divine sound of his Lyre. Others, however, understand the said attraction allegorically when...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "magnetic" or attractive power of music, transitioning from the general legend of Orpheus to specific historical and natural examples of music's influence on the cosmos, the human soul, and even physical health.</meta>

# Universal Music-Making

For they say that Orpheus was a distinguished Astrologer and Musician, perfectly skilled in both arts, and that he so opportunely tempered and mixed sounds that he might best understand and imitate the harmony of the celestial stars. He provoked the celestial harmony toward this earthly one in such a way that he drew into himself all their influx and power; relying on this, he could draw and determine whatever he wished by playing his lyre. Some also add that since he knew perfectly by what proportion and what harmony each thing was constituted and composed by nature—and which star each thing obeyed and was subject to—he adapted musical ratios to those stars. By their motion, he would lure inanimate things through the power of the stars, which he would, as it were, draw out from where it lay hidden within them by his own external harmony. This is not unlike how iron strikes hidden fire out of flint, or how the blast of a bellows brings forth hidden flame. For there are in all things certain "latent little sparks," as it were, and seeds of harmony or sense; so much so that the ancients even said God himself was the <note>original: ἁρμονίαν πάντων</note> harmony of all things.

<margin>The power of harmony lies hidden in all things.</margin>
Hence, by the authority of Proclus, <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who believed the entire universe was connected through "sympathies."</note> all things compose hymns to the Leaders of their Order; but some do so intellectually, some rationally, some naturally, and others by sense alone. And indeed, if anyone (he says) could hear the vibration which individual things produce in the air in a circle—such as solar things toward the sun, and lunar things toward the moon—he would surely perceive a certain sound of that kind, aptly composed toward their King, whatever kind each individual thing is able to produce.

<margin>The power of Music over human minds.</margin>
The magnetic power of Music, therefore, which moves all things, is well known for how much it can achieve in human beings. For no heart can be so harsh and wild that it is not softened by apt melodies and songs that soothe the soul; conversely, by unseemly and discordant sounds, the soul is tightened and restrained. Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and philosopher of ancient Greece.</note> brought forth song as the sweetest thing given to mortals from heaven, soothing all things. In war, drums resound to add courage to those about to battle; trumpets and flutes echo to arouse the spirits of soldiers in fighting. Timotheus the Musician, whenever he pleased, so inflamed the mind of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note> with the Phrygian mode <note>An ancient musical scale associated by the Greeks with martial energy and excitement.</note> that, driven wild, he would run to arms; and when he wished otherwise, by changing the tone, he suppressed the ferocity of his mind and drew his softened spirit to feasts and banquets. Something similar is read concerning a certain Lutenist of the King of Denmark. Did not Pythagoras—according to the testimony of Cicero—render peaceful and mild a certain youth of Tauromenium who was spurred on by insane love, as if by a gadfly, by the sounding of a spondee? <note>A "spondee" is a slow, solemn musical foot consisting of two long syllables.</note> Certainly, Theophrastus is said to have employed musical sounds to restrain the impulses and disturbances of the mind. The histories of the Trojans tell of Clytemnestra, who was incited to continence and modesty by a Lutenist left behind for that reason by Agamemnon. Plutarch testifies of himself that he was so inflamed by the harmonic modes of a certain Lutenist that, seizing nearby weapons, he laid violent hands on whoever was sitting near him.

<margin>The power of Music as a Healer of diseases.</margin>
Not only humans, but even animals themselves are captured by musical modes. Elephants, according to the testimony of Strabo, are lured by drums; swans by the lyre; and the fowler sings sweetly with his pipe when he deceives the bird. The innate ferocity and savage cruelty of bears is not halted unless the sound of the pipe is heard. By the modes of the flute, Pythagoras is said to have restrained the attack of wolves. Finally, music is a most excellent medicine, suitable for dispelling all diseases; sacred and profane histories abundantly relate that those suffering from sciatica, <note>original: ischiaticos</note> melancholy, madness, demonic possession, and poisoning have been cured by this, as will be said later.

<margin>How to understand the trumpet mode for the deaf.</margin>
However, as for the fact that Asclepiades <note>An ancient Greek physician.</note> is everywhere alleged by ignorant authors to have cured the deaf with a trumpet, I would not want it understood as if he performed this by the sound and melodies of the trumpet. Rather, it was because of an instrument fashioned in the shape of a trumpet, inserted into the ears of the deaf (as many hard-of-hearing people still use today, the construction of which I will provide in the following pages). By this, the species of sound and words were unified and increased by various reflections, so that they might reach the auditory organ of the deaf person more effectively. While the deaf were wonderfully helped by this, the story was taken up as a fable: that Asclepiades cured the deaf by the *sound* of a trumpet.

With these things thus prefaced, let us now see: what is this "Magnetism" implanted for drawing souls? What proportion of consonance do they have with the ears, that we are so greatly delighted by them? And what might number, weight, and measure be, both in sounds and in the ears, or in the soul, insofar as it is delighted by sounds, or seized by I know not what passion upon hearing them? For some sounds are so troublesome and discordant that by their harshness the teeth themselves chatter; others are so apt and harmonious, flowing in so sweetly, that they seem to snatch the soul out of itself—

Kircher also provides a rational, acoustic explanation for 'miraculous' cures for deafness using ear-trumpet technology.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the mythical and philosophical powers of music attributed to figures like Orpheus to a scientific and physical investigation into the nature of sound. It begins Book IX, which focuses on the "magic" or physical effects of harmony and discord.</meta>

Book IX. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance.

<margin>Various opinions regarding the power of Music.</margin>
Indeed, as I examine these things, it can scarcely be said how much controversy and disagreement exists among authors regarding the power and efficacy of this kind of harmony; how discordant are the opinions of almost all writers concerning the consonances of melodies. Some attribute this power to God, the source of all consonance, or to a soul composed of numbers; some to I-know-not-what celestial influences or the Cabalistic <term>decachordum<note>A mystical ten-stringed instrument or mathematical system used in Kabbalistic thought to represent the divine order.</note></term>; others to an occult sympathy of the soul with musical numbers; and many to geometric ratios. Having left behind all these opinions, which are out of tune and, as it were, greatly discordant with the truth, let us finally reveal what we ourselves determine regarding this "attractive" faculty of Music which draws the soul, and by what reasoning and process it produces such varied effects, not only in humans, but even in brute animals themselves.

# CHAPTER II.
## On the nature and production of Consonance and Dissonance.

Everyone marvels at why the soul is so greatly affected by consonances, yet shrinks so much from dissonances; the causes and reasons for this must be understood.

<margin>The tension and relaxation of sound from speed or slowness.</margin>
It must first be noted that two things are to be considered in consonances: the collision of bodies, which occurs through the motion of sounds; and proportion. These are, as it were, two principles—the former being Physical, the latter Mathematical—by which all consonances are caused. Physics considers the motion; Mathematics considers the quantity, numbers, weight, measure, and evaluates every proportion of one sound to another. Furthermore, since every <term>intension<note>In this context, "intension" refers to the tightening of a string or the raising of pitch.</note></term> or <term>remission<note>"Remission" refers to the loosening of a string or the lowering of pitch.</note></term> of voices and sounds flows from the speed or slowness of motion, a voice or sound will necessarily be caused to be more intense, sharper, and denser as the motion is faster; it will be more relaxed and thinner as the motion is slower. All of these things are learnedly evaluated by Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> in Book I of *Music*, chapter 3, where he teaches that those sounds are necessarily lower which are made by slower and thinner motions by the very slowness and thinness of the striking; they are sharper, however, if the motions are faster and denser. Thus, the same string sounds sharper if it is tightened, and lower if it is loosened; because when it is more tense, it gives back a faster pulse, returns more quickly, and strikes the air more frequently and densely. That which is looser, however, produces more relaxed pulses, and by the very weakness of the striking, being made thin, it trembles for a shorter time. Hence flutes or pipes—as we demonstrated in the *Organic Musurgia* <note>Referring to Kircher's own "Musurgia Universalis," specifically the sections on organ building and mechanical music.</note> and in the 7th book—sound now sharper, now more muffled and lower, according to the ratio of closed and open holes due to compressed or loosened air. This is evident in organ pipes and in the human <term>larynx<note>The "voice box" or upper part of the windpipe.</note></term> or windpipe. For the longer the tongue, or the <term>epiglottis<note>The flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe; Kircher here uses it to describe the mechanics of vocal pitch.</note></term>, or that fissure where the striking of air causes sound, and the wider the pipe, the lower the sound it will give; <margin>The cause of a sharp or low voice in humans.</margin> the shorter and narrower it is, the sharper the sound it will emit. From this it follows that those whose larynx is wide and long are accustomed to intone with a low and bass voice, but those whose larynx is narrow and small, with a high and sharp voice. But of these things we have spoken extensively in the first book.

<margin>Sound is not a single contrary, but composed of many parts of sounds.</margin>
It must be noted secondly that the sound of a moved string or an emitted voice is not a continuous thing, but is composed of discrete and interrupted motions. Such a sound is "fused together," as was said above in *Chordosophia* <note>original: "Chordofophia" — likely a section or term referring to the "wisdom of strings" or string theory.</note>, even if our ears are not at all able to perceive its intervals. This is no different than how the eyes cannot judge whether a burning coal, which someone swings very quickly in a circle, exists in the whole circle, or if the whole circle is made of fire. Boethius declares this with the example of a top spun by boys: if a stripe of red color is applied along the length or height of the cone, the whole cone will appear stained with red color when it spins, not because it is actually so, but because the speed of the red mark catches the parts that are not colored and does not allow the others to appear. Similarly, a more intense string rebounds and trembles with more strikes, a more relaxed one with fewer; for as often as a string is struck, not only is one sound emitted or one percussion made, but the air is struck as many times as the trembling string hits it. Hence, by the addition of motions, sharpness is intensified from gravity,

However, how we may cut any given number or magnitude so that the divided parts are in a given harmonic proportion, we have handed down extensively in our *Harmonic Algebra*.

<margin>Wherein the power of music consists.</margin>
With these things established, I finally conclude that the wonderful power of Music, which it holds in moving the passions of the mind, does not flow immediately from the soul; for since the soul is immortal and immaterial, it shares no direct proportion with voices and sounds, nor can it be changed by them. Rather, it flows from the <term>spirit<note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" (spiritus) were thought to be subtle, vaporous substances that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note></term>, which is the instrument of the soul, or from the primary union of the soul by which it is joined to the body. For a spirit of this kind, being a certain very subtle, blood-like vapor that is extremely mobile and thin, is easily stirred by harmonically excited air. When the soul perceives this stirring, it induces various effects according to the different excitations of the spirit. Hence, when the spirit is stirred by faster and denser harmonic motions and is, as it were, "rippled," there arises from that rippling a certain rarefaction. From this thinning of the spirit, an expansion arises, followed by gladness and joy. All these things will produce greater passions the more fitting and appropriate the melodies are, and the more they are proportioned to the natural <term>complexion<note>The specific balance of "humors" (fluids) that determined an individual's temperament and health.</note></term> and constitution of the person. From this it happens that while we perceive a perfectly composed harmony and a most sweet melody, we seem to feel a certain tingling in the heart and the mind, as if we were drawn and absorbed by this fitting agitation. Different musical modes or tones, which were discussed extensively in the preceding sections, promote this variety of passions most effectively; furthermore, the shortening of notes, the various reciprocations of ascent and descent, and the varied combination of dissonances artfully mixed with consonances also contribute. I shall make it clear through this experiment that the spirit is moved in this way and no other.

# Musical Experiments.

Take a glass cup of any size and fill it with pure, clear water. Once done, if you rub the outer rim of the glass in a circle with a moistened index finger for a short time, you will finally perceive a certain wonderful sound like ringing metal. The water, stirred by this, ripples so vehemently that it appears to be agitated by a wind. If you fill this cup only to the middle, you will indeed hear a sound, but twice as deep as the other, so that this sound resonates at a perfect <term>octave<note>original Greek: Διὰ πασῶν (*dia pason*), meaning "through all [notes]," the standard term for an octave.</note></term> to the first; consequently, you will also notice a slower rippling of the water. If you divide this same cup into five parts and fill three with water, leaving two empty, the glass will resonate a consonance <note>A ratio of 3:2, which creates a musical fifth.</note> accompanied by an even weaker rippling. Likewise, if the vessel is divided into seven parts and you fill four, leaving three empty, you will perceive a consonance <note>A ratio of 4:3, which creates a musical fourth.</note> followed by a rippling even weaker than the previous one. From this, it is clearly evident that our humors—and principally the spirit, which has its seat and dominion in the heart, the workshop of all passions—are moved in exactly the same way.

<margin>Why they are terrified by a violent sound.</margin>
Hence, when we perceive some violent sound like thunder or the explosion of a cannon, we are seized by a certain horror, because the spirit suffers a too-violent striking and dissipation from a sound out of proportion to itself; hence arise horror and terror. For this reason also, we cannot bear the screeching if someone scrapes iron with a knife, as it affects the muscles leading to the teeth and brain poorly by plucking at them with its harshness.

<margin>How beasts are delighted by Music.</margin>
All these things apply to animals as well; for there are those that rejoice and are soothed by melodies, which could not happen if that power of music flowed immediately from the rational soul. Nevertheless, man is delighted by Music in infinitely more ways than animals, because he understands the melodies better and more perfectly.

# CHAPTER III.
## On the affections of the soul to which Music incites.

<margin>The passions of the soul which are moved the most.</margin>
<margin>Why Music does not please those set in sadness.</margin>
Therefore, the soul, according to the diversity of the harmony, takes on various affections: joy, impulse, relaxation, fear, hope, anger, and compassion. For musical modulations move us most toward eight affections—as was stated in the preceding book—either because they are consonant or dissonant, or because they are fast or slow, or (what is more significant) because they tend toward a high pitch for cheerfulness, or sink into a low, relaxed sound for compassion and tears. However, Music does not excite love and hatred, even though these are the most powerful of all affections, because love and hatred are always directed toward a specific object <note>Original Latin: "amor & odium alicuius sunt." Kircher argues that music triggers general emotional states rather than specific feelings toward a particular person.</note>, as has been said elsewhere. Nevertheless, love is excited by joy, which is a general affection, as if by a certain friction. But since Music cannot generate sadness, it cannot generate hatred either. That Music cannot generate sadness is evident from the fact that sadness leads toward death, while Music leads toward life.

As for why Music—as <term>Ecclesiastes<note>Kircher likely refers here to Sirach 22:6: "A tale out of season is as music in mourning."</note></term> rightly says—is like an inopportune story in a time of mourning, and why we, when mourning or suppressed by a heavy sadness of heart, reject all Music, this is the reason: the spirit or <term>humor<note>In ancient and medieval medicine, humors were bodily fluids thought to govern personality and health.</note></term> is frozen and constricted by fear or sadness through a strong imagination of impending evils. In this state, the spirit rejects all movement and renders itself incapable of it. Therefore, if there were a Musician who could dissolve this condensed spirit with well-ordered Music, he would not move the listener to sadness, but would instead bring a relief of pain by causing the spirit to expand slightly. We have said that we are moved by Music toward eight primary affections, which can however be conveniently reduced to these three: joy, relaxation, and mercy (as also stated above). That other affections—such as love, sadness, audacity, fury, temperance, indignation, gravity, and religious devotion—result from these afterwards is "by accident" <note>In philosophical terms, "by accident" means a secondary effect that is not part of the essential nature of the thing itself.</note>; for all these follow from those three general affections of the mind, as we have taught in our *Musical Rhetoric*.

<margin>What is required for the increase of the drawing power of Music.</margin>
<margin>The agreement of harmony with the vital spirits.</margin>
Therefore, the various tensions and relaxations of tones, the various rises and falls and turnings, and the various and differing repercussions of voices, are the cause of a magnetic drawing of souls. Four things greatly increase these effects. First, the artistic mixture of tones and the various bindings of sounds through <term>arsis and thesis<note>The upward and downward motion of a musical beat or melody.</note></term> or syncopations, by which consonants are joined to dissonants by such strict laws of friendship that nothing sweeter can be perceived; these effects are greatly increased by the various "diminutions" <note>The breaking of long notes into many shorter, faster notes.</note> of voices and the mutual, friendly pursuits of artistically woven fugues. Second, a determined rhythm, contained within a verse. Third, the words themselves or the text of the songs. Finally, the disposition of the listener themselves; if these elements are missing, no emotional movement will follow from the harmony. 

For the diverse dispositions of men arise from no other cause than the motions of the <term>spirit<note>The "vital spirit" mentioned on the previous page as the bridge between body and soul.</note></term>—the chief organ and instrument of all powers of both the sensing and moving soul. This spirit is moved either through physical alteration or vocal motions. By these motions, the spirit is sometimes gathered together, sometimes distracted, now loosened, and shortly after intensified. Consequently, it undergoes various turns of changes caused by sonorous harmony; it follows necessarily that the soul is inclined to whatever state and disposition the spirit is in. 

Hence the lustful delight in charming, soft, and higher melodies, because the effect these produce in the excitation of the spirit is proportionate and similar to the affection toward which they already incline. From this, two people—one burning with heavenly love, the other with earthly love—might be stirred by different motions or desires by one and same <term>Dorian<note>A musical mode often characterized as serious, stable, and solemn.</note></term> or <term>Lydian<note>A musical mode traditionally associated with softness, longing, or even mourning.</note></term> tone. The first is moved with a desire for the heavenly Homeland joined with a contempt for earthly things; the second is moved by the heat of carnal fellowship joined to a desire for fleeting things. The same judgment applies to the rest. Thus, everyone is most delighted by that harmony which is most similar and proportionate to their own nature and temperament, and which is most agreeable to their present mood.

# CHAPTER IV.
## Investigation into the causes of consonant and dissonant numbers.

<margin>Why some numbers are sonorous, and others are not.</margin>
<margin>What consonance and dissonance are.</margin>
Furthermore, how Music moves the affections of the soul through its melodies is easily understood from what has been said previously. Now it only remains to explain how some sounds are consonant and others are not, and why only consonant sounds move the affections while dissonant ones do not. To understand this, one must know that just as **consonance** is a proportion of dissimilar voices or sounds reduced into one, or a mixture of high and low sound falling sweetly and uniformly upon the ears; so **dissonance** is a harsh and unpleasant striking of mixed high and low sounds coming to the ear.

Since, therefore, delight is perceived from the hearing of two different tones, the cause is that the tremors resulting from the vibration of a string are often united and agree as one. By this union and agreement, the "spirit" <note>In 17th-century physiology, the "spirit" was a subtle vapor that carried sensory information to the soul.</note> is similarly excited and stimulates the imaginative power toward delight. On the other hand, it leads to displeasure if the said tremors either do not unite at all, or do so only rarely. So that anyone may know how this union occurs, it seemed best to demonstrate the whole matter here through several propositions.

### Proposition I.

->*Two strings of equal tension, when struck at the same time, necessarily produce a unison, and they unite themselves perfectly and in equal time with each individual vibration.*<-

Although we have demonstrated all these things at length and from first principles in our *Chordosophia* <note>Literal: "String-wisdom"; Kircher refers to his own mathematical study of stringed instruments</note>, which is the first part of Book VI entitled *Organological Music-making*; nevertheless, because this place demands, as if by its own right, the "genesis" or origin of consonances, we have decided to briefly repeat the same things here. I assume, therefore, from the demonstrations in the cited book, that all the vibrations <note>original: "diadromos"; a term for the back-and-forth path of a vibrating string</note>—whether equal or unequal—of a single string are of equal duration. Let there be, therefore, two strings equal in both tension and thickness, AB and CD; I say that from their striking, a unison is necessarily produced.

<note>A diagram shows two vibrating strings, AB and CD. String AB is surrounded by a diamond shape formed by lines extending to point E above and M below, with a central intersection point S. String CD is similarly surrounded by lines extending to point F above and I below, with a central intersection point T. This illustrates the physical path of a vibrating string as it oscillates.</note>

Because, as shown in the cited place, strings of equal tension <note>original: "Isotonæ"</note> relate to one another as 1 to 1. The time also becomes equal and of equal duration; the end-point of the vibrations in each string will necessarily be isochronous <note>original: "iσοχρoνoς", meaning occurring in the same amount of time</note>, that is, it will happen at the same time. For both strings—AB being pulled to E, and CD being pulled to F—at one and the same time, this one striking the air at point M and that one at point I (the points of reflection), will cause exactly the same tones. In their return, at one and the same moment of time striking the air at S and T, they will cause the same tones as before, and thus they will always bring forth the same and identical sounds until the trembling strings, having reached their center of gravity, come to rest. Since, therefore, the blows to the air at the points of reflection unite themselves perfectly at the same moment of time, and this happens with each individual swing or back-and-forth motion, it necessarily follows therefrom, as was said, that the tone of the **unison** results—the fountain and origin of all consonances. Therefore, two strings of equal tension necessarily produce a unison, which was to be demonstrated, etc.

# Proposition II.

->**Two strings of equal thickness, where one is double the length of the other, will necessarily produce a Diapason (or octave) when struck, and they will unite their sounds at unequal intervals of time.**<-

Now consider two strings, AB and BC, where the latter is in a double proportion to the former <note>original: "proportione dupla"; in modern terms, a 2:1 ratio where one string is twice as long as the other</note>. I maintain that the sounds of these strings, once struck, will be united not in equal time, but in unequal time. Since the duration of one motion relates to the duration of the other just as the length of one string relates to the other (according to Book VI, Proposition 6), it necessarily follows that string AB completes its vibrations <note>original: "diadromos," a term referring to the back-and-forth path of a vibrating string</note> twice as fast as string BC. Suppose both strings are struck at the same moment; string AB at point G and BC at point F. String AB will necessarily travel the entire distance G to O once, while in that same time, string BC has only traveled from F to D. At that moment, the first string is at O (its limit), while the second is still at D (in mid-flow); thus, no union of sounds occurs. However, when string BC finally reaches point V, string AB will have reached point S for the second time. There, both strings have reached their respective limits—this one at V, that one at S—and the sounds caused by the striking of the air are perfectly united for the first time. Since string AB runs twice as fast as string BC, it necessarily sounds a <term>Diapason<gloss>An octave; the interval between the first and eighth notes of a scale.</gloss></term> (or octave) against the other at the moment of union. Therefore, the Diapason is caused by the union of sounds flowing in unequal time, which was to be demonstrated. But let us demonstrate this another way.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the physical paths of vibrating strings. A diamond-shaped figure with internal crossing lines connects points A, G, B, E, D, and C, representing the range of a string's vibration. Below it, two horizontal lines of different lengths are labeled B-S-V-I-C and F-S-G to show the comparative distances traveled by the high and low notes.</note>

## Another demonstration of the same principle.

Let the larger string be the <term>Hypate<gloss>The lowest-sounding string in ancient Greek music theory.</gloss></term>, and let the smaller string be the <term>Nete<gloss>The highest-sounding string in ancient Greek music theory.</gloss></term> (or octave G), which is half the length of the larger string. Let the space BC be the path through which the vibrating Hypate string runs back and forth, and let FG be the space for the Nete, which is half the size of the first. The ratio of the strings will be the same as the ratio of the spaces they traverse. Let us suppose these strings are struck simultaneously at points B and F. Both strings will travel from B and F: the larger to S, and the smaller to G. When the smaller string reaches G, having attained the limit of its motion, it strikes the air and causes a sound; meanwhile, the string BC is at point S, still as far from the limit C as it has traveled from B, and thus remains silent. Soon, however, it reaches C, where it resonates from the striking of the air. But in that same interval of time, the smaller string has returned from G to F. Because it travels half the distance in the same time it took the larger string to move from S to C, it resonates at F (the other limit of its path) at the exact same moment the larger string BC resonates at its limit C.

<margin>How the Diapason consists in a double proportion.</margin>
Thus, the first union of the sounds of both strings occurs here, and this will happen every time the trembling string BC strikes the air. Furthermore, since the smaller string traverses its space twice while the larger string traverses BC once, the smaller string will necessarily strike the air twice as fast as the larger one. Consequently, it will sound higher in pitch. Through the frequent union of these vibrations, it affects the "vital spirits" <note>In the 17th century, these were believed to be subtle fluids in the body that transmitted sensory perceptions to the soul.</note> so pleasantly that it creates that delight in the soul which we have called the first degree of harmony. For this reason, in strings of equal tension where the striking of the air occurs in equal time and space, a "unison" is caused; this relates to harmony as unity relates to number, or a point to a line—which is why it cannot properly be called "harmonic" in itself. Yet the Diapason is the sweetest of all consonances because the union of the perfectly mixed low and high sounds is so frequent.

<summary>This page mathematically demonstrates that the musical octave (Diapason) is created by a 2:1 ratio in string length, resulting in vibrations that coincide every second stroke. The author argues that this physical frequency of "union" is what creates the sensation of harmony in the human soul.</summary>

...more frequently than happens in any other consonances, since there was only one sound from the shorter string that was not united with the longer string. But the remaining consonances have more sounds that do not unite, and consequently, they unite more and more rarely the further they depart from the <term>diapason<gloss>An octave; the most perfect consonance after the unison.</gloss></term> when they sound with the <term>hypate<gloss>The lowest string or note in the ancient Greek musical system.</gloss></term>. # Proposition III.

->*If two strings of equal thickness sound a <term>diapente<gloss>A perfect fifth.</gloss></term>—the sounds will unite in a <term>sesquialtera<gloss>A ratio of 3:2.</gloss></term> proportion of time.*<-

You should imagine these lines below represent the transverse paths which the <term>diadromi<gloss>The back-and-forth vibrations or "runs" of a string.</gloss></term> of the struck strings complete. Let there be, therefore, a certain larger string AD, and let the space it traverses when struck be AB. ED; and let another smaller string, EFG, relate to the former as two relates to three, which is the proportion of the diapente. Let both be moved at the same moment (for we are speaking here not of a string traveling from one place to another, but of the sound which is propelled in the string from this end to that, where, in our way of conceiving it, by striking the air, it causes sound—I would like you to note this well).

Both will run, therefore: the larger from A toward D, and the smaller from E into G. Soon, therefore, while the smaller comes into F, the larger will begin to resound at D; thus no union of these sounds will occur here, since the sound of the larger string at D occurs later than the sound of the smaller string at G. Nor will a union of sounds occur in EF, since the motion of the larger string has not yet reached the end of its movement at E. Since, therefore, the motion of the larger string from E into A must still cover as much space as the smaller string from E into G, the motions of both strings will first be united at the sound-boundaries A and G.

You see, therefore, that as the vibration of the strings is, so are the sounds to one another; since the vibration of the smaller string relates to the vibration—that is, the course and recourse—of the larger string as 3 to 2, so also do the sounds of the smaller string relate to the larger. Therefore, the smaller string, always omitting two sounds which do not unite, will join the sound resulting from the third vibration to the larger string. Hence, the union of low and high sounds in a diapente happens more slowly than in a diapason, and consequently, it gradually moves away from the sweetness of the former.

<note>A technical diagram illustrates musical proportions through parallel lines. The top line is marked with points A, B, E, and D. A lower line is marked E, F, and G. Roman numeral 'II' marks denote segments between vertical guides connecting the two systems of motion.</note>

# Proposition IV.

->*Two strings of equal thickness sound a <term>diatessaron<gloss>A perfect fourth.</gloss></term>, because the sounds unite in a <term>sesquitertia<gloss>A ratio of 4:3.</gloss></term> proportion of time.*<-

<margin>Diatessaron.</margin>
First, let the space of the larger string be A, through which it runs when struck, AVXBC. Let the space of the smaller string be DFE, and let string relate to string, and space to space, as 3 to 4—namely, in the sesquitertia proportion, in which the proportion of the diatessaron consists. Having moved both strings from the boundaries A and D toward C and E, it is certain that the motion of the smaller, when it reaches E, will first resound upon being struck back, and when it has run back from E to F, then first...

# Book X. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance

...the motion of the larger string will first begin to sound at point C; then, when the smaller string reaching D resounds for the second time, the returning motion of the larger string from C will be imminent at point X. When the smaller reaches F, the larger will hold point A, where, having reached its limit, it will resound upon being struck a second time. The smaller string, however, moved from F into E, will resound there for the third time, while the larger string is moved to point V. Thus, no union of sounds has yet been made; they will first acquire this union when the motion of the larger string arrives from V to C, and the smaller from E to D. For since they reach the limits of their motion in equal time and space—namely, the larger at C and the smaller at D—the first union will occur there. Thus, in this consonance, the smaller string always passes over three sounds which do not unite with the sounds of the larger string, finally uniting the sound resulting from the fourth vibration. <note>Kircher is describing the physical "coincidence" of vibrations. In a perfect fifth (ratio 3:2), the vibrations meet up at regular intervals, but many of the individual oscillations of the faster string occur while the slower string is still mid-swing.</note> The same judgment applies to the other consonances, which will always be more imperfect the further they depart from the simplest <term>diapason<gloss>An octave; the most fundamental interval where the vibrations align in a 2:1 ratio.</gloss></term>, and the more rarely they unite their sounds. This occurs in the <term>ditone<gloss>A major third (ratio 81:64 in Pythagorean tuning, or 5:4 in just intonation).</gloss></term>, the <term>semiditone<gloss>A minor third (ratio 6:5).</gloss></term>, the <term>hexachord<gloss>A sixth (ratio 5:3 or 8:5).</gloss></term>, and similar intervals. Thus, the ditone always passes over four sounds that do not mix, uniting only the fifth; the semiditone, however, passing over five unsociable sounds, joins to the larger string only the sound resulting from the sixth vibration. See those things which we have treated most extensively in the *Chordosophia*. <note>original: "Chordosophia" — This refers to Kircher’s own theoretical work on the "wisdom of strings," likely a section within this larger volume.</note>

<margin>The Diapason is the most perfect of all consonances.</margin>
<margin>All Music consists of 3 consonances.</margin>
Therefore, if slow and fast motions are proportioned together and easily mixed among themselves, a consonance arises. If, however, they are disproportionate and admit no mixture or coming together, a dissonance is born. Furthermore, they will mix more easily the more similar they are, and the closer they are to the source—that is, to unity or the <term>unison<gloss>Two notes of the exact same pitch.</gloss></term>. Hence, the diapason consonance is the most perfect of all consonances, because it is perfected by the first, most perfect, and simplest proportion, standing only one step away from the <term>monad<gloss>The number one; representing unity and the Divine.</gloss></term>; such is the <term>duple<gloss>The 2:1 ratio.</gloss></term> proportion, relating as one to two. Closest to this in perfection is the <term>superparticular<gloss>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3/2, 4/3).</gloss></term> proportion—specifically the <term>sesquialtera<gloss>The 3:2 ratio, which produces the perfect fifth.</gloss></term> or <term>diapente<gloss>The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</gloss></term>, which relates as 2 to 3. This is followed immediately by the <term>sesquitertia<gloss>The 4:3 ratio.</gloss></term> proportion, relating as 3 to 4, which corresponds to the <term>diatessaron<gloss>The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</gloss></term> consonance. In the harmonic arrangement of tones, the fourth is considered perfect, but in the arithmetic arrangement, it is judged imperfect and dissonant; hence it is only "perfect" and "consonant" in a relative sense. <note>In 17th-century theory, the perfect fourth was often a "stable" interval in melody but was treated as a dissonance in counterpoint if it appeared against the bass.</note> It follows that these proportions, the sesquialtera and sesquitertia, are consonant because the diapason is constituted from them when joined together; they could not constitute the most consonant interval of all if they themselves were not consonant. And indeed, all Music consists of these three consonances, nor is all Music anything other than a harmony consisting of these three consonances, nor is any symphony possible without these three.

The ratio of perfect consonances—whether simple or composite—consists, therefore, in the number four. Moving from this up to the number six, the consonances depart from their perfection; such are the Ditone, the Semiditone, and the <term>greater hexachord<gloss>The major sixth.</gloss></term>. The first of these, consisting in the <term>sesquiquarta<gloss>The 5:4 ratio.</gloss></term> proportion, relates as 4 to 5; the second, in the <term>sesquiquinta<gloss>The 6:5 ratio.</gloss></term>, relates as 5 to 6. The third, in the <term>superbipartient<gloss>A complex ratio where the numerator is two greater than the denominator (specifically 5:3 here).</gloss></term> proportion of thirds, relates as 3 to 5. These are called "imperfect consonances," and together with the perfect ones, the entire circle of consonances is completed. You see, therefore, how the consonances flowing from unity complete the circuit of their total perfection in the number six (the senary), so that no other consonances besides those mentioned can be assigned. Whoever penetrates these things more deeply will see clearly how **GOD**, the Best and Greatest, is the source of all harmony, and how the world flowed forth from Him, and how the <term>hexameron<gloss>original: ἑξάμερον — The "Six Days" of creation described in Genesis.</gloss></term> was established by Him. But we have handed these things down more extensively in Books III and IV, on pages 100 and 187.

These consonances, therefore, according to their different arrangement in the musical scale, also cause a different constitution of tones, semitones, <term>dieses<gloss>Tiny musical intervals, smaller than a semitone.</gloss></term>, and <term>chromas<gloss>Colors or specific tunings of notes.</gloss></term>. From their various combinations, the human spirit is also variously affected according to the different complexions of men. From this, as was said a little earlier, various emotions and impulses of the soul result. For our spirit is moved according to the nature of the stirred air, just as a struck string stirs another that is untouched. Whence, if our spirits were strings, they—having been stirred by musical measures—would perfectly express harmony, which I make manifest by the following experiments.

# Universal Music-Making

### Experiment I.

<margin>One string is known to set a distant string in motion.</margin>
Upon a solid, smooth, and hollow board, let nine strings be stretched in the order shown in the following diagram. First, let two strings, A and F, be equal in both quantity and quality—that is, in their tension—so that they resound with a unison pitch; let the remaining strings be arranged step-by-step according to the diagram below. If you strike this first string, F, with a plectrum, it will cause all the strings that are <term>isotonous<gloss>From the Greek "ἰσοτόνυς"; meaning of equal tension or pitch.</gloss></term> to it to resound, no matter how untouched they remain. There is, however, this difference: the string that is closer to the unison will resound more and appear to move more noticeably. Thus, the motion and sound of the untouched unison string F will be felt most strongly in response to the sound of the first; it will also incite the octave <note>labeled "a" in the text</note> to sound, though a little more weakly than the former, as it departs somewhat from the unison. It will also incite the fifth, but scarcely perceptibly, as it departs more than is ideal from the unison. Indeed, if you place a feather upon it, you will feel a certain tremor in the string, however slight. I have found this hardly noted by anyone else, as most have thought that only the <term>hypate<gloss>The lowest-pitched string in the ancient Greek musical system.</gloss></term> in unison, and the <term>nete<gloss>The highest-pitched string in the ancient Greek musical system.</gloss></term>, could be moved by another untouched string. But long experience has taught me the contrary: for all strings consonant with the *hypate* are moved, but as I have said, they move more effectively the closer they are to their source. Dissonant strings, however, being unable to be moved by this friendly provocation, will persist in their stubbornness.

->*Nete.*<-

<note>A diagram represents a set of musical strings stretched within a rectangular frame. On the left side, the horizontal strings are labeled from top to bottom with the letters: A, E, D, C, B, A, G, F. On the right side, the top string is labeled "Nete" (the highest note) and the bottom string is labeled "Hypate" (the lowest note). The word "Nete" is centered above the top string to indicate the highest point of the scale.</note>

Furthermore, it is not only strings that incite other similarly stretched strings; organ pipes and trumpets <margin>The pipes of organs also move strings that are stretched in proportion to them.</margin> also cause strings enjoying a similar tone to resound. So that the truth of this matter may be more fully demonstrated, I will recount here what once happened to me in Mainz. While I was occupied with certain business in a choir room separated from the church during the time of a solemn Mass, I suddenly perceived a <term>large viol<gloss>original: "chelis maiorem"; likely a bass viol or cello-like instrument.</gloss></term> resounding at intervals. A singer had previously tuned it exactly to the church organ and left it hanging on the wall of the choir room without loosening the strings. It was untouched, and with no one present, it began to resound by some hidden motion. Astonished by the novelty of the thing, I drew closer to examine this prodigious sound more deeply. While doing so, I discovered that as soon as the organist played the pipes that exactly corresponded to the strings of the said viol, the strings themselves were incited by that tone, just as if they had been struck with a plectrum. I later demonstrated this "harmonic sympathy" to many others, to their great admiration. I subsequently attempted to exhibit this <term>phonurgy<gloss>The art or science of sound-manipulation or "sound-work."</gloss></term> in other places, but it was not possible to find a room arrangement similar to the one mentioned, which was found by chance rather than by art. For in a harmonic wonder of this kind, I noted that a perfect adaptation of the pipes to the strings is required, as well as an exact distance of the pipes from the strings, along with a specific arrangement of the room and the walls that propagate the sound. But regarding the construction of such a thing, since it does not belong in this section, we shall perhaps speak more fully elsewhere, God willing. For now, only the cause of this prodigious effect remains to be investigated.

## CHAPTER V.

### On the principle of the sympathy and antipathy of sounds.

Note first, that in this kind of sound, three things can be considered. First, the body which moves by sounding, and the body which is moved by another toward sound. Second, a certain proportion or likeness between the sounding bodies. Third, a suitable medium, such as the air.

<margin>How one string may move another untouched string.</margin>
Note second, that sound is not propagated through the medium of air alone, but wherever it finds a body in the medium suited to its preservation, it exerts its forces therein. For the air, which has been dispersed by sound, seeks a union out of its own nature; truly, the motion or sound preserves its character better and more faithfully in a body apt and skillful for its propagation, such as stretched strings. From this, I infer that a string set in motion will incite another similarly stretched but untouched string, either because of the greatest likeness and proportion which the sounding body and the soundable body have toward each other—since likeness and proportion are a kind of <term>mimicry of likeness<gloss>Kircher uses the phrase "simia similitudinis," implying that proportion acts as a natural imitation or mirror of the original motion.</gloss></term>, serving as a certain basis and foundation for the whole motion. Second, it is because of the moved air; for since the air is moved toward the motion of the sound, and the proportion of sound to sound is the same as the proportion of moved air to moved air (as was shown in the preceding pages), it follows that the air incited by the sound is still imbued with the <term>image<gloss>original: "simulachro"; a philosophical term for the form or representation of a thing carried through a medium.</gloss></term> of the sound it carries. When it falls upon a similar, proportioned sounding body capable of receiving the quality it carries, it strikes it in the same way that the air was struck by the original sound. Both the air and the sound seek union and propagation within the body, which is highly resonant and "airy" by its inherent nature.

Hence, a string moves a string that is equally stretched, or any other body or harmonic instrument, just as it would a string similar and corresponding to itself in sound. This happens because the equally incited air falls upon a body similar in both quantity and quality to that from which it was incited. Therefore, the body—already disposed of itself and longing for its own perfection or "good"—is similarly incited by the plucking of the surrounding air. Furthermore, a string sounding an <term>Octave<gloss>original: "Octavam" or "Diapason."</gloss></term>, though untouched, is nevertheless incited by a lower string because of the greatest likeness and proportion it has to it. For in the opinion of everyone, it does not differ from the lower string except by its high-pitched sound; thus it is judged to be the same. Indeed, it is virtually contained within the lower, just as the high is in the low <note>According to the testimony of Aristotle.</note>, and it is nothing other than a certain sharper and more intense repetition of the lower voice. This is why women naturally sing the interval of the <term>diapason<gloss>The interval of an octave.</gloss></term> with men, and boys and eunuchs with men of more advanced age. Bells and other sounding instruments also ring out a diapason mixed, as it were, with the lower tone, which would not happen unless the greatest likeness and proportion came between them.

Furthermore, since the external air is related to the internal air of the string just as the extension of one string is to another—and a string sounding a diapason is in a <term>sub-double proportion<gloss>A ratio of 1:2.</gloss></term>—it follows that the air, according to this proportion, also moves and incites the air that is internal and innate to the auditory organ, contained within its membranes.

From what has been said, it is clear by what means music incites various affections of the mind. It has the power of moving the hearing either with delight or compassion, or in another similar way, according to the variety of the sound and the moved air, which moves the hearing with such-and-such a proportion. For while the air, moved in this or that way and inhaled by a person, moves the <term>spirit<gloss>Kircher refers to "vital spirits," the subtle fluids that early modern science believed carried sensory information and emotions through the body.</gloss></term> in the same way, various affections are incited in animals according to the variety of the sounds, just as the spirit is moved in various ways when the air is moved. Since the heart is the "throne of the spirits," they receive the trembling and leaping air into the chest and sound as one with their own kind. The remaining spirits located in the other parts of the body follow these; they move the muscles or restrain them according as the law of numbers either increases with incitements or rests with a composed tenor, or imitates rest with slowness. This is no different than in the strings mentioned a little before: when one string is touched, another equally stretched string trembles in response. For the spirits that are in the heart are excited by the motion of an external sound all the more easily than strings, insofar as their union is greater. Hence, a depressed and withered soul finds rest through much care, once the accession of the entering external air has been made, and is uplifted...

Universal Musurgy

...while the elevated [spirit] is restrained or even drawn down from that height by the contrary reason. From this, the reason is also clear why many people, even while doing other things, join in with those singing; why when one person shouts, the urge to shout seizes everyone; and why in battle or in an assembly, when one person cries out or laments, immediately the whole line or assembly cries out or groans. But I have decided that this agitation of our spirit by external sound should be demonstrated through an extraordinary experiment.

### Experiment.

<margin>Sound moves various humors in different ways.</margin>
Take five glass cups, all of the same size and capacity, which you will arrange in the order expressed here in the diagram below; let one cup be filled with <term>spirit of wine<gloss>Original: "aqua vitæ." In the 17th century, this referred to distilled alcohol or brandy, considered "fiery" in nature.</gloss></term>, another cup with a better quality wine, another with subtle [thin] water, another with thick water, such as seawater or oil; and the middle one with common water. This being done, with the tip of a moistened finger, rub the rim of the cup until you perceive the ringing sound, which we taught how to excite a little above in the experiments. For this most acute sound, not without wonder, will agitate all the remaining liquids, and indeed more vehemently the more subtle one liquid is than the other. Hence, the spirit of wine in the cup, which represents a fiery nature or a <term>choleric temperament<gloss>In the ancient theory of the four humors, the choleric temperament was associated with fire and yellow bile, characterized by a quick, hot disposition.</gloss></term>, will leap up most of all compared to the others; the wine in the cup representing the <term>sanguine<gloss>The sanguine temperament was associated with the element of air and a cheerful, active disposition.</gloss></term> or airy complexion will undergo a moderate agitation; the subtle water, exhibiting a <term>phlegmatic<gloss>The phlegmatic temperament was associated with the element of water and a slow, calm disposition.</gloss></term> constitution, will cause a slow and dull commotion compared to the others; and the thick water contained in the cup, on account of its earthy <note>This refers to the melancholic temperament, associated with the element of earth.</note> complexion, will scarcely be capable of motion. Music must be judged to excite the affections of our soul in no different way. If, therefore, our spirit be subtle and hot, Music will excite proud, insolent, and angry motions; if it be more subtle and of a moderate quality, it will incite to loves, joys, gladness, and amorous affections; if it be more condensed, it will move to tears, religion, restraint, and other pathetic affections; finally, if it be thick, as in men weighed down by sorrow, it will be incapable of all commotion, and therefore "music in mourning is an untimely tale." <note>original: "musica in luctu importuna narratio est." This is a reference to the biblical book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:6, which suggests that trying to cheer someone in deep grief with music is inappropriate and ineffective.</note>

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a four-legged wooden table. On the table's surface are five glass bowls, arranged in a cross pattern with one bowl in the center and four surrounding it. Each bowl contains liquid, and the illustration uses internal circular lines to suggest the presence of fluids or vibrations within the vessels, representing the "jumping" of the liquids in response to sound.</note>

From this experiment it also becomes clear how one sound achieves different effects in men of different <term>complexions<gloss>Original: "complexio." In early modern medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual that determines their temperament.</gloss></term>; for the choleric man is moved in one way, the sanguine in another, and finally the phlegmatic in yet another. All these things shine forth so clearly in this single experiment that they demonstrate the moving power of Music almost <term>apodictically<gloss>A term meaning a proof that is clearly demonstrated or certain.</gloss></term>, which also holds true in strings of equal length but made from the intestines of different animals or from different metals. For just as there is a weight of metal to metal, so there is string to string, and sound to sound, etc.

Book IX. The Magic of the Consonant and Dissonant.

# P A R T  I I.

# THE MAGIC OF THE CONSONANT AND DISSONANT
## Music-Medical Magic, or the Medicine and Cure of Diseases to be Healed through Music.

### P R E F A C E.

<margin>The wondrous effects of Music.</margin>
*We call Music-Medical <note>Original: "Iatricam." From the Greek 'iatrikos', relating to medicine.</note> Magic that which performs quite exotic and prodigious effects in curing diseases of the soul and body. For just as was demonstrated at length in the seventh book, it is known from the testimony of almost all historians that Terpander <note>A Greek poet and musician of the 7th century BCE, credited with the invention of the seven-stringed lyre.</note> and Arion <note>A legendary Greek harper said to have been saved from the sea by a dolphin attracted by his music.</note> freed men from the gravest diseases by song; that Herophilus <note>A famous physician of Alexandria who was the first to realize that the pulse is a rhythm that can be measured like music.</note> measured the veins of the sick by musical numbers; that Xenocrates <note>A Platonist philosopher who reportedly used musical melodies to cure those suffering from mental disturbances.</note> delivered the frenzied from their madness by the measures of songs; and others, to whom they attribute such musical science that they even restored the use of hearing to the deaf. Since these things have been partly declared in the preceding sections and are partly to be declared in what follows, they are by no means to be repeated; rather, we have thought it best to bring forward the reasoning behind each one in this place.*

---

# C H A P T E R  I.
## On the causes of that prodigious cure of diseases to be carried out by the help of Music.

<margin>The Cabalists attribute everything to the Sephirothic channels.</margin>
<margin>The Platonists attribute exotic effects to the World Soul.</margin>
<margin>Astrologers and Alchemists to the influence of celestial bodies.</margin>
**V**arious people assign various reasons and causes for this prodigious cure. The Cabalists, after their own fashion, attribute everything to the <term>Sephirothic channels<gloss>In the Jewish mystical tradition of Kabbalah, the Sephiroth are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself. Kircher believed these were 'channels' of divine energy.</gloss></term>, through which divine power flows into individual things of the world. We shall speak of the manner in which they assert this happens, God willing, in our <term>Egyptian Oedipus<gloss>Kircher's "Oedipus Aegyptiacus" (1652–54) was his massive work attempting to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs and explain ancient esoteric wisdom.</gloss></term>, in the treatise on the explanation of the Tree of the 10 Sephiroth. The Platonists, in their way, establish the causes of these marvelous effects in the bonds of the <term>World Soul<gloss>Anima Mundi; the concept that the entire universe is a living, breathing entity governed by a single soul.</gloss></term>, which joins all things to itself harmonically (and which they also call the <term>Colchodea<gloss>A term used by Neoplatonists and Hermeticists to describe the world-soul's animating and binding spirit.</gloss></term>). The Astrologers and Alchemists attribute everything to the influences of the superior bodies [the stars and planets]; since we have treated the reasons for all of these in the "Astrology of the Consonant and Dissonant," or in <term>Worldly Music<gloss>Musica Mundana; the Pythagorean concept of the "Music of the Spheres."</gloss></term>, we refer the reader there.

And I truly marvel that men so wise, having abandoned natural causes, have fallen into such absurd opinions so remote from all human intellect. They seem to have done the same as those who, leaving behind their domestic wealth, migrate to the Indies to acquire those riches which they believe are more abundant there, exposing themselves to innumerable dangers. But before we assign the genuine causes of these individual effects, let us first, in our usual manner, suppose certain things to establish our demonstrations on a more solid foundation.

<margin>How the air ought to be conceived.</margin>
I suppose, therefore, First: That the <term>Air<gloss>Kircher views air not just as empty space, but as a medium that carries vibrations and "spirits."</gloss></term>—not only the external air, but also the internal air present in every single thing—is moved according to the nature of sound. Thus, if the sounds are in a <term>double proportion<gloss>The musical interval of an octave (2:1).</gloss></term>, they imprint that same proportion on the air; if in a triple, a triple; if in a quadruple, a quadruple; and so on for the rest. And just as <term>visible species<gloss>In 17th-century optics, "species" were the invisible images or forms that traveled from an object to the eye.</gloss></term> emanating conically from objects do not become sensible in the medium unless they are actually perceived by the organ and the visual power—even though the "species" of all visible things persist in the air without confusion or mixing (as we have demonstrated at length in *The Art of Light and Shadow*)—so too the air is perpetually full of the simulacra of infinite species carried through it from objects of every kind.

<summary>Kircher introduces the concept of music as a medicinal tool, citing historical examples like Terpander and Arion, and begins to critique mystical explanations (Kabalistic, Platonic) in favor of his own theory based on the physical properties of air and "species."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the physical properties of sound to its medical application. Kircher establishes several "suppositions" or axioms to explain how music interacts with the human body and soul before beginning a case study on the biblical story of David and Saul.</meta>

Universal Music-making

<margin>Audible species follow the properties of visible ones.</margin>
Just as visible species <note>original: "species". In the science of this period, "species" were the sensible forms or images emitted by objects that travel through a medium like air to reach the senses.</note> persist in the air, so do audible species. There is only this difference: the former are present permanently, while the latter are transient. Thus, if the harmonic motion of the air were sensible to our sight, we would perceive the same harmony in any part of the air that musicians produce. Truly, all these things will be more clearly demonstrated in what follows.

<margin>A miraculous cure through music can sometimes occur by the help of the devil through a pact.</margin>
I suppose, secondly, that a miraculous cure of diseases of this kind can be considered in three ways: First, supernaturally; Second, by the art of the Demon; Third, naturally. To the first kind belong all those cures which have a manifest miracle attached to them. Thus Christ our Savior called Lazarus back from the dead with a loud voice, and restored hearing to the deaf man by whispering this word *Ephphatha* <note>Aramaic for "be opened," spoken by Jesus in Mark 7:34.</note> into his ears; and similar things which we read both in the Holy Scriptures and in the lives of the Saints. Secondly, it is certain that such miraculous cures produced by Music are sometimes performed by the help of the demon, through an implicit or explicit pact. For just as Magi, having made a pact with the demon, can set any sign they wish—upon which the Devil provides the effect of health—so he can also take up Music or any Musical instrument to perform the said effect. By this art, the Brothers of the Rosy Cross <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret brotherhood of sages and alchemists rumored to possess the power to cure all diseases.</note> are said to heal any diseases, even incurable ones; these things will be explained more fully later. Thirdly, there is the natural power of Music, of which we have spoken partly in the preceding sections and will speak in the following. And it is only this natural power that we have undertaken to treat in this place.

<margin>Just as strings, so also muscles and nerves can be stirred by music.</margin>
I suppose, thirdly, that our whole body is porous <note>original: "transpirabile", meaning able to be permeated or "breathed through" by external influences.</note>, and that the nerves and muscles receive the same impression through external material sound as strings stretched over smooth and resonant wood acquire. And just as these strings are stirred not only by an external sound but also by an internal sound of the air proportioned to them, so also the nerves and muscles are agitated by the air and the "implanted spirit" (the director of the motor faculty) enclosed within them. When the soul then perceives this proportioned form, it is necessary that it undergoes the highest alterations of either joy or sadness.

I suppose, fourthly, that not just any diseases indiscriminately, but those which depend immediately on black and yellow bile <note>Referring to the Four Humors: black bile (melancholy) and yellow bile (choleric/anger).</note>, can be cured by the help of music. For I judge it to be impossible <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note> to cure wasting diseases, epilepsy, gout, and the slowest-moving ailments, or even those which have some vital organ already corrupted.

I suppose, fifthly, that it is necessary for the Musician to have a deep understanding of the nature and complexion of the person he wishes to cure. Furthermore, the greatest account must be taken of the time, the place, and similar circumstances, without which I judge it impossible to reach the intended effect. These things being supposed, let us now bring the miraculous cure of certain diseases to examination, so that the curious reader may know what is to be thought of them.

---

# C H A P T E R  I I.

## How David, by playing the lyre, rescued Saul from the evil spirit.

To better untangle this question, we will first bring forward the words of Holy Scripture; for it is held thus in the first book of Kings, chapter sixteen <note>Now known as 1 Samuel 16:23.</note>: *Whenever, therefore, the evil spirit from God seized Saul, David took the lyre and struck it with his hand, and Saul was refreshed, and it was better for him; for the evil spirit departed from him.* The words of the Sacred text teach most clearly that some kind of evil spirit from God was driven out by Music; however, how this happened is explained by various people in various ways.

<margin>The Rabbis assert that David cured Saul by the power of the ten-stringed Psaltery.</margin>
The Rabbis say in this place that David, while he cured Saul, played a ten-stringed Lyre constructed according to the pattern of the Sephirotic Tree <note>original: "arboris Zephyroticae". This refers to the Sephiroth, the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>, and being fruitful with the outflows of the ten divine Virtues as if with certain fruits, it produced this effect. For they say that David knew that star to which the harmony should be joined, so that the frenzy might easily be blunted and he might feel better; so says Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a prolific Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note>, in the *Micra heggadolah*. Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Renaissance philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man" and his interest in Christian Kabbalah.</note>...

### Book IX. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance. 215

<margin>Rabbi Ibn Ezra devises trifling astrological reasons for the cure of Saul.</margin>
<note>original: "R. Abenezræ"</note> Cardan, in his 7th and 8th Mathematical Theses, says that Music moves the <term>spirits</term><note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle, vapor-like substances that carried out the functions of the soul within the body.</note> so that they may serve the soul, just as medicine agitates them to rule the body; and that music heals the body through the soul, just as medicine cures the soul by means of the body. From these points, one can easily gather by what reasoning David so easily repressed the raging Saul. From this, who does not see that the commentary of Ibn Ezra is most vain? For David did not look upon the aspects of the stars while he soothed Saul's madness, but rather he struck the strings with his hand as often as Saul commanded, regardless of whether these or other astrological aspects were in force.

<margin>What things dissipate the melancholic humor.</margin>
But we, having rejected all the aforementioned sayings, say that David liberated Saul from <term>melancholy</term><note>One of the four humors, associated with black bile and states of depression or madness.</note> and from a species of madness (which he himself perfectly understood) and subsequently also from a demon—not with herbs, juices, pills, or other substances that dissipate melancholy, but by the power and efficacy of Music alone. And to demonstrate the matter more clearly: Note that those things cure madness or mania which open the pores, ward off <term>sooty vapors</term><note>original: "fuligines". These were thought to be dark, smoky waste products of metabolism that clouded the brain.</note>, clear obstructions, and refresh the heart. A harmonic concert is able to accomplish this. Since Music consists of sounds produced by the commotion of the air, when you use those sounds which move the airy spirits of the madman, these spirits—having been made warmer and swifter by the motion (according to our 3rd Supposition)—will eventually thin and dissipate the entire mixture of the melancholic humor.

<margin>By what means David cured Saul with music.</margin>
Or, if you prefer that we relax those spirits and make them more quiet, so that they do not so pierce the <term>meninges</term><note>The membranes surrounding the brain.</note> of the brain, we ought to use very slow sounds and small intervals. Thus, through the harmony of slow motions, those spirits and biting vapors that fly from the stomach, spleen, and <term>hypochondria</term><note>The upper lateral regions of the abdomen, then thought to be the seat of melancholic vapors.</note> into the brain, being made slower, may leave the man in peace. Therefore, Davidic Music was able to settle Saul in two ways: First, by moving, heating, and thinning Saul’s spirits and fumes so that the dissipated melancholic juice was driven out of the cells of the brain or dissolved into thin air, passing away through insensible transpiration, sweat, and the pores. Secondly, once those spirits left the melancholic juice, the juice could not rage (as it is by nature "earthy" and lacking in action) until the vital and animal spirits moved it and carried it here and there. They left it, however, when they flew to the ears as if with loose reins for the sake of catching the harmony. While the harmony lasted, the madness ceased; when it ceased, the spirits returned, but having been made lighter and more free, they were able for a time to expel, thin, or diminish the melancholy, and perhaps convert some part of it into a more benign vapor or habit. 

From this it is manifest that this matter proceeded not from a casual sound of the lyre, but from the greatest art and David’s supreme skill in playing. For David, being of the highest and most sagacious genius, and furthermore, as Saul's armor-bearer, always enjoying his presence, knew Saul's character, inclinations, mental impulses, and the other <term>passions</term><note>original: "pathemata". Emotional or physical sufferings/states.</note> by which he was agitated, through the great familiarity he enjoyed with him. Whence, urged not so much by his own instinct as by a divine one, he took up the lyre or some other instrument without doubt. For as it is recorded in the *Shields of the Mighty* <note>original: "Schilte gilbormi", referring to the Hebrew work *Shiltei ha-Gibborim* by Abraham Portaleone.</note>, David knew the use of thirty-six musical instruments and played each most skillfully (as has been said regarding the instrumental music of the Hebrews). He knew how to adapt his playing so dexterously and with such appropriate sound to the King’s humor—perhaps by reciting certain rhythms which he knew were most pleasing to Saul's ear and suited to the task, or even by provoking him with a metric dance until he finally achieved the intended effect. For with the harmonic motion of the lyre added—by which Saul was accustomed to be wonderfully affected at the sight of his armor-bearer, a beautiful and graceful youth—the spirits of the muscles were excited. The words, joined harmonically and plucking at the hearing rhythmically, lifted the soul as if from a dark prison into a high region of light. By this, the sooty spirits pressing upon the heart were dissipated, finally offering the heart a place to dilate itself; from which dilation, joy and the rest from troubles necessarily followed.
