### Universal Musurgy

### Corollary I.

<margin>How does Music heal those afflicted by melancholy or demons?</margin>
It is clear from what has been said how, once the misty vapors of the heart have been dissipated, the <term>spirit of the Lord</term><note>In the context of the story of Saul, this refers to the evil spirit permitted by the Lord, which Kircher argues finds a physical "seat" in the dark, melancholic vapors of the body.</note> was consequently driven out. For since the <term>melancholic humor</term><note>The "black bile," one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with darkness, coldness, and depression.</note> is misty, obscure, and dark, it truly offers itself as a most suitable seat for demons. This is evident in the demon-possessed, the <term>phrenetic</term><note>Those suffering from brain inflammation or delirium.</note>, the <term>energumen</term><note>A historical term for individuals believed to be possessed by evil spirits.</note>, and the <term>menstruating</term><note>original: "menstruatis". In the medicine of Kircher's time, it was believed that certain physiological cycles involved the accumulation of "vapors" that could affect the spirit.</note>; since these abound in much <term>black bile</term><note>original: "atra bile"</note>, they render themselves susceptible to the various illusions of demons, who fix their seat in that misty vapor and agitate the soul in diverse ways. The most manifest signs of this matter are the exotic operations they perform—now speaking in tongues they do not know, now divining the future, now perpetrating various other things which can by no means be ascribed to pure human nature. Therefore, since the viscous and dreg-filled melancholic humor is, as it were, a certain instrument for the demon, suited for agitating the mind in wondrous ways, it is no wonder that once the humor is dissipated, the soul is restored to its former tranquility by <term>reinstatement</term><note>original: "postliminio", a legal term for the restoration of rights, here used metaphorically for the return of health.</note>, as we shall later discuss regarding those suffering from <term>Tarantism</term><note>A psychological and physical phenomenon in Southern Italy where victims of a spider bite were said to be cured only by frenetic dancing and music.</note>.

---

### Corollary II.

It is clear from what has been said by what reasoning Music removes the plague, <term>Lycanthropy</term><note>The delusion of having transformed into a wolf.</note>, fury of the mind, and other disturbances in all those cases we mentioned previously. This occurs by the benefit of the <term>spirits</term><note>In early modern physiology, "spirits" were subtle fluids that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note>, which, having been rendered thinner, faster, and warmer, dissipate those humors and thin or mitigate those things by which diseases are procreated. Consequently, the mind—its <term>phantasia</term><note>The faculty of the soul responsible for forming mental images.</note> being diverted for a time from the apprehension of the disease that was afflicting the soul more than is right—is so cheered that, once excited, it directs all the spirits to drive out the infirmity. These spirits, on account of the effective command of the mind, run hither and thither and fly together until they have fulfilled the orders, in much the same way that certain <term>North Winds</term><note>original: "Aquilonares". The North Wind was traditionally associated with cold, dry, and purifying air.</note>, when stirred up, perfectly purge the air infected by contagion and ward off the rot of that same air mixed with foul vapors. For since the vital spirit is airy or ethereal, as soon as it perceives sharp sounds and air moving quickly, it imitates that motion and its <term>Rhythm or cadence</term><note>original: "Rhythmum siue clausulam"</note>. For just as the operation of the intellect follows the actions of the phantasia, and the will and sensitive appetite follow the acts of the mind and the motions of the imagination—so much so that you can hardly distinguish the motion of one from the other—so those corporeal spirits, which are the primary instruments of the soul, easily follow the impressions and motions of the alteration of the air.

# CHAPTER III.

## Regarding the wondrous history of a certain King of Denmark driven insane by the power of Music.

The following example will teach that Music does not only release one from fury, but can also incite one into fury. <term>Krantz</term><note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian.</note> relates the case in Book 5 of *Denmark*, Chapter 3, and <term>Olaus Magnus</term><note>A Swedish ecclesiastic and writer (1490–1557) known for his descriptions of Northern peoples.</note> records it in these words: "While <term>Eric</term><note>King Erik Ejegod of Denmark (reigned 1095–1103).</note>, having meanwhile returned to his kingdom, was holding a solemn court and delighting in the industry of many soldiers and craftsmen alike, there was present among others a Musician. This man claimed to possess such skill in the art that he could call men into whatever passions he wished: making the joyful from the sad, the sad from the cheerful, the appeased from the indignant, and the indignant from the placid—even boasting that he could make them insane unto fury. And the more he made these claims of great things he could do, the more he made the King eager to experience them. And now the craftsman repented of his boasting and wished he had not proclaimed such great things about himself, for truly to test these things on a King was not without danger; furthermore, if he failed to prove what he said by the deed..."

He feared, not without reason, that he would be considered a liar and a pretender; he pleaded with whomever he could to turn the King away from that desire, but he achieved nothing. For the more he refused the trial of his art, the more he inflamed the King’s curiosity. When he saw that he would not escape even if he fulfilled what he had boasted, he begged that all weapons by which injury might be inflicted be carried away; then, he arranged for several people to stand outside the sound of the <term>cithara</term><note>A stringed instrument similar to a lyre or lute, often used in classical and medieval literature to represent the power of music.</note> so they could be called to him, and they were ordered to smash the cithara, once snatched from his hands, against the head of the player. When everything was now properly prepared, he approached the King, who was shut in the hall with a few attendants, with his cithara. At first, with a heavy tone, he instilled a certain sorrow in the listeners; then, by singing more pleasingly, he turned it into joy, so that they were not far from leaping about jokingly. <margin>The King of Denmark driven into a frenzy by the power of Music.</margin> Then, having attempted more sharp modes, he stirred up a certain indignation, which, when it grew strong, one could see the King and those standing by beginning to rage. Soon he gave the signal to those hiding to enter and restrain the now-raging King; first, according to the agreement, they smashed the cithara, and then they moved to restrain the King. But the man’s strength was so great that he killed some with his fist; then, overwhelmed by many pillows, that fire subsided. But when he had recovered himself, he grieved vehemently that he had raged against those whom he previously held most faithful.

Behold this truly marvelous history, which <term>Saxo Grammaticus</term><note>A medieval Danish historian (c. 1160 – c. 1220) known for the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> also relates in Book 12. They say that this King, named Eric and surnamed "the Good," burst into such a fury that, having broken the doors of the hall and seized a sword, he ran through four men; but when his mind was restored, having left his son as Regent of the kingdom, he set out for Jerusalem for the sake of expiating the homicides and died in Cyprus. Here, surely, no small doubt arises: how could the sound of the cithara have such ineffable power that it could snatch a King, who was by his very nature good, merciful, and mild, into such great furies? For that Alexander was driven into a rage by Timotheus and incited to take up arms by the cithara was not so surprising in a King of boiling bile and a thoroughly <term>Martial soul</term><note>A personality dominated by the influence of Mars—warlike, aggressive, and hot-tempered.</note>; for since he was filled with fiery spirits, these, having been stirred by a Martial rhythm, could easily induce the effect of fury through a skilled cithara-player who knew Alexander's temperament.

But how it incited this "best" King of Denmark into such excessive mental ardor, I do not clearly see. Certainly, several circumstances persuade me that this effect was not entirely natural. For the cithara-player requested that, while the King was raging, the cithara be smashed against his own head, and that only after it was smashed should the King be restrained. This action implies I know not what kind of <term>pact</term><note>Kircher suggests that the musician may have had a demonic contract or used "black magic" rather than pure musical science.</note>. For if, as he boasted, he knew how to excite changes of affect and mind in men by the sound of the cithara, why did he not recall the raging King from that vehement commotion of the soul to a milder state by using more relaxed rhythms? Just as historians report that Timotheus and Pythagoras recalled youths burning with lust to self-restraint. The hesitation also, by which he regretted the promised effect, clearly shows that he foresaw an infallible effect in the King, and consequently feared lest great danger hang over his own head. Why he also wanted the guards to stand outside the sound of the cithara, I see no reason; for Music, as has been said, is not fit for stirring all people in the same way, but according to the different conditions of their natures, one was moved differently than another. Therefore, there was undoubtedly some implicit pact here, by which he produced the same effect so powerfully in everyone.

Or, if there was no pact, I would say that a Demon mixed himself into this action, as in the case of <term>Saul</term><note>The first King of Israel, who was famously soothed by David’s harp playing, though Kircher notes here that the music eventually failed to curb Saul's violence.</note>, whom we read became so insane as soon as the evil spirit invaded him that no Davidic cithara was sufficient to repel it; for it is certain that Saul was not always cured by David, since twice he tried to transfix the player with his spear; the harmonious sound being insufficient to dissipate such a violent commotion of <term>black bile</term><note>original: "atræ bilis"</note> maintained by a Demon. Although also Saul's hatred, conceived against David, could have greatly detracted from the skill of David’s art. In a word, in such prodigious cures performed through harmony, I would believe that something preternatural always coexisted with the natural action, especially if they are so maddened by the power of music that they are carried away even into open homicides, as was evident in this present example and in King Saul. For those afflicted by <term>Tarantism</term><note>A phenomenon in southern Italy where victims of a spider bite were said to dance uncontrollably; Kircher was a leading researcher on this topic.</note>, although they assume entirely exotic behaviors by the power of Music and are close to being "water-crazed" [delirious], it has never been heard that they inflicted violence on anyone, as will be said later. Furthermore, how the hard of hearing, those with sciatica, and other diseases...

### Question I.
## Why can those suffering from Tarantism be cured by no other means than a harmonic medium, or by Music alone?

How great the power of Music is in stirring the passions of the mind, and what the cause of this harmonic energy might be, has been shown at length in the preceding chapters; it remains now for us to finally show how the force of the disease in those suffering from Tarantism can be driven out by the force of music, and the sick person restored to full health. Therefore, without any verbal ambiguity, let us begin the reasoning we have set before us.

<margin>The power of harmonic sound.</margin>
When strings or chords (as we taught in the preceding pages) have the greatest power to stir the air in the same manner in which they themselves are moved, and excite a harmony pleasing to the ears and the mind through this proportional mixture of sounds, it happens that by this stringed harmony—derived from the various and proportioned motion of the strings—the air is harmonically stirred. The air, in turn, similarly stirred according to the harmonic motions impressed upon it, penetrates within. Once the <term>phantastic faculty</term><note>In early modern psychology, the "phantasy" or "imagination" was the faculty that received sensory data and mediated between the physical body and the soul.</note> is occupied by this pleasant motion, it similarly moves the <term>spirit</term><note>Kircher refers to "animal spirits," a subtle fluid thought to travel through the nerves to communicate between the mind and the muscles.</note> by thinning it out. The spirit, thinned and rarefied by this motion, suitably affects the muscles, arteries, and the innermost fibers, which are the receptacles of these spirits. 

<margin>How the sick person is freed by music.</margin>
Since the vehicle of the hidden poison is a sharp, biting, and bilious humor hidden in the innermost marrow of the fibers, it happens that when this humor is stirred up along with the poison, it becomes rarefied and heated. This affects the entire system of muscles with a certain itching or twitching sensation. The patient, sweetly affected by this twitching that is pleasing to them, is compelled to break out into jumping—or at least, a commotion of the entire body and the humors follows. This commotion leads to heat; heat leads to a relaxation of the entire body and the opening of the pores; and finally, the opening of the pores is necessarily followed by the breathing out (transpiration) of the poisonous vapors. Since, however, the poison is so deeply rooted that it cannot be exhaled in a single bout of dancing, a certain portion evaporates gradually through movement every year until the whole is consumed.

<margin>Different people are affected by different instruments according to the poison, complexion, and constitution of the person.</margin>
As for why different people are affected by different musical instruments, I believe this should be ascribed to the diversity of "complexions" (temperaments) or of the Tarantulas themselves, or of the humans. For those who are <term>melancholic</term><note>In the system of the four humors, a melancholic person was thought to have an excess of "black bile," making them slow, cold, and prone to sadness.</note>, or those struck by Tarantulas with a duller venom, are affected by noisy drums and loud instruments rather than by strings and lutes; for since their humor is thick and sluggish, and the spirits follow the disposition of the humor...

The Tarantula, through its bite, infuses into humans a certain subtle humor, which acts as a vehicle for the hidden and penetrating poison. When this is excited by the periodic heat of the summer sun, it spreads throughout the whole body—especially into the arteries, muscles, and innermost fibers. In this way, the body is gradually disposed to receive harmonic motions. Once it is disposed, the poison finally twitches the muscles according to the proportions of the harmony, forcing the sick person, whether they wish it or not, to break out into leaps, and thus the intended effect of healing is achieved.

## Corollary II.

<margin>
Which music is most suitable for those afflicted by the Tarantula.
</margin>
Secondly, you will gather that just as not every melody suits every Tarantula, but specific melodies suit specific spiders, so too for a person bitten by this or that Tarantula, this or that melody is appropriate. For some, as has been said, are not moved except by a violent noise—as happens with those Tarantulas endowed with a more tenacious humor; the same is true in humans. Others are easily moved by any sound proportioned to them, such as those endowed with a subtle and bilious humor. For by motion, the poisonous spirits in them are easily thinned; since these spirits are sharp and biting, they vehemently entice the person to jump by plucking at the muscular system. 

If, therefore, a "melangoga" <note>original: *melangoga*; a term Kircher uses for a spider that stirs "black bile" or melancholy.</note> bites a melancholic person, it will make him sluggish and sleepy; if a "cholerogoga" <note>original: *cholerogoga*; a spider stirring "yellow bile" or choler.</note> bites him, it will make him choleric, mobile, unstable, frenzied, and breathing "Martial furies" <note>Refers to a warlike or aggressive madness associated with the god Mars.</note>. And so it goes with the others, especially if the music corresponds to the specific "Tarantism." 

One might rightly wonder what sound is proportioned to the poison. I say, therefore, that the quality of the poison—excited at fixed times just like all periodic diseases—causes a certain boiling or commotion of the humor. This humor, thinned by the power of the poison, is scattered into certain very subtle threads, like fibers, between the <unclear>diashuara</unclear> <note>This likely refers to the "diastemata" or the gaps/intervals between the muscles.</note> of the muscles. If, by the condition of the humors, these threads are such that they are easily stirred harmonically by an external sound, they will vibrate like a proportioned object. These vibrations then provoke the muscles to which they adhere into leaps, caused by both the twitching and the biting nature of the poisonous matter. 

Hence, the more a sound utilizes "diminutions" <term>diminution: a musical technique of breaking long notes into many fast, short notes</term> of voices and notes, and the greater the mixture of high and low voices in a Tone full of frequent semitones, the more pleasing the music will be to those affected by this disease. Because of the speed of the motion, it plucks the muscles more violently and consequently urges the person more strongly to dance. Hence, Lute players <note>original: *Cytharędi*</note>, as much as possible, tend to adorn their melodies with various diminutions of voices, and mostly in the Phrygian mode, because of the frequent semitones of which it consists.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the diverse properties of different Tarantulas.

<margin>
A wondrous story confirms that Tarantulas are imbued with contrary powers.
</margin>
**F**urthermore, it might rightly appear to anyone as almost miraculous and entirely paradoxical that one Tarantula, by some dissimilarity of nature, could be completely opposed to another; for they do not all respond to the same instrument, nor the same leaps, gestures, or symptoms, but rather to entirely different ones. When this was reported to a certain Spaniard then staying in Taranto, he is said to have first received the news with laughter. Despite the testimony of many trustworthy people, he refused to believe it until he had tested the danger upon himself. Therefore, having sought out two Tarantulas of different color and quality, he placed them on his hand and voluntarily allowed them to inflict punctures in different parts of his hand. Once the diseases were contracted and the poison gradually spread through his whole body, he soon felt the most severe paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or increases in symptoms, often involving convulsions.</note> and the agonies of death. Lute-players, flute-players, and musicians of every kind were immediately summoned, and various types of harmonies were attempted. At last, the sick man felt himself strongly urged to dance by one specific melody, but in vain; for as much as the poison of one Tarantula urged him toward the dance, the other poison—being contrary in its entire substance—resisted and pulled him back from the dance. Other types of melodies were attempted again with different instruments; he felt himself powerfully incited to dance by one of them once more, but again, it was in vain. For this poison, which incited him to dance, was so inhibited by the prior incompatible and entirely contrary poison that what the power of one allowed, the other irremediably denied. Thus, caught in this struggle of contrary qualities, while the sick man found no remedy for his resisting nature and the ferocity of the hostile humors <note>In 17th-century medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, and since no exhalation of the poisonous quality was permitted, he finally departed this life miserably, not without the grief and pity of those present. By his example, he taught how reckless and dangerous it is to expose oneself to such fatal experiments without caution and foresight.

<margin>
Music must cause the poison to transpire.
</margin>
Unless, therefore, the music causes the poison to transpire <note>To "transpire" here means to be breathed out or expelled through the skin via sweat, which Kircher believed was the primary way to purge the spider's venom.</note>, it is certain that the victim of the Tarantula cannot live, or at least must lead a miserable life full of the most severe symptoms. Two other examples confirm this: a certain member of the Holy Order of Capuchins in Taranto was bitten by a Tarantula, and his natural appetite was driven toward clear waters. While he was carried away by this appetite—arising from a certain magnetic kinship and relationship between the victim and the spider—his superiors did not permit him a bath, nor the remedy common to all, namely the dance, to break the force of the disease. Finally, he was incited by such great efficacy of the biting quality that one day he slipped out of the monastery like one out of his mind and entered the sea, toward which he was carried with the greatest force, hoping to find in this coolness some salutary remedy for the atrocity of the stimulating disease. But it happened otherwise: where he sought health, he found death; for to the great sorrow of all, he was submerged and perished in the sea.

Roberto Santoro, a Nobleman of Taranto, was bitten by a Tarantula; because he did not know it, he was gradually brought to the brink of death. Since the physicians were unable to discern any signs of the disease, it finally occurred to one of the bystanders that the Nobleman was suffering from Tarantism <note>The disease or state of being bitten by a tarantula and requiring musical therapy.</note>. The conjecture was accepted in the medical council. Soon a skilled musician was summoned and brought to the man in his death-agony; in place of mourning, the usual types of melodies were attempted. To one of these, which was proportioned to his ailment, the man—who had been lying motionless and deprived of the use of his senses, fixed to his bed—was finally roused by the grateful repercussions of the harmonic air. From his lethargic and death-bearing stupor, he began at last to move his languid limbs slightly, then to toss his arms, and soon, as the sound continued and his strength was resumed, to sit up in bed and twist his neck, giving manifest signs of the internal delight perceived from the Music. Then, as the lute-player played more briskly, he even raised himself onto his feet; what more?

## Question II.
### Why are those affected by Tarantism so greatly delighted by certain colors?

**I**t has been said that different Tarantulas excite those affected by Tarantism toward different colors; the reason why this happens must now be explained. I suppose, therefore, as something proven by experience, that those bitten incline toward the color which the tarantulas themselves prefer. Thus, those who are wounded by red Tarantulas are inclined toward the color red and flame-like hues; those bitten by green ones incline toward green, and so on for the rest. Likewise, those Tarantulas found near waters, rivers, or the rims of cisterns similarly incline the bitten person toward water; whereas those from hot and dry places usually incite the victims of the Tarantula toward bilious <note>Relating to "yellow bile," one of the four bodily humors thought to cause irritability or heat.</note> actions.

If the **temperament** <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of humors in a person's body.</note> of the man corresponds to that of the Tarantula, it will produce a much more powerful effect. There are, therefore, certain venomous animals that transfer the very same affection which they themselves suffer into others by their bite. So it is with the **Dipsas serpent** <note>A legendary snake whose bite was said to cause intense, unquenchable thirst.</note>; since it is always tortured by a burning thirst, it produces the same in a man by biting, according to the verse:

> As the thirst twisting this creature is quenched by no waters,
> So does she stir up that same rabid thirst with her bite.
<note>original Latin: "Ut sitis hanc torquens nullis extinguitur udis, / Sic rabidam morsu concitat illa sitim."</note>

In the same way, the bite of a rabid dog produces that same passion in a man which it produces in the dog—namely, **hydrophobia** <note>original: "υδροφοβίαν"; fear of water.</note>, or the dread of water. The **Cerastes** <note>The horned viper.</note> also, as I have learned from the Egyptians, instills **pyrophobia** <note>original: "πυροφοβίαν"; fear of fire.</note>, or a fear of fire and light, both in the serpent and in the man infected by its venom. Likewise, the **torpedo fish** <note>An electric ray known for its numbing sting.</note>, being torpid itself, renders limbs torpid. And just as a parent suffering from gout, leprosy, or epilepsy communicates those same diseases to a son through his seed, in no different a way do the venoms of various Tarantulas—by a property implanted within them—seem to incline the mind of the bitten person toward the color which they themselves reflect, or by which they themselves are refreshed, through a hidden **Magnetism** or a blind similarity of nature. That the Tarantula is refreshed by a certain color is evident from the fact that, when placed on various colored surfaces, they seek out that surface which is similar in color to themselves.

<margin>
The cause of 
**chromatophilia** 
<note>original: "χρωματο-φιλίας"; a love or affinity for colors.</note>.
</margin>
From this it follows that, just as the venomous humor proper to this animal inclines its own imagination toward this or that color as being agreeable or contrary to its nature, so too will that same humor—transfused into the human body by a bite—produce the same effect through a certain Magnetic relation and a hidden, wondrous correspondence. For as soon as a color sympathetic to the venom (for example) meets the affected man, he immediately feels himself well and pleasantly affected by it, but poorly if he gazes upon a color contrary to himself. For the appearance of the color perceived by sight is presented to the imagination as something pleasing, which causes a **dilation of the spirit** <note>In Kircher’s medical theory, "vital spirits" were subtle fluids that carried sensations; "dilation" meant they expanded in a state of joy or health.</note>. The dilated spirit, acting as the carrier of the pleasing image, joins itself to the humor that is sympathetic to the image being carried. From this mutual marriage of natures, a certain pleasing affection or a **prickling titillation** results, diffused through all the fibers of the body, from which finally arises pleasure and a vehement desire to join and unite oneself with the desired object. 

Just as a person suffering from Tarantism is so affected by the proportion of numbers and the mixture of high and low voices (which is proportioned and similar to the venomous humor) that, with ears applied to the instruments, they perceive a harmony of this kind as if drunk in by the ears and incorporated into themselves because of a certain titillation of the reflected harmonic air; so too is the sight of the bitten person carried toward a sympathetic color with such ardor that they seem to want to drink it in with their eyes and incorporate it into themselves, owing to the pleasing affection and titillation of the spirit produced from it. For the individual powers, directed by the spirit, are carried toward their own objects

...by exactly the same reasoning as was stated regarding the **magnetism of the imagination** <note>original: "phantasię magnetismo"; the theory that the mind can exert a magnetic-like pull on the body’s "spirits" and humors.</note>.

At this point, one might not undeservedly ask: in what way does the color white dissipate, black collect, red inflame, and green, purple, or gold delight? Why, in those affected by Tarantism, do green and blue delight so greatly, while red and glittering colors hurry them away into certain exotic **apparitions** <note>original: "φάσματα" (phasmata); ghostly visions or spectral appearances.</note>? For these colors can only perform such feats through **species** <term>images or sensory forms that travel from an object to the eye</term>, which in themselves produce no real action; this is because they have only an imperfect and diminished essence, which some call "real" and others "intentional," being midway between the nature of real things and mental concepts.

I respond that the sensible species of colors are qualities endowed with the power of acting, though to a lesser degree than the qualities from which they are shed. For who would deny that the light scattered from the sun through the air, or the heat poured out from a fire, has the power of heating? Light is the image and **species** of the Sun, just as heat is the representative form of fire; nothing, therefore, prevents objects from changing the organs of the senses through these species, acting as their own natural instruments. Added to this is the fact that the venom of the Tarantulas claims this specific property: it inclines the victim toward one color or another according to its own condition. For the **humor** <note>One of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> in the human body is so tempered that it is carried toward the imagination, guided by the **spirit** <term>animal spirits: a subtle, fluid-like substance thought to carry sensory information through the nerves</term>, which has been shaped by the "species" of the colored thing. Thus, experience teaches that the color red wonderfully excites those who have been bitten by "analogous" <note>Spiders whose own coloring matches the red color mentioned.</note> Tarantulas. Since redness, by its peculiar action, inflames the eyes due to its similarity to the nature of fire and twitches the visual muscles—as is apparent in Lions and Buffaloes—and since the greatest force of the spirits is collected in the eyes, these spirits, being dilated and ignited by the flaming color, twitch both the visual muscles and other nearby muscles corresponding to the rest of the limbs. It happens that from this twitching, a certain immense itching is felt, giving rise to movements which Music greatly promotes with its harmonic air. Whence a man, feeling the greatest pleasure from that most pleasing object of color along with the Music, is driven, whether he wills it or not, into leaps and dances.

<margin>Harmony exists within colors.</margin>
For there is also a harmony in colors, which recreates the mind no less than Music, and this analogy of harmonies possesses the greatest power in arousingly the affections of the soul. For just as from yellow, red, and blue, the most pleasing colors of gold and purple arise, so from these two comes green, the most pleasant of all colors. By the same reasoning, since green is composed of the most pleasing colors, gold and purple, it is most perfectly tempered—not unlike the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> consonance, which is composed of the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> and the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. Just as the Octave moves the ears most perfectly of all, so green moves the eyes, such that nature seems to have given it solely for pleasure and the recreation of the eyes.

## Question III.
### Why do those affected by Tarantism mimic such diverse movements?

It has often been said that those affected by Tarantism assume diverse behaviors during the time of their **paroxysm** <note>A sudden attack or violent expression of a disease.</note>; some act as soldiers, some as Leaders and Governors, others as prize-fighters, and some as preachers. It is asked, therefore, from where do these affections arise? For it is certain that such passions did not exist before, yet they are notably transformed as soon as they perceive the sound of musical instruments. To explain this, it must be noted that there are certain poisons which, in a peculiar way, have power over the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note>. By their force, the humors throughout the entire body are stirred up and elevated into the brain; afterward the spirits, and finally the imagination, are invaded by them. Finally, by the aid of the spirits, the humors of the whole body are excited according to the "species" conceived in the imagination, based on the varying ratio of the person's temperament.

<margin>The imagination, when vehemently occupied with something, is transformed as if into the thing it desires.</margin>
Thus, it is no wonder if those infected, by the aid of the spirits, believe themselves to be that which is presented to them by the imagination. Thus the venom brought in by the **dipsas** <note>A legendary serpent whose bite caused a fatal, unquenchable thirst.</note>, as well as **aconite** <note>Wolfsbane, a highly toxic flowering plant.</note> taken in larger amounts, seems to transmute men into fish, geese, ducks, or divers. For since poison of that kind, by its own force, inclines one toward water due to the intolerable thirst it excites, the imagination—having immediately assumed those images toward which it inclines by the power of the spirits—anxiously and laboriously fashions waters for itself, and rejoices insatiably in the sight and drinking of them; whence it will necessarily desire to be that

...that [the imagination] usually enjoys desired things, such as all aquatic creatures, and consequently, by the force of a persistent disease, the phantasy <note>original: "phantasia"; in early modern psychology, this was the faculty that processed sensory images and "spirits" within the brain.</note> is stimulated toward the desired thing. From this soon arise movements conforming to the excited humor—acts, I say, of indignation, anger, fury, and mental instability; and similar passions of the rational soul are excited, which are furthered more and more by the glint of unsheathed swords and the sight of red objects, as was also said in the preceding sections. However, the bile-inducing venom acts more mildly in a phlegmatic person; and you may reason the same way regarding blood-inducing <term>hemagogis</term>, phlegm-inducing <term>phlegmagogis</term>, and black-bile-inducing <term>melangogis</term> Tarantulas in people of sanguine, phlegmatic, or melancholic temperaments. Since these points are clear from what has gone before, I will gladly omit them here.

# CHAPTER VI.

## How Prophecy and Divination Can Be Caused by Harmonic Melodies.

It is known from the Holy Scripture that prophecy has occasionally occurred through the power of musical harmony. This is seen especially in the first Book of Kings, chapter 10 <note>Kircher cites "lib. 1. Reg. à 5," referring to the Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 10:5–10.</note>, where Samuel sent Saul, who had been anointed king, to a group of Prophets. When they met, Saul saw them with a psaltery, a drum, a flute, and a lyre before them, and they were prophesying; then the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him and he prophesied in their midst. Also, in 1 Chronicles chapter 25, the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun <note>original: "Iditpia," a variant spelling of Jeduthun.</note>, who were set apart for service by David, prophesied with lyres, psalteries, and cymbals. And in 2 Kings chapter 3, verse 15 <note>original: "lib. 3. Reg. c. 4. num. 15."; Kircher follows the Vulgate numbering where 1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings are 1–4 Kings.</note>, while the minstrel played, the "hand of the Lord" came upon Elisha. Therefore, the question is asked: what power and efficacy can Music have to produce such a wonderful effect even in men who are not supernaturally endowed with the gift of prophecy? But so that these matters may be discussed more solidly, we shall first declare how we define "prophecy" in this context.

Prophecy, therefore, is nothing other than that foreknowledge or prediction of future events, or a divine instinct by which someone, being inspired, reveals the secrets of the heart or other mysteries that cannot be known through natural means. Thus, one who knows those secrets and counsels of God through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit without their own labor is called a Prophet. It can also be called "prophecy" when many things beyond human sense are accomplished by the help of a malignant spirit, as happens in those possessed by demons, and formerly in those who were agitated by "poetic fury." We are not dealing here with the miraculous production of Prophecy, but with the natural kind; we ask whether this can truly be produced by Music, a topic on which there are various opinions from different people.

The Astrologers, along with the Magi, assign the cause to the "Soul of the World" <note>original: "Colcodeam Animam"; likely referring to the *Alcocoden*, a term from Hellenistic and Arabic astrology for the "giver of life," which Kircher links to a soul that distributes forms.</note>, the distributor of forms. They foolishly claim that the power of all Magic is to be drawn from this, and that this is why Saul became a prophet when the musician played. For they think that the soul performs wonders according to various degrees of "fury," so that a soul stirred by musical fury exits its prison and transcends the bonds of the limbs without restraint; being incited by a divine Spirit, it understands all things and foresees the future. I pass over many unworthy things they devise to establish their opinions; while I reserve these for refutation in other works, I did not wish to be more lengthy here—

### Book IX. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance. ###

...we have established. Some argue that when the mind hears musical concord, it meditates on **celestial harmony** <note>This refers to the "Music of the Spheres," an ancient belief that the movement of celestial bodies creates a divine, mathematical harmony inaudible to human ears.</note>. They believe the mind, enticed by that sweetness, remembers the wondrous harmony of the celestial spheres and takes flight from its bodily chains. It remains aloft until, filled with knowledge of future things, it returns to agitate the whole body as if seized by a divine frenzy. However, these trifles are refuted in other places.

I shall now reveal how I believe the knowledge of divination and prophecy can result from harmonic modes. I say that music assists prophecy only externally, insofar as it makes the mind attentive and calls it back from any other thoughts so that it may be free for the single harmony. Indeed, musicians and lute players say they are never more successful than when expressing a song on the lute. This is not because God requires such preparation—any more than He requires dreams—to reveal something or enlighten the mind. Rather, it is so that the mind may, in some way, accommodate itself to the nature of things. For this reason, the prophets often wished to use a psaltery <note>An ancient stringed instrument similar to a harp.</note>, so that the mind, attuned to harmony, might receive the divine influence without being disturbed by the imaginations and phantasms <note>In early modern psychology, "phantasms" were the mental images or "spirits" that occupied the imagination.</note> of fleeting, worldly things.

Since God is Himself harmony, He willed to prepare the minds of the prophets through harmonic song so they could participate in His influence. Through this harmonic movement of the soul toward God, they are more perfectly united to Him. From this union follows the movement of the soul toward the hidden knowledge of future things. For the more a person becomes like God through various preparations, the more united to God they will be; and the more united they are, the more they will be filled with the gift of a greater grace. This is why we know that the holy men of God, withdrawn from the care of fleeting things and devoted solely to the contemplation of heavenly matters, are most often gifted with the power of Prophecy.

<margin>Opinions on the cause of Prophecy.</margin>
Therefore, harmony concurs with prophecy only **dispositively** <note>Meaning it "disposes" or prepares the mind to receive the gift, but does not cause the gift itself.</note>, and not **effectively**, since this effect far exceeds all the natural powers of music.

There are some foolish "philosophers" of our time who think there is a certain *panspermia* <note>original: "πανσπερμία"; a Greek term meaning a "universal seeding" or a mixture of all possible seeds/ideas in the air.</note> or "Idea" in the air—whether they believe it to be the Platonic World Soul, or the influence of the heavens, or a clumping of atoms—through which a mutual communication of emotions and concepts occurs. They think that, by natural means, certain people can know things from great distances, and thus "natural prophecy" is generated in the human mind. From this, it appears that nothing is so absurd that it does not have its followers. Just as mortal weakness cannot grasp how free actions could leave a "trace" or image of themselves in the air, I consider it **impossible** <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton).</note> for such things to be explained this way.

Certain Platonists, however, establish the cause of this admirable effect as the intelligent "World Soul" (*Anima Mundi*). They think the human soul, when excited by harmony, acts as a small fragment of that greater soul. When it is freed from bodily images, it shares in the same knowledge possessed by the World Soul. Since they claim the entire body and the entire world are penetrated by that Soul, they only require that individual souls be freed from every impediment so that, united through "harmonic union," they may know the same things the universal soul knows.

But since this Platonic fiction regarding a World Soul contradicts orthodox doctrine, it is seen to refute itself.

There are others who include the power of the whole world within our own soul, to the extent that they believe the soul knows all things when it contemplates itself. They believe that when the soul leaves all external things and retreats to the "center of the mind," it finds this knowledge. Some of these thinkers even claim the <term>active intellect: the part of the mind that transforms sensory experiences into abstract concepts</term> is freed from mental images even while living in the body, so it can understand without turning to physical forms; from this, they say, prophecy is born.

However, since I have refuted these ideas elsewhere, the fact remains that the prophecy spoken of in Holy Scripture, which occurs while the psaltery is playing, happens only "dispositively." In this way, God uses many elemental things as signs or vessels to confer grace upon mankind.

But since I treat these and similar matters at length in my *Egyptian Magic* <note>original: "Magia Ægyptiorum"; likely referring to another of Kircher’s works on esoteric philosophy and ancient wisdom.</note>, I refer the reader there.

<header>Universal Music-Making</header>

## CHAPTER VII.
# On the greatest effect of music, which it has in stirring up bodies, and consequently on those bodies which can partly be harmed or partly benefited by its sound.

There should be no doubt that music possesses the greatest power in stirring up physical bodies. For when large bells are rung, when cannons are fired, or when thunderous echoes roar, how great is the movement of the air, of buildings, of windows, and of towers? These movements often grow so violent that men are not only stunned by the vehement sound but may even fall down lifeless. However, we are not speaking of this kind of sound, but rather of that by which certain things are moved by *this specific sound alone*, and not by any other, even a louder one. It is a wonder why one string should sound in response to another of equal tension, yet not respond to the blast of a cannon. Indeed, there is a hidden power within certain sounds directed toward specific bodies, so perfectly proportioned that the sound moves those bodies and no others; it impresses its force upon some, but not upon others. Just as a magnet does not exert its power on wood, lead, or similar things, but only upon a body of its own kind, so there are certain sounds which are fit and proportioned for the exciting of specific bodies. If anyone knew these proportions, he could undoubtedly perform the greatest miracles of nature by their means.

<margin>Wondrous experiments concerning sound</margin>
It happens from time to time that while many people are talking together, one particular voice makes a bench tremble, while the voices of the rest leave no impression upon it. I have also noticed occasionally that a single pipe of an organ has moved a specific string of a large lute <note>original: "chelis maioris"; here referring to a theorbo or large stringed instrument.</note> so sharply that the string seemed to have been plucked by a plectrum. Even a stone of immense mass has been known to tremble at the sound of a specific organ pipe, yet when that pipe was silent and the others were sounding, no movement was perceived. Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and music theorist who corresponded frequently with Kircher.</note> reports a similar wonder among the Franciscan Fathers in Paris: when the organs are played, the floor—near the end of the diameter rising from the square where the organs are situated—is shaken so much that you would almost fear the earth was opening up; yet you feel this not at all if you move closer to the organs or further away from them. From this are drawn the greatest arguments for **Natural Magic** <note>In the 17th century, "Natural Magic" referred to the study of the hidden, yet purely physical, forces of nature, such as magnetism or acoustics, rather than the supernatural.</note>, as well as the solutions to entirely paradoxical effects—such as when statues are moved by one certain sound and not another, a topic which will be treated specifically in our work on the *Wonder-working of Sounds*. In this same manner, at the waterfalls of Tivoli <note>original: "catadupas Tybu-tinas"; referring to the famous Cascata Grande in Italy.</note>, a certain iron ring fixed into a neighboring house is seen to be in perpetual motion due to the vehement sound of the falling river. I also have in my Museum a **polychord** <note>A multi-stringed experimental instrument used for studying acoustics.</note>, one string of which, though none of the others do so, is animated into sound with wonderful force at the ringing of a nearby bell. Truly, we shall speak of these things most extensively in what follows. There is no other reason for this phenomenon than the proportionate harmonic disturbance of the air; wherever the air finds a body proportioned to itself, it affects that body with a similar kind of motion. All those experiments which we produced in the first part of this work aim toward this conclusion.

From this I conclude that if someone knew the proportion that the sound of a particular instrument has to the **spirits** <note>The "animal spirits," thought at the time to be a subtle fluid that transmitted sensory information through the nerves.</note>, muscles, and arteries of the human body, nothing would be easier for him than to sweep a person into any emotion whatsoever. He could rouse them into dances proportioned to the nature of the musical measures, as we have said regarding those afflicted with **Tarantism** <note>A supposed dancing mania thought to be caused by the bite of a tarantula, which Kircher believed could be cured by specific musical frequencies.</note>. Furthermore, I am persuaded that if one knew the proportion of sound which each person possesses in relation to the **four humors** <note>The traditional medical theory that health is governed by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> of the human body, there would be no evil so obstinate, nor any infirmity so deeply rooted, that he could not dispel it by the power of this sound alone. We treat this at length and specifically in our *Medicine of Consonance and Dissonance*. Such sounds can be considered in two ways: either as being proportioned or disproportioned. We have proved that the former, being harmonic, are most healthful to the human body. Regarding disproportionate sounds, we say they produce the opposite effect in human bodies; for we call a sound "disproportionate" either because it is [violent] due to its vehemence...

## Digression on the capture of the Swordfish <note>original: *Pxyphiæ*, commonly called *pesce Spada*</note> which is carried out in the Strait of Messina <note>original: *freto Mamertino*</note> at certain times of the year, and whether Music holds any power over animals.

<margin>The wondrous hunting of the Swordfish by means of certain words.</margin>
It is a wonder, and scarcely believable to those who have either not seen this hunt or did not take part in it. This hunt is carried out in no other sea in Europe, as far as I know, except in Sicily, and especially in the Strait; it is arranged beforehand in the month of May. Expert fishermen in the said month, and on an appointed day very early in the morning, enter the Sicilian sea—which they call the *Pharo* <note>The Strait of Messina, named after its famous lighthouse or "Pharos."</note>—with a boat prepared for this peculiar business. One among the fishermen, more skillful and robust than the rest, occupies the prow of the boat, likewise equipped for this specific task with a harpoon <note>original: *hasta*, literally a spear or lance</note>; another invites the fish, which may be hiding somewhere, with singular words. As soon as the fish perceives the words—wondrous to say—it immediately presents itself as if lured by them. The harpooner at the prow, watching for the fish to present itself at the opportune moment, strikes it with a spear thrown with great skill; he finally makes the fish a rich and sumptuous prey for the tables of the Great Lords. But it is not necessary to recount the particular method of this hunt here, as it is outside our scope; instead, I shall explain how these fish present themselves at certain words and peculiar voices, and not at others. Many have thought those words were made up, and known only to sailors of this kind. Some have believed that the fish are enticed by these words as if by a kind of incantation. While I was passing through Messina on May 17, 1638, I received the whole method of proceeding from the fishermen themselves while present at the hunt. The words with which they are accustomed to lure the fish are as follows:

->Come, Mother of the song<- <note>original: "Mamassu di paianu"</note>
->Little ball of the song<- <note>original: "Pallettu di paianu"</note>
->Stay there, little one<- <note>original: "Maiaffu stignela"</note>
->Little ball of the song, again<- <note>original: "Pallettu di paenu palè"</note>
->The stay<- <note>original: "La stagnela"</note>
->Missing the stay<- <note>original: "Mancata stignela"</note>
->Toward the boat we look, near the face, and from the land.<- <note>original: "Pro nastu vardu, pressu da visu, & da terra."</note>

And these are the words taken from the mouths of the fishermen, at the utterance of which the fish, as if attracted, soon presents itself to the boat. How this happens, since it has tormented the wits of many, remains for us to explain.

It must be noted, therefore, that this effect of attracting the fish through words can happen in two ways: physically (through a natural cause) or paraphysically (beyond nature, either from a certain pact with a demon, whether implied or explicit). If the effect happens in the latter way, as many think, it can rightly be recorded among incantations. For we know that many snakes, birds, and wild beasts were accustomed to be gathered into one place, enchanted by certain mutterings of words fashioned from a pact. Truly, since in operations established by a pact there usually intervene certain other things that are more truly superstitions than physical operations—and other corrupt circumstances concerning time, place, position, and the number of words, which are entirely contrary to physical operations—a skilled philosopher will also easily discern true physical operations from superstitious ones by these listed circumstances. And certainly, I was for a long time much persuaded that the said capture of the swordfish was done through certain incantations and deceptions, until, finally, having inspected and discussed it more deeply, I found the operation to be done without any superstition...

<header>Universal Musurgia</header>

...I have detected. From this, I suspected that some physical efficiency lies hidden beneath these phenomena. To explain this: I first suppose, as we have explained elsewhere in various places, that every sound produced by an efficient cause spreads out spherically into every surrounding space and immediately acts upon any bodies it encounters. Since some of these are more and others less movable, it happens that wherever a sound strikes a proportionate and consonant subject, it moves that thing alone, while leaving countless others unmoved because they are disproportionate—as we have shown at length in "The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance" and other parts of this work. Hence, among many strings, only those that respond in unison or the octave will sound, while the others remain still. Thus, a certain sound from a pipe might move a specific stone, seat, railing, or statue <note>original: *imaginem*</note>, which no other pipe is able to move.

<margin>Why animals are delighted by some sounds or abhor others.</margin>
In like manner, experience teaches us that animals abhor certain sounds and, conversely, are delighted by others. Almost all animals abhor the grunting of a pig because of the violence it inflicts upon the spirit. A bear, on the other hand, is delighted by a pipe, because such a sound soothingly affects its spirit; similarly, the nightingale affects all things with its musical melodies because of the natural disposition of its vital spirit and its innate inclination toward harmonic measures. The same must be said of artificial or articulated sound <note>Structured sound such as speech or song</note>, which possesses greater power in almost all animals than inarticulate sound; for that sound affects more deeply and moves the imagination <note>original: *phantasiam*; in 17th-century science, this was the faculty that processed sensory data</note> of animals more powerfully than the latter. This is why shepherds give names to dogs, horses, sheep, and goats, so that when called, they stop and follow the shepherd. Certainly, the Dolphin, when called by a boy by the name of Simon, always appeared, as authors write. Peter Martyr, in his book on American affairs, also tells of a fish of immense size called the Manatee <note>original: *Manati*</note>, which, when called by the name "Martin," would come out of the waters and take food from the hands of any bystanders. Thus, animals are captured by certain words and not others, because such words, and no others, have a power proportionate to their articulated sound to move the spirit and imagination of animals, by which movement they follow the sound.

Therefore, the same thing may happen in the capture of the swordfish <note>original: *psyphiæ*</note>; for only these recited words have the power to excite the indwelling spirit and imagination of this animal and affect it soothingly, and no others, as is established by certain and indubitable experience. Since only those words have the proportion required to rouse the animal spirits, and no others; just as among men, not all are delighted by the same music, but by that which is more proportionate to their temperament <note>original: *complexioni*</note>, the same must be said of animals. The words, however, are not entirely made up, but are true words, corrupted over time so that they might seem meaningless <note>original: *ἀσήματα* (asēmata)</note>. And this, I believe, is the reason why the swordfish appears at the spoken words, saving the judgment of better philosophers; to whose opinions I promise I shall not be unwilling to subscribe, if they bring forward anything better.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## Whether the natural power of herbs, plants, and animals, joined with musical melodies, possesses any power in the cure of infirmities.

There was no lack among the ancient philosophers—Pythagoras, Theophrastus, Ismenias of Thebes—whom Joannes Baptista Porta followed more superstitiously than is right among the moderns, who not only believed, but tried to persuade many others, that a lute equipped with wolf-gut strings <note>original: *lupinis fidibus*</note>, when played, would leave sheep stunned and lifeless with fear; also that horses are put to flight and driven into a frenzy by the sound of drums made from elephant, camel, or wolf skins; and that lutes equipped with viper or snake gut strings would cause miscarriages in pregnant women. I, certainly, so as to leave nothing untried, conducted an experiment on wolf-gut strings; for I took care to have two multi-stringed instruments <note>original: *polychorda*</note> prepared at no small expense, one of which was equipped with wolf-gut strings and the other with sheep-gut strings; and

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s exploration of "The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance," moving from general theories of resonance to a skeptical, experimental critique of popular myths regarding "antipathy" and the medicinal properties of musical materials.</meta>

### Book IX. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance.

<margin>The Author’s experiments on wolf and sheep strings.</margin>
I once arranged for a wolf-gut stringed instrument <note>original: *lupinum polychordum*</note> to be played inside a sheepfold; then, I had both a wolf-string and a sheep-string instrument played together outside. However, I was unable to observe by any means that terror among the sheep, nor that famous breaking of strings born from "antipathy," which many claim occurs. I did not stop there: I placed a wolf’s head upon the sheepfold and tied a wolf’s heart and genitals <note>original: *veretrum*</note> to the necks of the sheep. Yet, I could never detect those "fantastic terrors" which they say seize sheep when they encounter such things. On the contrary, I even saw a wolf cub living with sheep, interacting just as trustingly as a dog and without any terror. Therefore, from that time on, I resolved that I would never believe anything of this sort unless my own experiments first made me certain of the report.

If those who investigate the "more secret philosophy" <note>Kircher refers here to "occult" or "hermetic" philosophers who believed in hidden, magical connections between objects.</note> would only employ such experiments, their volumes would not be stuffed with so many monsters and portents, nor would the chairs of the Masters be filled with so many fables and false deceptions. I consider it unworthy of a Philosopher to put forward anything of this kind for which they have not first conducted an experiment. But I return to the matter proposed at the beginning.

<margin>How sounds can be curative of diseases.</margin>
Giambattista della Porta <note>original: *Ioannes Baptista Porta*; a famous Neapolitan scholar and polymath (1535–1615) known for his work on natural magic.</note>—whom I otherwise admire as a wise man—thought that any disease could be dispelled by the power of music, provided that the pipes were constructed from the wood of plants that regard said diseases with a "natural sympathy." For example: if one were to make a pipe from the stalks of Hellebore, the "lymphatics" <note>original: *lymphaticos*; those suffering from madness or delirious states</note> could be cured by its sound, since hellebore is said to cure them when ingested. In the same way, he claimed a pipe made from a poplar tree would mitigate sciatic pains <note>original: *Ischiadicos dolores*</note> with its sound, because poplar ointment is especially beneficial for hip pains. Likewise, he claimed a listener would be incited to lust <note>original: *ad Venerem incitari*</note> if they used a pipe constructed from the stalks of the Satyrium plant; or that an instrument made from cinnamon bark would cure fainting or a loss of consciousness <note>original: *lipothymiam*</note>. In the same manner, he believed a pipe made from the legs of a kite <note>a bird of prey</note> would, by the force of antipathy, render larks and other small birds motionless.

Time would fail me if I wished to cite every single raving of the unskilled and these old wives' tales. For who is so moderately—and, so to speak, only on the "tips of the lips"—dipped in philosophy that they do not see these things have absolutely no affinity with Music? For if these things possess a curative power for certain diseases, they can certainly exercise it through natural application alone, without any help from sound. Furthermore, I argue as follows: either the harmonic sound produces these effects, or the medicinal power implanted in the pipe does, or both do so together. If it is the first, then the power joined to the material is superfluous. If it is the second, then the sound is unnecessary for producing the effect, since it is pointless to do through many means what can be done through fewer. 

Finally, if it is the third, it would happen either because the sound carries that curative power like a vehicle, or through some hidden "sympathy" resulting anew from the union of both; neither of these can or should be admitted. Not the first, since the virtues of natural things have a sufficient faculty in themselves to change and alter objects placed within their sphere without needing a "vehicle" to carry them. Add to this that an "intentional species" <note>original: *species intentionalis*; in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to the immaterial form or "image" of a sensation, such as a sound, as it travels to the senses</note> is entirely unfit for carrying anything else, as it requires the vehicle of air just to propagate itself in length and breadth; certainly, it cannot give to another what it lacks itself. That is, even if a "vehicle" could be substituted for the flow of powers into another thing, no new sympathy could result from it, since the power of sound and the occult power implanted in the pipe have very different essences, and "intentional species" are not capable of receiving any such physical impression. 

Therefore, whatever the wits of malicious men devise regarding these matters is false. Sound is not "sympathetic" in itself, nor is it the cause of the aforementioned effects; rather, it is the harmonious air exciting the spirit according to the various laws of numbers. It matters little, therefore, whether the pipe with which a shepherd soothes his sheep is made of elderwood or of wolf bones; they will be captivated by the sound of either pipe. For the same reason, it was not necessary for Hismenia the Theban <note>a famous ancient Greek flute player</note> to use a poplar instrument to banish sciatic pains, or for Xenocrates to use hollow Hellebore stalks to heal the delirious; they could have performed this with instruments constructed from any suitable material. For Music cures diseases by no other quality than that which disperses and loosens "thick spirits," refines them once loosened, lifts the soul weighed down by the dissolution of lethargic and melancholic fumes, and finally restores health by removing the causes of the diseases. Those who... are also to be laughed at.

He has just finished dismissing the idea that the physical material of an instrument (like wolf-skin or sheep-gut) possesses inherent magical antipathies. Here, he extends this skepticism to the choice of wood used for instruments, arguing that the effect of music lies in its mathematical proportions (rhythm) and its physical impact on the body's "spirits," rather than the material's occult properties. Those who wish to heal those afflicted by the plague foolishly believe that a lute <note>original: *cytharæ*</note> must be constructed from the wood of a grapevine or a laurel tree, on the grounds that wine, vinegar, and laurel are known to ward off the pestilence. Similarly, they foolishly believe that a pipe made from a <term>Thyrsus</term> <note>The Thyrsus was a staff associated with Dionysus and his followers, often made of giant fennel and topped with a pine cone, linked here to the "Satyrium" plant, thought to be an aphrodisiac.</note> excites lust, while one constructed from the wood of the Chaste Tree <note>original: *Viticis, siue Agni casti*</note> leads to chastity. In truth, either instrument will incite one to impudicity if you play lascivious melodies, and either will lead to modesty if you employ chaste and temperate melodies. Therefore, that harmonious air alone—producing rhythmic movements of a similar harmony—ought to be called the cause of such a prodigious cure. For the musician creates a harmonious rhythm in the air; this air, shaped by that same harmonic rhythm, communicates it through the power of hearing to the <term>spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, "spirits" were subtle, vaporous substances that acted as the bridge between the soul and the physical body, carrying sensations and commands.</note>. Finally, these spirits, stirred by this harmonic rhythm, move the soul to various affections—of love, joy, or sorrow—according to the quality of the motion. From these motions, in turn, arises the dissipation of "sooty" or dross-like vapors <note>original: *fuliginum*</note> that occupy the vital organs. Once these causes of disease are dissipated, the intended health must necessarily follow.

<margin>How Saul was liberated from an evil spirit by the power of music.</margin>
From these principles, it is clearly evident how Saul, when he was seized by an evil spirit, was soon restored to himself while David played his music. For since Saul, out of envy and sadness, suffered from an abundance of "melancholic humor" <note>Black bile, associated with depression and thought to be the physical environment most attractive to demonic influence.</note>—which is the proper and most suitable seat for demons—it happened (as is evident in those who are demonically possessed, frenzied, or energized) that these vaporous spirits were dispersed by David’s melodies. The cloud of the heavy-laden mind was dissolved, and with it dissolved, the evil demon, as if driven from its own seat, vanished. From this came the immediate composure and tranquility of his mind. But perhaps I have dwelt on these matters more extensively than was necessary. Therefore, let these remarks on the prodigious cure of diseases through music suffice. Should anyone desire to know more curiously about the harmony of pulses, the "syndrome of spirits," and the wonderful sympathy or antipathy between human beings—or what is the same, the consonance and dissonance of natures and temperaments shining forth between different men—let him consult my *Iatrice* or *Medicine of the Consonant and Dissonant*, where he will find many new and hitherto unknown things regarding this matter.

## CHAPTER I.
->On the definition and division of prodigious sound.<-

A prodigious sound is nothing other than an unusual noise intended to signify something, which, while it strikes the ears vehemently and its cause remains unknown to the listeners, ravishes them with the greatest wonder. It is of three types: natural, preternatural, and supernatural (or miraculous).

To the category of miraculous sound belongs that great sound which, while Christ was preaching in John 6, suddenly arose and filled all the listeners with great wonder; such also was the Music of the Angels at the Nativity of Christ; such was the sound on the day of Pentecost, according to that passage in

# CHAPTER II.
## On the fall of the walls of Jericho following the sound of the trumpets.

<margin>The walls of Jericho collapsed by a miracle.</margin>
Whether that prodigious sound of trumpets and the shouting of the people caused the fall of the walls of Jericho through physical means <note>original: *physicè*</note> or through a miracle is a matter of dispute. Among the Rabbis, <term>Ralbag</term> <note>Rabbi Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher known for seeking naturalistic explanations for miracles.</note> was the first to think they collapsed due to the sheer violence of the sound. The Holy Fathers held the same opinion, namely St. Augustine in his 206th sermon *On Time* <note>original: *de tempore*</note>; he says that after reaching the city of Jericho, its walls were cast down to their very foundations by the shouting of the people and the sound of trumpets. St. Jerome, in his letter to Abigaus, says the walls of Jericho fell, overthrown by the blasts of the priestly trumpets. St. Ambrose asserts the same in Book 30, Chapter 10, as does Origen in his 6th homily. Among more recent authors, <term>Mersenne</term> <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and music theorist, often considered the father of acoustics.</note> thinks they collapsed entirely due to the violence of the sound; indeed, he even prescribes a mathematical proportion between the "moving force" and the "mobile object." Since these theories are more clever than they are true, we shall not dwell on them. Rather, we say briefly that the walls collapsed miraculously at the sound, serving as a sign of the Divine will. However, I shall prove that they could not have been moved by natural means (regardless of what Mersenne says). No sound of men or trumpets, no matter how great, intense, or multiplied, can naturally cast down or move a wall or a massive structure on its own, which I demonstrate as follows.

Three things must concur to produce a sound: first, the collision of two bodies, either solid or nearly solid. Second, the "breaking" or crushing of the air (or a similar body) trapped between those two. Third, the diffusion of this broken and crushed air, which acts as a sort of flight or retreat. It is this movement that can move or impel something; for while the air "flees" and recedes, it strikes any bodies it encounters and, if it can, pushes them forward. It always moves and pushes the nearby and immediately adjacent air, otherwise there would be a "penetration of dimensions" <note>In Aristotelian physics, two bodies cannot occupy the same space at once; therefore, the air must move out of the way.</note>; and air is naturally very easy to set in motion. However, it does not always move distant air, because the force of that "fleeing" air gradually weakens, and thus it ceases to advance or push forward of its own accord. But in this progression and the impulse it gives to other bodies, one must consider that for sound to travel far and push strongly, it is necessary, first, that it be broken, crushed, and thrust out with great force; and second, that it be not a thin or meager thing, but possess a greater quantity. For if the first is lacking, the "flight" is stopped immediately, and it will not move the nearby air vehemently even at the start. If the second is lacking, the voice will be stifled by the surrounding air, which is spread far and wide, and it will be unable to either advance or push anything. To this we must add that even the greatest sounds have very little force in an open medium, such as open fields, and that the sound is easily dissolved and dissipated into the vast air that surrounds us. So much so, that most philosophers assert that what reaches ears that are somewhat distant is not the actual, real sound, but only its <term>species</term> <note>In 17th-century physics, a "species" was a non-physical "likeness" or sensory image of an object that traveled through a medium to the senses, rather than the physical force itself.</note> or shadow.

<margin>How sound moves things.</margin>
If sound possessed this power, then in the besieging of cities, there would be no need for battering rams and catapults, but only the disorganized noise of men, horses, drums, trumpets, and cannons. As for what we said in the preceding part—that sound possesses great power to move certain things, such as when an organ makes a stone or a statue tremble with its sound—I would not have this understood as anything other than a "harmonious agitation" of the air. For even a single small pipe can move a massive weight, whereas ten pipes larger than said pipe might not move it at all. Therefore, in that passage, we were not speaking precisely of the violent agitation of the air, but of that phenomenon where we say a sound moves another body that is "proportioned" to itself, in the same way that one string [moves another]...

as we said, one string moves another. For if twelve strings are stretched on any <term>polychord</term> <note>A multi-stringed instrument, like a harp or harpsichord.</note>, of which the first and the last are <term>equally tuned</term> <note>original Latin: *isotonae*, meaning tuned to the same pitch and tension.</note>, I say that one of these will move the other, but none of the other ten strings listed can move either of them, even if they are all set in motion. As for the testimonies of the Holy Fathers cited shortly before, I say that none of the Holy Fathers believed the walls of Jericho fell solely by the natural power of trumpets and shouting, but rather by a sign, through which God—either by Himself or through the ministry of Angels—destroyed and laid waste to the City. It remains the case, then, that the ruin of the walls of Jericho was not caused by the natural sound of the trumpets, but was entirely miraculous. # CHAPTER III.
## On the portentous sounds of the second class, that is, those which occur by a natural agent, but by a power greater than human.

We speak here of certain portentous sounds which seem to have neither a purely supernatural nor a purely natural force, but are produced for good or evil by Angels, or by good or evil Spirits <note>original: *Genijs*, referring here to tutelary spirits or demons.</note>.

->A Marvelous History of a certain Sorcerer, who charmed<-
->children with sound.<-

<margin>Mice attracted by the sound of a pipe.</margin>
In the year of Christ 1284, a wonder happened in Hamelin, a town of Lower Saxony situated on the Weser river, which is almost beyond belief; the history is as follows: When the inhabitants were infested that year by huge swarms of mice and rats, and the evil grew to such an extent that almost nothing—whether fruit or grain—could be found that was not subject to the gnawing of the rats, and consequently various plans were being debated for removing such an intrusive and ruinous plague; meanwhile, a man never seen before, and of prodigious stature, suddenly appeared. He soon promised that he would immediately remove whatever mice were in that district, provided they agreed with him on a certain sum of money. No sooner said than done; the reward being promised, the said man drew a pipe from the pouch he wore at his waist, and as soon as he sounded it, behold! huge swarms of mice, bursting forth from every corner of the houses, the ledges of the roofs, and the holes in the floors, followed that unusual sound of the piper all the way to the river. There, the piper, with his garments tucked up, entered the river, and the rats followed him, where they were all extinguished by a voluntary drowning. After the enchantment was finished, the man demanded the agreed-upon reward, but when the citizens hesitated over the promised sum, he rebuked them with threatening words, saying that unless they gave the reward, he would exact another much heavier than the one promised. The threats were received with laughter. But the next day around noon, the said man appeared again, in the habit of a Hunter, with a terrible face and a purple hat of unusual design. As soon as he sounded another pipe, far different from the first, behold! all the children of the whole town, from four-year-olds up to twelve-year-olds, went out and followed the prodigious sound. Now, outside the town on the bank of the Weser, there is a certain cavern in a mountain, large enough for the stabling of beasts; into this cavern the hunter led all the children along with himself. And from that time, none of the children ever appeared again, nor was it ever discovered afterward what happened to the children or where they went. Because of this so wonderful event, the whole town, widowed of its children, is accustomed to this very day to calculate its years from the "departure of our children." I myself have been in that same city, I have seen the mountain itself, and I viewed with great admiration the history shown in a detailed painting in the Church—
