# CHAPTER IV.
## On the prodigious sounds of Bells.

Among the various bells that have stunned the world with their prodigious sound, the first place is surely held by that Bell of Velilla <note>Velilla de Ebro, a town in Aragon, Spain, famous for its "miraculous bell" that supposedly rang of its own accord.</note>, a continuous miracle of Spain, of which Varius writes in Book 2 of *On Enchantment*, chapter 14: "In the Kingdom of Spain, in the town called Velilla in the diocese of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsaraugustanæ diœceſis"</note>, there is a certain bell which they call 'miraculous.' This bell, for several months before any adversity occurs in the Christian Republic, rings of its own accord without anyone pushing it. I myself have read the testimony of this fact, documented by public notaries with many witnesses present, which the Viceroy of that Kingdom provided in his letters." Our fellow Jesuit Mariana describes it in these words: "Thirty-six miles below the City of Zaragoza, the town of Velilla is situated on the banks of the Ebro, built from the ancient Roman ruins of the colony of Julia Celsa. It is famous for nothing in this age or in the memory of our ancestors more than for its Bell. The people are convinced that when it rings—unmoved by anyone and with an unusual and persistent tolling—it signifies most notable events, for better or worse. Whether they believe this foolishly or truly, I do not dispute; nevertheless, men of no small standing are cited as eyewitnesses to this miracle. They say that the Bell rang of its own accord on the day before the Kings were captured. It sounded a second time on the third day before the Kalends of November, and again on the nones of January—sounding a third time when, after the treaty of Milan was concluded, the King of Aragon was restored to liberty. Furthermore, witnesses beyond all exception heard it ring before the death of Philip II, and several times in these recent years, as Nieremberg testifies."

<margin>Various examples of the prodigious sound of bells.</margin>
There is a similar Bell among the Japanese which rings of its own accord whenever great seditions and tumults threaten the kingdom. Juan Lopez, Bishop of Monopoli, relates that a small bell in the Monastery of the Dominican Fathers in Zamora <note>original: "Camorensi", likely referring to Zamora.</note> was accustomed to ring spontaneously three days before the death of any member of the order, even if no one was then lying ill in bed. The same author reports that there was a similar small bell in the Monastery of St. Dominic in Cordoba, which by its own sound portended the fate of either a brother of that monastery or some distinguished man of the same order. Angelus Rocha relates similar things regarding the prodigious sound of another bell in the Dominican monastery of Salerno, which announced those about to die. Gibellinus, in the *Life of St. Menulphus*, reports that in Germany, in the Monastery of Böddeken, a bell similarly signaled the death of a nun by a spontaneous tolling.

There are also other musical instruments that sound of their own accord when the more serious dangers of a kingdom are imminent. Thus, at the Tomb of Saint James of Compostela, future seditions are declared by war-like instruments and noises. Some signify the victories of Catholics against infidels, such as the clashing of the bones of Fernán González <note>A legendary Count of Castile; Kircher refers to the folk belief that his bones rattled in his tomb when Spain was in danger.</note>, concerning which see Nieremberg. I could bring forward innumerable examples of prodigious sounds in this place, but he who desires more of this kind should read the *Theater of Human Life* concerning prodigies, Hegesippus and Josephus concerning the signs preceding the destruction of Jerusalem, Cornelius Gemma in his *Cosmocritica*, and others. It remains to be investigated how that sound is produced. Certainly, it is not natural; therefore, it must occur beyond nature. I say, then, that these prodigious sounds are caused by the help of Guardian Angels through the merits of some Saint, both for certain ends and reasons known to God alone, and to warn of imminent evils in a kingdom...

# CHAPTER V.
## On the hidden causes of certain sounds, such as the formidable sound of the Smellen cave in Finland.

<margin>The admirable power of the sound of a cave in Finland.</margin>
Let us now consider that terrible cave of **Finland**, which **Olaus Magnus** <note>A Swedish archbishop and cartographer (1490–1557) famous for his descriptions of Northern Europe.</note> beautifully describes in Book 11, Chapter 3 of his *History*. It is located near the coastal city of **Vyborg** <note>original: "Viburgium"</note>, close to the Russian lands. Such is its secret power that if a living animal is cast into it, the formidable sound excited within it—by its sheer intensity—so overwhelms the ears of those standing nearby that they can neither hear, nor speak, nor remain standing. It strikes the ears with this power much more severely than the loudest **cannon** <note>original: "bombarda"</note>, or weakens them in a moment to the point that they are hardly masters of themselves. 

But this work of nature does not seem to be idle; for when a hostile invasion threatens, the governor of the land orders everyone's ears to be plugged with wax, and those who are to survive are hidden in cellars and caves. Finally, protecting himself, he precipitates some animal, suspended by a rope or a spear, into the mouth of the cave. From this, such a horrific sound is immediately stirred up that the enemies besieging the area fall down like cattle to be slaughtered, and having fallen, they remain there for a long time to be plundered. When they return to their senses, they no longer arrange to fight, but prepare to look to their own lives in flight. Thus it happens that those who could not be repressed by arms or force from their warlike fury are conquered, wasting away from the mere horror of bellowing nature. He asserts, moreover, that this cavern is surrounded by several walls to ward off the dangers of those who might approach it rashly. According to the same witness, the **Russians** <note>original: "Rutheni"</note>, having lost many thousands of their men, left behind for posterity examples of this calamity that are truly to be pitied above all other enemies. 

**Pliny** tells of a similar cave in **Dalmatia** with a vast, steep opening, into which if even a light weight is thrown on a calm day, a storm like a whirlwind bursts forth. **Peter Martyr** <note>An Italian-born historian of Spain's explorations in the Americas.</note> tells of a similar cave on the island of **Hispaniola** in America, of such horrendous sound and such a cruel storm perpetually following it, that no one dares to approach within five miles of it with impunity—that is, without danger to life or risk of deafness.

<margin>The cause of such a great effect.</margin>
The cause of such a prodigious sound, if the things Olaus reports are true, is none other than the natural internal constitution of the mountain. This multiplies the sound through an infinite **reflection** of the voice <note>Kircher is describing what we now call resonance and echoes.</note> and stirs the air; and since the agitated air can have no other exit except through the hole and orifice of the cavity, it is no wonder that the sound, constricted and narrowed there, should excite such a formidable noise along with the violence of a storm. 

I hear that something similar is found in the **Swiss** mountains, especially on the mountain they call the **Cucumber** <note>original: "Cucumerem"; likely referring to a peak with a distinct shape, possibly near Mount Pilatus.</note> because of its shape. At its summit, a deep abyss is seen, and if even a single stone is thrown through its orifice into the interior of the mountain, it excites such violent sounds that it not only strikes terror into those standing by, but forces them to flee by the violence of the wind coming out. For there is a wonderful power in enclosed mountains for multiplying sound, which experience also teaches us in very deep wells. 

In my own homeland, in **Fulda**, on the **Mount of the Blessed Virgin** <note>The Frauenberg in Fulda, Germany.</note>, there is a certain well nearly 300 spans deep, in which a stone thrown in excites such a sound that it might seem like the explosion of a piece of artillery. I remember observing the same thing on a certain mountain of the **Lipari Island**. Therefore, I do not think Olaus’s cave is entirely fabulous, since wonders of these kinds of sounds frequently occur to those traveling the world. But since we have reserved these miracles of the mountains for our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "subterraneo mundo"; a reference to Kircher's famous geological work *Mundus Subterraneus*.</note>, we refer the curious reader there.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the prodigious sound of certain shores of the Bothnian Sea.

<margin>Terrible sounds of the shores in the Bothnian Sea.</margin>
When **Olaus Magnus** <note>A Swedish archbishop and author of the 1555 *History of the Northern Peoples* (*Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus*).</note> treats the very high mountains of the **Bothnian Sea** <note>The northernmost arm of the Baltic Sea, between Sweden and Finland.</note>, he also mentions the prodigious sound of the coastal caverns. He says that no one can approach the roots of these mountains because of the intensity of the sound; for they perceive such horror from the deep collision of the waves that, unless they escape by swift rowing or a strong wind, they become almost lifeless from fear alone. Moreover, the bases of these mountains have certain winding fissures and internal receptacles where the waves enter and exit, fabricated by the stupendous craftsmanship of nature. In these, within a long abyss, that formidable sound generates a kind of subterranean noise. Just as many people once attempted to investigate the cause of this somewhat recklessly, so too did they lose their lives in wonder, their ships immediately filled with water. Indeed, that deadly sound, reaching the ears of sailors from many miles away, warns them to flee far from the snares of that most mournful "chattering" <note>original: "garrulitatis"; Kircher uses this term to personify the sound of the water as a dangerous, deceptive speech.</note>, which those positioned nearby cannot endure. **Vincent of Beauvais** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and encyclopedist.</note> tells of a similar mountain in these words: Among the **Tartars** <note>A historical term used by Europeans for the peoples of Central and North Asia.</note> there is a certain small mountain, in which there is said to be a hole, from which in winter such great windstorms emerge that men can hardly pass through there, and not without manifest danger. The cause of this thing is nothing other than the hidden **cataracts** <term>catadupae</term> <note>From the Greek *katadoupoi*, referring to the roar of falling water; Kircher uses it for powerful subterranean water flows.</note> of underground waters, as we shall demonstrate at length in our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "mundo noſtro ſubterraneo"; Kircher's famous 1641 work *Mundus Subterraneus*.</note>, and as is clear from the cave of **Hispaniola** <note>Modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note> mentioned above.

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note> reports that the shore of the **Aegean Sea** rivals the sound of a **cithara** <note>An ancient Greek musical instrument in the lyre family.</note>, certainly for no other reason than the varied composition of the cavernous shores. Receiving the force of the rushing waves and multiplying the sounds, they exhibit something harmonic—I know not what—to those listening from a distance. For I think no one can doubt that the size or smallness of caverns performs the same role in the production of sound as hollow resonant bodies, such as jars of differing sizes. From this, another difficulty is solved concerning the prodigious sound which **Laetius** <note>Joannes de Laet (1581–1649), a Dutch geographer who wrote a history of the New World.</note> reports is heard in his *History of the New World* in a mountain near the shore of the sea of **Guatemala** <note>original: "Quatomalenſis"</note> in **New Spain** when the East wind blows. For he says the sound so closely rivals the sound of our **organ** that the natives call it the **Dance of the Gods** <note>original: "Choream Deorum"</note>. The cause of this thing is nothing else but the channels of the mountain being of different sizes, in which the air, driven and packed through the caverns by the violence of the sea, performs the same thing as is done in trumpets, pipes, and bodies exposed to the wind when it is variously agitated and struck against the openings of the channels.

<margin>A wonderful history of three mountains in Persia.</margin>
To these, we shall add what **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 150 – c. 215 AD).</note> tells as a wonder about certain British and Persian mountains in Book 6 of his *Stromata* <note>The *Stromata*, or "Miscellanies," is one of Clement's major works.</note> in these words: [They also say, those who have written histories, that there is in the island of **Britain** a certain cave situated under a mountain, with a gap at the summit. When the wind falls into the cave and is struck against the fold of the trench, the sound of **Cymbals** is heard, as if they were being struck rhythmically. Often, when the leaves are moved in the woods by a sudden and thick rush of wind, a sound is emitted similar to the song of birds. Furthermore, those who composed Persian histories regarding places in the more eminent region of the **Magi** <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia.</note>, report that three mountains are placed one after another in a long plain. The first emits a sound like that of not a few thousands of men shouting, just as if they were in the air. When they come to the middle one, they perceive a greater and more evident noise at the same time. Finally, at the end, they hear people singing a **Paean** <note>A song of triumph or thanksgiving, originally to Apollo.</note> just like those who have conquered. The cause of any such sound is, as I think, both the smoothness and the concavity of the places; and so the breath <note>original: "spiritus"; here meaning air or wind.</note> which has entered, being thrown back and proceeding into the same place, sounds more violently.] If what Clement reports about the British mountains is true, certainly the cause of that prodigious sound can be nothing other than the cavernous and pierced channels of the mountain being of different sizes, from which such a disposition is born; for the cave situated under the mountain sends in the captured wind...

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s discussion of natural acoustic phenomena. ...it sends the air into channels where, more tightly compressed and striking against the openings, it produces various sounds, just as we said before regarding the mountains of Guatemala.

The triple variation of the murmur, which Clement <note>Likely referring to Titus Flavius Clemens, known as Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who wrote on Persian customs.</note> reports that three Persian mountains produce, must be attributed in the same way to the arrangement of the mountains. For the din of an army or a passing caravan, reflected in that place and multiplied by various reflections within the cavities of the mountains, reproduces the murmur of a passing army; it is no wonder, then, that the noise of a tumultuous host is perceived. Furthermore, because the reflection from the hollow of the second mountain doubles the din from the sounds—both direct and reflected—of the passing caravan from the first mountain, it is no wonder that the noises are heard more loudly. As for the third mountain, being more remote due to the natural arrangement of the ground and the alpine cavities, one who has deeply contemplated the preceding wonders of sound will not be surprised that it reproduces something similar to choirs singing <note>original: "Pæana"; a Paean was a Greek song of triumph, thanksgiving, or praise.</note> hymns of praise.

# COROLLARY.

<margin>The miracles of nature in an acoustic mirror, or listening place.</margin>
From this it is evident that a huge rock, hollowed out in a parabolic shape, can return a whispered voice at a distance of fifty paces, such as Father João Pais <note>A Portuguese Jesuit missionary (1564–1622) who wrote about his travels in Ethiopia (Abyssinia).</note> describes as being found in the mountains of Gojjam in his *History of the Abyssinians*. In these mountains, he says, there is a huge rock hollowed out with such natural industry that it appears like a mirror to those looking from a distance. Opposite this, he says, is another rock, on whose summit nothing can be said so softly, even from a great distance, that it is not heard. Indeed, for those shouting in said place, the sound is so intensified that it seems like the voice of an entire army. The petty priests of that place know this hidden power of resonant nature; in order to show themselves to be divine, they warn men positioned on the mountain peak of future events using these hidden voices. Those men, thinking they are inspired by the voice of a Deity, not infrequently fall into the greatest calamities while they hasten too thoughtlessly to execute the commands. If these things are true, I would believe it happens by no other means than through a <term>Phonokapoptikon<note>From the Greek roots "phono" (voice/sound) and "katoptrikon" (mirror-like). Kircher uses this to describe a "sound-mirror" that reflects acoustic waves to a single focal point.</note></term> object endowed by nature with a parabolic shape, by which the species of sound flow together into a single point on the rock positioned opposite. By this means, many things reported by historians are explained, which were widely regarded by most people as fables and superstitions. <margin>From Herberstein in the *History of Russia*.</margin> Sigismund von Herberstein <note>A 16th-century diplomat whose *Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii* was the primary Western source on Russia.</note> relates that in the province of "Candora," in the farthest land of the North, there is a river which no one has yet crossed because of the frequent ghosts that suddenly appear there, and the voices of men and animals usually heard on the opposite bank. He also says that hardly a day or a week passes, especially in the summer time, in which such prodigious voices are not heard. I certainly believe these are no other portents than the true voices of men and animals arising in the fields on the near side of the river, reflected from the hollow "mirrors" of the rocks across the water, which strike the simple and inexperienced men stationed on the banks with this vain dread and a kind of panic fear; for nothing can more easily deceive men than this talkative playfulness of nature. <margin>An extraordinary case.</margin> Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician.</note>, in Book 18 of *On Subtlety*, tells of a similar deception involving a certain acquaintance of his. A certain friend of ours, he says, when he was traveling near a river and did not know the ford, began to shout, *“Oh?”* to which a hidden Echo replied, *“Oh?”* He, thinking it was a man, asked in Italian: *“Where should I cross?”* <note>original: "Onde deuo paſſar?"</note> *“Cross!”* <note>original: "paſſa"</note> was the reply. Then he asked, *“Here?”* <note>original: "qui?"</note> *“Here!”* <note>original: "qui"</note> was repeated. But at that spot, the waters were roaring loudly in a deep whirlpool; from which he, terrified, asked again, *“Should I cross here?”* The Echo replied, *“Cross here!”* To him asking the same thing many times, it replied the same. Therefore, since the friend was between the fear and the necessity of swimming, and a dark and unseasonable night was pressing in, he thought some Demon wanted to persuade him to throw himself headlong into that torrent. Returning from there, he told the whole story to Cardano, who demonstrated by the facts themselves that it was not the snares of a Demon, nor the illusion of a phantom, but a game of jesting nature. You might perceive a similar portent of nature in Syracuse, in the ruins of the Palace of Dionysius <note>Referring to the "Ear of Dionysius," a famous limestone cave in Syracuse, Sicily, known for its incredible acoustics.</note>, where in a certain receptacle nature reflects sounds so perfectly that I cannot recall having heard anything more marvelous in a similar subject. Many things would have to be said in this place concerning the prodigious reflection of the voice and sounds, but since we have reserved all these for the following treatise, here putting an end to "Teratology" <note>The study of marvels or "monstrous" wonders.</note>, we proceed to "Echosophia" <note>Kircher’s term for the "wisdom" or science of echoes.</note>.

<summary>Kircher explains how natural rock formations and mountain cavities act as acoustic mirrors (Phonokapoptikon), creating echoes that mimic armies or human voices. He uses these natural principles to debunk historical accounts of "demonic" or "divine" voices, citing examples from Ethiopia, Russia, and the Ear of Dionysius in Syracuse.</summary>

## PART IV.
# PHONOCAMPTIC MAGIC
### O R
### On the Wondrous Works and Effects of the Reflected Voice.
## P R E F A C E.

<margin>What is an Echo?</margin>
<margin>Description of the nature of the Echo.</margin>
An Echo is a joke of a playful nature, called by the Poets "the image of the voice," according to that line from Virgil:
> The rocks resound, and the struck image leaps back in various ways. <note>original: "Saxa ſonant, varijſq; offenſa reſultat imago." From Virgil's *Georgics* or *Aeneid*, describing how sound reflects off physical obstacles.</note>
By philosophers, it is called the reflected, reverberated, or reciprocal voice; by the Hebrews, it is called *Bat kol* <note>original: "Bat col"; literally "daughter of a voice," a Hebrew term referring to a divine resonance or a heavenly echo.</note>, the daughter of the voice. Its nature is so hidden that to this day there is hardly anyone who has explained its latent essence. It is well known, and almost common knowledge, that an echo is a reflected voice, but how, from what sources, by what propagation, at what speed, and at what distance it is produced is so unknown that it rivals any mystery; nor does it seem that the vastness of the difficulties encountered can be exhausted by any reasoning, except by one who, equipped with the greatest experience and singular industry, has finally caught this fugitive Nymph after she has been toyed with by wondrous arts. Since no one has performed this until now, I—driven by the desire to investigate her—have searched the hidden recesses of the woods, the secret retreats of groves and mountains, and the rough plains of valleys, ruins, fields, and marshes, leaving nothing untried to reach her hidden nature. But while I pursue her, she flees; while I flee, she pursues; while I speak soothingly, she mockingly eludes me; when I shout loudly, she doubles the voices as if she had summoned followers to herself, knowing not how to yield. Occasionally, as if indignant, she turns away and avoids a response; sometimes, with a completely unusual talkativeness, she pours back ten words for every one. Mocked so often by this variety and inconstancy, I have tried to stop this most fleeting "goddess-ling" by every means—partly with songs, partly with musical instruments of every kind—and attempted to appease her in every way with words composed now to severity, now to flattery; but she, as one accustomed to woods and solitudes, knows not how to be tamed, and easily eluded all my efforts.

<margin>The nature of the Echo is to be investigated with the help of Geometry.</margin>
Finally, joining with me Geometry <term>anacamptic</term> <note>The science of reflection; usually applied to light (catoptrics) but here applied by Kircher to sound.</note> as a companion, I attacked her more fiercely once again. By her sagacity, it finally happened that she stood still, and my wishes were fully satisfied. Therefore, I have seen fit to communicate to the curious Reader in this treatise what I observed regarding her during my various travels in different places. To ensure the reader recognizes the immense riches of sounds more clearly, I have decided to exhibit a certain specimen of truly admirable things in this three-part treatise. First, we shall set forth new principles and canons of the <term>phonocamptic</term> <note>From the Greek "phone" (voice) and "kamptein" (to bend or reflect); the art of reflected sound.</note> art; second, we shall unlock <term>Phonocamptic Architecture</term>, or the art of <term>Echometry</term> <note>The measurement of echoes and acoustic distances.</note>, from the deepest secrets of nature. Third, we shall produce <term>Echotectonics</term> <note>The construction of acoustic devices or spaces.</note>, or the fabrication of Acoustic instruments, which we also call <term>Phonocamptic Catoptrics</term> <note>Acoustic mirrors. "Catoptrics" usually refers to the study of light mirrors; Kircher applies the same mathematical principles to sound.</note>. Indeed, we shall demonstrate in many ways—and perhaps through inventions not to be despised—that nothing is contained in that prodigious Catoptric Magic that Phonocamptics cannot also exhibit.

<margin>Blancanus was the first to write about Echometry.</margin>
<margin>What the author has achieved.</margin>
And although our fellow <note>Kircher refers to him as "nostre" (ours) because both were members of the Jesuit order.</note> Blancanus <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who wrote on the geometry of echoes.</note> was the first, as far as I know, to write about Echometry (in which he clearly deserved distinguished praise from posterity), we, following in his footsteps yet not at all content with what was handed down by him, raising our minds to higher things and opening a new and ever-flowing spring of various inventions, have endeavored to raise this <term>Echosophy</term> <note>A term coined by Kircher for the "wisdom" or scientific study of echoes.</note> to that degree which a science so hidden, and thus known to few, seemed to demand by its own right. I do not doubt that Kings and Princes, enticed by these things, will in the future restore with all zeal the magical structures of the ancients for the exhibition of any sounds whatsoever. But leaving behind the ambages of words, let us proceed to the matter itself; and so that we may proceed more solidly in our Echosophy, I have seen fit first to set forth definitions, Axioms, and Postulates in the manner customary to Geometers, so that, strictly observing the rule of the art, we may proceed in all things <note>original: "νόμῳ δίχως" (nomō dichōs); likely meaning "methodically" or "by the law of distinction."</note> according to law.

# DEFINITIONS.

**1** Phonocamptic Magic, or the Art of Sound-Reflection, is the more hidden science of sounds, by which we perform marvelous and—to those ignorant of the causes—miraculous effects through the power of the reflected and multiplied voice. <note>The term "Phonocamptic" is derived from the Greek words *phōnē* (voice/sound) and *kampsis* (bending or reflection). In the 17th century, "magic" often referred to "natural magic"—the study of hidden natural laws to produce amazing effects.</note>

**2** *Phonocampsis* <note>original: "Φωνόκαμψις"</note> is nothing other than the reflection of the voice, which the Greeks and then others call an Echo.

**3** The *Phonic Center* <note>original: "Κέντρον φωνικόν" or "centrum phonicum"</note> is the name given to the point from which the sound-lines originate, such as point **A** in the following figure.

**4** The *Phonocamptic Center* <note>original: "Κέντρον φωνοκαμπτικόν"</note> is the endpoint on the phonocamptic line where the reflected voice meets the ears, such as centers **B**, **O**, **V**, **C**, and **E**.

<note>A perspective geometrical diagram illustrates the principles of sound reflection (acoustics). A point labeled 'A' on the right represents the source of sound, the "phonic center." Lines representing sound rays radiate from A toward a large vertical stone or brick wall labeled with the corner points G, K, H, and I. The lines strike the wall at various points (L, C, B, E, P, Q) and reflect according to geometric laws. Point B is hit perpendicularly by sound from A, representing the "Orthophonous Line" (a direct reflection back to the source). Other rays hit the wall at angles and reflect toward points such as O, V, D, and K. The wall is depicted with a grid-like pattern suggesting masonry. Various letters label the intersection points and sound paths to demonstrate the definitions of phonic lines and different types of acoustic reflection.</note>

**5** The *Phonocamptic Object* is the name for any obstacle reflecting the voice, such as the wall **G K H I**.

**6** We call the *Phonocamptic Medium* that substance through which the sound is propagated <note>Usually air, though Kircher explores other media in his wider work.</note>.

**7** A *Phonic Line*, or a sound or vocal line, is that path through which the voice travels and returns, such as **A B** in the figure. It is of many types, as follows.

**8** An *Orthophonous Line* <note>original: "Ορθόφωνος"; literally "straight-sounding"</note>, or a direct sound line, is that through which the voice flows back to the place from which it originated, as are all lines reflected perpendicularly from a wall back to the sounding body. In the figure, line **AB** represents this, and it corresponds to a perpendicular ray of light.

**9** A *Loxophonous Line* <note>original: "Λοξόφωνος"; literally "oblique-sounding"</note> is a sound line that strikes the opposite wall at an angle and reflects at that same angle, such as lines **OS** and **CD** in the figure. It is fourfold, for either...

**13** The **angle of sound confusion** is the angle caused by two conical or cylindrical sound-paths intersecting one another.

**14** **Polyphonism** is the multiplication of the voice by being variously reflected within a concave body. In this sense, **phonism** is nothing other than the act of sound spreading itself out in a spherical, conical, or cylindrical manner.

# Axioms and Hypotheses.

**1** Every angle of sound-fall is equal to the phonocamptic angle; or, what is the same thing, every angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

**2** Every phonic or sound center radiates outward into a sphere in straight lines.

**3** Nature, in the matter of sound, only achieves its end through the shortest possible lines.

**4** Everything—and only that—can be heard which a sound-line is able to reach.

**5** Sound is vehemently intensified by multiple reflections radiating into a single point.

**6** Every reflection of sound occurs either back upon itself or toward the opposite side.

**7** The voice reaches the ears more slowly the farther away the reflecting object is, and more quickly the closer it is.

**8** Sound is measured by the activity of the sound-line.

# Postulates and Data.

**1** Given any point on a reflecting object where reflection occurs, to determine the reflected line.

**2** From any point of the object, a reflection can be established to any other point.

# Physiological Preludes on the Nature of the Echo, or the Reflected Voice.

### PRELUDE I.

### *Sound is the Ape of Light.*

<margin>What is Sound?</margin>
Sound, as was demonstrated in the first book, is nothing other than a sensible quality that can be perceived by hearing. It is not the motion of bodies colliding with each other, as some believe; however, sound follows the motion of colliding bodies, though indeed not immedia—

# Universal Music

<margin>
A collision of two solid bodies is not always necessary for sound.
Water is a medium for sound.
Fish hear.
Similarity of the direct and reflected ray to sound in air and in water.
Why sound is not so pure in a hall decorated with tapestries.
</margin>
...immediately, but by means of the breaking of the intermediate air; hence bodies which contain more air and smoothness possess the greatest power for sounding, because air is broken more in smooth and airy bodies than in those that are non-airy and thick. For this reason, it is not always necessary for two solid bodies to collide for a sound to occur; rather, the impulse of air and water is most suitable for producing sound, as pipes, the roaring of the sea, and thunder clearly teach. Therefore, when the air is broken by the collision of any bodies whatsoever, a sound is made, which is diffused from the point of collision no differently than a species <note>In 17th-century physics, a "species" refers to the sensory image or representation of an object that travels through a medium to the senses.</note> of colors radiating into a sphere. For just as colors emit their species everywhere through radiation, as if they were representatives of the object, so too does sound emit its species. Furthermore, the mediums of sound, by which its species are carried to the hearing, are not the subject of the sounds themselves, but are air and water. Regarding air, there is no doubt; regarding water, experience also makes us more certain. Indeed, Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), a Roman naturalist who wrote "Natural History."</note> reports that fish are accustomed to being gathered by a certain sound. The same Pliny relates that fish have appeared when called by name; furthermore, they are vehemently terrified of thunder, which would not happen unless they heard beneath the waves. Divers also assert that they perceive more forceful sounds under the water, and they do so more easily the closer they are to the surface of the water. This is a manifest sign that sound penetrates to the power of hearing through the air within porous bodies, such as water, wood, and walls. Water, therefore, is a medium for sound, although sounds are carried much more clearly and easily through air than through water. For just as a ray of light behaves toward a denser medium—in which it is refracted and dulled—so the sound ray <note>original: "radius sonorus"</note> is also refracted in a denser medium. Thus, the sounding species are dulled and blunted by the thickness of water, just as visible species are by a denser medium. Hence, in rainy weather and vaporous air, we hear less than when the air is clear. In great halls draped with tapestries, the voice is also blunted and absorbed, being perceived with more difficulty than when the walls are stripped of their hangings. From this, the reason is also deduced why music grows faint in a place full of people: because the sound, absorbed within the hollow mouths <note>or "cavities"</note> of human bodies, loses its force. In the same way, a hall spread with wool or straw so blunts the sound that it is scarcely perceived. More will be said on these matters in what follows.

<margin>
Sound imitates light.
</margin>
These things having been established, it must now be shown that sound is the "Ape of Light"—that is, that it emulates light in almost all its operations—which I shall now do. It must first be noted that a sound creates a sphere of its own power <note>original: "virtutis suae sphaeram"</note> within which that sound may be perceived, but outside of it, not at all. This sphere cannot be formed unless it is constituted by straight lines diffused everywhere from the sounding subject through the medium, as if from a center. Therefore, the radiation of sound mimics the flow of light very closely, nor is there any difference in the <term>radiation of rays <note>original Greek: ἀκτινοβολίας (actinobolias)</note></term> except that light is propagated by instantaneous motion, and sound by successive motion through the air. Certainly Virgil himself seems to suggest that light and sound are in some way the same thing when he says:

->Then the clearer fire is heard.<-
<note>original Latin: "Tum clarior ignis auditur." From the Aeneid, Book II. Kircher uses this poetic license to argue that ancient authors saw a link between the physics of fire/light and sound.</note>
->As also in Book 6: And dogs were seen to bark through the shadows.<-
<note>original Latin: "Visaeque canes latrare per umbram." From Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

<margin>
Parallel comparison of light to sound.
</margin>
Indeed, nothing can meet the eyes that cannot also present itself to the ears under a certain analogous reasoning. Just as it is the property of light to represent the different colors of bodies according to the different directions of rays—sometimes incident, sometimes reflected—upon surfaces, and from there to the eyes; so it is the property of sounds to represent the different qualities of bodies by the help of moved air striking and hitting their surfaces. Thus, we may say without incongruity that colors are nothing other than the different immersion and reflection of rays in a medium, just as sounds are nothing other than different motions of the air. For if anyone could see the most subtle motions of the air while some musical instrument was sounding, he would certainly see nothing else than a kind of painting sketched with a remarkable variety of colors, by which the diverse qualities of the sounding bodies would present themselves to the eyes, as has been said. Furthermore, just as light considered abstractly is invisible, so is sound. For we cannot see anything in this world except colored surfaces representing as much as possible the Sun and other luminous bodies. That light is invisible is shown more than enough by concave mirrors, which leave no trace of the rays except at the point where the rays meet and are...

# Book IX. The Magic of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>
No accident is sensible by itself.
Light reaches the eyes by the same reasoning as sound reaches the ears.
</margin>
...by applying an opaque reflecting body; indeed, to speak more strictly, I say that no accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a property (like color or sound) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a physical substance</term> is sensible by itself, except through the bodies by which it is sustained, or through quantity, which gives them extension, without which it would vanish into a point and nothingness. Therefore, just as light is invisible without air, so too is sound; for while sound makes the air sensible to us, it reveals many qualities of bodies that we would not know how to recognize except by the help of sounds. And if anyone looks a little more deeply into the nature of light, he will find it to be nothing other than a certain motion of the air, as it were, which carries with it the image of the first mover—namely, the luminous body—to present it to the eyes under the name and appearance of color or light. In the same way, sound is nothing other than the motion of that same air, which carries with it the different qualities of its cause—namely, the bodies moving it. Thus, it presents an image to us under the name and appearance of sound. For the sensible form of, for example, a certain sounding bell, presents itself to the eyes of a deaf person in much the same way as it occurs to the ears of a blind person. Furthermore, just as light cannot be preserved without the body from which it flows by an actual influence, so neither can sound exist without the motion of the air.

Therefore, we must laugh at all those who think that sound, enclosed in a pipe, can be preserved for a long time, as will be discussed more fully in our *Echotectonica* <note>Kircher's term for the "architecture of echoes" or the science of managing reflected sound.</note>; indeed, experience teaches us better, and that we are affected with greater pleasure when we read a certain history or a vivid description of a thing, or hear it sketched out by a distinguished Orator with various figures of words and sentences (like colors), than if we were to look at those same things with our own eyes.

Furthermore, just as the species <note>The "species" refers to the sensory representation or "image" of an object that travels through a medium.</note> of the objects affect the eye and the optic nerve by a certain hidden reasoning to produce a similar image by the help of the spirits; so too the image of a sounding body, carried by the air, affects the air implanted in the acoustic or auricular nerve to represent the image of the sounding body. From these things, unless I am mistaken, the immense similarity between optical and acoustic bodies in acting upon and producing both sight and hearing in humans is clearly shown.

<margin>
The refraction and reflection of sound.
</margin>
Finally, just as sight is refracted in a denser medium, so also is sound; as will be shown extensively later. For what else is sound received in a very porous and soft body, if not a certain shadow of sound, presenting an obstacle to prevent it from extending further?

### Corollary

<margin>
How much deeper a sound is inside water than the same sound outside water.
</margin>
From this follows a certain method of determining how much deeper a sound made inside water is compared to the sound of the same body made outside water, and consequently, how much thinner air is than water. For it was discovered by experience by a distinguished Mathematician not long ago that the sound of a certain bell, which was two degrees (for example) outside the water, was five degrees inside the water, and was consequently deeper by one minor harmonic tenth <note>An interval of an octave plus a minor third.</note>. Indeed, the cause of this thing is nothing other than the rarity and density of the different media. For water resists the species of a sounding body more inside the water than outside; from this resistance arises a slowness of the medium's motion, which slowness the sound follows by becoming deeper. For as one medium relates to another, so do the vibrations made in one medium relate to the vibrations made in the other; and as vibrations relate to vibrations, so sound relates to sound. If, therefore, as in the proposed example, it was as 5 to 2, the motion of the air and the motion of the water will hold themselves in the same proportion: from which the rarity of the air compared to the density of the water will be as 125 to 8.

<margin>
Phonism is similar to photism.
</margin>
You see, therefore, that Phonisms <note>Kircher's term for sound-phenomena.</note> are entirely parallel to Photisms <note>Kircher's term for light-phenomena.</note> in their operations, except for the motion, which is instantaneous in the diffusion of light, but successive in sound. Sound also is not only capable of being propagated along straight lines, but also along curves, as is evident when it passes through channels and tubes, or through similar sound-ducts, in which it is not only conveniently carried but is also greatly increased and strengthened; indeed, it is propagated further than in the open air, as will be proven later by various experiments.

# PRELUDE II.
## On the Phonocamptic Object.

<margin>
The hidden power of the Echo.
</margin>
**A** phonocamptic <term>phonocamptic: from the Greek "phone" (sound) and "kamptos" (bent); a technical term for a surface that reflects sound waves</term> object is not only made of walls, cliffs, partitions, and similar hard and solid bodies, but even earth, trees, leaves, wood, simple earth however porous, and especially water and any suitable liquids will be fit to reflect voices and sounds. This fact has perplexed me in a wonderful way more than once; for more than once in the middle of the fields located between Rome and Tusculum—where no wall, no trees, but only shrubs and inhospitable rocks and the furrows of the fields dominated—it was possible to perceive an Echo, not without admiration. Thus, a frequently small thing can cause a wonderful effect. However, it was established for me that the shrubs and the furrows of said fields had caused the Echo because, passing through the same agreed-upon place at another time when the furrows had been overturned and the shrubs cut down, it was no longer possible to hear the Echo. Many Echoes of the greatest former celebrity have also failed in our times, either because walls were overturned or because the reflecting <term>anacamptic: a general term for reflecting; in this context, it refers to the reflection of sound or light</term> objects were changed and altered. Certainly, at the tomb of Cecilia Metella—which today is called *Capo di Bove* <note>Italian: "Head of the Ox," named for the bull-skull decorations on the frieze.</note> situated near the Praetorian camp—Boissard reports in his *Topography of Rome* that there was once an Echo of the greatest celebrity, which, though sought out with singular study, cannot now be found. Truly, I have cited Boissard's words so that the reader may know what to think of his account; he speaks thus in the *Topography of the City*:

> *The Tomb of the Metelli, he says, is of a round shape made of squared white marble like a very large tower, hollow inside, and open at the upper part; its walls are about 24 feet thick. It lies near the corner of the walls, and in its circuit are carved marble bull heads stripped of skin and flesh, as was customary in sacrifices, which are held by ribbons and wraps of bandages joining a heap of fruits, flowers, and leaves (commonly called festoons), and in the intervals, the platters of the sacrifices are placed. There are nearly two hundred bull heads; therefore it is called Capo di Bove. Antiquarians maintain that a double Hecatomb <note>Hecatomb: a large-scale public sacrifice, literally of 100 oxen.</note> was made at the famous funeral of Cecilia Metella, whose name is read on the front of the tomb on a huge marble tablet facing the gate of the Praetorian fortress: "To Cecilia, daughter of Quintus Creticus, wife of Metellus Crassus." At the base of the hill on which the tower is built, if anyone pronounces a full heroic verse <note>heroic verse: the dactylic hexameter used by epic poets like Virgil.</note>, a wonderful Echo will return the same verse, often quite articulately. I myself heard that first Virgilian line from the Aeneid distinctly eight times in full, and afterwards several times confusedly. Nowhere in the world is an Echo of this kind heard; it is said to have been excited by such great artifice so that at the funeral of this Cecilia, the wails of the mourners, the exclamations, and the funeral laments would be multiplied immensely while that double Hecatomb was celebrated and funeral games were provided in honor of the Matron. Thus says Boissard.*

Truly, driven by the desire for this curiosity, I sought this so prodigious Echo two or three times with the greatest zeal, but in vain; I was never able to find the same, nor could any other of the curious men here in Rome. Certainly, one who examines our following phonic exercises <note>original: "progymnasmata phonica"</note> will easily see that the layout of this place is very little capable of such an Echo. Whence I do not know how the Author pronounced these things so boldly. Was the nature of the site perhaps changed? Or was a neighboring building that stood in the way destroyed? Certainly, searching these things with the greatest care, I found nothing so destroyed within the hundred years since he himself testified to hearing the Echo; hence we leave these things to be examined further by others more curious. I certainly, as I said, explored all the walls round about several times, but I confess I could find nothing such as that which said Boissard describes.

<margin>
Why Echo does not occur in straight-built wells.
Echo in the Vatican Palace.
</margin>
Furthermore, experience teaches that water can be a reflecting object, since almost all wells produce a very distinct Echo, as is testified by the well in the courtyard of the Vatican Palace, which returns the voices of men—even the lowest whispers—so distinctly that you would swear men were hiding inside. And indeed, it returns everything the more perfectly the more the well is exposed to the free air; for if covered by a roof or a cloth, it performs nothing; the cause of which thing is not...

<margin>
Why wells are so resonant.
</margin>
...is nothing other than a double reflection, one of which reflects downward from the vault <note>original: "ex fornice"; referring to the arched ceiling or top of a structure</note>, and the other reflects upward from the water; thus, they return in a confused manner, for it is not necessary that they return anything distinct. Furthermore, since water has an extremely polished and mirror-like surface and is most suitable for reflecting, it is no wonder that the Echo dwells more willingly at the pools of lakes, rivers, and seas than elsewhere. Certainly, wells declare this above all other things; those abundant in water are ten times more resonant than those stripped of water, especially if the interior concave surface approaches a spherical shape. We conclude, therefore, that every solid or even liquid object can be <term>anacamptic: a general term for a reflecting surface, used here for sound reflection</term>; and indeed, they will strike back the sound more vigorously the more they are polished, just as a very clean mirror shows light and figures better than one less clean and polished. Secondly, water is most capable of reflection due to its entirely mirror-like surface.

<margin>
Water is most suitable for reflection.
</margin>
Thirdly, all other rough and soft objects do reflect, but more weakly and inordinately, as on the grassy slopes of mountains or in forests enjoying a great crowding of massive trees. In these, there is no ordered reflection; instead, from the various and multiple reflections of the voice from tree to tree, nothing is left but a certain vehement <term>phonism: a resonant sound effect or sonic phenomenon</term> or a confused humming and a tinkling similar to those heard in wells. Truly, we shall pursue all these matters more extensively in the following sections.

<margin>
Whence the humming in forests.
</margin>

# PRELUDE III.
## On the Phonocamptic Medium, or the Line of Action.

<margin>
The phonocamptic medium is twofold: physical and mathematical.
</margin>
In this place, the medium must be considered in two ways: the Physical and the Mathematical. The physical medium is that aerial space through which the voice is propagated, and it is of diverse quality and constitution. The mathematical medium is the magnitude or smallness of the interval measuring the duration of the propagated voice. We shall treat both briefly in this prelude, beginning with the Mathematical medium.

### §. I.
### On the Line of Phonic Action.

<margin>
What the line of action is and its types.
</margin>
We call the "line of action" or "phonic line" 그 that which limits the action of radiant or phonic diffusion; it is twofold: simple and mixed. The simple or direct line of action is that which limits the propagation of the voice and is called the semi-diameter of the sphere of phonic activity. The mixed line is that which is constituted from the incident <note>the path of the sound hitting the object</note> and the reflected line, which we therefore call the "direct-reflected" line. Although Blancanus <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who wrote on echoes</note> considers this equal to the direct or simple line, in strictness it must necessarily be smaller. For it is certain that a voice struck against a wall, as if broken there and having suffered some loss of vigor, returns more weakly than the direct voice, which is known to be propagated in a uniformly-difform manner <note>a technical term in physics of the period meaning the speed or intensity changes at a constant rate</note> when hindered by no obstacle; we have demonstrated this at length in our *Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Ars Lucis & Umbræ"; Kircher's 1646 work on optics and catoptrics</note>. How much smaller this mixed line of action is than the simple one can be determined only with difficulty; certainly, I judge the difference to be so meager that it might be said to belong to reason rather than to the senses. Therefore, without scruple, it can be physically established as equal to the direct line. And thus we have accepted it both here and in the *Art of Light and Shadow*, page 576. Since the voice is increased somewhat by the repercussion in the nearby medium, it easily restores what was lost by the collision.

<margin>
The direct line is strictly greater than the reflected line.
</margin>

<margin>
The first case.
</margin>
Moreover, this line can be considered according to three cases. The first is: either the reflected line is equal to the incident line, and then the phonocamptic obstacle will necessarily occupy the midpoint of the line of action. For example, if in the first case the line of action is AC and the <term>anacamptic: reflecting</term> obstacle is at B, the midpoint of the line, the radius AB reflected from B to A <note>The OCR reads "V," likely a misread of "A" or a point designating the listener</note> will be as great as AB or BC, which is half of the entire line of phonic action AC.

The second case: If indeed the reflected <term>phonic line: the path sound travels</term> is longer than the incident (incoming) line, then the <term>phonocamptic obstacle: the object that reflects the sound</term> will be positioned beyond the midpoint, as shown at point S. <note>A technical diagram illustrating the geometric principles of sound reflection (phonics). It contains two labeled cases. The larger central diagram shows a horizontal line AB with two reflection points, S and P, and their corresponding reflected paths SR and PX, demonstrating how the position of an obstacle relates to the length of the reflected sound path.</note>

<margin>
The Third Case.
</margin>
Third: If the reflected phonic line is greater than half of the total, then the sound-reflecting obstacle must necessarily be placed on this side of the midpoint of the line of action, as seen at point P. The reflected path PX will then be equal to PB, the remainder of the total direct line AB. From these examples, it is clearly evident that lines—whether they are <term>Orthophonic: sound traveling in a straight line</term> or <term>loxophonic: sound traveling at an angle or slant</term>—when combined with their reflected paths, always equal the total length of the direct path.

->### §. I I.<-
->### On the speed of sound as it passes through a medium, or on the extent of phonic space.<-

<margin>
Great difficulty in determining the distance for an Echo.
</margin>
I have found nothing so doubtful and perplexing as the uncertain determination of the distance required for an Echo. <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician.</note> Biancanus determines the minimum space to be 24 geometric paces; this minimum space is the distance required to return one distinct syllable to the ears of the speaker after the first is uttered. <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath often called the "father of acoustics."</note> Mersennus sets it at 69 feet. I, taking the most exact measurements of all through experience, have always found different results; so much so that, despairing at last, I thought hardly anything certain could be determined in this matter. For having attempted experiments with the voice, a trumpet, and a gunshot from one and the same place, I discovered that the more violent the sound, the faster it is reflected. Thus, the sound of the trumpet blurred the voice that had previously returned a syllable distinctly, and the sound of the gunshot absorbed it so much that hardly anything distinct could be heard. Therefore, I wonder greatly what the excellent Mersennus was thinking when he asserted that every sound from one and the same place is always equally fast. For if the <term>species of sound: a philosophical term for the "form" or "image" of sound as it exists in the air</term> were merely <term>intentional: existing as a mental representation rather than a physical substance</term>, then no doubt—as appears in visible images—something could be concluded regarding that equal speed. But since the species of sound are for the most part real, and are carried by the <term>undulation of the air: an early description of sound waves</term> as if by a vehicle, it is certain that sound will always be carried faster and faster according to the violence of the agitated air. Just as a ball is struck against a wall with greater force, it is reflected with faster motion and consequently to a more remote distance; sensible experience teaches us that the motion of the voice behaves in exactly the same way. These things are so true that even Mersennus himself admits it in his *French Universal Harmony*, book 3, page 214. There, he says he observed an Echo in the Montmorency valley near the Ormesson estate which, while it repeated 14 syllables at night, repeated only 7 during the day—that is, only half of them. The cause of this is nothing other than the extreme tranquility and undisturbed consistency of the night air, whereas the daytime air is divided and discontinued by countless movements. Consequently, the voice, hindered by various obstacles as it were, shows itself to be less swift.

<margin>
Experience gathered from every kind of instrument.
</margin>

<margin>
Species of sound are defined by the undulation of the air.
</margin>

<margin>
Why an Echo is perceived more perfectly at night than by day.
</margin>

<margin>
The fallacy of the chronometer instrument based on string vibrations.
</margin>
...persists; for if such obstacles do not stand in the way, and the sonorous motion is always <term>isochronous: occurring in equal time</term> <note>original Greek: ἰσοχρόνος</note> or equally swift within a determined interval, I do not see why an Echo would not repeat as many syllables during the day as it does at night. Therefore, the fact that it repeats only seven syllables by day, but fourteen by night, is a manifest sign that sound moves more slowly by day for the reason mentioned shortly before. Consequently, the final seven syllables, in a medium that is disturbed and agitated by various movements, gradually grow faint and die away. Certainly, if one had fired a <term>sclopus: an early type of firearm or scatter-gun</term> in the same place, there should be no doubt that even by day it would have repeated all the syllables. Nor does the equal duration of vibrations in a chronometer instrument, or the <term>isochronous</term> motion of two different types of spheres falling from a height to the ground, support this experiment. For these experiments, if they take place over a larger space, are highly suspect and full of fallacy, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere; for experience alone will show that they strike the ground at unequal intervals of time from a height of 500 feet. But more on these matters elsewhere.

<margin>
A monosyllabic Echo requires a space of 110 Roman feet.
</margin>
Since, therefore, I find the task of determining a certain measure to be difficult, and moreover find that the experiments of various authors differ greatly, I myself did not wish to be idle in this business. Indeed, bringing the experiments performed by others back to the anvil <note>a metaphor for refining or re-testing ideas</note>, I began all kinds of experiments with a monosyllabic Echo. Using the voice, a trumpet, and a gun, I tested the whole matter and found that a monosyllable admits no change at all within a space of 20 feet. Thus, I found the distance for a monosyllabic Echo to be about 110 feet, which had, as I said, a "breadth" of 20 feet, within which space it always repeated the same syllable. A trumpet, however, rendered the first sound distinctly within a space of 90 to 110 feet. A gun, within this same space, was somewhat confused with the original sound. Within 400 to 900 feet, however, it perfectly and distinctly returned a seven-syllable phrase—for example, *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original Latin: "Arma virumque cano," the opening of Virgil's Aeneid</note>—within the time in which one could most swiftly recite the *Hail Mary* <note>original Latin: "Ave Maria"</note> up to and including the words *blessed art thou* <note>original Latin: "Benedicta tu"</note>.

<margin>
Various experiments conducted.
</margin>
<margin>
Sound is returned best of all at night and in the evening; worst in the morning and at noon.
</margin>
I also used the vibration of a chronometer, but always with little success. Then, at different times—morning, noon, evening, and night—I took care to have experiments performed either by myself or by others who were first excellently and carefully instructed. We always found a different speed of sound and a different quantity of intervals. In the silence of the dead of night, the Echo seemed to exercise its dominion best for the reasons stated shortly before. We found the least success in the morning due to the dewy and foggy constitution of the air; at noon it performed better, as the air was thinner; and even better in the evening due to the perfect "cooking" <note>an alchemical/Aristotelian term meaning the sun has processed or refined the atmosphere</note> of the air.

<margin>
Changing weather changes the Echo.
</margin>
Furthermore, I observed the weather with great study and diligence. In rainy or snowy weather, the Echo is dulled in a wonderful way, so that it hardly seems to have any power. After heavy rains, as the air is very much purified, it acquires a great deal of strength. Here in Rome, strange to say, it acquires the greatest vigor when the <term>Boreas: the North Wind</term> is blowing; it grows faint with the <term>Auster: the South Wind</term>, and behaves moderately with the <term>Eurus: the East Wind</term> and the <term>Subsolanus: the East-Southeast Wind</term>.

<margin>
The Echonic Paradox.
</margin>
When a wall is exposed to the North Wind, while that wind is blowing, it is strange to say that the direct sound reflected is notably slower. Yet at the same time, a direct voice striking a southern surface is faster when reflected. For in the first experiment, the direct voice, being contrary to the wind, is carried through the medium with more difficulty than the reflected voice; the reflected voice, however, being spread by a favorable wind, returns more quickly to the ears, so that what it had previously lost due to the resistance of the medium, it now recovers through speed. The same must be said of the other quarters of the sky, so that from this it appears that there is a great diversity in the speed of sound spread through a medium.

---

### Corollary I.

<margin>
Difficult determination of the Echonic distance.
</margin>
From this infinite diversity and variation of media, it is clearly evident that every determination of the distance required for an Echo is doubtful, fallacious, and utterly uncertain. Nor is it ever consistent with itself—whatever <term>Blancanus: Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer</term> and <term>Mersennus: Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a polymath who studied acoustics</term> may say—unless it is subjected to geometric laws through <term>Catoptrics: the study of reflection, usually of light but here applied to sound</term> constrained by acoustic instruments (which will be treated later). Therefore, whatever shall be said hereafter must be taken only hypothetically.

# Universal Musurgia

## Corollary II.

<margin>
The fallacy of the chronometric instrument, by which some believe they can determine the extent of phonic space.
</margin>
Secondly, it is evident that the use of a chronometric instrument—whether based on vibrations or the pulse—is superfluous in this business. Sound travels through the medium with such incomprehensible speed that by the time the string begins its motion, the voice has already completed its circuit <note>original: *peridromo*</note> and presented itself to the ears. Therefore, he who trusts he will certainly grasp the quantity of such swift motions with any chronometric instrument is merely "drawing water with a sieve" <note>An ancient idiom for performing a useless or impossible task.</note>. Even with all possible diligence applied, one will wander from the truth by a space of 10, 20, or even 30 feet. This is the same reason why a monosyllabic Echo persists within a gap of 20 feet at most; for a space of 5, 10, or 15 feet is scarcely perceptible in relation to the increasing speed of the motion. 

As for Mersenne’s belief that a monosyllabic Echo covers a space of 100 geometric paces in the time of one second; this is by no means to be understood geometrically, but rather physically and as a "rough measure"—that is, as much as is granted to the senses to discern. I do not say this because I wish to deter the curious reader from such a laudable study of observations, but rather to point out the difficulty of the task and how much diligence, liveliness, and dexterity of wit is needed in properly conducting experiments, so that at last some measure suitable for investigating the Echo may be obtained. 

Since, therefore, Biancani <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician.</note> has found the space for forming a monosyllabic Echo to be 24 geometric paces—or, what is the same, 120 geometric feet—while Mersenne wishes it to be 100 geometric feet; I judge that a middle ground 

<margin>
What quality of space is likely for returning an Echo.
</margin>
should be held more securely: a hypothetical space of 110 feet. This nearly matches the truth when compared with the observations of the cited authors. The reason why observations rarely agree is the diversity of the medium and the inequality of voices and sounds. For, as I said above, the Echo has different strengths at different times of the day; there are different conditions in Winter, Summer, Autumn, and Spring. 

<margin>
The four seasons of the year, as well as the natural day, and even diverse climates, affect the Echo in different ways.
</margin>
I do not doubt that a monosyllabic Echo, which here under the Roman climate covers a space of 110 geometric feet in the time of one second, would take up a different time and space in other climates. We also find the quality of the reflected sound to be different according to the diversity of the <term>anacamptic: reflecting</term> objects. Some Echoes are weak and languid, some are strong, some are shrill and noisy; others are pleasant and sweet, while others are mournful and mimic a lament; furthermore, some are tinkling and clear. 

This diversity comes from nothing other than the different constitution of the reflecting bodies. According to 

<margin>
The diverse constitution of phonocamptic objects varies the Echo.
</margin>
whether they are more or less porous, they are found to be less or more sonorous, clear, and vigorous. For, as was shown in Book 1, individual bodies have different ways in which their parts are joined together. Because of this, each body is allotted different and distinct sounds: smooth and porous bodies produce a clear and tinkling sound, while dense and rough bodies produce a dull and deep sound. Thus it happens that a voice striking any body returns imbued with the quality and property with which that body itself is imbued. For just as light striking a surface is "dyed" by the color of that surface, so the voice is "dyed," as it were, by the sound of the body upon which it falls. This is the reason why a reflected voice is returned now clear, now dull, now pleasant, now mournful. But having examined all these things which seemed somewhat required for knowing the nature of the Echo, nothing remains but for us to establish the nature of reflection by irrefragable reasons.

Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic.

# CHAPTER I.
# CANONS AND RULES OF THE PHONOCAMPTIC ART OR ECHOMETRY
<note>The "Phonocamptic Art" refers to the science of reflected sound (from the Greek *phone*, sound, and *kamptos*, bent). "Echometry" is the measurement of echoes.</note>

### Echo-Reflective Lemma.
<note>A "lemma" is a preliminary proposition in a mathematical argument. Here, Kircher proves that the path of reflection is the shortest possible path between two points and a surface.</note>

If from two points to any point on a straight line (which is the common intersection of a plane drawn through those two points with another plane), two straight lines are drawn making two equal angles with it; these two straight lines will be shorter than any other two straight lines drawn from the same two points to any other point on that same straight line.

From two points **A** and **B** to point **C** on the straight line **CD**, let two straight lines **AC** and **BC** be drawn so that the plane drawn through **CD** passes through **A** and **B** when rotated, making the angles **ACF** and **BCD** equal. From the same points **A** and **B**, first let two other straight lines **AD** and **BD** be drawn to another point **D** to the right of **C**. I say that **AC** and **BC** together are shorter than **AD** and **BD**. For if **AC** is extended through **C**, let **CE** be made equal to **CB**, and let **DE** be joined. And because angle **ACF** is assumed to be equal to angle **BCD**, and angle **ACF** is equal to the vertical angle **ECD** <note>Vertical angles are opposite angles formed by intersecting lines; they are always equal.</note>, angle **BCD** will also be equal to angle **ECD**. Therefore, since the two sides **BC** and **CD** are equal to the two sides **EC** and **CD**, the base **DB** will be equal to the base **DE**; and consequently, **AD** and **DB** together will be equal to **AD** and **DE** together. But **AD** and **DE** are greater than **AE** <note>According to the geometric principle that any two sides of a triangle must be longer than the third side.</note>—that is, greater than **AC** and **CB**, since **CB** and **CE** were made equal. Therefore, **AD** and **BD** will be greater than **AC** and **BC**, which is what was to be shown.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the law of reflection. It shows two points, A and B, above a horizontal line representing a reflective plane. Lines connect A and B to a central point C on the line, where the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. Additional points F and D are marked on the horizontal line to the left and right of C, with lines connecting them to A and B to demonstrate that these alternative paths (AD+DB and AF+FB) are longer than the path through C. A point E is shown below the line, extending from line AC, as a construction to prove the equality of the triangles used in the demonstration.</note>

Next, let two other straight lines **AF** and **BF** be drawn from points **A** and **B** to another point **F** to the left of **C**. Again, I say that **AC** and **BC** are shorter than **AF** and **BF**. For by extending **AC** again and taking **CE** equal to **CB**, let **EF** be joined. And since angles **ACF** and **BCD** are assumed to be equal, and **ACF** is equal to the vertical angle **ECD**, the angles **BCD** and **ECD** will also be equal. Consequently, since the two sides **BC** and **CF** are equal to the two sides **EC** and **CF**, the base **BF** will also be equal to the base **EF**; and therefore **AF** and **FE** will be equal to **AF** and **BF**. But **AF** and **FE** are greater than **AE**, which is to say, greater than **AC** and **BC**, because **BC** and **CE** were made equal. Therefore, **AF** and **BF** will be greater than **AC** and **CB**, which is what was to be shown.

Therefore, because Nature, when unimpeded, acts through the shortest lines <note>original: *Natura non impedita agit per lineas breuiſſimas*</note>; it happens that a ray of the Sun or a visual ray falling from **A** onto the plane toward **DF**, so that it is reflected to point **B**, must necessarily fall on point **C**, where the angle **ACF** (which perspectivists call the "angle of incidence" <note>original: *angulum incidentiæ*</note>) is made equal to the angle **BCD**, which they call the "angle of reflection" <note>original: *reflexionis*</note>. For if the ray fell on **D** or **F** and were reflected to **B**, nature would not be acting through the shortest lines, since both **AD**, **BD** and **AF**, **BF** are longer than **AC**, **BC**, as we have demonstrated. This would be absurd. And thus it is demonstrated what perspectivists <note>Historical scholars of optics and geometry.</note> assume: namely, that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

<meta>catchword: Pro-</meta>

<summary>Kircher establishes the geometric foundation of acoustics by proving that sound reflection follows the law of equality between the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection. He argues that sound, like light, follows the "path of least resistance" or the shortest possible distance when reflecting off a surface.</summary>

## Proposition I.

### ->Every incident angle of sound is equal to the reflected angle of sound, or, what is the same thing, the angle of incidence of sound is equal to its angle of reflection.<-

**W**hatever we have demonstrated regarding the reflection of light in the *Anacamptic Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: *Arte Anacamptica Lucis & Umbræ*; Kircher refers to his previous work on optics and catoptrics</note> can be brought back to our attention here. This is because the operations of sound are parallel to the operations of light in nearly all respects, with only a few exceptions. First, therefore, it must be shown that the incident angle of sound <term>phonoptotus: from the Greek phone (sound) and ptotos (falling)</term> is equal to the reflected angle of sound <term>phonocampticus: from the Greek phone (sound) and kamptos (bent)</term>, which we do as follows. Let the reflecting object be **AB**, the phonic center <term>the source of the sound</term> be **C**, and the reflected point <note>the location of the listener or the echo's destination</note> be **D**. I say that the sound from **C** striking at point **E** will be reflected toward **D**. For according to our first hypothesis, the reflected angle **AED** is equal to the incident angle **BEC**.

<note>This page contains two geometric diagrams. The upper, larger diagram illustrates a reflecting surface represented by a horizontal line segment marked A and B at either end. A point E sits on this line. A line segment CE represents the path of incident sound from a source C, and line segment ED represents the reflected path to point D. A vertical line dropped from E and another line ER to a point R to the left of D are used for the geometric proof. The angles AED and BEC are shown as equal. The lower diagram is a simplified version of the first, showing the same relationship between points A, B, C, D, and E to reinforce the principle of equal angles of incidence and reflection.</note>

If the angle of reflection is not equal to the angle of incidence—that is, if angle **AED** is not equal to angle **BEC**—then let us suppose the sound reflected from **E** is instead struck back toward point **R**. Therefore, the angle **AER** would be either equal or unequal to the angle **AED**. If the former were true, and angle **AER** were equal to angle **AED**, the part would be equal to the whole, which is absurd. If the latter were true—that is, if angle **AER** is not equal to angle **AED** or **BEC**, and yet the reflection still occurs at point **R**—then nature would not be achieving its end via the shortest possible lines. This contradicts our third Axiom and is a physical absurdity. Therefore, it is necessary that the incident angle **BEC** be equal to the reflected angle **AED**, which was to be demonstrated. Furthermore, that nature establishes its operations under the equality of the angles of incidence and reflection—or via the shortest lines—was demonstrated at length in the *Anacamptic Art*, part 2, proposition 1, to which proposition we refer the curious reader. But
