## Proposition II.

### ->Whenever a voice falls upon any orthophonic [direct-sounding] object, or one that is perpendicular, it will be reflected back upon itself.<-

Let the phonic center <term>the source or origin of the sound</term> be at **A**, <note>see the preceding figure</note> and let the orthophonic <note>original: ὀρθόφωνον (*orthophōnon*), meaning "straight-sounding" or perpendicular</note> object be **CD**. Let the voice flow from **A** to **B** orthogonally <note>original: ὀρθογώνως (*orthogōnōs*), meaning at right angles</note> or at a ninety-degree angle. I say that the voice will be reverberated from **B** back to **A**. I demonstrate the matter thus: if, by some impossibility, it were not reflected from **B** back to **A**, let us suppose it were reflected to **V**. Therefore, by the fourth hypothesis, the angle of incidence **DBA** would be equal to the angle of reflection **CBV**, which would mean an acute angle is equal to an obtuse one, which is absurd. We have supposed, moreover, that the voice is carried from **A** to the wall normally <note>at a right angle</note>, and consequently forms a right angle of incidence **ABD**; therefore, the angle of reflection must also necessarily be a right angle according to the cited fourth hypothesis. It will therefore reflect back upon itself, specifically through the line **BA** along which it traveled from **A** to **B**, which was to be demonstrated. The truth of this proposition is taught not only by light falling normally, but also by a ball when it is struck normally against a wall and is bounced back upon itself, and countless other examples, for which see our *Anacamptic Art of Light* <note>Kircher refers to his 1646 work *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, where he discusses the physics of reflection (catoptrics)</note>.

## Proposition III.

### ->Whenever a voice falls upon some loxophonic [oblique-sounding] object or falls obliquely; the voice will be reflected not back upon itself, but to the opposite side.<-

There can be four cases of this proposition. Either the voice falls obliquely onto a vertically standing wall, in which case it reflects either to the right or the left depending on the position of the sound source; or the voice, emitted from below, falls obliquely on a higher phonocamptic <term>sound-reflecting</term> object and thus reflects upward; or if the voice is emitted from above and falls obliquely on a lower wall, it will then be reflected downward. We shall demonstrate each case separately.

Let the wall be at **DE**, <note>see the figure for Prop. 1</note> and the phonic center be at **C**, with the voice falling loxophonically <note>original: λοξοφώνως (*loxophōnōs*), meaning obliquely or at a slant</note> at **B**. I say the voice will be reflected from **B** to the opposite side, namely to **A**, with the angles being equal. For if it were not reflected to **A**, it would reflect either upon itself (back to **C**) or to **I**, or to any other place outside **AB**. But it will not reflect upon itself, since by the preceding proposition only a perpendicular line reflects back upon itself; and the line **CB** is, by our supposition, loxophonic, that is, falling obliquely onto the wall. Nor will it reflect to **I**, because the angle **IBD** would then be equal to the angle **CBE**, which would make the part equal to the whole—an absurdity. Therefore, it will reflect to no other part but **A**, for in this way the angle of incidence **EBC** and the angle of reflection **ABD** will be established as equal, and nature will reach its end via the shortest lines. Whenever, therefore, a sonorous line falls obliquely upon a wall, it will necessarily fall upon the opposite side with equality of angles, which was to be demonstrated. From this it is clear that a sound source placed at **A** will reflect sound to **C** on the left, and one placed at **C** will reflect to **A** on the right.

Furthermore, if the voice is located at **A** and the phonocamptic object is a tower **BC** placed on a mountain: I say the voice from **A** to **B** will be reverberated from there to **V**. The reason is exactly the same as in the preceding cases; for since it falls obliquely at **B**, the voice will necessarily be reverberated to **V** with equality of angles. The same would happen if the voice of the tones were located—

# PHONOCAMPTIC CANONS

# ECHOMETRIC CANONS.

## CANON I.

Since the phonocamptic art <term>the science of sound reflection</term> follows the laws of photocamptics <term>the science of light reflection</term> in all things, it preserves not only the principal differences of position—which are upward, downward, to the left, and to the right—during reflection, but also any intermediate directions depending on the placement of the anacamptic <term>reflecting</term> object. If the echoing or phonic surface is perpendicular to the reflecting object and simultaneously parallel to the horizon, the Echo will be born as either orthophonic <note>original: *orthophona*, meaning "straight-sounding" or direct</note> or loxophonic <note>original: *loxophona*, meaning "oblique-sounding" or slanted</note>, according to the different right or left placement of the vocal source.

If, however, the phonic surface falls obliquely upward or downward upon some azimuthal surface <note>a vertical plane used for measuring direction</note> of the reflecting object, reflections will be produced that are anophonic <note>original: *anophonę*, upward-sounding</note> or catophonic <note>original: *catophonæ*, downward-sounding</note>, meaning Echoes reverberating upward and downward.

Finally, if the phonic surface falls upon some phonocamptic plane that is parallel to neither the vertical nor the horizontal circle, but is inclined obliquely and laterally, the reflections produced will be lateral and loxophonic, intermediate between the horizon and the zenith; just as we have demonstrated in the anacamptic art of light.

## CANON II.

Whenever, therefore, the phonocamptic object is both parallel and perpendicular to the sound source, then the surface of reflection will be straight to the horizon. But if it is a parallel loxophone—that is, if the phonocamptic object is equidistant from the sound source but not perpendicular, such as walls that are slanted yet straight, or towers on mountains relative to a sound source placed in a valley—then the surface of reflection will be equidistant to one of the azimuthal lines, or, what is the same thing, it will match one of the vertical lines. If, however, the phonocamptic object is neither parallel nor perpendicular to the sound source, then the phonocamptic surface (the surface of reflection) will be equidistant to one of the inclining or inclined planes.

## CANON III.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the reflection of sound. A point labeled 'A' on a horizontal plane represents the center of the sound source. A rectangular block labeled 'C' represents the phonocamptic (reflecting) object. A line rises vertically from the object to a point 'V', representing the upward reflection of the sound.</note>

Whenever the sound source **A** is on a horizontal plane, and the phonocamptic object **C** is on the same horizontal plane, a reflection upward to **V** will necessarily follow. If the object is both inclining and inclined, it will reflect not upward, but by a middle path according to the ratio of its inclination and declination, so that the entire doctrine of dial-making planes <note>original: *sciatericorum*, referring to the geometry of sundials</note>, which we handed down in the *Great Art of Light and Shadow*, can be beautifully adapted to this Echometry.

Since, therefore, they all reflect back upon themselves and reflect at the same time, they will vehemently intensify the Echo, which was the point to be proven.

## Corollary.

From this it is evident: The further someone is from the center of a circular concave, the more imperfect the Echo is returned; yet the closer one is to the center of the concave wall, the more confused the sound becomes. Therefore, a middle distance must be maintained.

# Proposition VI.

> *The closer the vocal source, or sound-maker, is to the phonocamptic <term>phonocamptic: an object that reflects sound, from the Greek words for "sound" and "bent"</term> object, the further away the reflected voice will be perceived; and the further the vocal source is from the phonocamptic object, the closer the reflected voice will be perceived.*

Since it was shown in the third prelude that the direct-reflected line of activity is always as long as the line of action (that is, the semi-diameter of the sphere of activity), it necessarily follows that the reflected line is longer in proportion to how short the direct line is, and shorter in proportion to how long the direct line is. Let the phonocamptic object be HBI. And let the direct-reflected line of activity SBF be equal to the line of direct action VR; I say that the reflected voice will be perceived further from the object the closer the direct voice was to it.

### Book IX. The Magic of Sound Reflection.

...the sound will be repeated for a third time. Since, by our premise, the objects E, F, and G are perpendicular to the voice and are "orthophonic" <term>orthophonic: from the Greek for "straight-sounding," referring to surfaces that reflect sound directly back to its source</term>, the lines DE, DF, and DG will necessarily reflect from points E, F, and G back to the speaker at D. Because the line DE is the shortest, it will reflect back to D most quickly. Since DF is longer than DE, it takes more time to return to D; consequently, the reflected voice from F will be perceived after the reflected voice from E. Furthermore, because DG is even longer than DF, it will reach the ears at D even later. Thus, a "triple echo" <note>original: "Echo triphona"</note> of DE, DF, and DG is produced by these different, unequal travel times caused by the varying lengths of the lines. Therefore, if the sound-reflecting <term>phonocamptic: an object that reflects sound, from the Greek "phone" (sound) and "kamptein" (to bend)</term> objects are arranged in this order, etc., which was the point to be demonstrated.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the reflection of sound from surfaces at different distances. On the right, three vertical rectangular objects are labeled A, B, and C. On the left, a single point D represents the listener or source. Three lines of different lengths radiate from D to points E, F, and G located on the surfaces of objects A, B, and C respectively. The diagram illustrates how sound waves reflecting from surfaces at different distances (DE, DF, DG) return to the source at different times, creating a triple echo ("Echo triphona").</note>

<margin>How an echo is generated.</margin>
It should be noted here that we can consider two types of duration for the voice. First, there is the sound of the voice itself, which lasts as long as it is being spoken and is vigorous and strong during its initial production. Second, there is the propagation of the voice along a "line of action." This propagation is such that while the initial voice lasts, the propagation also lasts; however, once the sound has traveled further and the primary voice has fallen silent, the propagation continues until it strikes an obstacle and is reflected, generating an echo along a "direct-reflected" line. Experience teaches us that we eventually hear the reflected voice quite some time after the primary voice is spoken. Therefore, the total duration of a voice, from its first production to its end, is measured by the space through which the voice travels and returns. Thus, if the distance is shorter, the reflected voice will return sooner; if the distance is greater, it returns later. Consequently, at a shorter distance, the echo can repeat fewer syllables, while at a greater distance, it can repeat more. Even though all the syllables of the primary voice are reflected, they are not all heard; this is because the stronger primary voice "blunts" or drowns out the weaker reflected sounds so that they cannot be heard while the speaker is still talking. Once the primary voice ceases, the reflections are finally heard, either sooner or later depending on the distance.

## Corollary.

**H**ence it is clear why sometimes only the last syllables of a word are heard and never the first: because the reflected voice returns while the primary voice is still being spoken. When the speaker finally stops, the remaining reflected syllables are perceived. Imagine a wall AB at a short distance CD, from which someone shouts the word *PARATIS* <note>Latin for "You are ready."</note> with a strong voice. It is certain that the first syllable *PA* strikes the wall first, then the second syllable *RA*, and thirdly *TIS*, in a direct sequence. However, they reflect in the same order, so that *PA* presents itself to the ears first, followed by the next two syllables, *RA* and *TIS*. If the distance is only suitable for producing a single syllable (monosyllabic), then when the word *PARATIS* is shouted, only the syllable *TIS* will be perceived. This is because the first syllable *PA*, upon reaching the reflection point at D and reflecting back, arrives at C while the speaker is still vocalizing. The same happens with *RA* at point *e* and *TIS* at point *f*. The syllables become confused and return nothing intelligible. While the reflected voice of *PA* reaches C, the direct sound of *RA* is moving from D to *f* and from *f* to *e*. Meanwhile, the final direct syllable *TIS* reaches D. Confusion occurs again in the same spot, so that the echo cannot be heard until the two syllables *PA* and *RA* have ceased; finally, the last syllable *TIS* is perceived alone at C without confusion. Having seen the nature of sound according to simple lines, nothing remains but to speak of composite lines.

<note>A diagram illustrates the phonetic overlap of an echo. A vertical line on the right represents a wall AB. A horizontal line segment CD represents the distance between the speaker at C and the wall at D. The word "PARATIS" is broken into syllables ("pa", "ra", "tis") placed along the path from C towards the wall at D. Below these, the reflected syllables are shown returning towards C. Points 'e' and 'f' are marked on the horizontal line between C and D. The diagram visualizes how initial syllables can be "drowned out" by the ongoing direct sound, leaving only the final syllable "TIS" to be clearly heard as an echo.</note>

## Universal Music-making

## §. I.
## On Phonic Projections:

Phonic projection <term>phonismus: Kircher’s term for the spatial behavior or "field" of sound</term>, as is evident from the definition, is the diffusion of the voice in a cylindrical or conical shape, or the radiation of the voice in the manner of a cone or cylinder. It must be noted, however, that sound does not occur through a simple projection of lines, or ray-emission <term>actinobolia: from the Greek for the emission of rays, usually used in optics or radiation</term>; otherwise, nothing at all could be heard. In this regard, it differs from light. Instead, in its projection and reflection, it acts by means of a sonorous cylinder or cone. Therefore, sound does not have a purely mathematical width, but a thoroughly sensible and corporeal one, so that in reflection, it is not a single line but a continuous multitude of lines that produces the sound. For example, let the source of the sound be **A**, the endpoint of reflection be **B**, and the object or reflecting wall be **CD**. Let the motion of the sound begin at **A**. I say that not just a single line **AO**, after reflection is made at **O**, will produce sound at **B**, but the entire cylindrical cone **AFE** will be reflected toward **B** through the cylinder **EFB**. But let us demonstrate the matter a bit more precisely.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the reflection of sound from a surface. A drum, labeled **A**, emits a beam of sound represented as a cylinder or cone (**AFE**). The sound travels to a vertical wall labeled **CD**, hitting it at points **E** and **F**. The sound then reflects off the wall towards a point **B** on the right. A central axis **AO** passes through point **X** on the wall to point **B**. Between the wall and point **B**, there is a shaded triangular region labeled **H**, where the lines of reflection intersect, representing the "triangle of confusion."</note>

## Proposition VIII.
### A cylindrical phonic projection is reflected to the opposite side as a cylindrical projection.

Let there be some drum in **A** whose sound falls upon the surface **CD**. I say that the phonic projection will be cylindrical—that is, the reflection will not be linear, but cylindrical. For if one imagines phonic lines being drawn from each individual point of the drum at **A** to the surface **EF**, these will undoubtedly constitute a phonic projection in the shape of a cylinder. I say that this same projection will be reflected in the shape of a cylinder toward **B**. Since all the phonic lines in the phonic cylinder **AFE** are parallel to each other (according to the 11th theorem of this book and the 6th of our *Anacamptic Art* <note>original: "artis nostræ anacampticæ," referring to the science of reflected waves</note>), they will reflect in parallel <note>original: "παραλλήλως" (parallēlōs)</note> toward **B**, the base of the sound-reflecting <term>phonocamptic: sound-reflecting, from the Greek "phone" (sound) and "kamptein" (to bend)</term> cylinder. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<margin>What the triangle of confusion is in the cylindrical projection of sound.</margin>
But these points are most true based on what has preceded. It should be noted, however, that the triangle **FHE** is called by us the **triangle of confusion** of sound. For as long as the ear is positioned within it, the reflected voice will be imperceptible; moreover, the reflected sound will be confused with the direct sound. But outside of it, in that entire space **BHF**, it is perceived more distinctly the closer the ear <gloss>**B**</gloss> is to the source of reflection.

It should be noted, secondly, that this triangle will be sharper at **H** the more the line **AO** approaches a right angle at **XO**.

## Proposition X.

### *In a conical phonic projection <term>phonismus: Kircher’s term for the spatial field or "shape" of a sound</term>, only the axis is reflected according to the equality of angles, while the reflected sound field will be a truncated cone. Just as in optical projections and ray-emissions <term>actinobilismus: the science of how rays are emitted and travel</term>, the axis of the pyramid of light—whether it be the light itself or the visual image—possesses the primary power both for illuminating and for representing things distinctly; the same is true in a Conical Phonic Projection.*

Let there be a direct or incident sound-cone **ABC** <term>phonoptotus: from Greek, meaning "falling sound," or sound striking a surface</term>; let the reflecting object <term>phonocampticum: the surface that causes an echo</term> be **CHB**. I say that only the axis **AH** is reflected at equal angles toward **D**, the midpoint of the base of the cone. For since these two lines constitute the axes of the cones, the endpoints of these axes will necessarily be the centers of the bases of the cones, both the direct one and the reflected one. Therefore, they form an angle of incidence **AHB** equal to the angle of reflection **DHC**; thus, this axis alone will be reflected toward **D**. All the other rays will be reflected into various other parts according to the equality of angles: specifically, **AB** will reflect toward **F**, **AK** toward **G**, **AL** toward **D**, **AM** toward **N**, and finally **AC** toward **I**. If they did not reflect to these specific points, but instead all reflected toward **D**, then the angle of reflection for each individual ray would be unequal to its angle of incidence. This is absurd and contrary to our hypothesis. Therefore, only the axis is reflected toward **D** at equal angles, and no other ray; consequently, the reflected sound field will not be a perfect cone, but will take on the form of something like an inverted and truncated cone.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the reflection of a conical sound wave. A source point A emits a cone of sound rays labeled ABC toward a flat wall surface CHB. The central axis AH hits the wall at point H and reflects to point D on a parallel plane labeled PN. Other rays AB, AK, AL, AM, and AC reflect off points B, K, L, M, and C on the wall to corresponding points F, G, D, N, and I on the plane. The resulting reflected volume forms a truncated cone shape.</note>

## Proposition XI.

### *A conical phonic projection hitting a wall perpendicularly creates an inverted, truncated phonic cone through its reflection.*

Let the Conical Phonic Projection **ABC** be perpendicular to the wall **BDC**. I say that the reflected sound field will form an inverted truncated cone. Because, according to the second proposition of this book, none of the lines falling from **A** onto the wall are reflected back onto themselves except for the axis (the middle line), all the other rays will reflect to various points outside of point **A**. Since those points are reflected at equal angles from the periphery of the circle (which is the base of the phonic cone), the boundary of the reflected lines **VX** must necessarily be a circle. The center of this circle, **A**, will be the phonic center <term>centrum phonicum: the point of origin for the sound</term>, or the source of the sound, or what is the same thing, the peak...

<note>A geometric diagram showing a conical sound wave originating from point A and hitting a perpendicular wall BDC. The central ray reflects directly back along its path, while peripheral rays reflect outward, creating a reflected sound field that forms an inverted truncated cone. The outer boundary of this reflected cone is represented by the circular base VX, with the source point A at its center.</note>

->§. II.<-

->On Polyphonisms, or the Prodigious Increase of Sounds.<-

<margin>What polyphonism and polyphotism are.</margin>
**J**ust as light acquires its greatest increase when compressed within concave bodies, so also does sound. What burning mirrors <note>original: "caustica specula"</note> accomplish in the convergence of light-projections <term>photismi: the spatial fields or "shapes" of light</term>, Acoustic <note>original: "Otica"</note> or Auditory organs accomplish in the convergence of sound-projections. Thus, a "polyphonism" is nothing other than the convergence of many sound-fields or vocal cones into a single point. Just as "polyphotism" is nothing other than the meeting of many light-projections in one point. Since this polyphonism properly belongs to concave bodies—some polygonal, some circular—I have decided it is my duty to explain such a subtle and illustrious subject at greater length, especially since, as far as I know, there is no one else who has touched upon it.

I suppose first, then, that a voice in an open field is subject to no reflection, but radiates spherically in every direction. However, as soon as it encounters some obstacle perpendicular to it, it then establishes its first sound-projection <term>phonismus</term>. If the voice is positioned between two obstacles or walls, it establishes two sound-projections in that position, and so on for others. This being supposed, it only remains for us to see how many and what kind of sound-projections the voice produces within various bodies. Let it be as follows.

## Proposition XII.

### With the phonic center <term>centrum phonicum: the point where the sound originates</term> positioned on the axis of a concave equilateral <term>isopleuri: from Greek, meaning "equal-sided"</term> triangular prism, the emitted voice, increased by a threefold sound-projection, will return to its own center.

<note>A geometric diagram shows the cross-section of a triangular prism labeled **ABC**. Inside the triangle is a central point **D**, representing the "phonic center" (the source of the sound). Three lines (**DE**, **DF**, **DG**) extend perpendicularly from point **D** to the midpoints of the triangle's sides, illustrating the path of sound rays reflecting back to the source. The triangular structure is depicted resting on a base of masonry stonework, suggesting a physical architectural model.</note>

**L**et there be a concave three-sided prism **ABC**. Let the phonic center be established at **D** on the axis of the prism. I say that the emitted voice, increased by a threefold sound-projection, returns to its center. For since the rays or axes of the sound-projections **DE**, **DF**, and **DG** are perpendicular to the sides of the prism (according to Proposition 2), they will necessarily return upon themselves, increased threefold. Since all the neighboring rays are also received in a near-perpendicular manner, they too (according to Hypothesis 3) will meet around the same center **D**. In that spot, the voice will be miraculously intensified by the various meetings of the reflected lines. Therefore, the rays near the perpendiculars will run back to **D**; the remaining rays (according to Proposition 4) will produce a ringing or a confused humming <note>original: "confusum bombum"</note> through various secondary reflections off the sides. Thus, with the phonic center positioned on the axis of a concave three-sided prism, the emitted voice, increased by a threefold sound-projection, will return to its own center, which was to be demonstrated.

## Proposition XIII.

### With the Phonic Center placed on the axis of a quadrilateral concave prism, the voice emitted will return to that same center increased by a fourfold sound-projection.

<note>A diagram illustrating the cross-section of a rectangular shaft or prism. A central point is labeled E. Straight lines extend perpendicularly from E to the midpoints of the four walls, which are labeled C (top), D (bottom), A (left), and B (right). The wall at the bottom is shaded to represent masonry or brickwork.</note>

**L**et **ABCD** be a quadrilateral concave prism <note>essentially a square or rectangular tube or shaft</note>, with the phonic center at **E**. I say that the voice emitted will return to **E** increased by a fourfold sound-projection <term>phonismo: Kircher’s term for the spatial field or shape of a sound</term>. Since the rays or axes of the sound-projections **EB**, **EC**, **ED**, and **EA** are perpendicular <note>original: "normales"</note> to the sides, the voice will be reflected back upon itself according to Proposition 2 of this book. Furthermore, since these rays are equal in length, they will also sound together at point **E** at the same time. Since the neighboring rays are received in the same manner as the perpendiculars, they too will reflect around **E** to the width of the listener's ears. Therefore, the voice will return to the center **E** increased by the four sound-projections which the four sides of the prism produce, which was to be demonstrated.

We must now explain how the remaining lines of sound eventually return to the center **E** through various reflections. We have already spoken of the perpendicular lines; let us now speak of the oblique ones. As is clear in Figure 2, let **EC** and **BE** be oblique <term>loxophonę: from the Greek for "slanted sound," referring to paths that do not hit the wall at a right angle</term> lines. I say they will return to **E**. For **EC**, reflected at **C** according to the equality of the angles **ECI** and **VCD**, will be reflected to **D**; from here, under the same equality of angles **VDC** and **SDO**, it will be reflected to **O**, and finally from **O**, under the equality of angles **SQD** and **XOE**, it will return to the center **E**. In like manner, **EB** is reflected from **B** into **G**, and from there into **F**, and finally into **E**. Likewise, **EF** will be reflected from **F** by the reverse path into **G**, from there into **B**, and finally into **E**. So too **EO** will return from **O** into **D**, and from **D** into **C**, and finally into **E**, similarly by a path contrary to the first.

<note>A set of three diagrams labeled 1, 2, and 3, contained within rectangular borders, showing the geometric paths of reflected sound. Box 1 shows perpendicular rays from the center E to the walls. Box 2 shows an oblique (loxophonic) path reflecting off several surfaces before returning to the center. Box 3 displays a more complex seven-reflection path. Various points along the paths and walls are labeled with letters including A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, N, O, P, S, V, and X.</note>

Again, as is clear in Figure 3, the line **EF** is reflected from **F** into **G**, from here into **V**, and from here into **I**, and from here into **N**, then into **O**, and from **O** into **P**, and finally into **E**, always reflecting under the equality of angles, so that after seven reflections it finally returns to **E**. If the flow of the voice were directed by the opposite path from **E** into **P**, after the same number of reflections it would finally return to **E**. The same must be said for the remaining lines intermediate between **O** and **F**.

For sound lines reflected in various ways and returning to the same starting point are accustomed to intensify the sound wonderfully. It also demonstrates the marvelous industry of nature in increasing the voice within concave bodies.

## Proposition XIV.

### With the phonic center established on the axis of an equilateral pentagonal prism, the voice emitted, increased by five sound-projections, will return to the place from which it flowed.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates a regular pentagon labeled with vertices A, B, C, D, and E. The center point is labeled L. Straight lines, representing the "axes" of the sound, are drawn from the center L to the midpoints of the five sides, labeled G (on side AB), I (on side BC), K (on side CD), F (on side DE), and H (on side EA). A zigzag line tracks the path of a single sound ray reflecting off the interior walls at points O, P, V, and S, eventually returning to the center L.</note>

**L**et there be an equilateral pentagonal prism **ABCDE**, and let the voice emitted from point **L** on the axis (the phonic center) be propagated in every direction. I say that the voice, increased by five sound-projections <term>phonismus: Kircher’s term for the specific shape or "image" of a reflected sound</term> — **LBC**, **LCD**, **LDE**, **LEA**, and **LAB** — will return to **L**. 

First, according to Proposition 2, the axes of the sound-cones **LG**, **LI**, **LK**, **LF**, and **LH**, since they are perpendicular <note>original: "normales"</note> to the sides, must necessarily return to **L**. Furthermore, the other neighboring rays, though moved by various reflections, will also eventually be reflected back to **L**. For a voice falling from **L** onto point **O** will be reflected from there to **P**; from **P** to **V**, from **V** to **S**, and from **S** to **I**, and from here it will finally return to **L**. You see, therefore, that there is no phonic line intercepted between points **HA** or **HB** which does not eventually return to the center **L** after various reflections. The same must be said of the other phonic lines falling upon any other side. Therefore, with the ear placed on the axis of an equilateral pentagonal prism, etc., which was to be demonstrated.

## Proposition XV.

### With the phonic center established on the axis of an equilateral hexagonal prism, the voice emitted, increased by 6 sound-projections, will return to itself.

<note>A geometric diagram shows a regular hexagon with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E, and F. The center is marked O. The midpoints of the six sides are labeled G, H, I, K, L, and M. Several lines radiate from the center to the sides and corners. Internal reflection paths are illustrated with zigzag lines hitting points labeled m, N, P, and Q, demonstrating how sound waves bounce within the hexagonal structure to return to the center point O.</note>

**L**et there be a hollow, equilateral <note>original: "isopleurum"</note> hexagonal prism **ABCDEF**, and a center on the axis **O**. A voice emitted there, increased by 6 sound-projections, will return to the place from which it flowed, namely to **O**. Since all the lines (the axes of the sound-cones) reaching the midpoints of sides **ABCDEF** are perpendicular according to Proposition 2, they will be reflected back onto themselves, back to **O**. The other neighboring rays, wandering back and forth through various reflections, also eventually reflect back to **O** as per the preceding proof. Consequently, a most powerful booming <note>original: "bombus": a deep, resonant humming or droning sound</note> will be perceived. 

For the voice falling from **O** to **m** will be reflected to **K**; from **K** to **N**, and finally back to **O**. Similarly, the voice falling to **P** will be reflected from there to **I**; from **I** to **Q**, and from **Q** finally back to **O**. The same must be said for every other phonic line intercepted between **MA** and **AG**. Therefore, with the ear so placed, etc., which was the goal.

**Note** that if someone were to place surfaces perpendicular to the rays at points **G**, **H**, **I**, **K**, **L**, and **M**, I say that the Echo, by its reflected lines, would describe a perfect hexagon. For the voice falling from **A** to **G** would necessarily be reflected from **G** to **H**, from **H** to **I**, from **I** to **K**, from **K** to **L**, from **L** to **M**, and finally from there back to **A** under the equality of angles. Likewise, in the preceding pentagon, the voice at **H** would be reflected from **B** to **C**, from **C** to **D**, from **D** to **E**, from **E** to **A**, and finally back to **H**—provided, that is, that surfaces were erected at points **ABCDE** perpendicular to the rays of the figure. The same must be said for all other polygons.

## Corollary I.

<margin>The logic of reflection in concave solid bodies</margin>

**F**inally, from what has been said, it is most clearly evident that the more sides concave prisms possess, the more the sound will be increased; for when the sound-projections <term>phonismus: Kircher’s term for the specific geometric path or "image" of a reflected sound ray</term> are multiplied, the sound is amplified. These sound-projections increase according to the number of sides. Furthermore, the more sides there are, the closer the angles of incidence and reflection will be to a right angle <note>original: "recto viciniores"</note>, and consequently, the sound-projections—according to the third hypothesis—are united more closely around the center. However, it should suffice to explain the matter with a single example. Let there be a dodecagonal <note>A twelve-sided polygon</note> prism as the following figure shows, whose center is **O**. Let **ACBO** be one of the twelve sound-projections. I say that the sound emitted from **O**, besides being increased by twelve projections, will also be amplified by the lines approaching more closely to the normal <note>The perpendicular line to a surface</note>, such as all those intermediate lines between **A** and **B**. The outer lines **OA** and **OB** of each projection will be as far from the center in their first reflection as the width of the polygon's side; after multiple reflections, however, they will all eventually converge at the center, as seen in the preceding sections.

## Corollary II.

**I**t is also evident that if, for example, at point **A** and at each of the angles, perpendicular surfaces were erected, the sound would describe a dodecagon through its reflection. By its circular reflection, it would form a hexagon. From point **F**, however, reflected through **B**, **K**, **N**, and back to **F**, it would describe a square, as the figure clearly shows. Again, if reflected from **F** to **H**, then to **M**, and back to **F**, it would describe an equilateral triangle through a triple reflection. You see, therefore, how the voice in a single dodecagon describes all the lines of the astrological aspects <note>Kircher links the geometric paths of sound to the "aspects" or angles used in astrology, such as the sextile (60°), square (90°), and trine (120°)</note> through sound reflection. Many other secret wonders of reflection lie hidden within such figures, which will be revealed only to those who have deeply examined what we have presented here.

## Proposition XVI.

->When the sound center is established on the axis of a hollow cylinder, the sound emitted from all points of the circumference will reflect back into itself.<-

<note>A circular diagram illustrates a cylinder's cross-section with a center point labeled N. Radial lines extend from N to points labeled A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L on the circumference. This shows sound rays traveling from the central axis to the perimeter and reflecting directly back to the center.</note>

Let there be a hollow cylinder **XY**, with the voice established at the center **N**. I say that from all points of the circumference **A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, B, G, H, I, K, L**, and any other infinite points, the sound will be reflected back to **N**. Since all lines drawn from the center to the circumference are perpendicular <note>original: "rectæ"</note> to it, and according to Proposition 2, straight lines are reflected back upon themselves, all lines from the perimeter will therefore be reflected back to **N**, where they are all united; thus, the Proposition is clear. Furthermore, since the voice does not fall upon the points of only one circle, but upon as many points as can be considered along the length of the cylinder, and since all these longitudinal lines are parallel to the axis, all points of these longitudinal lines will be reverberated somewhere onto the axis. From this, the wonderful and truly miraculous multiplication of sound—such as we experience in deep wells <term>puteus: a well or deep shaft</term>—will be evident without any difficulty. Let there be a well **ABCD**, with the central axis **OP** and the sound center **N**. Let the voice emitted from **N** fall on **E**; it will then be reflected from **E** to **G**, and from **G** to **F**, always intersecting the axis at points **M** and **V**. Similarly, the voice falling on **H** will be reverberated to **I**, and from **I** to **K**, crossing the axis at **R** and **S**. Similar reflections occur at all points of the lines of the well's depth, such as **AC** and **BD** in the present diagram.

<note>A rectangular diagram represents a well labeled ABCD with a central vertical axis OP. A sound source N is located on the axis. Lines trace the path of sound rays reflecting between the side walls AC and BD, crossing the axis at points M, V, R, and S as they zigzag along the length of the shaft.</note>

## Proposition XVII.

->*In pyramids of any number of sides, as well as in hollow cones, if the ear is placed on the axis, the sound emitted will never return to the source, except at points L and M, but not at other points.*<-

<note>A triangular diagram depicts an inverted pyramid or cone labeled ABC, with its point (apex) A at the bottom and the base BC at the top. A central axis AO is shown. From a sound source K on the axis, rays reflect off the internal walls at points G, E, H, F, N, and O. Instead of returning to K, the lines move progressively upward toward the open top at points L and M.</note>

**S**ounds do not return to their source within hollow conical bodies outside of points **M** and **L**; consequently, such bodies are unsuitable for multiplying sound in this manner. For since the voice strikes each side obliquely <note>original Greek: "loxophōnōs" (λoξoφώνως), meaning at a slant or diagonally</note>, it reflects itself upward. Let there be a pyramid **ABC**, with the sound center at **K**. The voice falling from there onto **G** will reflect to **E**, and from **H** to **F**, from **N** to **O**, and from there again to **L**. From this, it is clear that the reflection always strives upward and does not return to itself, except at the two points **L** and **M**, as has been stated.

## Proposition XVIII.

->*When the phonic center is established in the center of the five regular hollow solids, the reflected voice, increased by as many phonisms as the body has sides, will return into itself.*<-

The five regular solids <note>Known today as the Platonic solids.</note> are the tetrahedron, the cube, the octahedron, the dodecahedron, and the icosahedron; they are called "regular" because they have equal sides and because they are the only ones that can be inscribed within a sphere; for each of their planes is equidistant from the center. From this, and even from the very definition of each, it is clear how the voice is propagated within them. For when the phonic center <note>The point where the sound originates.</note> is placed in the center of a tetrahedron, the voice, increased by 4 <term>phonisms</term> <note>Kircher uses "phonism" to describe a discrete unit of reflected sound or an echo-reflection.</note>, will return into itself; in an octahedron it returns by 8; in a dodecahedron by 12; and finally, in an icosahedron, the voice will return to itself increased by 20 phonisms. The demonstration of all these depends on what has preceded, and it is so easy that it requires no further explanation.

## Proposition XIX.

->*A hollow sphere is the most suitable of all bodies for propagating sound.*<-

Since all lines drawn from every point of a circular surface to the center are equal to one another, and all are perpendicular to the spherical surface, it follows that they must necessarily reflect back into themselves. All these "species" of sounds <note>In 17th-century physics, "species" referred to the form or image of a sensory perception—in this case, the sound waves themselves.</note> will unite at the center; therefore, the most powerful sound will be produced there. Thus, the hollow sphere is not only the most capacious of all bodies for propagating sound, but also the most suitable for multiplying it, which was the point to be proven.

## Problem II.

->Given two points or stations, to determine both the position of the reflecting object and the angles under which the loxophonic voice travels and returns.<-

**LET** there be two given points A and B; of which B is the center of sound production, and the other, A, is the terminus of the reflected voice. It is required [to find] how a reflecting object <note>original: *obiectum anacampticū*; from the Greek *anakamptos*, meaning "bent back" or reflecting.</note> should be positioned so that A can perceive the voice reflected from B. Let two lines be drawn from B and A in any manner, provided they meet somewhere, for example, at C. Let a triangle ABC be formed, and once this is done, let the triangle ACB be divided in half; for a line drawn perpendicular to the end of the dividing line at point C will designate the position of the wall or whatever reflecting body is used. For the voice from B, striking this wall, will necessarily be reflected to A. I demonstrate the matter as follows: since, according to Proposition 1, an Echo occurs under the equality of the angles of incidence and reflection, and here the **cathetus** <note>original: *cathetus*; a technical term for a perpendicular line used in geometric proofs.</note> CS is the line dividing the phonocamptic triangle in half, and the line LCM represents the reflecting object perpendicular to the cathetus CS, the lines LCA and MCB will necessarily give equal angles of incidence and reflection. Moreover, the angles adjacent to the cathetus are equal; therefore, the voice from B striking the already determined object LCM will be reflected to A under equal angles. Therefore, given any two points or stations, we have determined both the position of the object and the angles under which the **loxophonic** <note>original: *vox loxophona*; Kircher uses this to describe sound that travels along an oblique or "slanting" path rather than a straight line.</note> voice goes and returns, which was what was to be done.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrating the law of reflection for sound. A triangle is formed by points A, C, and B. A vertical line (cathetus) CS bisects the angle at C. A horizontal line LCM is drawn perpendicular to CS at point C, representing the reflecting surface. Lines AC and BC represent the paths of sound reflection, demonstrating that the angle at which sound hits a surface equals the angle at which it bounces off.</note>

## Problem III.

->*Given any points or stations arranged in any manner, provided they have the proper distance for producing an Echo, to arrange the reflecting objects so that the reflected voice becomes known only to those occupying the said stations or the direct-reflected lines.*<-

**LET** the given stations be A, B, C, D, E, F, G. Let the first voice be at A. It is required to arrange the **phonocamptic** <note>original: *anacamptica*; Kircher uses this term for objects that reflect sound, from the Greek 'anakamptein' meaning to bend back.</note> objects according to the given points so that the reflected voice is known to no one else except those occupying the points of the stated stations. Let the said points be joined by straight lines; once this is done, bisect each angle into two equal parts according to the preceding rule. I say that normals <note>lines at a 90-degree angle</note> erected at the endpoints of the lines bisecting the angles will designate the required position of the objects, and the reflected voice will be perceived only by those occupying the given stations or the direct-reflected lines. For since the lines bisecting the angles are nothing other than the **normals** <note>original: *catheti*; a term from optics and acoustics referring to the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection.</note> of the reflecting surface, the voice will everywhere make the angles of the normals equal according to Supposition 6.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the law of reflection across multiple surfaces. Points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H are arranged in a wide polygonal arc. Solid lines connect these points in sequence (A to B, B to C, etc.), representing the path of a sound wave. At each vertex (B, C, D, E, F, G), a dashed line (the normal or cathetus) bisects the angle formed by the incoming and outgoing sound paths. A central point H is connected to the vertices by dotted lines to show the geometric center of the arrangement.</note>

If, therefore, normals are erected at the endpoints, they will establish two right angles with the **normal** <note>original: *catheto*</note> at each point. If you subtract the prior normal angles from these, the remaining angles will be, according to the 6th definition of Euclid, the direct-reflected angles—that is, the angle of incidence will be equal to the angle of reflection. The voice, therefore, falling from A onto wall B, departs from there reflected into C, and from here into D, and from D into E, from E into F, and from F into G, and finally from G into H. The voice, therefore, having struck each object, will reflect toward the given points with equality of angles. Thus, with the points given, etc. Which was to be done.

## Corollary.

**IT IS EVIDENT**, therefore, that with the ear positioned at any of the given points, the Echo will be perceived, and to seven different men standing at seven points, the Echo originating from A will be revealed to each one; indeed, it will be revealed not only at the given points, but in any part of the lines joining the points, which we call the direct-reflected lines.

I say that the objects arranged upon the normals in this way will cause the voice, partly internally,

## Problem V.

->*To construct a polyphonic echo, or one which repeats the same voice and other propositions several times after they are first uttered.*<-

<margin>How a polyphonic echo is to be constructed.</margin>
At this point, one must recall those things which we handed down in the third Prelude concerning the interval of an Echo. For since a certain and mathematical distance cannot be given in this slippery business, he will do best of all who investigates the said distance by the senses or mechanically. He shall do it thus: let him select for himself a solid, polished wall, most fit for the reflection of the voice; then let him approach and recede from it perpendicularly until it perfectly returns one syllable, and let him carefully investigate that space by some known measure. Then let him move back in a straight path until it perfectly returns a two-syllable word, and let him measure the space carefully. Afterwards, let him move back so far until the Echo returns three syllables, and so always receding more and more from the wall until it perfectly returns ten syllables or some verse, observing the distance perfectly in all the polysyllables. And experience will find that the spaces by which an Echo is increased by one syllable are not equal, but always smaller and smaller; in like manner, so that the Echo may be polyphonic and repeat a syllable several times, the spaces by which the seven-syllable sounds distinctly increase are not equal, but always smaller and smaller.

<margin>Why the spaces in a polysyllabic Echo are not equal.</margin>
The reason for this thing is nothing other than the weakness <note>original: *languor*</note> of the voice, which, the more remote a space it traverses, the more it always flags and weakens until it is utterly exhausted. Since, therefore, the voice is always more and more weakened, it is certain that the spaces can by no means be equal, but the more remote ones must always be closer together (as happens in the perspective of columns). By what proportion they decrease, however, is difficult to know, since the velocity of motion can hardly admit an exact and certain proportion to the space. He will act more securely, therefore, if he investigates the spaces of a polyphonic Echo by the senses, just as he did the polysyllabic spaces. Thus the matter can be investigated mechanically with the help of several people. Let AB be a wall from which the echo-measurer <note>original: *Echometra*</note> recedes so far until he perfectly returns that phrase: *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original: *arma virumque cano*; the famous opening of Virgil's Aeneid</note>, which happens at point C...

Therefore, the ear placed at X will perceive a seven-fold echo; thus we have constructed a seven-fold echo, which was the thing to be done.

## Problem VI.

->*Given any points arranged in a circle, to construct a circular and polyphonic [many-voiced] echo. See Figure III in Plate XV.*<-

Let the echo-reflecting points <term>phonocamptica: points or objects capable of reflecting sound back to its source</term> be arranged in any way on a circle ABCDEFGHIKLM. From the phonic center A, let the sound lines AB, AC, AD, etc., be drawn. I say that from point G on the radius of the circle, the lines GB, GC, GD, GE, GF, GH, GI, GK, and GL being drawn will assign the positions of the echo-reflecting objects. For since, by the 16th proposition of the 4th book of the *Elements* <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements of Geometry, specifically the properties of angles within a circle</note>, angles in a semicircle are right angles, the lines drawn from G to the sound lines drawn from A will be perpendicular. Therefore, the voice from A onto the echo-reflecting object situated above line B will reflect the voice back to A. And since the lines C, D, E, F, I, H, K, L are perpendicular to the sound lines described from A, the echo-reflecting objects founded upon them will similarly reflect the voice back to A. Furthermore, since the lines produced from A are always longer and longer, it follows also that the voice will be reflected back to A later and later; thus a polyphonic <note>many-voiced</note> echo will be born, repeating the voices successively as many times as there were points arranged in the circle. If these points have an equal distance from A in both semicircles, they will reverberate into an echo at the same time and render it twice as strong.

### Problem VII.

#### To construct the choir of a church with such artifice that only three singers perform as much as a hundred.

Let the dome <note>original: "tholus"</note> of the choir be arranged so that it has a spherical surface on the inside, and let the organ and the singers be placed around the center of this dome. You will then achieve your goal; for since all the vocal lines are perpendicular to the dome, they will return to the place from which they flowed, and they will intensify the sound most vehemently. Furthermore, if a distance is taken from the choir that is sufficient for a three-syllable Echo to be repeated, and a spherical surface is made on the wall at that location—described as if from a center at that place in the temple where people usually indulge in devotion—the voices will not only be most vehemently intensified in this spot, but they will also constitute a different choir from the first. For if they arrange the songs through three-note phrases <term>clausula: a short musical phrase or cadence</term>, such that after the given phrases a pause is always held for as long as the said phrases last, the people existing in said location will be entirely persuaded that there are two choirs, and that they are constituted by a great crowd of singers; we have placed the musical phrase here:

The church of St. James of the Incurables <note>San Giacomo degli Incurabili, a church in Rome</note> here in Rome is also so suited to this business that it seems the Architect had this in mind.

### Inquiry.

#### Whether a heterophonic echo can be constructed, which returns words different from the original ones.

<margin>
The manifold nature of the heterophonic echo.
</margin>
**A**t first glance, this business seems to involve I know not what impossibility <note>original Greek: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamia), meaning inability or impossibility</note>. For how, you will ask, can a voice differ from itself? Since an Echo is nothing else than a certain flow of the first voice continued and reflected, and it cannot by any means bring forth something else by reflecting except what was first uttered, it therefore seems to involve a contradiction that an Echo could represent something else. I respond that an Echo is considered in many ways: either as **orthophonic** (that is, direct) or as **loxophonic** (that is, oblique); again, either as **monophonic** (reflecting one syllable) or **polyphonic** (reflecting many syllables). I say therefore that it is true that an orthophonic and monophonic Echo cannot represent anything other than what was uttered. However, I say that some loxophonic Echoes <term>loxophonic: from the Greek 'loxos' (slanting) and 'phono' (sound); an echo that hits a surface at an angle.</term> are possible, which we say can be suited to represent something other than what was uttered. Some think even an orthophonic Echo can be arranged so that the direct voice carries one thing, and the reflected voice another. Thus, some people, while they utter Greek words, make the Echo respond in Latin, as is clear in the following words.

-> The gods sell all things for labors. — to the good. <-
<note>original: "οἱ θεοὶ πάντα πωλοῦσι πόνοις. — bonis." The Greek word 'ponois' (labors) sounds like the Latin 'bonis' (good men/things).</note>
-> They sell all things. — I have played. <-
<note>original: "πάντα πωλοῦσι — luſi." The Greek 'pōlousi' sounds like the Latin 'lusi' (I have played or I have deceived).</note>
-> The gods are here. — in age. <-
<note>original: "οἱ θεοὶ ἐνθάδε — ætate." The Greek 'enthade' sounds like the Latin 'aetate' (in time/age).</note>

In this or a similar way, words with similar endings could be selected from any language, yet such that they have different meanings in the different languages. But as such things are forced and require little genius, so they are not easily put into practice except with long study and little fruit. Perhaps these things could be better achieved in one and the same language, of which we will provide some examples. *See Figure II, Illustration XV.*

<margin>
SHOUTING
  WITH LOVE
   BY CUSTOM
    BY MOUTH
     BY DEED
</margin>
<note>original Latin: CLAMORE / AMORE / MORE / ORE / RE. These are Latin puns where removing the first letter of each word creates a new valid word.</note>
Suppose, for example, a four-syllable Echo is to be established; let the objects BCDEF be so arranged that each reflects one syllable later. And let the following word be **CLAMORE**. Let the source of the sounds or the speaker be at A. Since the objects are assumed to be so arranged that each reflects a syllable later, it is certain that the individual objects reflect different words with different meanings. Thus, object B returns **CLAMORE** (Shouting); object C returns **AMORE** (with Love); object D returns **MORE** (by Custom); object E returns **ORE** (by Mouth); and finally, object F returns **RE** (by Deed). Therefore, a polyphonic Echo will always repeat different and distinct words, as if someone should cry out: "In what way shall I give thanks to you, by SHOUTING?" <note>original: "tibi verò gratias agam, quo CLAMORE?"</note> The Echo will respond: "I will give thanks by **SHOUTING**, with **LOVE**, by **CUSTOM**, by **MOUTH**, by **DEED**."

<margin>
YOU WILL STAND FIRM
  YOU WILL STAND
   YOU DEPART
    TWICE
     HE GOES
</margin>
<note>original Latin: CONSTABIS / STABIS / ABIS / BIS / IS. Like the previous example, the echo "eats" the front of the word to create new meanings.</note>
Likewise, the word **CONSTABIS** will always reflect different words in different objects, as is clear here. Innumerable examples of this kind can be found, reflecting one after another from the prior voice, so that the Echo no longer returns the first word, but always returns other and different words. In these two ways, therefore, an orthophonic Echo (and indeed in various objects) can return different words from the prior ones, but not otherwise. The question then is whether a loxophonic Echo can be so constructed that it can respond to questions in any other language.

# Universal Music-making

## Problem VIII

### To construct a heterophonic echo, whose reflected voice always responds with different words and in any language.

<margin>What a heterophonic echo is</margin>
**T**his Echo requires the cooperation of two people and should be arranged as follows: first, a space should be determined that is suitable for perfectly pronouncing a word of four or five syllables—that is, a space that can clearly carry a word of that length. Once this is done, the reflecting object should be positioned with this specific strategy: the voice of someone standing at the first station, hitting the object, should be reflected to the ears of someone standing at a second station; however, the arrangement must be such that the first person cannot see the second, but only hear them. For this reason, the reflecting surface should be placed at the meeting point of two walls or a certain promontory, as shown in the diagram. In this figure, EF represents walls joined at point D; the obstacle that reflects the sound (the "Rupes") may be either natural or artificial.

The reciprocal phonic center should be located at points A and B, at such a distance from the object DC that it perfectly returns four or five syllables, as I mentioned. By this arrangement, as soon as the first person at point A begins to shout, the voice will hit point C <term>loxophonically</term> <note>original: "loxophonè"—meaning on a slanted or oblique path</note>. It will not be reflected back to A, but rather to B. As soon as the person standing at B hears it, they respond with other words uttered in any language, which will then immediately strike the ears of the person standing at A. He will therefore perceive something different than what was first spoken. For example, if the first person shouts the question, *“What is your name?”* <note>original: "quod nomen tibi"</note> and the other person positioned at B responds, *“Constantine,”* the person at A will perceive, immediately following the words of his question, a response that is not his own words, but the reflected words of another. 

Certainly, this trick—especially when staged with care—is so mysterious that when I tested it here in Rome at our estate, there was almost no one who understood how it worked. Everyone was amazed and stood as if stunned when they heard the Echo respond to every question with different words. To hide the trick effectively, however, the two people should be endowed with voices that are as similar as possible; in this way, the illusion will remain better hidden. Thus, we have constructed a <term>heterophonic</term> <note>original Greek: "ἑτερόφωνον" (heterophonon)—meaning "different-sounding"</note> echo, etc., which was the goal.

<note>A scientific diagram illustrates an acoustic setup for creating a heterophonic echo. Two walls, labeled E and F, meet at a right-angle corner labeled D. Two figures are positioned at points A and B in the foreground. Point C is indicated on the wall where sound waves reflect. A line of sound traveling from figure A to point C is labeled with the question "What is your name?" (original: "quod nomen tibi?"). A corresponding line of sound traveling from figure B to point C is labeled with the response "Constantine" (original: "Constantinus."). The background depicts a rural landscape with a large building, trees, and rocky cliffs (labeled "Rupes").</note>

<margin>Corollary I.</margin>
From what has been said, it is clear that two people at points A and B can signal anything to each other by this method. Indeed, two choirs could even perform together in alternating voices in a wonderful manner, and other feats could be performed at the discretion of a clever craftsman.

<margin>Corollary II.</margin>
It is also clear that just as there are optical illusions for the sense of sight, so too are there acoustic illusions. For the person positioned at A will clearly believe the voice comes from point D, and even that it is the very voice he emitted. This trick will be all the more secret the more similar the voices are, and the less the two people know about each other. However, there will be more extensive material regarding these matters in the following sections.

# PHONOCAMPTIC TRIGONOMETRY
->OR<-
### On the measurement of phonic lines.

## Problem I.

> *Given the perpendicular distance from a wall together with the angle of reflection or incidence of all oblique phonic points, to find the distance from the perpendicular point B.*

**L**et the wall be FDB, with the perpendicular distance known to be a measure of 25 paces, and the <term>loxophonous</term> <note>original: "loxophonophorum"—referring to sound traveling on a slanted or oblique path rather than a straight line</note> lines be AD and DE. I maintain that if either angle CAG or GAI—or what is the same thing, the angle of reflection DAB or of incidence EDF—and the phonic <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "catheti"—a geometric term for a perpendicular line, in this case, the line CDA</note> angle CDA are known, then the lines BD, AD, AC, CD, and ED become known. Let the angle CAD, which is equal to the angle of incidence ADB, be known through a <term>dioptric instrument</term> <note>A surveying tool used for measuring angles, similar to a primitive theodolite</note> as 76 degrees. When subtracted from 90, this leaves 14 degrees for GI, the angle of the phonic perpendicular CDA. Therefore, to find the line DB (or the oblique phonic point DB), let the calculation be: as the sine of the angle of sound-incidence <note>original: "phonoptoti"</note> (76 degrees) is to the sine of the angle of the phonic perpendicular (14 degrees), so is the distance of 25 paces to the other; the operation being completed, the line DB, the distance of the point of reflection from point B, will be produced. If, however, you desire the length of the oblique-falling line AD, let it be: as the sine of the angle of incidence ADB is to the <term>total sine</term> <note>In historical trigonometry, the "total sine" refers to the radius of the circle used in the calculation, usually assigned a large whole number like 10,000 or 100,000 to avoid decimals</note>, so is the known measure of 25 paces to the other; the sought oblique-falling line AD will be produced. Since the reflected line ED is equal to it, its length is known by extension.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates how sound reflects off a wall. The wall is represented by a vertical line labeled FDB. A horizontal base line contains points A, I, and B. A sound path (line AD) starts at point A, strikes the wall at D, and bounces back along the path DE. Point G is marked on the initial path AD, and point C is on the reflected path DE. Vertical lines GI and CD are drawn to show the heights. The angle CAG is labeled 76 degrees. The distance IB is marked "25 pass." (25 paces), and a small box nearby contains "625" (which is 25 squared). Near the wall segment DB, the numbers 8 and 64 (8 squared) are boxed. A value that looks like "26 + 13/8" is written near the line segment GD to indicate a calculated distance.</note>

If you truly wish to know at which point on line AX the voice from D is reflected, proceed as follows. Double the distance BD from point A along the line AX, and you will have point E, the sought point where the voice from A, reflected from D, will be perceived. For since the perpendicular CD cuts the triangle of reflection EDA exactly in half, the angles EDC and CDA will be equal; therefore, the sines subtending them will also be equal—namely AC and CE. The endpoints of these, A and E, determine the space between the phonic center A and the point E where the reflection ends. Thus, given the distance, etc.

## Corollary.

**H**ence it is clear: first, that oblique-sounding lines that are directly reflected between two parallels are always equal. Second, that the straight-sounding <note>original: "orthophonum"</note> radius AB or CD to the echo-reflecting <note>original: "phonocampticum"</note> object FDB is always equal to the phonic perpendicular CD situated between the parallels EA and FB. Third, that the space BD, whatever and however great it may be, when doubled always measures the distance AE, at the endpoint of which (E) the voice reflected from D terminates.

## Problem II.

->Given the distance of the phonic center from the terminal point of reflection,<-
->to determine the straight phonic line.<-

**L**et the distance AC or CE be known, and the center of reflection E or A. The <term>orthophonic</term> <note>original: "orthophona"—referring to a straight or perpendicular sound path</note> line AB or CD will become known if the calculation is made thus: as the sine of the angle GAI of the phonic <term>cathetus</term> <note>A vertical line dropped to a surface; the "leg" of a right triangle</note> is to the sine of the angle of incidence ADB (noted on the arc CG), so is the known measure DB to the other value. Once the operation is completed, AB or CD is produced. If, however, you wish to know the <term>loxophonic</term> <note>original: "loxophonas"—referring to slanted or oblique sound paths</note> lines AD and DE, let it be: as the sine of the angle of the phonic cathetus is to the <term>total sine</term> <note>original: "sinum totum"—in early trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle used in the table, acting as a base value (usually 1 or 100,000)</note>, so is DB to the other value. Once the operation is completed, the sought-after loxophonic lines AD and DE will be produced. The logic is clear from the 15th proposition on the resolution of triangles in the works of <term>Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a renowned Jesuit mathematician and astronomer whom the author frequently cites</note>, whom you may consult regarding geometric problems 1, 2, and 3.

## Problem III.

->With the oblique line known, to find the straight line and the distance of the phonic center<-
->from the normal point or center of reflection.<-

**L**et the loxophonic line AD be known. First, you shall investigate the orthophonic line CD in this manner: let it be as the total sine is to the sine of the <term>phonoptotic</term> <note>original: "phonoptoti"—the angle at which the sound "falls" or hits the reflecting surface</note> angle ADB, so is the known measure AD to the other value; once the operation is completed, the sought-after AB or CD will be produced. Again, to find the quantity of the line DB, let it be as the total sine is to the sine of the angle of the phonic cathetus GAI, so is the known measure AD to the other value; once the operation is performed, the sought-after BD will be produced.

## Problem IV.

->With the straight line known, to find the oblique lines and the distance of the phonic center<-
->from the center of reflection by means of tangents and secants.<-

**L**et AB be the known orthophonic line; and should you desire to know the loxophonic line AD, let it be as the total sine AI is to the <term>secant</term> AG of the phonic cathetus angle of 14 degrees, so is the known measure AB of 25 paces to the other value, and the sought-after quantity of the loxophonic AD will be produced. Again, to investigate BD, let it be as the total sine AI is to the <term>tangent</term> IG of the 14-degree angle; so is the known measure of 25 paces to the other value, and the sought-after quantity BD will be produced. If, however, BD is known, AB and AD will become known in this way: let it be as the tangent GI is to the total sine, so is the known measure BD to the other value, and the orthophonic line AB will be obtained. Again, for the loxophonic line AD, let it be as the tangent GI of the 14-degree angle is to the secant AG, so is the known BD to the other value, and the sought-after quantity AD will be produced.

### III. Given the oblique quantity, you shall seek the straight line CD and BD in this manner.

**L**et it be as the secant AG is to AI, so is the known AD to the other value, and the sought-after orthophonic CD or AB will be obtained. Again, as the secant AG is to the tangent GI, so is AD to the other value, and the sought-after quantity BD will be produced. With this completed, all lines pertaining to phonic matters will have been investigated.

Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic.

## Problem V.

->Given two sides in a phonic triangle, to find the third<-
->by the extraction of the square root.<-

**F**irstly, in the phonic triangle ADB, let the <term>orthophonic</term> <note>original: "orthophonum"—referring to a straight or perpendicular sound path</note> side AB be given as 25 paces, and the line AC (the distance of the phonic center from the phonic <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "catheto"—a vertical line used in geometric construction</note>) as 8 paces; you will find the third side AD in this manner. Let the given sides be multiplied by themselves [squared], and from the sum of the two sides joined together, let the <term>square root</term> <note>original: "℞. quadr." or "radix quadrata"</note> be extracted. You will then have the sought-after line AD, according to the 47th proposition of the 1st book of <term>Euclid's Elements</term> <note>The OCR reads "4. lib. 1.", but the text describes the Pythagorean theorem, which is Proposition 47 in Euclid's first book</note>.
Secondly, if the sides BD and AD are known, you will find the third, AB, if you subtract the square of line DB from the square of the whole AD. For the root of the remaining square will give the sought-after line AB.
Thirdly, if the two sides AB and AD are given, you will find the third, BD, in this manner: Subtract the square of AB from the square of AD, and the root of the remaining square will give the sought-after line BD.

## Corollary.

**F**rom these briefly stated points, it is clear how phonic lines are typically measured in all other <term>Echometric</term> <note>The science of measuring echoes</note> cases. Since in the entire phonocamptic system the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, once any side is known along with an angle in the phonic triangle, the remaining parts will be investigated by the exact same method we have prescribed. Therefore, whether the reflection occurs on regular or irregular bodies, the same ratio of dimension must always be observed. I wished to indicate this briefly here so that nothing might seem to be missing from our phonocamptic art.

<margin>
Wonders concerning the construction of acoustic instruments
</margin>
**W**e give the name "acoustic instruments" to those devices by which we present remote sounds to the ears—sounds otherwise inaccessible to the sense of hearing—just as we do with optical instruments for distant objects that are entirely hidden from the sense of sight (which we have treated at length in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte Magna Lucis et Umbrae"—Kircher's 1646 work on optics and projection</note>). These sounds are confined within organs constructed after the model of nature with wonderful industry and skill. 
This study first contains the construction of halls, chambers, and galleries arranged with such ingenuity that in a certain and determined point, Princes may be able to hear every utterance of words, no matter how whispered. Secondly, it covers the construction of acoustic instruments for the use of the hard of hearing, along with acoustic <term>Cryptology</term> <note>The study of secret or hidden communication</note>, or the occult communication of mutual concepts through sounds, and other new and most hidden inventions. But before we approach the matter itself, we have seen fit to set forth the experiments themselves which we shall use in the architecture of the work.

# Acoustic Experiments I.
## Channels or siphons propagate sound miraculously.

<margin>
Roman Aqueducts propagate sonic species across a great distance.
</margin>
**J**ust as light enclosed in polished containers gains a maximum increase in intensity, so too does sound propagated through channels. For I believe that if a cylinder one mile long were provided for the entire sonic sphere, with a capacity equal to that sphere, a sound which in open air has a line of action of only 24 paces would propagate its line of action beyond a thousand paces in that cylindrical channel. Experience itself supports my opinion; for the Overseers of the Roman Aqueducts say that within the aqueducts, the voice of speakers is perceived across a very long distance, even at five hundred feet, as if the speaker were present, especially if the channel was remarkably polished. Experience also teaches that a channel of two hundred feet renders even whispered voices audible at either end. Nor should this seem strange to anyone; since the voice enclosed in channels, while it cannot escape, strives to recover through longitudinal propagation what it had lost in the open air through diffusion, dispersion, and dissipation of its <term>species</term> <note>In 17th-century physics, "species" refers to the "form" or "image" of a sound as it travels through a medium like air.</note>. For in these narrow spaces, being repeatedly reflected and multiplied, it acquires both a huge increase and the most remote boundaries of its propagation. But at this point, I cannot omit a notable question, not yet decided by anyone as far as I know, which follows.

## A Curious Question.
->Whether the voice, tightly enclosed in channels, remains<-
->there for some space of time.<-

<margin>
The fraud of Porta and Cornelius Agrippa.
</margin>
**T**here were some, among them Giambattista della Porta and Cornelius Agrippa, who not only held this opinion but also tried to persuade others of it as an infallible truth: that a voice whispered into a very long, clean, and polished channel, before the sonic species exit, if closed very tightly from the other end, persists within the said channel so that several days later, when either end is opened, the voices soon present themselves to the listener's ears as if released from a certain captivity. And this fabrication was so plausible that it gained not only many patrons but also its sharpest defenders. Wecker, Alessio, and others have tried to defend the matter as most certain, true, and beyond all doubt—even adding fabricated stories about the great utility of such an experiment—defending it as if for their <term>altars and hearths</term> <note>original: "pro aris & focis"—a Latin idiom meaning to defend something with the utmost zeal, as if protecting one's home or religion.</note>. So it happens when Experience, the "Mistress of Things," is not consulted, and we rashly and headlong subscribe to the fantastic agitations of anyone's mind; in this way, intolerable errors are propagated by substitute teachers in the lecture halls. If they had previously conducted an experiment of this thing, or had properly understood the nature of sound, they would never have fallen into such a shameful opinion. I say, therefore, that water will sooner be drawn with a sieve than a voice be enclosed in channels; and I conclude this from the <term>impossibility</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamian)</note> of the matter with the following argument.

**F**or either the voice is carried through the channel by real species or <term>intentional species</term> <note>Kircher is distinguishing between "real" physical movement of air and "intentional" forms that exist in the mind or medium.</note>; neither can be said. Not the former, for the real species of sound are nothing other than the continuous and successive agitation of the air carrying the voice, which, while enclosed, finds the exit obstructed at both ends; nor can it be reflected because of the air left behind that does not know how to yield. Therefore, all agitation of the air will necessarily cease in a moment, and with that cessation, the sonic motion also ends. Indeed, he who would attempt to enclose sound within a channel would be doing the same as one who believed he could draw water with a sieve. Let there be, for example, a channel AB of 400 feet, which is a length sufficient for forming a three-syllable Echo. Thus, with someone occupying station A whispering a voice—for example, "Sing!" <note>original: "cantate"</note>—another at station B, at the sign of the end of the uttered voice at B, whe—

<summary>Kircher explains how enclosed channels like aqueducts can amplify sound and carry it over long distances. He then debunkers the popular myth held by Agrippa and Porta that sound can be "trapped" in a pipe and released days later, arguing that sound is merely a temporary agitation of air.</summary>
