<meta>This page continues Kircher’s investigation into the physics of sound. Having previously discussed how sound travels through aqueducts and pipes, he now addresses a popular myth of his time: the idea that one could "capture" a voice inside a tube and release it later. He uses Aristotelian physics to debunk this "imposture" before moving on to the conduction of sound through solid materials like wood.</meta>

<margin>
Explanation of a false experiment.
</margin>
...it should be closed as quickly as possible; the sealing must occur while the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciebus"; refers to the formal qualities or "images" of sound that travel through a medium.</note> of the sound are still dwelling within the channel. For this reason, they require a very long channel. They say, therefore, that in this way a trapped voice can remain for a long time, and when the channel is finally opened, it presents itself to the ears like a captive.

<note>A horizontal line is labeled with points A, C, D, and B. Between points C and D, the Latin word "cantate" (meaning "sing ye") is written to represent the sound traveling through the tube.</note>

<margin>
Refutation.
</margin>
They claim that just as in the open air, both direct and reflected voice can remain without any further dependence on the original source. O foolish device! These impostors do not see the manifest contradiction of their own opinion, for it would clearly follow from this that a voice both exists and does not exist. For a voice exists and remains only as long as the motion of the air remains; when that motion ceases, the voice itself ceases. As was stated in Book 1, all sound essentially depends upon the motion of the air as its vehicle. Therefore, if both ends A and B of the tube are closed, either the sonorous air will still be moved, or it will be at rest. I shall demonstrate that it certainly cannot be moved: imagine the voice is propagated in the section CD while both ends are now closed; I say that all motion will cease simultaneously, since neither the air in front (CA) nor the air behind (BD) can give way in any manner. Nor can any reflection occur, since in every reflection the air first set in motion is driven backward by the reflection itself; but here the air at BD cannot be driven back because of the compression of the forward air at AC, which does not know how to give way. Thus, at the very moment both ends are closed, the entire body of air comes to rest, and with it, the propagation of the voice. But they will say that the "sonorous species" remain there unmoved. Even if I were to grant—though I do not—that the species remain there, I still say that once the opening B is opened, the motionless species could not possibly exit, as there would be nothing to impel them. Since sound, as has been said, essentially depends on motion, when that motion ceases, the sound itself is destroyed. Nor is it a similar case to how a voice remains in the open air without dependence on the source; for in the open air, the air does not rest at all, but the sonorous air is in continuous motion, as the nature of an Echo sufficiently declares. Therefore, real sonorous species cannot be permanently enclosed within a channel, which was the first point to be proven.

<margin>
Intentional species of sound cannot be enclosed.
</margin>
Nor can <term>intentional species</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, these are the "immaterial" versions of sensory information that travel to the senses.</note> be enclosed; for since they have an entity close to the spiritual and incorporeal, no obstacles could be so great as to block them. Daily experience teaches that sound is permeable even through the thickest walls. It is therefore ridiculous, not to say foolish, to wish to restrain sound with barriers, since once enclosed, it would pass through the barrier as easily as it passes through a window or a wall. You see, therefore, from this discussion of ours, how contrary to reason and how discordant the reasonings of these impostors are. Thus, that fabulous invention about enclosing sound in channels, which has occupied the academic chairs until now, should be abolished. Let investigators of the truth learn not to give credit to any matter unless it has first been weighed perfectly in the balance of reason. But having explained these things, let us now return to our purpose.

# Experiment II.
## Voice is propagated miraculously through long beams.

**T**his is also an admirable, though almost common experiment, regarding the propagation of sound in long beams, and it is performed in this way: let there be a beam AB, two hundred feet long. I say that at either end, A or B, no noise can be made so small that it is not perceived at the other end as if it were present.

<note>A drawing depicts a long rectangular wooden beam or log, oriented horizontally and labeled with 'A' at the left end and 'B' at the right end.</note>

The cause of this matter is sought; for a voice that is imperceptible across a space of 200 feet seems a paradox to many when it is perceived through the intervention of a beam. But those who remember what was said about the nature of sound in the first...

# Universal Music-making

<margin>
What is the reason why a scraping sound produced at one end of a long wooden beam is perceived so easily at the other end?
</margin>
...if one has understood well what we said in the first book, they will find no difficulty here either. To declare the effect of this experiment more precisely, however, two things must be noted: first, the efficient cause of sound, which we have said is nothing other than a certain <term>tremor</term> <note>Kircher uses "tremor" to mean a physical vibration or oscillation of a solid body.</note> of colliding bodies; second, the material object of sound, which is the air. Since a wooden beam is exceedingly porous, it is also highly suited for the propagation of sound and extremely receptive to vibration. Thus, a scraping sound produced at one end (B) will be easily perceived by an ear placed at the other end (A), since the beam, acting as a single sonorous body, is moved to vibrate throughout. Consequently, it communicates these <term>sonorous species</term> <note>original: "species sonoras"; in 17th-century physics, these were the "audible forms" or qualities of a sound that travel through a medium to the senses.</note> partly to the internal air within its pores and partly to the surrounding external air. It is necessary for the ear at end A to perceive this continued vibration of the air, which serves as the vehicle for the voice. The truth of this matter is proven by experiments: for if the beam is cut through anywhere, or if you bind it tightly with a strap, or if you apply a thick board to the other end, you will perceive nothing at all. This is because the sonorous vibration is now interrupted and can no longer reach the air, much like a bell tied with a cord is deprived of its proper sound because its vibration is stopped.

## Corollary.

And from this it is clear why the experiment is less successful if the entire beam lies upon the ground or is enclosed within a wall; for it is hindered from vibrating by the surrounding earth or wall. Therefore, the experiment succeeds best with a beam lightly placed upon two supports, and even better if it could be suspended in the open air. Whether a similar success occurs in beams of bronze or metal has not yet been fully established; however, I do not doubt that the same thing happens in every sonorous body, even glass. For the more vibrating, polished, smooth, and porous these bodies are, the better the effect they will produce. As we have said, the entire logic of this experiment depends on the vibration of a long body; strings testify that sound is propagated better along a long body than a wide one. For this reason, thicker walls, because they cannot easily vibrate, lack this effect.

# Experiment III.

## *The voice is better propagated and more powerfully intensified through circular tubes than through straight ones.*

Daily experience teaches that sound is more powerfully intensified in a curved tube than in a straight one. This is shown primarily by trumpets, and by the "Horn of Alexander the Great," with which he used to assemble his entire army, and which was twisted into a circle, as was mentioned in our history of marvelous sounds. The cause of this is sought. It must be noted, therefore, that just as the multiplication of light and heat occurs through the multiple reflection of light—as we taught in our book *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*—so the intensity of sound is created by the multiple reflection of sound within a circular hollow. For in a straight tube, there is only the propagation of sounds that are narrowed and collected into one; but in a circular tube, the sound is not only collected, but is greatly increased and intensified by a certain infinite reflection of sonorous lines.

Zig-zagging lines originate from this opening, reflecting off the inner and outer curves of the tube's walls at points labeled B, Z, D, F, H, K on the inner side and Y, E, G, I, L on the outer side. The lines converge and exit through a narrower opening on the right, labeled S, V, and X, demonstrating how the circular shape intensifies sound through multiple reflections.</note>

# Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic
<note>Phonocamptic: from the Greek *phonē* (sound) and *kamptos* (bent or turned). This branch of magic or science deals with the reflection of sound, much like catoptrics deals with the reflection of light.</note>

Let the tube AV be bent into an arc; I maintain that the sound is intensified more within it than in a straight tube. For besides the collection of sound, a manifold reflection of the same occurs, from which a powerful intensification is born. Thus, you see the <term>sonorous ray</term> <note>Kircher envisions sound traveling in straight "rays" similar to light, which can be reflected off surfaces.</note> reflected from A to B, from B to C, and from there to D; from D to E and so on, intensified through multiple points of reflection. Similarly, the opposite ray X is reflected to Y and from there to Z; and from Z to alpha and from there to beta, following another series of reflections. Since infinite sound lines enter the mouth of the tube AX, each will observe its own laws in reflecting. Therefore, since there is an infinite piling up of sound lines, a <term>polyphonism</term> <note>original: "polyphonismus"; here meaning a multiplication or layering of sounds that increases volume.</note> will necessarily be born from their reflection, becoming more intense as the sound is more compressed toward V. This occurs least of all in a straight tube; for in such a tube, as has been said, the propagation occurs only by the sound being collected and narrowed, without such great reflection.

### Corollary.

<margin>
A conical channel intensifies the voice more than a cylindrical one.
</margin>
From this it is clear that a conical tube intensifies the voice more than a cylindrical tube, for the former is more suited to reflecting the <term>sonorous species</term>. Hence, if you twist both a conical and a cylindrical tube into a circle, the conical one twisted into a circle will be more effective than the cylindrical one twisted into a circle. For as the circular conical tube moves from wide to narrow, the constricted and packed sound images will be vehemently intensified, not unlike wind which gains greater force when constricted in narrow places. In a circular cylindrical tube, however, the packing of the sound is equal everywhere. Because of this, the Horn of Alexander the Great was constructed so that it dilated from narrow to wide; but regarding this, see the history of miraculous sounds and my work *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*. <note>original: "Artem lucis & umbrae"; Kircher refers to his own 1646 treatise on optics and acoustics.</note>

## Experiment IV.

->*Sound propagated along circular surfaces acquires immense power.*<-

<margin>
Sound carried through circular surfaces is most perceptible.
</margin>
Experience has many times taught me in various buildings that sound propagated along circular surfaces is extremely intense. There is in Heidelberg, Germany, a certain very large round tower, constructed with such artifice that two people diametrically opposite one another may speak whatever they wish, even in the lowest whispers. I hear there is a similar hall in the Palace of the Duke of Mantua; I have experienced the same in the arches of great bridges. I also undertook an experiment of this matter with remarkable success in the dome of Saint Peter’s here in Rome. In the interior dome, there is a <term>cornice</term> <note>A decorative ledge or walkway high up in the dome.</note> of such great width that a chariot could comfortably travel there without danger. In places at opposite diameters of this encompassing cornice, a distance of nearly one hundred geometric feet, two people opposite each other talk to one another even in the lowest whispers, despite the clamor of a crowd of men and musicians making a noise below. Yet, at the remaining points of the wall, nothing is perceived. There is no doubt that the same thing happens in all circular structures. To reveal the cause of this, it must be known that sound has this particular quality over light: it is propagated according to the movement of the air. Thus, if the movement of the air is in a straight line, the sound will also be propagated in a straight line; if in a circle, the sound will also be propagated according to the circle, and so it must be said of other surfaces. Furthermore, when the sound—diffused spherically—seeks to escape in a circular surface, but finds no place to escape because the walls block it, it is constricted along the circular surface. Finally, meeting at the diametrically opposite point with the vocal air arriving there at the same moment from the other side of the wall, it is vehemently intensified. From this kind of conjunction and confluence of species, that great intensification of the carried voice is born; and thus it happens that this <term>phonophonism</term> <note>A term Kircher uses to describe the reinforcement of sound by sound, specifically in a "whispering gallery" effect.</note> occurs nowhere else but in the opposite locations. However, we have decided that this matter must be demonstrated more deeply.

Let the cornice AB be circular, and in it let there be two diametrically opposite places A and B; I say that one standing at A and murmuring any words however softly, the one standing at B...

...the words will be perceived in the opposite place and nowhere else. Since sound is propagated in a circle according to what was stated, and in its diffusion is carried from part A into the opposite parts with equal motion, it will necessarily complete both semicircles ADB and ACB in the same amount of time. It will, therefore, reach point B at the exact same moment. Since a union of <term>phonisms</term> <note>original: "phonismorum"; Kircher uses this term to describe the individual units or reflections of sound waves that combine to create an audible effect.</note> occurs there, it is necessary that the voice—which was previously imperceptible—becomes strongly intensified and begins to present itself to the senses at that specific point. 

I prove that the voice is perceptible in no other point of the circuit except in B as follows: Let the ear be placed at point C, and let someone standing at A whisper; I say that nothing will be perceived at C. For since the arc AC is an unequal part of the total circuit compared to the arc ADBC—the former being very short and the latter very long—it happens that the voice carried from A to C flies away too quickly, while the voice carried from A through D and B to C arrives too late. Thus, a union of the voices and phonisms cannot occur there, and consequently, nothing is perceptible. Since all other arcs chosen in this manner are unequal and the sound travels them in unequal times, no intensification of the voice can happen in any place except in the opposite point B, where the motion of equal duration will perfectly correspond to the equality of the lines.

### Corollary I.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates a hemispherical dome representing the propagation of sound. Curved lines radiate from point A across the surface of the hemisphere, converging again at point C, showing how sound waves are focused by the architecture.</note>

From this it follows: A spherical quadrant, such as the <term>tholus</term> <note>original: "tholus"; the internal vault or cupola of a dome, often found above a church choir.</note> of a choir might be, is most suitable for this purpose. Let ABCD be a spherical quadrant. Let A and C be two diametrically opposite places. I say that voices uttered softly at A will be perceived at C; for since all lines from A to C are semicircles, the voice—carried through innumerable semicircles according to the preceding principles—will finally be strongly intensified at C by all those semicircles, as if they were united at a pole.

### Corollary II.

From this it follows secondly: this intensification of phonisms at the opposite ends of any semicircular vault or hemispherical cupola will be twice as great if the surface is very flat and highly polished, since all the sound lines in the entire hemisphere will meet at point C at the same time.

### Corollary III.

From this it is clear thirdly: in any sphere with a diameter of 90 geometric feet, at opposite poles, this increase of phonisms would be truly prodigious, since the semicircular lines of the entire spherical surface flow together at the opposite pole at exactly the same time.

### Experiment V.

->*The voice in spiral shells, or a conical tube twisted along a helical or spiral line; as it is the most suitable of all shapes, so it also possesses the greatest power.*<-

<margin>The power of spiral tubes in multiplying sound.</margin>
This experiment is indeed most worthy of observation: sound within a conical tube twisted into a spiral—of the kind seen in snail shells—is increased in a wonderful manner beyond all other objects mentioned thus far. I would never have believed it had experience not made me certain of it time and again. I have seen nothing more wonderful in this category than the Grotto of Dionysius the Tyrant, <note>original: "Antro Dionysij Tyranni"; a famous limestone cave in Syracuse, Sicily, carved in antiquity and known for its extraordinary acoustic properties which allowed a listener to overhear whispers from far away.</note> constructed in the shape of an inner ear, which still survives in Syracuse in Sicily; see the description of it in the history of prodigious sounds. Certainly, in the architecture of the ear, we showed in Book 1, in the chapter on the anatomy of the ears of all kinds of animals, that the most wise Nature chose this spiral tube above all other shapes. We showed that the more certain animals were of a more perfect sense of hearing, the more open and perfect a <term>cochlea</term> <note>The spiral-shaped cavity of the inner ear.</note> she granted them, as is most clearly seen in the ears of pigs, hares, mice, dogs, and especially donkeys. In the construction of their ears, Nature established tubes that are perfectly helical; for which reason, we have deemed it worthwhile to declare Nature’s design.

Regarding why a spiral tube intensifies sound more than all others, I assign this cause: whatever has been said of conical and cylindrical tubes—whether straight or twisted—applies most perfectly to this spiral cone. For it not only perfectly collects the "sonorous species" <note>The perceived qualities or images of sound.</note> and reflects them many times over, but it reflects them in every direction—backward and forward—mostly by <term>orthophonic</term> <note>original: "orthophona"; a reflection that returns directly back toward the source.</note> reflection. Furthermore, since the helical passages are separated only by a thin diaphragm, by striking against the sides, it does not just increase the sound by reflecting it, but by penetrating into the other passages, it wonderfully intensifies the <term>phonisms</term>. <note>Kircher uses this term to describe the individual units or impacts of sound that combine to create an audible effect.</note> But let these things be better understood.

<note>A detailed geometric diagram shows a spiral conical tube labeled with letters. A sound source at point A emits rays that reflect off the inner walls of the spiral. Let there be a conical tube twisted into a spiral helix, labeled AMQC. I say that in this tube, voices are intensified more than in all other hollow bodies. Let the voice be at point A, from which the sound is propagated within the hollow of the tube. Because the interior of the tube is arranged with an irregular curvature, it happens that a certain "star-like" reflection is perpetually born. The further this penetrates inside, the more sharply and acutely it will always reflect, until finally, in the orthophonic reflection, it produces a most intense sound. Thus, you see the voice from A falling upon E, and from there reflected to F, and hence to G, H, I, K, and L. Since this line is orthophonic, being reflected back into itself, it will vehemently intensify the sound. In the same way, the vocal line from A falling on M will be reflected from there into N, O, P, Q and the remaining points in a star-like pattern, until in R and S, it again produces a most intense sound through orthophonic reflection. Since, however, infinite lines can be drawn from point A, each hitting different parts of the interior surface...

# Problem I.
## To describe an ellipse with the single stroke of a string.

<margin>
Book 3...
in the
con-
struc-
tion
</margin>
Since in Books 3 and 10 of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Lucis & Vmbræ"; Kircher’s 1646 treatise on optics and gnomonics</note> we have handed down various methods for describing ellipses and other conic sections, we did not wish to repeat them here. Instead, we shall teach only that method which seemed more suited to mechanical Echotectonics <term>Echotectonics: the architectural art of designing buildings and rooms specifically to produce desired acoustic or echo effects</term>. Thus, in this way, you may describe an ellipse with a single stroke of a string.

<margin>The wonderful power of the Ellipse.</margin>
Every ellipse consists of two diameters: a major and a minor. For if they were equal, it would not be an ellipse but a circle. The more the minor diameter decreases, the sharper the ellipse will be; the more it increases, the more obtuse the ellipse will be and more similar to a circle, until the diameters become equal in size and the ellipse vanishes into a perfect circle. Note, moreover, that in every ellipse except the circular one, two points are found which Geometers commonly call "foci" <term>foci: literally "hearths" or "fireplaces" in Latin; the two central points that define an ellipse's shape</term>, because in those points ignition occurs when using caustic mirrors <note>original: "speculis causticis"; mirrors designed to focus sunlight into a single point to generate intense heat or fire</note>. These two points are situated on the major semi-diameter; they will always be further from each other the sharper the ellipse is (that is, the more it differs from a circle). Conversely, they will be closer together as the ellipse nears a circular shape, until they meet in a single point, which is the center of the circle.

With these things observed: Let the diameters of the ellipse to be formed be given as AB (the major) and CD (the minor). Let the minor diameter CD be placed at right angles at the center point E of the major, so that the ends of the minor diameter are equidistant from the center point E. This being established, you will find the foci or "points of comparison" thus: take the major semi-diameter AE or BE with a compass. Placing the compass at either end of the minor diameter (C or D), transfer this distance onto the major diameter AB. Where the compass cuts the line AB on both sides, there will be the two foci, namely at I and L. Having found these focal points I and L, fix two pins into them. Around these pins, place a string double the length of LA or IB. Within this loop of string, a stylus <note>original: "graphium"</note> drawn around will describe the desired ellipse. The string is represented to us by the two lines LR and RI; it is tied at the two points I and L and applied with the stylus R precisely at point A. Then, as the stylus R is drawn around from A within that string, it will describe the sought-after ellipse. From this, it is clearly evident that the two parts of the string extended from R toward either focus (specifically the lengths LR and RI) will always be equal to the major diameter of the ellipse. For the mathematical demonstration of all these things, see the *Art of Light and Shadow*, Book 4, in the treatise on conic sections.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the "gardener's method" for drawing an ellipse. A horizontal line AB represents the major axis with center point E and two focal points I and L. A vertical line CD represents the minor axis. A triangular arrangement of lines represents a string anchored at the foci I and L and pulled taut by a stylus at point R on the perimeter. The diagram demonstrates how the sum of the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci remains constant.</note>

This form or rule we call an Ellipsoplast, serving as a potter's mold for the Ellipse.

# Problem III.
## To describe a parabola with a single stroke of a string.

A parabola is a section of a cone parallel to its side, within which there is a point where all lines incident parallel within its surface are united upon reflection. Since we have demonstrated all these matters at length in the cited books of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Lucis & Vmbræ"; Kircher’s monumental 1646 work on optics and geometry</note>, we refer the reader there, where he will also find various descriptions of parabolas. Consequently, in this place, we have thought it necessary to propose only one method, which is easier and more suited to our purpose.

Let a very flat board XY be prepared, to which a square rule DE is applied at right angles, so that the rule applied to the side EG scrapes the side of the board EG perpendicularly and, as it is moved, always remains equidistant to the axis of the parabola. Therefore, to describe the parabola with the help of this instrument, let a very fine string be attached to the center L. Then, with the rule placed over LB, the string—wrapped around the stylus D—should be secured with a small nail at the base of the rule E, so that the string has a length double that of LB. Since, indeed,

<note>A geometric diagram showing the construction of a parabola on a rectangular board labeled X and Y. A sliding rule DE is used to guide a string-and-stylus construction. The resulting parabola is labeled FBG, with its axis BL, focus O, and a vertical line NR representing the "latus rectum" or the chord passing through the focus.</note>

according to Proposition 10 of conic doctrine demonstrated in *The Art of Light and Shadow*, all lines from the center to the perimeter of the parabola, together with those which fall from there onto the semi-ordinate, are equal, the stylus D will necessarily describe the parabola FBG by the motion of the rule. You will find its phonic point <term>phonic point: the acoustic focus where sound waves converge after reflecting off a surface</term> of reflection O, if you move any rule perpendicularly over the axis BL of the parabola until you intercept a fourth part of the line NR (applied as an ordinate, or the *latus rectum* <term>latus rectum: literally the "right side," a technical term for the chord through the focus of a conic section parallel to the directrix</term>) on the axis BL. For this point will be the focus of the parabola, as shown in the figure.

# Problem IV.
## To build a Parabola-maker form.

On any flat and polished floor, let a parabola of the size you desire and which best suits your purpose be described according to the established rules and the stated method. According to this, you shall cut another out of wooden boards or iron plates so that the piece cut out exactly matches the one drawn on the floor. You will then have a parabola-maker <note>original: "paraboloplasten"</note> ready in the shape shown in the following figure, in which the vertex A is equipped with a sharp iron point. CD, however, with the handle IMP, and the sharp iron point continued along the axis, is fixed into the wall during the description of the parabola, so that the surface is not altered by a change in the axis. Then, with the handle placed under another fulcrum <term>hypomochlio: from the Greek 'hypomochlion,' meaning a pivot or the point on which a lever turns</term> and rotated within lime, gypsum, or other material heaped around it, it will describe the desired parabola in that material.

# Problem V.
## To describe a hyperbola with a single stroke of a string, and to build a hyperbola-maker from the described form.

Let the center of reflection be A; the opposite center B, and C the vertex of the hyperbola. With these three given, you shall describe the hyperbola by the drawing of a string in this way: In both centers (or points made by comparison in opposite hyperbolas), let needles be fixed, to each of which a string is tied. Next, have a stylus <note>original: "graphium," a writing or drawing tool</note> perforated at its base in the manner of a needle's eye, as is seen at F. Through this hole, let both strings fastened at A and B be drawn. Then, let the stylus F be moved to both sides so that the two strings are always loosened by the motion, and by this movement, the desired parabola <note>The original text says "parabola" here, though the context and heading indicate the author intended to say "hyperbola."</note> is described.

The base of the device has a crank handle labeled M and P, used to rotate the template to create a three-dimensional hyperbolic vessel or surface.</note>

# Problem VII.
## To describe a spiral line.

<margin>V</margin>
To describe a spiral line, take two points I and K at any distance, and through them draw a straight line BA of a given size. Then, placing the compass at center K, describe a semicircle BCA from A; next, placing the compass at center I, describe a semicircle DGA from D. Then again, with the compass at center K, describe another semicircle DEF from D. Again, with the compass at point D, let a semicircle DEI be drawn, and then with the compass at center K, draw another semicircle from point I; and so on for the others, and you will have a perfect snail-like <term>cochleatam: a spiral or screw-like shape, from the Latin 'cochlea' (snail shell)</term> figure, as the diagram shows. If you draw this figure out lengthwise from its center I, having cut it into an iron plate along the helical line, it will be born— <note>original: "na-", completed by catchword "scetur" as "nascetur" (will be born/produced).</note>

<note>A geometrical diagram illustrating the construction of a spiral (helix). The spiral is formed by a series of connected semicircles of increasing radii, centered alternately on points K and I. Various points along the spiral are labeled with letters: G, H, F, A, C, E, B, D, and V. A horizontal line BA passes through the central points to guide the compass placements.</note>

## CHAPTER IV.
# ECHO-BUILDING MAGIC
->OR<-
### On Acoustic Structures.
## PREFACE.

<margin>Whatever has been stated regarding the Magic of Mirrors can also be applied to sound-reflection.</margin>
<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicts a landscape featuring a building and trees.</note> Whatever wonders we have displayed in our *Magic of Mirrors* <note>original: "Magia Catoptrica," referring to the study of reflected light and mirrors</note>—such as when we used telescopes to bring the appearance of distant objects before us as if they were present, or when we provided the wonderful composition of tiny things, both animate and inanimate, to be viewed through microscopes—we are confident we shall achieve the same in this present treatise regarding the representation of distant sounds. We shall present voices, otherwise imperceptible, compressed within instruments so vividly and sonorously to the ears of the listeners that they might not unfairly seem to be recalled from death to life. We undertake this all the more gladly because the subject is both more profound and more highly anticipated. Let no one persuade themselves that we will present things here that are certain only in *theory* but meet with no success when brought into *practice*. On the contrary, let the reader be certain that we shall exhibit no clever devices whose infallible certainty has not first been confirmed by undeniable experiments observed in various parts of the world. With these things established, let us proceed to the matter at hand.

## Prelude I.
### Concerning the Vitruvian Theater and the Sound-Vessels placed within it.
->*See Illustration XVI, fig. I.*<-

It can hardly be explained how great a variety of opinions and how much disagreement exists among authors regarding the structure of this Acoustic Theater. Almost none of those who have commented on Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of "De Architectura," the foundational text for Renaissance builders.</note> show that they have properly understood it. But, as is common in such difficulties, when they cannot penetrate an obscure matter, most have substituted a borrowed opinion for their own so as not to seem to have said nothing—or so that, by passing over such a memorable thing in silence, they do not prove themselves to have "drawn water with a sieve" <note>An ancient idiom for performing a futile or impossible task.</note>, as the old saying goes.

Considering often that this confusion arises solely from an ignorance of Music, I believed I would perform a worthwhile service if, in this treatise on Echo-building <note>original: "Echotectonicæ"</note>, I inserted my own opinion regarding the structure of the said Theater at this opportune point and explained what those famous sound-vessels <term>Echeia <gloss>resonant bronze jars or vessels used in ancient Greek and Roman theaters to amplify the actors' voices</gloss></term> actually were. This shall be done after I have first cited the text of Vitruvius.

# Universal Music-Making

->Thus Vitruvius in Book 5, Chapter 5, describes the Resonant Theater<-
->in this manner.<-

> *Therefore, from these mathematical investigations, bronze vessels are produced according to the size of the theater; let them be so manufactured that, when they are struck, they can produce the sounds of a fourth, a fifth, and so on in order, up to the double octave. Afterwards, having established chambers among the seats of the theater according to musical principles, let the vessels be placed there so that they touch no wall, and have an empty space around them and a gap at the top. Let them be placed upside down, and on the side facing the stage, let them have wedges placed under them no less than half a foot high; and opposite these chambers, let openings be left in the lower steps two feet long and half a foot high. The designations of the places where they are to be positioned are explained thus: If the theater is not of vast size, let a transverse region at mid-height be designated, and in it thirteen chambers, separated by twelve equal intervals, shall be arched over. These Resonant Vessels <note>original: "Echæa"</note>, described above, should sound in their chambers as follows: in the extreme corners, let the first ones be placed on each side sounding the highest note of the system <note>original: "netem hyperbolæon"; the highest note of the ancient Greek Greater Perfect System</note>; the second from the ends a fourth below that, at the "disjointed" high note <note>original: "netem diezeugmenon"</note>; the third a fourth below that at the "middle-adjacent" note <note>original: "netem parameſon"</note>; the fourth a fourth below at the "conjunction" note <note>original: "netem ſynnemmenon"</note>; the fifth a fourth below at the "middle" note <note>original: "meſon"</note>; the sixth a fourth below at the "middle-lowest" note <note>original: "hypaten meſon"</note>; and in the center, one at a fourth below at the "lowest of the low" <note>original: "hypaten hypaton"</note>. Thus, by this reasoning, the voice pouring forth from the stage as if from a center, expanding in a circle and striking the cavities of the individual vessels, will arouse an increased clarity and a harmony suited to itself by its resonance. Thus says Vitruvius.*

<margin>Explanation of the theater according to all its parts.</margin> The vessels, therefore, should be so manufactured that, when placed and struck, they return all the differences of the harmonies, such as the fourth <term>diatessaron</term>, the fifth <term>diapente</term>, and the octave <term>diapason</term>; the octave plus a fourth; the octave plus a fifth; and the double octave <term>disdiapason</term>. That is, according to the ratios of the intervals: 4:3 <term>sesquitertia</term>, 3:2 <term>sesquialtera</term>, 2:1 <term>dupla</term>, 8:3 <term>dupla sesquitertia</term>, 3:1 <term>tripla</term>, and 4:1 <term>quadrupla</term>, within which six consonances <note>original: "sexphtongis"</note> the Pythagoreans enclosed the entire harmony of voices. But for them to provide this, they require certain places, which Vitruvius calls "cells" or chambers, which must touch nothing, because otherwise they would hardly return a sound; indeed, they would make everything dull. Let them be in an empty space so they may resonate better; let them have a gap at the top so that the voice, having struck the cavity of the chambers, may shine forth more vehemently by its manifold reflection. He wants them placed upside down so the voice enters better; he wants the vessels supported by wedges so that, exposed to freer air, they might resonate without hindrance, not unlike our bells, distant at least half a foot from the floor. He also leaves openings on the opposite side of the chambers two feet long and half a foot high, through which the voice might exit. Having noted these things, Vitruvius shows in what place and by what method the said vessels ought to be positioned. If the area at mid-height around the theater is divided into twelve equal parts by thirteen chambers, it is certain that two will be in the extreme corners, one in the middle, and five on each side from the middle to the ends. In the extremes, which he calls the "first," let the vessels be in unison with the highest note <note>original: "neten hyperbolæon"</note>, that is, the fifteenth or double octave, and therefore they maintain a quadruple proportion of equal size to the largest vessel.

The second vessels from the ends are a fourth away, reaching the "disjointed" high note <note>original: "neten diezeugmenon"</note>; that is, let them be in unison, and compared to the largest vessel, let them sound an octave plus a fifth, which is the twelfth, and let them be in a 3:1 <term>tripla</term> proportion to the said "lowest of the low" <note>original: "hypates hypaton"</note> vessel. The vessels disposed in the third place on each side shall be in unison, and resonating a fourth plus an octave compared to the largest vessel; hence, consequently, it is necessary that they be in a 8:3 <term>dupla sesquitertia</term> proportion to it, sounding the eleventh.

Furthermore, the vessels disposed in the fourth place on each side shall be in unison and resonate an octave compared to the largest vessel; hence, consequently, they must be in a 2:1 <term>dupla</term> proportion to the said middle vessel. I have found in this place a notable error which cannot stand with musical precepts: it says "a fourth to the conjunction note" <note>original: "diateſſaron ad neten ſynnemmenon"</note>, which can by no means subsist while preserving the harmony. Therefore, the word "fourth" <note>original: "diateſſaron"</note> must be struck out; for in this way the error will be perfectly amended, by whatever means it finally crept in. Moreover, the vessels disposed in the fifth place on each side shall be in unison, resonating a fifth to the largest vessel; hence in a 3:2 <term>sesquialtera</term> proportion...

It should be noted that in small theaters, according to the description of **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose "De Architectura" is the primary source for these acoustic jars</note>, the lowest row or level should be moved to the middle, with the chromatic and diatonic levels omitted. But in larger theaters, such as this one, the theater is to be divided according to its height into three levels by four arches, and then the lowest is to be assigned to harmony <note>meaning the Enharmonic genus</note>, the second, as stated, to the chromatic, and the third to the diatonic. How the vessels of the remaining chromatic and diatonic levels are to be arranged, Vitruvius shows in these words:

> *But if the size of the theater be larger, then the height should be divided into four parts, so that three horizontal tiers of cells are created: one for harmony, another for the chromatic, and the third for the diatonic. Starting from the bottom, let the first tier be placed according to the harmonic genus, just as was described for the smaller theater. In the middle tier, first, let vessels be placed in the extreme corners that have a sound matching the **chromatic hyperbolaion** <note>The highest tetrachord in the Greek scale</note>; in the second positions from these, a fourth to the **chromatic diezeugmenon**; in the third, a fourth to the **chromatic synnemeno**; in the fourth, a fourth to the **chromatic meson**; in the fifth, a fourth to the **chromatic hypaton**; in the sixth, a fourth to the **paramesen**, which has a commonality of consonance as a fifth to the chromatic hyperbolaion and a fourth to the chromatic meson. In the middle, nothing is to be placed, because no other quality of sound in the chromatic genus can have a symphonic consonance. In the highest division and tier of cells, let vessels be built in the first corners with a sound for the **diatonic hyperbolaion**; in the second, a fourth to the **diatonic diezeugmenon**; in the third, a fourth to the **diatonic synnemeno**; in the fourth, a fourth to the **diatonic meson**; in the fifth, a fourth to the **diatonic hypaton**; in the sixth, a fourth to the **proslambanomenon**; and in the middle, to the **mesen**, because it has the commonalities of symphonies as an octave to the proslambanomenon and a fifth to the diatonic hypaton.*

Now that I have laid out before the eyes of the curious reader a most accurate description of the theater—one which, as far as I know, has been attempted by no one until now—let us discuss the individual parts a little more precisely. Note that in Figure I of the Illustration <note>original: "Iconif." (Iconismus)</note>, we have left only nine cells open; in the highest level, we have represented the size, position, and shape of the Resonant Vessels in three open cells; in the second open level, we have shown the cavity and interior arrangement of the cells along with the wedges <note>original: "cuneis"</note> upon which the Resonant vessels were to be placed. In the third open level, we have shown only the interior arrangement of the cells; the remaining closed cells show the exterior appearance facing the theater. These must be dealt with individually in order.

### §. I.
### On the Cells.

There were thirteen cells arranged in order within the interior level, separated from one another in such a way that each had certain passages or channels on the sides, through which the voice, propagated into neighboring cells, would always receive greater and greater increase...

### Book IX. Sound-Reflecting Magic.

...so that it might take up the sound. The shape of the interior surface of the cells could be none other than circular, as this is most suitable for propagating and amplifying the voice, as we have described here. The size of the cells corresponded to the size of the theater; indeed, the cells were not visible, as they were hidden within the floorboards. However, they had an opening on the outside that was either rectangular or oval, two feet long and half a foot high, such as those we have illustrated in spaces CM and DP in the compartments 1, 2, 3, and the rest in order within specific cells. Through these openings, the voice of the actors, insinuating itself, was multiplied there by various reflections. Once multiplied and driven through various turns, the sound was finally communicated through the lateral passages (which we have depicted on the side in the open cells MLR) to the neighboring cells, and from each individual cell to the next in order. Thus, it was no wonder that such great resonance was produced in the theater. I specified "through lateral passages," because without these, the voice could by no means gain its vigor, but would instead be absorbed and suffocated within the cells without an exit.

### §. II.
## Concerning the Echæa or Bronze Vessels.

<margin>The form and figure of the Echæa.</margin>
The *Echæa*—so named from the Greek *ēchein*, meaning "to sound"—or bronze vessels, were placed into each individual cell in the following manner. In the middle of the floor of the cell, a wedge or fulcrum was erected, as cell ML indicates. This was inserted into the bottom of the vessel with great skill so that the vessel rested upon it quite freely, just as is often done with our bells; for vessels placed on sharp points resonate better, since there is no obstacle to impede the vibration of the bell. The shape of the vessels could be no other than that of our modern bells, from which they differed in no way. They could not be angular, because the corners would have hindered the sound; nor could they be spherical, as some authors claim. Such a shape would contradict the intent of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BC), the Roman architect whose works are the primary source for ancient acoustic jar theory.</note>, who expressly states that the vessels were open at the bottom and supported on wedges. Others believe they were shaped like mortars <note>A heavy bowl used for grinding; in the 17th century, these were often cast in bronze and had a bell-like resonance.</note>, a view I do not oppose, for a mortar is entirely similar to a bell, differing only in that a bell is somewhat more tapered. They had, therefore, a somewhat conical shape, like our bells and mortars. Experience over many centuries has taught that this shape produces the best resonance of all, a fact we have shown extensively in our treatise on bells.

### §. III.
## How the Echæa Vessels Sounded and by What Means They Were Stimulated.

<margin>An experiment on the sound of the Echæa.</margin>
There is a great controversy in this place regarding the stimulation of the vessels, as many cannot grasp how these harmonic vessels produced their sound. Some think the vessels had little hammers attached to wires or iron cords which, when pulled, struck the bells to make them sound, much like the mechanism in modern bell-organs; this is the opinion of Cesare Cesariano <note>An Italian architect (1475–1543) known for his 1521 commentary on Vitruvius.</note> in his commentaries. Others believe the vessels sounded solely by the impact and force of the air moved by the voice of the actors. However, this theory cannot hold up, since no voice is powerful enough to stimulate a heavy bell. This is evident with our own bells: if they could sound by the movement of air alone, they would produce a perpetual noise, as they are constantly exposed to the air and usually situated in high places where the wind is strong. Yet no experience has ever shown that even the most impetuous wind caused such a sound. Indeed, to test this, I had glass bells cast and carefully arranged them in concave spaces according to the Vitruvian method. I applied voices at every level of intensity, yet no distinct musical sound was perceived—only a ringing <note>original: "tinnitus"; refers here to a general metallic humming or echoing rather than the medical condition.</note> such as is felt in wells and concave places. Nevertheless, most scholars hold that those concave cells and vessels were used solely to provide a great resonance to the theater; a point I do not deny;

# Universal Musurgy

I deny [that this was the case]; for I do not see what such ingenious effort in proportioning the vessels according to harmonic consonances would contribute without them being physically struck. I am completely unable to discern to what end such a studious and subtle distribution of vessels—ordered according to the triple musical genre of diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic <note>These are the three "genera" of Greek music theory: the standard scale (diatonic), the scale using half-steps (chromatic), and the scale using quarter-tones (enharmonic).</note>—was arranged, since without an actual symphony <note>original: "symphonia actuali," meaning a sounding musical harmony.</note> all these things would have been useless and of no benefit. Either we must say they were instituted merely to amplify the voices of the actors, or they had some other use. However, it is not likely that the <term>Echæa</term> <note>From the Greek *ēcheia*, these were bronze sounding-vessels placed in theaters to improve acoustics.</note> were constructed with such great harmonic artifice solely for a greater resonance of the voice. Nor can it be said, as was proven just before, that they were stirred into harmonic symphony by the voice alone, or by the striking of the air made within them.

For this reason, Bonaventura Cavalieri <note>An Italian mathematician (1598–1647) known for his work on optics and geometry.</note> in his short work *On the Burning Mirror* <note>original: "de speculo Ustorio"</note>, thinks these Vitruvian cells, as well as the Echæa, were of a partly parabolic and partly hyperbolic figure. In these, the voice, having entered and been struck, was increased by a certain infinite multiplication of rays. To prove this, 

<margin>
How the 
Echæa vessels 
were stirred 
into harmony.
</margin>

he introduces a construction of this theater much different from the one we read described by Vitruvius. From the place of the voice all the way to the cells, he imagines parabolic arches, in which the voice—diffused as if from the center of parabolic arches and multiplied infinitely—produced a wonderful effect, both in the intensity of the voice and in the stirring of the Echæa. But since, as I have said, by this reasoning he imagines a new theater of which nothing similar is read in Vitruvius, he does not seem to have satisfied architects very much; for by abstracting from the text of Vitruvius, anyone could easily devise new Echæan structures.

It is asked, therefore, how these theaters had such great resonance, and how the vessels were disposed for such a brilliant effect as historians report? It should be noted, therefore, that a double harmonic sound can be considered in this kind of Echæa. The first was produced by a certain ringing or harmonic hum, while the external voices, entering the cells and being struck by various agitations, finally rendered that ringing which the trembling of the vessels exhibited by a multiplied sound and a certain force. The second could be established by little hammers <note>original: "malleolos"</note> pulled by cords and struck against the Echæa. 

The use of the former seems to have been so that the voice of the actors, received into those cavities and multiplied there, might acquire greater resonance, as has been said; and all commentators on Vitruvius agree with me on this. This was indeed nothing other than a certain symphonic ringing, caused by the trembling of the Echæa distributed in various harmonic proportions. 

The other use could have been in the preludes or interludes. For, in order to excite the listeners and sharpen their expectation of the things to follow, before the characters entered the theater, the Echæa were sounded. But they could not sound unless iron wires <note>original: "filis ferreis"</note> equipped with their own hammers were led through all the cells. Indeed, with this wire industriously drawn through all the cells, someone specially assigned to this task stirred all the vessels into a most perfect harmony. These vessels excited a vehement sound in the cells, perceptible far and wide, and of all the greater wonder because the "musurgical" machinery <note>The hidden acoustic engineering.</note> was hidden. And Vitruvius himself hints that this was the principal use with these words:

->*He stirred up an increased clarity and a harmony suited to the concord.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Excitauit auctam claritatem & concentu conuenientem ſibi conſonantiam."</note>

Therefore, there was a concord of vessels arranged according to musical consonances. But it was said above that a similar vehement concord cannot be made by the striking of the voice alone. Therefore, by the stated reasoning, they sounded when stirred into harmony by hidden cords, which Cesare Cesariano <note>The first translator of Vitruvius into a modern language (Italian, 1521).</note>, cited above, also suspected. And unless it happened by this reasoning, I do not see what other way there could have been by which they were stirred into consonance. For by this same artifice, according to Pliny, they exhibited thunders and other murmurs. 

The fact that Vitruvius says nothing openly about these cords and hammers happened because he himself never saw such a theater, but only received the account from the Greeks. Hence he frequently alleges Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist of the 4th century BCE.</note>—who likely stood as the author of this kind of theater—and follows his musical precepts while being himself doubtful. Nor was there any other theater of this kind in Greece or Rome besides that Corinthian one, from which we read that Pericles (according to the same Vitruvius) took the Echæa to be hung in the Temple of Fortune at Rome. <note>Kircher's memory or source here conflates Pericles with Lucius Mummius, who famously brought the bronze vessels from Corinth to Rome after the city's destruction in 146 BCE.</note> And certainly Vitruvius himself seems to have had some objection regarding the construction of this theater from the more skilled architects of his time, which he attempts to propose and solve at once with these words.

Having previously questioned the mechanical possibility of voice-activated resonance, Kircher now examines the ancient sources and historical claims regarding these acoustic devices, before transitioning to a famous contemporary example of architectural acoustics at the Villa Simonetta.</meta>

Book IX. Reflective Sound Magic

*Perhaps someone will say that many theaters were built in Rome every year, and no account of these things was found in them; but they erred in this, because all public wooden theaters have floorboards that resonate in harmony. This can even be observed by lute-players <note>original: "cytharædis," referring to performers on the kithara or ancient lute.</note>, who, when they wish to sing in a higher tone, turn themselves toward the doors of the stage, and thus receive the aid of the consonance of their voice from them. However, when theaters are constructed from solid materials—that is, from structures of cement, stone, and marble which cannot resonate—then these vessels must be deployed for this reason. But if it is asked in which theater in Rome these were made, we cannot show one, but rather in the regions of Italy and many cities of the Greeks. We also have the authority of Lucius Mummius, who, after the theater of the Corinthians was destroyed, brought its bronze vessels to Rome and dedicated them from the spoils at the Temple of the Moon. Many skillful architects, due to a lack of funds, chose earthenware jars that sounded in this way and, arranged by this reasoning, achieved very useful effects.*

And indeed, this invention of the theater so pleased Vitruvius that for its sake he set forth the foundations of the whole of "oceanic" music <note>Vitruvius used the metaphor of waves in a pond (oceanic) to explain how sound travels in concentric circles through the air.</note>, although he himself, being uncertain in many things, did not foresee the difficulties that would arise. For if he had possessed a perfect knowledge of musical science, he would never have used the <term>enharmonic genus</term> <note>A complex Greek musical scale using quarter-tones, which Kircher considers too delicate and impractical for large bronze vessels.</note> in describing the <term>Echæa</term> <note>Sounding vessels or acoustic jars.</note> of a smaller theater. This genus is useless for exhibiting harmony because of the sounds of various mixtures entering into the bronze vessels, as we have proved at length in Book 7; nor could it have happened that those bronze vessels were cast so exactly that they could distinctly exhibit <term>dieses</term> and <term>dieses</term> <note>A diesis is a tiny musical interval, specifically a quarter-tone in this context.</note> in the smallest intervals. He ought, therefore, to have more prudently applied the <term>diatonic genus</term> <note>The standard scale of whole and half steps, which is much more stable and resonant.</note> as most suitable for this task. For when he employs the <term>fourth</term> and <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron & diapente."</note> in the enharmonic genus, what else is he describing but the diatonic?

From this it is clear how many errors lie hidden even in the monuments of the greatest authors; if these were intimately discussed, unsightly spots would be detected even on the sun itself. From this I conclude it is likely that he presented the construction of such a theater to posterity simply copied from some manuscript of Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum was a Greek philosopher and a major authority on ancient music theory.</note>, since many things occur in the description of the three genera that cannot agree with musical rules.

But I hear some murmuring that the Greeks had many wonders whose logic has escaped posterity, and that the Vitruvian theater was one such thing, in which the <term>Echæa</term> were adapted with such industry and some incomprehensible art that they were excited by the voice alone. But since such a thing contradicts all experience, no wise man should debate it—unless perhaps they persuade us that some hidden intelligence stirred them at the sound of the voice, which would be ridiculous, not to say foolish, to assert. For it is characteristic of the admirers of such Greek things to invent dreams for themselves and to devise anything to establish their whims, even if discordant with reason and experience. However, I would not deny, as was also said above, that some symphonic ringing was perceived from the recitation of the actors <note>original: "comedorum."</note>, just as experience above has taught us; but it was by no means sufficient to achieve the end intended by the ancients. Some, noticing in the remains of the Roman Hippodrome <note>A stadium for horse and chariot racing.</note> that still survives certain earthenware vessels inserted into the bowels of the walls, have come to this opinion: that such vessels were arranged there for no other reason than to increase the resonance of the theater. But they are wandering in a great hallucination, since the said Hippodrome had neither the form of a theater nor—much less—required resonance due to the noise of running horses and tumultuous crowds. I say, therefore, that those earthenware vessels were inserted to lighten the weight of the walls, just as we see being done today in tufa vaults to relieve the weight. And these are the things that occurred to us to say about the Theater of Vitruvius; but let us now turn our pen to other matters.

->Universal Music-making<-

[they] possess, being so named. In this villa, Ferdinand Gonzaga, once Governor of Milan, erected a building famous not so much for its architectural symmetry as for its marvelous Echo. On the highest floor of this building, a certain window opens (as will be explained shortly), in which they say a spoken word is multiplied twenty-four times—and even more depending on the intensity of the voice and sound—indeed, almost infinitely. When I heard this from several trustworthy Fathers, a great desire seized me to investigate the cause of such manifold reflection. I therefore gave the task of drawing the entire structure and site as accurately as possible to Father Matthäus Storr, a priest of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits.</note>, a most trustworthy man, notable for his varied learning as well as his genuine integrity. He measured the structure of the entire building in detail and recently sent me the drawings, along with a perspective view and other circumstances concerning the Echo. So that it may be clear what the cause of such a portentous Echo is, let us first place the dimensions of the building, explained by its parts, before the reader's eyes.

The height of the entire building, as is clear from *Figure II, Plate XV*, has two floors separated by a walkway. The lower floor boasts peristyles <note>Rows of columns surrounding a courtyard.</note> built beneath the walkway. **K** is the area paved with stones. The upper floor contains three parts especially worthy of consideration; the first is the interior and principal part of the palace, **FLXM**; then there are two lateral and parallel buildings, **XMVN** and **GFHL**. Their dimensions are as follows: the width **FX** or **LM** is 62 Milanese paces and four inches; and so that we may proceed more exactly in this matter, we have seen fit to include in the figure a fourth part of a pace or a Milanese ell, indicated by the letters **XZ**. The height **FL** or **XM** is 16 paces and 4 inches. The length **MN** or **HL** is 33 paces and 3 inches. The width of the walkway **HL** is 8 paces and 6 inches. The window from which the Echo is provoked is the only one in the middle of the highest part of the wall **XVMN**, marked with the letters **RS**. Let these suffice as far as dimensions are concerned. Therefore, that window **RS** is the one and only place for hearing the Echo, for it does not resonate elsewhere. I have received testimony from many that a voice sent out from there is returned twenty-four times, even thirty times and more, depending on the greater or lesser effort of the voice. Indeed, I believe there is no fixed and determined number of reflections for the voice, but that it can be multiplied infinitely; the same thing happens as in the vibrations of a string, whose strokes appear clearly at the beginning, but at the end disappear due to extreme speed, and the sound gradually dies away. The same appears in the reflection of mirrors. The cause of this Echo is therefore asked? I answer that the cause is the positioning of two parallel buildings situated at a proportionate distance. Furthermore, since the said walls have the highest degree of uniformity and a flatness devoid of all roughness, the voice is reflected with the greatest ease. I demonstrate the matter thus.

Let the walls **AC** and **BD** in the figure placed here be parallel and perfectly flat, having a distance proportioned to returning a two-syllable word. I say that a voice sent from window **E** must necessarily be returned very many times; for the <term>phonism</term> <note>Kircher's term for a sound-path or the physical manifestation of a sound-wave.</note> according to Proposition 1 of <term>Echometria</term> <note>The science of measuring or calculating echoes.</note> is propagated from **E** to **I**, and returns from there by the same path to **E**; from **E** again to **I**, and from **I** once more to **E**, and so by infinite alternating repercussions until the voice, weakened by too much reflection, finally fails. This is no different than a ball which, being struck forcefully back and forth between two narrow walls, finally fails after five or six rebounds as its momentum ceases. And it is certain that there is no other cause for this thing than what we have said, because since according to Proposition 1 of Echometria the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, an Echo can be made by no other means except through that normal <note>In geometry, "normal" means perpendicular.</note> cylindrical phonism established between two parallel walls. For if other parts of the wall, for example **A** and **C**, were to reflect the voice, the angles at **A** and **C** would necessarily be right angles; but according to Book 1, Proposition 15 [of Euclid], they are acute, and they propagate the voice into other parts, for example through **K** and **N**. Therefore, from **I**, and from no other place, does such a manifold reflection of the voice occur; although...

A horizontal line labeled IE connects the two walls at their midpoints. Lines originate from point E and reflect off wall AC at point I, or extend diagonally to points A and C. Further lines extend from point I to external points K and N, illustrating the laws of acoustic reflection where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.</note>

And this is the reason why many wells and cisterns also produce such a significant reflection of the voice. Let **ABCD** be the well, and **DEB** the water; let the opening of the well's cover or the cistern be **I**, and the ceiling of the cistern be **CA**. I say that a voice introduced through **I** is returned many times for the reason that the <term>phonismus</term> <note>Kircher's term for a sound-wave or the physical impulse of sound.</note>, falling upon the very flat and calm surface of the water **EF**, is struck back from the same into the ceiling of the cistern, and then once more onto the surface of the water, and this happens so many times until it eventually fails, weakened. This matter requires no further demonstration, as it is self-evident. Thus, the cause of such a manifold Echo in the Villa Simonetta is clear.

## Corollary I.

From these facts it is established that if someone were to construct a similar structure—that is, two walls separated by a distance of about 63 paces—he would have a similar Echo, since nothing else is required for the voice to be returned distinctly except for a proportionate distance, which 63 paces will provide. If someone were to make a cistern or well just as many paces deep, he would find a similar Echo there too.

## Corollary II.

It is therefore clear that neither the substructures, nor the courtyard, nor the intermediate palace equipped with many windows, nor the walkways cause this prodigious Echo; rather, as I said, it is the parallel placement of very flat walls unobstructed by any roughness. Nor must a window necessarily be situated at the position marked **RS**. For if it were made in another part of the wall, it is certain that you would have the same Echo, and perhaps a window at the midpoint **I** of the wall would achieve a much greater effect; but let us leave these things to be considered by architects. These are the few points we wished to describe regarding the Echo of the Villa Simonetta.

# Prelude III.
## Concerning the Ear of Dionysius, still surviving in Syracuse.

A most famous structure is still on display today in Syracuse, Sicily, which some call the Prison of the Tyrant Dionysius, others the Little Ear, and others by various names. It was architected with such ingenuity that someone standing opposite the entrance hears whatever was spoken returned perfectly and with multiplied sound. Having heard much about this, partly from authors and partly from the reports of others, I undertook an investigation of it in the year 1638 when I passed through Syracuse, and finally uncovered its causes. Mirabella <note>Vincenzo Mirabella (1570–1624), a Sicilian archaeologist and author of "The Ancient Syracuse."</note> describes this with singular care in his *Ichnography of Syracuse*. The structure is as follows: the location is outside the walls of the city of Syracuse, commonly called Dionysius's Prison. Anyone who carefully considers the artifice and industry with which it was architected by the Tyrant will see that the cause of this structure was none other than that the captives held within could not even breathe without being heard by the prison guard. It was constructed by the Tyrant in the shape of an ear, following the model of nature, with singular ingenuity and industry.

It is carved out of the living rock, which, ending in a narrow channel through a spiral path, was directed into the guard's chamber placed above the cavern. Thus it happened that every sound, even the slightest...

# Universal Musurgy

<margin>The wonderful Echo of Syracuse.</margin>
...any noise or whispering entering the spiral work was diverted into the chamber of the guard, where anything uttered softly was perceived as if the speakers were present. Today, with the channel in the wall blocked, the whispered voices transform into a most beautiful and miraculous Echo; hence it is commonly called *la grotta della favella* <note>Italian: "the cave of speech."</note>. It does not return the voices in the same way as other echoes, but rather elevates a soft voice into a shout; the sound of clearing one's throat sounds like thunder, and the striking of a cloak with a flat hand might seem like the explosion of a cannon. Indeed, it does not merely intensify the voice but repeats it several times. Because of this, a musical canon sung here by two people soon turns into a four-voice harmony, as the reflected voice of the first beautifully catches up with the voice of the second—a thing truly most worthy of hearing.

This truly wonderful architecture has taught me much concerning the engineering of hidden sounds and deeper knowledge exceeding all understanding. Since I have explained these things in the preceding pages, I did not wish to be tedious in recounting them again here. However, lest we seem to have hidden anything from the curious Reader, I have decided to include a figure of this structure here, so that from the diagram itself one may deduce the cause of the miraculous sound. Our Jesuit Fathers in Syracuse sent this <term>ichnography</term> <note>From the Greek *ichnos* (track/footprint) and *graphē* (writing); a ground plan or floor plan of a building.</note> to Rome, having recorded it from the cliff with the greatest care. An eyewitness, Jacobus Masò, a student of Theology in our Society and highly skilled in the Mathematical sciences, also contributed greatly to this drawing.

To this I shall subjoin another marvelous building, still standing in Pavia, constructed with such artistry that a person standing in the doorway perceives an echo that is miraculously prodigious. For it seems to respond thirty times to one who questions it; it does so with such distinctness and such exact pronunciation of every syllable that many have simply persuaded themselves it is not a work of nature, but an illusion of a demon bound to that place. Among these people was Girolamo Cardano <note>Hieronymus Cardanus (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath, physician, and mathematician.</note>, which is indeed surprising in a man so ingenious and by no means unacquainted with the secrets of nature. But let us hear the words of the said Cardano, who describes it in his book *On Subtlety* in these words:

<margin>The Echo of Pavia.</margin>
Girolamo Cardano of Milan, in his books *On Subtlety*, Book 18, *On Wonders*, printed in Nuremberg, says this at the end of the book:

> *The third kind of watch is pure and sincere, in which one may see wonders in many ways: as when an Echo resounds, then especially it is multiple; it happens that sometimes it returns voices seven times. At night this is marvelous in a wonderful way, and unless the thing were common knowledge, it could terrify anyone, so clearly and sometimes slowly does it return the voices. The cause is the air, which is struck back by flat surfaces and hollows; for nothing resounds except caves or walls, and they resound more from old buildings, and more from a distance than from nearby. It is necessary for the voice in an Echo to be sent out and returned by an intermediate flat surface. It is very often multiple: we ourselves have heard a triple one.*

And the ancients did not only know examples of a multiple voice or one returned seven times. Truly in Pavia (formerly called *Ticinum*), there is a great hall—the Italians call it the *Salàm* <note>Italian: *Sala*, meaning a large hall or room.</note>—which, near the city citadel, sends back voices from the doorway so many times that you cannot count them; sometimes a thirteenth voice is heard. Many witnesses were present, and among others, that distinguished professor of the medical arts, Melchior Malheuser the German, our pupil. *You would have believed someone was answering or mocking you. The voices die away gradually and cease. From this, in a wonderful way, "Ahime"* <note>Italian: "Alas" or "Woe is me."</note> *—which in Latin sounds like "heu"—is returned like the voice of someone dying and failing. This building is square, and is illuminated by several open windows on the upper sides. Otherwise, the front and the wall placed opposite are solid, except that there is a door in the front. The length is about a hundred feet, the width nearly twenty-five. The voice also resounds and is multiple if you stand near the other wall opposite the door. And it seems then to be returned from the high part of the door. Thus, the voice resounds for those standing on either side, and especially outside the door itself, but not at all in the middle. From this, no one can doubt it is either a Demon or a trick. For it can scarcely be believed to be an Echo, so clearly, so easily, so often, and in such a certain order are all the voices heard. The height, I believe, is half again as much as the width; for this hall is lofty. I have chosen to describe it thus so that men may know where it is convenient to experience such things, or if it pleases them to reconstruct another example. I learned from those standing by that formerly, in front of the door, there was a vaulted porch placed in that region, of which a large part still remains. They said the accustomed voices were returned much better to those standing outside the door under the vault, and much more richly and with a greater "interest" (as it were), so that they sometimes resounded thirty times. It is certain that the more quickly the voice is brought forth, and with a louder and more excited tone, the more clearly and frequently it is returned.*

But since not long ago Salvator Scarduccius, a Priest of our Society and a man by no means unskilled in music, gave me a complete account both of the quality of this Echo and the construction of the building, I thought the description he sent should be opportunely inserted in this place. In this way, the reasoning behind such a famous and celebrated Echo might become more deeply known to the curious Reader. The matter stands thus: The building is in the city of Ticino, commonly called Pavia, in the highest part of the city near...
