...the castle or Ducal Palace, commonly called the *Salone* <note>original: "Salone," Italian for a large hall.</note> or the Arsenal, once served for public games but now is a storehouse for military equipment. Its shape is quadrangular; its height is 35 Roman cubits <note>original: "brachiorum Romanorum." A "brachium" or arm's length was a common unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to a cubit or 2-3 feet depending on local standards.</note> up to the ceiling; its length is 124 Roman cubits; and its width is 24. It has two doors: one in the front facing North, 6 Roman cubits high and 4 wide (formerly 5). In the part opposite the front, namely the South, three windows are seen, of which the middle one is larger than the lateral ones; below these, a door opens of the same size as the northern door, through which access is made to the portico indicated by Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who studied acoustics.</note>; it now serves as a workshop. We have briefly explained the description of the entire structure as far as it pertains to our purpose, so nothing remains but to explain the reason for such a manifold Echo.

<margin>The cause of the Pavia Echo explained.</margin>
With the north and south doors open—the latter being about 30 paces from the city walls—the Echo responds eleven times; with the southern door closed, eight times; and with both closed, only six times, to someone standing in the middle. The reason for this can be none other than the obstacles of the walls outside the doors, which reflect the "sound-species" <note>Kircher uses the term "species" to describe the physical form or image of a sound wave as it travels through the air.</note> eleven times when the doors are open, in proportion to the calculated distance. When the doors are closed, however, because the distance is shorter, it is necessary that there be fewer reflections. It has been observed, however, that this Echo has its greatest power in reflecting disyllables <note>words with two syllables.</note>, just as was said of the Milanese Echo. The natural voice is most suitable for forming an Echo in this place; but an artificial sound produced by a trumpet or drum confuses the Echo because of the violence of the sound. (We have shown the reason for this at length in preceding sections.) It is written, however, that if a trumpet or the pipe commonly called a <term>cornetto</term> <note>A Renaissance wind instrument with a mouthpiece like a trumpet but finger holes like a recorder.</note> sounds these intervals: *ut, mi, sol* <note>The musical notes C, E, and G.</note> in monosyllables, the Echo forms a certain harmony in the manner of an eleven-voice <term>fugue</term> <note>A musical composition where a short melody is introduced by one part and successively taken up by others.</note>, a thing wonderful to hear. Furthermore, this Echo has different properties depending on the various positions of those shouting. For it appears differently to those positioned in the middle from those shouting at the front or side, and differently again to those at the gates from those shouting in the middle; the reason for this is nothing else but the position of the opposite walls, in which, through either intentional or accidental distance, the reflected species of sounds, being repeatedly struck back, present various deceptions to the ears. No one will be unable to know the cause of all these things except he who has either not read our preceding reasoning on <term>polyphonisms</term> <note>Kircher’s technical term for the study of multiple echoes or complex sound reflections.</note>, or if he has read them, has not understood. The reason why today it does not produce those miracles of the reflected voice as it once did in the time of Cardano and Biancani <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who wrote on acoustics.</note> is that this place is now filled with various military apparatuses, which hinder the manifold reflection of the voice. And a clear proof of this is that from the western side, where obstacles of this kind are seen placed, the Echo is not perceived by those standing there, the species being scattered and absorbed. These are the things I thought should be said about this famous Echo of the city of Pavia.

# PRACTICE I.

## To arrange the Halls of Princes in such a way that nothing can be said so softly that it is not heard, either in the same room or in another.

<margin>Channels have a wonderful power for gathering voices.</margin>
Some have thought this could be done through a hidden duct of channels, such as Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615) was an Italian polymath who wrote extensively on "natural magic," including acoustics and optics.</note> suggests; namely, that when channels are led from different rooms into a single location, the Prince, by applying his ears to the opening where all the channels meet, will perceive the voices from the various rooms. If this is understood to mean that any soft words spoken in the chambers fly through the channels and present themselves to the Prince's ears, it is false; for voices uttered in a room are by no means gathered at the opening of a channel, but being variously dispersed and absorbed in the open air, they expire, already weakened, before they reach the channel. But if the mouth is applied directly to the channel and the voices are whispered into it, there is no doubt that the Prince will distinctly perceive those whispered words from each room. For not only have I heard a voice over 500 feet away in a lead pipe of great length, but others have heard it with me in an earthen pipe.
<margin>A channel of 500 feet conveys voices.</margin>
However, the tube must not be too wide, nor too narrow; the true width or diameter of tubes for transmitting voices ought to be three inches <note>original: "trium pollicum." The "pollex" or thumb-width was roughly equivalent to an inch.</note>. For drums and trumpets, the channels can be made somewhat larger.
<margin>Why tubes set in a wall return the voice better than those exposed to the open air.</margin>
These tubes convey the voice better when built into a wall than when they are exposed to the open air. The reason for this is nothing else than that, being encased in the wall, they do not permit such a noticeable vibration as they would if they were free; vibration greatly hinders the conveyance of voices, as it easily confuses them with its own shaking.
<margin>The opposite happens in a solid beam.</margin>
The complete opposite is found in beams and other solid, long bodies, which lose all the power of a whispered voice [when encased in a wall]; however, they acquire a greater power for conveying the voice the more they are exposed to a free medium, as was demonstrated above. For since the vibration of the whole object delivers the noise excited at one end to the other end, if a beam is buried in the earth or encased in a wall, it loses its freedom to vibrate, and it must necessarily lose its ability to propagate the voice along with it.

<margin>The Author's experiment regarding subterranean channels.</margin>
And although this matter regarding channels is very simple, it must not be denied that many truly paradoxical things can be achieved by the help of such secretly directed channels, if the craftsman and wise <term>Echotechnus</term> <note>Kircher's term for a specialist in acoustic engineering, literally an "echo-technician."</note> uses the required skill. A certain chemist's subterranean workshop taught me the truth of this matter; it was built without any hole or window, using only a single channel to draw off smoke and equipped with a very small door. When the door was closed, any voices spoken inside were perfectly presented at the far opening of the channel, to great wonder. Made wiser by this experiment, I am thoroughly persuaded that something similar can undoubtedly be put into effect in the palaces of Princes. This is how the <term>Echotectus</term> <note>Another of Kircher's invented terms, an "echo-architect."</note> should arrange the matter:

<margin>How the acoustic channel ought to be directed.</margin>
Let a chamber be made capable of holding a few people, 8 palms <note>The "palmus" or palm was a common unit of measurement; the Roman architectural palm was about 8.8 inches or 22.3 cm.</note> long, as shown in the following figure, and just as many wide and high. In the figure, the width RX is 8 palms, and the height DV is the same. It should have a very small and low door A, which can be closed very tightly. A window of very thick crystal should also be inserted into the side, set into the wall in such a way that, when voices resonate inside, the sound cannot escape through the window or the door, but only through the channel DE. This channel, led through a hidden passage of the house into room F, you will connect with the dome <note>original: "tholo," a circular or domed ceiling structure.</note> of Chamber D (which, according to the proposed model, ought to be very polished, like a twisted cone) so that it appears as one continuous surface. At the other end, let the channel have a flared opening at E, so that the sound coming out can spread itself freely, and you will have a completed structure. For if anyone enters Chamber AD with the door and window closed and makes any sounds, since the sound of those voices cannot escape elsewhere, through...

# Practice III.

## How to arrange halls designed with parabolic surfaces so that an ear placed at a certain point perceives whatever is spoken softly.

Although the nature and properties of the parabola have been discussed at length above, lest you commit some error in practice, I thought certain difficulties should be addressed here first. It must be understood, therefore, that a parabolic surface can be considered in two ways: obtuse and acute. The more obtuse <note>wide or flattened</note> the concave surface is, the closer it will have its focus, or acoustic point, to the vertex <note>the center point of the curve</note> of the parabola. Conversely, the more acute <note>narrow or sharp</note> the same surface is, the farther the acoustic point will be from the vertex of the parabola. This point, where the rays converge, is always located on the axis of the parabola.

<margin>It is necessary for lines converging to a single point within a parabola to be parallel.</margin>
Second, it must be known that for all sound-lines <term>lineae sonorae: the paths along which sound travels, treated here like rays of light</term> to flow together into the acoustic point, it is necessary that the sound-lines falling upon the interior concave parabolic surface be parallel to the axis. Hence, if the parabola is sufficiently wide, even the smallest "species" <note>original: "species" — the intelligible forms or waves of the voice</note> of the voice will all flow together into a single point. But let us demonstrate the matter a little more clearly: let ABC be the parabola and D the focus. I say that the voice's forms will not radiate into point D unless they are all carried parallel to the axis BDE. For suppose the voice radiates from E to O and I (for we showed above that the voice is propagated through conical sound-forms <term>phonismos conicos: the cone-shaped expansion of sound waves from a source</term>). It is certain, according to the rules of reflection handed down above, that lines falling from E onto O and I will reflect not into D, but into X; for in this case, the angle of incidence will equal the angle of reflection. Again, if a voice placed outside the axis radiates into the concave surface, it is indeed true that only one single ray will be reflected into D; the other radiations, however, will establish different centers of reflection outside the axis, as is clear from the sound-line falling from G to V, and from there reflected into D. But the lines radiating from G to R and Z will converge neither in D nor in X, but in P.

<note>A geometric diagram of a parabola labeled ABC with its central axis BDE. Various points (E, G) represent origins of sound waves, and lines demonstrate their reflection off the interior surface of the parabola toward specific focal points (D, X, P). A large circle is drawn near the opening of the parabola, representing the base of a cone of sound (phonismus conicus) used in the acoustic demonstration.</note>

<margin>A conical sound-form in a parabola acquires different centers or reflections on the axis.</margin>
You see, therefore, that a voice radiating conically within a parabola achieves nothing remarkable unless it is positioned on the axis; for then, the lines of only one conical sound-form will converge into a single point. Let ABC be the conical sound-form in the following figure, BDC the parabola, and let the sound source be on the axis of the parabola AD. I say that the lines of the conical sound-form ABC falling on the concave surface of the parabola will reflect into D. For since all the lines establish a circle on the concave surface of the parabola, which is the same as the base of the cone, it is certain that all will reflect at equal angles into a certain and determined point of the axis. Since, however, this cone is not of one type only,

But if the sound-flow <note>original: "phonismus" — Kircher's term for the propagation or flow of sound waves, modeled on the behavior of light.</note> is not conical, but cylindrical, then I assert that all sound lines parallel to the axis will converge at one single point; you may see the demonstration of this matter in my work *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte Magna Lucis & Vmbrę" — Kircher's 1646 treatise on optics and light.</note>.

<note>A small geometric diagram in the upper right margin shows a parabola labeled ABC with an axis BE and a focal point D. Lines parallel to the axis are shown entering the parabola and reflecting off the inner surface to converge at the focal point D.</note>

With these things properly arranged; if it is your intention to construct a similar device in some palace, you may conveniently install it in a long hallway in this manner: at each end, using a parabola-shaping tool <term>paraboloplastę: a specialized template or instrument used by builders to ensure a perfect parabolic curve</term>, a parabolic surface should be described so that if the axis were extended, it would pass through the center of both parabolas.

Let there be a parabola at each end of the hallway; the first ABC, the second GEF. Let the common axis for both be E.B. and let the focal points of each parabola be H and I. Let the source of the sound be at point O in the middle of the axis EB. If it radiates with a conical sound-flow, it will indeed have an effect, but not as intense as the parabola promises for the reasons mentioned just before; but if the sound-flow were cylindrical from POR—

<note>A large horizontal diagram depicts a long architectural hall with parabolic reflectors at each end (marked GEF and ABC). A central axis line runs through the room. Sound produced in the center (near points P, X, O, Y, Z, R) travels in parallel lines to the parabolic ends, where it reflects and concentrates at the focal points H and I. This illustrates how someone standing at the ends can hear whispers from the middle, and vice versa.</note>

<margin>The wonderful power of the parabola in transmitting voices.</margin>
—and propagated toward either end, an ear placed at either focal point H or I will find what it desired; for all the sound lines, however softly the voice is imbued, will nevertheless reflect into H or I, where they will increase the sound in a marvelous way. Therefore, whatever was whispered in the middle at POR will be understood at H or I. This device will be all the more hidden the more obtuse <note>flatter or wider</note> the parabolas are; for from this it happens that the focal points are positioned far outside the concavity of the parabolas. Indeed, listeners will wonder how they perceive such clear voices at that specific point in the middle of the air, when nevertheless neither an arch nor any other surface appears within the hallway which could be the cause of such a prodigious sound. Furthermore, if six different people were standing at points P, X, O, Y, Z, and R, they could communicate different things to the person standing at H or I; and those nearby would not even notice what was shared in such a low whisper. Moreover, the person standing at the focal point H of the parabola, by whispering against the parabola, will reveal whatever he wishes to those standing at P, X, O, Y, Z, and R. But if he wishes to speak to only one of the six—for example, the one standing at P—he would accomplish it through a tube directed at point G of the parabola; for the voice falling on G will necessarily present itself to the ears of the one positioned at P, since a ray, by that nature with which it falls, is necessarily reflected.

->Another method.<-

Mersenne, in his *Universal Harmony* <note>original: "harmonia vniuersali" — refers to Marin Mersenne’s 1636 work *Harmonie universelle*, a foundational text in music theory and acoustics.</note>, provides another method which I shall add here so that it may be judged for what it is worth. For since he saw that cylindrical sound-flow <term>phonismum: the propagation or movement of sound waves</term> was difficult to achieve, and the conical was not sufficient, he hoped he could achieve something better by doubling the parabola. He turned a smaller concave parabola toward a larger one, so that they shared a common focal point. In this way, the sound-flow falling into the larger concave surface would be reflected through the focus into the smaller concave surface, and from there finally propagated in a parallel flow outside the surface of the larger parabola (which must be cut away according to the size of the smaller parabola) to the ears of someone standing behind it.

<margin>Another method for increasing parabolic sound-reflection.</margin>

<note>A geometric diagram shows a large parabolic arc ABC with a smaller parabola E inside it. An axis line passes through the center. From two source points X and Y at the bottom, sound rays extend upwards to hit the inner surface of the large parabola. These rays reflect toward a common focal point G, but are intercepted by the small parabola E. From there, the rays are reflected straight down in parallel vertical lines, terminating at points H, I, L, and M where the listener's ears would be.</note>

Let the larger parabola be ABC and the smaller DEF, applied to one another in such a way that the focus G is common to both. Let the larger parabola be cut away from V to P. Once this is done, let the sources of sounds be at X and Y. The sound lines XT, XV, YP, and YQ, falling upon the concave surface of the larger parabola, will be reflected from there through G toward S and R; but XT and XV, falling upon N and O, will be reflected again from there into LM and HI, until they finally present themselves as a cylindrical sound-flow to the ears placed at HILM. Certainly, these things have a beautiful appearance of theory at first glance, but in practice they achieve no success at all. For besides the very few lines that the larger parabola is capable of catching, the smaller one also transmits very few, and those are significantly weakened by that parallelism; thus, I would dare to say that the method we described previously is a hundred times better than this one. Indeed, Mersenne himself, foreseeing the difficulty of the matter, abandoned it as if it were a lost cause and fled to another, which is nonetheless not much better. For it is clearly evident that no success can come from this mechanism, both for the reasons stated and because of the focus; since it is common to both parabolas, it would require a precision more than Archimedean <note>original: "industria plusquam Archimedea" — a reference to the legendary mechanical precision and ingenuity of Archimedes.</note> to arrange both exactly. Let the larger parabola be ABC, and let the smaller one D be placed opposite it as appears in the figure, having a convex parabolic surface and a common focus at E.

<margin>Many things proven in theory can only be reduced to practice with difficulty.</margin>

<note>A second geometric diagram illustrates a different parabolic arrangement. A large parabola ABC has two sound sources F and G at its base. Rays from these sources hit the inner surface of the large parabola. These rays reflect toward a central focus E but are intercepted by a small convex parabolic surface D. Upon hitting D, the rays reflect back down as parallel vertical lines to points I and R.</note>

With the machine arranged in this way, the sound lines from G and F falling onto the concave surface of the larger parabola reflect from points *onxh*, not into the focus E, but onto the convex surface of the smaller parabola D. Finally, they will reverberate the captured sound in a cylindrical flow to the ears of the listener at I and R. But who does not see that this too contains nothing within it besides mere speculation?

<header>Universal Music-making</header>

For a smaller parabola, besides the fact that it aligns with the focus of a larger one only with difficulty, it also reflects so few and such weak reflections onto the convex surface of the smaller one that I think someone placed at IR <note>referring to a point in the diagram on the previous page</note> could hardly acquire any singular increase in voice. Even if this significant increase in voice were granted—though I do not concede it <note>original: "dato tamen non concesso" — a rhetorical device used in logic to argue that even if an opponent's premise were true, the conclusion would still fail</note>—I still believe this device would be so difficult in practice that it could hardly achieve any success. For there are many things which are most beautiful according to theory, yet can almost never be put into work. To ensure that the same could not be said of our own inventions and acoustic structures in this place, we have taken singular care not to propose anything that has not first been proven by experiment. Therefore, whoever intends to build an acoustic structure using parabolas should proceed by no other method than the one we have described, and they will achieve an infallible effect. For it is not necessary for the parabolic surfaces in this business of echo-building <term>echotectonico: Kircher’s term for the architectural science of controlling and directing sound</term> to be as mathematically exact as is required for burning mirrors <note>original: "speculis causticis" — mirrors designed to focus sunlight into a point of intense heat to start fires</note>. A shape elaborated with as much diligence as possible with the help of a parabolic mold <term>paraboloplastæ: a physical template or "form-maker" used by masons to ensure a wall follows a perfect parabolic curve</term> will suffice. For since sound lines have their own width—and quite a notable one at that—only someone who has failed to understand the preceding points could be ignorant of the fact that the acoustic center of a parabola is not a mathematical point, but a physical one, endowed with its own breadth.

## Practical Exercise IV.

->Constructing a hyperbolic structure to gather sounds.<-

<margin>The principle of the hyperbolic structure.</margin>
Whatever we have said concerning the parabola must also be applied to hyperbolic surfaces, so that nothing further remains to be said about forming surfaces of this kind. If someone possesses a hyperbolic mold <term>hyperboloplasten: a template for shaping a hyperbolic curve</term> suitable for the size of the location, they may describe two hyperbolic surfaces along with their acoustic centers in some walkway. There, an ear placed at the center will perceive voices, however softly uttered, just as in the parabolic structures. Let us therefore hasten to other matters.

## Practical Exercise V.

->To construct elliptical structures that intensify sounds wonderfully.<-

Compared to other conic sections, the ellipse is the most suitable of all for this business of echo-building. For this reason, we have decided to treat elliptical structures more extensively here. What an ellipse is and how it is drawn has been stated above; let us therefore proceed to the instruction. The elliptical vaults <note>original: "tholi" — domes or vaulted ceilings</note> of these structures have this unique property: they always produce two points or centers in the open space. First, let there be an elliptical mold <term>Ellipticoplastes: a tool used for forming an elliptical curve in plaster or stone</term> of a length equal to the oval length of the vault.

Points A and B indicate the vertices of the major axis of the ellipse, where the curvature is shaped.</note>

Let the vault AHB, then, be made of plaster. To this, at the poles A and B, you should apply the elliptical mold; and let the acoustic centers be C and D, which should be marked most diligently. Once the mold has been rotated...

...[with the aid of] the ellipse-shaper <term>ellipsioplastæ: a tool designed by Kircher to trace or carve a perfect ellipse in wet plaster</term> within the plaster using a semicircular motion for as long as needed, until the form has left a perfect elliptical surface inside the vault. Since the voice from D, however it strikes the elliptical vault, is always reflected to C, and since there infinite sound-images <note>original: "species soni" — in the physics of the time, these were the "auditory forms" or representations of sound that traveled through the air to the ear</note> reach it at one and the same moment of time, there the intensified images will present themselves perfectly to the ears.

Note, however, that the surface should be as polished as possible, and to make it more like a mirror, it ought to be soaked in water mixed with glue or even gum arabic; for by this, all cracks and minute roughnesses will be removed, and the voice will reflect better.

## Practical Application VI.

->To construct an acoustic ellipse in some palace in such a way that two Princes, situated in separate chambers, can converse about any matter as if they were present together.<-

**T**his is an invention of the greatest utility in the mutual communication of counsel. Indeed, it is of the highest interest to confer in secret counsel, removed from all human knowledge, lest the plans become known before their time through the snares of spies; it seems that those secret staircases and entrances to the chambers of Princes were ordered for no other end than that they might meet to communicate their counsels on matters of great importance more secretly and thus more securely.

How we may therefore architect something similar through the art of Echo-building <term>Echotectonica: Kircher's term for the architectural science of controlling and directing sound</term> is now to be seen; so that two Princes in different chambers might safely and securely communicate their plans to one another, the structure must be built by this art. Let a space of 100 feet, or even more (it makes no difference), be taken between two chambers and enclosed by two walls. Within this space, you shall form an acoustic ellipse, constructed by this artifice so that the two foci of the ellipse terminate in little windows <note>original: "fenestrellis"</note> in each chamber, arranged for this purpose. You will then have what you sought, but a visual demonstration will make the matter clearer.

Let there be two chambers D and E, and let the space lying between them and enclosed by walls be DE. Within this space, by the help of the ellipse-shaper form, you shall describe a concave elliptical vault

## Practical Application VII.

->To construct the same structure by another method with much greater skill, and to extend it across a larger space.<-

But if anyone should wish to architect a similar work of art for a very remote distance, he shall begin the task in this way: within the two walls determining the chosen space, let 4, 5, 6, or 7 elliptical "eggs" <note>Kircher uses the term "ova" (eggs) to describe the shape of the elliptical vaults.</note> be formed in exactly the same manner as you see done in the preceding figure. However, the ellipses must be so constructed that each is truncated along the lines applied in order passing through the focal points, as is clearly evident in the following figure.

<note>A technical diagram illustrates the principles of acoustic reflection within a series of four connected elliptical vaults. Two parallel walls, labeled FG at the top and HI at the bottom, bound the structure. Inside, four elliptical segments (AB, BC, CD, DE) are arranged linearly. A series of lines radiate from point A (where a human head is illustrated), reflecting off the surfaces of the ellipses and converging at focal points B, C, and D before reaching the final point E (where another head is shown). Vertical lines marked V (top) and X (bottom) indicate where the ellipses are cut or joined at their focal points.</note>

<margin>A remarkable elliptical architecture for broadcasting voices.</margin>

In this figure, within the walls FG and HI, let four elliptical vaults be arranged so that the acoustic centers or focal points are common to each pair of ellipses. Thus, the acoustic center B of ellipse AB is also the center for ellipse BC, and the acoustic center C of ellipse BC is common to ellipse CD; and the acoustic center D of ellipse CD is common to ellipse DE. Therefore, the ellipses should be truncated <note>cut off or opened</note> according to the lines VX passing through the centers, so that the individual ellipses appear like hollowed-out casks. By this, you will have a remarkable secret prepared. 

For if someone situated at A whispers even the lowest voice, another person as far as five hundred feet away at E will perceive it as clearly as if it were whispered directly into their ears. This happens because all the sound lines reflected in the elliptical vault AB will converge at B as a center; there, multiplied and intensified without confusion, each line progresses further to form another reflection in the second elliptical vault at C. In this center, once again united and multiplied, they will enter the elliptical vault CD, and being reflected there, they will join at D. From here, finally, reflected again in the fourth vault, they will at last arrive, intensified and multiplied, at the ears of the person situated at E, who will perceive the sound-images <note>original: "sonoras species" — the physical forms or "shades" of sound that Kircher believed traveled through the air.</note> as clearly as if he were present at A. The demonstration of this matter is so clear that nothing seems to be required for its understanding beyond a careful consideration of the figure.

## Corollary.

From what has been said, it is clear how many miracles of echo-architecture <term>Echotectonica: a term coined by Kircher for the architectural science of controlling and reflecting sound.</term> can be performed by this single proposed application. Indeed, with the help of this machine, you will be able to exhibit musical concerts of every kind, with no one even suspecting where the sound originates. But let these things suffice for the ingenious reader to discover innumerable other inventions.

### Practical Application VIII.

> How to arrange a twisted spiral cone, or a snail-shell tube, within some structure so that it conveys any articulated sounds from a public place, however distant, into an inner chamber so surely and distinctly as if they were right at the ears, with no one suspecting where they might come from. See Illustration XVI.

<margin>A marvelous acoustic structure using a snail-shell tube.</margin>
We have rightly reserved for last the most perfect and most admirable of all <term>Echotectonic</term> <note>From the Greek 'echo' and 'tekton' (builder), referring to the art of building structures for acoustic effects.</note> devices. I know not what could be achieved in natural magic more wonderful than this. But, lest I keep the curious reader in suspense any longer, I shall explain the matter in few words. Let a snail-shell tube, or a spirally twisted cone, be carved into natural stone or a cliff; or, if the location does not allow for that, let it be formed from plaster, clay, or <term>tufa</term> <note>A porous volcanic rock commonly used in Italian architecture.</note>. Let it be engineered so that it has a very wide opening extending outward toward some public place frequented by a multitude of people. Let the other end of the tube terminate in a small hole within an inner chamber, removed from the crowds. The interior spiral surface should be polished as exactly as possible in the stone material, or if the stone is too rough, the inner surface should be coated with plaster for a smoother polish.

With this device completed, I say that nothing can be spoken so secretly in the opposite forum, square, or public place—which the mouth of the snail-shell tube faces—that it is not carried through the spiral into that hidden chamber. In this room, therefore, you will perceive the various voices of animals, the secret whispers of men, singing, weeping, and wailing as distinctly and clearly as if they were happening in the chamber itself, with no one even suspecting from where such a prodigious effect of sounds proceeds. Observe the structure in the following Illustration XVI <note>original: iconismo XVI</note>, where the palace is represented by the letters ABCD; the snail-shell tube inserted into the wall or cut into the rock is G; its opening is H; its terminus is E; the forum is L. In that forum, nothing can be uttered so secretly that it is not perceived within the chamber, however far away it may be.

And this is a device that far surpasses not only parabolic but also elliptical acoustic structures, and all others proposed thus far, since it is constructed according to the pattern of nature observed in the anatomy of the ears <note>The author is likely referring to the cochlea, the spiral-shaped part of the inner ear.</note>, and it abounds with infinite reflections of voices (as we showed in problem 8, from which the voice is wonderfully intensified). Moreover, a tube of this kind can be positioned in two ways: either horizontally or sloping as at G, or vertically as at PO. Both produce remarkable effects, though the vertical is more powerful, because sound is carried more easily upward than downward or sideways. We have represented both paths of the tube here in the illustration. We discovered this admirable device on the occasion of the "Ear of Dionysius" <note>The 'Ear of Dionysius' is a famous limestone cave in Syracuse, Sicily, legendary for its acoustics; it was said the tyrant Dionysius I used it to eavesdrop on his prisoners.</note> which still survives in Syracuse; see its description in the history of echoes provided a little earlier.

### Digression on the Snail-Shell Cone.

Truly, why such a great power of sound multiplication exists in a twisted helical cone should rightly seem a wonder to anyone. Certainly, when I thought long and hard with myself about this matter, I finally discovered that a helical cone twisted in a certain ratio affects something parabolic; in which, while infinite clusters of sounds are formed, it is no wonder that it obtains such great power in multiplying sound.

Indeed, it is known that a helical line can be given that is equal to a parabolic one; so that the curious reader may understand this: Let the helical line within the circle *N g n o* be marked with the letters *a b c d e f n*. I say: If the axis of the parabola *G S* is taken as equal to the semi-perimeter *ngN* of the circle *nONg*, and the semi-ordinate <note>A term in geometry referring to a segment of a line used to define the curve of a parabola.</note> of the parabola *T S* is taken as equal to the semi-radius *ag* of said circle, then through the vertex *G* of the axis, a parabola *GT* is described which passes through the terminus of the semi-ordinate *ST*. I say, *GT*...

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof of how sound-collecting shapes—specifically spirals and parabolas—relate to one another mathematically, before transitioning to practical designs for hearing aids.</meta>

Universal Musurgy

...that the parabola will be made equal to the spiral line a b c d e f n. All of these depend on the different movements by which each line is similarly and equally described. For if you divide the tangent of the parabola Gm into any number of parts equal to the radius of the circle a g, the movement from a to g will be equal to the movement from G to Q; and the movement made from N through the semi-perimeter g h i k n is, by hypothesis, equal to the movement from G to S made along the axis of the parabola. From this it is clear that if you take a <term>semi-ordinate</term> <note>A geometric term referring to a line segment perpendicular to the axis of a curve, such as a parabola, reaching from the axis to the curve itself.</note> equal to GN or double ST, and you apply it to the continued parabola XV between GV and GX, the parabola GTX will be twice as large as the spiral line a b c d e f n, or equal to it taken twice. If, however, you apply a semi-ordinate three times larger than the diameter a g in the continued parabola, you will have a parabola three times larger than the spiral, and so on to infinity. All of which I would demonstrate here more extensively, had I not reserved those proofs for other places.

<note>A geometric diagram in the upper right margin illustrates the relationship between a circle and a parabola. It is sufficient, therefore, to know that the power of the snail-shell tube shares something entirely in common with parabolic tubes. I have thought these things should be indicated here so that I might encourage the minds of students to more deeply investigate such inexhaustible treasures of nature.

### The Spiral-Shaped Ear Trumpet.

<margin>Which animals possess a great power of hearing.</margin>
III. **Instruments made after the model of the ears of animals possessing great acoustic power also have great power for strengthening the hearing.** Moreover, animals endowed with exceedingly sharp ears are the deer, the dog, the hare, and all other animals with large ears. Among the others, the structure of the hare's ear is truly most admirable; because since it is a most timid animal and completely defenseless, nature seems to have fortified it both with the sharpest hearing—like a scout of enemies to sense dangers in advance—and with feet like weapons suited for running. Therefore, if anyone were to have an ear trumpet fashioned after the model of a hare's ear, he would find in it a wonderful secret for strengthening the hearing. An organ of this kind has, <margin>The structure of the hare's ear.</margin> first, a very long external ear and a sort of elliptical cartilaginous envelope, versatile in every direction for better gathering the sound rays within; then, from a narrow space, it is dilated into a long and cavernous space, finally ending in a <term>cochlea</term> <note>original: "cochleam"; referring here both to the snail-shell shape and the internal ear structure.</note>. Across this cochlea is stretched that membrane which in anatomy we call the <term>tympanum</term> <note>The eardrum.</note>, along with the <term>malleus</term>, <term>incus</term>, and <term>stapes</term> <note>The hammer, anvil, and stirrup—the three tiny bones of the middle ear.</note>. Thus, the voice is gathered by that oblong and versatile ear within the cavernous passage of the internal ear; where, increased by a single reflection, it glides with great force into the spiral labyrinth, and there, striking the tympanum, it moves the internal air, from which finally happens that most acute sensation which we admire in hares. Therefore, if you compare the ear trumpet to nature's industry, you will find, as I said, a certain wonderful secret for easily strengthening the hearing.

In order that we might proceed more securely in this imitation of nature, we have seen to it that the ears of certain animals possessing more power of hearing than others were made by most skilled anatomists; which we have also presented to be viewed in the first tube of <term>Illustration II</term> <note>original: "Iconiſmo II"; Kircher often refers to his plates as "Iconisms".</note>, so that, according to the hidden structure of nature in the organ of hearing now brought into the open, you might shape the work of your art and construct ear trumpets with practiced skill.

->How to set up a statue so that it repeats any words uttered in the manner of an Echo.<-

# RECAPITULATION
## OF NATURAL MAGIC.

->*I assert that a statue can be constructed, hanging in the middle of the air, which most perfectly pronounces any sounds, whether articulate or inarticulate.*<-

---

<margin>The marvelous construction of the Magic Statue</margin>
We rightly call this proposition a recapitulation <note>original: anacephaleosis; a summary or summing up of previous points</note>, since whatever descriptions of wondrous things have been brought forward thus far are contained here as if in a certain summary. For what I say is certain and beyond doubt, and has been wonderfully proven by experiment as far as possible: namely, I say that a statue can be made which, placed in the middle of a room, or even hanging in the air, performs all the things mentioned above. Thus, those standing by may see and hear the wonder of a speaking statue, yet they will in no way be able to penetrate the cause of such a hidden mystery. They will observe the movement of the eyes, marvel at the agility of the lips and tongue, and gaze with astonishment at the living structure of the entire body. But by what artifice the statue was built, or what hidden mechanism of its movement it possesses, no one will be able to discover, since the statue hangs in the middle of the air, supported by nothing, touching no conduit, and animated by no wheels; but rather, it is constituted by a purely natural artifice and a varied combination of more hidden arts.

Let no one, however, persuade himself that I am promising <term>impossibilities <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατα (adynata)</note></term>; whatever I promise can be brought to an infallible effect. However, I have thought it more prudent to suppress the method in silence, so that such sublime mysteries of secret things—which should be revealed only to Great Lords—do not become common knowledge to everyone. If the things commonly spread about the head of Albertus <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, who was legendary for creating a mechanical speaking head.</note> are true, I would certainly say that no skill remains in the world for building a similar head except the artifice I have described. Of such great importance is the <term>Combinatory Art <note>Ars combinatoria: a method of combining different scientific or mechanical principles to produce complex effects.</note></term>, by whose help alone all the secrets of the world are opened; whatever is hidden and admirable in any science is brought forth by it. He who is skilled in this art will be most successful in the investigation and scrutiny of secret things—

...for hydraulic machines as well; besides providing a copious supply of wind, they also turn a phonotactic drum <note>original: tympanum phonotacticum; a revolving cylinder with pins used to trigger musical notes or mechanical actions in a programmed sequence</note>. By these means, artificial animals of every kind are animated into song, along with many other things of which mention will be made in abundance in the following pages. Aeolian Chambers <note>term: Aeolian Chamber - a specialized vessel where falling water is used to trap and compress air to power organs or automata</note> can, moreover, be set up in various ways.

#### First method, see figure II in Illustration XVIII.

<margin>First method: construction of an Aeolian chamber.</margin>
Let a hollow receptacle be constructed of bricks in the shape you see here; at the bottom, let a marble stone **I** be erected, polished to a very smooth surface. From **A**, let a spiral pipe **A L** be led, which should be open at **A** and below at **L**, yet joined at the parts **A E** in such a way that the air enclosed within finds no exit other than **F**. Furthermore, let the Chamber have a drain <note>original: epistomium</note> at **C** suitable for drawing off the water. Finally, at **F**, let a pipe be led out to carry the air—commonly called a *wind-trunk* <note>original: porto vento</note>—and you will have a finished machine. For the water, diverted from either a spring or a river through the pipe **A K**, will discharge itself with great force into the spiral pipe (which ought to have very steep coils); through this, accompanied by a great quantity of crowded air, it will glide down onto the polished surface of stone **I** with great force and a very loud noise. From the violent impact of the rushing waters and the agitation of the spreading droplets, the air trapped inside will be greatly stirred up and, being constricted by these narrow spaces, while it seeks an exit and finds none except through pipe **F**, it will fly out through it with the greatest force into the chests designated for receiving the winds. And thus, finally, a perpetual wind will be supplied to the pneumatic organs.

<margin>Why more air is generated by a winding tube than by a cylindrical one.</margin>
I will briefly explain why we have employed a spiral siphon and the polished surface of the stone. It must be understood that rushing water is full of air, and it carries down a vast quantity of the same in all its falls. The reason for this is sufficiently demonstrated by the very abundant foam, like snow, which is nothing other than infinite little bubbles, all filled with air; from their infinite multitude and crowding, the water takes on a color that is, as it were, white and snowy. Since this is the case, as soon as the water drawn through pipe **A K** has wound itself through the spiral bends within pipe **A L** in its headlong fall, it will also generate a great deal of air by being struck repeatedly within those bends. This would not happen in a cylindrical tube; for in such a tube, since the water finds no impediment, rushing in a simple fall, it would not carry as much air with it onto stone **I** as it does through the aforementioned winding pipe. Therefore, the water, accompanied by copious air through said pipe, will rush onto the surface of stone **I** with the greatest force; from this impact and the shattering of the water particles, new air will be constantly generated. Constricted within the cavity of the receptacle, finding no other exit but through **F**, it will escape through there with the greatest force and noise. To ensure this wind is perpetual, and lest the receptacle be filled with water over time, we have arranged the drain **C**, through which as much water is always discharged as was let in through the winding pipe; and thus, finally, the wind will be made perpetual.

...[with the greatest] force, it soon excited a very powerful wind within; this wind was imbued with excessive humidity, so to ensure it exited purer and drier, those diaphragms—perforated in the middle like a sieve—were arranged. Hence, some even derive air into the chambers using bellows driven by water instead of using the Chambers themselves. But having touched upon these things first, let us now proceed to others.

### Practical Application III.

->Another construction of the Aeolian Chamber.<-

There are some who construct the Aeolian Chamber <note>term: Aeolian Chamber - a vessel where falling water traps and compresses air to power instruments</note> with this artifice. From certain bricks, they build a Chamber of any shape, spacious according to the size of the organ, such as may be seen in *Figure III of Illustration XVIII*. At the bottom of this, they erect another tube **FG** of square or cylindrical shape (it makes no difference), and within this, another tube **E** from the outside, led down within tube **FG** for the space of one foot as far as **H**. The structure will then be complete; for the perennial water flowing into tube **E** will exert itself within tube **FG** until it overflows. As the waters overflow with diffusion and force onto the bottom of the vessel **CD**, a powerful wind will be excited. Since this wind has no other exit except through **B**, it will discharge itself through this tube into the wind-chests or wind-boxes and channels. 

However, I would advise no one to use this artifice, for at the beginning it will have air that is more great and powerful than is proper, and at the end, air that is more meager and weak than is proper. For the water will continually rise within the Chamber until it is completely filled; once filled, it is emptied again through the drain **I** <note>original: epistomium; a valve or plug used to empty the water</note>. Therefore, the structures we taught in the two preceding practical applications are better and much more efficient than this present one, unless it were so adjusted that the water collected within the vessel, ascending by some force as in **MH**, neither increased nor decreased. In this way, it would always supply equal air to the wind-chests.

Having thus handed down the ways in which we force air into the wind-chests by the sole impetus of rushing water, the method must now also be handed down by which we can continue the same wind, forced within the channels by the artificial industry and help of bellows.

...a suitable shaft <term>CD [shaft/axle]</term>, into which a transverse beam is inserted at **R** in such a way that it can move at **R** up and down as if on a pivot. Next, let a wheel **NO** be made, equipped with its own buckets, whose extended axle should be bent exactly in the manner seen in the figure, inserted into the support **M** so that it can rotate upon it as if on a pivot. Above this, in a convenient place, two bellows equipped with weights should be secured at **G** and **F**. At the end **E** of the transverse beam, another rod **LK** should be lowered, inserted into the curved handle at **K** by an end-ring **K**, so that it can run freely within the axle **K**. Once these things are prepared, as the water **K** turns the wheel **NO** by the force of its fall, the wheel will simultaneously rotate both the axle and the curved handle **MK**. Since the rod is linked to this at **K**, as it descends toward the lower part, the handle **KE** to which it is attached will pull the transverse beam **AB** along with it. As this beam descends, one bellows (namely **G**) will necessarily be raised, while the other, **F**, by descending, will promote the ascent of bellows **G** by its own weight **M**. Conversely, when the handle **K** rises, the rod will lift bellows **F**, while the other bellows—pressed both by the weight **G** and the rod—will necessarily descend; and thus they will continue in alternating turns. From the pressure of the bellows, air is violently forced into the <term>Aeolian Chamber [a wind-chest or air reservoir]</term>, from where it will finally be channeled through pipes to wherever one desires.

<margin>Another method for bellows</margin> Anyone who wishes to increase the number of bellows can easily achieve this effect through many curved handles arranged in different ways, as appears in **Figure V** of the said illustration. In this figure, four bellows **A, B, C, D** are arranged in order, one after the other, lifting an axle **EF** equipped with four handles **K, I, H, G**, which will stir up a mighty wind. For the "living water" <note>original: "Aqua viva," referring to flowing or running water</note> falling upon wheel **E** moves the axle **EF**. The curved handles, corresponding to the rods supporting each individual bellows, now lift and now depress the bellows according to the position of the handles. However, the figure places the matter before the eyes better than I can explain with many words.

<margin>The use of bellows.</margin> The use of these bellows is varied and manifold; for by these, organs are brought to life, the songs of birds are staged, rooms are cooled, and various movements are set in motion, about which we shall speak partly here and partly in other places, God willing.

# Practice V.

## *How to arrange the prime mover for driving string instruments or lutes.*

<margin>The use of steel springs.</margin> Since instruments equipped with strings have a great enemy in moisture, and cannot remain in damp places for long without notable damage, craftsmen have found another way of driving said instruments. They prepare certain <term>steel springs [literally "steel feathers/pins"]</term> with singular industry, having a length determined by the size of the instruments. They are accustomed to coil these within cylinders and drums using tensioners; from their forced state and continuous struggle, the cylinder must necessarily turn, and thus it provides the same effect as the cylinders driven by water described previously. This craftsmanship is widely known; for the makers of wheeled clocks <note>clockmakers</note> apply almost every kind of motion to said machines through these steel springs. These springs, enclosed in cylinders, have such force that they can equal the power of huge weights. However, since we deal with these and their construction professionally in our *Universal Statics*, in the treatise on wheeled clocks, I did not wish to be more profuse here. Whoever desires a greater knowledge of these springs should, in the meantime, consult the clockmakers. If, therefore, in place of the wheel **NO** described in Practice 4, you place a cylinder animated by said steel plates or springs, it will lift the bellows **G** and **F** through the curved handle **K** just as easily as the wheel **NO**, though not with a motion of equal duration. For motion by water is perpetual, whereas by springs it will last only as much time as the duration of the organ's sound requires. These springs, however, have a double duty: they both lift the bellows and rotate the <term>phonotactic cylinder [the programmed musical barrel]</term> to perform the symphony, as will become clear in the following figures.

# Preliminary Exercise I.
## To construct a phonotactic cylinder.

<margin>What is a phonotactic cylinder?</margin>
In order for organs to play by themselves, it is necessary that the <term>keys [palmulæ]</term> of the harmonic console be pressed in a musical sequence. However, they cannot be pressed musically except by hands, or by something pressing the keys in place of hands, such as a pinned <term>cylinder [cylindrus]</term>. From the rotation of this cylinder, the pins pull the small arms of the keys, thereby producing a harmonic sound. We must now explain how a cylinder of this kind is constructed, how it is divided, and how it is equipped with its pins. Indeed, the preparation, division, and application of this device involve everything rare, hidden, and subtle in the business of <term>automata [automaton]</term>, so much so that without this, nothing can be constructed correctly or with ingenuity. We call it a **phonotactic cylinder** <note>literally "sound-arranging cylinder"</note> because, in its harmonic divisions, the melodies are arranged with the highest skill, as will become clear in the progress of the work.

# Paradigm I.
## To harmonically outline the phonotactic cylinder.

The phonotactic cylinder can be considered in two ways: either in the manner of an elongated column, or in the manner of a military drum; both can serve our purpose. The **columnar cylinder** serves shorter melodies of 15, 20, or 30 <term>measures [tactuum]</term>, for it

<note>A technical diagram illustrating two types of cylinders used in a musical automaton. Cylinder A is a long, slender 'columnar' cylinder with longitudinal lines. Cylinder B is a 'Tympanoides' cylinder, wider and shorter, resembling a drum, equipped with a crank and axis for rotation.</note>

makes shorter revolutions, as appears in cylinder **A**. The **drum-like cylinder B** <note>original: "Cylindrus Tympanoides"</note> serves longer melodies, for it has circles much larger than the columnar one, as is evident from the figure. You may choose whichever one suits your purpose. Let there be, then, a cylinder prepared in the stated manner, of such size as fits a melody of 14 measures or time-lengths, arranged beneath the console of keys or <term>keyboard [Tastaturam]</term> <note>Kircher notes that "Tastatura" is a "barbaric" or non-classical term for the keyboard.</note> in such a way that the length of the cylinder corresponds to the length of the console. It should be divided into as many equal parts or circles as the console contains keys, so that for every key (or *tasta*, to use the common term), a corresponding circular division exists on the cylinder.

Once the cylinder is positioned and prepared in this manner, you will select a beautiful and ingenious melody—one not exceeding 14 measures of time—which you will resolve into its individual voices. You will distinguish each measure with lines, adding the number of the measures at the bottom or the top, as is shown in the following paradigm. In this first example, it seemed best to show a simple song written in larger notes, so that we might make our way from simpler things to more perfect ones. We have, however, somewhat diminished the voice of the song <note>This refers to "diminution," the Renaissance practice of breaking long notes into faster, decorative passages.</note> so that you might have an example of how to execute the diminution of notes to be placed upon the cylinder.

### Sketching or transferring the song into the phonotactic cylinder.

Since the first note in the bass voice is a <term>semibreve</term> <note>a whole note</note> on G, look at the top of the square among the keys for the letter G or g. Then, within the parallels encompassing one beat, draw a solid line, yet in such a way that it does not fill the entire space from g to a; for although the line of the second space marks the beginning of the second beat, the end of the first beat ought not be placed precisely upon it, but a little bit before, as you see. Again, since in the bass of the song the notes of the second beat are two <term>minims</term> <note>half notes</note> equivalent to one whole time and occupying the same key, namely G; within the same space g of the phonotactic square, starting from the line of the second beat, you will mark a small line up to line 2 and 1/2, which represents a minim in g, and then from line 3 within the space up to line 4 and 1/2 you will mark another line equal to the first, which represents the other minim; and thus you have completed two beats.

Furthermore, since the notes of the third beat placed in the bass of the song are again minims in a; you will seek that 'a' at the top of the phonotactic square, and within the spaces of the 3rd beat, you will mark two small lines representing minims, as before. Again, since the notes of the fourth beat in the bass of the song are a dotted minim and a <term>semiminim</term> <note>quarter note</note> placed in g, you will arrange them entirely within the space of the 4th beat corresponding to g, just as you did for the notes of the second beat. Since the note of the fifth beat occupies the G key and is a minim, you will arrange it within the space of the fifth beat of the phonotactic square corresponding to g, as you see. But since the following note of the same beat in the bass of the song is a minim and occupies the f key, you will seek f at the top of the square and arrange the said minim within the space of the fifth beat from the third line to 4 and 1/2. 

Again, since the note of the 6th beat is a semibreve placed in E, you will mark a small line within column E of the square in the space of the 6th beat, from the first line of the beat to 4 and 1/2. In the same way, you will mark the note of the seventh beat placed in D, in the space of the 7th beat of the column from the first line of the 7th beat to 4 and 1/2, and you will have half of the song completed. Furthermore, since the note of the 8th beat is preceded by a minim rest, you will omit the line in the space of the 8th beat suitable for a minim; but since the note of this space is a minim and placed in d, you will arrange a minim within the middle of the space of the 8th beat from line 3 to 4 and 1/2. 

Besides, since the ninth beat contains 4 semiminims in D, you will mark them upon individual lines in the said space of column D, which will represent 4 semiminims, for a semiminim always occupies an incomplete part of the beat's space, as you see. Again, since the space of the 10th beat contains a dotted minim in D and a semiminim in b, you will transfer those into the appropriate spaces of the Cylinder; the notes of the eleventh beat are two minims in C; of the twelfth, one semibreve in D; and finally, the note of the thirteenth beat is the final note, of whatever duration, in G; all of these you will transfer into the appropriate spaces of the Cylinder, and you will have what was sought, as the figure of the Cylinder extended onto a square surface clearly teaches.

**O**ne must proceed in no different a way for the other voices of the Altus and Tenor; for there is a single method of operating for all of them. For the perfection of the entire harmony consists in this task. You see, then, how by turning the handle of the entire cylinder, the cylinder is moved and changed simultaneously, while the iron tongues of the keys <note>the metal parts that the teeth strike to produce sound</note> remain always unmoved.

## How multiple melodies can be transferred onto the same cylinder

**N**ote that multiple melodies can be transferred onto one and the same cylinder; for the wider the columns or the spaces between the keys are, the more melodies can be placed in them. For example: if the spaces were of the width AB, eight different melodies could be placed on the cylinder. Since the individual spaces are equal and divided into eight parts, the iron tongues at the ends of the <term>palmulæ</term><note>Latin: "little palms"; these are the small levers or pivoted fingers in a mechanical organ that are lifted by the pins on the cylinder to play a note.</note> in the organ’s <term>tastatura</term><note>The keyboard or key-action assembly.</note>, which catch the teeth of the cylinder, will correspond to one space AB—that is, they can be applied to one of the eight said parts. It is certain, therefore, that eight melodies can be placed on it. And for that reason, the axis of the cylinder must protrude outward, divided into as many <term>crenæ</term><note>Notches or grooves.</note> as there are divisions in the space. But you will more easily grasp my meaning from the following figure.

<note>A technical diagram illustrates a mechanical musical cylinder and its associated hardware. A horizontal cylinder is mounted on an axle, with its surface divided into three main segments labeled A, B, Y, and Z. Above each segment, a set of letters (c d e f g h i k) represents specific notes or key positions. Three vertical lever components, labeled 'X', are shown poised above the cylinder, interacting with the musical notation or "teeth" (pins). A detail on the upper right shows the construction of one such lever with parts labeled a, b, d, f. To the left, the axle extends through a support pillar (TL) and terminates in a handle (T) on a shaft (S). The protruding section of the axle is marked with a series of small notches or grooves labeled L, m, n, o, p, q, r, s; these allow the entire cylinder to be shifted laterally into fixed positions, aligning different sets of pins (representing different songs) with the fixed levers.</note>

Therefore, let the spaces AB, BY, and YZ be the cylinder's eight-part spaces marked with the letters c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, continued through the entire circumference of the cylinder, and corresponding to three keys <note>original: "b quad. CD"</note> <term>B-natural</term>, C, and D. We have chosen eight-part spaces instead of 36 <note>Kircher likely refers to a 36-key instrument here</note> so that the figure would not be extended beyond measure. Since each eight-part space corresponds to one of the 36 keys—that is, to one lever in the keyboard mechanism, which we have marked here with the letter X—it is certain that with the handle TS placed over the last notch L on the support TL, the levers X in all the eight-part spaces of the cylinder will be moved immediately over the column for 'c', as is apparent to the observer. Again, if the handle T is moved over the notch M on the said handle, I say that the iron tongues at the end of the levers X will no longer correspond to the spaces for 'c', but to the spaces for 'd', and consequently, a place for a second melody will be provided. Furthermore, if you set the handle T upon the support TL at point 'n', the iron tongues of the levers X will no longer correspond to 'd' but to 'e', and consequently, a place for a third melody will be provided. In this way, by moving the handle over the remaining points n, o, p, q, r, s, the levers X will necessarily change position, and new spaces for melodies to be applied will always open up on the cylinder, up to eight.

The following song is to be recorded on the cylinder; you shall proceed in exactly the same manner as was done in the previous example. To begin with the melody <note>original: "cantu"; referring here to the soprano or leading voice</note>, proceed as follows: since the melody begins with a <term>rest</term><note>original: "suspirium"; literally a "sigh," the standard term for a quarter-note rest in mensural notation</note> in the first position, do not make any division on the phonotactic cylinder for the first quarter-part of the beat. However, since the first note is a <term>minima</term><note>A "minim" or half-note in modern terms, though its duration depended on the time signature of the period.</note> and is set on the note *d*, you will arrange a line in the *d* column corresponding to half a beat, placed after the initial quarter-space; this will create the <term>syncopation</term><note>A rhythmic effect where a note begins on a weak beat and is held across a strong beat, creating a "suspended" or off-beat feel.</note> of the note. 

Then, you will determine the next note, which is set on *c*, in the *c* column, leaving a quarter-part of the first beat in the first space and placing the other half of the *minima* in the space of the second beat. Proceed in this same order for the remaining keys assigned to the syncopated notes. You shall then record the second and third voices onto the cylinder with equal diligence. 

All of these instructions are presented so precisely in the following phonotactic grid that you can learn how to proceed simply by comparing the musical notes with the teeth of the said cylinder. For anyone who has deeply understood the previous instructions will encounter no difficulty here at all. 

Note, however, that here in the keyboard layout of the phonotactic cylinder, the key **b** always corresponds to the <term>soft signature</term><note>original: "molli signaturæ"; refers to B-flat.</note>; on the keyboard <note>original: "tastaturā"</note> this belongs to the third position of the black keys <note>original: "palmulæ nigræ"</note>. On the other hand, the **$\natural$** <note>original: "b quadratum"</note> corresponds to the <term>hard signature</term><note>original: "duræ signaturæ"; refers to B-natural.</note> and belongs to the fifth white key. To whatever key you find this sign **#** attached—for example, c#, d#, f#, etc.—it will indicate the positions of the semitones on the black keys marked with those letters. The keys written simply, without signs, will indicate the positions of the white keys on the <term>abacus</term><note>Here referring to the physical key-bed or the layout chart for the cylinder's pins.</note>.

### The Phonotactic Cylinder projected onto a plane, together with the harmonic arrangement of the pins, by which the voices of the preceding three-part song, the placement of the notes, and the measurement of time are exactly indicated.

<note>A large rectangular grid represents a "Phonotactic Cylinder" <note>original: "Cylindrus Phonotacticus"</note> projected onto a flat plane. The grid functions as a graphical musical score or a template for pinning a mechanical musical instrument. 

Vertical Axis: The left side is numbered from 1 to 14, representing measures or temporal divisions.
Horizontal Axis: The top edge is labeled with musical pitches across several octaves. The labels include "F G A" followed by repeating sequences of "b c d e f g a" in different scripts and cases, some including accidental signs like sharps (#).
Internal Data: The grid is populated with numerous small, white horizontal bars, representing the "teeth" <note>original: "dentes"</note> or pins of the cylinder. These bars are placed at specific intersections of pitch (columns) and time (rows). The arrangement shows three distinct voices (a <term>triphonium</term><note>A composition for three voices.</note>) moving through the 14 measures, including syncopated rhythms as indicated by the offset placement of bars within the grid squares.</note>

Although this three-voice piece <note>original: "triphonium"</note>, as was stated in the preceding section <note>original: "§."</note>, could be transposed into one and the same grid, we have nevertheless, for the sake of avoiding confusion, arranged a separate grid corresponding to the cylindrical surface. It is the one shown above. Regarding the understanding of this, nothing more seems to be required than an inspection of the notes shown in the said grid by various marks <note>original: "apices"; referring to the visual indicators in the grid</note> matching the value of the notes, and a diligent comparison of one with the other. Thus, you see the first note of the bass voice <note>original: "basis"</note>, which is a <term>minim</term> <note>original: "minima"; a half-note in the musical notation of the time.</note> on *g*, proceeding in the *g* column by a mark equivalent to a minim. You will also see that the remaining two voices—following initial rests equivalent to one minim—begin with a <term>syncopation</term><note>A rhythmic technique where the note starts on a weak beat and is held over onto a strong beat.</note>, and so on for the rest. These things will be better understood through a diligent examination of the individual parts than by many circuitous words <note>original: "ambagibus"</note>.

# Paradigm 1.
## How notes of the smallest value can be inscribed onto the cylinder.

This geometric division offers such great utility that no manual dexterity of a craftsman could ever match it. In order to transfer these "twitterings" <note>original: *teretismos*; a term borrowed from Greek music theory referring to rapid, bird-like vocal flourishes</note> onto the cylinder, you must divide the space of a single beat <note>original: *tactus*</note> into 32 parts. For this many "three-tailed" notes constitute one unit of time or beat. Then, you shall proceed as you see has been done in the following example, in which you will find the arrangement for only two beats. If, however, 16 notes were to correspond to one unit of time, as happens in "two-tailed" or semiquaver notes, then the space of one beat would need to be divided into 16 parts. If, indeed, 64 notes were to correspond to one unit of time, as happens with the fastest three-tailed notes, then each beat-space would have to be divided into 64 parts; and one would then proceed according to the rules delivered, and so on unto infinity.

->### Corollary<-

From this it follows that no motion of notes can be devised so swift that it cannot be exhibited by the help of this mechanical practice. Consequently, our automatic art can reach those heights where no manual dexterity can go; nor will any Organist <note>original: *Orgonædus*, a Latinized Greek term for an organ player</note> be found in the world who could achieve anything similar with his hands.

# Paradigm IV.

## How Triple, Sesquialtera, and similar proportions of time can be introduced onto the phonotactic cylinder.

Since motions of "perfect time" <note>In early music theory, "perfect time" refers to triple meter, symbolized by the circle, representing the Trinity.</note> occur quite frequently in harmonies, and some of them are so difficult that there are scarcely any—even among the most excellent musicians—who are able, I will not say to sing them, but even to play them on instruments. We shall show here by what method the cylinder is to be divided so that their most perfect motion may be exhibited. For nothing in the entire treasury of music is so hidden that our phonotactic division cannot make it manifest. Let the following song, therefore, serve as our example to be transferred onto the cylinder. Note, however, Reader, that we here take "triple" in a broad sense for any proportion of perfect time in which three <term>minims</term> <note>A half-note in modern notation.</note> are equivalent to one minim of "imperfect" (duple) time. We did not wish to use more obscure terms in this place, lest we entangle the craftsman in terminology he does not understand. Commonly, however, all those songs that have the numbers 3, or 3/1, or 3/2 prefixed to them are called "triples." You may draw the genuine reasoning and true knowledge of these from our 7th Book, to which we refer the studious Reader; there he will find treated whatever can be desired regarding this business. The following song is by Simplicio Todeschi of Verona, printed in Venice in the year 1627. Although the author committed many errors against the precepts of music in it, we have thought it best to place it here, corrected as much as possible, because it suited our purpose.

# Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<note>The upper portion of the page features a musical score arranged in five systems of three staves each, representing a three-part polyphonic composition. The music is written in mensural notation—an early system of musical notation used before modern bar lines—with diamond-shaped and rectangular note heads. Clefs, including C-clefs and F-clefs, are placed at the start of the staves. This notation provides a musical example of a composition <note>original: melothesia</note> featuring complex "triple" <note>original: tripla</note> rhythms and syncopations intended for mechanical reproduction. On the far right edge, a vertical scale labeled "Beat" <note>original: tactus</note> and numbered from 1 to 24 is partially visible, serving as a coordinate system for a musical cylinder.</note>

When you are about to transfer this musical composition <note>original: melothesiam</note> onto the cylinder, you must first divide the individual beat <note>original: tactuũ</note> spaces into three, six, or twelve equal parts, if you wish to play with diminutions <note>the ornamental breaking down of long notes into many rapid ones</note>. One-third of a part will serve for minims; two-thirds for semiminims; and finally one-sixth for the quavers of the triple meter <note>original: fusis triplę</note>, as is clear in the preceding example.

Indeed, triple rhythms occasionally occur with such ingenious syncopation that a singer must be exceedingly skilled to either sing or play them. You can arrange these triple rhythms on the cylinder with the same ease as the previous ones; and thus it will come to pass that nothing in music is so intricate or perplexed that it cannot be performed by this automatic musical <term>phonotactic cylinder</term>. Not long ago, I composed a triple-time piece of this kind as an example, so roughened with pure syncopations that even the most expert Roman musicians were scarcely able to sing it at last, and only after great practice. The French, however, being more accustomed to this style of singing, performed it accurately—though not without causing confusion among the others. This piece is presented in Book 7.

If, therefore, you wish to transfer the preceding song in <term>perfect time</term> <note>a Renaissance term for triple meter, where a note is divided into three smaller units instead of two</note> onto the cylinder, proceed in this way: since the first two notes of the voice, the breve and semibreve, are set at pitch *a* and correspond to one beat <note>original: tactui</note>, you will first look for the key *a* at the top of the grid on the cylinder. Then, for the breve, you will apply a small line within column *a* in the first tripartite space, occupying nearly two-thirds of the first space. Next, in the same column, you will apply another small line for the semibreve, filling nearly the third division. In the second space, however, you will apply small lines corresponding to the notes of the second beat: specifically, one for the semiminim in column *d* in the second space, marking out one-third of the space; then nearly two-thirds of the second space for the dot <note>the musical dot used to extend a note's duration</note>; next for the minim set at *e*, in the second beat space, from the middle of the second line of said space up to the third line; and finally for the semibreve set at *f*, in the column of the *f* clef in the space of the second beat from the third line to nearly the fourth. You will then determine the small line for the beginning of the third beat, and thus you will have the locations for the pins <note>original: dentibus, literally "teeth"</note> of the cylinder, fixed within the second space.
