## Example V.

### Transferring Chromatic and Enharmonic phrases onto a cylinder.

The **Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** genres <note>In ancient Greek music theory, there were three "genera" or styles of scales: the Diatonic (familiar today), the Chromatic (using semitones), and the Enharmonic (using tiny quarter-tones called diesis).</note> are so difficult and arduous that many musicians—I will not say they cannot sing or play them—do not even understand what the names signify. They consider such music to be a paradox and impossible to sing <note>original: ἀδύνατον (*adynaton*)</note>. I myself admit the difficulty of the matter; since these genres possess such extremely subtle intervals, it seems scarcely possible for the human voice to exhibit such minute divisions accurately and distinctly. On instruments, the matter may meet with slightly better success; however, because there are hardly any craftsmen capable of striking such subtle intervals exactly, the matter still suffers from the greatest difficulty. 

Yet, on our **phonotactic cylinder** <note>Kircher’s term for the pinned barrel used in automated organs or music boxes to "program" a song.</note>, the task is entirely easy. Indeed, I believe there is no other way to perfectly, exactly, and distinctly exhibit these genres than through such **automata**. In these devices, all intervals—no matter how small—can be arranged with such an exact division that they achieve an infallible effect. So that you may see a specimen of this, we will here teach how to transfer a **chromatic-enharmonic monody** <note>A monody is a single, solo melodic line.</note> onto the cylinder. This demonstrates that nothing in the whole of Music is so abstruse or hidden that our **phonotactic art** cannot exhibit it.

### A Diatonic-Chromatic-Enharmonic Monody to be displayed on the Phonotactic Cylinder.

<note>A large woodcut diagram is printed in "negative," showing white lines and text against a solid black background. This diagram represents a phonotactic grid—a map for placing pins on a musical cylinder. The horizontal axis across the top serves as a musical scale or "gamut," featuring a very dense array of pitches. These are labeled with letter names (A, a, b, C, c, D, d, E, e, f, G, g) and interspersed with various sharp and cross symbols to indicate the microtonal (enharmonic) divisions between standard notes. The vertical axis represents time or the "tactus" (the beat). Inside the grid, white rectangular blocks of varying lengths are placed. These blocks represent the pins that would be hammered into the physical cylinder; their horizontal position determines the pitch (including the microtonal chromatic and enharmonic notes), and their vertical length determines how long the note lasts. This grid allows a composer to precisely "program" a melody that would be nearly impossible for a human to perform accurately.</note>

Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic.

<note>Five musical staves display a complex melodic line filled with numerous accidentals, including sharps and flats. This illustrates the chromatic-enharmonic genus discussed in the text, which uses intervals smaller than a semitone, such as quarter-tones.</note>

Who, I ask, possesses a voice so skilled and flexible that they could perfectly perform the intervals placed here? Certainly, all musicians seem to despair at the very first sight of them. Yet, in our **phonotactic cylinder** <note>A rotating barrel with pins or "teeth" used to trigger notes in an automated instrument, similar to a music box mechanism.</note>, all these things are arranged and composed with the same ease as the other examples we have proposed thus far. However, it should be noted that the **keyboard** <note>original: *Abacum clauiarium* or, as it is commonly called, *tastaturam*</note> must be arranged quite differently for this musical genre. In an ordinary keyboard, one generally finds only the steps of the Diatonic and Chromatic scales, and thus a single octave on a common keyboard has only 12 **keys** <note>original: *palmulas*</note>, as we showed in the section on keyboards in *Musica Organica*. But a **Chromatic-enharmonic keyboard** possesses a total of 32 keys per octave; we have described four such types in the previously cited location. Therefore, since a keyboard consists of at least 4 octaves, and one octave consists of 32 steps or keys, the entire four-octave keyboard will have 128 keys. Once the organ is tuned in this manner, if you determine the placement of the cylinder's teeth according to the value of the notes within the spaces assigned to the chromatic-enharmonic signs, you will obtain the sought-after, hitherto unheard-of Chromatic-enharmonic music. In the preceding example, we have shown only a single voice for the sake of avoiding confusion, so that no doubt remains in your mind.

## Corollary.

From this it is clear that if someone were to divide a whole tone into 5, 6, 7, or 8 intervals or steps, and were to arrange the keyboard and the organ pipes to correspond to each of these different intervals—and finally, if they transferred a song composed according to these steps onto a cylinder—this **automaton** <note>A self-playing mechanical device.</note> organ would exactly reproduce every subtle difference in those steps. This is truly a miraculous machine, reaching a level of precision that no human voice or industry could seem to achieve.

## Paradigm VI.

### Arranging the harmony of multiple voices on the cylinder.

<margin>The utility of the phonotactic cylinder in wonderful compositions.</margin>

It is certain that our phonotactic cylinder can perform those melodies which no manual agility or skill of the hands would be sufficient to render. For if someone were to compose an ingenious and however complex **fugue** <note>A musical composition where a theme is repeated and overlapped by multiple voices.</note> of 12 voices, it is certain that there is no Master in the world who could purely perform it by the service of his hands alone. Yet, on a phonotactic cylinder prepared with geometric division, not only will the said fugue be exactly arranged, but it will be rendered perfectly—without a single missing note—with the same naturalness and clarity with which it was composed. Indeed, if someone were to construct an organ with a keyboard of 10 octaves, they could perform on that organ a fugue of not just 10, 12, 30, or 50, but even a hundred voices with infinite variety. We do not provide an example of many voices here, as you can easily figure out how to transfer them to the cylinder from the preceding instructions. While we were writing this, by order of Pope **INNOCENT X**, we arranged for a **hydraulic organ** <note>A water-powered organ, a marvel of Renaissance and Baroque engineering often used in gardens.</note> a cylinder with a diameter of 8 palms <note>A "palm" was a traditional unit of measurement; 8 palms would be roughly 6 feet or 1.8 meters.</note>, upon which we set a **Symphony** <note>A harmonious composition for multiple instruments or voices.</note> of 6 voices woven with ingenious fugues and syncopations of 73 beats, which consequently provides a symphony most worthy of being heard.

## Conclusion.

From these things, which have perhaps been discussed more at length than was necessary, it is most clearly evident that no artifice in Music can be imagined so hidden or abstruse that it cannot be achieved through our phonotactic art.

## Paradigm VII.
### On the toothed wheels that move the cylinder in a rotation, and on the speed of tempo.

The cylinder can be driven in a circle in two ways: either by the aid of water or by springs <note>original: *pinnarum*. In this context, Kircher refers to the coiled metal springs used in clockwork or mechanical instruments.</note>. In hydraulic organs, water not only moves the cylinder but also supplies the necessary wind by its fall within the Aeolian Chamber <note>A specialized vessel where falling water creates air pressure to blow through organ pipes.</note>. Other instruments, however, such as Harpsichords <note>original: *Clauecymbala*</note>, which are enemies of moisture, are brought to life into harmony by springs violently twisted and wound within the cylinders. The difference between the two instruments is that those driven by water promise perpetual motion, while those driven by springs last only for a certain time. Now, giving motion to a machine is indeed easy; but making it proportional—"here is Rhodes, here is the jump" <note>original: *hic Rhodus hic saltus*. A Latin proverb based on Aesop, meaning "now prove what you can do," referring to the difficulty of maintaining a steady tempo in mechanical music.</note>. For without an even progression and revolution of the cylinder, the harmony would lose all its value.

Therefore, a wheel driven by water must have another toothed gear at the end of its axis, which is commonly called a *Rochetto* <note>A ratchet or small sprocket wheel.</note>. This gear, with its teeth, will catch another toothed wheel placed at the end of the cylinder, and thus, finally, a proportional motion for the harmony is introduced. In order for the harmony to be presented with a suitable and proportional motion, the gear as well as the toothed wheel it catches must consist of a certain number of teeth. For this gear will perform the same function in the fast or slow rotation of the cylinder as the fast or slow beat <note>original: *tactus*</note> produced by the hand of a conductor; for the more teeth the gear has, the faster the wheel will turn; the fewer it has, the slower. But these things will be better understood from the following figures than from many words. Clockmakers <note>original: *Horologiarij*</note> should also be consulted regarding this business, as it is their specialty to determine a given time by wheels. We shall also deal with these matters most extensively in our *Great Art of Heaviness and Lightness* <note>Kircher's *Ars magna lucis et umbrae* or more likely his work on mechanics, *Physiologia Kircheriana* or *Mechanica Statica*.</note>, specifically in the chapter on static mechanics, God willing.

## Mechanism I.
### On Hydraulic Organs.

There are various opinions by various authors regarding hydraulic organs, and they were described so obscurely by Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a 1st-century BC Roman architect whose descriptions of ancient technology were famously difficult for Renaissance scholars to reconstruct.</note> that it can hardly be discerned what should be concluded about them; and this is no wonder. For if we also proposed to describe the organs we use, we could by no means describe the matter so exactly that all difficulty would be immediately removed, especially for those who have no knowledge of such organs. All the more will antiquity and the novelty of the vocabulary and objects torment us if we attempt to understand and build the Vitruvian machine as described. Nevertheless, lest we leave anything unattempted in this work, we shall try to show what kind of machine it was, as far as we have been able to gather from an exact examination of the Vitruvian description and various conjectures.

In some respects, those organs were similar to ours; in others, they differed, as will be seen in the context of the description. For the purpose of these organs was undoubtedly to emit sound, but they could not give this except from the impulse of air and spirit. Truly, air and spirit could not be impelled unless they were forced into one place, and they could not be forced except by instruments prepared and suited for that purpose. Therefore, instruments had to be prepared that were fit and suitable for this, which would stir up the air, tighten the stirred-up air within channels, and thus the compressed air would emit sound—all of which are common to our organs. But before we describe the individual parts, it is worthwhile...

# Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic <note>The study of sound reflection and mechanical sound production.</note>

->Tt 2<-

I thought it would be best if I first provided the text of Vitruvius in this place; so that the curious reader, comparing each detail with the text, might perceive what we have achieved in the clarification of this most intricate matter. Vitruvius, Book X, Chapter XIII:

> *Regarding the principles of hydraulic organs, I shall not fail to touch upon them as briefly and as closely as I can in writing. On a base constructed of solid material, a chest made of bronze is placed. Above the base, rungs are erected on the right and left, joined in the form of a ladder, which enclose bronze cylinders <note>original: "modiolos"</note> with movable pistons <note>original: "fundulis ambulatilibus"</note> finely finished on a lathe. These have iron cranks <note>original: "ancones"</note> fixed in the center, joined by pins to levers, and wrapped in woolly skins. Likewise, on the top surface, there are holes about three fingers wide; near these holes, bronze dolphins are placed on pivots, holding cymbals <note>In this context, these function as valves.</note> hanging by chains from the holes of the cylinders down into the chest where the water is held. Inside this chest is something like an inverted funnel <note>term: "pnigeus" (Kircher writes "phigeus"). An air chamber used to regulate water pressure.</note>, under which small blocks about three fingers high are placed to level the space at the bottom between the lower edges of the funnel and the floor of the chest. Above its neck, a small joined chest supports the head of the machine, which in Greek is called the <term>κανὼν μουσικὸς</term> <note>original: "kanon mousikos", meaning a musical rule or frame.</note>. Along its length, channels are made—four if it is a tetrachord, six if a hexachord, and eight if an octochord. Within each channel, stopcocks <note>original: "epistomia"</note> are enclosed, fitted with iron handles; when these handles are turned, they open the vents from the chest into the channels. From the channels, the frame has holes arranged transversely, corresponding to the vents in the top board, which is called the <term>πίναξ</term> <note>original: "pinax", meaning a tablet or display board.</note> by the Greeks. Between the board and the frame, sliders are placed, drilled in the same manner and treated with oil so they may be pushed easily; their movement back and forth alternately closes some holes and opens others. These sliders have iron mechanisms <note>original: "choragia"</note> fixed and joined to keys <note>original: "pinnis"</note>, the touch of which effects the motion of the sliders. Above the board, holes are contained which allow the breath to exit the channels. Rings are attached to the sliders, into which the individual pipes of all the instruments are enclosed. From the cylinders, pipes are continuously joined by wooden necks reaching to the vents in the small chest, where valves <note>original: "axes"</note> finished on a lathe are placed; when the chest receives the "soul" <note>The "anima" or pressurized air.</note>, these prevent the breath from escaping back out by blocking the holes. Thus, when the levers are raised, the cranks pull the piston-heads to the bottom, and the dolphins on their pivots, dropping the cymbals into the openings, fill the space of the cylinders. Then the cranks, lifting the pistons within the cylinders with great speed and force, and the cymbals blocking the holes above, force the air trapped there by pressure into the pipes, through which it rushes into the wooden necks and through the neck into the chest. By the more forceful motion of the levers, the breath flows in through the openings of the stopcocks and fills the channels with "soul." Thus, when the keys are touched by hand, they move the sliders back and forth, alternately closing and opening the holes, and produce sounding voices in many variations of melodies according to the musical arts. I have strived as much as I could to state this obscure matter clearly in writing. But this is not an easy system, nor is it readily understood by everyone except those who have experience in these kinds of things. If some do not understand from these writings, when they see the thing itself, they will find everything arranged perfectly, with care and precision. Thus far Vitruvius.*

<margin>Explanation of the hydraulic organ.</margin>
This machine has four principal parts which must be considered according to the mind of Vitruvius. The first part is the **Bronze Chest**, with the inverted funnel, which he calls the *pnigeus*. The second is the **Construction of the Cylinders**, together with the channels, levers, and dolphins; for this is the primary part that animates the machine by supplying the wind. The third is the **Small Chest** <note>original: "Arcula"</note> with the sliders, keys, mechanisms, vents, and the *pinax*; these are the ways and paths of the winds, with covers to either open or close them. The "Small Chest" is the same as what modern organ-builders call the **windchest** <note>original: "secretum"</note>; the "sliders" are the same as those commonly called **stop-valves** <note>original: "battiuenti"</note>; the "mechanisms" <note>original: "choragia"</note> are the same as **keys** <note>original: "tasti"</note>; the "pins" <note>original: "pinnae"</note> are the same as the **trackers** or iron wires which, when the keys to which they are attached are pressed, push the valves they are connected to and open the holes through which the wind trapped in the *pnigeus* is given passage into the organ pipes. The fourth part consists of the **Organ Pipes** or reeds; if there were four, the organ was called a *tetrachord*; if six, a *hexachord*; if eight, an *octochord*; if twelve, a *dodecachord*. These were arranged according to the intervals of the scale <note>original: "diaphon"</note>. And with these four parts, the entire hydraulic organ of Vitruvius is completed; however, let us teach its structure a little more deeply.

# Universal Musurgia, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Therefore, in the first place, a wooden base was positioned to serve as a support for the whole structure; above this, a bronze chest (labeled ABCD) was placed to hold the water, which Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria (c. 10–70 AD), an engineer and mathematician who described early steam and hydraulic machines.</note> refers to as the "Altar." From this base, vertical beams were erected, between which transverse pieces of wood were placed; Vitruvius calls these "ladder-like rules" <note>original: *scalares Regulas*</note>. In our diagram, we have indicated the whole mechanism using only one beam (α β), so that the illustration would not be made too confusing by a multitude of ladder-like supports. Through these supports, long rods (VX, XY) were guided like pistons; beneath these were placed cylinders (Yy) or boxes similar to the machine of Ctesibius <note>Ctesibius (285–222 BC), the Greek inventor often credited with the invention of the hydraulic organ.</note>, which we call a pump <term>Anthleam</term> <note>original: *Anthleam*, from the Greek *antlia*.</note>, or commonly a "Tromba."

These cylinders contained valves <note>original: *pulcos*</note> or pistons (Z, Z), which Vitruvius calls "elbows" <term>ancones</term>; these were disks and small bottoms <term>fundulas</term>, or small flat plates <term>platismatia</term>, surrounded by circles of wool and leather. These entered into the cylinders like plungers <term>Emboli</term> to either draw in or expel the water. However, the cylinders or "mortars" (YY) were positioned outside, within the bronze chest (ABCD). At the very top, they were equipped with certain handles

From their mouths, chains emerged which were joined to the pistons (VY). When one was pressed down, the other was raised, in exactly the same way as occurs in our common pumps <term>Anthleis</term>. # Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic.

It is nothing other than a certain air-pump <term>anthlea</term> <note>original: *anthlea*</note>, or a device arranged for compressing air into the air-reservoir <term>pighæum</term> <note>original: *pighæum*</note>. Indeed, from the cylinders **YY**, air was thrust through the channels **T** into the receptacle which Vitruvius calls an "inverted funnel" <note>original: *infundibulum inuersum*</note>. Thus, these two cylinders, along with the pistons or valves **VY** and the small flat plates **d**, represented nothing other than that machine which we call an "Aeolian gun" <note>original: *sclopum Aeolium*; a device used to demonstrate the power of compressed air, described in Kircher's earlier work *Ars Magnetica*.</note>, the mechanism of which we handed down in the third book of *The Magnetic Art*. These corresponded to two bellows supplying wind to the air-reservoir. Within the chest **ABCD**, there was a kind of inverted funnel **EFGH**, placed three inches from the bottom and supported by certain small blocks marked **λ** and **ε** as props, so that water could enter from the bottom into the funnel (which lacked a base). However, the chest **ABCD** was not entirely filled with water, but only to a certain level, so that air occupied the space between the water and the uppermost part of the funnel, as appears in the figure. From this, it happened that just as a shepherd's bagpipe <note>original: *vtriculus pastoritius*</note>, when squeezed, supplies a copious amount of air, so this air—pressed by the incoming air supplied by the pump in alternating turns through the internal channels—was thrust into the wind-chest **X** and there compressed for the use of the sounds.

<margin>The nature of Vitruvius’s hydraulic organ is explained part by part.</margin>
The air-reservoir <term>pighæus</term> <note>original: *pighæus*</note> had certain spatulas or handles inside, which Vitruvius calls *choragia* <note>original: *choragia*; Vitruvius uses this term to refer to the mechanical parts of the organ's action.</note>, and these corresponded to the individual spatulas of our own organs, which, when opened by iron wires, provided the wind with access to the pipes. We have marked these spatulas in the figure with the letter **I**. These rested upon the openings, driven by certain springs, in exactly the same way that modern organ builders are accustomed to arrange the "tongues," which they call "wind-strikers" <term>Battiuentos</term> <note>original: *Battiuentos*; likely referring to pallets or valves.</note>. Above these corresponded the keys **S** <note>original: *Choragia*, here used as *Tasti*</note>, which were joined to the spatulas **I** by brass wires. It happened that when the keys were pressed by the hand of the organist, they pressed the corresponding spatulas inward toward the wind-chest <term>Anomothecam</term> <note>original: *Anomothecam*; wind-chest.</note> through the iron wires **I** and **S**. When these were pressed in this manner, the air enclosed and compressed in the wind-chest entered through the openings into the corresponding pipe-channel, causing the desired sound. We have expressed this entire operation in the figure through the key **V**, the spatula **y**, and the opening **X** placed beneath it. From this, it is clearly evident that, except for the method of supplying the wind, almost everything was common to our own organs. For the man operating the pump thrust the air latent in the cylinders by alternating plates through the channels **T** into the funnel, in which the compressed air departed into the wind-chest or "chest of winds." There, once collected, the air entered into the open pipes upon the pressure of the springs or keys made through the *choragia*, producing the sound desired for that pressure of the keys. One thing seemed worth explaining here that neither Vitruvius nor any other commentator on him has noted.

Namely, why organs of this type are called "hydraulic," when no mention is made of the use of water [for sound]; and for what purpose Vitruvius kept water in the chest. I answer briefly, therefore: the water was placed there so that, when agitated by the movement of the air compressed in the reservoir or funnel, it would impart a certain singular "tremor" <note>A vibrato or tremolo effect.</note> to the sound. From this tremulous sound alone, the organ was called "hydraulic," for in such a tremulous sound there appeared something strange and especially pleasant to the ear. And we say that the water was placed in the chest for this use, even if Vitruvius hints at nothing concerning it. And let these remarks suffice for the hydraulic organ of Vitruvius.

From this description, it is most clearly evident that if organs of this type are compared with our modern organs, they were utterly childish, and the work was exceedingly meager, thin, and crude. For I do not see what kind of harmony a layout of 4, 5, 6, or 8 pipes could stir up, so that I marvel greatly that Nero could be so intensely moved by such a cheap and tiny hydraulic organ that—as Vitruvius testifies—amidst the dangers to his life and empire, and amidst the sedition of soldiers and leaders, with the imminent ruin of everything, he did not abandon his care and study of it. But if he had possessed an abundance of modern organs, animated not with 4, 5, 6, or 8 pipes, but as in the larger organs of Germany with 1,152 pipes <note>original: *1152 duabus fistulis*</note> through the help of 24 different registers—if he had heard such machines acting as automata without any service of hands, with what great pleasure would we judge him to have been delighted? Truly, these most enlightened ages have discovered many things to which the inventions of the Ancients can in no way be compared, as has been shown elsewhere. But with these things premised, let us now approach the Mechanics itself.

## Mechanism II.

### To construct an automatic hydraulic organ.

For a hydraulic organ, three things are required: Water, air, and a <term>phonotactic wheel</term> <note>original: *rota phonotactica*; a pinned cylinder or barrel used to "program" the music, similar to a music box</note>. Water is the prime mover, air is the soul of the organ, and the phonotactic wheel is the instrument of <term>autophony</term> <note>original: *αυτοφωνίας*; Greek for "self-sounding" or automatic performance</note>. You shall proceed in this manner: once the organ has been constructed in a suitable location according to the rules handed down in the section on Organic Music, you must first and foremost construct an "Aeolian Chamber" <note>original: *Cameram æoliam*</note>, as was described a little earlier in Practice II.

<note>A complex technical diagram illustrating the mechanics of an automatic hydraulic organ.
- Figure I shows the main organ assembly, featuring a large pinned cylinder (H, K) driven by a water wheel (R) via a geared axle (L). Above the cylinder, a series of levers or "keys" (E, F) numbered 1-11 are triggered by the pins on the cylinder to play a row of organ pipes.
- Figure II and Figure III depict auxiliary mechanical components, including pulleys (C, D), frames (B, E, F), and gear systems.
- Figure IV shows the 'Aeolian Chamber' (VXYR), a vertical air-compression vessel. Water enters from a pipe with a valve (T) and falls through perforated diaphragms to force air through a curved pipe (Z) into the organ's wind chest.
The diagram includes various letter labels (A, B, C, D, E, F, H, K, L, P, Q, R, T, Z) corresponding to the technical description in the text.</note>

Therefore, let the Aeolian Chamber **VXYR** be 5 palms <note>A "palm" was a historical unit of measurement, roughly 3 to 4 inches or the width of a hand</note> in height and 3 1/2 in width, equipped with diaphragms pierced in the manner of a sieve, and provided with two channels. The larger of these, **TS**, should supply "living" <note>flowing</note> water; it should, however, have a stopcock <term>epistomium</term> <note>original: *epistomium*</note> at **T**, to...

<header>Book IX. Echo-Reflecting Magic.</header>

...to the water, to be stopped whenever it is pleasing. Let the aforementioned channel be diverted into the lower part of the vessel; let it also have another channel above, marked V, Z, which transfers the air stirred up within the <term>Aeolian chamber</term> <note>original: *cameram æoliam*; a specialized vessel where falling water traps and compresses air to create a steady wind supply</note> into the <term>wind-chest</term> <note>original: *anemothecam*; literally "wind-container," the reservoir that holds pressurized air for the pipes</note> of the organ. For the water, rushing with great force through channel TS into the inner part of the vessel R, will agitate both the air already there and the new air being generated. Seeking a wider space and finding none, the air will fly out through VZ into the wind-chest. Furthermore, the water escaping with very violent force through the opening R will turn the wheel MR, which is fitted with a manifold cycle of buckets. This wheel, through a gear L attached to its axle, will rotate the <term>phonotactic cylinder</term> <note>original: *cylindrum fiue rotam phonotacticam*; the pinned barrel that "programs" the music</note> or wheel HK. This cylinder, by means of its "teeth" or pins arranged harmonically according to the preceding patterns, will catch each of the levers inserted in order on the iron wire AB. Finally, the levers, caught by the teeth of the wheel, will depress the keys of the keyboard EF (to which they are connected by iron wires 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc.). Once depressed, these will open the <term>valves</term> <note>original: *paltismatia* or *Battiuentos*; the mechanisms that allow air into specific pipes</note>, and thus the wind, now violently forced into the wind-chest, will enter the pipes through the open valves; and at last, the desired harmony will be perceived. We do not teach the internal structure of the organ and its individual parts here, as we have already delivered that in our section on Organic Music.

<margin>Movable and immobile teeth of the cylinder.</margin>
Note in this place that the phonotactic cylinder can have both movable and immobile teeth. They are immobile when they are fixed into the cylinder so that they can no longer be removed. They are movable when they can be removed at will and others put in their place, so that any <term>musical composition</term> <note>original: *melothesia*; the arrangement or setting of a melody</note> can be adapted to it at any time. For this, in a cylinder divided into 24 beats, and each beat again into 8 (for the performance of notes called <term>eighth notes</term> <note>original: *fusas*</note>), you shall make holes at every point of division. Thus, various teeth prepared in great quantity for different note values, contained in a certain small box connected to the organ, can be inserted at the will of the musician. However, this can properly be done only in larger and wider cylinders; in very small ones, this will not meet with such good success.

Note secondly: This automatic artifice can be applied not only to organs but also to any kind of stringed instrument.

## Mechanism III.

### To construct an automatic stringed instrument by another method.

<margin>Construction of the automatic stringed instrument according to all its parts.</margin>
Some people, including <term>Robert Fludd</term> <note>original: *Robertus de Fluctibus* (1574–1637), an English physician and mystical philosopher who wrote extensively on mechanical music</note>, construct this kind of automaton by another method, for which three things are required. One part sounds with strings stretched for harmony. The second, positioned distinctly among the strings, strikes them. The third regulates the striking of the strings themselves with certain balanced weights. First, a triangular or square shape BB is constructed from three fir planks (as shown in Mechanism II, Figure II); on its two equal sides, about 40 brass wires are stretched, hung from their own tuning pins, so that they can be tightened and loosened according to the laws of music. The middle of the base at BB must be slightly slotted, so that the sounding machine can move steadily through the openings at BB. Furthermore, a square CDEF should be formed from more solid wood, marked off by parallel bars; this is nothing other than a phonotactic wheel flattened out into a plane. This must be inserted within the sides of the <term>lute</term> <note>original: *barbiti*; a general term for a stringed instrument</note> at the openings BB so that it may move lightly up and down. Upon this, you will distribute your musical composition with its teeth and pins according to the practical rules delivered a little earlier, so that they can be removed if desired. The width of this phonotactic square should have as many parallel wooden bars as there are keys on the keyboard; the length should be divided into the beats appropriate to the composition. In the center of each division, holes should be made into which small pegs are inserted, exactly like those which can easily be bent to strike the string and return to an upright position after the string is plucked, as is usually done in <term>harpsichords</term> <note>original: *clauecymbalis*</note>. Finally, lest the strings, once struck, give off a longer sound than is proper, other plectra stuffed with thin cloth should be fixed above the pegs...

# Book IX. Phonotactic Magic.

->The spindle, commonly called a <term>rocchetto</term> <note>Italian for a small bobbin or spool; here referring to the gear or spindle of the cylinder.</note>, is turned into the <term>phonotactic cylinder</term> A; as this is rotated, its teeth, which are harmonically arranged, will press the teeth of the pallets BC. When these are pressed, they will strike the small hammers against the corresponding bells via their axles, and thus the harmony will be completed. However, so that the cylinder may proceed more evenly, a <term>chronometer</term> <note>A mechanical regulator or fly-governor used to maintain a constant speed in clockwork.</note> X is arranged, as shown in Figure I of Illustration XIX, in exactly the same way as is usually done in clocks. Generally, two cylinders are placed: the larger one for turning the wheel A, and the other for showing the hours on the index <term>η</term> <note>The Greek letter eta.</note>. The bells or chimes must be cast harmonically; the method by which this should be done we have shown in the treatise on bells in *Organic Music*, and the preceding figure teaches it beautifully. In this, the diameter AB represents the diameter of the larger bell in **C** <note>original: "C sol, fa, ut"</note>; CB represents the diameter of the second bell in **D** <note>original: "D la, sol, re"</note>; DE shows the diameter of the third bell in **E** <note>original: "E la, mi, re"</note>; EB shows the diameter of the fourth bell in **F** <note>original: "F fa, ut"</note>; FB shows the diameter of the fifth bell in **G** <note>original: "G sol, re, ut"</note>; GB shows the diameter of the sixth bell in **A** <note>original: "A la, mi, re"</note>; HB gives the diameter of the seventh bell in **B** <note>original: "B fa, ♮ mi"</note>; and finally IB gives the diameter of the eighth bell in **C** <note>original: "C sol, fa, ut"</note>, as the attached figure beautifully demonstrates. How these diameters are actually found, however, we have taught at length in Book 6, Chapter II, to which we refer the reader. The site or position of the bells can also be varied; I preferred the one made in the manner of a small tower, as can be seen in the present Illustration XIX. In this, the phonotactic cylinder A is rotated internally by the twisting and forceful winding of a steel blade <note>A mainspring.</note>; with its teeth, it moves the small levers BC placed in order. These, through the iron wires to which they are attached, lift the hammers of the bells corresponding to them in the tower; when these return to their natural state, they strike the small bells harmonically. From this, the desired effect of harmony is finally achieved, as we have said. Each hammer, however, must be restrained by certain pins, which we have expressed in Figure II by the letters <term>ρ</term> <note>The Greek letter rho.</note>, lest they remain resting upon the bells after falling, but instead are pulled back slightly to avoid the confusion and dulling of the sounds. But let us explain the matter better in Figure II of Illustration XIX.<-

Let the phonotactic wheel A be equipped with teeth harmonically arranged. Let the board or <term>keyboard</term> <note>original: "Clauiarium"</note> be BC, whose pallets are one and a half feet in length, inserted into the iron wire DE as an axle; let the extreme part IS represent the keyboard. Each pallet should have rings within the line DE, connected by iron wires; let the iron wires then be connected to the hammers of the bells, as can be seen in the iron wire HK, the hammer KL, and the small bell M. It will thus happen that as soon as the cylinder A is rotated by the automaton, and strikes the ends of the pallets at BC with its harmonically arranged teeth, pressing each one by lifting it, the pallets IS (inserted on the iron wire DE as a <term>hypomochlion</term> <note>A Greek term for a fulcrum or pivot point.</note>) are depressed. From this depression, the iron wire HK will depress the hammer KL, which, when depressed, strikes the bell M with force and finally produces the desired sound; you shall judge the other wires in the same way. Since, however, the bells are always larger and larger, the iron wires cannot be led straight to their hammers; therefore, lest the various wires become entangled by slanted angles, the masters have arranged certain oblong iron instruments, which are commonly called <term>cadences</term> <note>Mechanical linkages or trackers that transmit motion across a distance.</note> and which we call axles. Each of these has two small arms somewhere, to which two wires are attached: one that lifts the hammer, and the other which, connected to the iron of the pallet, moves the <term>dybrachium</term> <note>A "two-armed" lever or rocker arm.</note>. The axles or cadences in Figure II are marked with the letters NO, PQ, SS, each of which has two arms—whence we also call them *dybrachia*, as if you were to say "two-armed." These are marked with the letters TV, XY, Z<term>β</term> <note>The Greek letter beta.</note>, to which iron wires are attached; the first of these, TXZ, are attached to the pallets a, b, x, while the remaining three, VY<term>β</term>, are attached to the hammers <term>δ</term>, <term>ϕ</term>, <term>λ</term> <note>The Greek letters delta, phi, and lambda.</note>. It happens, therefore, that as soon as the pallets a, b, x are pressed, the three arms TXZ turn the axles: T turns axle NO, X turns axle PQ, and finally Z turns axle SS. By their attraction and pressure, the remaining arms VY<term>β</term> will also be depressed; these, being inclined by the pressure, will strike the hammers <term>δ</term>, <term>ϕ</term>, <term>λ</term> against the bells by the iron wires to which they are attached, and thus the intended harmony will finally be achieved. By this practice, you will be able to assign any location to the bells. Truly, the figure will teach you better in all things.

# Device V.

## Concerning Hanging Bell-Wheels. See Illustration XX.

<margin>The origin of the Bell-Star of the Church of Fulda.</margin>
I happened to see this device nowhere else but in the great church of the Monastery of Fulda <note>A major Benedictine abbey in Germany, founded by St. Sturm, a disciple of St. Boniface.</note>, and I judged it most worthy of being described in somewhat more detail. After Saint Boniface had completed the construction of the church in said location and had devoted himself entirely to the conversion of souls, it happened that among other most illustrious women, he also converted an Englishwoman. While she had previously worshipped a golden star as a deity, once converted to Christ, she wished to install a golden star—resounding with countless small bells—in the church founded by St. Boniface, as a monument to her perceived return to the faith. After this had endured for several hundred years as the greatest ornament of the church, it eventually happened that, amid the encroaching disturbances of wars, the Abbot, being in need of money, was forced to take down the golden star and spend it on military expenses. So that such a famous monument should not perish, he ordered a bronze star of the same shape and size, equal to the former, to be put back in its place. To this very day, it is viewed in said church with the greatest admiration by all, and is perceived by the ears to be no less pleasantly resonant with its sweet sound than the original. Both ends of its axle rest upon silk ropes, twisted with singular skill, which are lowered from the very high dome of the temple, so that the star hangs suspended in the air, as you see in Figure IV. These ropes are wound around an axle in a windlass above the dome, inside the wheel of which a man walking turns the star, which is bright with 14 rays. Each of these rays has a length of **12 feet** from the center to the tip. These are equipped with countless little bells and, when the wheel is turned, it produces a sound that—though very large and powerful—is nevertheless sweet and most pleasing to the ears, and full of majesty (especially if it harmonizes with the massive organ on the opposite side during the greater festivities and public celebrations of the City). However, I did not think I should omit here a very detailed description of the said star, which the most Illustrious and Reverend Abbot of the Monastery of Fulda, Joachim <note>Joachim von Gravenegg, Prince-Abbot of Fulda from 1644–1671.</note>, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire and Arch-chancellor of the Empress, took care to have most accurately drawn and transmitted to me by his most learned secretary, Master Christopher Emerus—a man most ready not only of hand, but also of wit. It is as follows: See Illustration XX.

### *A description of the bell-machine, or hanging star, in the Basilica of the Monastery of Fulda, which they commonly call the "Golden Wheel," most worthy of being seen and heard.*

<margin>Figure I.</margin>
From what metal this hanging Star is fabricated remains as yet unknown; however, it seems to be partly cast and partly forged. The length of one half-foot is designated in the third figure after the drawing of the axle. The special division of the principal parts and the proportion of this wheel—of the circles and spaces as well as the rays—can easily be found from the drawing with the help of a compass. This Star consists of fourteen rays, which, as far as the interior decoration of the openwork is concerned, are so varied and of such most skillful workmanship that no one ray corresponds to another in this regard, but is plainly different; yet a similar and equal exterior decoration and proportion is maintained. In every one of these rays, there were at minimum nineteen little bells or chimes, and although some have fallen off, many still hang there, which, by the treading of a certain machine like a pulley, [are moved] to a length—

### Corollary

<margin>How the Cymbal Wheel might be made into a perpetual motion machine.</margin>
From these details, it is evident that this cymbal wheel would be even more worthy of admiration if it were adorned with harmonically cast small bells and various types of <term>crotals<gloss>ancient percussion instruments similar to rattles or small cymbals</gloss></term>. Thus, one ray could be equipped with bells arranged in the stated manner, another with rattles, another with cymbals, and similar types of tinkling bells. It would also be possible to make such a wheel perpetually mobile; specifically, if an <term>Aeolian machine<gloss>a wind-powered mechanism</gloss></term>, constructed in the manner of wind-driven mills, were built outside the dome of the church to turn the internal axis. We leave the realization of all these things to ingenious architects.

Let an instrument be made about 6 feet long, marked ABCD, with an arched exterior surface similar to that of the larger <term>chelybus</term> <note>Kircher uses the Greek-derived word "chelys" (tortoise shell/lyre) to refer to stringed instruments</note>, which are barbarously called <term>violones</term> <note>The violone is the precursor to the modern double bass</note>.

Then, let a wheel be made with a diameter of 4 spans, whose width should be only 2 or 3 fingers thick. This wheel, revolving on its own axis, you shall hide within the interior body of the instrument with such ingenuity that only a sixth part of the wheel's circumference emerges from the arched exterior surface of the instrument. We have marked this sixth part of the wheel protruding beyond the surface with the letters NG. Let the edges of the instrument, AC and BD, be parallel to this wheel, of equal height, and equally arched. When this is done, let the instrument be equipped with strings made of animal intestines (for brass strings have no place here) in the quantity and thickness usually found in Harps. Arrange them so that the largest string always corresponds to the lowest key or paddle, C-sol-fa-ut; the remaining strings should be smaller and smaller, decreasing proportionally, and arranged to correspond in order with the following keys, just as in Harps. This is continued until the whole task is completed with 49 strings (the number of paddles or keys that an ordinary <term>Abacus Clavicymbalorum</term> <note>Literally "the table of the harpsichord," referring to the keyboard</note> possesses). The keyboard of 49 keys is represented here by XZ. To ensure that each individual string maintains its proportional length, you will glue a curved bar or bridge OP to the arched surface of the instrument; this bridge, by gripping the strings obliquely within iron pins, will determine their length from P to O. The strings should be fastened at the end BD with other iron or wooden pins; at the end AC, tuning pegs should be fitted, around which the strings are wound so they can be tightened or loosened according to the judgment of the person tuning them. The strings, however, should not touch the Wheel GN, but should remain a distance of half a finger from its outer circumference. Handles, which we also call <term>choragia</term> <note>Mechanical levers or pullers</note>, should be applied within the space HL, so that each string has its own handle. These are to be attached with such industry to the shafts of the keyboard paddles (which incline inward) that as soon as the keys are pressed, the handles attached to the shafts are pulled downward, forcing the strings they correspond with against the wheel. Once the wheel is set in motion—having been previously rubbed thoroughly with <term>colophonia</term> <note>Rosin, used to create friction between a bow and a string</note>—it will finally produce the sound of a stringed instrument. To better understand these things, it seemed appropriate to display the hidden mechanism separately.

Therefore, within the space HL, let a curved arc or fulcrum be made of wood, carved with as many notches as the instrument has handles or strings. An iron or brass wire should be passed through these notches and simultaneously through the tails of the handles, so that the handles can be raised or lowered around the iron wire as if around an axis. But let us explain the matter more deeply with one or two handles and keys: let N be the paddle of the keyboard, and NML its shaft, which is fixed by a pin within the wood KL arranged inside. Let the handles be represented by SVT, which are fixed by an iron wire passed through the notches *rm* of the fulcrum QR. Furthermore, the handles should have rings at V, through which a wire is inserted to connect them with the rings of the key shaft NL at point M. Let the extremity of the handles at T be slightly curved, so that with this curvature it can more easily grip the strings at T. Let the string *ab* be placed immediately beneath the handle, yet in such a way that it does not touch the end of the handle at all, but is a little distance from it, as string *ab* shows. Thus it will happen that as soon as the key N on the keyboard XZ is pressed, the wire MV (affixed at M to the key and at V to the handle) pulls the handle SVT so that its extremity T presses the string against the wheel (which was previously well-roughened with rosin). By its revolution, the wheel vibrates the string *ab* and finally produces the desired sound of a bowed instrument. What we have said concerning one key and handle must be understood to apply to all others in a similar manner and arrangement. The wheel in the instrument is marked with the letter NG and should be equipped with teeth so that a gear—commonly called a <term>rocchettum</term> <note>A pinion or small cogwheel</note>—marked with the number 2 can engage them. The wheel can then be turned from the outside by a handle or crank 2-3 through a hole in the opening Z where its axis passes; this can be done by a person, by an automaton, or by some other ingenuity, as has been discussed previously and will be discussed in the following pages.

When these things have been properly carried out, you will thoroughly coat the surface of the Wheel NG (the sixth part of the circle protruding beyond the instrument, being 2 or 3 fingers wide) with rosin or colophony pitch. Or, if the craftsman is skillful, he might cover the entire circumference with horsehair that has been well-rubbed with rosin...

# Universal Musurgia, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Because the mere rubbing <note>original: "rasura"</note> of the strings does not create harmony unless an artful application of fingers touching the strings in various ways is added to create the intended music. Thus, this wheel, by rubbing the strings, also produces no harmony unless the artful movement of the keys <note>original: "tastorum abaci"</note> is added. For when these keys, artfully attached to their levers, are pressed, the movement of the lever drives the "fingertips" <note>small mechanical strikers or tangents</note> down onto the strings positioned below. From this, the desired harmony is produced so exactly and ingeniously by the player that whoever hears this instrument would believe they are perceiving the sweetest symphony of viols <note>original: "Chelyum symphoniam"</note>.

In order to make this machine automatic, the resin-coated wheel must be powered by weights, a cylinder, or a very strong tensioned steel plate; or, as was said previously, it can be driven by the motion of water. If the teeth of this drive-wheel are engaged with the teeth of a <term>phonotactic wheel</term> <note>a pinned cylinder or drum used to program and play music automatically, like a music box</note>, and both are moved at the same time, the latter will take over the work of the hands by lifting the levers and keys, while the former will take over the work of the horsehair bow. However, all these things will be better understood from the illustration than from many words.

## Mechanism VII.

### *To construct an automatic machine that exhibits a symphony of every kind of instrument.*

So that one might exhibit the symphony of the lyre <note>original: "Chelium"</note>, harps, lutes, theorbos, harpsichords, organs, regals, and other instruments in a single device, one shall construct another machine using the following ingenuity.

Let the body of the entire preceding instrument, marked ABCD, be divided into three levels <note>original: "contignationes"</note>. The first of these, XZ, shall contain the harpsichord with all its relevant parts. The second level, B, which is slightly larger than the first, shall contain systems of pipes for every kind of organ and regals <note>small portable reed organs</note> of the lower registers, each arranged with its own stops <note>original: "registris"</note>, laid horizontally to the horizon to save space. The third level, I, shall be occupied by the bellows, cylinders, and wheels. I have no doubt that organ-builders <note>original: "Organopęi"</note> will grasp my meaning without any difficulty. To describe everything here with total precision is forbidden by both the capacity of the paper and the constraints of time, especially since we described those matters in the preceding Book VI. Finally, the principal machine—that is, the structure that exhibits the symphony of every kind of stringed instrument—is placed on top, in exactly the same manner described in the preceding Mechanism VI; but let us explain the details more specifically.

The first interior level will contain a harpsichord equipped with brass strings and distinguished by three stops <note>original: "Registris"</note>, as the names attached to the instrument indicate. The first of these produces the simple and ordinary sound of a harpsichord. The second, by moving the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "capreoli"; Kircher notes these are the feathered wooden pieces that strike the strings, so named because they "leap" (saltu)</note>, produces the most perfect sound of a Harp; this change in sound consists of a specific adjustment of the woods which, when struck by the strings, acquire the sound of a harp. This is a matter well known to more experienced craftsmen. If you move the third stop, using hollow jacks and split pegs <note>original: "taxillis"</note> which jump onto the strings, they will emit a sound exactly like the trumpets that they call "mutes" <note>original: "surdinas"</note>. You have, therefore, in this triple register a triple harmony of instruments: harpsichord, harp, and trumpet-like sounds. To this is added the mechanism described in the previous proposition (for this must always occupy the highest place and the outermost surface), so that you may hear in it the symphony of every kind of instrument that can be categorized as lyres, viols, or lutes.

Furthermore, each individual key of the upper keyboard has pegs placed beneath it, which rest upon the keys of the keyboard of the second level (the harpsichord). The keys of this second level have other brass rods <note>original: "stylos"</note> beneath them, which rest upon the <term>pallets</term> <note>original: "platismatijs"; internal valves of an organ windchest</note> of the interior organ in the third level. From this it happens that while the keys of the upper and outermost keyboard are pressed, these, being pushed down, depress the keys of the harpsichord keyboard via their pegs. And these, being pressed, push down the brass rods to activate the pneumatic mechanisms of the organ in the third level...

Book IX. Phonotactic Magic <note>The art of "programming" sound using pinned cylinders.</note>

...valves <note>original: "platismatia"</note> upon which they rest. Therefore, when these valves are opened by the pressure of the pins, they admit the collected wind into the pipes, from which emerges an organic harmony.

To understand how each part sounds **automatically** <note>original: "αὐτοφώνως"</note>, listen: The resin-coated wheel <note>A wheel used to vibrate strings through friction, similar to a hurdy-gurdy.</note> is moved in the exact same way we previously taught—using weighted plates or a constant flow of water—to turn wheels with great force. As this wheel turns, it rubs against the strings to produce a unique sound, while simultaneously turning the **phonotactic cylinder** <note>A rotating drum with pins, like those in a music box, that "programs" the music.</note> via an intermediate wheel through a system of interlocking teeth. The teeth arranged on the rotating phonotactic cylinder catch and press down on the ends of the levers <note>original: "palmularium"</note> of the keyboard, which strike the strings to create harmony and a concert of all kinds of lutes and lyres. These levers, in turn, press down on the levers of a harpsichord hidden on a second level by means of pins placed beneath them. According to the triple arrangement of the registers, they will perform a triple symphony composed of bells, harps, and trumpets. Finally, the levers of the harpsichord press the valves of the organ hidden on the third level via iron styli, letting wind into the pipes. Depending on the setting of the registers, these pipes produce the sound of flutes, regals <note>A small, portable pipe organ with reed pipes.</note>, or even tibiae <note>A type of ancient flute or reed pipe.</note>. You can change these with infinite variety by adjusting the registers, so that one moment you hear a symphony of lutes, then harps, trumpets, and bells; a moment later, an organ or flutes of every kind; and finally, a concert made of all these sounds mixed together in various ways. Thus, in a single instrument, every kind of musical instrument is represented, with no human player actually touching it. You will understand my intention more easily from the accompanying figure; it is impossible to describe every single detail with perfect accuracy, but a curious reader who has practiced with the previous examples will easily grasp my meaning from the illustration provided.

# Invention VIII.

->To construct an automatic Organ Machine that produces the voices of animals and the song of birds. See Illustration XXI.<-

**In order** for this machine to display everything skillfully, we thought it best to first describe the movements and voices of the animals separately. Anyone who intends to display the voice of a **Cuckoo** <note>original: "Coccygis siue cuculi"</note> along with its natural movements should, as mentioned before, set up an "Aeolian Chamber" <note>A device that uses falling water to compress air.</note> in a place where water is abundant. This chamber gathers the created wind into a wind-chest <note>original: "anemothecam"</note>. The water, rushing through an opening, forcefully turns a wheel, while the axle of the wheel catches the teeth of the cylinder where you will arrange the animal voices in this manner:

<margin>The construction and sound of the Cuckoo.</margin>
You shall fashion a likeness of a cuckoo to sit upon the wind-chest. It should have a movable tail and beak, which is achieved through a system of levers <note>labeled α, β, and γ in the diagrams</note>. A cord is attached to a lever or key; when this is pressed, one lever strikes another to open the bird's beak, while another lever connected to the tail is raised. Thus, the cuckoo will appear to dance with its tail and sing with its beak.

<note>A five-line musical staff displaying diamond-shaped notes. The notation represents the cuckoo's call as pairs of descending notes (minor thirds). The triggers for these notes are labeled with the letters I, H, and K above the staff.</note>

Since two notes correspond to one beat of time, you shall insert one tooth in line ks to occupy the first beat, and another in line ty equal to the first, leaving a space for a half-pause; and thus continue with alternating repetitions until you have filled the cylinder. When this is finished, two iron wires, Hr and Kt, should be connected to the levers of the valves <note>original: "platismatiorum"; these are the valves that let air into the organ pipes.</note>, r-t. Once opened, the wind enters the pipes and expresses the desired sound of the cuckoo, while the handle OI expresses the movement of the bird, as was said.

## Corollary I.

->To express the song of a Rooster flapping its wings.<-

<margin>Construction and song of the Rooster</margin>
By this very same method, you may express the song of a rooster flapping its wings. Let there be four other circles on the cylinder, ms, et, lo, and nr, to which the same number of handles Ls, MT, NO, and rV correspond. Let the body of the rooster, Z, be formed from any material, with movable wings and beak. Beneath it, a certain kind of pipe expressing the song of the rooster should be placed (which organ-builders are familiar with), together with the pins RST of the valves <term>valves<span>Kircher uses "platismatia," referring to the pallets that open the airway in an organ windchest.</span></term>, enclosed within the valve-box <note>original: "anomotheca"</note> e-b, which you will connect by iron wires to the handles LMNs. In the first circle of the cylinder, ms, the teeth should be arranged to produce the movement of the rooster's wings, either in a continuous or interrupted motion, as you please. In the other circles of the cylinder, et, lo, and nr, you will express the song of the rooster with teeth according to the musical notes shown here and according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections.

<note>Three staves of musical notation using mensural notation (diamond and square notes) representing the crowing of a rooster. The staves are simplified, focusing on the rhythmic and melodic patterns characteristic of the bird.</note>

When this is completed and the cylinder is rotated, the teeth representing these notes on the cylinder will lift the levers of the handles MT, NO, and rV, which in turn depress the pins of the valves RST. By this pressure, the valves T are opened; once opened, the sound entering the pipes will express the rooster's crow. Meanwhile, the handle Ls, connected by an iron wire to three other wires at the knot s (two of which are connected to the wings and the third to the beak), will open both the wings and the beak, according to the arrangement of the teeth on the cylinder. Thus, we have exhibited the song and movement of the rooster, which was the task at hand.

The task is easy and presents no difficulty, especially if the Artisan has correctly understood what has been said up to this point. Therefore, in place of many words, I trust the Illustration placed here will make the matter entirely clear.

# Machine IX.
## To exhibit automated Pythagorean music arranged according to the hammers of three Cyclopes in proportion. See Illustration XXII.

Among the other harmonic machines, the one that follows deservedly holds first place. It is the Pythagorean music established for hammers, which we have often exhibited in various places before different Princes with such great applause and admiration that they seemed hardly able to be satisfied by its repetition. This music especially finds its place in the ingenious performance of comedies. The eight-voice modulation <note>original: "modulatio octophona"</note> is distributed into two choirs. The tempo perpetually follows triple proportion <note>A musical time signature where three notes are played in the time of two, creating a dancing rhythm.</note>; the hammers give the measure in such a proportion that the largest to the middle hammer has a sesquialteran proportion <note>A 3:2 ratio, which produces the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note>, and to the smallest it has a double proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio, which produces the interval of an octave.</note>. Words are attributed to Vulcan, encouraging his Cyclopes to forge weapons for some distinguished expedition; these, being called, beat the anvil, and with the tripled sound of the hammers while they strike the anvil, the singers follow the tripled measure precisely with both voice, dance, and gesture, presenting a wondrous spectacle to the eyes and ears. Therefore, let us see how we might exhibit through an inanimate automated machine this representation which has hitherto been performed in comedies with living voices, dancing, and movement.

We assume here the organ with all its parts—wheels, wind chamber <note>original: "camera æolia"</note>, and the wheels driving the machine—from the preceding sections. The Pythagorean musical composition <term>melothesia: the art or rules of musical composition</term> truly composed by us, along with the text and the proportion of the hammers, is as follows.

->Create a melody with rhythms; let us sing, let us applaud. Strike with hammers and dance.<-

This musical arrangement <term>Melothesia; Kircher’s term for the art of setting a melody or composing for an automated instrument</term>, which is set in triple meter <note>original: "triplæ proportionis"</note> and distributed among eight voices, you shall transpose onto the phonotactic cylinder <note>the revolving pinned barrel that "programs" the music</note> using the exact same method we provided above in the second exercise <note>original: "progymnasmate"</note>. Since the piece consists of 54 units of time—that is, beats—the entire circumference of the cylinder must be divided into 54 parts. Then, each of those parts is divided again into three smaller sections, because each note of this musical arrangement is worth one-third of a beat. The length of the cylinder, however, should be laid out according to the order and sequence of the keys or levers <note>original: "palmularum sive tastorum"</note>, as you have seen done previously. 

Handles should also be adapted to the cylinder and connected by flat iron wires to the wind-chest <term>anemotheca; the chamber in an organ that holds and distributes compressed air to the pipes</term>, as was explained in the preceding sections. Once these tasks are completed, you will transfer the eight-voice <note>original: "octophonam"</note> musical arrangement provided here onto the cylinder, with the pins <note>the "teeth" or pegs on the barrel</note> firmly fixed in their proper places, each corresponding correctly to the individual notes. Finally, the handle *mn*, depressed by the teeth of space *HG*, will pull down the escapement *RS* (to which it is joined by an iron wire through arm *X*), and will simultaneously pull down arm *Y*. By the lowering of this arm, it is necessary that a raising and lowering of the conductor's arm *N* follows. Thus, the statue *N* will be seen to give the beat or applause according to the measure of time, perfectly expressing the <term>upbeat and downbeat</term><note>original: "ἄρσιν & θέσιν" (arsin & thesin). We have therefore exhibited an automatic Pythagorean and Cyclopean musical machine, which was the task to be performed.

Furthermore, if you close all the windows of the room, the sound, likewise shut in, will fall silent; but as soon as even one is opened, it will flood those present with its accustomed sound and wonderful pleasure.

# Universal Music, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### Corollary I.
### On the construction of the aforementioned machine for perpetual resonance.

If anyone should wish to continue this kind of harmonious sound perpetually, he should set the machine in an open location on some tower, adjusted in such a way that it turns in the manner of a <term>weather-vane</term><note>original: "aplustri," a term originally referring to the curved ornament on a ship's stern, here used for a wind-vane mechanism.</note> or wind indicator toward whichever wind is currently blowing. Thus, having captured the air, it will be animated of its own accord and will always resonate regardless of the wind's direction.

<note>A woodcut illustration shows a rotating wind-vane mechanism. A horizontal beam is mounted on a vertical pivot. On one end of the beam is a large funnel-shaped sail labeled B, designed to catch the wind. On the other end is a rectangular musical box labeled A. The entire apparatus is designed to rotate so that the funnel always faces the wind, directing airflow into the box to vibrate its strings.</note>

### Corollary II.
### So that a marvelous Music may be perceived high in the air.

In order that this marvelous harmonic sound may be perceived with astonishment high in the air, you shall adorn a flying fish or <term>Dragon</term><note>A "flying dragon" was a common early modern term for a kite.</note> (the construction of which we have described at length in the "Representative Magic" section of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*) in such a way that strings are stretched to <term>unison</term><note>original: "æquisonū."</note> on both sides. As soon as you have committed this to the open air, whether the rope is pulled in or let out, the strings will always be excited with great force and a deliberate musical effect. But if, in place of

Innumerable other mechanisms can be made by this means, not unlike <term>stage illusions</term><note>original: "præstigijs."</note>; however, we leave these to the skillful craftsman. Nothing remains, therefore, except for us to show why strings stretched in unison nevertheless produce diverse harmony. For this, I first propose the following experiment.

### Experiment.

If someone exposes a string made of animal intestines, stretched in the place prepared a little earlier, to the wind, he will observe that the string soon sounds—not with the note expected of a stretched string, but with something entirely different. For now it maintains a third, now a fifth, now a fifteenth, or a twenty-second; and then a third, fourth, or sixth. Since there has been no one who could explain the reason for this, we considered it our duty to reveal the genuine cause of this matter here.

I propose, therefore, first: that the wind is not always carried against the string with a uniform force, but strikes now this part of the string, now that, like certain rays, sometimes with a slower and sometimes with a faster impetus. I shall show that this unequal force of the wind is the cause of such diverse sounds as follows.

### Book IX. Phonotactic Magic.

Let AF be the string and G be the wind; if the wind should strike the entire string AF with a single and undivided force, it is certain that the string will produce that specific sound which corresponds to its tension.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the physics of wind hitting a string. A personified wind, depicted as a blowing head labeled G, directs a triangular gust of air toward a vertical string marked AF. Various points (A, B, C, D, and F) are marked along the string to show different points of contact or harmonic division. Point A is the top and F is the bottom. Horizontal lines connect the wind source G to points B, C, and D on the string.</note>

If, however, the ray of wind C alone touches the string—that is, if it divides the string in two—it will happen that the remaining parts CA and CF will sound an <term>octave</term><note>original: "diapason"; the interval of an eighth.</note> compared to the whole string, just as we have demonstrated in the division of the <term>monochord</term><note>original: "monochordi"; a single-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note>.

<margin>Why wind produces different tones on a stretched string.</margin>

For the ray of wind serves in the place of a <term>plectrum</term><note>original: "plectri"; a pick or tool used to pluck a string.</note>; when it touches point C, the vibration of the whole string in parts CA and CF will sound twice as fast, and thus the string will necessarily ring out higher by the interval of one octave. If, however, the ray of wind presses at AB, the remaining part of the string BF will necessarily sound a <term>fifth</term><note>original: "quintam" or "diapente"; the interval of five notes.</note> for the reasons already assigned in the division of the monochord. If the wind should press the entire space AD, the segment DF will necessarily sound a <term>double octave</term><note>original: "disdiapason"; also known as a fifteenth.</note>, and so on for the rest. Therefore, the ray of wind will produce different sounds in the string according to the different points where it falls upon it. Thus, the larger the part of the string the wind leaves untouched, the deeper the sound it produces; and the smaller the part, the higher the sound. What the wind does in one string, it will do in countless other strings tuned to the same pitch, and this is the true cause of such a great variety of sounds perceived in this instrument. From this, a certain tremulous sound is born, affecting the ears wonderfully, which certainly has no other origin than the undulation of the wind, which does not always strike with a straight force, but glides against the string in the manner of waves; consequently, it excites the string with the same motion with which it strikes it.

### Corollary.

From these points, it is also clear that one and the same string can produce infinite different sounds. For even if the wind presses the string more strongly in one place, by pressing it more weakly in various other places, it will give birth to new and different distinctions of sounds. For if, for example, it presses strongly at C and weakly at B, it is certain that segment CA will not sound a perfect octave, but will strive toward some intermediate tone. But let these explanations suffice regarding the cause of the diversity of sounds in a single string.

## Mechanism XI.

### Exhibiting all kinds of sympathetic harmonic experiments.

We call "sympathetic experiments" those in which objects resonate without being touched when another sound is made, due to a certain marvelous proportion and similarity between sounding bodies. This causes one body to move, untouched, at the sound of another. This proportion occurs not only in bodies made of the same material, but even in different materials. From this arise many miracles of nature, the reasons for which no one can easily explain unless they possess a distinguished knowledge of the secrets of music. It is almost common knowledge that one string can move another untouched string, not only when they are tuned to <term>unison</term><note>original: "vnisonum"; two strings tuned to the exact same pitch.</note>, but also when they are tuned to the <term>octave</term><note>original: "diapason"</note> and the <term>fifth</term><note>original: "diapente"</note>. However, the untouched string always trembles more vehemently the closer it is to a unison pitch. We will not assign the reason for this effect here, since we have discussed it most extensively in the preceding sections, but we will merely reveal the manner in which many admirable things in <term>natural magic</term><note>A branch of science in the early modern period that sought to understand the hidden "occult" forces of nature, such as magnetism or resonance, through observation and experiment.</note> may occur.

# Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

## Experiment I.

### To exhibit Sympathetic Music; that is, to prepare an instrument which, with no other agent acting upon it except Sympathy, produces a harmonious sound.

<margin>A stringed instrument can be stirred to action by the sound of an Organ.</margin>
In this section, we shall not establish harmony between <term>homogeneous</term><note>original: "homogeneis"; objects of the same kind, such as two identical lutes.</note> bodies, such as two stringed instruments might be, but rather between <term>heterogeneous</term><note>original: "heterogeneis"; objects of different types, such as an organ and a lute.</note> ones—that is, between an organ and a stringed instrument, or others—for in this way, the harmony will be perceived more distinctly. Take an instrument fitted with strings and constructed from the most resonant wood, of the kind we proposed in Machine X; you shall tune its strings to a certain very perfect organ, so that each individual string is in perfect <term>unison</term><note>original: "vnisonent"; sounding at exactly the same pitch.</note> with the individual pipes of the organ. Once this is done, you shall move back from the sound of the organ with your instrument until you see the strings move and find them returning a perfect sound; and this will be its <term>proportionate distance</term><note>The specific physical space required for sound waves to effectively trigger resonance in another object.</note>. If some strings do not move, it will be a sign that the pipe does not correspond perfectly to the string, or that it is an <term>octave</term><note>original: "octaua"; an interval of eight notes.</note> higher. Or, you might work more deliberately: apply the instrument here and there to the interior walls of neighboring rooms, or best of all, upon a beam continuous with the organ, until you detect the motion and sound of the strings, and you will have found what you seek. 

For the stringed instrument will perfectly exhibit every harmony of the organ within a separate place. And lest you think I am merely passing on a theory, read what we reported above regarding the Organ of Mainz, which by chance stirred a <term>lute</term><note>original: "Chelyn"; from the Greek "chelys" (tortoise), referring to a lyre or lute-style instrument.</note> hanging in a nearby choir loft; no doubt will remain as to the truth of the matter. In this, there is only one difficulty: that one must find the perfect similarity and proportion of the bodies along with the proportionate distance. Whoever finds this can undoubtedly boast that they have found something marvelous in nature. For there is such a mutual similarity among certain sounding bodies that as soon as one sounds, the other is found to sound as well, as we have curiously shown in parts 1 and 2 of this book. Another experiment teaches us all these things: if someone were to lightly suspend harps, theorbos, lutes, harpsichords, and similar stringed instruments in a very resonant room (after first removing all tapestries that dull the sound), he will perceive—not without wonder—a certain exotic harmony caused solely by the motion of the air from the voices of speakers or from the voices of those playing an organ.

## Corollary.

### Concerning Statues that move themselves to a certain sound.

We reported in the place cited above that there were certain statues in a particular church which, at the sound of a nearby bell or even a certain organ pipe, would move (while all those present cried out as if it were a miraculous motion of the statues). It is clear, therefore, from the preceding points, how statues that provide a similar effect can be manufactured in any church. For a statue made of porous wood and proportioned to a sounding body, if balanced with extreme precision upon a porous beam continuous with the organ or the location of a bell, will undoubtedly provide the intended effect. Regarding these types of "Magic" Egyptian statues manufactured for the deception of the common people, see our work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where you will find many curious and hidden things.
