Book IX. Phonotactic Magic.

## Experiment II.

### On sympathetic harmony via conic bodies.

If anyone should know how to fashion a parabolic or hyperbolic cylinder, he should know that he has penetrated the greatest secret in <term>music-making</term><note>original: "musurgia"; the art of composing or creating music through mechanical or mathematical means.</note>. Let us reveal the secret: let a concave parabolic semi-cylinder be fashioned by means of a <term>parabola-shaping form</term><note>original: "paraboloplastæ"; a template or mold used to create a parabolic curve.</note>. This is done if you draw the parabola-shaping form with a steady and straight motion through suitable material along its length; for by that motion, as the material yields and is soft, the aforementioned parabolic semi-cylinder will be formed, possessing wondrous power in exhibiting sympathetic harmony.

The business should be arranged as follows: observe with the greatest diligence the two <term>foci</term><note>original: "foci"; the central points of a geometric curve where rays—or in this case, sound waves—converge.</note> in the bounding parabolas. If a string is drawn from one focus and terminated and tightened at the other opposite focus of the parabola, the instrument will be prepared for sympathetic sound. But let us declare the matter with letters and a figure. Let ABCDEF be the parabolic cylinder; the two parabolas bounding the cylinder are ABC (the upper) and DEF (the lower); H and G are the foci of these equal parabolas. I say that the string or nerve HG, extended through both foci, will be stirred by any motion, even the smallest. For since any section of the semi-cylinder made normally to the axis is a parabola, and infinite parabolas can be conceived within that semi-cylindrical surface, it happens that any voice or sound and motion of the air falling upon this parabolic semi-cylindrical surface—provided it falls upon the cylinder at right angles—forms as many <term>projections of rays</term><note>original: "actinobolismos"; from the Greek for "throwing out rays," referring here to the reflection of sound waves.</note> as there are equal parabolas that can be conceived in said semi-cylinder. Furthermore, since the string is extended through the foci H and G, it will consequently pass through the foci of all the other conceivable parabolas in the said semi-cylinder. Since the union and confluence of rays occurs in the centers of the foci, the intensification of sound will also occur in them. Therefore, the entire string, agitated by the multiple confluence of rays and the multiplication of impulses, will tremble and sound.

<note>A diagram shows a vertical semicylindrical apparatus labeled with geometric points. The top parabolic curve is labeled A, B, and C with focal point H. The bottom parabolic curve is labeled D and E with focal point G. A vertical line representing a musical string connects points H and G. To the right of the cylinder is a small illustration of a figurine labeled 'I' on a pedestal. At the bottom right is another illustration labeled 'V' showing a similar figurine or mechanical part, connected to the description of a perpetual motion statue.</note>

<margin>A string which, as it were, gives forth a perpetual sound.</margin>

## Corollary I.

<margin>How a perpetual harmony might be made.</margin>

From this it is clear that if one were to stretch three or four strings near each other around the foci according to the consonance of the 3rd, 5th, and 8th <note>The fundamental musical intervals that create a major chord.</note>, the machine would exhibit a perpetual harmonic murmur in an appropriate place or when exposed to the wind. For this sonorous line HG has a certain physical width and some space within which the intensification of the rays and the <term>caustic</term><note>original: "caustici"; Kircher borrows this term from optics, where it refers to the burning point of light, to describe the "burning" or intense concentration of sound.</note> or sonorous effects occur.

## Corollary III.

## Experiment III.

### To stimulate untouched strings by the sound of glass.

If someone rubs the rim of a <term>glass cup</term><note>original: "scyphi vitrei."</note> with fingers previously moistened, they will soon perceive a certain ringing sound. If, moreover, they extend a string over the cup tuned to that same pitch, they will perfectly perceive not only the trembling of the string, but also its sound. If, therefore, someone extends corresponding strings over several glass cups, they will have music composed of a wondrous ringing and the sound of strings. Regarding this experiment, see our more extensive treatment in the first part of this book.

## Experiment IV.

### To make one believe they hear the great roaring of bells.

This is a remarkable experiment that fills listeners with the greatest admiration. Take one of the strings from a <term>large viol</term><note>original: "Violone"; at this time, it usually referred to a large stringed instrument of the viol family, a precursor to the double bass.</note>; to this, hang a <term>brass plate</term><note>original: "laminam æneam."</note> or any other ringing and sonorous body. Then, wrap both ends of the string around your fingers and insert them into your ears. When the hanging plate strikes another nearby object, you will perceive a sound that you would never have believed at first—namely, a sound far exceeding the tolling of all bells. If, instead of a plate, you take a brass rule (the longer it is, the better suited for the purpose), you will perceive a truly formidable sound composed of deep and sharp tones; and indeed, the longer the string, the more intense the sound it will emit. 

The cause of this thing is nothing other than the trembling of the ringing metal, which, while it communicates its ringing to the string, the string <note>original: "fibichorda"; literally a 'fiber-string'.</note> conveys the communicated roar to the hearing. There, the enclosed and internal air is violently shaken through its <term>acoustic muscles</term><note>original: "musculos suos acusticos"; Kircher’s term for the anatomical structures of the inner ear that he believed responded to vibration.</note>, and thus presents a most powerful sound. It is indeed wonderful that no other bodies, but only those that delight in ringing—such as all metallic plates and rules—produce this effect.

## Corollary.

If you lower an instrument of this kind into a cistern that resonates strongly by means of a string, and insert both ends of the string into your ears, and then strike the plate against the wall, you will hear a roar composed of various voices, powerful beyond what can be described.

Book IX. Phonotactic Magic <note>Phonotactic: derived from the Greek words for "sound" and "arrangement." This refers to the art of organizing sounds through mechanical or spatial means.</note>

## Experiment V.
### *To establish music with every kind of wood, metal, or glass.*

The manner in which the <term>Zylorganum</term><note>A precursor to the modern xylophone or glockenspiel; literally a "wood-organ."</note>—that is, an instrument constructed from various harmonious arrangements of wooden or glass tiles of different sizes—is to be built, has been discussed at length in the section on Musical Instruments <note>original: "Organica Musica."</note>; for this reason, you may refer to that cited location.

## Experiment VI.
### *On the various alterations of sound in strings.*

A string produces a sound according to the condition of the objects placed beneath its bridge. Thus, if you place a wind-inflated bladder containing small pebbles beneath a larger stretched string and scrape the string with a hair-bow, you will hear a certain ridiculous sound, well-suited for <term>theatrical interludes</term><note>original: "scenicis intermedijs"; these were musical or comedic performances held between the acts of a play.</note>. If you place a glass body beneath the same string, the string will emulate a certain strange ringing; and so it goes for other materials. All of these provide an immense wealth of material for creating unusual instruments.

## Experiment VII.
### *So that a deaf person may perceive music.*

A <term>Lute</term><note>original: "Testudo," literally "tortoise," referring to the rounded shape of the lute's body.</note> with a long neck will achieve the intended purpose. Let the Lute be fitted with strings, and let the deaf person grip the end of the neck with their teeth; afterward, let the lute be set into harmonious motion. I say that the deaf person will perceive the harmony; indeed, nothing but an experiment performed on a deaf person has taught us the truth of this matter. For the sound of the lute, propagated through the neck into the mouth, wonderfully excites the auditory power through the nerves in the <term>acoustic organ</term><note>The inner ear and its associated nerves.</note>. I am also persuaded that through Experiment V, a deaf person would perceive that powerful sound of bells.

## Corollary.

From these things it is clear that if, in any stringed instruments, a certain neck or long arm continuous with them is extended to any distance—such as through intervening walls, provided it does not touch the walls—the end of the neck, when gripped by the teeth, will provide the sound of the lute just as if it were present. For we have said in the preceding pages that the propagation of sound performs the same effect in the neck of a lute as it does in long beams. Since the neck is continuous with the body of the whole, certainly the closer parts, the more remote parts, and thus the entire body will tremble at the sound of the strings. Since this tremor is a harmonious propagation of air, it will consequently provide the sound to the acoustic organ through the mouth and teeth at a distance, as distinctly as if it were present.

And let these remarks on Mechanical Music suffice. Nothing remains, therefore, except that we should also say something regarding <term>Steganographic</term><note>Secret or encoded communication.</note> or Cryptological Music.

Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance

## PART V.
# MUSICAL CRYPTOLOGY
### OR
## The Steganographic Art, by which the secret concepts of the mind can be communicated through sounds to two or more distant friends.

<note>A large woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a figure in a classical landscape with a tree and a distant building.</note> Just as we have taught in the *Great Art* <note>original: "Arte Magna"; this refers to Kircher’s previous work, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (The Great Art of Light and Shadow), which dealt with optical communication.</note> how the secret concepts of the mind can be communicated to those who are absent through Light and Shadow, so too can it be done through sound. Even if such secret communication of things can be established across a greater distance through sight than through sound, nonetheless, so that nothing is lacking from this Musurgy of ours, we will not so much teach as merely suggest in this place how this might be achieved through sound.

It must therefore be noted that the art of Cryptology is twofold: the first is vocal, the second is mute. It is "vocal" when the secret thoughts of the mind are opened to a friend in a distant space through a manifest sound. It is "mute" when those same thoughts of the mind are communicated through letters or musical characters woven together in an impenetrable kind of writing. We will explain both in a few words.

->§. I.<-
### On Musical Cryptology.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' with floral motifs.</note> Since <term>Cryptology</term><note>The study of hidden or secret communication.</note> consists in this—that the secret concepts of the mind are revealed to a friend in a distant space—it can be done in several ways altogether. First, across a very remote space through louder sounds; second, across a nearer space through hidden tubes constructed by the art of <term>Echotectonics</term><note>A term coined by Kircher meaning "the architecture of echoes," or the engineering of acoustic spaces to manipulate sound.</note>, as was shown above. To the first kind belong the explosions of war engines <note>Cannons or artillery.</note>, which we showed in the first book can sometimes be heard at a distance of ninety miles, especially with a favorable wind. Such was the horn of <term>Alexander the Great</term>, of such a powerful sound that with it he could perfectly halt his entire army, however dispersed, as if he were speaking in person to each individual; see the description of it given elsewhere. For an alphabet could be so arranged that a specific number of sounds would respond to such and such a letter, as we have taught elsewhere; and thus knowledge of the intention of any absent friend could be reached. To this belongs the sound of trumpets, the noise of drums, the ringing of bells, and any other instrument of louder sound. However, this business has this inherent difficulty: that besides being very expensive, it also makes the secret plot <note>original: "machinationem"</note> established through such louder sounds immediately suspect and betrays it, since it cannot be hidden. If, however, we speak of this business speculatively or mathematically, and experience in <term>Echonic Musurgy</term><note>The science of acoustics and sound reflection.</note> shows that sound travels 100 geometric feet in the space of one second, and consequently 2 leagues in the space of one minute of an hour. It is certain that with such powerful sounds produced successively by a distribution of vocal instruments around the entire 
<margin>How news of the whole world can be known in the space of two days.</margin>mass of the earth in 60 hours—that is, in a space of two days and 12 hours—whatever happens in the whole world could be known. And perhaps by this method we could come to know the longitude of regions, as we shall say elsewhere.

# Book IX. Musical Cryptology.

When <term>Cryptology</term><note>The art of hidden or secret communication.</note> is to be established over a relatively short distance, it can easily be achieved using instruments described in the art of <term>Echotectonica</term><note>original: "Echotectonica"; Kircher’s term for "echo-architecture," or the engineering of sound and acoustics within buildings.</note>. These consist primarily of pipes of all kinds—straight, conical, elliptical, and spiral—conducted from place to place through hidden passages. By their help, two Princes can reveal whatever they wish to each other, even when absent from one another, as if they were present together. However, since I have already described the construction and use of all these acoustic instruments most precisely in the aforementioned art of Echotectonica, I have judged it superfluous to deal with them here at length with tedious repetition; for the reader will be able to derive countless other things pertaining to this subject from the instruments already cited.

Furthermore, all the musical instruments discussed in the preceding sections can serve this Cryptology. Indeed, as many differences as there are in sounds, so many ways can there be to reveal one's thoughts to another. For the sound of pipes, cymbals, bells, strings, and the human voice (whether simple or singing) can be used as signals. To provide an introduction to this matter, let the alphabet be divided into six rows, assigning four letters to each row; you will then assign a specific type of sound to each row, as is shown in the following table.

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Pipe** | A | B | C | D | } Order 1. |
| | O | O | O | O | |
| **Cymbal** | E | F | G | H | } Order 2. |
| | O | O | O | O | |
| **Little Bell** | I | K | L | M | } Order 3. |
| | O | O | O | O | |
| **String** | N | O | P | Q | } Order 4. |
| | O | O | O | O | |
| **Clapper** | R | S | T | V | } Order 5. |
| | O | O | O | O | |
| **Voice** | W | X | Y | Z | } Order 6. |
| | O | O | O | O | |

<margin>A method for secret manifestation.</margin> The use of this alphabet is as follows. Suppose these words are to be signaled to a friend: *Come quickly* <note>original: "Veni cito"</note>. Since the first letter of the word *Veni* is V, and V holds the fourth position in the fifth row of letters, four strikes of the <term>clapper</term><note>original: "crepitaculum"; a percussion instrument like a rattle or wooden clapper.</note> will represent V. E, the second letter of the word, is contained in the second row of letters (corresponding to the cymbals) and occupies the first position; this signifies that one strike of the cymbal should be given. N, indeed, holds the first place in the fourth row of letters [signified by the string]. Finally, I, corresponding to number 1 in the third series of letters, will instruct you to give one strike of the little bell to signify I. Thus you see that the letter C signifies three sounds of the pipe; I signifies one strike of the little bell; T signifies three sounds of the clapper; and finally, the letter O signifies two strikes of a string. In this way, you may signal anything you like. The white circles in the table represent a board equipped with holes, so that as soon as you hear a specific sound, you may mark the place with a peg, arranging the individual tablets in order.

Furthermore, you can combine all the instruments listed in the previous table into one very simple instrument consisting of four handles. Since you can produce the sound of pipes with your mouth, you need not be forced to add bellows to the instrument. The first handle will serve for striking the cymbal; the second for the bell; the third for the string; and the fourth for the rattle.

From these examples, it is clear that an alphabet can be constructed in which each of the twenty-four letters corresponds to different types of sound, so that for any specific type of sound, a letter is immediately recognized. However, since all these matters are too minor to be explained at greater length, let us leave them to be refined by others.

## §. II.
## Musical Steganography.

Another form of <term>Musical Steganography</term><note>The practice of hiding a secret message within a musical composition.</note> consists of an impenetrable method of writing using musical characters, and it is multi-faceted. First, all the keyboards (or <term>tastaturæ</term><note>From the Italian "tastatura," meaning the keys or fingerboard of a musical instrument.</note>) of the aforementioned instruments can serve this purpose, so that individual letters written on the keys correspond to the individual letters of the alphabet. This can also be done through musical notes, and again by the ascent and descent of the notes—yet in such a way that <term>breves</term><note>original: "breues"; a long note value in early music notation.</note> denote an ascent and <term>semibreves</term><note>original: "semibreues"; a shorter note value.</note> a descent, as seen in the following example.

## P R E F A C E.

<note>A large decorative square woodcut initial 'V' featuring scrolling floral and leaf patterns.</note>

While the ancients were carefully contemplating that admirable order in the universe of things and the great majesty of nature, they found themselves unable to do anything but believe in a Divinity <note>original Latin: *Numen*</note>. They saw the mechanism of the world constructed with such an admirable succession of events, and with such remarkable wisdom and foresight. However, as they were deprived of the light of faith, they fell into various errors and gave birth to various and utterly discordant monsters of the intellect. For some, thinking the world itself to be a certain great God and Spirit <note>original Latin: *Daemonem*</note>, worshiped it in place of the true Divinity. Others believed in a Spirit or <term>World-Soul</term> <note>original Latin: *Anima mundi*; the philosophical concept that a rational soul animates the entire physical universe just as a soul animates a human body</note> permeating and constituting all things by its own power. Some even fashioned a <term>Calchodea</term> <note>A term used in Hermetic and Neoplatonic philosophy to refer to a presiding spirit or "Guardian of the Worldly Ideas" that distributes forms to material things</note>—that is, a Governor of worldly Ideas—bestowing their forms upon all things.

<summary>This page introduces Book X, where Kircher argues that the universe is a musical instrument designed by God. He begins the preface by discussing how ancient philosophers recognized the divine order of the world but, lacking Christian revelation, mistakenly deified the world or invented spirits like the World-Soul.</summary>

...they said; We, however, investigating the nature of things and its innermost recesses somewhat more deeply, have found that this **world-soul**—or as the Arabs call it, the **Calchodea**—is nothing other than Nature itself, the true and unique **art of God** <note>original: *τέχνην τοῦ θεοῦ*</note>, who establishes all things through it. We assert that its power, which permeates all things, is nothing other than an **adapting and arranging power** <note>original: *δύναμιν ἁρμόζουσαν*</note>—namely, a **harmonic proportion by which all things are disposed and preserved; the sole cause and origin of all the wondrous effects and operations hidden within the womb of nature.** 

And so that the target of our intention may become clearer and clearer, we have progressed through every grade of natural beings, showing that the hidden harmonies and discords of things—the laws of hatred and friendship by which individuals are joined in a friendly gathering or separated in an unfriendly one—consist of the consonant and the dissonant. We show that these things possess their own harmonic ratios, which, if you were to separate them from Nature, would necessarily cause all things to collapse into a confused chaos and an abyss of nothingness.

Here the curious reader will find **the causes of the powers of stones, herbs, animals, and their affections detected, and a door opened to a new workshop of Natural Magic, which, by applying consonances to dissonances in all things, produces stupendous effects**; thus, he will find almost nothing in the entire womb of nature so hidden or abstruse that it will remain concealed from him with the help of this book, or by which he cannot perform wonders.

We have called it the **Decachordon** <note>A "Ten-stringed instrument," usually referring to the biblical ten-stringed lute or psaltery mentioned in the Psalms.</note>, so that we might more perfectly contemplate the harmony of natural things set out in a ten-fold order. This is expressed through ten strings in a perfectly arranged lute, or as ten registers in a ten-piped organ. Thus, having been raised higher through the contemplation of worldly harmony, we might finally rest most sweetly in the unison of such an admirable and incomprehensible **Organ-Player** <note>original: *Organædi*</note>—in God, I say, the center of all harmony.

# PART I.
## THE TEN-PIPED ORGAN.
### CHAPTER I.
#### GOD, the Best and Greatest, is compared to an Organist; the World is compared to an Organ.

<note>A large ornamental square woodcut initial 'M' is decorated with intricate scrolling foliage and floral motifs, common in 17th-century printing to mark the start of a major section.</note>

THAT GREAT and incomprehensible GOD from eternity, before any condition of created nature, was most sufficient unto Himself alone. He was compelled by no necessity or need, but solely from the abundance of His infinite goodness, to show the infinite riches of His glory and bounty, He was pleased to establish the world in time. He arranged it not in a confused order of things, nor by some rash efficiency of beings, but by a certain supreme and ineffable providence, so that man—the son of the world—contemplating the **Cosmos** <note>original: *κόσμον*; meaning the "ornament" or the "order of all things connected by an inviolable law"</note> of this machine, might recognize the Author of inexhaustible power. By recognizing Him, man might wonder; by wondering, he might desire; by desiring, he might love; and by loving and worshipping Him, he might finally possess Him eternally. **The order and beauty of the World, therefore, is a certain Idea of the divinity, displaying that Idea of Ideas which enfolds all things most perfectly; it is that Monad** <note>The "Monad" refers to the number one, representing unity and the source of all other numbers and proportions.</note> **which involves the proportion of all numbers within the ineffable amplitude of its center.** And just as He is the number of infinite perfection, He willed to show all things disposed in **number**; as **weight**, He willed to show all things in weight—that is, the multitude and variety of scattered things drawn into one as if to a center of gravity; and finally as **measure**, He willed to show every single thing adorned with a certain infinite symmetry and harmonic proportion. He did this so that there might be a perpetual love, agreement, and consensus of created things, both with their Author and among themselves—a symphony most absolute in all its numbers. Since, therefore, **Music or harmony is nothing other than number,**

...number, measure, and weight, as has been shown extensively in the preceding pages. Furthermore, the world, according to the testimony of Plato, is a **harmony holding all things together** <note>original Greek: *ἁρμονία πάντα κατέχουσα*</note>. Indeed, Nature is the art of God, a **fitting power** <note>original Greek: *vis ἁρμόζουσα*</note> that adapts all things. Since the world is also a perfect likeness of God, it necessarily follows that according to the likeness and analogy of that Archetypal harmony, the **cosmos** <note>original Greek: *κόσμον*, meaning the world as an ordered system</note>—that is, the harmonic world—was established. It follows that Nature, as the art of God, has looked toward musical proportions in all worldly operations. However, lest the assertion of our contemplation seem vain or idle, let us now show how God, the Creator of all things and the **Master Organ-Player** <note>original Latin: *Organædus*</note>, played during that primeval origin of things.

<margin>God as the Organ-Player.</margin>
Therefore, just as a craftsman about to build an Organ first lays down various foundations as the first rough elements of the work, then fashions pipes of every kind, arranges the channels that conduct the air and wind, and adapts various rules—which the common people call **Registers** <note>Also known as "stops" on an organ, which control the variety of sounds</note>—to demonstrate a greater variety of harmony; and afterwards organizes the bellows as certain receptacles of the winds, by whose perpetual motion the air is constricted and forced into the wind-channels to be supplied; and finally, he arranges the **Keyboard** <note>original: *Clauiarium*</note> as the ultimate director of his art; and at last, with the help of his fingers and the various combinations of the registers, striking the keys—which they call *tasti*—he produces that variety of harmony which we perceive with admiration in organs. In a not dissimilar manner, God, the Best and Greatest, being about to fashion this worldly organ with an inexhaustible variety of the dissonant-consonant, did, by the Word of His power, first establish that formless **matter** <margin>The production of Hyle (Matter).</margin> <note>original Greek: *hylen*</note> and indigestible chaos, as the foundations and preludes of the future organ. Then, He sketched out the pipes as certain rough drafts of forms lying hidden in that formless chaos. Thirdly, by the Spirit of His divinity brooding over the formless waters, He brought forth the air and winds necessary for the future organ by blowing (so to speak). Fourthly, He arranged that formless mass of matter, imbued by His Spirit with various differences of sounds, into different classes of things as if into certain registers. Fifthly, He produced the Keyboard of the entire organ as a kind of soul and His own art—that is, Nature, implanted in individual things. And finally, when the work was perfected, that **Supreme Musician** <note>original: *Archimusus*</note>, urging the keyboard (that is, His art) by the breath of His spirit animating the organ, produced that admirable harmony of things which we admire to this very day; but let us see how He produced it.

<margin>The Register or Prelude of the first day.</margin>
And so, as soon as the first Register of this organ—like the **lowest note of the scale** <note>original: *proslambanomenōn*, the fundamental note in the ancient Greek musical system</note>—was opened and sounded by the Word of His power; behold, the **Empyrean Heaven** <note>The highest heaven, believed to be the realm of pure fire and the dwelling place of God</note> was filled with an innumerable variety of blessed minds distributed into nine orders of choirs. What did this present but a kind of **ten-stringed instrument** <note>original: *decachordon*</note> or a certain harmonic scale? Its nine strings denote the distinct Choirs of Angels, while the tenth denotes the **Leader of the Choir** <note>original: *Choragum*</note>, God Himself, the Best and Greatest, the celestial Apollo and the ultimate completion of the entire harmony in the number ten. What did the Earth, together with that Light created on the first day, intimate, if not a certain first prelude of the variety of forms soon to be introduced into matter? Yet, because the lower part of this Register resonated with I-know-not-what unpleasantness due to a confused melody, it had not yet acquired the perfection due to it.

<margin>The Register or prelude of the second day.</margin>
Behold, as soon as the Register of the second day was opened and sounded by the Word of His power and the breath of the Holy Spirit, the Waters were immediately segregated from the waters and enclosed in the channels of the earth; the Dry Land was uncovered and detected; and the air, stretched far and wide in 그 expansion of space, displayed a beautiful **stage** <note>original: *proscenium*</note>. In a word, the primordial nature of the Elements and their neat connection brought forth a certain new harmony; yet, since the intended perfection of the harmony was not yet consistent with itself:

<margin>The Register or prelude of the third day.</margin>
Behold, the third Register was opened and sounded by the Word of His power and the cooperation of the breath of the Holy Spirit. Behold, the Earth, struck by the art of the Organ-Player, germinated an innumerable variety of herbs, plants, trees, seeds, flowers, and fruits. What else did this exhibit but just as many different melodies of divine art in such a great diversity of natures—which, although dissonant, were nevertheless consonant in their beautiful mixture?

<margin>The Register or prelude of the fourth day.</margin>
Furthermore, the fourth Register was opened and sounded by the Word of His power and the breath of the Holy Spirit: behold the Heaven, the Sun, the Moon, and the Planets, emerging as if from a certain chamber...

But so that the supreme <term>Organ-player<note>Latin: "Organædus"; here referring to God as the performer of the "World Organ."</note></term> might vary and increase the equipment of worldly harmony:

You have here, then, the preludes of the 6 Registers of created things, corresponding beautifully to the <term>six days of creation<note>original: "hexamero"; the Hexameron refers to the biblical six days of creation.</note></term>. But just as organists, after the preludes of the individual registers have been properly performed, arrange all the registers together to exhibit the universal harmony of all the pipes at once; so that eternal <term>Master Musician<note>original: "Archimusicus"</note></term>, after the six preludes of created things, produced Man—the most excellent of corporeal creatures. Opening all the Registers of the world-organ, He performed a prelude of universal harmony in him, as if in the measure and end of all things. For besides his soul, which is heaped with so many gifts of grace and nature, God also fashioned his body with such symmetry and proportion that the concords divided among the individual classes of created things seem to be collected in a single human being, as if in a compendium and <term>recapitulation<note>original: "anacephaleosi"; from the Greek 'anakephalaiosis,' meaning a summing up or bringing together under one head.</note></term> of the greater world. We have seen, therefore, curious Reader, the fabric of the world-organ; we have considered the arrangement of the Registers, the paths of the winds, and the variety of the pipes; and we have listened to the Organ-player's inimitable skill in playing and his wonderful concord. Nothing further remains, therefore, except that we search a little more deeply into the harmonies and concords hidden in the individual classes of created things. And so that we may proceed with harmonic order, we shall follow the order of the 10 registers—that is, the order of the 10 distinct types of beings which represent to us nothing other than a certain <term>ten-stringed instrument of nature<note>original: "decachordum sive decaulum"; 'Decachord' refers to a ten-stringed lute or harp.</note></term>. We shall clearly demonstrate that in each of these, God and His art, Nature, have looked toward harmonic proportions and forms.

### Of the Four Elements

Since the four Elements hold the lowest place in this organ of the world, we must rightly discuss their Symphonism in the first place, as if it were the <term>lowest note of all<note>original: "ὑπατάτω" (hypatato); in the ancient Greek musical system, this was the name for the lowest string or note of a tetrachord.</note></term>. # The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

A certain celestial Apollo, according as he strikes with his <term>plectrum<note>A small flat tool used to pluck the strings of a musical instrument.</note></term>—that is, through the various vibrations of his rays—awakens different harmonies in the lower world. These things are so true that Vitruvius himself considered this contemplation a great secret of nature to be left to posterity; indeed, he asserted in these words that the diversity of human voices arises solely from the different constitutions of the climate.

> *For in those places where the sun pours forth vapors in moderation, it preserves bodies in a temperate state; but where it burns nearby in its course, it snatches away and dries up the temperate moisture. Conversely, in regions with cooled vapors because they are far from the south, the moisture is not exhausted by heat; instead, the dewy air from the sky pours moisture into bodies, producing larger frames and higher-pitched [acute] sounds of the voice. For this reason, nations in the north are nourished with massive bodies, fair complexions, straight red hair, blue-gray eyes, and much blood, because they are shaped by the fullness of moisture and the coolness of the sky. However, those closest to the southern axis and subjected to the sun's path are produced with smaller bodies, dark complexions, curly hair, black eyes, weak legs, and little blood by the force of the sun.*

And a little later, he says:

> *Therefore, since we hold this certain in our minds, if a line is drawn from the edge in the northern region to that which is above the southern axis, and another oblique line from there to the highest point at the summit, we will undoubtedly perceive that therein lies the scheme of the "world-triangle," like the instrument the Greeks call the <term>sambuca<note>An ancient triangular stringed instrument, similar to a small harp, known for its high, shrill tone.</note></term>. Thus, because the space closest to the bottom of the strings is from the axis line in the southern borders, those nations, due to the shortness of the height relative to the world, produce a thin [acute] vocal sound, just like the highest-pitched string in an instrument closest to the angle. Following this, the other nations up to central Greece produce sounds at more relaxed [lower] intervals. Likewise, increasing in order from the middle to the far north, the voices of nations are expressed by nature with heavier [grave] sounds due to the height of the sky. Thus, the entire conception of the world seems to be most harmoniously composed through the sun's temperament, according to the inclination of the sky.*

Thus says Vitruvius. But so that these things may be better and more clearly perceived, I have decided to demonstrate that triangle, or "harmonic sambuca," a little more extensively.

Therefore, to show the differences in the vocal sounds of various nations, Vitruvius, having established the horizon, creates a certain diagram in the likeness of the instrument the Greeks call the *sambuca*—namely, a triangular one equipped with strings, shaped much like our own Harps. The sum of it is this: those for whom the northern pole [axis] of the world is less elevated above the horizon have a higher and more subtle voice than those for whom the same pole is higher, for these latter have a deeper and lower sound of the voice.

<note>A circular geometric diagram titled "Vitruvian Heptachord" (Heptachordon Vitruuianum). A semicircle is divided by degree marks (10 through 80) and letters. Below the horizontal diameter line AEC, there is a triangular structure labeled with letters (H, I, N, M) and a point F at the bottom, creating a harp-like shape (the Sambuca) that relates the pole's altitude to a musical scale.</note>

We demonstrate this according to Vitruvius's mind as follows. Let the meridian circle be ABC, the center of the world E, the horizon AEC, and the north pole F. Let a perpendicular FH fall from F to the horizon AC, and let a line FE be drawn from F to the center E; thus the triangle FHE will be formed. Again...

# Book X. The Nature of the Ten-Stringed Instrument

From the pole raised at G, let another perpendicular line GI descend to the horizon AC, and let another line drawn from G to E close the triangle GIE. I say that those for whom the pole is higher at F have a sharper voice than those for whom the same pole is at point G. Let line EH be drawn within the larger triangle GIH, and let it there be called MH; it is certain that line GI is longer than line MN. If, therefore, line GI were the string of an instrument, it would produce a deeper and lower sound than string MN, which, because it is closer to the angle and therefore shorter, will also make a sharper sound. Thus, the individual <term>sines<note>In this context, the vertical lines representing the elevation or height within the geometric diagram.</note></term> of the polar elevations fitted within the triangle correspond to the strings of the <term>Sambuca<note>An ancient triangular stringed instrument, similar to a harp or lyre.</note></term>; the voices of people born under various climates are entirely in harmony with these, according to the mind of Vitruvius; see the figure added here.

But when I considered this ingenious fabrication of Vitruvius a little more deeply, I saw that while it holds much agreement with reality, for the most part it cannot stand, since experience teaches us that sharp, deep, and temperate voices are found under one and the same climate. Indeed, under the equator, where Vitruvius placed the <term>Nete<note>The highest note in the ancient Greek musical system (the *systema teleion*).</note></term>—that is, the maximum sharpness of harmonic voices—experience teaches that men mostly have the thickest and dullest voices, as seen in New Spain <note>Mexico and Central America</note> and other parts subject to the Torrid Zone. In the Frigid Zone, however, men mostly have the sharpest voices, as is apparent among the <term>Laplanders, Icelanders, and Skridfinns<note>The 'Scrikfinni' or 'Skridfinns' was a historical name for the Sami people of Northern Scandinavia.</note></term>. For although these cold parts have much moisture, as Vitruvius rightly notes, the cold there has joined to it a certain parching power by which bodies are not only constricted but also entirely dried out, which a sharp voice necessarily follows. But the Torrid Zone, while having maximum heat, also has maximum moisture due to frequent rains, rivers, vast lakes, and the proximity of the ocean; certainly, it is so far from producing sharp voices that it instead produces dull and deep ones. Truly, this error is easily forgiven in Vitruvius (as he had no knowledge of these zones in his time), and he is to be highly praised for rightly attributing the cause of the sharpness and depth of voices to dryness, heat, cold, and moisture. Therefore, let us arrange this harmony of the terrestrial world differently.

I say first that all places on earth imbued with moderate moisture and cold generate deep and profound voices, while those excelling in dryness and heat generate high and sharp voices, regardless of the specific climate. Thus, the <term>Portuguese<note>original: "Lusitani"</note></term>, despite being further south, have a deeper voice than the <term>Castilians<note>original: "Castellani"</note></term>; for no other reason than that Portugal is more humid than the mountainous region of Castile. For this reason, sulfurous and dry lands like Sicily and Calabria produce much sharper voices than the humid Roman countryside, not because they are further south, but because of the dry and hot condition of the soil. Therefore, the diverse constitution and unique property of horizons is the sole cause of the diversity of voices, if indeed it is to be taken from the four elementary qualities.

<margin>The cause of the diversity of voices in different Regions.</margin>

But since the combination of these qualities in the generation of the voice was discussed most extensively in the first book, we refer the reader there. In this way, through eight combinations, we can derive eight different intensities of the voices of the inhabitants of the earth, which indeed correspond perfectly to the degrees of one <term>octave<note>original: "diapason"</note></term>. For first, those who are born in the most humid and simultaneously coldest places, such as those born and living near lakes and stagnant marshes enclosed within mountains, acquire a thick and profound voice, such as the <term>hypate<note>The lowest string/note in the ancient Greek octave.</note></term> is in the eight-stringed scale; for cold in a humid environment is the greatest expander of the limbs. Second, those who are born and raised in the hottest and driest places have a very high, shrill voice, similar to eunuchs, such as the <term>Nete</term> is in the eight-stringed scale. Those who are born in the most temperate places acquire a perfectly temperate voice from the hot, dry, moist, and cold, corresponding to the <term>Mese<note>The "middle" note of the ancient scale, serving as the functional center.</note></term> in the octave. Those born in places approaching more heat and dryness, but retaining some degrees of cold and moisture, acquire a voice corresponding to the <term>Parhypate<note>The note just above the lowest note.</note></term> and <term>Hypomese<note>A note below the middle.</note></term>; likewise, those who approach more cold and moisture while retaining some degrees of heat and dryness acquire a voice corresponding to the <term>Hypoparanete<note>A note below the next-to-highest.</note></term> and <term>Paranete<note>The note next to the highest.</note></term>. See the following diagram.

# The Great Art of Consonance ⊕ Dissonance

<note>A marginal diagram shows a right-angled triangle with its vertex at G and its base at AC. Multiple lines radiate from vertex G to various points along the base, each labeled with terms from the ancient Greek musical scale: Nete, Paranete, Hypoparanete, Paramese, Mese, Hypomese, Parhypate, and Hypate. This geometric model represents the "Vitruvian instrument" mentioned in the text, illustrating how geographical latitude relates to musical pitch.</note>
In this way, the Vitruvian instrument can be understood; where it must also be noted that the individual climates of the temperate zone have this quality: they sharpen or dull voices depending on whether they have a greater or lesser latitude. Thus in Germany, because of the cold, the <term>hypate<note>original: "hypate"; the lowest note in the ancient Greek tetrachord system.</note></term> in human voices is usually a whole tone deeper than the Italian *hypate*, and consequently the entire system of the octave or <term>diapason<note>The Greek term for an octave.</note></term> follows suit. The same is to be understood for the rest. Indeed, for these reasons, this system undergoes change according to the different seasons of the year; since in winter it turns out much lower than in summer.

For as Vitruvius rightly observes, this kind of variation is noted even in instruments themselves; for two baked clay cups, one of which is less fired than the other and consequently holds more moisture, also allow for a notable variety in sounding; which experience forces us to admit in strings and sinews as well.

<margin>The variation of the tone, which the <term>Chorister<note>original: "Chorista"; likely referring to the standard pitch used by choir masters or musicians.</note></term> commonly calls "pitch," in different regions.</margin>
But why we experience the exact opposite in artificial sounds is worthy of the greatest wonder. For it is known that here in Rome, organs and harpsichords are tuned a whole tone lower than in Naples; in Florence, they are a semitone deeper than Roman instruments; but in Venice, they are tuned a whole <term>ditone<note>A major third, or two whole tones.</note></term> higher than the Neapolitan ones. We attribute the cause of this thing in places so close together not so much to the nature of the locations, but to long-standing custom; for this matter can depend on the temperament of men, some of whom are moved by higher melodies, others by lower ones. This is clearly evident in the ancient peoples of Greece—the Aeolians, Dorians, and Ionians—who, just as they differed in customs and temperament, also disagreed in the quality of their music. The Dorians observed a grave manner of singing, the Lydians a cheerful and sharp one, and the Phrygians a softer one, as has been explained at length in the preceding books. Having seen, therefore, the harmony that the diverse disposition of the earth brings to things, we must now also see what <term>Symphonism<note>A term for the harmonious blending or agreement of different elements.</note></term> the four Elements obtain when conspiring together.

# SYMPHONISM
### of the IV Elements.

Various authors explain the harmony of the four elements in different ways. Alchemists report it by this example: they extract the spirit from wine, then the oil that is innate to the spirit, thirdly the phlegm, after which the dregs remain, which they call the <term>caput mortuum<note>Literally "dead head"; the useless residue left over after distillation or sublimation.</note></term>. These, enclosed in a hermetically sealed glass, are continuously distinguished into five distinct regions, as it were. The lowest of these, being black, represents Earth; the next, an aqueous substance extracted, represents Water; the subtle and spiritual part represents Air; and finally, the fourth, oily and flammable, represents Fire. Above all these floats a certain "fifth essence" <note>the *quinta essentia* or quintessence</note>, far removed from all impurity and the dregs of earthly contagion, representing Heaven. These, by a certain harmonic analogy, surpass one another according to the degrees of being proper to each, so that they closely express harmonic intervals; and they claim the created world was made according to this model of art and nature, as will be shown more fully hereafter.

Others compare the whole world to a harmonic <term>monochord<note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical relationships between musical intervals.</note></term>, in which the spirit or soul of the world—or better, God Himself—placed outside the monochord, produces all consonances. He makes the voices sharper in creatures that are closer to Him, and deeper in those that are more remote from Him. Thus, the deepest voice, approaching more toward silence, darkness, and the horror of matter because of the excessive density of the air and the resistance of the spirit, can represent the Earth. For they maintain that Light acts upon the matter of the world in the same way that the human spirit acts upon the air. They say the string is the matter of the world, and the instrument is the <term>mega-cosmic<note>Referring to the "great world" or universe as a whole.</note></term> monochord, in which the harmonic degrees perfectly reflect the arrangement of the harmonic scale. Thus <term>Robert Fludd<note>original: "Robertus de fluctibus"; a prominent English Paracelsian physician and mystic known for his complex diagrams of the macrocosm and microcosm.</note></term> places cold, thickness, and weight in the earth, which relate to the cold and matter of the lowest region extending all the way to the Moon as 4 to 3, which is the pro-

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

...the <term>sesquitertia proportion<note>original: "portio sesquitertia"; a ratio of 4:3, which in music corresponds to the interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term>, because in this region a fourth part of light and color is present; and let a <term>diatessaron<note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term> be formed from water, air, and fire. The earth holds itself as the Greek letter Gamma (Γ) does on the <term>monochord<note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical musical ratios.</note></term>, like the number one in arithmetic, and a point in geometry. To better explain these proportions, one might imagine a double pyramid—one luminous or "formal," the other "material"—inserted into each other in such a way that the luminous pyramid has its base fixed in the Empyrean heaven, while its tip reaches down to the earth. The dark pyramid, however, fixes its base upon the earth and its tip in the Empyrean. These two intersect around the sphere of the Sun, creating a wondrous mixture and equality of light and darkness through a continuous harmonic progression. 

In this arrangement, there is one whole tone from the earth to the water, another from the water to the air, and a <term>semitone<note>A half-step in music.</note></term> from the air to the fire (which is nothing other than the highest peak of the air). From the fire to the Sun, three more tones are established; a semitone is formed from the Moon to Mercury, from there to Venus, and finally from there to the Sun. Thus, the interval between the earth and the Sun consists of five tones and two semitones, creating an octave or <term>diapason<note>original: "diapason"; the interval of an octave, composed of a perfect fourth (diatessaron) and a perfect fifth (diapente).</note></term> in the sphere of equality, just as if a string were divided in half. From the Sun to the Empyrean, he imagines another "spiritual" octave; and so he composes the entire world from a double octave, both material and formal. These are subordinated to one another so perfectly that they represent the system of a musical scale, or a <term>pentadecachordon<note>A fifteen-stringed musical scale used in ancient Greek theory.</note></term>. When this scale is struck by the hand of God, it excites certain wondrous harmonies between both worlds, the figure of which you may contemplate in the final register.

When the ancients looked upon the elemental world and saw it was constituted from a certain "concordant discord," and perceived a wonderful temperament of diverse qualities, they compared the elements to a <term>tetrachord<note>A series of four notes.</note></term>. For Orpheus, as <term>Bryennius<note>Manuel Bryennius, a 14th-century Byzantine music theorist who preserved ancient Greek musical knowledge.</note></term> testifies, constructed a four-stringed Lyre after this model and arranged all its sounds according to the steps of the perfect fourth. The first string, the <term>hypate<note>The lowest note of the tetrachord.</note></term>, represented the Earth; the second, the <term>parhypate</term>, represented Water; the third, the <term>paranete</term>, represented Air; and the fourth, the <term>nete<note>The highest note of the tetrachord.</note></term>, represented Fire, as is clear in the diagram.

<note>A schematic diagram illustrates the correspondence between musical notes and the four elements. Four horizontal lines connect the names of the notes on the left to the elements on the right: The Nete corresponds to Fire, the Paranete to Air, the Parhypate to Water, and the Hypate to Earth.</note>

Thus, the first and deepest note is analogous to the earth, while the fourth and highest is analogous to fire; the second to water, and the third to air. Just as among the elements there are two heavy and two light, and one is heavier or lighter than the other, so in the said tetrachord there are two low sounds and two high, and one is lower or higher than the other. Again, just as the four elements, changed this way and that toward one another, acquire various thicknesses, temperaments, and qualities—from which the different species of things emerge—so in the said tetrachord, the sounds changed and compared to each other produce various differences in tone. Furthermore, just as three intervals are recognized in the four elements, from which the mutations and qualities of physical forms are born, so too in the tetrachord of four tones, various forms of consonances arise. This is evident in the fourfold division of the seasons, in which this elemental tetrachord, struck by the <term>plectrum<note>A small tool used to pluck a stringed instrument.</note></term> of Apollo, provides that harmony and "symphonism" which we experience with wonder every year in the generation of things and the production of other effects. Though this tetrachord is discordant and devoid of harmony by itself, as soon as those radiant fingers of Apollo strike and stir it, it immediately exhibits a marvelous harmony, joining consonants with dissonances so that entirely disparate and contrary things nevertheless run together into a single composition with a wonderful concord and friendship.

Furthermore, when Pythagoras examined this harmonic secret a little more deeply, he finally found nature hidden with truly wonderful skill in the five regular bodies. For he found the harmony of the earth in the "harmonic cube"; for the cube has six flat faces;

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>A marvelous comparison of the cube to musical proportions.</margin> It has 8 solid angles, 24 plane angles, and 12 lines. Within these, 12 to 6 creates a <term>diapason<note>The musical interval of an octave, representing a 2:1 ratio.</note></term>; 8 to 12 a <term>diapente<note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth, representing a 3:2 ratio.</note></term>; 6 to 8 a <term>diatessaron<note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth, representing a 4:3 ratio.</note></term>; 24 to 6 a <term>disdiapason<note>A double octave, representing a 4:1 ratio.</note></term>; and 24 to 8 a diapason with a diapente <note>An octave plus a fifth, or a perfect twelfth, representing a 3:1 ratio.</note>. Thus, the entire series of musical harmonies is found within this single body. This should not seem strange to anyone, for within the earth—serving as the foundation and base—lie the <term>proslambanomena<note>original: "proslambanomena"; in the Ancient Greek musical system, this was the lowest note of the scale, providing the foundation for all other intervals.</note></term> and the harmonic seeds of all things to be generated, as shall be said later. Just as in a <term>polychord<note>An instrument with many strings.</note></term> all the strings acquire a certain relationship by being tuned to the first, so do the remaining elements relate to the earth.

Furthermore, he <note>Likely referring to a philosopher like Plato or a generic "Geometer."</note> discovered Fire within the Pyramid <note>The tetrahedron, the four-sided Platonic solid.</note>, for it consists of 4 sides and 4 solid angles. It also has 12 plane angles, from which arises a certain simpler nature that we observe in fire. For 4 to 4 constitutes a <term>unison</term>, and 4 to 12 a diapason with a diapente, through which the sharpness or subtlety of this harmony is understood. In the Octahedron, he found the harmony of Air; it consists of 8 solid angles, just as many sides, and 24 plane angles. Finally, in the Icosahedron of 20 sides, 12 solid angles, and 36 plane angles, he found the nature of Water, as will be discussed in what follows. The harmonic proportions of these bodies are gathered in relation to one another as follows: the Octahedron compared to the Pyramid is a <term>duple proportion<note>2:1 ratio.</note></term> in its sides; a <term>sesquialter<note>3:2 ratio.</note></term> in its solid angles, and duple in its plane angles, from which emerge the harmonies of the octave and the fifth. The proportion of the Pyramid to the Cube is sesquialter in its sides and duple in its angles, again establishing the fifth and the octave. The Cube has a <term>triple proportion<note>3:1 ratio.</note></term> to the Icosahedron in its sides, a <term>sesquitertia<note>4:3 ratio.</note></term> in its bases, and a sesquialter in its angles, from which emerge the twelfth, the fifth, and the fourth. You see, therefore, that the closer these bodies approach the earth, the greater the harmony of properties born within them. Thus you see the Cube and Icosahedron—which represent Earth and Water, female and male—swelling with harmonic seeds: the "bed of the Nymphs" <note>original: "cubile Nympharum"; a poetic reference to the fertile union of earth and water.</note>, most fit for the generation of things. Hence, the inscription of the Icosahedron within the Cube represents the most fruitful marriage of water and earth for the purpose of generating all life.

We have shown the harmony of the elements according to the analogy of the proportions shining forth within them; now it remains to declare that sensible "symphonism" of the elements, by which they harmonize with one another truly and realistically. For it is certain that from the various agitations of the elements, a sensible harmony is born according to the condition of the bodies striking one another. For what else does the earth represent to us but a kind of pipe organ, equipped with hidden channels like pipes? Through these narrow passages, that fiery spirit <note>Kircher often uses "spiritus" to refer to geological gases or pneumatic forces.</note> diffused throughout the entire body of the earth rushes with force. It acts just like the wind in our artificial organs, producing deep sounds mixed with high ones depending on whether the passages are wide or narrow. I first became aware of this kind of music during those wonderful earthquakes in Calabria in 1638. As the force of the trapped spirits shook the mountainsides and escaped through whatever "gate" was opened, I heard sounds sometimes like a trumpet, sometimes like the murmurs of echoing waters, occasionally like violent thunder, and at other times like the wailing of men or the whistling of winds. The <term>Catadupae<note>Great waterfalls or cataracts.</note></term> of water within the bowels of the mountains are also the cause of that prodigious "concert" which, as was said above, history records as being heard at certain openings in the mountains. We shall assign the reasons for these more fully in our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo Nostro Subterraneo"; Kircher is referencing his own major work on geology and the earth's interior.</note>.

Furthermore, the perpetual agitations of the earth and water establish another kind of harmony. As they perpetually strike the shores, they create a harmony determined by the size of the caverns and channels, which history says various sea coasts exhibit. Thus the shores of the Aegean Sea, according to the testimony of Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note>, give off the sound of a <term>Cythara<note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre.</note></term>. The banks of certain islands produce the symphony of organs and every kind of pipe. The shores of the Baltic Sea, according to the testimony of Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus, a 16th-century Swedish writer.</note>, echo with the wailing of men. For as we have shown elsewhere, the hollows of coastal caves and grottoes pour forth every kind of harmony. If their capacity holds a ratio of 1 to 2, they will necessarily return an octave when struck by the waves and floods as if by a <term>plectrum<note>A pick used to pluck a stringed instrument.</note></term>. If 2 to 3, a fifth; if 3 to 4, a fourth; if 8 to 9, a whole tone; and so on for the rest. It is therefore no wonder that their murmur and noise, containing the hidden seeds of harmony within themselves, is pleasing to the ear.

Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature: 373

Furthermore, Air, sometimes with earth and sometimes with water, gives birth to various distinctions of harmonic sounds. When it is mixed through violent agitation with mountains, rocks, caves, narrow passages, trees, and the waves of the waters, it produces a marvelous harmony, as if from consonant and dissonant tones, and from deep and high voices. This is first evident in the narrow passes of mountains of various sizes, where the wind, striking them in different ways, displays a wonderful variety of sounds. Thus, on Mount Etna, near certain cavernous cliffs, when the <term>South-east wind<note>original: "Euronotho"; the Euronotus is a classical name for the wind blowing from the south-east.</note></term> blows, a perpetual and harmonious whispering is perceived, just as if one were hearing strings stretched at intervals of the fifth, the third, and the octave. I remember observing the same thing in the sounds of trees of different sizes shaken by the wind. For if one tree is double the size of another, as is most apparent in Cypresses and Poplars, their whispers will express a <term>diapason<note>The musical interval of an octave, representing a 2:1 ratio.</note></term>; if one is to the other in a ratio of three to two, a <term>diapente<note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth, representing a 3:2 ratio.</note></term>; and so on for the others. The same usually happens in the proportion of the waves of the sea; indeed, in paper windows, when a certain wind blows, I excite a perpetual music by the benefit of the air alone in this manner:

<margin>A beautiful experiment</margin>
In a certain paper window, let any number of circles be formed in the same proportion as the diameters of the pipes of an organ have to one another—namely, as 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, 1 to 3, 1 to 4, and so on. Once this is done, let the circles drawn on the paper be very finely cut out, but with this caution: that they remain attached at some point. Let them be like certain "lips," plectrums, or tongues that form a voice by the collision of the wind, and the instrument will be ready. For when the wind strikes the said window, the "lip" within the circular slit, being set in motion, will soon return a certain tremulous sound. And since all the circles are shaped harmoniously, they will all together emit a harmonic sound, to the great admiration of those listening. The instrument of strings moved by the wind <note>A reference to the Aeolian Harp.</note>, which we described in the preceding pages, also belongs to this category. In <term>Aeolipiles<note>original: "Aeolijs... pilis"; these were hollow metal globes with a small hole, which, when filled with water and heated, produced a whistling sound from the escaping steam.</note></term> of different sizes, air agitated by the heat of fire excites a strange and harmonic noise. I could bring forth innumerable portents of this elementary symphony in this place, had I not demonstrated them everywhere throughout this whole work. Certainly, if our ear were placed in such a location that it could distinctly hear the roar of the winds and the Ocean striking the various shores of the lands, I say it would perceive nothing but a symphony perfect in every measure. Thus, we are incited by this to sing the praises of the Creator with unwearied labor, when we behold even the elements themselves harmonizing in a unanimous conspiracy to pay perpetual hymns to Almighty GOD their maker, as if with the four voices of bass, tenor, alto, and soprano.

# REGISTER II.
## The Symphony of the Heavens.

I undertake a truly arduous task as I attempt to investigate that musical harmony of the celestial bodies; a business attempted by many, yet performed correctly by no one until now, with everyone failing to grasp the symphonies of such unusual harmony. Certainly, the <term>Archetypal Ideas<note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, original patterns of all things existing in the mind of God.</note></term> of things necessarily persuade us that this world was composed with musical artistry. For since GOD is the harmonic Archetype of things, and wished to describe the species of individual things in this book of the universe in a rhythmic order, like certain poems, He seems to have busied Himself with this above all: that through this mundane organ—disposed in a due, most congruent order conforming to the <term>Harmostes<note>original: "Harmoştæ"; a Greek term meaning 'one who fits together' or an 'arranger,' here referring to God as the divine Tuner of the world.</note></term> (that is, the Fount of Ideas)—He might exhibit the said poems of most elegant music to the ears of mortals. Augustine, a great light of the Church, agrees with our words in these terms: *“God has made the order of the ages beautiful, like a most lovely poem, through the use of certain antitheses.”* And shortly after: *“Just as contraries opposed to contraries render the beauty of speech, so is the beauty of the age composed by a certain eloquence, not of words, but of things, through the opposition of contraries.”* He calls this world a certain poem and epigram, in which there are as many voices and things as there are antitheses; as many battles of things as there are contrarieties seen, according to that saying:

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

->*Within a single body*<-
->*Cold things fought with hot, moist with dry,*<-
->*Soft with hard, and weightless things with those having weight.*<-
<note>original: "Corpore in uno / Frigida pugnabant calidis, humentia siccis, / Mollia cum duris, sine pondere habentia pondus." These lines are from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* (1.18–20), describing the state of Chaos before the world was ordered by a divine hand.</note>

<margin>The Lyre imitates the harmony and music of the world.</margin>
There are, therefore, most elegant songs of things in this world: for the all-encompassing variety of contraries and their discord, arranged by the divine genius of the eternal craftsman and perfected by his numbers, renders a most concordant and sweet music to the eyes, just as another variety of words and a well-tempered discord of sounds renders music to the ears. <term>Quintilian<note>A Roman educator and rhetorician (c. 35–100 AD).</note></term> in Book 1, Chapter 6, says it was the opinion of <term>Pythagoras<note>The Greek philosopher who first proposed that the universe is governed by mathematical and musical ratios.</note></term> and all his followers that the World was composed according to musical reason, and that the lyre was subsequently made in imitation of it. Moreover, what this "Music of Things" might be—what their opposites are, what order they follow, what song they sing, and finally, what the beauty of the universe is—let anyone who has not yet seen it with their eyes perceive it with their ears as described by the most wise Seneca in these words:

<margin>The most beautiful structure of the universe is described by Seneca.</margin>
> Imagine, he says, O Marcia, that I am coming to give you counsel as you are being born. You are about to enter a City common to gods and men, embracing all things, bound by certain and eternal laws. You will see there innumerable stars; you will marvel that all things are filled by a single star, the sun, marking the spaces of day and night with his daily course, and dividing the year equally into summer and winter. You will see the nightly succession of the Moon, borrowing a gentle and diminished light from her brother's encounters; now hidden, now hanging over the earth with her full face, changeable in her waxings and wanings, always different from her nearest state. You will marvel at the gathered clouds, the falling waters, the slanting rivers, and the crashing of the heavens. When you have lowered your eyes to the earth, satisfied with the spectacle of higher things, another form of things will meet you, marvelous in a different way. Here is the spreading level of plains extending to infinity; there, the lofty peaks of mountains rising in great and wonderful ridges toward the sublime; the downward rush of rivers, and all of them flowing from a single source toward the East and the West; the nodding forests on the highest summits, and the singing of the woods with their animals, and the dissonant harmony of the birds. The various locations of cities, and nations secluded by the difficulty of their terrain, etc. And shortly after: What of the brightness of stones and gems? And the gold flowing among the sands of rapid torrents? And the glowing torches of fire in the midst of the lands, and again in the midst of the sea? <note>original: A paraphrase from Seneca the Younger’s *To Marcia, On Consolation*.</note>

<margin>Augustine’s words also on the beauty of the world.</margin>
Similar to these are the things which Saint Augustine wrote in *On True Religion*, Chapter 29: One ought not to look fruitlessly or in vain upon the beauty of the heaven, the order of the stars, the brightness of light, the vicissitudes of days and nights, the monthly courses of the moon, the fourfold tempering of the year congruent with the fourfold elements, the great power of seeds, the species and numbers of living things, and all things preserving their own measure and nature in their kind, etc. Again, <term>Tertullian<note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note></term>, in Book 1 *Against Marcion* before the middle, weighs how beautiful the order of the Universe is, how fit and excellently fabricated, so that philosophers, considering the magnitude, force, power, honor, beauty, wealth, faithfulness, and law of the elements, were at first struck with awe and hesitated to say that the world could exist without a divine mind.

<margin>Psalm 18.</margin>
Saint Augustine considered the order of the ages to be like a most beautiful poem, composed by God out of certain "antitheses" <note>The use of opposites in a composition to create beauty.</note> of honor; the beauty of the age is composed not of things, but of the eloquence of words. And so that we do not draw nothing from the sacred treasures, the royal Prophet <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note> clearly described this most orderly Music of the Universe and most elegant song of things in his own most elegant verses: *The heavens declare...* etc. Down to these words: *Their sound went out into all the earth,* or as the Hebrew texts have it: *Their line went out,* or *their measuring-rule.* <note>original: "Cœli enarrant" (Psalm 19:1, or 18:1 in the Vulgate). The author notes that where the Latin says "sound," the Hebrew *qaw* implies a "measuring line," suggesting the world is built to a precise architectural and musical scale.</note>

<margin>The world consists of perfect diapason harmony.</margin>
That is, their Music is so harmonized according to rule and measure that nothing more exact can be investigated. So that this may be more evident, let us observe, if you please, what <term>Georgius Venetus<note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Franciscan friar and author of *De Harmonia Mundi*, who blended Neoplatonism with Christian theology.</note></term> related in his *Problems*, having drawn it from the Pythagorean workshop of Censorinus, Pliny, and Eratosthenes: that from the earth all the way to the sphere of the zodiac signs, there is a perfect <term>diapason<note>An octave.</note></term> harmony. From the earth to the moon is a tone; from the moon to Mercury, a semitone; from Mercury to Venus, the same; from Venus to the Sun, a tone and a half, etc.

Do you see the music of this divine worldly temple? The concord of all nature? Does not Augustine, therefore, by the best right, call the world a most beautiful song and epigram? Who would now deny that the entire study of poetry consists in the imitation of nature?
