# Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature.

Furthermore, Pythagoras, Plato, <term>Tullius<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman orator and philosopher whose works were foundational to Western thought.</note></term>, Pliny, <term>Macrobius<note>A 5th-century Roman philosopher famous for his commentary on Cicero’s "Dream of Scipio," which preserved many Pythagorean musical ideas.</note></term>, <term>Proclus<note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who saw the universe as a series of cascading harmonies.</note></term>, <term>Chalcidius<note>A 4th-century commentator whose Latin translation of Plato’s *Timaeus* was the primary source of Platonic thought in the Middle Ages.</note></term>, and countless others—even the Holy Fathers—astounded by this miraculous arrangement of things, believed that the heavens emit a true and most sweet sound.

Tullius, in his *Dream of Scipio*, perceiving the most sweet song of the heavens with his ear and reflecting on it in his mind, says: *What is this great and so sweet sound that fills my ears? This is that sound which, formed by the impulse and motion of the orbs themselves at intervals that are unequal but yet distinct in fixed proportions, and tempering high notes with low, produces various harmonies equally.* And further below: *For which reason that highest course of the star-bearing heaven, whose rotation is swifter, is stirred and moved with a sharp sound.* <note>original: "Quis est qui complet aures meas, tantus & tam dulcis sonus? Hic est ille qui interuallis coniunctis imparibus..." This is a famous passage where Scipio Africanus explains the "Music of the Spheres" to his grandson.</note>

<margin>The words of Macrobius.</margin>
These are the words of Tullius. Macrobius, in Book 2 of his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, Chapter 1, comments on them thus, bringing Pythagoras and Plato to the same opinion. Therefore he says: *It is necessary that sound be born from the very rotation of the orbs: because the air, struck by the intervention of the blow, emits a force of crashing from itself, nature itself compelling that the violent collision of two bodies result in a sound.* And immediately: *From these things it is gathered by unassailable reason that musical sounds proceed from the rotation of the celestial spheres: because it is necessary for sound to be made from motion, and the reason which is inherent in divine things is the cause of the melody in the sound.* <note>original: "Ex ipso circumductu orbium sonum nasci necesse est..." Macrobius argues that because the planets move at such high speeds through the ether, they must logically produce sound.</note>

<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
Pythagoras was the first of all the men of the Greek nation to conceive and understand this in his mind: that something composed from the spheres sounds because of the necessity of reason, which does not depart from celestial things. These are his words, which he proves and explains from the same philosophers in the following chapter. And in Chapter 3, he begins thus:

<margin>Plato</margin>
Hence Plato in his *Republic*, when he treated the rotation of the celestial spheres, says that individual <term>Sirens<note>In the Platonic tradition, these Sirens are not the dangerous temptresses of the sea, but celestial spirits who sing the single note of their respective planetary sphere to create the cosmic harmony.</note></term> sit upon individual orbs. He signifies that by the motion of the spheres, a song is presented to the divinities: for "Siren," singing to GOD, is the meaning in the Greek understanding. 
<margin>A single singing Siren exists in each of the heavens.</margin>
And soon after: *Therefore the Theologians, also proving that the heaven sings, employed musical sounds in sacrifices, etc.* These things are there, and others which I pass over for the sake of brevity. And that one Siren resides in each of the heavens was reported by <term>Georgius Venetus<note>Francesco Zorzi (1453–1540), a Venetian friar and Christian Kabbalist who synthesized Hermetic, Platonic, and Christian thought in his work *On the Harmony of the World*.</note></term> in Volume 5, Problem Section 5, Number 321, drawing from Plato’s *Republic*, Proclus in his commentary on the *Cratylus* and the *Republic*, and Chalcidius in his commentary on the *Timaeus*. The half-line of <term>Angelo Poliziano<note>An influential Italian Renaissance scholar and poet (1454–1494).</note></term> looks toward this:

->*To each its own harmless Siren.*<-
<note>original: "Sua cuique innoxia Syren."</note>

<margin>Pliny on the same subject.</margin>
Pliny, in Book 2, Chapter 3, says the same thing: *In a harmony of sweet and indeed incredible pleasantness, the world glides silently by, night and day, for us who act within it.* <term>Caelius Rhodiginus<note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), a humanist whose "Ancient Lessons" served as an encyclopedia of classical lore.</note></term> in Book 5, Chapter 25, speaks thus: *How does it happen that the rotated whirling of such great orbs is carried along in a silent and quiet circuit, even if the wondrous delight of sounds passes by our ears which hear too little?* Plato asserted this; all who followed him approved it; and it was not displeasing to <term>Boethius<note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), whose work *On the Institution of Music* was the standard musical textbook for a thousand years.</note></term>.

<margin>Philo the Jew says the same most elegantly.</margin>
Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, in his book *On Dreams*, describes this music in words most worthy of note: *The heaven, by the perpetual concord of its motions, renders a most sweet harmony: which, if it were able to reach our ears, would stir in us powerless loves and an insane desire; spurred by which we would forget the things necessary for sustenance, not being fed by food and drink sent down through the throat, but like candidates for immortality, by the divine songs of perfected music—the kind which Moses is said to have heard when he was snatched out of his body, and for forty days and as many nights he tasted neither bread nor water.* <note>original: "Cælum perpetuò concentu suorum motuum reddit harmoniam suauissimam..." Philo suggests that celestial music is so perfect it provides spiritual nourishment that replaces physical food.</note>

<margin>The heaven is an instrument with which GOD is sung.</margin>
And what follows is divine: *Therefore the heaven, the archetypal instrument of Music, seems to me to have been fashioned for no other reason than that hymns might be skillfully and musically chanted to the Parent of all things.* These are the words of Philo. St. Ambrose harmonizes with this in his preface to the Psalms, saying: *The Angels praise the Lord; the Powers of the heavens sing psalms to him. A more expressive speech reports that the very axis of heaven turns with a certain sweetness of perpetual concord, so that by the habit of nature, it seems foreign to us.* <note>original: "Laudant Angeli Dominum..." St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD) was one of the four original Doctors of the Church and a pioneer in Christian hymnody.</note>

<margin>Boethius also.</margin>
These are the words of Ambrose. Anicius Severinus Boethius also says, in *On Music*, Book 1, Chapter 2: *How can it be that such a swift machine of heaven moves in a silent and quiet course, even if that sound does not reach our ears?*

<margin>St. Isidore.</margin>
And other things in the same place. St. Isidore, in Book 3 of his *Etymologies*, Chapter 16, says: *The world itself is said to be arranged by a certain harmony of sounds, and the heaven itself revolves under the modulation of harmony.* <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD) compiled all known human knowledge of his time into his *Etymologies*.</note>

<margin>Licentius, a Christian poet.</margin>
But also a certain Licentius, whom <term>Sixtus of Siena<note>A 16th-century theologian and biblical scholar.</note></term> mentions in Book 5 of his *Library*, Annotation 105, speaking of GOD, elegantly sang this very thing, saying:

> *He fitted numbers to the heavens; and commanded*
> *Sounding modes to be practiced, and equal dances to be driven.*
<note>original: "Aptauit numeros cælis: iussitque sonoros / Exercere modos, parilesque agitare choræas."</note>

<margin>And St. Anselm.</margin>
Anselm, in the first book of *The Image of the World*, says as follows: *The seven orbits of the heavens revolve with the sweetest harmony, and most delightful concerts are produced by their circling. This sound does not reach our
<margin>Why we do not hear the sounds of the heavens.</margin>
ears because it occurs beyond the air, and its great magnitude exceeds our narrow sense of hearing.* <note>original: "Septem cælorum orbes cum dulcissima harmonia voluuntur... eius magnitudo nostrum angustum auditum excedit." Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) was a Benedictine monk and philosopher; "De Imagine Mundi" is a work often attributed to Honorius Augustodunensis, though Kircher here attributes it to Anselm.</note> Thus says Anselm.

<margin>This world is the temple of God; therefore, it should not lack musical instruments. Psalm 8. Wisdom 1.</margin>
The reasoning that moved them to assert this celestial melody is that this world was called the "Temple of God" by the ancients, namely by <term>Tullius<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note></term> in *The Dream of Scipio* and by Seneca.

Since this world is the temple of God, and it is not fitting for temples and churches of the Divine to be without organs and singers, the ancients held that in this temple of the universe, the sound and harmony of the heavens were devised by God to take the place of organs and singers. In this way, it is true that "the heavens declare the glory of God" and the universe possesses "the knowledge of the voice"—that is, a most learned voice and sound, as the Scriptures say.

->§. I.<-

### On the admirable proportion of the worldly bodies to one another.

<note>A circular astronomical diagram illustrates Johannes Kepler's model of the universe based on nested Platonic solids. The outermost sphere is labeled "Orbit of Saturn," nested within a "Cube." Inside this is the "Orbit of Jupiter" nested within a "Tetrahedron." Further inside are nested spheres and geometric shapes labeled "Octahedron," "Icosahedron," and "Dodecahedron." The central part of the diagram depicts the orbits of "Mars," "Earth and Moon," "Venus," and "Mercury," with the "Path of the Sun" and a reference to "Tycho Brahe." This model attempted to explain the distances between planets through the geometry of perfect solids.</note>

From the time of <term>Hipparchus<note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190 – 120 BC) who is considered the founder of trigonometry.</note></term> until these most recent times of ours, scarcely any astronomer has been found who has correctly assigned the true proportion of the worldly bodies, whether in their bulk or in their distance from one another. Everyone differs in determining these things, and the reason for this is nothing other than the diversity of the solar medium, the deception of the eyes and instruments, as well as the incorrect determination of the apparent diameters of the celestial globes. No hope seems left to us for reaching this secret of the world; nevertheless, it is as certain that there is an admirable and thoroughly harmonic proportion in these worldly bodies as it is certain that God, the Most Wise Architect, created all things in "number, weight, and measure." <note>A reference to Wisdom 11:20, a cornerstone of the belief that the universe is mathematically ordered.</note> Since the Cause is most orderly, it is impossible for the effects to be disorderly, though various men assign this proportion in various ways. The belief of the ancients—that a perceptible harmony was forced out by the collision of the celestial bodies—is widely rejected in these most recent times, since neither the solidity of the heavens nor the order of the spheres subsists according to the arrangement of the ancients. *Ptolemy, in his Harmonics, arranges the spheres in a double order like a musical scale, in this way: first, so that the Moon represents the <term>hypate<note>The lowest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term> (that is, the lowest string) and Saturn the <term>nete<note>The highest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term> (the highest), with the remaining planets representing the intermediate strings; and second, in a contrary series, so that Saturn represents the hypate and the Moon the nete.* But these reasonings, aside from certain frivolous and very improper congruencies, conclude nothing certain or solid. Therefore, by no reasoning can the harmony of heaven be considered under these terms. When Kepler also considered this vanity, he designed another harmony, but one so obscure and entangled in mystical veils of words that his meaning is understood with difficulty. For while he attempts to demonstrate everything according to it, differing from himself and carried away by a tide of the mind, he finally placed the harmonic secret in the five regular solids...

<header>Book X. The Decachord of Nature.</header>

[Kepler] boasts that he has uncovered [these secrets]. For he says that if the angle of a **Cube** is applied to the innermost circle of **Saturn**, the centers of its planes almost touch the middle circle of **Jupiter** (for he assumes that each planet consists of three "heavens": the <term>Apogee<note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note></term>, the middle, and the <term>Perigee<note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note></term>; he also establishes the sun as immobile and the earth as moving). Truly, with the angles of the **Tetrahedron** resting on the innermost circle of **Jupiter**, the centers of the tetrahedron’s planes almost touch the outermost circle of **Mars**. Likewise, with the angles of the **Octahedron** rising from any circle of **Jupiter**, the centers of the octahedron's planes seem to descend below the outermost circle of **Jupiter**, yet do not reach the middle. 

<margin>5. The regular bodies contain the harmony of the world.</margin>

Finally, with the proportions of the **Dodecahedral** and **Icosahedral** orbits being equal to one another, the proportions or intervals between the circles of **Mars** and the **Earth**, and between the **Earth** and **Venus**, are very nearly equal. These proportions are themselves similarly equal if we calculate from the innermost part of **Mars** to the middle of the **Earth**, and from there to the middle of **Venus**; but look upon this matter in the preceding figure. <note>Kircher is discussing Johannes Kepler's famous theory from *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), where he proposed that the distances between the planets could be explained by nesting the five Platonic solids within each other.</note> And these are the speculations of **Kepler**. However, I do not see how the harmony of the heavens intended by Philosophers and Mathematicians can be demonstrated from these things, since he himself might be said to have violently distorted the heavens to fit his five solid bodies, rather than applying the bodies to the heavens. For if a certain and determined quantity had been found in the distances of the mundane bodies, something analogous to the five regular solids could undoubtedly be concluded regarding the proportions of the celestial bodies. But since all Astronomers from the time of **Ptolemy** even unto this day labor in assigning them, and disagree almost infinitely, the harmony of the heavens can certainly least of all be demonstrated from these; nor can the same be concluded from the periodic motions of the planets, which I show as follows. According to **Kepler**, the periodic motions of the Planets are as they appear in the following Table.

<note>In this table, "Scruples" (Scrup.), "min.", "sec.", and "ter." (thirds) refer to subdivisions of time or arc used in 17th-century astronomical calculations. A "third" is 1/60th of a second.</note>

In these periodic times, there are no harmonic proportions, which is easily seen if the larger periods are continually bisected and the smaller ones continually doubled. For if one takes the number of days as 120, which is the division of a musical string, there would come in this measure for the sixteenth part, a little more than 117. For **Jupiter**, for the eighth part, less than 95. For the **Earth**, less than 64. For **Venus**, for the double, more than 78. For **Mercury**, for the quadruple, 61 plus. And these numbers do not make any harmonic proportion with 120. Nor can the harmony of the heavens be concluded from the proportions of the <term>Aphelion<note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note></term> and <term>Perihelion<note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note></term> intervals, as **Kepler** thinks. For the diurnal motion of **Saturn** at aphelion is 1 min. and 46 sec., and at perihelion 2 min. 15 sec., which is not a third larger; but if the former had 1 min. 48 sec., then 1 min. 48 sec. to 2 min. 15 sec. would have the same proportion as 5 to 4, which is the proportion of a <term>ditone<note>A major third.</note></term>. But if the diurnal motion of **Jupiter** at 4 min. 30 sec. to the perihelion at 5 min. 30 sec. has a proportion of 5 min. to 6 sec., a <term>semiditone<note>A minor third.</note></term>, as **Kepler** thinks, yet 5 seconds are missing to establish it. Nor is the proportion of a <term>diapente<note>A perfect fifth.</note></term> established between the aphelion of **Mars** at 26 min. 14 sec. and its perihelion at 3 min. 81 sec. <note>original: "3 min. 81 fecu." likely a typo in the original Latin for 38 min.</note>, but it falls short of it by 7 seconds. Furthermore, the perihelion of the **Earth** at 61 min. 18 sec. diurnal motion and the aphelion at 57 min. 3 sec. falls short of a semitone by 25 seconds. And thus in the remaining proportions of diurnal motions in aphelions and perihelions, you will find no perfect consonance. If, however, we were granted a certain "Keplerian license" to apply the motions mentioned just before to harmonic proportions, the harmony of the motions would be that which follows.

# Book 10. The Nature's Ten-Stringed Lute

...shows quite the opposite; therefore, nothing certain or solid can be concluded from these theories regarding the harmony of the heavens. Furthermore, no harmony can even be conceived across such vast intervals of delay. To play with mere proportions is a feat of no great genius, since there are hardly any things subject to numbers that do not possess some name derived from musical proportions. It remains to be said, then, what celestial music truly is and in what it consists.

Abenragel the Arab <note>Abu l-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal, a 11th-century astrologer.</note>, in the book he calls *Hesban elladonia*—that is, *The Calculation of the World*—says that the bodies of the world have the same proportion to one another as roots have to squares and cubes, a concept which Kepler also suggests in his *Cosmographic Mystery*.

<margin>How great is the apparent diameter of the Sun</margin>
This is finally explained at length by Reita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660), an astronomer and optician.</note> in his *Eye of Enoch and Elijah*. It is certainly an ingenious invention compared to others and most suited for celestial harmony—if only his fabrication were consistent throughout. But let us bring forward his invention. He says the proportion of the Earth to the Sun is as 10 is to 100—that is, as a <term>root<note>The base number (10).</note></term> to a <term>square<note>The number multiplied by itself (10 x 10 = 100).</note></term>—so that the root of the Earth (10) is squared to reach the mass of the Sun (100), and is cubed to reach the distance (1000) <note>10 x 10 x 10 = 1000.</note>. Furthermore, he shows the solar diameter, relative to the radius of its orbit divided into 10,000 equal parts, to be as a root to a square. Since the apparent diameter of the Sun at a middle distance from the Earth is 34 minutes and 41 seconds according to his observations, the <term>sine<note>A trigonometric function used to calculate sides of triangles.</note></term> subtending the visual arc of 34 minutes and 41 seconds will necessarily be 100 from the table of sines. With this faithful observation established, it is well demonstrated—indeed, it necessarily follows—that the visual diameter (if correctly measured) has the same relationship to the Earth’s distance as a root does to 10,000, assuming the center of the Sun's orbit coincides with the center of the Earth.

He then supposes that the Earth's diameter of 10 parts is a <term>cube root<note>The value which, when cubed, produces the total volume.</note></term>, and consequently this root of 10, according to the tables of sines, subtends 3 minutes and 30 seconds. From this, he infers the distance of the Sun from the Earth is 100 solar diameters, just as that same distance is one thousand terrestrial diameters. But for the truth of this speculation, nothing more would be required than a determination of the Earth's apparent diameter as seen from the solar or lunar globe. This could be determined mechanically from such a hypothesis by means of a **cosmic triangle**, whose legs BA and CA would meet at the center of the Sun (A), while the base BC would encompass the diameter of the Earth. In this triangle, since the Earth's diameter BC is known, the legs would also be known by supposition—specifically from the radius AI of the Sun's orbit, taken as 100 solar diameters. Furthermore, since the diameter of the solar disk is known in parts of its own orbit by supposition, the diameter of the Earth applied to the solar diameter would easily assign how many times the former is contained in the latter. In this way, we could truly arrive at knowledge of the proportion of both the diameters and the distance. If these results were to flow from that, as Reita wishes, I would say that a truly admirable proportion of world harmony had been found; the bodies would relate to each other and to their distance from Earth in the same way that the harmonic intervals of stretched strings relate to the weights extending them. However, I strongly doubt whether Reita did not choose such a beautiful and plausible proportion at his own whim, rather than observing it in reality.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the "Cosmic Triangle." The vertex, labeled Point A, is placed at the center of the Sun ("centro Solis A"), while the base, labeled BC, represents the diameter of the Earth. A horizontal line, labeled AI, bisects the triangle from the vertex to the base, representing the radius of the orbit or the distance between the two bodies used for trigonometric calculation.</note>

<margin>The proportion of the Sun, Moon, and Earth both to each other and to their distances.</margin>
Therefore, according to what has been said, the proportion of the Moon's distance to the Earth in its own diameters is the same as that of the Sun to the Earth in its own. Since 34 minutes and 41 seconds are assigned to the 100 solar parts, he necessarily concludes that 3 minutes and 43 seconds must be assigned to the Earth's diameter, and barely 1 minute and 9 seconds to the Moon's. Consequently, the Earth exceeds the lunar mass 43 times, as they relate to each other as 4 to 14. For the cube of 14 is 2744, while the cube of 4 is 64; and 64 is contained in 2744 about 43 and a half times. Therefore, the Earth exceeds the Moon by that many times. Since the Sun and Moon, in parts of the radius of their own orbits divided into 10,000, are the squares of their distances from the Earth, and the Sun is to the Moon as 4 to 64, the Sun will be 42,875 times larger than the Moon, as is clear from cubing the terms of the proportion. From this proportion—always assuming faithful observation—another secret is drawn: namely, that the semi-diameter of the Earth subtends 1 minute, 52 seconds, and 30 thirds of its orbit, which in the table of sines...

# The Consonance and Dissonance of the Great Art

<margin>The marvelous proportion of the Celestial Bodies.</margin>
183 parts are assigned to the parts of the "whole sine" <note>In historical trigonometry, the 'whole sine' refers to the total radius of a circle, which was often divided into 10,000 parts for ease of calculation.</note> divided into 10,000 parts. This number, when doubled, gives 366, which is the number of days in the Sun's annual revolution. You see, therefore, that a solar diameter of 100 parts (where the radius of the orbit is 10,000) is the square root of its average distance from the Earth. The Earth, indeed, being 10 parts, is the cube root of that same radius. Furthermore, the diameter of the Moon is considered to contain as many minutes <note>Arc-minutes of its orbital path.</note> of its own orbit as the Sun contains of its own. Yet another wonder shines through here: namely, that the average distance of the Moon from the Earth contains as many terrestrial diameters as the number of days the Moon takes to complete its monthly period around the Earth—which is approximately 29 days—and the Earth is distant from the Moon by that same number of terrestrial diameters. Likewise, the number 365—the annual motion of the Sun expressed in parts of the radius of its orbit divided into 10,000—presently reveals the solar eccentricity <note>The degree to which the Sun's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> to be that same number of parts. You see here a beautiful harmony.

->Corollary.<-

**F**rom these things it is further deduced that the proportions of all the Planets are the square roots of their periodic revolutions. For example, since Saturn revolves in 10,747 days and Jupiter in 4,330, the root <note>original: "Radix"</note> of this latter revolution number will be 66, and of the former 107. Such a proportion is shown to exist between Saturn and Jupiter, and so it is for the rest of the Planets, as is evident in the following table.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature.

<margin>The marvelous arrangement of celestial proportions.</margin>
And all these things follow of necessity if, as I have said, they rest upon a faithful foundation of observations. However, not content with these alone, certain thinkers rise even higher in their assumed proportions, trusting that they can use this method to extract the distances not only of the Sun, but also of Saturn, the fixed stars, and even the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest heaven in medieval and Renaissance cosmology, the dwelling place of God and the angels.</note>. For it is necessary that the symmetry of the remaining parts be assigned according to a proportion founded and propagated in the nature of things. If you take the 10,000 parts of the radius of the Sun’s orbit and multiply them by 10, the result will be the semi-diameter of the final Saturnian sphere from the Earth, equaling 100,000 parts. Just as the diameter of the Earth is contained a thousand times in the radius of the solar orbit, so the diameter of the Sun is contained a thousand times in the radius of Saturn's orbit. Thus, just as the Sun is the square root in its diameters to its distance from the Earth, so too is it the square root to the distance of Saturn in terrestrial diameters. By a not dissimilar reasoning, they say the diameter of Saturn is the square root, in solar diameters, to the semi-diameter of the firmament; so that the semi-diameter of the firmament is 1,000,000 solar diameters, or 10,000,000 diameters of the Earth. Moving at an equal pace, the entire diameter of the firmament in diameters of the sphere of Saturn is the square root of the semi-diameter of the Empyrean heaven, such that the distance of 1,000,000,000 diameters of the region and system of the wandering Planets <note>original: "systematis vagi Planetarum," referring to the solar system where planets "wander" against the fixed stars.</note> is utterly inconceivable. Indeed, if someone were to measure a space in the Empyrean every single day equal to the entire circumference of the Earth, they would not actually finish traversing the circumference of such an Empyrean heaven in ten thousand million years.

You have here, therefore, the proportion of the worldly bodies according to the conjecture of Rheita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660), a Capuchin astronomer and optician who proposed a harmonic system of the universe.</note>. If these should prove to agree with nature, I would certainly say that God, the Most Wise Architect, ordered the entire world and the disposition of the bodies within it according to the degrees of algebraic powers. But since we treat these matters specifically in our work *The Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte Lucis & Umbræ," referring to Kircher’s own book *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (1646).</note>, we refer the reader there.

---

### §. I I.

->What that Music of the heavenly bodies might be, and in what it consists.<-

**T**hat there is a certain harmonic concord of the celestial bodies—one most worthy of that eternal and infinitely sweet Arranger <note>original: "Harmostæ," a term for one who joins or tunes things together.</note>—is a concept received by the unanimous consent of the Sacred Scriptures, as well as all theologians and philosophers. Yet, it is scarcely explainable by numbers, since the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man to conceive that ineffable concord of the celestial bodies. For it is reserved by that eternal and supramundane Organist <note>original: "Organædo," literally an organ-player.</note> for His elect alone, to be enjoyed in the sweetness of eternal life. However, as much as the weakness of our human ingenuity and the intuition of our clouded minds can grasp, I would truly say that this harmony of the heavens consists not in the periodic numbers of their motions, nor in some sensible collision of the celestial bodies, but in nothing else than their admirable arrangement and a certain ineffable proportion breathing together into a union. By this union, these worldly bodies correspond to one another in such a way that if one were removed or changed, the harmony of the whole would deservedly perish. Thus the Sun, exercising its command over the entire Economy of the Planets subject to it, like a certain *Choragus* <note>The leader or conductor of a Greek choir.</note>, rouses them all into harmony with the plectrums <note>The pick or tool used to pluck the strings of a lyre or lute.</note> of its rays. This harmony, as we have said, consists both in an admirable arrangement and a most proportionate distance of one worldly body from another, as well as in the most exact analogy of size or magnitude appropriated to each for obtaining its purpose.
<margin>In what the true harmony of the world consists.</margin>
Thus the Sun to the Moon and the Earth, and the Earth to the Sun and the Moon, have such a distance and such a necessity of magnitude that without it, the world would necessarily perish. For by these intervals, the worldly things are perfectly able to help and preserve one another through their mutual influences. So that this may be understood, it must be noted that with fiery bodies (such as we say the Sun is, and indeed the fire of all nature), it is so arranged that they produce different temperaments in bodies situated at different distances. This is taught to us clearly not only by nature, but also by the empirical arts. First, the rays of the sun reflected upon the earth in various ways teach us this; they produce one effect under the Frigid Zone, another under the Temperate, and yet another under the Torrid—

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...finally they present another constitution; as we have demonstrated at length in our *Anacamptic Art* <note>original: "Arte nostra Anacamptica". Anacamptics is the study of reflected light or catoptrics, which the author uses here to explain how light and heat are distributed.</note>; and this wonderful variety of diverse effects is so harmonious that, if the Earth were without it, she would not know how to be preserved and would instead bring about a perpetual dissonance in all things.

<margin>How great a significance the distance of the Sun from the Earth has in the nature of things.</margin>
Therefore, the distance of the Earth from the Sun, combined with a specific magnitude of its body, produces a particular disposition of the Earth and no other, a specific temperament and no other, and a specific harmonic variety and no other. Again, this distance, along with the specific size of the Earth, creates a most equal portion of light and shadow in all places—as we have shown in many ways in the cited *Anacamptic Art*. If the distance were greater or smaller, the entire harmony would now be reduced to a most confused dissonance. Just as musical strings of a certain length are consonant, but as soon as they deviate from their proper length, they produce a strange mixture of consonance and dissonance instead of melody. Thus, if the Earth were closer to the Sun or further from it than it truly is (while remaining the same size), it would be struck by more effective solar rays if closer, or by weaker rays if further away. Besides inducing a massive inequality of light and shadow, this would produce a temperament for human life that is not only harmful but altogether unsuitable. The same would happen if, at the same distance, the masses of the Sun or the Earth were larger or smaller. For just as in burning mirrors <term>speculis ustorijs: parabolic or concave mirrors used to concentrate sunlight to ignite objects at a distance</term> a certain and determined distance of the focal point from the surface of the mirror is required to achieve the effect of combustion, so also between the Sun and the Earth, the eternal wisdom of GOD established a most proportionate and entirely harmonic distance for the balanced increase of heat.

<margin>The light of the Sun, whether further or closer, is the cause of change in all things.</margin>
Furthermore, that the various effects on the Earth arise from different degrees of heat—caused by the continuous movement of the Sun between the two tropics, projecting its rays perpendicularly in some parts, obliquely in others, and at obtuse angles in yet others—is clearly taught by the Empirical Art <note>Referring here to the "art of experience," specifically alchemy or early chemistry.</note>. This art produces different degrees of heat through the action of fire applied in various ways and intensities. By these means, a simple substance to be distilled acquires a different constitution through a wonderful process, symbolizing a certain harmony with the elements. What previously lay confused in a single homogeneous mass is now, by the help of fire, separated into various natures, exhibiting different bodies of diverse quality through varying **fermentation, coagulation, fixation, dissolution, composition, softening, and hardening**.

Just as the Sun is thus arranged entirely harmonically in relation to the Earth, so too the Moon, Venus, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn <note>The original uses the symbols ♂, ♃, and ♄.</note> possess their own harmonic ratios of intervals and magnitudes required by nature, both toward one another and toward the Earth and Sun. Indeed, the Moon has received such a distance from the Sun and Earth, with a proper proportion of magnitude, that if its size or its distance from either the Sun or Earth were changed by Divine power, the entire harmony would necessarily be thrown into confusion, and the Earth would inevitably perish. For at its specific distance, it can properly nourish the Earth with its influence; at no other distance could it break the heat of the Sun. Conversely, the Sun so tempers the moisture and coldness of the Moon with the mixture of its rays that it produces the effect intended by nature to be bestowed upon the Earth. For if the Moon <note>original: "))", a symbol for the lunar crescent.</note> were closer to the Earth, it would produce entirely dissonant and incongruous effects on the Earth through its excessive moisture. On the other hand, if it were closer to the Sun, the Sun acting more effectively upon the Moon would consume its moisture, and everything in the terrestrial world would be destroyed by excessive heat.

<margin>Nature being preserved, the distance of the Sun, Moon, and Earth could not be other than what it now is.</margin>
Therefore, nature opposed the watery Lunar body to the fiery Solar body in such a proportion of distance that one might restrain the force of the other upon the earth, binding and tightening the dissonant with the consonant, as it were. Because the Sun does not always strike the earth with the same heat, but varies according to its annual and daily ascent and descent, nature likewise did not wish the Moon to always strike the Earth with the same degree of moisture and coldness. Instead, this varies according to the different alterations of the lunar phases, as well as the ratio of its ascent and descent in its apogees and perigees <note>Apogee is the furthest point from Earth in an orbit; perigee is the closest.</note>. Thus you see that in the hottest summer, a full Moon—being at its lowest and smallest—has little power. Conversely, in the freezing depths of winter, when the Sun is positioned in a low place, the Moon rises as a sort of deputy for the Sun. This was done by the hidden counsel of nature so that the lower world might be preserved in its perfection through this exact variety, like a "consonant-dissonant" mixture.

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature.

Yet because the most scorching Sun, together with the most moist Moon, could not establish a perfect harmony of humors on the terrestrial globe (as if under a perpetual octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>) without the intervention of other bodies, Divine Providence therefore placed two other worldly bodies—namely Venus and Mercury—between the Moon and the Sun. These bodies excel with diverse powers, so that the vehemence of the solar rays might be carded <note>meaning filtered or combed through, like wool</note> and, as it were, blunted; from this, their strength is increased with the moisture necessary for the Moon, so that they might bless the earth with greater variety. For the fertilizing power of the body of Venus, communicated through its influential influx to the Moon, similarly fertilizes her moisture. Mercury, however, is the separator of the consonant from the dissonant; he tempers and diverts into himself whatever is harmful or superfluous in both the Sun and Venus. Thus, at last, he pours forth another kind of harmony necessary for the lower world. All these things, through the passage of time, bring about ever-diverse combinations of effects according to their various aspects and the eccentric positions of the aforementioned stars. Furthermore, because no organ is so perfectly constructed that it does not, over time, incur dissonance—either from strings becoming too loose or stretched beyond measure—it is impossible for the lower world not to occasionally fall into a bad mixture <note>original: "δυσκρασίαν" (dyskrasian); a medical term for an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> due to the distance or proximity of these bodies from the earth, as well as their various configurations. Nevertheless, just as a body filled with various humors over time and seized by fever is eventually restored to health by the evacuation of moisture, so too is the world restored.

<margin>Why Nature established the dissonant bodies of Saturn and Mars in the world.</margin>

And toward this end, God, through Nature—which is His art—placed two entirely dissonant bodies in the heavens: Mars and Saturn. From their pestilential exhalations, all the evils of the sublunary world take their origin. Lest these lead the economy of the entire lower world into an open cacophony <note>original: "κακοφωνίαν" (kakophonian)</note>, He placed the benign star Jupiter between them as an intermediary. By Jupiter's health-giving influx, the deadly and utterly ruinous power exhaled by both of them is restrained and held back. Moreover, lest the earth be openly exposed to ruin when attacked by the virulence of Mars, Nature willed him to be placed in the largest eccentric orbit of all, so that—coerced from below by the Sun and Venus and from above by Jupiter—he might desist for a time from his ferocity. Yet, Nature should not be accused of being a stepmother for creating such ruinous bodies; rather, she must be judged to have disposed them thus by some supreme and hidden counsel, as the world could not be preserved without them. Indeed, they seem to perform the same function in the "Greater World" <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> when it is burdened by a great mass of vicious humors, as is performed in the "Little World" <note>the Microcosm or human body</note> by Spanish Fly <term>Cantharides; a beetle used in historical medicine to create blisters and "draw out" bad humors</term> and caustic medicines. By the power of these things, the gathering of disease-causing matter is attracted and dissipated from the center to the extremities, freeing the person in danger. Thus, there is no evil in the nature of things that does not eventually yield to the good and the conservation of the whole universe. For what else are Mars and Saturn but certain dissonances? Yet, when they are bound and resolved into a perfect consonance by Jupiter, they provide not only a sweetness to the Music, but also its greatest ornament. What else is Mercury but a certain dissonance bound and tied between Venus and the Moon (like two consonances), lest, having obtained freedom and being bound to nothing, he might defile the earth despite the benign influx of the Sun, Venus, and the Moon? Certainly, whoever considers these things more deeply will find that the seven planets with the earth perpetually sing a perfect four-voice harmony <note>original: "tetraphoniam"</note>, in which the dissonant elements are joined to the consonant with such skill that they provide a most sweet harmony to the world. And so that the curious reader might have an example of this celestial four-voice song, I have seen fit to exhibit here the idea of our speculation in musical notes, where Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars sing the *Netodus* (the highest voice), in whose notes the consonant Jupiter always binds and breaks the dissonant Mars and Saturn. The Sun, singing the *Mesodus* (the middle voice), proceeds with the most perfect consonances, while the Earth as the *Proslambanomena* (the lowest note) is positioned above through the dia-

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Indeed, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon sing the *Hypatodon* <note>original: "Hypatodon"; the lowest tetrachord in the ancient Greek musical system, representing the lowest pitch range</note>. Venus and the Moon, being consonant, draw the intermediate and dissonant Mercury into their friendship, binding him with such harmonic measures that they render him entirely consonant, as can be seen in the musical notation for the *Hypatodon*. The Earth, however, lying beneath all things, receives a mixture of consonance and dissonance so perfect that it constitutes from this point the most perfect music with the planets—a harmony such as we might imagine here.

Since nature is perpetually eager for variety, she does not always offer the same harmony to the lower world over the course of time. Hence, the individual planets—both by rotating around their own centers and by their moving further away or closer to one another in their eccentric orbits <note>elliptical or non-circular paths</note>, as well as by the various positions and relations of their "aspects" <note>astrological angles</note> under the signs of the Zodiac—always pour forth new and ever-new kinds of harmony. These always remain, however, within determined limits intended by nature. Thus, in these eccentric orbits, which are like the boundaries of planetary motions, they gradually change ascending or descending tones or modes as they move—proceeding now from Dorian to Phrygian, then to Lydian, then to Aeolian, and so on through the rest—until they finally return to the tone assumed at the beginning once the entire circulation of tones is completed. 

Because the parts of the planetary globes or bodies are heterogeneous—having received different natures, qualities, properties, and powers due to their diverse positions relative to the other surrounding planets—nature willed them to turn about their own centers. This ensures they always present different sides to the earth, performing the same role in celestial music as the mixing of dissonances with consonances does in artificial <note>man-made</note> music. You see, therefore, that the planets are arranged in such an order that if even one were to recede from its determined limit (like a harmonic interval), the entire harmony would be rightfully destroyed.

## Corollary.

From this it is clear that the Earth serves as a kind of base <note>original: "basin"; here meaning the 'bass' or foundation of a musical composition</note> upon which the rest of the universe's harmony is built. For if the Earth were removed, the remaining voices would leave a harmony that is imperfect and subject to many dissonances. But enough has been said thus far, if I am not mistaken, regarding the universal symphonism <note>the harmonious blending of sounds</note> of the planets; now let us return to their particular symphonisms.

### §. III.
### Concerning the Particular Symphonism of the Planets.

<margin>The two companions of Saturn.</margin>
Lest the harmony of many voices echoing perpetually should become a burden to the ears through continuous sound, it was provided by the Composers <note>original: "Musurgis"; the divine architects of music</note> that they should distribute the harmony of many voices into several choirs. Thus, with alternating choirs equipped with various ranks of instruments, a greater variety and delight might arise for the listeners. By no different reasoning, Nature the Harmonizer distinguished those Celestial Singers <note>original: "Phonascos"; vocal leaders or instructors</note> into various choirs. Although they differ in the nature of their sounds, they all conspire toward a consonant-dissonant union, both adorning the world with variety and commending the ineffable wisdom of that supramundane Harmonizer. 

To begin with Saturn, the highest choir of the planetary harmony: in these recent times, the truly lynx-eyed <note>keen-sighted</note> school of astronomers has detected its marvelous constitution. It clearly appears that God Most Good and Great, in order to draw us into admiration and love of His wisdom, has unlocked a new register of the celestial organ. Saturn was first observed as if "triple-bodied" <note>original: "tricorporeus"; a reference to Galileo's early observation of Saturn's rings, which he initially mistook for two smaller bodies on either side of the planet</note>. It was later discovered that two bodies perpetually circle it like vocal attendants, guarding him. For since the Sun, the choir leader <note>original: "choragus"</note>, could not reach Saturn with the plectrum of his light due to the vast distance, he provided Saturn with two companions to attend him perpetually as deputies of the Sun. These nourish him by the mutual communication of powers, lest Saturn remain dissonant to himself. And by this marvelous conspiracy, that harmony which...

### Book X. The Decachord of Nature

The Sun, the Moon, and our Earth would, among themselves, form a distinct Choir, just as the Saturnian Orb (for so we shall henceforth call this planet) together with its two companions and attendants, the *Phonasci* <note>original: "Phonascis"; from the Greek for "vocal trainers" or "singers," here personifying the moons as members of a musical choir</note>—one of which reflects the Saturnian Sun and the other the Saturnian Moon quite appropriately—would produce a distinct harmony.

<margin>A matter worthy of note regarding the motion of Saturn’s companions.</margin>
And so that there might always be constant changes upon its own axis, [the Creator] willed the central Saturnian Orb to rotate in a space of 29 days and 10 hours—precisely as many days as the years it takes to complete its greater eccentric circle. This is a truly wondrous thing, first observed in these recent times; thus, if God were to place us on the Saturnian Orb, each natural day would not be 24 hours, but 706 hours and 38 minutes long. Furthermore, lest the subpolar parts of Saturn be condemned to perpetual darkness, He willed it to incline somewhat toward each companion; thus it happened that the entire globe is imbued with equal light. It is also probable that the attendants wander both around their own centers and around the Saturnian Orb in some period suitable for its preservation. To create a greater variety of influences, it is also likely that the Saturnian companions are of a heterogeneous nature; as they revolve, they turn different parts of themselves, imbued with various qualities, to induce a better temperament <note>a balanced mixture of qualities</note> in the Saturnian globe. Thus, by mixing concordant things with discordant ones, they bring about the perfect harmony of this choir, as is evident in the present figure, in which globe **A** represents Saturn and its axis **BC**. **ED** are the Saturnian companions, and **FG** their orbit; while **EAD** is the eccentric path of the Saturnian companions. These things, when compared with what has been said, will reveal the aforementioned harmony.

## Corollary.

From the stated harmonic arrangement, it necessarily follows that Saturn, because of its excessive distance, cannot be sufficiently illuminated by the Sun, and therefore provision was made for it by the light of its two companions. For since, according to the calculation of certain moderns, Saturn is distant from the Sun by 20,000,000 hourly leagues <note>a "leuca" or league was a common unit of distance; Kircher is emphasizing the vastness of the outer solar system</note>, it is certain that an eye placed on Saturn would perceive the solar diameter as measuring no more than 3 minutes and 11 seconds. From that distance, the Sun would appear little larger than Venus, Jupiter, or a star of the first magnitude, and consequently, Saturn requires light other than that of the Sun. 

It follows, moreover, that if we were situated on Saturn, we would have a day lasting 29 [Earth] days. We would never see the other "inferior" planets <note>planets closer to the sun than the observer</note> recede more than 40 degrees from the Sun: Jupiter would appear at 40 degrees, Mars at 12, Venus at 4, and Mercury at 2. The Moon and Earth would be scarcely perceptible. Therefore, you would conclude that all these planets are merely companions of the Sun, and you would recognize the Sun's 29-year period within the Zodiac, while believing Saturn itself to be fixed, submerged in the center of the universe. I could demonstrate all these things here, but since we have reserved those observations for the second edition of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Lucis & Vmbrę"; Kircher’s 1646 treatise on optics and astronomy</note>, following the findings of more recent authors, we refer the reader there. Let it suffice for now that we have demonstrated the admirable harmony of the Saturnian Choir in this place.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

## §. IV.
## Concerning the Jovian Choir.

<margin>
A description of the globe of Jupiter with its four companions.
</margin>

It has become known through frequent observation in these recent times that the Architect of Celestial Harmony adorned this Jovian Choir with a truly singular artifice above all others. While Jupiter, powerful in magnitude and glory, presented himself to be seen by this lower world with an unheard-of and unseen retinue of four companions <note>referring to the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto</note>, he did so in that concord of all things which we shall describe. This globe, much larger than the Earth, is so remote from the Sun that—just as with Saturn—the Sun seems hardly sufficient to illuminate it. Lest such an immense mass, imbued with the most excellent virtues, should be devoid of light and, wasting away in perpetual gloom, bring dissonance to the remaining bodies of the world, it was brought about by a certain admirable counsel of nature that four Choir Leaders <note>original: "Choragi"</note>, perpetually striking this immense mass with the plectrums of their rays, should stir it into the most beautiful harmony by their harmonic motions.

For it has been observed that the periodic motion of the first singer <note>original: "phonasci," a term for a vocal teacher or choir leader</note>, which is closer to Jupiter, is completed in the space of nearly 42 hours; the period of the second in 3 days and 13 hours; the third in 7 days and 4 hours; and finally, the period of the last or fourth in the space of 16 days and nearly as many hours. And if we believe the calculations of Rheita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660), an astronomer and priest who claimed to have discovered additional moons</note>, the first is distant from Jupiter by 20 ¾, the second by 27, the third by 41, and the fourth by 69 semidiameters of the Earth. Truly, see the calculation performed by Rheita for the four Jovian companions in the following table.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

Reader, having seen the description, position, and size of the Jovian Choir Leaders <note>The "Choragi" or Choir Leaders are the four Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.</note>; let us now see what harmony they effect in the Jovian Choir. In the preceding figure, the first is marked with the letter A, the second B, the third C, the fourth D, while Jupiter, situated as if in the center, is marked with the letter V.

<margin>
Jupiter is illuminated by his companions.
</margin>
<margin>
What is the Jovian Zone?
</margin>
When, therefore, God—the Arranger <note>original: "Harmosta," a Greek term for one who fits things together or a regulator of a chorus.</note> of immense and incomprehensible wisdom—decreed to build the world with an innumerable variety of things, He established in this mundane temple a second Choir, remarkable for the manifold power of its Choir Leaders: namely, the celestial globe which we call Jupiter. For this Jovian Sphere is much larger than our Earthly Sphere and is imbued with the most excellent virtues with which it might influence this lower world. Since it required a position most remote from the Earth and Sun, and could not conveniently draw sufficient light from the Sun, God assigned to it, as if they were substitutes, two Suns (the first and third) and just as many substitute Moons (the second and fourth) <note>Kircher classifies the moons as "suns" or "moons" based on their perceived brightness or roles in his harmonic system.</note>. He ordered them with such ingenuity and admirable providence that they would illuminate the Jovian globe perpetually and in alternating turns; so that what one Sun and Moon could not achieve, the auxiliary Suns and Moons would provide. 

By their harmonic motion, the Jovian Sphere is struck by a continuous succession of light and shadow, which causes a truly great and admirable diversity of natures in the said body. It is necessary that days and nights happen very unequally, not so much in the duration of time as in the intensity of light. For who doubts that two, three, or four Choir Leaders rising together for Jupiter bring more daylight to it than one Sun alone? Certainly, it is beyond what can be said: that a day there is of the most intense light. When, however, the said four Choir Leaders are joined together <note>in conjunction</note>, they will cause night in the opposite parts of the Jovian body, though a brief one due to the velocity of their motion. 

Lest that harmonic constitution of the Jovian body be disturbed by excessive light, He willed Jupiter not to rest, but to turn perpetually around its own center, so that one such revolution would consist of as many days as its periodic revolution in its eccentric orbit—namely, 12 years. Thus, for us if we were stationed on Jupiter, one natural day would not be 24 hours, but nearly 268 hours <note>Kircher is speculating on the rotation of Jupiter; modern science knows it rotates very quickly, in about 10 hours, but Kircher’s calculations were based on the theories of his time.</note>. Furthermore, it is brought about by a most pleasant and perpetual reciprocation that, as the light of the first Choir Leader withdraws more quickly than is equal, the lunar light of the second Choir Leader succeeds it; then the solar light of the third Choir Leader follows; and finally, as this sets, the lunar light of the fourth rises for Jupiter. From this, again, to blunt the violence of the light, frequent eclipses necessarily follow the motion of the Jovian body; so much so that I consider those "Jovian Zones" <note>The atmospheric bands or belts of Jupiter.</note> to be nothing other than the shadows of the lunar bodies projected onto the Jovian disk. Truly, concerning all these matters, see the extensive and curious treatment in the second edition of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* in the section on *Cosmometry*.

When all these things are compared together, the Reader will find a certain most absolute harmony, tempered from dissonances and consonances with such wondrous art that nothing more tuneful could be devised. Thus, it is necessary from a harmonic constitution of this kind that the Jovian body be rendered most beautiful and imbued with the most excellent qualities, such as we experience with admiration in its influence upon this lower world.

## Corollary I.

It also follows for the harmony of the world that Jupiter ought to have been neither larger nor smaller, nor ought it to have approached or receded closer to the Sun or further from it than its eccentric orbit prescribed, without manifest detriment to the harmony of the universe.

Whether the Jovian globe is inhabited.

## Corollary II.

It also follows that men can by no means dwell there, both on account of the excessive intensity of light and because of the temperament of the place, which is entirely unsuitable to human nature. As for those who wish to believe that creatures of a different nature were created there: since nothing is certain to us concerning them, nor can it be certain—indeed, it seems dangerous to the Faith—who does not see that this is nothing but a rash fiction devised without any foundation by the followers of novelties? But having seen the Jovian harmony, let us now proceed to the other choirs.

Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

## §. V.
### On the Solar and Martian Choir.

<margin>
The nature of the globe of Mars.
</margin>
The Solar or Apolline Choir <note>Kircher associates the Sun with Apollo, the leader of the Muses.</note> contains within its domain Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Earth, and it is almost parallel to the Jovian Choir; since enough was said concerning its harmony at the beginning, we did not wish to repeat the same things here. Between this Solar and Jovian choir, nature ordained another arrangement in the world’s harmony: namely, the globe of Mars. Since this globe was dissonant with the others, yet necessary for preserving the harmony of the world, it was placed in the middle, between the consonant Solar and Jovian choirs, so that by being tied or "syncopated" <note>In music, syncopation involves shifting the regular accent; Kircher uses this as a metaphor for how a seemingly disruptive planet like Mars is "bound" into the cosmic rhythm by its neighbors.</note> to them, it might breathe together into a most beautiful harmony. And so that this syncopation might occur with greater benefit, it was necessary to place him in the largest eccentric orbit of all, in which, while he sometimes descends below the Sun itself and at other times attacks the most remote empire of Jupiter, it happens that he is kept in his duty—sometimes caught by the light of the Sun, sometimes by Jupiter—lest, having become a law unto himself, he should turn everything upside down and disturb the harmony of the whole. Since he wanders alone, associated with no other choir leaders <note>Mars has no moons known to Kircher (Phobos and Deimos were not discovered until 1877).</note> along the path of his eccentric orbit, he is forced to beg for all his light from either the Sun or Jupiter. 

But since light of this kind was by no means sufficient to exercise his innate power, it was brought about by the hidden counsel of nature that the Martian globe should be furnished, as it were, with subterranean fires, becoming a fountain of darkness and of fires filled with pestilential fumes, excessive and deadly heats, and indeed the worst poisonous evaporations. The derivation of his virulent influence would not only infect but utterly destroy all other mundane bodies, had not nature placed him in such an opportune location to restrain his power. For since he is in the middle between the celestial choirs, it happens that by being variously bound and "syncopated" by Venus, Jupiter, and their companions, as has been said, he finally breathes in perfect harmony. And this is that ingenious "syncopsis" <note>original: "syncopsis," a musical binding or contraction.</note> which Nature seems to have affected in the harmonic concert of mundane bodies and the "good temperament" <note>original: "ἐυκρασία" (eukrasia), a Greek medical and philosophical term for a healthy balance of qualities.</note> of their influences.

## §. VI.
### On the Choir of Choirs, that is, on the harmony of the fixed stars in the firmament.

<margin>
What is the orbit of the Cynosure around the pole?
</margin>
Just as in the various distributions of Choirs, one is rightly called the "Choir of Choirs," from which, as if from a fountain and measure, the beauty of the entire harmony flows into the others; so that admirable Chief Choir Leader <note>original: "Archichoragus," the leader of a dance or chorus.</note>, GOD, has placed beside the planetary choirs a most eminent choir: the firmament, I say, filled with an innumerable multitude of stars like so many voices continually praising GOD. The firmament, however, does not have its stars fixed in a solid orb like nails in a wheel, as the Ancients more simply believed; nor are there any holes pierced in the firmament through which the Empyrean heaven might shine, as some in these times have foolishly asserted. Rather, they are globes of immense magnitude, removed from one another by different spaces in every variation of place, like certain particular systems, each founded on its own centers, and wandering with movements just as varied as our planets, here and there in their own eccentric circles and orbits within that immense expanse, mirroring this world of planets. 

The cause of their appearing motionless to us is their ineffable distance from the center of the earth; certainly the Pole Star <note>original: "stella polaris."</note>, which recedes from the pole by no more than 3 degrees and therefore appears to us entirely unmoved, is said to complete a circle around the pole of such vast amplitude that the entire Solar heaven, together with the orbits of Venus and Mercury, could be included within it. If we were to suppose the Sun were placed in that same spot, it would be thought by us to be perpetually immobile and to always have the same distance from Venus, Mercury, and the Earth, were they also placed there.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

I say further that if the height of the firmament is as great as Copernicus and Rheita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660), an astronomer and optician known for improving the telescope.</note> have determined, it can be demonstrated through the discipline of Optics that, for example, the Eye of the Bull <note>The star Aldebaran.</note> or the Lyre <note>The star Vega.</note>, even if they were carried in an orbit three or four times larger than the Sun’s, they would still be observed by us stationed on Earth as entirely immobile and maintaining the same distance from one another.

<margin>
Various comparisons made of an eye positioned on different globes in relation to other globes.
</margin>
Conversely, if our eye were positioned in a star of the first magnitude in Lyra, it would look upon the Sun under the size of a fixed star, while the remaining lower planets would vanish entirely. Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars would appear around the Sun in the same arrangement as the four Jovian companions or "chorus-leaders" <note>The Galilean moons of Jupiter.</note> appear to us around Jupiter—that is, entirely imperceptible without a telescope <note>original: *astroscopio*</note>. From this I conclude that there is an entirely innumerable multitude of fixed stars, differing in magnitude, distance, and intensity of light. Some of these match the Sun in light, some the Moon—that is, some enjoy their own light, and some enjoy a borrowed light like moons. Many of these are separated by a gap as great as the distance that divides the firmament from the Earth. In the constellation Orion alone, Rheita believes he has counted more than two thousand stars with the help of a telescope <note>original: *helioscopij*</note>—more than Antiquity found in the entire firmament; although others have not found so many. Who does not know that the Galaxy <note>The Milky Way.</note> is an innumerable multitude of crowded stars? Therefore, inaccessible distance is the reason why neither their motion nor their magnitude becomes perceivable to us. Indeed, through divine power, we could recede so far from the firmament that the Great Dog <note>The star Sirius.</note> and the Lyre, stars separated by the whole sky, would nonetheless become so close that they would appear as the two horns of Aries; until, as we receded further and further, they would finally merge into one. Likewise, undoubtedly, if our Sun were placed in the furthest inner reaches of the firmament,

<margin>
The Sun, if placed in the furthest inner reaches of the firmament, would be imperceptible due to the distance.
</margin>
it is certain that nothing of it would appear at all. From this another point is drawn: those stars in the firmament which seem to us to be separated by the space of one pace must actually be distant from each other by as much space as the diameter of the solar heaven can occupy, if the opinion of Copernicus were true. Although these things may seem paradoxical <note>original: *παράδοξα*</note> and unbelievable, nevertheless, given the foundational principles of optics, they can be demonstrated without difficulty under this view.

From this I certainly gather that, assuming the distances of Copernicus, Rheita, and Kepler, no star in the firmament is illuminated by the Sun; and this was made clear enough in the preceding section from the reasoning regarding Saturn. But concerning these things, I have written more curiously in *The Art of Light and Shadow*. And from these things said perhaps more extensively than was proper, that marvelous harmony of the world is clearly evident. If anyone judges these things to be incredible, he clearly places a bridle upon divine power. For the works of the Most High are wonderful, as Ecclesiasticus witnesses, both glorious and hidden; and His works are entirely immense; and in chapter 43: 
> *Many things are hidden, greater than these, and we know few of His works.*

But if anyone should ask me why divine providence wished these things to be hidden from men, and why He chose this Earth above all the bodies of the world to manifest the great wonders of His grace, I would in turn desire to know from him: why did He wish to hide the New World <note>The Americas.</note>, filled with an infinite multitude of men, until these latter times? And why has He not yet wished several provinces of this earthly globe (such as the sub-polar regions and the greater portion of the Southern Hemisphere) to be uncovered? Why also did divine goodness wish the mysteries of His Faith to be revealed to so few men? And from these, why did He predestine so few to life? These things are stored away in the abyss of the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God.
> *For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor?* <note>A reference to Romans 11:34.</note>
These things are reserved for the knowledge not of this life, but of another, more blessed one.

<margin>
Why God created such a great multitude of stars.
</margin>
Therefore, for what end God created such an infinite multitude of worldly bodies, even if it remains hidden from us, they are not for that reason deprived of their most efficacious effects. It suffices for us to know that all things breathe together into one harmony. Certainly, if there is nothing in the nature of lower things so slight and minute that it was not most wisely established for certain ends, how much more those greatest and vastly sized worldly bodies, which have their greatest and most eminent uses, to be revealed only in the next life. Who among physicians has until now certainly indicated the number and multitude of the muscles, cartilages, small veins, fibers, and other most minute parts of the human body? Yet it is certain that if even a single one were separated from the whole body, the harmony of the whole body would be destroyed. We do not, indeed, know the virtues and effects of the particular stars at present, but then perhaps we shall know them, those which we experience...

All things were made for the sake of man.

certain to us that all things were made for the sake of this Earth, since it was here that the Divine Majesty, clothed in flesh, deigned to live among men and was pleased to show the wonders of His works. Furthermore, the earth was established for the sake of man, its inhabitant, so that man—the most noble of creatures, the son and heir of the world—might consider this admirable **machine of the world** <term>machine of the world: *machina mundi*, a common Renaissance metaphor describing the universe as a complex, divinely-crafted mechanism like a clock</term> and recognize the infinite and inexhaustible power, wisdom, and goodness of the Creator. Thus, stirred by the most harmonious music of every individual part, man might be encouraged to offer praises to the most sweet Creator continually and steadfastly. In this way, after the passing of this corruptible life, full of God in the Word of Life, man might deserve to contemplate the Creator and all things in Him eternally, just as he is the most beautiful **idea** <note>original: *idea*; here meaning the divine blueprint or archetype</note> of all things and of the entire worldly machine.

Therefore, let mortals learn from this: with how much labor, sweat, danger, and various afflictions do they expose themselves to acquire even the smallest portion in the narrow huts of this earthly point? How small is the portion of what they obtain compared to those dwellings in the highest habitations of the heavens which God has prepared for His elect? I do not doubt that these dwellings far exceed the number of mortals who have existed from the beginning of the world until these times. For as the eternal Wisdom of God rightly said: *In my Father's house there are many mansions;* that is, they are innumerable and inconceivable to the human mind. Therefore, let mortals frequently stir up within themselves a desire for the eternal hills; let them often look with their minds and eyes toward those lights, which are like shadows of the eternal light. For in this way, stripped of the love of earthly things, they may live more abundantly with the children of light and in the company of the children of God.

# REGISTER III.
## The Symphonism of Stones, Plants, and Animals
## with the Heavens.

In the preceding Register, God the Best and Greatest displayed the admirable harmony of the celestial bodies to us; in this one, however, He offers to mortals another astounding **symphony** <term>symphonism: *symphonismus*, the resonant or harmonic correspondence between different levels of creation</term> of sublunary things—both among themselves and with the stars and worldly bodies—which is entirely in consonance with the higher world. It is, as it were, a reflected harmony from the celestial realms, for as **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the divine nature of harmony and the soul.</note> rightly says: the harmony of lower things is nothing other than certain voices of an **Echo** of the celestial ones, reverberating the higher sounds into this lower world according to a manner agreeable to their nature.

And although we have treated the matter of the Sun's wonderful effects and the secrets of the world's craftsmanship more 

<margin>
The Sun's benevolence toward these lower things.
</margin>

extensively in our *Arte Anacamptica* and *Gnomonica Physico-Astrologica* <note>Kircher is referencing his previous works on mirrors (*catoptrics*) and sundials, which he viewed as physical expressions of light and time.</note>, it nevertheless seemed appropriate to touch upon certain things here that contribute to harmonic adaptations, lest we seem to have omitted anything in this *Great Art*. The Sun, therefore, the Leader, Prince, and **Chorus-leader** <note>original: *Choragus*; the leader of a choir or theatrical performance</note> of all the heavenly bodies, picking its way through the paths of the world in an oblique course, cheers, fertilizes, brightens, and gives life to everything it can reach. Whatever it cannot reach, it leaves behind as foul, filthy, squalid, misty, dark, and imperfect. By its departure and distancing, it provides space for the Earth’s conceptions, so that soon, by its arrival and proximity, it may look after them and help them with a silent power. For it withdraws for a time until the Earth, imbued with suitable and timely moisture through a certain **sympathy** <term>sympathy: *sympathia*, the natural attraction or occult connection between things that share a similar essence</term>, becomes fit to bear the encounters of such a powerful friend. The Sun then finally returns by such degrees that, once the uppermost parts of the lands are dried, its power (restrained until its arrival and sight) first produces the fibers of plants within, then draws forth the budding greenness, and finally leads all things to maturity. In this task, it is not left without the aid and retinue of the celestial fires and stars—especially the planets. These planets, as if they were about to attempt something new on Earth with the Sun, now join together as one, and from one and the same side, having gathered their strength, they seem to stir up and threaten war against lower nature; at other times, scattered in different places and widely separated, and variously sown on high, they promise peace to the world. Now, as if there were not otherwise enough strength, but earthly things required their more immediate help...
