->### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.<-

<note>original: *Decachordon Naturæ*; a title referring to the universe as a ten-stringed instrument played by God.</note>

...[the celestial spheres] <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the spheres</note>, they lower themselves closer to those things; now, as if sparing the lower things, they withdraw further away, lifting themselves on high in both instances. Now, as if more diligent work were not needed, they linger or hesitate somewhere; now, as if they might be hindered by delay, they fly together swiftly; often, as if the place invites them, or indeed as if some worthwhile task was missed, they return on a reversed course. All these things have been most wisely ordained by **God** to produce corresponding effects in the terrestrial world. Hence, the heaven is full of a harmony and fitness of motions.

<margin>
Superior things flow into inferior things harmoniously.
</margin>

When **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "chains" of influence connecting the divine to the material world.</note> observed this, he believed that the Divine Beings above us were the first to participate in the harmony proceeding from the heavens. From these, man then receives a rightly ordered life, constancy of character, and fitness of actions; he believed that this gift of the heavens descends even to the brute animals, plants, and stones, insofar as they are capable of receiving said harmony. For superior things contain and perfect all worldly things by a harmonic principle, and they accommodate each other to bring the world into balance. Hence the ancient Egyptians, while considering the harmony of celestial things in the matters of the lower world, observed a certain sympathy, consensus, and kinship of some things to others, and of manifest things to occult powers. They established a certain sacred and mystical philosophy exhibited under various symbols and ingenious coverings of things, which they also call "hieroglyphic." This science, which has been lost until our day, we are restoring—God willing—in our work **Oedipus Aegyptiacus** <note>Kircher’s own massive 1655 treatise attempting to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs through a symbolic, mystical lens.</note>.

For they saw that the highest things lie hidden in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest; in heaven, indeed, earthly things exist in a celestial way, but on earth, celestial things exist in an earthly way. For why else do we think those plants we call **heliotropes** <term>heliotropia: from the Greek "helios" (sun) and "trepein" (to turn); plants that turn toward the sun.</term>, that is, "sun-followers" (about which we have written extensively in our **Magnetic Art** <note>Referencing Kircher’s book *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* or *Magnes*, where he discusses biological "magnetism" or attraction.</note>), turn toward the rising of the sun? Or the **selenotropes**, or "moon-followers," toward the Moon?

<margin>
All things are turned toward the Sun.
</margin>

Truly, driven by nothing other than that harmonic appetite lying hidden in all things, they all offer prayers and sing hymns to the leaders of their own order; but some in an intellectual way, others in a rational way, some in a natural way, and others in a sensory way. Do you not see how plants, even if violently pressed down, rise up with great effort to conform themselves to the heaven? Even the branches of trees, if drawn through an oblique hole, as soon as they find freer air, eagerly lift their heads upward, as if impatient out of love for the heaven.

Therefore, any "sun-follower" moves toward the Sun in whatever way it can. If anyone could hear the vibration made by them in the air by the circular motion of the plant, they would surely perceive a certain sound of that kind, composed for its "king," as much as plants or other things are able to produce. On earth, therefore, one may behold the Sun, Moon, and stars, but in an earthly condition; in heaven, one may see plants, animals, and stones, but in a celestial condition, according to a certain analogy.

There are, therefore, stones, plants, and animals that are "Solar," others that are "Saturnine," or "Jovial" <note>relating to Jupiter</note>; others are "Martial" <note>relating to Mars</note>, or "Venereal" <note>relating to Venus</note>; and finally others are "Mercurial" or "Lunar." Indeed, according to the more secret **Cabalists**, there is no herb on earth that does not have its own star in the firmament which says to it, "Grow."

And to begin with stones, who does not know that there is a very great appetite in them for the superior bodies and all those things that correspond to them in nature by any means? **Proclus** relates that the stone *Helitis* <note>likely an ancient name for a sunstone or hematite</note> imitates the Sun with its golden rays and its movement. Not unlike this was that gem which **Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician.</note> writes was on the finger of **Pope Clement VII**; it had a golden spot that was moved around daily, rising and setting according to the motion of the Sun. There are, therefore,

<margin>
The consensus and dissensus of plants and stones in heaven.
</margin>

Solar stones, such as all **Carbuncles** and **Pyropes** <note>Ancient terms for deep red, glowing gemstones like garnets or rubies.</note>. There are also Lunar stones, called **Selenites** <term>Selenite: named for Selene (the Moon); historically believed to wax and wane in luster with the moon's phases.</term> for that reason; it is written that **Pope Gregory X** had one of this kind, which mimicked the metamorphoses of the Moon, passing from blue to a white color according to the variation of the lunar light. Furthermore, the **Magnet** belongs to Mars; the **Sapphire** to Jupiter; the **Agate** to Mercury; all these stones are imbued with parallel virtues.

The various movements of herbs, plants, and trees also clearly declare the consensus of vegetable nature with the heavens. Among these, some follow the daily motion of the Sun, like the heliotropes described in the *Magnetic Art*; some follow the proper motion of the Sun, such as the leaves of the Willow, the White Poplar, the Elm, the Lime, and the Olive, which experience has shown are turned completely over on the very day of the Solstice; some of which...

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Some flowers open at sunrise, dilate as much as they can at noon, and close at sunset with such a love for the stars that, following and chasing the sun in its circuit, they even twist their own stems. At night, out of longing for the sun, they contract as if wasting away. Others, such as **Licorice** <note>original: *Glycyrrhiza*</note> and **Acacia**, raise their leaves toward the presence of the Sun like arms reaching up to embrace it, and lower them when it is absent, as if seeking it below the horizon and holding it tightly. There are also many types of **Moonwort** <note>original: *Lunaria*; plants historically believed to be influenced by the phases of the moon</note> which, stirred by love for the Moon, follow it with unceasing motion, taking on various forms just as the Moon itself takes on various phases. 

Likewise, the other planets have their corresponding plants: **Saturn** is represented on earth by the Cypress, Hellebore, and Monkshood <note>original: *Napellus*</note>; **Jupiter** by Rosemary, Citron, Betony, and Valerian; **Mars** by the Oak, Vervain <note>original: *Verbena*</note>, and Wormwood <note>original: *Absynthium*</note>; **Venus** by the Myrtle, Vine-leaf, and Savin; and finally **Mercury** by pomegranates, hyacinth, and narcissus.

Finally, in the economy of animals, this kind of consensus <note>A term used here to mean "harmonious agreement" or "sympathy"</note> is observed even more clearly. Some animals express their love for the stars to which they are subject through song, some through their gaze, and others through their gestures. Since I have already delivered the history of all these things partly in my *Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's *Magnes; sive de arte magnetica* (1641)</note> and intend to deliver it more fully in the *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>*Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652-54), Kircher's massive work on Egyptology and hermeticism</note>, I do not wish to dwell on them here. What else is the **Lion** and the **Rooster** but a kind of terrestrial Sun? What is the **Cat** but the Moon? What is the **Wolf** but Mars? What else do the **Dog**, **Horse**, **Deer**, and **Donkey** represent but Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn on earth? The voice, motion, and liveliness of the Rooster, the bird of the Sun, declare this clearly enough. 

It is a wondrous thing that **Proclus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> relates: that Solar demons, while appearing with the face of a lion, vanished immediately at the sight and song of a white rooster. He adds the reason: because those things established in the same order of being always revere the superior things, and freely yield to and serve them. All these things seem to testify and signify, with such a wonderful and pleasant spectacle, that heaven and earth have entered into a treaty and a kind of harmonic consensus to greatly congratulate mankind, and to diligently invite them to look up to, cultivate, and venerate the **Author** of so many goods, the **Craftsman** of such great miracles, and the most wise **Architect** of the most beautiful things. Indeed, the whole earth, together with the mass of water and whatever dwells in them, is so fitted to the superior elements, and those elements are so exposed to the heaven and stars, and in turn both are so ruled, tempered, and established by the counsel of inscrutable divine wisdom and prudence through hierarchical orders, that the whole of what we call **Nature**—connected by mutual embraces, bonds, duties, and functions—dwells concordantly in a marvelous harmony, as one from all, and all from one, amidst such a multitude of dissimilar and disagreeing things. But so that this harmony may appear more clearly, we have decided to subjoin here a schema of the entire harmony.

<margin>
Angels

Sulfur
Magnet

Shrubs
Serpentine things

</margin>

And so that we may better declare the **Sympathies and Antipathies** (or what is the same thing, the consonance and dissonance) in nature, imagine ten **enneachords** <note>Instruments with nine strings</note>, all of which are tuned in unison. That is, the first consists of nine strings and expresses the harmonic degrees of a single octave <note>original: *diapason*</note>, and all the others are tuned according to this one. Thus, all strings that represent the *proslambanomenon* <note>The lowest note</note> sound as a unison, and likewise for the *hypate*, *parhypate*, *lichanos*, and *mese* <note>Names of specific notes in the ancient Greek musical system</note>, as is clear in the following schema.

With all these enneachords placed continuously next to one another, it is certain (from what we declared in the first part of the preceding book) that if one *proslambanomenon* is struck, all the *proslambanomenas* of the remaining enneachords will also be set in motion, even if untouched. Again, if the *mese* of the first enneachord is struck, it will move the *meses* of all the remaining instruments by a certain hidden consensus, even if untouched; and so on for the rest. Therefore, if someone were to strike four strings—the *proslambanomenon*, *parhypate*, *mese*, and *nete*—at once, it is certain that all the others would respond similarly, even if untouched, and would thus exhibit a beautiful harmony woven from a fourth <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>, a major third <note>original: *ditono*</note>, and an octave <note>original: *diapason*</note>. Thus, no other strings will sound in consonance except those that respond in unison to the others. This harmony will become much more perceptible if the eight-stringed instruments <note>original: *octochorda*</note> were composed of different strings and resonant bodies. # Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance
<page-num>394</page-num>

<margin>The consonance and dissonance of things.</margin>
He established various Nine-stringed scales <note>original: *Enneachorda*; referencing a musical system of nine strings</note> of this kind in the world of the Nature of things, all arranged according to the celestial nine-stringed scale, such that when one is plucked, all the others are set in motion. Thus, in the preceding diagram: I. is the Nine-stringed scale of the Angelic world; II. is of the celestial bodies; III. is of metals; IV. of stones; V. of herbs; VI. of trees; VII. of aquatic creatures; VIII. of birds; IX. of quadrupeds; X. of colors, to which tastes and smells could be added, and so proceeding according to each order and degree of natural beings. And whatever is found on the individual strings—for instance, those on the *nete* <note>the highest string in the ancient Greek musical system</note> of each nine-stringed scale—are said to symbolize with Saturn ♄; for I know not what Saturnine nature they might represent, and they are so subordinated to each other that when one is plucked, the others (as was said of the strings) are all set in motion and sound a unison with one another. Likewise, all things that correspond to the *paranete* <note>the "next-to-highest" string</note> string in the individual nine-stringed scales symbolize with Jupiter ♃, and adopt entirely Jovian characters. And just as the string *proslambanomena* <note>the lowest string in the Greek system</note> does not accord with the *hypate* <note>the lowest string of the middle tetrachord</note> because of the "tone" <note>a major second interval</note>—which forms a dissonant interval—so Jovian things are entirely dissonant with Saturnine ones because of the "tone" by which they are distant, unless, as will be said later, they are corrected by syncopation <note>a musical technique of suspension that resolves a dissonance into a consonance</note>. Furthermore, just as the *proslambanomena* accords with the *parhypate* in a major third <term>ditono: an interval of two whole tones</term> as an imperfect consonance, so Martial things [related to Mars] also accord imperfectly with Saturnine things. Moreover, just as the perfect fifth <term>diapente</term> and perfect fourth <term>diatessaron</term> constitute a perfect octave <term>diapason</term>, so do the species of things corresponding to these. In a word: if you gather strings that are concordant in nature, you must produce concordant effects; if discordant, you will necessarily produce discordant ones. But how Man accords with all these things will be discussed more extensively in what follows.

## PRACTICAL CANONS
### Of Natural Magic, bound by Harmonic Laws.

<margin>How Orpheus, from his knowledge of proportions, drew all things to himself.</margin>
It is well established that natural magic is nothing other than a certain hidden and harmonic application of active things to passive things. Whoever knows this will, through suitable natural incitements musically combined, undoubtedly show himself to be a performer of wonders, and will think nothing in nature so closed and hidden that access to it is not opened to him by the help of this art. For nature is so benevolent toward certain individual things that she has bestowed upon them certain divine-like powers and gifts as excellent as those usually found in entire species. Between these, she placed proportions and similarities as if they were baits and lures for attracting one to another; by these, things are joined together and rejoice, as if by the same instinct of nature. And conversely, she inserted certain laws of agreement and disagreement—which we, not without merit, explain through consonances and dissonances—by which one thing separated far from another, yet artfully bound, is recalled again into a single harmony. He who considers these things will easily come to the opinion that nothing is denied to nature; for she takes great delight in these miracles. This is why she gave to individual things a certain power of "coagulation" <term>coaguli vim: the power to bind, set, or draw things together</term> and of attracting anything not unlike itself—as if it were bait—and the faculty of rejecting adverse things. Since we have dealt most extensively with each of these in our work on the *Magnetisms of Natural Things* <note>original: *Magnetismis rerum naturalium*; referring to Kircher’s 1641 book *Magnes*, which discussed physical and metaphorical magnetism</note>, we refer the reader there. Certainly, we read that Orpheus drew stones and wild beasts by no other means than analogical reasoning. Since he was a most wise Musician, Astrologer, and Magus, and knew perfectly well in what proportion and by what harmony each thing was composed by nature, and to which star it was subject, he adapted harmonic ratios to them. He brought forth even inanimate things through the power of the stars lying hidden within them by means of this external harmony—just as iron brings out hidden fire from flint, or as the blast of a bellows reveals a hidden flame. In this way, by timely tempering and mixing sounds, he imitated the harmony of the celestial stars, which he understood perfectly. He called the celestial harmony down to this earthly one, such that he could draw and charm whatever he wished by playing, even against every [other] influence and power, according to the very actions and proportions in which harmony exists in all things—even, if it is right to speak thus, the very stones and trees...

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

...trees and animals, once stirred, are driven toward whatever motion he desired through a harmonic arrangement—acting as a sort of preliminary preparation. This preparation is achieved through harmony; for since the heavens were established according to harmonic principles, and they accomplish all things through harmonic motions and sounds, it is only right that not just humans, but all lower things that obey the heavens, should be prepared to receive those celestial influences through harmonic means.

<margin>The composition of harmonic Theriac.</margin>
Therefore, just as a common form—a kind of harmony—is forged from a specific composition and mixture of herbs and other substances through the medical and astronomical arts, so too is a substance like Theriac <note>Theriac was a famous "universal antidote" or polypharmacy medicine in the Renaissance, often containing dozens of ingredients meant to create a perfect balance.</note> wonderfully enriched by the gifts and "dowry" of the stars. This occurs, as we shall later show regarding Theriac, through three virtues that harmonize toward the same end: the celestial virtue summoned through the skill of timely mixing, the celestial virtue naturally inherent in its parts, and the elemental virtue. The situation is exactly the same in every harmonic composition of <term>synergy</term> <note>original: *συνεργεία*; a working together of different forces</note>. Therefore, what Orpheus himself says concerning his seven-stringed Lyre—and as Briennius <note>Manuel Bryennios, a 14th-century Byzantine music theorist</note> speaks of it <term>more skillfully</term> <note>original: *ἐχμοτέρως*; perhaps meaning more scientifically or melodiously</note>—about it stirring rocks, plants, and animals, I might with better right apply to our preceding Nine-stringed Scale <note>original: *Enneachordo*</note>.

But so that you may see at least some practical application of this matter, we prescribe here certain rules <note>original: *canones*</note> so that the curious reader may learn what must be observed in the various harmonic compositions of nature. To proceed skillfully, let it be thus:

## CANON I.

<margin>The nature and character of individual things must be considered.</margin>
First, the nature and character of each star must be understood above all else. Then, one must study the individual classes of things in the earthly world that correspond to those stars. Thus, in the individual orders of stones, metals, plants, and animals, one must diligently consider which enjoy a Lunar, Solar, Jovian, or Saturnine character, and so on for the rest. Once these are reduced into certain classes, you shall also investigate the "strifes" and "hatreds" <note>This refers to the concept of antipathy and sympathy in nature—some things naturally repel each other while others attract.</note> between things with singular skill; for in magical operations, these provide the dissonance and consonance found in music, and they can be so artistically bound together that they produce a most beautiful harmony. Above all things, the opportune time, days, and hours must be observed, and they must be analogous to the things being adapted by physical skill; for this is of the greatest importance. One thing is more readily applied in winter, another in summer, another in autumn, and another in the springtime. Once these are properly understood, proceed to practice.

## CANON II.

<margin>What must be observed in the mixing of medicines.</margin>
All species of things that belong to a single string in the nine-stringed scale of the preceding diagram are so matched that they aim toward providing a single, extraordinary effect. Thus, Solar things joined together provide a most excellent Solar effect, Lunar things a Lunar effect, Jovian things a Jovian, and so on for the rest; they correspond to a "unison" in the nine-stringed scale of Nature. In this way, if you mix Saturnine things with Jovian or Martian things, you will not achieve the intended effect because their natures disagree. However, you will succeed if you join both Saturnine and Martian things to Jovian ones; for in this way they will bind each other, and one will break the force of the other so that the intended effect may emerge. Martian things are usually distant from Saturnine things by a "ditone" or "semiditone" <note>In musical terms, a major or minor third; here used to describe the degree of natural "distance" or discord between planetary influences.</note>. Likewise, Venusian things, which are distant from Saturnine things by a "diapente" <note>A perfect fifth.</note>...

## CANON III. Chemical

<margin>A secret in Chemistry.</margin>
Whoever wishes to proceed in chemical operations with caution and the desired effect, it is necessary above all else that he possess the knowledge of dissonance and consonance. This dissonance and consonance consists in this: that you recognize which minerals are consonant to one another, which are dissonant, and by which intermediaries they may be bound and recalled into concord. For example, if one wishes to produce a "Solar" effect, he will first take care that all Solar elements conspire into one by way of the **diapason** <note>An octave.</note>; then, through a **ditone** or **diapente** <note>A major third or a perfect fifth.</note>, a harmony is produced that is most absolute in all its proportions. Let all heterogeneous things be kept far from here, as they are dissonant—such as herbs, juices, gums, and similar things not contained within the natural class of minerals. However, dissonant things of the same natural order may be included in a most perfect harmony if they are syncopated by intermediaries in the prescribed manner. If anyone were able to divide the "metallic tone" in two, using Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note> as the mediator, he would undoubtedly have found that which has been most zealously sought from ages past to this very day <note>A reference to the Alkahest or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; yet "the Moon" <note>Silver</note> will be easily obtained if Mercury <note>☿</note> is syncopated with Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄; lead</note>—constituting a sixth interval—by means of a "Venereal" ligature <note>A binding agent associated with Venus/Copper.</note>. Truly, the harmonic exemplar of nature must be set forth in all things so that you may achieve a harmonic effect. But since we have reserved this harmonic application in chemical business for our work *The Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's massive 1665 encyclopedia of geology and chemistry, *Mundus Subterraneus*.</note>, we refer the reader there, where they will find everything they might desire concerning this matter, proven by innumerable experiments. For neither time nor the sheer bulk of this current work allowed us to include everything here.

## CANON IV. Botanical.

<margin>Things to be observed in the nature of plants.</margin>
In the "Economy of Plants and Trees," diligently examine which herbs symbolize <note>Have a natural affinity or "correspondence" with one another.</note> and which do not; what character each possesses in the heavens, and which string each refers to on our nine-stringed instrument <note>The Enneachord of nature described on previous pages.</note>. If you do this, you will know you have found a nursery of prodigious effects. Separate the Dissonant from the Consonant, unless you know how to bind them together so artfully that you make them not only concordant, but altogether conspiring in the highest sweetness. Solar, Jovial, and Venereal substances joined together perform the same role as the **diapason** (octave), the **ditone** (third), or the **diapente** (fifth) in music: a perfect harmony. Conversely, Saturnine, Martial, Lunar, and Mercurial substances will induce the greatest dissonance in things, performing the same as the intervals of the 2nd, 4th, and 7th in music. If, however, they are "corrected" by being bound with Jovial, Solar, and Venereal elements, they perform the same effect as syncopated 2nds, 4ths, 5ths, and 7ths in music—a sound harsher indeed to those unaccustomed to it, but bringing the greatest benefits with it. Of this kind are the **Alexiterics** <note>Protective medicines or charms against poison.</note>, **Antidotes**, and similar things; since these hold a middle place between the life-giving and the deadly, they are judged as dissonant, yet once mixed, they become consonant through "correction." For when taken internally, even if they are repugnant to the taste, they nevertheless restore the body to complete health by freeing it from superfluous humors. This kind of most perfect harmony shines forth especially in that most famous preparation of **Theriac** <note>A legendary polypharmacy "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients.</note>, where mixed Solar, Jovial, and Venereal elements are bound and syncopated with dissonant Saturnine, Martial, and Lunar elements through the artifice of joining, so that they produce a most absolute harmony in all proportions...

## CANON V. The Physician.

Since all members of the human body symbolize <note>resonate or correspond</note> with created things, it is certain that all worldly materials—having been created solely for the sake of man—conspire into the most absolute harmony, which is the health and optimal constitution of the human body. For just as individual members respond to individual planets, so also those things which regard the planets of both the greater world <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> and the lesser world <note>the microcosm or human body</note> have a certain innate appetite for preserving the members of the microcosm, which they exert at the opportune place and time when they are received.

Hence, just as Solar things are carried by an implanted appetite toward the Sun (☉), Lunar things toward the Moon (☾), Mercurial things toward Mercury (☿), Venereal things toward Venus (♀), Martial things toward Mars (♂), Jovial things toward Jupiter (♃), and finally Saturnine things toward Saturn (♄), and harmonize with them—each paying its own hymns as it were—so too all cardiac things harmonize with the Sun of the microcosm, cephalic <note>head-related</note> with the Moon, spermatic <note>reproductive</note> with Venus, pulmonary <note>lung-related</note> with Mercury, bilious <note>gall-related</note> with Mars, hepatic <note>liver-related</note> with Jupiter, splenetic <note>spleen-related</note> with Saturn, and finally stomachic things harmonize to a certain extent with the Earth—as if with a certain kitchen and pantry of all. Kircher visualizes the human anatomy as a vertical scale of nine "notes" or organs.</note>. In which

However, because it would produce not harmony but confusion and a dissonant melody if one were to excite all strings at once, hence, by a certain harmonic proportion, nutrients will be so tempered that, omitting the dissonances, they always bring about a harmonic temperament forged from perfect consonances. <header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

<margin>Whatever has some similarity with a part of the human body is usually its medicine.</margin>
...he will undoubtedly find. For just as a musical string moves another string tensioned in the same way; so any thing, whether taken from the order of mineral, vegetable, or sentient nature, which represents some member, part, or humor by the "character of similarity"—that is, by form, figure, color, or a similar habit of the body—is believed to excite that same member, part, or humor, either for the attraction of good or the repelling of evil. Hence, fleshy things increase and nourish flesh, bony things bones, bloody things blood, bilious things bile, and nervous things nerves. So things expressing diseases by similarity contribute to driving them out.

In this way, the *Galgulus* <note>original: *Galgulus*; the Golden Oriole, a yellow bird believed in folklore to cure jaundice if the patient looked at it.</note> cures the jaundiced; the *Alce* <note>original: *Alce*; the elk. Its hoof was a traditional remedy for epilepsy (the "falling sickness").</note> cures the epileptic; for a stomach ailment, the *lupine* <note>A type of legume.</note> cures stomachs; for diseases of snakes, snakes themselves; the liver of a rabid dog cures hydrophobia <note>Rabies.</note>; and countless others, regarding which see our *Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's book *Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica*.</note>. Likewise, all stony and gravelly things, or those that have obtained some shadow of similarity to a stone, are a remedy against the stone <note>Kidney stones or bladder stones, often called "calculus" in Latin.</note>. For the "sinning humor" <note>original: *humor peccans*; a medical term for an imbalanced bodily fluid causing illness.</note> existing unnaturally in some member, being dissonant to it, is torn away, attracted, and expelled by a medicine taken that is consonant with that sinning humor; thus it finally frees the member from the sinning humor, that dissonant guest. And so that I may explain the causes of this kind of sympathy more deeply in a harmonic way, it seemed best to start a little further back.

That "healing nature of diseases" was called by *Hippocrates* the "instrumental cause," which the soul uses immediately to exercise the principal faculties in the vital vapor, for the sake of either restoring or preserving health. You should understand this not only as an elementary mixture of parts and a temperament of the primary qualities, but most importantly as that substance composed of the *radical moisture* <note>The essential life-fluid thought to be consumed over a lifetime.</note>, the *primigenial heat* <note>The innate warmth of a living being.</note>, and the *innate spirit*, which acts as the bond of soul and body, the essential foundation of celestial and terrestrial things, which the more secret Philosophers call the "elementary heaven" or the "celestial element." This, according to the mind of Hippocrates, falling from individual bodies, informs, ferments, and disposes the seed; and it forms the body for the soul that is to enter it, from the matter subjected to it, into similar parts from which it flowed out, by a new harmonic mixture of the offspring. For a part cut from the head forms a new head, the idea of which it retained; that from the heart, a new heart; from the liver, a new liver; from the lung, a new lung; and so on for the rest. Moreover, the member it formed for itself in the unborn fetus, it is the office of the same nature to preserve unharmed in the child once born, or to restore it to health if it should happen to fall away from it. Although that whole nature concurs for the integrity, preservation, and safety of the whole body, nevertheless its various particles primarily bring aid and help to the different parts of the body in which they are innate, which Physicians are accustomed to call the "disposition" of the parts proceeding from the whole substance. For although these particles of innate substance differ very little from each other in nature, they nevertheless have a certain proper **sympathy** <term>original: *συμπάθειαν* (sympatheian); a natural affinity or "feeling together" between parts of a whole.</term> with the parts of the body in which they reside; for they are consonant with these; they reside in them and not others, they preside over them, and they heal them.

<margin>What things are most to be observed by the Physician.</margin>
Since, therefore, according to that saying of *Hippocrates*, "Natures are the healers of diseases," <term>original: *νόσων φύσεις ἰατροὶ* (noson physeis iatroi); the fundamental principle of Greek medicine that the body heals itself.</term> and nature itself immediately heals diseases, the Physician, as the servant of nature, must take the greatest care that he joins those three things which constitute implanted nature—namely, the radical moisture, the innate spirit, and the innate heat—in a suitable bond and a thoroughly harmonic proportion. He must ensure that the oily moisture does not fail the heat, nor the heat itself devastate its food by excess and defraud the spirit; if he provides this harmony, let him not doubt that nature, by its own character, will soon bring our body back to perfect integrity. But what that harmonic connection is, and how it ought to be provided by the Physician, remains to be investigated. The *Arabs* and *Egyptians* say that Medicine is the "Universal" preserver of nature's strength and the extirpator of diseased affections; the Alchemists call it the "Life-giving Stone"; *Paracelsus* calls it "Azoth" or "Potable Gold"; *Lullus* asserts it to be the "Quintessence" made from the dregs of wine, which he calls "Heaven." But since many have sought this, few have found it, and none have left it to posterity, it has happened that Physicians—deterred partly by weariness and partly by difficulty and expense—have descended from the *universal* medicine which benefits the whole body, to the *particular* medicine which benefits individual parts. Hence, as was said a little before, medicines for the head, the heart, the spleen, the liver, the lungs, and similar things—detected both by experiment and by "character" and "signature"—are used among Physicians today...

<margin>Universal Medicine extracted from the Microcosm <note>Man viewed as a "little world" reflecting the universe.</note>.</margin>
It is certainly well known that powders and salts of the human skull, when properly prepared, possess the greatest power even in desperate conditions of the head. I also hear that among the Arabs, a medicine suitable for dispelling all diseases is prepared from mummies. As I said above, a medicine will be all the more effective the closer it is in affinity of substance to the parts being treated. Indeed, one should not simply take any and every part of various plants and animals, but only those that form a major third, a fifth, an octave, or a unison <note>original: *ditonum*, *diapente*, *diapason*, *vnisonum*; Kircher uses these musical intervals to classify the "strength" of the medicinal relationship.</note> with the analogous members of the body. The remaining parts should be neglected as if they were dissonant, as is clear from the "nine-stringed instrument of nature" <note>original: *enneachordo naturae*.</note>. Nor should these be taken from diseased plants or animals, but from those in which the radical moisture <note>The essential life-fluid believed to sustain vitality.</note> remains for some time due to violent suffocation. See what we have said more extensively on these matters in our *Magnetic Art*.

## On the harmonic proportion and form to be induced in things.

<margin>What is harmonic proportion?</margin>
Harmonic proportion, as has been said, is a certain universal form existing in all things arranged in an orderly fashion. It causes all the harmony of things because, since all nature is harmonic, the chain of Ideal forms—continued from the first Archetype <note>The divine original pattern or model.</note> down to the last—demanded above all else that all other things participate in its harmony. Therefore, it is my intention to explain here, as briefly as I can, how this harmonic form is found in things for the purpose of procuring the intended harmony.

In the classes of all natural things, there are certain analogs that are carried along by an innate desire, proportioned to each other in exactly the same way; these provide the intended harmony. The elements of this worldly music are the radical moisture, the implanted spirit, and natural heat. These three exist not only in living beings but also, according to a certain analogy, in the heavens and in all inanimate things.

<margin>How consonances and dissonances occur in the things of the world.</margin>
Therefore, as long as these three are well-constituted in any order of beings, that thing is judged to maintain its proper harmony and a temperament that is most perfect in all its numbers. But if the radical moisture acts more than is right upon the spirit and heat, or if these act upon the moisture, dissonance will immediately be born. In the celestial world, we might not incongruously call this radical moisture the "Lunar influence"; the life-giving heat, the "Solar influence"; and the worldly spirit, the "bond" between the two. If these influences become immoderate, whether due to the conjunction or the dissonant aspects of neighboring planets, they will lead not only themselves but all sublunary things into disorder <note>original: *ἀταξίαν* (ataxian)</note> and a manifest imbalance of temperament <note>original: *δυσκρασίαν* (dyskrasian)</note>. We shall heal these if—at the appropriate time and place, and under the appropriate astrological aspect—we restore the moisture (which is failing due to excess or deficiency) to harmonic medicine by means of proportional heat and the mediation of the spirit, as we taught a little earlier. In this way, the harmony of the lower world, having been led into disharmony through the unhappy configurations and influences of the planets, induces storms, floods, sterility, famine, plague, and epidemic diseases as time passes. These things, however, having obtained a better position and disposition toward one another in the course of time, introduce a healthful influence to the intemperance of things...

### The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

brought back, they reduce it to a moderate state; from this, there continuously arises a serenity of the air, fertility, and the greatest abundance of all things, as well as the joy and concord of peoples—all of which are the highest signs of a harmonic constitution. In the elemental world, the clouds are the receptacles for this moisture, established for the greatest necessity. Surely, with the heavens as their guide and by that life-giving heat, they pour back the waters—which have been inhaled and drawn upward—onto this earth which craves them. If they should abound with more moisture than is right, it is sucked back from the earth, drawn away, and with the favor of the heavens, carried elsewhere by another carrier: the spirit of the wind. Using the wind as a vehicle, the clouds are carried to their respective lands to distribute a kind of "provisions," supplying them wherever there is a need. If, however, the earth is moistened more than is right by long-lasting rains, behold! That wind is sent forth to bring serenity and dryness, restoring the earth to its harmony in the space of even a single night. Thus, to complete the harmony of the universe, the rains provide water for irrigating the lands; the clouds serve as the vessel in which the waters are contained; the winds provide the chariot on which they are carried; Necessity is the horse, the Law of Nature is the driver, and the Moderator of all these is He who does what He wills in Heaven, Earth, Air, and Water.

Following this harmony of nature is the Law of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a traditional philosophical concept that the human body reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note>, in which the principal members correspond to the principal parts of the world. Since, therefore, the radical moisture <note>term: *humidum radicale*; the vital fluid believed in medieval medicine to sustain life, similar to oil in a lamp.</note>, the spirit, and the innate heat are present in each limb in the proportion required by that limb's condition, if those three should fall into dissonance through excess or defect, they must be brought back to a harmonic moderation by the application of analogous things, following the method indicated just a little earlier.

<margin>The mixing of wine with water to settle one's character must be harmonic.</margin>
Plutarch certainly prescribes a harmonic proportion for the mixing of wine with water, both for health and for settling the character of the soul. For if you mix 3 parts of water with 4 parts of wine, a *diatessaron* <note>original: *diatessaron*; the musical interval of a Fourth.</note> is born—an imperfect consonance, separated from others and unpleasant. Just as wine from such a mixture is almost watery and unpleasant, it is specifically suited for serious men intent on matters of great weight. If, however, you mix two parts of water with three parts of wine, a *diapente* <note>original: *diapente*; the musical interval of a Fifth.</note> is born—a charming and pleasant consonance, and such a temperament makes for a pleasant drink. But if you mix two parts of water with two parts of wine, the *diapason* <note>original: *diapason*; the musical interval of an Octave.</note> consonance is born—the sweetest and most pleasant of all. Such a mixture will always be rendered pleasant, provided one respects the place, time, custom, the persons involved, and the quality of the wine.

But to return to the works of nature: all species—whether inanimate, vegetable, or sentient—unite themselves to one another by a harmonic bond, for without this they could not be preserved. Metallic veins draw from the bowels of the earth the moisture and vapors necessary for the generation of any metal, according to the proportion suitable for the metal they are producing. Among plants, each one sucks from the "breasts of the earth" that nourishment which is most agreeable to its preservation, in such and such a proportion; if they were to overstep this, they would necessarily fail.

Following this application of nature is Art, which, in the business of grafting, never inserts trees of a dissonant nature into one another, but only those that are consonant and closer to each other in natural similarity. A miracle of this kind is seen here in Rome, to the great admiration of all, in the private garden of the Discalced Augustinian Fathers. There, a Citrus tree <note>original: *Citrus*; likely referring to a lemon or citron tree.</note> hangs in the air without a root, yet it produces leaves, flowers, and fruit solely from the nourishment it receives from neighboring similar trees, whose branches are entwined with its own. From this, it is clear that plants are so eager for the heavens that they break through all obstacles to satisfy their appetite. They also studiously avoid other things dissonant to them, just as the cabbage turns away from the vine by the flight of its stalks and leaves; the squash so hates a vessel full of oil placed beneath it that it seems to contract itself entirely.

In animals, too, each one seeks by natural instinct that food which is most agreeable to its preservation. It flees by every means from that which could bring about any kind of destruction. Hence, by Divine Providence, every creature has learned its own antidote, by which it may timely repel the evils it incautiously encounters. And all these things prove nothing else but a certain harmonic form latent in all things, by which the excesses and defects of things are called back to a middle balance. Truly, more will be said on these matters in what follows. To conclude everything summarily: the disharmony of the aforementioned things will be called back to harmony when, according to nature...

## REGISTER IV.

### The Sympathy of the Microcosm with the Macrocosm, or on Human Music.

<margin>The logic of the three worlds</margin>
According to the teachings of the ancients, the world is a kind of living animal. It was believed—demonstrated by the power of reason, though perhaps erroneously—that a single mind or soul, endowed with a single spirit, is diffused through a single body with the highest degree of uniformity. This was suggested not so much by human logic as by the conspiracy <note>In the Latin sense of "conspiratio," meaning "breathing together" or harmonious agreement.</note> of the beauty of all its individual parts and actions. For we consider it fitting that this world, being both one and manifold at the same time, is distributed into many worlds like joints and members of nature—some similar, some dissimilar—which come together from strife into friendship, and are brought back from dissonance into consonance, and from infinite plurality into a true form. Therefore, besides that supreme and incorporeal world upon which all others depend, there are three worlds joined by a continuous bond, like a golden chain: the Greater World (Macrocosm), the Lesser World (Microcosm), and the Political World, which is established from both. Man, the microcosm, was created after the rest so that the Divine Goodness might express within him, as a brief compendium, whatever He had previously made in a diffused manner. For if we undertake an exact comparison of individuals, we will find nothing in the greater world whose property does not also shine forth in man—the son of the world—as if in a measure and compendium of all things. For there is in man a certain celestial portion, another sublunary portion, and a third placed at the boundary of both which joins their forces like a kind of ether. This is especially clear if you see the agreement of the internal organs with external seats through the intermediate rivers of humors and spirits, or again among the organs themselves, in the way that the highest things are joined to the lowest through the middle; this corresponds in equal proportion to both the spirits and the parts of the whole soul. Similarly, in the body, in the soul, and in the spirit, there are their own stars, their own axes, centers, and circles, zones and elements. Conversely, in the heavens, there are their own plants and animals, their own organs, membranes, muscles, veins, arteries, and nerves; their own head, heart, and liver; their own vital, animal, and natural spirit; and their own faculties of desire, anger, and reason. Thus, no saying among the Philosophers is truer or more famous than that "all things are in all things," and that even the smallest things maintain a perpetual <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "συμπάθειαν" (sympatheian). A fundamental concept in Renaissance philosophy where all parts of the universe feel or react to one another due to a hidden connection.</note> with the greatest. While considering this kinship of nature and the laws of perennial fellowship, the ancients—eventually mixing all things with amorous affects—believed this universe to be a certain <term>breathing and exhalation</term> <note>original: "ἅπνουν καὶ ἔκπνουν" (apnoun kai ekpnoun). This refers to the Stoic idea of the universe as a living organism that "breathes" through cycles of expansion and contraction.</note>, an animal that is entirely "conspirable" and "exspirable." From this, they composed their science under the name of "True Magic," which is fixed upon that mutual conspiracy and symphony of causes and effects among all universal parts.

<margin>Which are the plants of the microcosm.</margin>
You see, therefore, how man expresses the celestial <term>enneachordon</term> <note>A nine-stringed instrument. Here, it refers to the nine-fold harmony of the celestial bodies (the seven planets plus the sphere of fixed stars and the First Mover) reflected in the human constitution.</note> within himself, and what an apt harmony it is: the Heart represents the Sun, the source of all life and motion; the Brain is the Moon, the mother of moist fertility; the Liver is Jupiter, fostering all things with mild heat; the Spleen is Saturn, the seat of all melancholy; the Gallbladder is Mars, ordained by nature to strengthen the expulsive force; the Kidneys and other spermatic parts are Venus, a benign structure for promoting the movement of the generative nature; the Lungs are Mercury, connecting all things with breath; and finally, the Stomach represents the Earth, serving as the receptacle for the whole. You see how beautifully the four humors in the elements of the world harmonize with the four elements: the bilious with fire, the phlegmatic with water, the sanguine with air, and the melancholic with earth. Here, the veins represent the abundance of rivers; the bladder, the Ocean; the vessels, the ponds and lakes; the seven cited principal members, the seven metallic bodies; the bones, the stone-quarries of the earth; the flesh, the soil; and the hair, the grass—all corresponding with the most exact harmony and agreement. Thus, the hidden signature of herbs refers to the individual parts of the Microcosm...

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature.

For the **ears**, there is **asarum** <note>Hazelwort</note> and **shells**; for the **eyes**, **eyebright**, **marigold**, and **cinquefoil**; for the **nose**, **horsemint**; for the **teeth**, **henbane**, **toothwort**, and the **pits and berries** of fruits. **Uvularia** <note>Bellwort</note> is for the **throat**; **liverwort**, **lichen**, and **oak-fungus** are for the **liver**; **citron**, **balm**, **motherwort**, **nard**, and **cardamom** are for the **heart**; **lungwort** for the **lungs**; **hart's tongue fern**, **spleenwort**, and **ceterach** for the **spleen**; **cyclamen** and **galangal** for the **stomach**. All of these are like certain "strings" which, when properly tuned, resonate through a hidden consensus with the corresponding strings of the **microcosm** <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human body, seen as a miniature version of the entire universe</note>. Indeed, the head seems to leap for joy at the presence of "cephalic" <note>Head-healing</note> remedies, the liver at "hepatic" ones, the heart at "cardiac" ones, and so the other members seem to rejoice in a likeness of nature, meeting the things that correspond to them by analogy with open arms, as if they were friendly guests and preservers.

<margin>Those things which have a likeness to the body's members heal those same members.</margin>

In no different a way do we arrive at the knowledge of what each thing is useful for by observing the "characters" <note>The physical signs or "signatures" imprinted by nature</note> that mark diseases, through the hidden harmony of the worlds. For just as the preceding "terrestrial stars"—that is, the plants—are carried from the circumference to the centers of the parts and members they mark, acting as the guardians and preservers of those members; so the following indices of diseases and imbalances in the microcosm attract the morbid cause from the centers of the members to the circumference by a hidden reason, expelling it along with themselves. Once the cause is expelled, they restore the body to its original harmony. In this way, **crystal**, **flint**, **citrine stone**, **lynx-stone**, the **stone of the microcosm** <note>Kidney or bladder stones</note>, **gromwell** <note>original: *Lithospermon*, literally "stone-seed"</note>, the pits of almost all fruits, and six hundred species of **saxifrage** <note>Literally "stone-breaker"</note> seek out, dissolve, and shatter stony concretions in the kidneys and bladder by a wonderful consensus. Thus, the juices of herbs that resemble one of the four humors are ordained to draw out that humor. In this way, the **Crab** <note>original: *Cancer*</note> kills **cancer** <note>The disease was named after the crab due to the swollen veins resembling legs</note>; a **scorpion** crushed into a wound heals the same. **Worms** kill **worms**; a **wolf** kills a **wolf**. **Hemorrhoids** are cured by **pilewort** <note>original: *chondrilla*</note>, which reflects their shape and figure. A flow of **blood** is cured by blood ground into a powder; the powder of a **serpent** cures the bites of serpents. Time would fail me if I wished to bring forward every single example here.

<margin>Diseases are the weather patterns of the microcosm.</margin>

There are as many species of diseases in the microcosm as there are types of "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning</note> in the elemental world. Thus **Galen** showed that the generation of gases within us is the same as that which occurs in the sublunary world. **Hippocrates**, too, in his book *On the Nature of the Child*, sketched for us a common likeness with plants—not only in disease and health, but in our entire birth, death, growth, maturity, and decay. What else are **catarrhs** and **fluxes** (which the Greeks call <unclear>ἐφ-</unclear> <note>Word is heavily struck through in the original</note>) than **rains**, **snows**, and **hail**? What are **apoplexies**, **comas**, **lethargies**, and other sleep-inducing diseases, than the **failing of the lights** <note>Eclipses</note>, **inundations**, and **cataclysms**? What are **kidney pains** and **gouty pains**, other than **monstrous births** and things seen in places where they do not belong, entirely against nature? What else are **colic**, **hysterical**, and **hypochondriacal pains**, than **whirlwinds**, the **bursting of dikes**, and the most savage **earthquakes**, tangled together within the bowels of the earth by the clashing of the contrary elements of fire and water, or bile and phlegm? Indeed, not only can this admirable consensus be compared between the whole microcosm and the whole **megacosm** <note>The Great World or Universe</note>, but also in each individual part. So much so that in the human head alone, whatever nature has gathered into the entire universe is displayed for our viewing; thus it can truly be said: *the end of all things is nature perfected, a microcosm in a macrocosm* <note>original: ἁπάντων τέλος φύσις ἀποτελεσμένη μεγακόσμῳ μικρόκοσμος</note>. For since the things of the intellect, the intellect itself, and the intelligible world are the same, surely the intellect shall be the world, but as the **entelechy** <note>The realized potential or "soul"</note> of the human head. Therefore, the world is to be looked for within the same place. If indeed the intellect, while naked in itself, is clothed in all intelligible things, it takes the place of **prime matter**; it performs the duty of **Form** while it shadows the intelligible things so that it differs not at all from them. Thus the soul corresponds to **plants** by its vegetative faculty, to **animals** by its sensitive and motive faculty, and to **Angels and GOD** by its rational faculty. But to speak a little more exactly: we have the element of **Earth** in the head as the **skull**; **Water** as the **dura mater**; **Air** as the **pia mater** <note>The protective membranes of the brain</note>; and **Fire** as the **substance of the brain** itself; or if Earth is greater in taste...

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

You will note that touch corresponds to water; the eyes to light; the ears to air; and the smoky and fiery exhalations to the nostrils. The metals, which are excreted here and there, represent dross; hence the black humor <note>The "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> of iron, the verdigris of copper, the yellow of gold, the pale hue of tin, the white of silver, and the ash-gray of lead—which emulates bronze—are all produced from bile, phlegm, sulfur, and mercury. The Sea is present at the boundaries of the body, scattering many rivulets down into the brain; cities and houses are seen in the small swellings of the ventricles, and various paths are found in the ducts of the vessels. The forests are the hair; the wild beasts are lice, insects, and other creatures that occasionally arise from the brain. Distilling tears imitate the dew and frost, while the dross held in the larger corner of the eye resembles filth in the corners of the world. Foul vapors obscuring the sight are like mist; clouds are the windings of the brain; the ringing in the ears is the wind; and a runny nose represents falling rain. Saliva is foamy snow; hail is phlegm gathered together; thunder is the rumbling of wind in the gut; lightning is the shock of the eyes; and a thunderbolt is a terrible gaze. Comets and other fiery meteors are displayed by the streaks and redness of the face and forehead.

If we move past the elements and their compounds to traverse the ether, we find that the Sun flourishes in the innate heat of the brain, and the Moon in its primordial moisture—the two greatest lights of the body. Jupiter resides in the tempered blood, Saturn in the melancholic, Mars in the bilious, and Venus in the phlegmatic. Mercury, however, resides in the mouth and tongue. If we examine the fixed stars, the structure of the brain clearly displays the circles of the planetary spheres and images of the globe. You see, therefore, that the entire machine of the world is perfectly symmetrical not only to man, but even to a single part of him. It is no wonder, then, that man, being composed of all parts of the world, contains all things within himself. All of this Hugo the Cardinal <note>original: "Hugo Cardinalis," referring to Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican friar famous for his biblical commentaries.</note> beautifully describes in his own way: <margin>The analogy of the microcosm with the macrocosm.</margin>

> "Every creature," he says, "speaks to us with a triple voice. The first voice is: *Receive a benefit*; the second: *Pay your debt*; the third: *Flee punishment*. The first voice is that of the serving heavens, speaking thus: 'I minister light to you by day so that you may see, and darkness by night so that you may rest.' The Air says: 'I provide you with the breath of life and every kind of bird for your service.' The Water says: 'I give you drink, I purge filth, I water parched things, and I provide kinds of fish for your use.' The Earth says: 'I carry you, I nourish you with bread and wine, and I fill your tables with every kind of fruit and animal.' The second voice is that of the world warning: 'See, O man,' it says, 'how he who made me for your sake loved you; I serve you so that you may serve him who made both me and you.' The third voice is that of threat: Fire says, 'You shall be burned by me'; Water says, 'You shall be drowned in me'; Earth and Hell say, 'You shall be swallowed by us, unless you respond to the benefits granted by God shining out within us.'"

But to return to our goal: certainly the ancients, looking upon the mass of the most perfect figure in the microcosm, the diverse variety of celestial and elementary things, the elegant order of the most magnificent things, and the beautiful consensus and harmony of the most graceful things, discovered numbers, measures, proportions, and harmonies from this marvelous structure. They observed the strangely proportioned consonances and measurements of all the members with one another. Since these things are proper to this place, we have decided to treat them a little more extensively.

### §. I.
->On the harmonic proportion of the parts of the human body in numbers.<-

Architects, following Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect whose theories on the proportions of the human body influenced Renaissance art and the famous "Vitruvian Man" by Leonardo da Vinci.</note>, are generally accustomed to divide the stature of a man into 10 parts so that they may investigate the proportions of the remaining parts from these; others have found 7, and others different measures. We, following the harmonic architecture of nature, will first divide the measurement of the human body—being more consonant with nature—into 9 parts. For nature herself formed man in such a way that she proposed the face to be viewed in the highest place, and the other parts of the entire body take their measurement from there. The face itself consists of three dimensions: one shall be from the top of the forehead where the hair begins to the eyebrows; another from there to the bottom of the nostrils; the last from the nostrils to the chin. The first is the seat of **wisdom**, the second of **beauty**, and the third of **goodness**. These, when increased, yield the entire stature of the human body,

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature.

<margin>Measurements of the human body.</margin>
...into nine portions, distinguished into three quasi-Zones. The first portion will be the face itself; the chest will make the second portion. From the top of the stomach to the navel is the third. From here to the bottom of the thigh is the fourth; the two hips down to the back of the knee <note>original: "poplitem"</note> will contain two more. Finally, from there to the ankle <note>original: "nodum," literally 'the knot'</note> are the shins; however, this lowest part—which is from the ankle to the bottom of the sole—along with the small space of the throat (which is between the top of the chest and the top of the gullet), and the space from the start of the hair at the top of the forehead to the crown of the head; these three, I say, joined together, constitute another portion. Therefore, the total length of human nature will consist of exactly nine parts. We are speaking here, however, of the perfect and most consummate man of ideal proportions, not of the stature of infants, women, or the elderly, whose bodies differ marvelously from true proportion. Furthermore, from the outside of the shoulders to the joints of the limbs, and from the armpits <note>original: "axillis"</note> on the inside to the boundaries of the palm and fingers, is three faces. Thus, the total length of the arms consists of seven faces. The width of the chest from armpit to armpit is two faces, and thus the width—which is the span of the outstretched hands—is exactly as great as the height of the man. Indeed, the analogy and measure of the individual parts relative to each other is as follows:

The length from between the eyebrows to the top of the nostrils is equal to the extension of the chin from the throat. As much as it is from the top of the nostrils to the chin, so much it is from the throat to the bottom of the gullet, and therefore it provides what is a semitone in music. Again, the interval of the upper lip from the mouth to the bottom of the nose is the same as the prominence of the top of the nostrils from the lip, and the same as the depth of the eyes from between the eyebrows to the inner corners. The width of the chest will be contained in two faces, the space between each nipple in one, and their certain placement from the lower gullet will be found with a compass of the same dimension. The width of the palm and the sole is one portion and a half, of which nine portions constitute the total height.

Again, the parts of the height are found in this way: the height of the head through the middle of the forehead is three parts; likewise, the height of the top of the hip through the back of the head from the top of the forehead to the neck is two parts; likewise the hip, the neck two parts, the chest through the armpits to the back five; the belly through the middle four; the total circumference of the upper arms, hips, shins, thumbs, and other joints corresponds to the length of the limbs. The height from the bottom of the ankles to the top of the foot will correspond to the length from the top of the foot to the end of the nail. The circumference of the neck corresponds to that part which is from the top of the chest to the navel; so says Pomponius Gauricus <note>Pomponius Gauricus (c. 1482–1530) was an Italian Renaissance scholar whose work *De Sculptura* established rules for artistic proportion.</note>. But so that the proportions of the whole symmetry and harmony may be better known, we shall exhibit them by another method in smaller numbers, following Vitruvius <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose "Vitruvian Man" theory posited that the human body's proportions could be mapped into a square and a circle.</note>, who asserts that the body consists of ten heads. The difference of this system from the preceding one proceeds from nothing other than the measurement of human bodies that are either not similar or do not correspond to each other in proportion. If, therefore, we consider the length of the human body to be divided into 180 parts, the individual parts compared to each other will obtain the quantity of as many parts as the following table reports.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature.

Whoever properly compares these numbers will find all the ratios of the more perfect consonances within them. For first, 6 to 6, 30 to 30, and 18 to 18 <note>OCR text reads "18 ad 8", likely a typo for 18 ad 18</note> represent the **unison**. 1 to 2 and 12 to 24 represent the **octave** <term>diapason; the interval of an eighth</term>. 4 to 6 is the **fifth** <term>diapente; the interval of a fifth</term>; 18 to 24 is the **fourth** <term>diatessaron; the interval of a fourth</term>. 1 to 4 and 6 to 24 represent the **double octave** <term>disdiapason; an interval spanning two octaves</term>. Indeed, the parts of the face will not create harmony with the rest unless the equality of the 3 parts of length corresponds with the equality of the 3 parts of width. For in this way the forehead, nose, and chin—being equal in length—show a perfect unison with the 3 parts of the face's width (namely, the two eyes and the intervening space between them, which are likewise equal).

<margin>Human symmetry is commensurable with the square and the circle.</margin>
Again, just as the unison is the principle of beauty and harmony, if any of these three does not maintain an equally sounding proportion, immediately some foul dissonance emerges that destroys beauty and harmony. This is apparent in those men whose forehead is too extended and nose too contracted, or whose forehead is too contracted and nose longer than is right. You will find the same in the proportions of the other limbs, as is clear in the accompanying figure. In this figure, you also see that the most perfect man is commensurable with the square and the circle. Indeed, a double center can be established in man for the circle, according to the two-fold posture of the limbs. For if he adjusts his hands and feet, spread apart as much as possible, into the shape of a **St. Andrew’s cross**, the center of the circle touching the extremities of the hands and feet will be the navel itself; but if, with feet joined, he extends his hands straight out, the center of the circle touching the extremities of the hands and feet will be the middle of the reproductive parts.

<margin>The symmetry of Noah’s Ark and Solomon’s Temple.</margin>
From this, it happened that the wisest men, observing the marvelous proportion in the fabric of the human body, built the structures of temples dedicated to GOD according to the same model. For both **Salianus** and **Villalpandus** <note>Father Jean-Baptiste Salian and Juan Bautista Villalpando were famous 16th/17th-century scholars who wrote extensively on biblical architecture and proportions.</note> demonstrate at length that Noah's Ark and the Temple of Jerusalem corresponded to these kinds of measurements of the human body. These things having been shown, nothing remains except that we now contemplate the internal harmony as well.

### §. II.
### On the Internal Harmony of the Microcosm.

<margin>The wisdom of GOD in the construction of man.</margin>
The human body is divided into three zones or regions, as it were. The first is of the head, and it represents the **archetypal heaven**, the intellectual kingdom. The second is of the chest, and it exhibits the **starry heaven**, as it were, in which the Sun, the Moon, and the other Planets, having been established, exercise their operations. The third belongs to the **Belly**, and represents the **elemental world**, the kingdom of corruption and generation. These sound together with one another in a certain admirable harmony.

The head, the citadel of sacred **Pallas** <note>A poetic reference to Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom, whose "citadel" is the brain.</note>, contains the brain, the principal province of the microcosmic earth. Its skull consists of 8 bones, to which the structure of the entire head is entrusted, and the manifold vaulting of the interior house is bound together as if by certain walls. Amidst this truly stupendous workmanship are seen the marvelous paths of the veins, the halls, the sinuses, the columns, and the vaulted involution, the spirals of the brain and the aqueducts, the innumerable springs of the nerves, the white marrow or "silver cords" of admirable fecundity—all ordained by GOD with incomprehensible skill for the preservation of the brain. He made the skull hard so that it could withstand external blows; He also armed the interior substance of the brain with two membranes <note>original: "meningibus"</note> defending it against injuries. The first of these is called the **Dura Mater** <note>original: "dura Mater"; literally "Hard Mother," the tough outer membrane</note>, which fills all the internal sinuses and cavities. The other, called the **Pia Mater** <note>original: "pia Mater"; literally "Pious/Tender Mother," the delicate inner membrane</note>, distributes the whole brain into different compartments. 

Time would fail me if I wished to recount all the particles of the brain; if I were to attempt to trace that trunk of the brain, or **silver rope**, into its sacred pipe—namely, the spine of the back; if I wished to distribute all the pairs of nerves arising from that cord through all the limbs, which (although anatomists count them as 30, according to the number of vertebrae) are nevertheless infinite. But since we have treated these matters at length in the preceding [book], and in the first book concerning the construction of the ear and the tongue, we refer the reader there. Let us proceed, therefore, to the second region of the chest—namely, the chest as the receptacle of the spiritual parts and the home of the heart. This is seen to be formed in the likeness of a vault or a **microcosmic lute** <note>original: "cytharæ microcoſmicę"</note>, acting as a certain fountain and spring of all harmony, as will be said later; for in this, the 7 microcosmic planets...

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...the dwelling, like a certain seven-stringed lyre <term>heptachord; a seven-stringed instrument</term>, contains a marvelous consonance of all things. For if you compare this space to the visible and invisible world, the **spleen** corresponds to the earth, the **gallbladder** to fire, the **intestines** with their phlegm to the sea, and the **air** [in the lungs] to the heavens—moving with a double motion of expansion <term>systole</term> and contraction <term>diastole</term>, much like the movement from east to west and the reverse of the celestial bodies. 

<margin>The members of the microcosm are compared with the political world.</margin>
If, indeed, we were to compare the body to a **Republic**, **Reason** would be called the King, the **Will** would be the Queen, the **Intellect** the Counselor, and finally the **Heart** would represent the Nobles. For when the heart fails, all things collapse; the heart beats its drum with perpetual expansion and contraction, sounding now the "retreat" and now the "call to arms" <note>original: *classicum*, a Roman trumpet signal for battle</note>. Nor is it unfitting to compare it to a **private household**, in which the **legs** act as the chariot, the **brain** as the counselor, the **liver** and **stomach** represent the kitchen, the **spleen** and **kidneys** the sewers, and the **veins** show the way for the food. The **arteries** supply heat, the **nerves** prepare the seasoning; **melancholy** juice provides the lean, **phlegmatic** the fat, **bilious** the hot, and **sanguine** the tempered portions. **Imagination** suggests the paintings, **Memory** narrates the stories of those paintings, the **eyes** represent the candelabras, and the **heart** moderates everything, with the remaining members thronging about it like servants.

The **heart**, therefore, is the seat of the irascible soul, the source of faculty and vital spirit, the hearth of natural heat, and the **Sun of the microcosm**, by whose perennial influence all things are preserved; hence, to conserve its heat, it consists of a very dense and hard substance, woven together with every kind of fortification. Furthermore, the four vessels of the heart can be not unfittingly compared to the four rivers of Paradise. For on the right side there are two veins: the **vena cava** brings the blood, and the **arterial vein** <note>The pulmonary artery</note> carries it ready from the heart into the lungs. 

<margin>The use of the members in the human microcosm.</margin>
On the left side are situated two arteries: the **Aorta** distributes the vital spirit and blood to the whole body; finally, the **venous artery** <note>The pulmonary vein</note> carries the inspired air into the heart, brings back the "sooty vapors" <note>carbon dioxide/waste gases in 17th-century physiology</note> of the vital spirit, and supplies arterial blood to the lungs. The bellows of this most perfect organ are constituted by the spongy **lungs**, conspicuous with their five lobes; for while these are dilated, they draw in air like a bellows, and when pressed and constricted, they distribute it—diffused through innumerable channels—to all the members as a necessity, thus fanning the heat of the heart.

Next follows the **stomach**, the workshop of chylification <term>chyle; the milky fluid produced during digestion</term>, and the steward and butler. If this organ is poorly affected, it undermines the entire harmony of the body, like a troublesome collector of debts causing much business for a man. So that it might be kept in its duty and not fall into total dissonance, two bodies are placed around it—the **liver** and the **spleen**—like a pot between two fires, for by their warmth it is preserved in its natural heat. The **liver** nourishes the entire family of the body at its own expense; it is the seat of love and desire, and upon its good mixture <note>Greek: εὐκρασία (*eukrasia*)</note> or bad mixture <note>Greek: ἀκρασία (*akrasia*)</note> depend both the color of a man and all his vital faculties. It is connected to the brain through the nerves, to the heart through the arteries and the vena cava, to the stomach, intestines, and spleen through the splenic and rare mesenteric vessels, and to the other parts of the body through its own and common ligaments. The **gallbladder** purges the liver by attracting the thinner bile; the **spleen** frees and purges it of the melancholy humor; the **kidneys** do the same for the watery humor; and the **intestine** thrusts out the attracted earthy and dreg-like waste. The **mesenteric veins** prepare the chyle and contribute the first stage of blood-making, to which the liver gives form and redness; the **vena cava** distributes it, and the other parts purge the royal house of blood-making <note>Greek: αἱματώσεως (*haimatoseos*)</note>. If these are compared to the starry world, they are found to agree most exactly.

<margin>The kingdom of generation and corruption in the microcosm.</margin>
The third region follows: the kingdom of **generation and corruption**, filled with meteorological impressions <note>The lower abdomen was often compared to the lower atmosphere where weather/waste occurs</note>. This belly contains within itself the **intestines**, the **bladder**, and the **spermatic parts**. The intestine, which in a man is seven times his length, is marked with different names according to its different functions. The first part after the stomach is called the **pelorus** or **duodenum**; the second, the **jejunum**; the third, the **ileum**, placed between both hips (whence come iliac diseases and the womb); these three are the thin and narrow intestines. The thick ones follow: first the **caecum**, like a shaggy bag; then the **colon**, the largest of all, the prison of winds and flatulence and the source of colic diseases. Following this is the **rectum**, so named from its continuous length, which, inserted into the sacred bone <term>sacrum</term>, finally opens for evacuation. Next follows the **bladder** of the microcosmic sea, like a certain channel in which all the waters of the lesser world are gathered as if in a pool. Finally, the **spermatic vessels** follow, which contain within themselves the "virtual microcosm," ordained by nature for the propagation of the species. 

Who, however, could sufficiently marvel at the admirable wisdom of **GOD** even in the nature of the seed itself, who from such a tiny fluid fashioned so many various and distinct parts: more than two hundred bones, and as many cartilages...
