Who can sufficiently proclaim the miracle of the female womb? As soon as it has received the generative fluid, it forms a perfected human being within a strictly harmonic interval of time. For in the first six days, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> testifies, the seed is transformed into something frothy and similar to butter. Soon after three days, spots of blood and red filaments appear; after fifteen days have passed from conception, it resembles coagulated blood. After another twelve days, the flesh is seen with the distinction of the three principal organs <note>Usually referring to the heart, liver, and brain.</note>. Afterwards, the beginning of the spinal cord is discerned; finally, after nine days, the head is distinguished from the shoulders, and the extremities of the sides and the belly are clearly discerned by the senses. And thus the fetus, which occupies a minimum space of six months in the womb, is curled into a ball and perfected in a truly harmonic time, as is evident from the numbers written here <note>The author is linking the stages of fetal development (6, 3, 15, 12, 9 days) to musical ratios and proportions.</note>. Finally, after seven months, or most commonly nine (for an eight-month period of birth is dissonant), the fetus, with frequent quivering of the hands and feet, ruptures the membranes and stimulates the womb with the sharpness of the released fluid; then the womb, burdened by weight and stimulated by the expulsive force, finally excludes its burden. I have treated these things at length so that you may look up to this fabric, in which the admirable power of **GOD**, His supreme wisdom, and infinite goodness shine forth in a wonderful way, and that you may learn from this to love the Eternal God. ### Section III.
## *On the perceptible harmony and music of the Microcosm in relation to the*
## *Celestial and Elemental world.*

**In** the preceding sections, we showed that the distances of the **Stars** are like certain strings, and the globes of the stars themselves are like weights attached to those strings, ordered by the harmony of the world in such a proportion that—just as strings stretched by different weights produce different sounds—if the proportions of the weights are in a harmonic proportion to each other, the strings extended and struck by them will exhibit consonant intervals in the same ratio. Thus I say, if by divine power the worldly bodies were suspended from material strings, the struck strings would necessarily produce the same most perfect and most harmonious sound, all of which is clearly evident from the proportions of the worldly bodies to one another as presented above.

In a similar way, in the elemental world (of whose perceptible symphony much was said previously), a certain perceptible harmony lies hidden, which would shine forth most clearly if **Divine Wisdom** were to strengthen the weakness of our auditory faculty. Indeed, motion, as was said in the first book, causes the striking together of bodies; from this striking of bodies, with air or water intervening, sound is made. And if the motions are harmonically proportional, a harmonic sound will be stirred up; if not, dissonances will be born. Furthermore, if the motions are fast, high-pitched sounds will be born; if slow, low-pitched sounds. With these things supposed, a triple perceptible harmony can be considered here. The first is from the motion of flight and pursuit, which we see most clearly in the family of dissonant and consonant plants and animals in their strife and friendship. 
<margin>The sympathy of palm tree for palm tree.</margin> 
This wonderful harmony appears first in the **palm tree**, male and female, which love each other so much that one perishes entirely without the other; nor does it wish to be watered to grow unless the water is drawn from the other sex. The **Cacao tree** of America entirely wastes away without the **Ebony** shading it; and to embrace many things in a few words, there is no herb that does not harmonize or disharmonize with another. Thus the **fern** abominates the **reed**, and the **vine** hates the **cabbage** with a natural hatred; yet in a very damp place, the fern begins to harmonize with the reed, for while the reed is almost suffocated by too much moisture, the fern frees it by diverting what is superfluous into itself. ### Of the Consonance and Dissonance of Nature

[...beneficial] with the juice of the vine <note>original: "vitis liquore", meaning wine</note> as soon as it meets the stomach of a drunken man which is discordant with itself, it begins to harmonize; while the excessive vapor of the wine is overcome by the juice of the *cabbage*, it restores the man to his original harmony. Furthermore, *Olive trees* are discordant to the oak, *chaste-tree* to *Satyrium*, and *water-lilies* to *St. John’s wort*, yet they harmonize with man when prepared in a harmonic ratio. Ants flee from *oregano*; they are discordant with the wing of a bat and the heart of a hoopoe; a goat flees from wild marjoram; a sheep so dreads *spearwort* <note>original: "Apium raninum," literally "frog-parsley," a toxic buttercup</note>, which is lethal to it, that nature has even depicted the plant upon its liver. Why does the elephant dread the grunting of a pig, but not the roar of a lion? Why does the bustard bird fly away at the sight of a horse, or the deer at the sight of a ram? Who taught the lark to so dread the hawk, or the hen the kite, that they would rather die in the hands of men—as has occasionally happened to me—than in the jaws of their enemy? 

<margin>
Various sympathies and antipathies of things.
</margin>

Certainly, this is nothing other than a certain hidden music, by which consonant things are so aptly tempered with dissonant ones that a most beautiful harmony must necessarily arise from them. But concerning this species of perceptible music, see the more copious treatment in the preceding sections.

The other species is a certain interior motion, by which the spirit, being harmonically excited, likewise excites the muscles harmonically. In the microcosm <note>The "small world," a traditional term for the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note> there are two things that constitute sensible harmony: the first is the motion or pulse, which draws its origin from the left ventricle of the heart as the seat of vital power and the workshop of innate heat, which the right ventricle of the heart serves as the workshop of the arterial blood. From these, through continuous *systole* and *diastole*—that is, the dilation and constriction [of the heart]—the spirits are born, which are the second instrument of sensible harmony. For as **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE).</note> rightly discusses in his book *On Food*, the pulsations of the veins and the respiration of the spirit are signs of health and disease according to various states of consonances and dissonances. For from these, the motor faculties and vital actions depend solely as if upon prime movers. Indeed, these motions are different in the various members of the microcosm; for if the spirits in the heart excite the muscles and fibers with a swifter motion, they will exhibit a sound similar to small musical strings, which happens most especially when the heart, dilated by joy, leaps. But in sadness, when the heart is weighed down, the languishing spirits cause slower motions, whence an effect entirely contrary to the former occurs. 

<margin>
The music of the pulses in the microcosm.
</margin>

Furthermore, the motions of the animal spirits in the liver are, in a perfectly healthy man, in a *sesquialtera* proportion <note>A 3:2 ratio, which creates the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> to the motions of the heart, and consequently harmonize in a *fifth* <term>diapente; the interval of a fifth</term>. The motions of the animal spirits in the spleen relate to the heart in a double proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio.</note>, for they move twice as slowly as the spirits excited in the heart, from which an *octave* <term>diapason; the interval of an eighth</term> arises. The motions of the spirits in the brain harmonize with the heart in a *fourth* <term>diatessaron; the interval of a fourth</term>, and so on for the rest. Therefore, in a perfectly healthy man, there is a perfect consonance of all members—not only an analogous one, but a truly sensible one, if the weakness of our ears could reach that far. For the muscles and the blood, agitated by the spirits, are necessarily moved; and from motion, a striking <note>original: "illusio," here referring to the physical striking or vibration that produces sound</note> is necessarily born, which a sound necessarily follows. Since the motions of the vital members are ordained by nature according to these harmonic proportions, as has been said extensively elsewhere, they will necessarily exhibit some harmony. 

But if, through an imbalance of the humors, the motions of the animal spirits in some vital member are stretched or relaxed more than is right, a disharmony is immediately introduced, which we say is nothing other than disease. This will be more severe the more the members are discordant with one another through inelegant motions. That this is true was shown extensively in the first part of this book, where we demonstrated through various experiences that our vital spirit is also moved harmonically by harmonious air caused by instruments or voices. Those intoxicated by the venom of the *tarantula* demonstrate this clearly; for a harmonious sound, as soon as it has seized the spirit of those bitten by the tarantula, excites it harmonically, and this spirit excites the muscles and fibers according to the measures of the harmonious air, which finally excite the man into leaps proportioned to his motions. The same happens in us: for while we hear beautiful music, we are immediately excited to produce similar songs and modulations. This would not happen at all unless the said harmony, through air affected by a similar harmony, imbued our spirit with a similar harmony as well. Since, therefore, the motions of the spirits in the vital members—the heart, brain, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys, etc.—are different according to the natural constitution of the members, they will harmonize beautifully with different motions, provided they are harmonic.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature

## Corollary I.

From this it is gathered why certain animals cannot endure the voices of other animals; it is because they evidently inflict a certain force upon the vital spirits that is contrary to their nature. Just as certain screeching sounds bring upon us a most troublesome shuddering.

## Corollary II.

<margin>
Why do herbs heal the diseases of the members they correspond to?
</margin>
It is also clear why herbs heal the diseases of the members to which they correspond so easily. For example, in the case of a severe inflammation of the liver <note>original: "Hepati"</note>, as soon as it has fallen into dissonance with the heart, if liverwort <note>original: "hepatica"</note> is taken, it immediately aids the member destined for its preservation. By its specific power, it diminishes excessive heat; once this is diminished, the liver is recalled from its imbalance <note>original: "intemperie," an imbalance of the four humors</note> and restored to its former harmony. The same must be judged to happen with other herbs corresponding to various other members.

<margin>
The third species of perceptible harmony
</margin>
The third species of perceptible harmony consists of the parts of both vegetative and sensitive nature, which are not only harmonious but themselves concur like instruments to constitute music; so that nature seems to have established all things for the use of music. I begin with the family of plants: trees of various sizes, between which there is a harmonic proportion, emit a harmonious sound when shaken by the wind. In this way, if several pine trees <note>original: "Pini"</note> were of such a size relative to one another that the first is to the second in a double ratio <note>original: "in dupla," corresponding to an octave</note>, this one to the third in a ratio of three-to-two <note>original: "in sesquialtera," a perfect fifth</note>, and the third to the fourth in a ratio of four-to-three <note>original: "in sesquitertia," a perfect fourth</note>, the fourth to the first in a triple ratio <note>original: "in tripla"</note>, and finally the fifth to the first in a quadruple ratio <note>original: "in quadrupla"</note>, I say that when shaken by the wind, they will present to the ears a sound that is utterly and perfectly harmonic, composed of the ratios 4, 5, 8, 12, 15. The same must be said of each and every shrub. Indeed, if anyone could perceive the movement of the growth of herbs, he would undoubtedly perceive a certain perpetual and harmonious sound.

<margin>
Perceptible harmony in the arrangement of trees.
</margin>

...and they gather similar things; the shins and legs of birds, most especially, are converted into pipes, flutes, and trumpets <note>original: "lituos"</note> of every kind; the intestines are turned into strings for making all types of stringed instruments, such as Harps, lutes <note>original: "testudines cheles," referring to instruments with a tortoise-shell shape</note>, lyres, and others of this sort; finally, the skin is turned into a drum; and the skeleton, as in a lute, contributes entirely to the framework of the instrument. # REGISTER V.
## On the Harmony of Pulses and Rhythms in the Human Body.

Nothing in the human body is so commended by harmony or dissonance as that marvelous variety of pulses; if it were granted to us to hear them, an irrefragable judgment would immediately be given to us concerning the healthy balance <note>original: "eucrasia"</note> or the morbid imbalance <note>original: "dyscrasia"</note> of the offending humors.

These pulses affect the entire artistry of music, whether you consider the intervals, the tempo, or the tension and relaxation; and beneath these lie hidden the causes of the greatest and almost prodigious effects, which we shall manifest once we have begun to treat such a worthy subject a little more deeply.

The wonderful harmony of pulses.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...and its condition is not simple, nor does it consist of simple parts; rather, it is composed of several elements. If any of these are missing, the motion does not occur, and thus there are as many variations of motion as there are parts that constitute it. In the pulses, five things especially are necessary for the complete perfection and nature of motion.

<margin>
The nature of pulses in motion.
</margin>

<margin>
The space through which motion occurs.
</margin>

**First**, the space through which the mover effects the motion, or through which the artery is moved. If this space is large, it creates a **large** pulse; if small, a **small** pulse; and finally, if it is middling, it produces a **moderate** pulse. From this, a triple variation of pulses immediately arises: large, small, and moderate.

<margin>
The measure of time in pulses.
</margin>

**Second**, time is required, which the motor <note>the "motor" here refers to the force that initiates movement</note> consumes in the motion. From this, another variation emerges, which depends on the measure of time. For if the motor consumes little time in the motion, it produces a **fast** pulse; if it takes much time, a **slow** pulse; and if the time is middling, a **moderate** pulse arises.

<margin>
What is the upward and downward motion in pulses?
</margin>

**Third**, since motion of this kind is composed of motion <term>anō</term> <note>Greek: ἄνω, meaning upward</note> or <term>katō</term> <note>Greek: κάτω, meaning downward</note>—that is, upward and downward—it will necessarily require an intermediate rest. From these rests, a third variation of the pulse arises: for either the artery lingers briefly in rest, producing a **frequent** pulse; or it lingers long, producing a **rare** pulse; or it lingers moderately, causing a pulse halfway between the two.

<margin>
What is the motive force in pulses?
</margin>

**Fourth**, a Motor is required, which we say is nothing other than the **vital faculty** <note>original: "facultatem vitalem," the animating force of life in 17th-century medicine</note> residing in the left ventricle of the heart, as we indicated above, as if dwelling in a center. From this faculty, the entire harmonic craftsmanship of the pulsation is completed. If this force is robust and strong, it renders a **vehement** pulse; if languid and dejected, a **feeble** one; if middling, it renders a **moderate** pulse between the vehement and the feeble.

<margin>
The artery is the instrument of the pulse.
</margin>

**Fifth**, the instrument of the Artery is required, by which the entire craftsmanship of motion is perfected. According to the condition of this artery, another variation of pulse is born. For if the artery is hard, dense, solid, and tough, it produces a **hard**, dense, and tense pulse; if, however, it is soft, flaccid, and loose, it renders such a pulse—that is, a **soft** one; or if it is of a middle condition, the artery will likewise exhibit a moderate pulse.

From these, fifteen variations of simple pulses emerge, resulting from the multiplication of the three simple differences by the five requirements, as is clear in the following table.

<margin>
How the motive force produces the pulse.
</margin>

But let us explain a little more deeply the marvelous harmony and the never-sufficiently-praised concord of this craftsmanship in producing these variations. The vital faculty, then, aware of its duty and excited by the utility it naturally perceives, moves the instruments committed to it with whatever strength it possesses. First, it agitates the arteries with an unceasing motion according to their quality and condition, and distends them as much as it can. By this faculty acting upon the aforementioned instruments through the stated space, motion is produced of such a condition as necessity demands. From this, it is clearly established that magnitude or smallness are to be taken from the space traversed, while the state of the faculty is understood by the strength of the stroke or the striking of the artery against the fingers, perceived through a hard or soft stroke in the pulses. Whoever is perfectly skilled in these things will understand not only the physiology of motions and pulses, but also...

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>Various differences of pulses.</margin>
From these pulses, the mechanism of the <term>microcosm<note>The "small world"—a common Renaissance concept that the human body is a miniature reflection of the universe.</note></term> is set in motion whenever it encounters an imbalance or a "bad mixture" <note>original: "discrásiam"</note> of the humors. Physicians describe these using a wide variety of names depending on the condition of the diseases: equal and unequal, as well as ordered unequal and unordered unequal. When a pulse is unequal in its magnitude but always maintains the same method, order, and regularity in its cycles of inequality, it is called an **ordered unequal** pulse; for instance, when every third or fourth beat is larger or smaller than the others, but always follows that same pattern. However, if it does this without order—changing its size now at every beat, now at every third or fourth beat, or after a longer interval—it is called an **unordered unequal** pulse. Within this category, others are called *myuri* <note>original: "myuri"; from the Greek for "mouse-tail," referring to a pulse that gradually tapers off in strength.</note>.

<margin>The intercurrent pulse.</margin>
An **intercurrent** pulse is one that, between two normal beats, produces another middle beat against the natural order—that is, one faster than the surrounding beats—as is shown in the musical notation.

-> Ordered unequal. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Unordered unequal. <-

<note>Two musical staves are shown side-by-side using mensural notation with diamond-shaped notes. The left staff, representing the "Ordered unequal" pulse, shows a regular rhythmic pattern of three notes on the middle line followed by one note on the top line, repeating consistently. The right staff, representing the "Unordered unequal" pulse, shows a chaotic and irregular sequence of notes placed at different heights and intervals, indicating a lack of predictable rhythm.</note>

The **intermittent** pulse follows a path contrary to the one mentioned above; the artery indulges in such long pauses that several beats seem to be missing.

-> Intercurrent. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Intermittent. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Failing. <-

<note>A single continuous musical staff is divided into three sections. The "Intercurrent" section shows notes crowded together to represent extra, rapid beats. The "Intermittent" section shows regular notes followed by a vertical stroke through the staff, representing a rest or a skipped beat. The "Failing" section shows the notes becoming increasingly sparse and dropping lower on the staff, indicating a dying pulse.</note>

A **failing** pulse <note>original: "deficiens"</note> occurs when the artery seems almost devoid of motion due to the extreme weakness of the beat. It is called a **reciprocal failing** pulse when, after a certain interval of time, it returns to motion again. This is clearly shown in the notation for intermittent and failing pulses.

A **wave-like** pulse <note>original: "undosus"</note> occurs when some parts of the pulse rise more and others less, or move slower or faster like waves pushing against one another. Some people confuse this with the **vermicular** and **formicant** pulses. The difference, however, is this: <margin>What the vermicular and formicant pulses are.</margin> the **vermicular** <note>original: "vermicans"; worm-like</note> pulse imitates the crawling progress and wavy motion of earthworms, while the **formicant** <note>original: "formicans"; ant-like</note> pulse imitates the tiny, rapid steps of ants.

The **goat-leap** pulse <margin>The goat-leap pulse.</margin> <note>original: "caprizans"</note> is categorized among the unequal pulses and takes its name from the behavior of fighting goats. When a goat attacks another, it first rears up, then briefly restrains itself mid-charge, and immediately rushes forward with a second motion that is far faster and stronger. If the pulse produces a similar motion, it is called "goat-leaping."

Among these, physicians list others, such as the **spasmodic**, **palpitating**, **hectic**, and **noisy** pulses, which I shall refrain from discussing here so as not to be too long-winded.

### On the rhythms or harmony of the pulses.

<margin>The source of the motions of expansion and contraction.</margin>
One must understand, therefore, that the structure and character of the pulse consist primarily of four parts: specifically two motions, acting like an <term>arsis and thesis<note>Greek terms for the "lift" and "fall" of a musical beat.</note></term>. One occurs when the artery is lifted upward <note>dilation/diastole</note>, and the other when it is compressed toward the lower part <note>contraction/systole</note>. Since this cycle consists of opposites, it necessarily contains certain intermediate pauses. One is the external pause, which is the limit of the pulse's expansion; the other is the internal pause, the limit of the artery's contraction. The former was most wisely ordained by nature for drawing in air and moderating the innate heat; the latter for expelling smoky vapors. But which of these...

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature.

<margin>What is the rhythm of the pulse?</margin>
<margin>Double rhythm</margin>
...of these movements for forming a solid judgment about the state of the body and health, he alone shall know it who rightly understands Rhythm, or the knowledge of harmonic concord and modulation—the parity and disparity which the pulse maintains between its <term>dilation<note>The expansion of the artery, known medically as diastole.</note></term> and <term>compression<note>The contraction of the artery, known medically as systole.</note></term>. Rhythm in this context is therefore nothing other than the proportion of the times within the pulse to one another. Since indeed proportion is the relationship of two quantities of the same kind to one another, and time is a type of quantity, it follows that if you compare the quantity of the artery's expansion to the quantity of its contraction, you can judge perfectly concerning excess, deficiency, and equality. Rhythm is twofold: equal and unequal. The former occurs when the time of expansion is equal to the time of contraction—that is, when one duration does not exceed the other. The latter proceeds in the opposite order.

<margin>Pararythmic and eurythmic pulses</margin>
Equal rhythm—which Galen calls <term>eurythmic<note>From the Greek "eurythmos," meaning well-rhythmed or natural.</note></term>, the natural and best pulse—is properly suited to those enjoying optimal health. However, when a change in pulse occurs by reason of age, region, or temperament, it is called <insert>unequal</insert> or **pararythmic**. Unequal rhythm—which Galen calls <term>ekrythmic<note>From the Greek "ekrythmos," meaning out of rhythm or non-natural.</note></term>—exceeds equal rhythm by either a manifest or a hidden excess. If the former, it occurs either with a multiple proportion (such as double, triple, or quadruple, under which proportions the perfect musical consonances—the octave, the octave-and-fifth, and the double octave—are considered) or with a "superparticular" proportion (such as the <term>sesquialtera<note>A 3:2 ratio.</note></term> or <term>hemiola<note>A musical ratio where three notes are played in the time of two.</note></term>, the 4:3 ratio, the 5:4 ratio, the 9:8 ratio, and so on; namely, the musical fifth, fourth, and whole tone). If the latter—that is, by a hidden excess—then the pulse is <term>eurythmic<note>The author likely means "arythmic" or "un-rhythmed" here in the sense of being unpredictable, though the text uses the term "Eurythmus" to describe the difficulty of notation.</note></term> and cannot be expressed by any certain proportion or any musical note, and thus should not be dealt with here. We shall instead deal with that manifest excess which shows us clear traces of health or infirmity. Indeed, we must see how these rhythms are reduced to harmonic laws, once we have first expressed the rhythms of different ages using musical notes.

### The Song of the Boy.

<margin>Equal rhythm or equal proportion in fusa notes.</margin>
<note>A five-line musical staff in mensural notation featuring a series of eight fusa notes (diamond-shaped heads with stems and single flags) all on the same pitch.</note>
This corresponds to the age of childhood; it has a swift contraction or expansion of the artery, just as the <term>fusa<note>A fast musical note value, similar to a modern eighth or sixteenth note.</note></term> notes of the "Cantus" or highest voice express.

### The Alto of the Youth.

<margin>Equal rhythm or equal proportion in semiminim notes.</margin>
<note>A five-line musical staff in mensural notation featuring a series of six semiminim notes (filled diamond-shaped heads with stems) all on the same pitch.</note>
Corresponding to the age of adolescence, it has a contraction and expansion of the artery suited to the <term>semiminim<note>A moderate musical note value, similar to a modern quarter note.</note></term> notes of the "Altus" voice.

### The Tenor of the Man.

<margin>Equal rhythm or equal proportion in minim notes.</margin>
<note>A five-line musical staff in mensural notation featuring a series of four minim notes (hollow diamond-shaped heads with stems) all on the same pitch.</note>
Corresponding to the age of manhood, it has a contraction and expansion of the artery suited to the <term>minim<note>A slower musical note value, similar to a modern half note.</note></term> notes of the "Tenor" voice.

### The Bass of the Old Man.

<margin>Equal rhythm or equal proportion in semibreve notes.</margin>
<note>A five-line musical staff in mensural notation featuring a series of four semibreve notes (hollow diamond-shaped heads without stems) all on the same pitch.</note>
Corresponding to old age, the artery undergoes a contraction and expansion such as the <term>semibreve<note>A long musical note value, similar to a modern whole note.</note></term> notes in the "Basis" or bass voice represent.

<margin>What is the pulse in children?</margin>
You see, therefore, the harmony of the rhythmic pulse across the different ages of life. In children enjoying good health, the pulse is frequent and swift, which the highest voice (appropriate for boys) beautifully expresses. In youths, however, the pulse is indeed more moderate, but with an equal con—

<margin>What is it in men?</margin>
<margin>What is the pulse in the elderly?</margin>
...is more rapid, and for this reason it is compared to the <term>Alto<note>The second-highest voice part in a four-part musical texture.</note></term>; its <term>pararhythmus<note>original: "pararhythmus"; a pulse that deviates from the natural rhythm of its age group.</note></term> differs from the previous stage by the interval of a <term>diatessaron<note>A perfect fourth in music.</note></term>. In the age of manhood, the pulse attains a perfect moderation, which we therefore most aptly express with the smallest notes in the <term>Tenor<note>The third voice part, traditionally considered the "foundation" or steady part of a composition.</note></term> voice; the pararythmus of this age differs from the second stage by the interval of a <term>ditone<note>A major third.</note></term> and from the highest stage by a <term>hexachord<note>A musical interval of a sixth.</note></term>. Finally, in the elderly, the pulse grows faint, and thus it is most aptly expressed by <term>semibreves<note>A musical note of long duration; here, it signifies the slow, heavy heartbeat of old age.</note></term> in the <term>Bass<note>original: "basis"; the lowest voice part.</note></term> or bottom voice; for its pararythmus differs from that of manhood by a ditone, from youth by a <term>diapente<note>A perfect fifth.</note></term>, and finally from childhood by a <term>diapason<note>An octave.</note></term>.

You see, therefore, that among equal rhythms, some are of a short time, others long, and others even longer. Thus, if one considers the rhythm of a child, it is by its very nature of a shorter duration, yet found to be equally vigorous. If this changes into the rhythm of youth, it acquires a rhythm of longer duration and a more spirited nature. When changed into the rhythm of manhood, it becomes most temperate and most fit for performing actions worthy of a human being, until, changed at last into the rhythm of old age, it withers into ruin. However, so that we may apply this harmonic speculation to some practical use, it remains to be said how this kind of rhythm can be examined in all circumstances, so that we might divine the health of the sick from them.

### On the Harmony of Pulses by Reason of the Four Temperaments, the Air, the Region, and the Seasons.

<margin>How different temperaments are considered by the nature of the pulse.</margin>
Since it is clearly established that humans possess various temperaments, it is certain that any given <term>temperament<note>The ancient medical theory that health is determined by the balance of four bodily fluids or "humors."</note></term> produces various, diverse, and altogether different pulses. For bodies excelling in a hot temperament are found to necessarily have a large, fast, and frequent pulse, but not a vehement one; and just as this complexion admits various degrees of intensity and relaxation, so too does it have different pulses.

Bodies of a cold temperament are endowed with pulses entirely contrary to those mentioned: small, slow, and frequent. Humid temperaments are endowed with a pulse exactly equal to the pulse of women, as will be taught shortly. Dry temperaments produce a larger, hard, and exceedingly rare pulse, somewhat more vehement, such as we experience in slender bodies. We exhibit the harmony of these temperaments in the following notes.

<note>A musical notation diagram featuring four square notes on a five-line staff. The notes correspond to the four temperaments: Cold, Hot, Humid, and Dry. Above and below the staff, brackets identify musical intervals: a "Dissonant Tone" between Cold and Hot; an "Octave" spanning from Cold to Dry; another "Dissonant Tone" between Humid and Dry; a "Fourth" between Hot and Humid; a "Fifth" between Hot and Dry; and a larger "Octave" bracket at the bottom spanning from Cold to Dry.</note>

In this diagram, you see the difference of the pulses in the four temperaments shown by musical notes, together with the combinations made between them. Just as the cold and hot temperaments are opposites, so too do their pulses differ entirely in time. They produce the same effect in music as a <term>tone<note>A whole step; here considered a "dissonant" interval because it creates tension rather than resolution.</note></term>, which is the most dissonant among consonances. By a similar reasoning, the pulses of the humid and dry temperaments differ from one another, and it is impossible for them to sound together, just as in music a tone cannot be consonant.

Cold and humid temperaments, being <term>systata<note>original: "systata"; from the Greek for "standing together" or "compatible."</note></term>, can agree, though with difficulty; joined together, they produce the same effect as a fourth in music, which, depending on its position, is sometimes consonant and sometimes dissonant. However, because the moisture is friendly to the heat, the hot and humid temperaments are highly sociable, and thus produce the same effect as an octave in music.

<header>Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature</header>

<margin>The pulse changes based on the different constitution of the air.</margin>
<margin>The diversity of the pulse in the four seasons of the year.</margin>
<margin>Autumnal pulses.</margin>
Furthermore, you will undoubtedly find very similar pulses resulting from the temperament <note>In this context, "temperament" refers to the specific mixture of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in the atmosphere.</note> of the air, as it is completely changed by either the seasons of the year or the different nature of various regions. According to Galen <note>A Greek physician (129–216 AD) whose theories on the four humors dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, the seasons of the year are divided for the best of reasons into hot, cold, dry, and moist. He established their temperament as so effective that they change not only the pulse but also our actions and almost all bodily functions. Indeed, in balanced bodies, it produces the greatest and most vehement pulses; but if the bodies are less balanced, the pulses will differ from the aforesaid standard according to how much the temperament of the body whose pulse you touch differs from the median balance. The reason is that the vital faculty in unbalanced bodies is not as robust, nor are the other functions as they should be. For bilious bodies fare better in winter, phlegmatic bodies in summer, and balanced bodies in spring. In summer, pulses become small, fast, frequent, and weak; the reason for this is the dissipation of the innate heat, which makes them weak, yet because the need for cooling is increased at that time, it follows that the pulses must be fast and frequent. Furthermore, in winter, pulses are small, slow, rare, and weak according to Galen; but we assert that they are large and moderate in other respects, and not as vehement as in spring. For since the internal parts heat up more in winter through <term>antiperistasis<note>The opposition of properties, where an internal quality (like heat) increases when surrounded by its opposite (external cold), as if the heat is being compressed and concentrated.</note></term>, it is necessary that large pulses follow. In Autumn, the pulses are rendered weak and unequal for two reasons: the first is that Autumn is likened to diseases arising from corruption; the second is due to the sudden inequality of the weather at this time, which nature cannot endure without harm. Nature finds it very difficult to be cooled and then immediately warmed in the same period, for she is distracted toward different things at once. As the artery adapts to the sensation of the weather—moving now toward larger, faster, and more frequent pulses, and now toward their opposites—it is inevitable that weakness and listlessness of the pulse follow.

To these four seasons, the nature of the air and the region correspond in every way. If the air of a region has a summery constitution, it produces a pulse like summer; if it has a spring-like disposition, it returns spring pulses; if it is autumnal or wintery, it will manifest such pulses. This wonderful analogy is followed by the fourfold time of day: Dawn, Midday, Sunset, and Night. Dawn corresponds to spring, Midday to summer, Sunset to autumn, and Night to winter, producing corresponding pulses in each of those times.

### Corollary I.

<margin>Why was the diversity of pulses established by nature?</margin>
And from what has been said, the wonderful harmony of pulses in bodies clearly appears—hidden, indeed, but ordered by divine counsel so that without this variety, no perfect health could persist in its proper time, for the harmony of the pulses seeks to match the harmony of the seasons. Just as the elemental world could not persist for the generation of things without the variation of the annual seasons (as was said above), so pulses—now vehement, thick, and hard; now soft, slow, and weak; now maintaining a middle course—are absolutely necessary both for drawing in ever-new air and for expelling the <term>sooty vapors<note>original: "fuligines"; literally "soot" or "smoke," referring to the waste products of the blood's "combustion" in early medical theory.</note></term> of the blood. Since all these matters were touched upon in the preceding sections, we will not dwell on them longer.

### Corollary II.

<margin>The harmony of pulses in men of different ages.</margin>
It is also clear from the preceding discourse that if we were permitted to hear the pulses of various times and ages, we would perceive a certain harmonious symphony or <term>mixture<note>original Greek: "σύγκρασιν" (synkrasin); a blending of different qualities or musical tones.</note></term> composed of thirds, fifths, and octaves. Since the pulse of a child compared to that of an old man is in a double or even quadruple proportion, a <term>diapason<note>An octave (2:1 ratio).</note></term> or a <term>disdiapason<note>A double octave (4:1 ratio).</note></term> would necessarily be perceived. And since the pulse of a child compared to a youth is in a ratio of five to three <note>original: "superbipartiente tertias," a mathematical ratio of 1 2/3 or 5:3.</note>, a <term>semiditone<note>A minor third.</note></term> would be continuously manifested to us. Again, since the pulse of a child compared to a grown man is in a <term>sesquialtera<note>A ratio of 3:2, which in music typically forms a perfect fifth.</note></term> proportion, soon a <term>diatessaron<note>A perfect fourth (4:3 ratio). Note that the author's specific musical-medical mappings may vary from standard music theory ratios.</note></term> would be felt, and so on for the rest—assuming, however, that each individual is in the best of health.

<header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

In a very similar way, the pulse of a healthy person in winter compared to the pulse of that same person in summer would be found to exist in a double proportion <note>original: "dupla proportione"; this is the 2:1 ratio, which in music forms an octave.</note>; Autumnal pulses compared to summer pulses are in a ratio of four-to-three <note>original: "sesquitertia"; the musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, and these compared to spring pulses are in a ratio of three-to-two <note>original: "sesquialtera"; the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. This was most wisely established by nature according to the laws of the seasons, as it is entirely necessary for preserving the balance of the bodily temperament. But if the pulses are weakened through an imbalance of the humors and a lack of order <note>original: "ἀταξίαν" (ataxian); a Greek medical term for physiological disorder or irregularity.</note>—as when a confused symphony replaces the steady, even rhythm of the pulse—the unity of harmony must necessarily perish. You see, therefore, that the pulses perfectly measure harmonic time, while the animal spirits <note>In historical medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be refined substances that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>, like voices, complete the harmony with precision.

A similar harmony is carried out between the pulses of a man and a woman.

### Corollary III.

<margin>
What dissonance is.
</margin>
From this it follows: that whenever the harmonic proportion of the pulses is disturbed, disease necessarily rushes in. Disease is nothing other than a certain dissonance of the humors; and just as these humors are highly diverse, so their various imbalances cause different diseases. In this way, there is one pulse for those with fever, another for those with dropsy <note>An old medical term for swelling caused by excess fluid (edema).</note>, another for the consumptive <note>Those suffering from wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note>, another for the epileptic, and so on for every other individual disease. This is why nature resists disease so forcefully; for disharmony tortures both the soul and the body and brings manifest violence to nature.

### Corollary IV.

If, therefore, there were a Physician who possessed such knowledge of this great harmony that he could recognize the pulses of individual diseases, he could undoubtedly lead the body back to perfect harmony through harmonic means applied by contraries—now by adding, now by subtracting. And since nature has willed that few should be aware of this secret science of pulses, it is no wonder that so few Physicians are found today who achieve anything remarkable in the cure of diseases. Nevertheless, if any Physician understands our meaning well and practices correctly according to this secret document of Science, I have no doubt that, aided by these principles, he will achieve wonders.

## Music of the Five External Senses.

<margin>
The physician must be skilled in music.
</margin>
The external senses in man also have their own harmonic union, perfectly joined together from consonances and dissonances. Before we prepare to describe the harmony of the "inner man"—that is, the moving symphony of the internal senses—we wish first to explain the external senses here, lest we seem to have omitted anything in this Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.

Since we have already treated the harmony of sight and colors extensively in the fourth part of the preceding book, as well as in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, and since this entire work is concerned with the object of hearing (which is music), nothing remains but for us to pursue the harmony of the remaining senses: Smell, Taste, and Touch.

<margin>
The music of tastes.
</margin>
Therefore, as Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath who wrote extensively on medicine, mathematics, and music.</note> says, musical proportion in tastes can be considered in two ways: simply, and by comparison. Simply put, the highest sweetness is referred to as the octave <note>original: "diapason".</note>; for there is a most sweet concord in tastes, and therefore "sweet" corresponds to it as a simple element; for what can be sweeter in either category? But a rich or "fat" taste—such as in well-prepared meats and eggs—is referred to the perfect fifth <note>original: "diapente"; a 3:2 ratio.</note>; for it is itself most pleasant after sweetness and is perfect in its own kind. The perfect fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"; a 4:3 ratio.</note>, however, matches the salty taste best. By itself, salt is harsh and unpleasant, just as the salty taste is; however, the fourth combined with the fifth completes the octave, whereas the fourth by itself clashes with the octave. Likewise, a salty taste paired with a rich/fat one brings the greatest delight, but it accords so poorly with sweetness that it is better joined to bitter things, such as well-salted olives. Therefore, the salty taste corresponds exactly to the musical fourth.

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

Again, the **minor third** <note>original: "semiditonus"</note> corresponds perfectly with the **insipid** <note>tasteless or bland</note>, and the **astringent** corresponds with the **major third** <note>original: "ditonus"</note>; for both are not unpleasant and harmonize with the **sweet**, just as the minor and major thirds harmonize with the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>. Furthermore, each of these tastes moves the senses only slightly, and they are somewhat similar to one another, which is also the case with the major and minor thirds. However, neither of these fits with the **fatty** <note>rich or oily</note>, nor does the major or minor third agree with the **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>, for such a composition creates no small discord. Again, they are similar in this: that the **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> harmonizes greatly with the major and minor thirds, just as both the insipid and the astringent harmonize best with the **salty**. For a fourth added to a major third creates a **major sixth**, and with a minor third it creates a **minor sixth**. Both of these are consonant, yet they are not particularly sweet on their own because they lack the "sweetness" and "fatness" of the primary intervals, just as the major and minor sixths do not reach the perfection of the octave or the fifth. 

The **sharp** <note>acrid or pungent</note> taste is similar to the major sixth, while the **sour** <note>acidic</note> is similar to the minor sixth. The sharp and the insipid naturally agree, as do the sour and the astringent—just as the major sixth is joined with the minor third, and the minor sixth with the major third to complete an octave. However, this is less "sweet" because the fifth is absent, just as the "fatness" is absent. The **harsh** <note>austere or dry-bitter</note> taste agrees with a moderate sharpness; therefore, both are well-joined with the insipid, according to the saying:

->*So that the tasteless beets of the workers' meals might have flavor,*<-
->*Oh, how often does the cook seek out wine and pepper?*<-
<note>This is a reference to the Roman poet Martial (Epigrams 10.48). Pepper represents the "sharp" and wine the "harsh."</note>

For pepper is sharp and wine is harsh; both flavors harmonize with the sweet and the fatty, just as both the major and minor sixths harmonize with the octave and the fifth. Yet neither harmonizes with the salty; for the fourth cannot be joined to a major or minor sixth. 

The **bitter** taste is similar to the **whole tone** <note>original: "tonus"</note>. A tone is always dissonant by itself, and the bitter is unpleasant by itself. The tone is the origin of all musical consonances; likewise, all fruits—whether sweet, astringent, sour, or sharp—are bitter before they ripen. Furthermore, a whole tone combines with no consonance worse than it does with the octave; similarly, no taste is more unhappily joined than bitter with sweet. The bitter taste also agrees with nothing more than the salty; likewise, a tone added to a fourth completes the fifth, which is the sweetest consonance—just as we see in salted olives. 

A light bitter taste does not shrink from the fatty, though it makes it somewhat worse, as seen in cakes made with wormwood, eggs, and cheese, or in vines where wormwood foliage has been cooked in; yet that flavor deviates only slightly from the fatty. Similarly, when a tone is added to a fifth, it becomes a major sixth—not as sweet as the fifth, but not entirely unpleasant. In the same way, if a tone is added to a minor or major third, a fourth is made from each, which is not particularly consonant; but the **tritone** <note>the "devil in music," an interval of three whole tones</note> is the harshest of all. Therefore, the same occurs when bitter is joined with the insipid, and even worse with the astringent, as in bitter acorns, than which nothing more dismal can be tasted. It is manifest, therefore, that this division of tastes agrees perfectly with musical proportion.

When, therefore, among tastes that agree in any way, the ratio of the best taste to the worse is a **double proportion** <note>2:1, the octave</note>, while the middle to the worse is a **four-to-three ratio** <note>original: "sesquitertia," the fourth</note>, and the best to the middle is a **three-to-two ratio** <note>original: "sesquialtera," the fifth</note>, then that taste will certainly be the best. We see this first in the relationship of the fatty to the sharp and the insipid; for it is clear that the best of these is the insipid because it can be endured on its own, the salty is middle, and the sharp is the worst. Therefore, the insipid will surpass the salty by a three-to-two ratio, the sharp by a double ratio, and the salty will surpass the sharp by a four-to-three ratio. Again, if we join the sweet with the sharp and the insipid, or with the sour and the insipid, the sweet will prevail such that it surpasses the insipid by a double, quadruple, or eightfold ratio—that is, by an octave, a double octave, or a triple octave—while the sour will surpass the insipid by a four-to-three ratio.

Yet another logic in the joining of tastes must be referred to the individual's sense. For those tastes which provide the greatest pleasure to the palate, we can rightly designate as the octave. From the less pleasant, it is a four-to-three ratio; from the middle, a three-to-two ratio. For example, let us suppose that to someone, harsh things are most pleasant. Indeed, salty things are pleasant to no one; no animal besides man—not even plants, except for a very few of their own kind—can be nourished by salt. Since the salty is a part of the bitter, it is worse because it is sharp, which is why no animal is born in salt; whereas in wormwood, though it is very bitter, small flies...

<margin>The practice of harmonic tempering in flavors.</margin>
The black species <note>original: "genus nigrum"</note> arises all summer long, and little worms are found in rue; therefore, one should take as much of the **harsh** <note>original: "austere"</note> as is sufficient, and three-quarters of the **sweet**—as if it were the worst of the astringents—so that the ratio of sweet to astringent is a **double proportion** <note>The ratio of 2:1, which creates an octave.</note>. In this way, a most pleasant flavor is established according to the proper nature of musical proportion. Some propose the **bittersweet** <note>original: γλυκύπικρον (*glykypikron*)</note>, that is, the sweet-subacid, as the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>, with the sweet relating as a **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note> and the sour as a **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. When these are joined, the octave—the sweetest of all musical consonances—is born, which is to say, nearly the most pleasing of all flavors. It is certain that some cooks have attained such great skill in preparing food that they boast that no appetite is so diminished that a harmonic preparation of food could not stir a new craving <note>original: "orexin"</note> within it.

<margin>How individual names might be assigned to tastes and odors.</margin>
What has been said about flavors ought to be said in exactly the same way regarding odors and touch, since the same logic applies to all. For just as there are different variations of colors in visible things, it is certain there are just as many variations of tastes, smells, and sensations of touch. I truly wonder that until now there has been no one to assign specific names to each odor, taste, and touch, especially since I see no difficulty in this. For a flavor could be named from the things themselves; so that besides sweet, bitter, salty, acidic, styptic, astringent, and fatty, there would be the "flavor of such-and-such a fruit," the "flavor of such-and-such a meat," the "flavor of such-and-such a bread," or a cheese. In the very same way, names could easily be imposed on odors and fragrant things: from the violet, "violet-like"; from the pear, "pear-like"; and from aromatics, "the scent of such-and-such a spice," of "such-and-such a wine," or "such-and-such a flower," and so on for the rest. If these things were done, something more exact could be established regarding the nature and harmony of these senses. But let others see to this. For us, it is enough to have demonstrated in some way that a certain wondrous harmony lies hidden beneath all things, and likewise beneath the five senses.

# REGISTER IV.

## The Symphonism of the Passions, or on the Music of the Various Affections of the Soul toward one another.

<margin>The double appetite in man.</margin>
That Divine **Harmonizer** <note>original: "Harmosta," referring to God as the tuner of the universe.</note> of things, after He had formed man from clay with a certain harmonic proportion of limbs—so that there might be some use for such beautifully ordered parts, and that the instrument might emerge perfect in every measure—He placed within him the breath of life. I mean the spirit, or the rational soul, which is perpetually moved by a **double appetite** as if by two air-receptacles or bellows. The first of these is on the side of the **sensory** <note>original: αἰσθητικὸς (*aisthetikos*)</note>, which is the origin of the disturbances, passions, and perturbations of the soul. The other is on the side of **reason**, the author of habits both natural and supernatural. Thus, a most beautiful organ soon shone forth in this worldly temple. Its foundations are the framework of the human body; its **registers** <note>the sliders that control the pipes in an organ</note> are the principal organs of life—the heart, the liver, and the brain; the **bellows** are the sensory and rational appetites; the **spirit** or air is the vital faculty. The **keys** <note>original: "palmulae sive tacti"</note>, as they are commonly called, are the various **disturbances** <note>original: "pathemata"</note> which they call the passions of the soul. The **organist** <note>original: "Organaedum"</note> performs the acts of reason or the rational appetite. However, the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> or the sensory appetite—blind and headlong in its passions—solicits the keyboard with various apprehensions of good or evil. It acts just like an unskilled artist who does not know how to correctly blend consonant keys with dissonant ones, producing in place of harmony something ridiculous, foul-sounding, and intolerable to the ears...

# The Harmony and Dissonance of the Great Art

<margin>
How the soul is moved through the passions.
</margin>
...produces a harmony; for just as a healthy body is in consonance when all the **humors** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were fluids that needed to be balanced for a person to remain healthy.</note> are tempered and each is kept in its proper place, it becomes dissonant when they are so stirred up that one becomes too abundant and plots the destruction of the others. In no different way is our soul judged to be healthy when all its parts and faculties hold their proper place and do not rise up against the judgment of reason. It is dissonant, however, if they are so incited that, as if a sedition had occurred, the lower parts attack the superior. But let us now investigate the cause of this harmony and dissonance. Since the passions of the soul have their principal seats in the principal members of the human body, it is certain that the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia," the mental faculty that receives and processes sensory images.</note>, according to the quality of the object it perceives, excites the **vital spirits** <note>Subtle, vapor-like substances believed to circulate through the body, acting as the bridge between the soul and the physical organs.</note> dwelling in the members as if they were instruments of all vital motions. Once excited, these spirits move the person toward love or its opposite, hatred; toward joy or sadness; toward compassion or vengeance and indignation. And so, the same thing happens in the spirits as happens in strings stretched in various ways: when they endure the greatest tension, they produce a very sharp sound corresponding to **choler** <note>The "yellow bile" humor, associated with fire, anger, and high-pitched energy.</note>; but the more relaxed they are, the deeper the sound they emit, corresponding to **melancholy** <note>The "black bile" humor, associated with earth, sadness, and low-pitched energy.</note>. Experience teaches that the intermediate temperaments, the phlegmatic and the sanguine, likewise correspond to the middle sounds. For as soon as the soul, through the imagination, perceives something quite vehemently, the vital spirits—incited and transformed by it—are immediately agitated. From this agitation, it is necessary that motions arise: sometimes fast, sometimes slow; now frequent, now rare; now relaxed and intermittent; and various other differences of high and low pitch. However, since the imagination is blind and headstrong unless it is supported by the judgment of right reason, it is like a man unskilled at playing the organ. Even if he strikes the keys and mixes high and low sounds, because he lacks this art—that is, the dictates of right reason, the only **musician of the human mind** <note>original: "organædus," a player of the organ.</note>—he gives birth to a foul dissonance instead of harmony, and thus destroys the entire harmony of the mind. Furthermore, since the **desiring appetite** <note>original: "concupiscibilis appetitus," the drive toward things that bring pleasure.</note> has its seat partly in the heart and partly in the liver, and the **spirited appetite** <note>original: "irascibilis," the drive to resist obstacles or seek vengeance.</note> partly in the brain and partly in the liver, the imagination, moved by an object of anger, ripples the spirits hidden in the heart and liver through an effusion of bile with a most violent motion. The pulses are altered by this rippling of the spirits and are rendered exactly like it. When the imagination is agitated by a sad object, the spirits gathering from the extremities toward the brain induce fear, pallor, and **loss of voice** <note>original: ἀφωνίαν (*aphonian*)</note> in the mind; for a denser spirit reflects an affection like itself. Likewise, while someone is troubled by the heat of sensual love, the spirits derived from the brain, heart, and liver into the genital vessels produce motions there similar to the loving affection, as will be explained more fully later. Let the same judgment apply to other affections and disturbances. Since, therefore, all disturbances of the soul occur through the motion of the animal spirits, and these produce sometimes fast, sometimes slow pulsations according to the various affection, it is certain that if it were permitted for us to listen to such pulsations, we would perceive nothing but the most dissonant rhythms of disturbances produced by the sensory appetite. We would perceive the most consonant rhythms, however, if they were skillfully tempered by the judgment of right reason.

<margin>
The pulse reveals the affections.
</margin>
But to demonstrate the matter more clearly: let us examine the pulse of a man with seething bile, and we shall find in reality that it is, beyond the usual, large, high, fast, frequent, and vehement. For anger has a double consideration: one is when the appetite is for vengeance, in the beginning of which the soul is gathered into itself, affected by the object itself, and afterward rushes with a violent and powerful impetus toward external things and against the object, in order to pursue either flight or vengeance. The other is when, by the aforementioned motion of the soul, the blood near the heart is also moved simultaneously and is called back to external things to assist the soul itself. This is why anger is considered by many to be nothing other than a certain "ebullition" or seething of the blood around the heart; which motion will be all the more vehement the more turbulent the agitation of the blood and spirits is.

<margin>
The pulse of a joyful man.
</margin>
If we explore the pulse of a man leaping with joy, we will find it notably altered according to the magnitude of the joy. If the joy is moderate, it will produce large, slow, rare, and moderate pulses; for the joyful heart is diffused outward through the entire body and, because of that motion, acquires for itself a certain tension by which the pulse is increased. Consequently, the itching of the moderately leaping spirits affects the man in a kindly way. If, however, the joy is immoderate and excessive, the pulses will turn out altogether weak and **strong**...

# The Harmony and Dissonance of the Great Art

...crawling <note>original: "formicantes," referring to a "formicating pulse," a medical term for a pulse that feels like ants crawling under the skin.</note>, from which a total dissipation of the **vital spirits** and death must necessarily follow (according to various historical accounts of those who have died from excessive joy). <margin>The pulse of sadness.</margin> **Sadness** produces pulses that are the exact opposite of those mentioned above: namely small, slow, rare, and weak. In this suffering, the internal heat is suffocated because the spirits and blood are trodden down; this leads to coldness and a stiffness of the entire body. Therefore, just as it is necessary for those overwhelmed by excessive joy to perish from the scattering of their spirits, those overwhelmed by excessive sadness perish from the suffocation of the same. Indeed, a **string** that is stretched too tight breaks, while one that is too loose becomes unfit for movement.

From this, the difference between **anger** and **fear** is clear. In anger, the spirits retreat and are then poured out with the blood toward the external parts of the body; they are gradually kindled to such an extent that the person seems to breathe vengeance. In fear, however, the spirits indeed retreat, but they do not move outward. In anger, the effervescing spirits are agitated around the heart; in fear, these same spirits are trodden down as if suffocated. Long-standing fear produces pulses similar to those of sadness, but recent fear—especially if it is more vehement—produces pulses that are fast, turbulent, vibrating, disordered, and unequal. These disturb the mind and toss it here and there; one might say that nature is searching for a way to protect itself through this motion of the spirits and blood. This is also evident in the movement of **shame**. <margin>The movement of shame.</margin> However, the movement of shame is much more harmonious than that of fear. For even if the spirit in those who are ashamed suffers a certain retreat, **right reason**—as if confident in the goodness of the cause—brings the exiled spirit and heat back from the center to the circumference. This is why the face soon shines with a graceful and becoming redness, offering a kind of applause and a victory won over the suffocation of the spirit.

<margin>The passion of the irascible faculty, and the nature of its object.</margin> You see, therefore, that the disturbance of the **irascible faculty** <note>The "irascible faculty" was the part of the soul believed to be responsible for assertive emotions like anger, courage, and the desire to overcome obstacles.</note> is of the same nature as the mind’s disturbance resulting from the perception of an object. If the object is perceived as consonant (harmonious), the passion is consonant; if the object is dissonant—as when the mind judges that something must be fled—then by this very act, as if by an elevated bellows, a great influx occurs: **animal spirits** <note>The "animal spirits" (from the Latin 'anima', meaning soul) were thought to be refined fluids that traveled through the nerves to govern sensation and movement.</note> flow to the brain and vital spirits flow to the heart. As the faculty hides itself and flees from the object, great and varied changes in the pulse follow, as we described just a moment ago.

<margin>The origin of disturbances.</margin> The entire system of the **affections** <note>Emotions or passions.</note> has its origin in the agitation of heat and spirits incited by the **imaginative faculty**. Proportional pulses necessarily follow this agitation of the spirits. It is so much the case that, if the state of the pulse were perfectly known to us during every surge of emotion, we could perfectly judge the inner harmony of a human being and discern each individual affection through the pulse alone. But so that this harmony of pulses may be revealed more clearly and brilliantly, we must speak of the greatest of all disturbances: **Love**. Since Love contains all other passions folded within it, I hope that we may better conceive of its nature through harmonic principles.

### Section I.
## Concerning the Music of Love.

<margin>The Music of Love.</margin> Love, insofar as it is a disturbance of the soul, has such power over the pulse that many have convinced themselves that the arteries pulse "amorously," following the example of **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BCE) was a Greek physician famously said to have diagnosed a prince's secret love for his stepmother by observing the prince's racing pulse when she entered the room.</note>. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theories on the pulse remained standard for centuries.</note>, however, teaches professionally that there can be no specific "amorous pulse" as such. Instead, the alteration of the pulse in lovers occurs only from the previously mentioned passions of joy, sadness, anger, and the rest. 

For since love is a thing full of anxious fear, it seethes in a wondrous way with the effects of other disturbances. <margin>The effects of Love.</margin> Even though love has no pulse proper or unique to itself (because it is a desire or appetite), it nonetheless possesses "familiar" pulses—specifically those produced by whatever passion of the soul is joined to love at that moment. For those who love either waste away mourning in melancholic sadness, or are dissolved by great sorrow, or become angry, or fear. Consequently, such pulses grow within them as are dictated by the passions prevailing at that time. This is the most common characteristic of love; yet we should not say that these "amorous" pulses are identical to the pulses of pure sadness, anger, or envy as if they were distinct and isolated disturbances. Indeed, it is certain and proven by experience that the pulse in an angry lover...

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

...much different in an angry person than in one who is simply angry; much different in a melancholic lover suppressed by sadness than in a sad and simple man. In the latter, the pulses increase just as they do without love, and thus they also last for only a short time; but fear, or any other passion joined to love, lasts and persists so much that if you touch the pulse at intervals, you will easily find that same change persisting for a long time. Furthermore, since love is a desire to enjoy beauty, it usually has many other passions of the soul as companions, any of which has anger joined to it as a companion—either to pursue what it hopes will be pleasing and joyful, or to flee what is sad and troublesome. <margin>Variation of the pulse in lovers.</margin> Since these passions of the soul are entirely contrary to one another and produce contrary effects in the pulse, it happens beyond doubt that when the heart is forced to move with contrary motions, pulses also arise that are unequal and disordered <note>original Greek: *ataktoi*</note>, such as we find in those suffering from love-madness <note>original Greek: *philomania*</note>. Consequently, from this principle, the Ancients judged that there is a specific "amatory pulse."

From this it is also clear <margin>The illness of Antiochus.</margin> that **Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BCE).</note> recognized the love of **Antiochus**—by which he was pining away for **Queen Stratonice**—by no other means than from this kind of unequal equality and dissonant-consonant motion. For while the body is healthy, it is impossible for unequal and disordered pulses to exist, unless so many affections of the mind have grown together at once that they can effect such a change. <margin>The strange and contrary affects of lovers.</margin> For who, I ask, ever rejoices in the passions of the mind except a lover? Who is saddened in joy and gladness except a lover? Who ever works evil and rejoices, or does good and fears, except a lover?

It is not surprising, therefore, if we consider the proper pulse of love to be unequal and disordered <note>original Greek: *ataktos*</note> even without a morbid cause; for at the memory or sight <margin>Whence the madness of love arises.</margin> of the beloved, it heats up so much that it can be compared to feverish pulses. For **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> rightly feels that this love is born from a contagion of the blood, and therefore lacks alternating rest. For a continuous fever flourishes in the blood, whereas it rests for six hours in phlegm, one day in yellow bile, and two days in melancholy <note>referring to the traditional theory of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile (melancholy).</note>. It even brings about delirium and insanity at times, with excessive heat and spirit filling, drying, and disturbing the brain. This <margin>How many types of dementia.</margin> happens when either increased blood, yellow bile, or black bile occupies the brain too much; for these are the three species and causes of dementia.

If lovers are vexed by "burnt" blood <note>original: *adusto sanguine*, a medical term for humors that have become overheated and toxic.</note>, they break out into unrestrained laughter, they delight in song, they exult in dance, they promise wonderful things about themselves, and they boast beyond all custom. Those who have burnt yellow bile are easily angered, rush at those they meet, and strike themselves and others. But if they are oppressed by black bile, they mourn perpetually and invent dreams for themselves; and if those humors are detained in the heart, they cause anguish and anxiety. Therefore, lovers are usually delighted by sounds, melodies, and amatory songs in praise of the beloved, seeking relief and medicine for their sorrow. From this also come frequent sighs, groans, half-spoken words, lamentations, tears, <margin>Gestures and manners of lovers.</margin> sobs, and other things of that kind. These serve both to bring forth and lighten the misery of the soul, and to move the beloved to compassion toward them. For while the heat ascends to the upper parts and the soul is occupied there, the lower parts are destitute and constricted; and while the lover thinks attentively on the beloved, respiration is inhibited. Hence sighs arise, as afterward one breathes more abundantly with greater force. Furthermore, the humor flowing from the eyes when the brain is compressed causes tears; hence also the languor of the whole body and a kind of fainting <term>lipothymia<gloss>A medical term for a sudden loss of strength or a fainting fit.</gloss></term> of the lover.

Indeed, while the mind and the whole power of the lover tend toward the beloved, the exterior parts are deserted, and the entire body languishes and collapses. The lover even neglects himself and all other things while he thinks only of the beloved; he who is careless and idle in all other matters becomes anxious, astute, and cunning only in amatory affairs. Who, however, could easily describe that ebb and flow of most turbulent passions by which the lover is continually agitated? <margin>Contrary motions and affections of lovers.</margin> He hopes easily and despairs, hates and loves, rejoices and is saddened, is glad and grieves, laughs and weeps, speaks and is silent, turns red and turns pale, is hot and is cold, hates and loves, as soon as various thoughts about the beloved enter his mind. Indeed, what you may wonder at even more: he loves and hates the beloved at the same time. He hates her as the thief and killer of himself, yet he is compelled to love her because of her radiance and beauty. In this way, he is tormented and delighted at once; he wishes to love and wishes not to love. He would wish not to love, because he would not wish to die; he would wish to love, because he thinks her worthy of love. Thus he allows himself to be seized and killed, so that as a captive he may be redeemed, and having been killed, he may live again. Of all these affections...
