# The Great Art of the Consonant and Dissonant
<meta>catchword: let it-</meta>

<margin>The cure for lovers.</margin>
The sole cause of this contradiction is the varied alteration of heat and the spirits agitated through the imagination. There is no more effective means for restoring these to a proper balance <note>original: *temperiem*—referring to the healthy balance of bodily humors</note> than various musical modes. If someone knew how to apply these aptly to the commotion of the humors and spirits, they would undoubtedly cure love-sickness <note>original: *philomania*</note> perfectly. But see more on these matters in *The Magnetic Art*, concerning the magnetism of love.

->## § II.<-
->## On the harmonic fascination of Love.<-

<margin>The fascination of lovers.</margin>
That wondrous effect of reciprocal love has twisted the minds of almost all philosophers: that effect by which we see two people so tightly bound to one another, even at first sight, that they can hardly be torn apart from each other anymore. Someone may frequent the company of beautiful youths or other men and turn their eyes upon everyone; yet there is one who strikes, one who pleases, the friendship of one is sought, and one—even though unknown and never seen before—wounds the anxious mind above all others. There are indeed many in the company, many in a single school <note>original: *phrontisterio*—a place for study or reflection</note>, some beautiful and graceful, some deformed of body; others well-mannered and possessing beautiful characters, others endowed with rude and dissolute ways. Yet it happens that of these, only one pleases, one is desperately loved, and no other—even if another were more beautiful and endowed with better manners. This attraction is sometimes reciprocal, and sometimes, without reciprocation, it exerts its force upon another even if they are reluctant.

<margin>How the Platonists explain fascination.</margin>
Everyone has sought the cause of this, I say, but hardly any have assigned it correctly. The Platonists, in their fashion, attribute it to a certain "fascination." Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who blended Platonic philosophy with medical theory.</note> beautifully declares all these things by the example of **Lysias** and **Phaedrus**, who were desperately in love with one another:

> *Lysias,* he says, *gazes intently at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his own eyes into the eyes of the other, and along with the sparks, he transmits his spirit <note>original: *spiritum*—in pre-modern physiology, these were subtle vapors that carried life and emotion through the body</note> as well. The ray of Phaedrus is easily joined to the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated from the heart of Phaedrus, immediately seeks the vitals of Lysias, by whose dullness it becomes thicker and flows back into the former blood of Phaedrus, so that the blood of Phaedrus is now in the heart of Lysias. From this, both immediately break out into a cry: Lysias to Phaedrus, "My heart, Phaedrus, my dearest vitals!" and Phaedrus to Lysias, "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Lysias follows, because his heart demands its moisture; Phaedrus pursues Lysias, because the bloody moisture demands its own vessel and requires its own seat. But Lysias pursues Phaedrus more ardently, for a heart lives more easily without the smallest particle of its moisture than the moisture itself lives without its own heart; for a stream rejoices in its source more than the source in the stream, etc.*

<margin>Fascination does not happen through the eyes.</margin>
The Platonists therefore think that the fascination of love is caused through the eyes. If they mean visual rays <note>A reference to the ancient theory of "extramission," where the eye was thought to shoot out beams to see.</note>, this is utterly false, since according to the principles of Optics, rays are not emitted *out of* the eyes, but are emitted *from* the objects themselves into the visual faculty. Let us therefore explain how a fascination of this kind actually occurs.

<margin>How love is born between similar people.</margin>
It must be understood, therefore, that there is in the temperament of men some remarkable similarity founded upon a certain agitation of the spirits and the more subtle blood, which bestows a corresponding form upon each body in every part. From this follows a similarity of character and actions. Since, by a natural appetite, like seeks the company of like, the same thing happens in humans as happens in strings stretched to a unison: when one is struck, the other soon resonates. Thus, when someone situated in a common gathering looks at any other person, the reason they are suddenly captured by this one or that one, and not another, is because the pulses in the excitation of their spirits are equal. Since exactly the same actions and character proceed from this—and since traces of these exhibit themselves most especially in the eyes and in the conformity and correspondence of outward actions—it is no wonder that another person endowed with a similar temperament, a similar pulse, and a similar agitation of spirits is soon excited by this "unison" even at first sight, and blazes up in love as if toward a thing most identified with themselves. To this is added that by this effervescence of reciprocal love, the spirits—always more and more vehemently excited and dilated—burst out through the passages of the eyes, which are around the corners <note>original: *hirquos*—the "canthi" or corners of the eyes</note>...

<margin>The habits of those fascinated.</margin>
...and let there be a mutual communication of the most subtle blood and spirits, which produces certain shared habits in inseparable friends and most dissonant effects. From this are derived those vehement fears when loved ones are absent, the cruelty of suspicion joined with indignation and the most burning jealousy, ridiculous hope, disordered gestures, complaints, insomnia, continuous groans, and other delusions of lovers. But since the emotions follow the agitations of the vital spirits' pulses, and since the emotions in both absent parties are stirred by different laws of the pulse and different incitements of the spirits—so that while one is driven by anxiety for the beloved, another by jealousy and fear, or one by hope and confidence while the other is driven headlong by desperation—it happens that from this dissimilar mixture of affections and grief, something most dissonant is born. This, however, soon degenerates <note>In this context, "degenerates" means "to change back" or transform from a complex state to a simpler one.</note> into a most concordant unison as soon as they are present with one another again. For the presence of a friend soon drenches the heart of both with the greatest joy; the dilated heart summons the spirits into a union, and it happens that from an unequal pulse and unequal agitation of spirits, there soon arises an equal, orderly <note>original: *σύντακτος* (syntaktos) — well-ordered or arranged</note>, and unison pulse of the friends. From this unison is born pleasure, joy, and a certain harmonic and reciprocal enjoyment of the beloved thing, which is the ultimate goal and end of love.

<margin>The wondrous power of love and its origin.</margin>
Whatever we have said regarding the circle of beauty, moving from sensible things to the spirit and the inner soul, and from there back through the spirits to the bodily senses—understand the same regarding the offspring of beauty, which is love. For first, the force of external beauty strikes the outer sense, especially sight; hence the poet says: <note>original: "Ut vidi, ut perij, ut me malus abstulit error" — As I saw, how I perished, how a wicked delusion swept me away! From Virgil's Eclogues.</note>

<margin>How animalistic love is born.</margin>
From the external sense, stirred by sensible harmony, the spiritual beauty of the observed things—which we have defined as nothing other than a certain harmonic proportion fixed in the concord of movements, limbs, character, and actions—stirs the spirit of the onlooker. This spirit soon communicates the received image to the soul as well, causing the inward harmony of the perceived thing to affect the internal harmony of the perceiver in equal proportion, especially their "form" <note>In Aristotelian terms, "form" refers to the essential nature or organizing principle of a person.</note>. Indeed, the impressed images of beautiful things are often moved from their places by any occasion; once this principal form is disturbed, the spirit is troubled, and from the spirit, the external senses are troubled again. Here, a greater downward plunge soon appears, moving from the noble senses to the more base: from smell to taste, and from hearing and sight to the wicked touch. From there, progress is made to the final degree of pleasure, which philosophers take for a species of supreme madness or frenzy, and physicians take for the image of the "falling sickness" <note>original: *comitialis morbi* — epilepsy</note> or a convulsion. Yet the common people basely seek it as the height of supreme pleasure and the absolute summit of happiness in love.

<margin>By what things the transformation of lovers is fostered and nourished.</margin>
Furthermore, this transformation of the lover into the beloved is fostered and nourished either by affection, or by habits, actions, desires, clothing, and all other conditions of life through which the lover accommodates himself to the beloved person. He does this so that he may be as similar to them as possible and united to them in all things as much as he can. For there is nothing more powerful for binding the lover to the beloved than becoming most like those things which uniquely please the beloved, and "tuning one’s lute" to the other’s lute in all things. From these things, not only does love and return-love flow, but also a reciprocal transformation and a most perfect transition of one into the other. This love is found almost exclusively among the young and those of a "sanguine" bodily temperament, as we have said. For a similar age and a bodily complexion prone to loving excite a mutual harmony of love. If a choleric person loves a choleric person, they are indeed "consonant," as we said, but in a certain intolerable servitude; for although the similarity of complexion creates mutual love, the frequent anger of the bile <note>Choler was associated with yellow bile and an angry temperament.</note> disturbs the power of that love. Between the sanguine and the choleric, because of the mixing of sweet and sharp humors, there is a certain alteration of anger and grace, of pain and pleasure; but the condition of the choleric is better, because the sanguine person is more lovable and gracious. Hence it happens that from mutual syncopation, the dissonant is rendered consonant.

<margin>What kind of love exists between people of different temperaments.</margin>
Between the sanguine and the melancholic, the bond is firm and not at all wretched; for the sweetness of the blood tempers the bitterness of the melancholic, and thus it goes better for the Melancholic. But between the Choleric and the Melancholic, love is entirely wretched; for Choler provokes anger, bitterness, slaughter, and impatience, while melancholy provokes greater and perpetual complaining.

<margin>The origin of melancholy in lovers.</margin>
[Love] requires the most frequent fuel of the purest blood; however, once the purer and clearer blood is consumed, that which is left behind for the nourishment of the limbs is spotted, thick, and black. Thus the body becomes dried out and withered, and the lover becomes "melancholic" <note>In historical medicine, melancholy was thought to be caused by an excess of "black bile," leading to despondency and physical wasting.</note>, for this melancholy is generated from that same thick and black blood. When this substance fills the head with its vapors, it dries out the brain and disturbs the soul with foul and horrific visions. This leads to a change in the pulse and a massive, irregular agitation of the "spirits" <note>The "spirits" or *spiritus* were believed to be subtle fluids that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>; from these agitations, various kinds of intense emotions are born, acting as the instruments of our vital actions.

### Corollary III.

<margin>Why diseases are cured through music.</margin>
It follows also that Music is the most powerful of all means for curing the diseases of love. Since lovers for the most part become melancholic, and the aforementioned sufferings arise from that melancholy, if someone were to dissolve that thick mass of melancholic blood through a correctly proportioned harmony, he would restore the lover to his original harmony and balance of humors, as we taught previously in Book 9, Part 1.

It is also clear from this discourse—which was perhaps more extensive than was strictly necessary—that if someone understood the perfect temperament and natural inclination of men, he could make himself pleasing and lovable to everyone simply by conforming his outward manners and actions to theirs. This knowledge is of great value in every station of life, and especially in winning the friendship and favor of Princes.

### § III.

### On the Harmony of the Rational Appetite.

Having extensively explained the Music of the "sensitive appetite" <note>The sensitive appetite refers to the part of the soul shared with animals, dealing with basic desires and emotions.</note> and its effects in humans in the preceding sections, it remains for us to discuss the Music of the rational mind at an equal pace. Because the appetite is subject to frequent and turbulent sufferings, it produces such dissonances that we might not inappropriately compare it to a pipe organ. Therefore, just as a skilled organist must be called upon to make an organ produce music that is perfect in every measure, so too must we call upon the "rational appetite"—that is, the dictate of right reason. When reason tames the passions that are discordant and <term>disorderly <note>original: "ἀτάκτως" (ataktōs) — meaning in a confused or lawless manner.</note></term>, and when it pulls the reins on the lower appetite to subject it to the rational will, what else is it doing but bringing strings that are too tight or too loose back to a middle ground? It binds dissonances with consonances with such skill that it forms a beautiful harmony. For this to happen, however, the soul must be in agreement with itself. Just as we feel the torment of immense pain when the physical frame is dissolved or torn apart, so too does the soul suffer when it incurs a lack of balance in its virtues because the lower appetite has rebelled. When the framework of rational movements is loosened, the soul endures great punishments and torments; the punishment for this <term>disorder <note>original: "ἀταξίας" (ataxias) — a state of chaos or lack of arrangement.</note></term> is felt by all the senses and limbs, which should be governed by the soul, as if they were failing.

<margin>By what means the dissonances of the soul are to be cured.</margin>
The Soul must therefore be cured through true philosophy and the constant contemplation of virtue, through sacred rites, and the application of suitable purifications. Once restored to health, strengthened by truth, and fortified by such defenses, the soul will fear no onset of the shocks that arise. Instead, being in agreement with itself, it may then harmonize with others and find helpful support from all things. However, when the soul is at odds with itself, it is impossible for it to perceive the "harmonic symbols" <note>The hidden resonances or similarities between different parts of creation.</note> of others. For every mind disordered by passions is, as Saint Augustine testifies, its own punishment; indeed, when integrity is driven away, order is disturbed and true peace—which is the "tranquility of order"—is exiled. In its place, harsh and unpleasant dissonances arise, such as agitation, restlessness, inconsistency, affliction, and various types of torment. By these, the temperance of the mind—which is the best harmony of all virtues—is utterly destroyed.

Since, therefore, virtues are the delights of the soul and the remedies for its diseases, they must be harmonious, since health and delight are born only from consonances—or rather, beautiful...

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Certain things are, by their nature, consonances. For as we said above, the health of the body—which consists of the humors <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) had to be kept in balance to ensure health.</note> and those things pertaining to the body's substance—is a perfect harmonic temperament. The pleasure derived from health arises from the proportion of one's vital power to the subject; the greater the proportion, the greater the delight. Thus, the state of being healthy is also the state of being delighted. Both of these qualities are drawn from Apollo, the inventor of both the Lyre <note>original: "Cythara"</note> and of medicine, who exerts his power not only over the body but also over the soul. If artificial harmony <note>That is, man-made music played on instruments.</note> possesses such power to move the soul—as we have already described in various places—then surely that natural harmony must possess a much more excellent power. This natural harmony consists of the proportion and temperament of medicines relative to one another and to the qualities of the body to which they are given, provided that just and harmonic weights are used in their mixing.

<margin>The virtues are the medicines of the soul.</margin>
In the same way, the virtues—which are, in a sense, the medicines of the soul—must be tempered, both among themselves and in relation to the soul, so that they may bring health and delight. They must be harmonically balanced and aptly connected to one another. Indeed, this connection cannot happen without harmonic agreement. For just as vocal harmony (according to the testimony of Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was a standard textbook for a millennium.</note>) is "the concord of similar and dissimilar voices reduced into one," so the harmony that perfects the soul is "the chorus of similar and dissimilar virtues reduced into one."

The virtues are dissimilar: generosity is different from faith, thrift from hope, and contemplation from the busy work of charity in constant service, along with many others of this kind. Nevertheless, they all sound together in consonance. They are built upon the love of God and neighbor as if upon the bass <note>original: "basin," referring to the fundamental or lowest note in a musical structure.</note>, the root, and the foundation of the entire harmony. <margin>A twofold modulation in the virtues.</margin> However, it should be noted here that a twofold "modulation" <note>In this context, modulation refers to the regulation and tuning of the soul’s movements.</note> can be considered in the harmony of the virtues. The first is that by which each individual virtue is measured in the scale of what we rightly call Justice (common to all just people). By this, we weigh and balance every virtue as if on a pair of scales—adding or subtracting to constantly seek the middle point <note>A reference to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," where virtue is the balance between two extremes.</note>—so that it neither exceeds nor falls short. Some have called this "prudent discretion," while others call it "temperance." The second modulation is a beautiful arrangement of all the virtues together in a single chorus of charity and love for God or neighbor (or both at once). For by this charity, as if by a kind of seasoning, we temper and moderate all the virtues; through this, we direct every good work toward God, the Author of all symphony. By this, the mind—led by the divine spirit and sending away the divorce papers to its old, sluggish physical mass—is perfectly joined to God through union (for it is necessary that like should approach like).

<margin>How man can become supremely perfect.</margin>
If, therefore, a man desires to be divine, it is necessary that his spirit harmonize with that divine element which is within him, into which he may finally lead back his lower soul, once it has been imbued with that same spirit. We make the spirit harmonize with the divine through *syntheresis* <note>A scholastic term for the innate spark of conscience that inclines a human toward the good.</note> and through an obedience that always murmurs against evil and prays for the good. From this follows a most harmonious peace and tranquility, then joy of heart, jubilation of mind, the "earnest money" of blessedness, and finally an expansion of the heart and a swift flight to embrace the good. This is according to the scripture: "I ran the way of your commandments when you dilated my heart" <note>original: "viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, cum dilatasti cor meum." Psalm 119:32.</note>.

<margin>The method prescribed for reaching perfection.</margin>
But because in the care of bodies we seek not only the proportion of antidotes to one another, but also the harmonic method of applying them to the body, we must provide for the harmony of the soul with a similar logic of proportion. Since various virtues are more or less suitable for different people, each person should acquire those toward which their faithful genius, their nature, or rather the Supreme Distributor of all things has gently led them. The soul’s progress is promoted chiefly by that threefold genus of virtues first described by Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> and celebrated by all the wise: the **Political**, the **Purgative**, and the **Heroic**. These act as a most perfect lyre, stirring up the sweetest harmony within us. The **Political** genus corresponds to the *proslambanomena* <note>The lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system.</note> string of this lyre—the root and foundation of the instrument, its lowest chord. The **Heroic** corresponds to the *nete hyperboleon* <note>The highest note of the ancient Greek musical system.</note>, representing the highest and most acute voice. The **Purgative** genus holds the position of the *mese* <note>The middle note, which acted as the tuning anchor for the entire scale.</note> in the fifteen-stringed scale <note>original: "pentedecachordo."</note>. From the *proslambanomena* string to the *mese*, an octave <note>original: "diapason."</note> is formed; from there to the *nete hyperboleon* another octave is formed—perfect harmony on both sides. From the *proslambanomena* to the *hypate meson* is a fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>; to the *lychanos hypaton*, a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>; to the *nete diazeugmenon*, an octave plus a fifth; and finally to the *nete hyperboleon*, an octave; and so on for the rest, as appears in the following figure.

### The Five-Stringed Harp of the Soul

<note>A vertical diagram titled "The Five-Stringed Harp of the Soul" maps various human virtues to musical intervals. On the far left, a bracket labeled "Double Octave" <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note> encompasses the entire list of virtues. To its right, the list is divided by two smaller brackets, both labeled "Octave" <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. The upper Octave bracket includes: "Heroic, Divine Love & Contemplation," "Contempt for the World," "Humility," "Patience," "Mortification," and "Chastity." The lower Octave bracket includes: "Temperance," "Purifying Religion," "Vigilance," "Circumspection," "Prudence," "Punitive Justice," "Commutative Justice," "Distributive Justice," and "Political Virtues."</note>

But let us apply these things to the mystic Lyre <note>original: "Cythara"</note>: Man, therefore, ascending from the foundation of the civil virtues and raised up to the purifying virtues, seems to complete the first interval of an octave; but from this, being subjected to another octave of heroic virtues, he produces a most consummate harmony through the mediation of the remaining virtues. Indeed, the civil virtues—through discretion, prudence, and deliberation—temper the motions of the sensory appetite, so that nothing is committed against the right dictates of reason. The purifying virtues—Temperance, Chastity, Patience, and Humility—do not merely restrain these motions, but utterly exterminate them, to such an extent that the mere presence of reason, the empress of the appetites, suffices to suppress them. By these virtues, the soul, free from disturbances, renders itself a most tempered instrument. Since the political virtues arrange the exterior of men (that is, they establish the first steps of harmony), the purifying virtues through the first octave cleanse the spirit and, so that it may emerge entirely harmonic, render it melodious. The heroic virtues, however,

<margin>The harmony of the virtues.</margin>
elevate the mind to the supreme concert; they unite and identify man with the intelligences, and thus with GOD himself. For as the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or a Neoplatonic authority like Plotinus.</note> rightly says, men are made Gods through the excellence of virtue. And Plotinus says, "The study and the vow of the Heroic man is not only to be free from sin, but also to be GOD, and to return thither, from whence he proceeded." When we return to where we proceeded from, we then complete a perfect octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>, in which the tone returns to the same step and key from which it had departed, as is well known to musicians. You see, therefore, in the present diagram, how the Soul, beginning from Justice or conversion, arrives step by step through harmonic degrees until it reaches that unitive love, the double octave <note>original: "disdiapason"</note>, which is the goal and center of the entire harmonic system. But now that the symphony of the soul with the virtues has been examined, nothing remains but to show how, and by what means, we can arrange this harmony in the soul, so that we may finally attain that end of harmony—which is peace, tranquility, and a certain blessedness of the soul on this earth. For through this harmony, joined to the archetypal harmony, one is made happy in himself, blessed, and a companion to the children of GOD.

<margin>How we are united to GOD.</margin>
For since GOD is the first rule that governs all contingent things, He is necessarily always melodious; indeed, He is that One and harmonic power through which all things agree and are made harmonious. Hence the Sacraments were ordained as signs and, as it were, effective causes of a Sacred and Divine thing—namely, <term>proofs</term> <note>original Greek: "τεκμήρια" (tekmēria), meaning signs or sure markers.</note> of divine grace and heavenly favor, by whose help man is led to the proper concert with GOD. Since,

<margin>The harmony of the 7 Sacraments.</margin>
therefore, man is born a "child of wrath," discordant due to sin and turbulent passions, the Sacrament of Baptism was granted for his

<margin>Baptism.</margin>
tempering. In this sacrament, he is washed clean, and by the power and efficacy of the Sacrament itself instituted by CHRIST (provided no lack of disposition stands in the way), he is tuned into harmony with GOD.

<header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

<margin>Penance.</margin>
Furthermore, man is at odds with himself and fails in his daily operations, in which—according to the prescription of the law—neither the whole mind, nor the whole soul, nor all his strengths are in consonance; hence arise daily defects and dissonance. Therefore, to restore the Soul to its own harmony, the sacrament of penance was instituted, by which—through the reason of conversion to **GOD** and the efficacy of the Sacrament and absolution—discordant things are brought back into alignment. Truly, because man is rendered most dissonant by the daily 
<margin>The Eucharist.</margin>
provocations of gluttony, the Sacrament of the Eucharist was given to restore him to harmony, being the source and fountainhead of all spiritual harmony; for by this 
<margin>Marriage</margin>
we repair that which is infected by the contagious odor of the flesh, and we arrange the body of our humility so that it may be adapted and configured to the body of His charity. Moreover, that which is defiled and made discordant by the enticements of the flesh in the generation of offspring is duly preserved and repaired by the Sacrament of Marriage. By Confirmation, however, dissonant doubt is removed from the faith, 
<margin>Confirmation</margin>
and the soul is strengthened to run the path of the Lord's commandments. By Extreme Unction, man is freed from every contagion and all remaining dissonance, and is affirmed in absolute concord. Truly, by the Holy Chrism or the Sacrament of Orders, while a Vicar of Christ 
<margin>Extreme Unction.</margin>
on earth is established, he makes the most perfect harmony of all resonate in the minds of men through justice and the power divinely handed to him.
<margin>Holy Orders</margin>

You see, therefore, how man, purified and adorned by the Sacraments—and further stripped of all dissonance by the frequent exercise of virtues—conspires in perfect symphony both with himself, and with **GOD**, and with his neighbor.

# REGISTER VII.
## The Symphony of the Political World, or Concerning Political Music.

Just as in a single physical body the mind exerts and perfects its harmonic actions through the concord and connection of the limbs, and binds those same limbs together with one spirit; in no different a way does a single empire—while the Republic rules, commands, provides for each, and dictates laws by the power of one or several united persons—establish concord. It executes those things necessary for human society, communicates commerce, and preserves actions and friendships inviolate through suitable precepts suggested by nature or necessity. In this political world, it brings forth a most beautiful harmony, 
<margin>Political Harmony.</margin>
entirely analogous to the two worlds described just before <note>Referring to the physical and spiritual "worlds" or "harps" discussed in previous chapters.</note>. And just as in strings and pipes and in song itself a certain concord <note>original: "concentus"</note> must be maintained from distinct sounds—which educated ears cannot bear if changed or discordant—and from them a concordant and congruent harmony is produced by the moderation of very dissimilar voices; so from the highest, lowest, middle, and intermediate ranks and sounds, a city consists of the consensus of the most dissimilar parts through moderated reason. What is called harmony <note>original: "harmonia"</note> by musicians in song is concord <note>original: "concordia"</note> in a City or Republic—the tightest and best bond of safety in any Republic, which can in no way exist without justice. 

Justice, however, cannot achieve its effect unless by the authority of someone who holds supreme power, as Cicero <note>original: "Tullio," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> testifies. However many species of Republic there are, there must be as many supreme powers, one in each; just as in one physical body there is one soul that commands, one moderator of the vital operations diffused throughout the whole body, not 
<margin>Unity must be loved in a Republic.</margin>
two. In the World there is one **GOD** who, by his ineffable providence, moderates and directs everything in it with concord; however, it is impossible for there to be two supreme powers in a Republic administering affairs with equal power and command. Since a "supreme" does not admit a superior in its own order unless it is subordinated to something else, if you establish two, the dissonance of the political body is already at the doors; for the civil body being divided, it would be necessary for there to be two Republics instead of one. Nor does it stand in the way that the supreme power admits many administrators and distributors; for these do not hold supreme power, but all hold one power together, as happens in an Aristocracy and a Democracy. 
<margin>Monarchy.</margin>
In a Monarchy, truly, the power over all things lies with one person, from whom the rest, who are under him in the Republic...

<header>Book X. The Decachord of Nature.</header>
<sig>Iii</sig>

—public <note>Completing the word "Republic" from the previous page.</note> the prince or King governs the Kingdom through the parts entrusted to him. Just as the power of the soul is diffused through the whole body and its members as if through certain instruments, so the King exercises his Authority through the service of those placed in charge. This is because harmony consists in this one thing: that a single string or pipe always sounds lower and lower, or higher and higher <note>original: διατόνως (*diatonōs*), meaning step-by-step or according to the musical scale.</note>, from whose skillful symphonism <note>The blending of different sounds into a single harmony.</note> a purposeful melody is finally born.

<margin>The political state is the image of the governing GOD.</margin>
Hence, as soon as that supreme **Harmonizer** of things had founded that great harmonic system of the world with an ineffable variety of "registers," he acted as the **Grand Choirmaster** <note>original: *Archichoragus*, the leader of a choir or dance.</note>. For each and every creature—the heavens, the elements, animals, trees, springs, rivers, and the rest of the works he made—he appointed leaders and choir-captains proper to their own kind.

<margin>The example of natural things.</margin>
We observe the necessity of this arrangement in almost all classes of natural things. When a human is born, lest he perish, he requires another to direct him. A single man rules over all living creatures. Within man himself, the more divine part—the soul—rules; and within the soul itself, two parts (the irascible and the concupiscible) <note>These are the "passionate" and "desiring" parts of the soul in Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, which must be governed by reason.</note> must be subject to the dictates of reason. Among the members of the body, one is primary, by whose judgment all the rest are moved—whether that be the head, or as others say, the heart, which is related to the brain. In this way, God placed a Prince-Angel over the Angels, a spirit over spirits, a star over stars, a Demon over demons, a bird over birds, a beast over beasts, a serpent over serpents, a fish over fish, and over men he placed a Man: **CHRIST JESUS**, the Word Incarnate. Thus, to command, to be ruled, and to be governed is entirely in accordance with natural law, and with the divine, human, and civil law of nations. Certainly, since this marvelous diversity of the world consists of the four elements and the substances of contrary qualities—both spiritual and corporeal—unless they were bound together by a certain harmony and symmetry of subordination, and tempered by certain laws of subjection and governance, the beautiful harmonic body of the world would soon necessarily be thrown into confusion. For such diverse things could not persist within it if each performed its works by itself under a mixed and indifferent rule. Rather, power meeting equal power would possess everything in perpetual discord and irreconcilable disagreement, and would usurp foreign things which it does not know how to rule, nor which suit it, to its own destruction.

<margin>Order is necessary for the world.</margin>
Therefore, order is necessary in all things, as Boniface <note>Likely referring to Pope Boniface as cited in the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon law.</note> beautifully stated, as recorded by Gratian: "From this point," he says, "by the promise of divine providence, He established different ranks and orders to be distinct, so that while the lesser showed reverence to the more powerful, and the powerful bestowed love upon the lesser, a true concord might arise, a weaving together out of diversity, and the administration of individual offices might be rightly carried out." For the Universe could not subsist in any other way, unless this great order of difference preserved it. Because every creature cannot be governed or live in one and the same quality, the example of the celestial hosts instructs us: for while there are Angels, there are also Archangels, who, though they are not equal, differ from one another in power and order, as is well known. For just as was said above, from strings of different tones stretched into symmetry, a most sweet sound is born—indeed, from low, middle, and high tones joined together, the most pleasant melody arises—so in the Society of the Republic, a beautiful "concert," a praiseworthy concord, happy and almost divine, is produced from those who command and those who obey; the rich and the poor; the Nobles and the commoners; the Learned and the Artisans, and various degrees, persons, and statuses of that kind. For what is lacking in one voice is supplied by another, and what one lacks is communicated by another. A good harmony cannot be born from strings of a single tone, nor from an instrument whose strings are all stretched to a single unison. Thus a Republic could not possibly consist if all people were equal. This harmonic equality is apparent from the various states in which 

<margin>The power of Divine providence in the different states of men.</margin>
divine providence has placed men. We see one reach the highest peak of wisdom, while another, submerged in the abyss of ignorance, hardly differs from the beasts; we see one filled with every kind of virtue, and another endowed with no ornament of the soul; likewise, one raised to the highest peak of dignity, another depressed to the lowest poverty; one to abound, another to want; one rich, another poor; one to enjoy perpetual delights and an abundance of wealth, and another to lead a miserable life in perpetual labors. Why therefore...

# Of the Great Art of Harmony and Discord #

<margin>A marvelous distribution of things in the world.</margin>
...[Did not] God’s goodness make everyone of equal condition? This unequal lot of mortals is cast against us as a reproach by those who, impiously denying all providence, believe everything happens by chance. I ask them in return: why did the Creator himself not make all animals Angels, or all planets the Sun, or all limbs eyes? For if all limbs were eyes, where would be the hands, the feet, the mouth, the stomach, and other members necessary for the body? If all planets were the Sun, where would be the Moon, looking upon the birth of the stars so that she might bring forth offspring for us? Where would be Mars providing strength, Jupiter balancing, Mercury sharpening, Saturn consolidating, or Venus connecting all with love? And if all animals were Angels, where would be man, the unique image of GOD? Where the horses that carry him? Where the oxen and sheep, the ministers of human sustenance—indeed, our very food? Where would be the animals and beasts of burden, which were produced for the world’s adornment and man’s service? 

Just as, therefore, there is no consonance if every string of an instrument were the highest or the lowest note, the middle or the next-to-middle note, or some such <term>equal tone</term> <note>original: ἰσότονον (*isotonon*); in music theory, this refers to notes of the same pitch which cannot create harmony together.</note>, since harmony is generated from like and unlike strings or voices as the order of the world requires; so too, if all were Teachers, Wise Men, Princes, or the wealthy, it would be necessary for the world to perish. In this diversity 

<margin>The harmony of the political state.</margin>
of intellects and professions, and in this varied throw of fortune's dice, the "symphonism" of the political world primarily consists. Just as in the structure of the human body different limbs, destined for different duties, work together for the single good and healthy preservation of the individual, so also the different members of the political world must work together for the safety and preservation of the Republic. Therefore, the beauty of the whole human race lies in the variety of individuals, which the Supreme Moderator has drawn from the most diverse types into the harmony of one mystical body under CHRIST the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: θεανθρώπου (*theanthropou*); a theological term for Christ possessing both divine and human natures.</note>. This consonance of both the natural world and the political body is conducted with such elegance and sweetness that no more perfect arrangement could be found.

To these things, which differ by nature, various gifts have been assigned to each according to their own virtue and disposition. Rewards are also given according to their works by "geometric proportion"—meaning that whatever the proportion is of gifts to gifts and merits to merits, the same should be the proportion of rewards to rewards. By this proportion, not only does GOD give rewards to individuals, but the civil Republic—which is a certain image of the worldly, or rather the archetypal world—establishes its governance. Truly, we shall speak more extensively of this triple proportion later.

<margin>The harmony of the Republic consists in the obedience of subjects to be shown to the Prince.</margin>
Furthermore, the Republic preserves its harmonic state as long as the members are joined to the head—that is, the subjects to the Prince—in perfect concord and peace. But the entire harmony of the Empire and the Republic is soon destroyed when discord and dissension arise, or where a change of Religion and factions of minds against the Prince have sprung up.

<margin>In what the discord of the Republic consists.</margin>
If, moreover, a Prince should degenerate into a Tyrant and no longer seeks the good of his subjects; if he does not yield to the customs and inclinations of the people; if he overflows with luxury, pride, and greed; if, with justice cast aside, all things are thrown into confusion by a certain promiscuous and unpunished license to sin—then harmony is lost. Where life is not truly lived, where each person measures the public good only by his own profit, where one meditates on his own safety only through the destruction of another, where all justice lies numb, all order and discipline are torn apart, faith is broken, all piety is loosened, and where humanity toward any neighbor has chilled into a more-than-barbaric ferocity; for while one member of the Republic does not suffer with another, the whole withers and dissolves into rot. Just as a harmonic body is soon destroyed when a violent imbalance of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed in ancient medicine to control health and temperament.</note> relaxes its reins, so also is a Republic destroyed where the injustice of kings and the custom of the worst morals has arisen.

<margin>Religion is necessary for preserving the Republic.</margin>
Conversely, as the body is perfected by the soul, so the Republic is perfected by Religion (I speak here, however, of that true and only-saving, orthodox, Catholic Religion). For as the soul is whole in the whole body and whole in every part, so for preserving the harmony of the Republic, there must be one Religion and one set of articles of faith for all, which they must believe, hold, and observe. Without this Religion, neither the prince performs his duty, nor do the subjects; without it, there is no Society, because there is no faith; no justice, no virtue, but fraud, license, insolence, and in one word, a confusion of all men and things is born. And just as between the soul and the body, so between the King and his subjects, between the Prince and the people, there must be the highest "conspiracy" <note>Used here in its original Latin sense, *conspiratio*, meaning "breathing together" or total agreement and harmony.</note>, without which the foundations of the entire city are deservedly split apart as if by a dangerous lightning bolt.

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature #
Iii 2
<meta>catchword: perhaps</meta>

...[For how can a state be secure]? For what kingdom is safe when its guardian is the fear of the people? What city is secure in which the multitude lives suppressed by force and arms? Therefore, so that the <term>Republic</term> <note>original: *Respublica*; here referring to the "commonwealth" or any organized state.</note> may sound in perfect harmony with itself, the <term>tritone</term> <note>original: *tritonus*; a musical interval of three whole steps, traditionally considered the "Devil in music" because of its extreme dissonance.</note> must be removed; the tritone must be avoided along with the <term>fifth</term> <note>original: *diapente*.</note>; the <term>fourth</term> <note>original: *diatessaron*.</note> combined with the <term>minor third</term> <note>original: *semiditono*</note> or the <term>major third</term> <note>original: *ditono*</note> must be utterly rooted out; the <term>octave</term> <note>original: *diapason*</note> with the fourth, and similar monsters of maximum dissonance must be fled from in every way. This is to say that discord, tumult, the persistence of the worst morals, and the tearing apart of the established Religion into various heresies must by no means be permitted; for these have been, at all times, the greatest seeds of massive calamities and the overthrow of Kingdoms and Empires.

And from these matters, which have perhaps been declared more extensively than was proper, it is sufficiently clear in what true harmony in a Republic consists. Nothing remains, therefore, except that we now show which proportion is suitable for each of the three states of the political world—the Monarchic, Aristocratic, and Democratic—and for the household, so that they may coalesce into a perfect harmony.

### On the three proportions suitable for the threefold state of the world: ###

**T**hree species of proportions are considered by Geometers: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic. When equal amounts are added to some numbers, without regard to their size, then it is an arithmetic proportion.

<note>A visual representation of arithmetic proportions. To the right, three columns of numbers: the first row (3, 9, 5), the second row (3, 3, 3), and the result (6, 12, 8), with the word "Add" on the left and "equals" on the right of the middle row.</note>

->Disjoint Arithmetic Proportion.<-
For as much as 6 is greater than 3, so 12 is greater than 9 by the same number of units; this is a disjoint proportion.

3 &nbsp; 9 &nbsp; 5
Add &nbsp; 3 &nbsp; 3 &nbsp; 3 &nbsp; equals
\--- --- ---
6 &nbsp; 12 &nbsp; 8

It is conjunct when, starting from any number, equal amounts are continuously added to it.

->Conjunct Arithmetic Proportion.<-
Add 3 &nbsp; 6 &nbsp; 9 &nbsp; 12 &nbsp; equals

However, when similar parts are added to numbers with regard to their size, it is called a disjoint geometric proportion: For just as a triple (9) is added to 3, so a triple (27) is added to 9, and so on to infinity.

->Disjoint Geometric.<-
3 &nbsp; 9 &nbsp; 27

But when, starting from some number, either a similar part or a multiple is always added to it, it is called conjunct; for as 8 is to 12, so 12 is to 18, and 12 is the geometric mean; the proportional geometric mean between 12 and 27 is 18.

->Conjunct geometric proportion.<-
8 &nbsp; 12 &nbsp; 18

It is called a Harmonic proportion in which the proportion of the differences between three numbers is the same; as in 3, 4, 6. Whatever three numbers these may be, whether they are truly harmonic or not, it is always true in them that the ratios of the equals are confused in a certain way; but since these means were treated professionally and most extensively in the 3rd book, we refer the Reader there. Therefore, it remains for us to show how such proportions can be suitable for a political state.

<margin>
Three Political species.
</margin>
Thus, since there are three political forms—the Democratic or popular, the Aristocratic or that of the Nobles, and the Monarchic or Royal—the Arithmetic proportion beautifully suits the Democratic, the Geometric suits the Aristocratic, and finally, the Harmonic proportion suits the Monarchic form best of all. For just as in Arithmetic the increases of all numbers are equal, both for the large and the small, so in a Republic the people want all burdens,
<margin>
Democracy loves Arithmetic proportion.
</margin>
benefits, honors, and Magistracies to be equal. They do not wish to tolerate any respect for persons—for instance, when they want everyone to have the right of hunting, whether they be noble or ignoble, rich or poor. And if there is any matter that does not allow for division among many, the people want it decided by lot; because the lot is blind, not at all distinguishing the noble from the ignoble, the rich from the poor, the well-deserving from the undeserving, the virtuous from the vicious, or the ingenious from the stupid. Then also, an individual thinks himself equal to the others if he deals with them on such matters, whether they be good or bad...

<vocab>**tritonus**: a tritone, a musical interval spanning three whole tones. **diapente**: a perfect fifth. **diatessaron**: a perfect fourth. **semiditono**: a minor third. **ditono**: a major third. **diapason**: an octave. **Proportio Arithmetica**: Arithmetic Proportion, where the difference between terms is constant. **Proportio Geometrica**: Geometric Proportion, where the ratio between terms is constant. **Proportio Harmonica**: Harmonic Proportion, a complex ratio related to the lengths of vibrating strings. **Democratica**: Democracy. **Aristocratica**: Aristocracy. **Monarchica**: Monarchy. **Respublica**: Republic or the public state.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how mathematical proportions apply to political structures. Having established that different forms of government reflect different mathematical ratios, the author now explains how "Harmonic Proportion" serves as the ideal model for a stable Monarchy, using examples from law, medicine, marriage, and social gatherings.</meta>

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance #
Iii 3
<meta>catchword: in place</meta>

...perhaps he obtains it by lot; where in place of chance, other means of acquisition can also exist.

<margin>Aristocracy requires geometric proportion.</margin>
Conversely, just as in **geometric proportion** <note>In geometric proportion, ratios are equal (e.g., 2 is to 4 as 4 is to 8). In a social context, this means rewards are proportional to status or merit.</note> the differences between numbers are matched to the numbers themselves—so that a large number has a large difference—so too in a **Republic of the Nobility** <note>original: *Optimatum Republica*; a government ruled by the "best" or highest-ranking citizens.</note> are persons distinguished. Burdens, rewards, magistracies, and duties are all differentiated; the most excellent things are reserved for the Nobles, while the remainder is left to the people. In such a state, it is necessary for **arithmetic proportion** <note>Where the difference between numbers is constant (e.g., 2, 4, 6). Socially, this represents strict equality where everyone receives the same share regardless of status.</note> to be admitted separately within each faction. For among the things belonging to the people, everyone who is of the people shall receive an equal lot; and among the things belonging to the Nobles, all the Nobles shall do the same. Unless this is done, there would be a continuous ladder of ranks from the common people all the way to the lowest dregs, and continuously among the Nobles up to the Prince of the Republic—in which case it would not be a Republic, but a sort of Royal state of the City.

<margin>The Monarchic state loves harmonic proportion.</margin>
A Royal state, however, even if it is most closely compared to geometric proportion (because all rights of the Magistrate are reserved for the King, just as he himself surpasses everyone else by noble lineage, arms, or virtues), can nonetheless be most rightly tempered by both types of proportion in its method of governing. For the one King, as the arbiter of all things, dispenses everything between the Nobles and the people—not by blind impulse or chance, but by considerations of virtue, merit, order, and rank. He executes all parts of **distributive and commutative justice** <note>Distributive justice gives rewards based on merit; commutative justice ensures fair exchange and equality before the law.</note>. This union of both proportions is sufficient to constitute **harmonic proportion**. Thus, from Justice—which encompasses all methods of governing—a triple form of justice results: **commutative**, which consists in arithmetic proportion; **distributive**, which consists in geometric; and **musical**, which consists in a mixture of both proportions. To these respond the three daughters of **Themis** <note>The Greek Titaness of divine law and order.</note>: **Eunomia**, **Eirene**, and **Dike** <note>original: *εὐνομία, εἰρήνη, & δίκη*. In Greek mythology, these are Order, Peace, and Justice.</note>—Law, Equality, and Peace—acting as the guardians of the three proposed proportions.

<margin>A rare example of commutative justice.</margin>
A clear example of these proportions is found in the *Education of Cyrus* <note>Referring to the *Cyropaedia* by the Greek historian Xenophon.</note>. When Cyrus was a boy, he saw a tall man wearing a short tunic standing next to a small man wearing a wide, loose tunic. Cyrus judged that they should swap tunics so that what was suitable might go to each person. However, his teacher declared that each man’s own property should be left to him. If the tall man had been ordered to pay some money to the small man, and the exchange were made that way, the teacher might have seemed to advise his pupil most excellently. In this case, Cyrus pushed for **geometric proportion** by measuring the clothes to the bodies; the teacher maintained **arithmetic proportion** by protecting each man’s possession. But a third person would have looked at both simultaneously—the physical need as well as the preservation of each man's property—and thus would have chosen a **harmonic proportion** mixed from the previous two. In this way, the common benefit of both is compared to the sweetness of a musical harmony.

<margin>An example from a surgeon.</margin>
This temperament is also evident in payment for services. A doctor often demands 500 gold pieces to remove a bladder stone, but from a poor man, he takes only a few coins. If he followed arithmetic or geometric analogy strictly in all cases, one man would die from the stone and the other from hunger; but by **harmonic reasoning**, wealth is preserved for the one and health is provided for the other.

<margin>Harmonic proportion in the laws of marriage.</margin>
The use of these proportions is also seen in the laws of marriage. For example, if patricians were ordered to marry only patricians, and plebeians only plebeians, that is a **geometric similarity**. If, however, marriages were sought randomly by lot, or if people competed for beauty, wealth, or virtue without regard for lineage, that would be an **arithmetic condition**. But in the first case, the spirits of the citizens are torn into factions, and in the second, the social orders are confused; both are ruinous to the Republic. Therefore, legal experts persuade us to allow impoverished patricians to marry wealthy plebeians, and rich plebeians to marry poor patricians. This is beneficial to both orders: for the Nobles, it allows them to protect their status with increased wealth and ensures their women are married; for the commoners, it opens a path to honors and encourages them to work toward virtue; and finally, for the Republic, it ensures the social orders embrace each other with mutual affection.

<margin>Harmonic proportion must be observed in banquets.</margin>
The same must be observed in the law of **symposia** <note>original: *symposiacis*; referring to formal banquets or drinking parties where intellectual discussion took place.</note>, in which not geometric alone, nor arithmetic alone, but a harmonic proportion mixed from both holds place. For arithmetic equality is foolish in banquets if people sit together indiscriminately without regard for sex, condition, age, or status. Geometric equality is also tasteless; for if everyone is learned, how will they benefit the unlearned? If the boisterous sit with the boisterous, who shall provide them a model of modesty? If the melancholic sit with the melancholic, what [mirth will there be] in that place...

<summary>Kircher applies the mathematical concepts of Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic proportions to social and political life. He argues that Harmonic proportion, which balances strict equality with merit-based hierarchy, is the secret to a stable monarchy and a peaceful society.</summary>
<keywords>political harmony, geometric proportion, arithmetic proportion, harmonic proportion, justice, Cyrus the Great, social classes, marriage laws, medical ethics, banquets</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of mathematical ratios as models for social and political order. Building on the previous page's distinction between arithmetic equality (simple balance) and geometric proportion (relative balance), the author now introduces harmonic proportion as the ideal middle ground for laws, friendship, and the stability of the state.</meta>

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance #

<margin>In the laws of friendship, harmonic proportion must be observed.</margin>
<margin>The office of a judge corresponds to *arithmetic* proportion.</margin>
<margin>Geometric proportion belongs to the magistrate.</margin>
...in place of delights, there is pleasantness; therefore, the law ought to be tempered according to **harmonic** proportion. This **harmonic** proportion and concord is also seen in the whole scope of human life as love, which is the foundation of friendship. For if a mere equality of duties is introduced by **arithmetic** law <note>original: *lege arithmetica*; a system where everyone gives and receives exactly the same amount.</note>, there will be no friendship except between equals. But if between unequals there is a mere and exquisite similarity of duties according to **Geometric** proportion, there will be friendship in neither case, but rather a perpetual business transaction and a haggling of duties for the sake of one's own profit. From this arises the necessary association of patron and client, without which there is no freedom to demonstrate love, and nothing is spontaneous. Thus, this **arithmetic** equality is most beautifully likened to an iron rule which does not know how to bend; **Geometric** similarity is likened to a **Lesbian rule** <note>The "Lesbian rule" (*regula Lesbia*) was a flexible lead tool used by ancient masons to measure curved surfaces; here it represents a law that is too easily shaped to fit any situation.</note> made of lead, adaptable to all corners. But **Harmonic** proportion is likened to a wooden rule, which, when bent, immediately returns to its shape. In the governing of all types of polities, the rigor of the laws and the office of the judge are compared to **arithmetic** equality; this not only assigns to each person exactly what is theirs, but also imposes punishments on delinquents equally without respect of persons. By this, judges are bound to the laws and to the evidence and proofs, so that they may judge according to them, even if the laws seem unjust. Conversely, the equality and the mere discretion of the magistrate—provided he is good and acts from conscience—takes on the nature of **geometric** proportion. To these, others interpose the office of either the higher courts, or of all or the supreme magistrate, following the example of **harmonic** tempering; these are permitted neither to act from mere whim, nor are they strictly bound, but are allowed to bend the laws according to the reason of circumstances in the manner of a wooden rule, not breaking them, and to interpret them in judgments according to equity.

<margin>In sumptuary laws, geometric proportion must be observed.</margin>
<margin>In penal laws, harmonic proportion must be observed.</margin>
Furthermore, in sumptuary laws <note>original: *legibus vestiariis*; laws regulating clothing and luxury to reinforce social hierarchy.</note>, geometric proportion is most prevalent, so that the higher the rank of dignity someone holds, the more precious the adornment of clothing permitted to them; here, **arithmetic** equality is intolerable. However, because it is not only the variety of ranks that demands a distinction in dress, but some account must also be held here for wealth and some for merit, and because not all ranks can be constrained by a single law, a tempering of both proportions is usually inserted into the laws themselves, or partly left to the discretion of the moderators. This **harmonic** proportion is also observed in penal laws according to the requirement of vindictive justice <note>Justice that seeks to correct a wrong through punishment.</note>, namely, so that punishment is inflicted on delinquents according to the gravity of the crime. Indeed, the law of retaliation <note>original: *poena talionis*; "an eye for an eye."</note> favors **arithmetic** proportion, while the law of fines favors **geometric**. In this way, in all other laws—such as those concerning voting, creditors, restitution, interest, rewards, wages, and inheritances—just as a triple proportion can always be seen, so the best of all is the **harmonic**.

<margin>Geometric proportion belongs to the state of Aristocracy.</margin>
<margin>How harmonic proportion is disturbed in a Republic.</margin>
In a **Democratic Empire**, **Arithmetic** equality holds the greatest place. In an **Aristocratic** state, **geometric** similarity prevails, in which, however, a reason for tempering is often held; for instance, when the people themselves, being in power, voluntarily entrust honors, magistracies, and priesthoods chiefly to the **Patricians** <note>The hereditary noble class.</note>. Or when the **Nobles** <note>original: *Optimates*</note> make the common people partakers of some honors, granting the most profitable duties to the commoners alone, and most severely avenging injuries brought against them by the Nobles. They grant the freedom of enjoying pleasures, which in itself tastes of a popular state, and they permit a certain right of voting to the commoners in naming a certain number of candidates from the ranks of the Nobles, from which number the Nobles themselves afterwards entrust the magistracies to whomever they wish. Indeed, as long as this communion consists of the will of that order which holds supreme power, a most sweet harmony of concord among citizens endures. But if it is revoked, first complaints emerge from the penalized party, then discords follow as if the harmony were disturbed, and finally, either the empire is transferred, or the entire city falls to enemies.

<margin>In a monarchical state, arithmetic equality cannot exist.</margin>
The same must be held in a **Regal** or **monarchical** state, to which **harmonic** ratio is familiar. In this state, just as one person excels all others, so he alone possesses the supreme right of empire; the rest live under him in **arithmetic** equality. Therefore, in this form of politics, there can be three kinds of governing. For if the **King** communicates all duties equally, with no distinction between the nobility and the commoners, the moderation will be popular and like the **arithmetic** style, which is not becoming to the highest Majesty; for the highest person would then be coupled with the lowest commoner with no intermediate rank cast between them. Truly, the high-born citizens...

It applies these mathematical concepts to friendship, judicial discretion, sumptuary laws, and the stability of democracies, aristocracies, and monarchies.</summary>

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance #

<margin>In a monarchical state, arithmetic equality cannot exist.</margin>
...those of noble character will depart the kingdom if no respect is given to rank. But if the King, excluding the commoners, grants everything to the nobility, a **geometric similarity** <note>original: *geometrica similitudo*; a system where rewards are proportional to status, but may exclude lower classes entirely.</note> will arise in the form of government, which is utterly dangerous and lacking in **harmonic sweetness**; for the common people, who are powerful in their numbers, being at last offended, will strip the Nobility of their offices and honors, and the King himself of his power. And although a ruler might distinguish many levels of rank and divide duties, if he preserves for each rank its own exclusive domain—just as in Rome the tribunate belonged to the commoners alone and the consulship only to the patricians—the ranks will be alienated from one another, and they will not coalesce into a single body with firm concord among themselves. For the duties of the inferiors will be despised along with their rank; so much so that in Rome, a patrician could not hold the tribunate unless he had utterly sworn off his nobility. All these things are beautifully 

<margin>Geometric equality in a monarchical state is dangerous.</margin>
<margin>The ratios of states are demonstrated in numbers.</margin>
shown in the following numbers: 4, 6, and 7. Here, 4 represents the King, 6 the nobility, and between these, 5 represents the **harmonic mean** <note>original: *harmonicam medietatem*</note>, while 7 represents the common people, who are discordant with both of the former. Or, the matter is better illuminated in the following numbers: 4, 6, and 9. For 6 makes a harmony with 9 <note>a ratio of 2:3, the musical fifth</note>, but 4 makes no harmony with 9. Thus, it is easier for the nobility to associate with the commoners than it is for the King; and as 6 is the **geometric mean** <note>The middle term in a geometric progression (4:6 is the same ratio as 6:9)</note> between 4 and 9, being in accord with both, so the Nobility is cast as a bond between the King and the lowest commoners.

<margin>Which numbers represent the Aristocratic form.</margin>
Furthermore, the Aristocratic form of governing a kingdom is represented by numbers of **disjunct geometric proportion** <note>A proportion where the pairs are separated: A is to B as C is to D, but B and C are not related.</note>: 3, 6, 5, 10. This disjunction represents the discords in a city arising from too strict a seclusion of the ranks. Finally, the tempering of both forms of government in a Monarchical or Royal state is this: that some commoners, though few, equal in wealth to the burden or recommended by virtue or some other quality, should intervene in the duties of the nobility; and that sometimes the appointment of one of the lesser nobles to a fruitful commoner’s function might confer honor upon it by the splendor of his lineage, making it more commendable to the commoners in the future. For example, a **duumvirate** <note>A board of two officials acting together.</note> might be established consisting of one noble and one commoner, providing solace to both ranks; or courts might be composed of persons from all ranks; or in public deliberations regarding the common good, the poor might be mixed with the wealthy. Thus, not only the cultivators of virtue and piety would hold all things, but some things would also be reserved for the brave, some for the ingenious, some for the prudent, and some for those powerful in experience. These things are beautifully shown in the following numbers: 2, 3, 4, 6. Between these, the first to the second is a **fifth** <note>original: *diapente*</note>; the first to the third is a **fourth** <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>; the first to the third is an **octave** <note>original: *diapason*</note>; and finally, the first to the last is an **octave with a fifth** <note>original: *diapason cum diapente*</note>. Thus, each and every number is perfectly in consonance with one another.

## Corollary ##

<margin>The form of government that possesses harmonic equality is the best.</margin>
From this it is clear that the form of government is always better which approaches more closely to **harmonic proportion**; such is the Monarchical state. The Aristocratic and Democratic states, although they may emulate harmonic proportions in some way, for the most part they favor **geometric** and **arithmetic proportion**, and because of the many intervening dissonances, they are mostly exposed to discords and turmoils. Add to this that the Monarchical state, like a genus, includes the Aristocratic and Democratic states as species, as is clearly seen in the Empire <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. And the free cities, what else do they represent but a certain Democracy, even if not most absolute in every respect, but dependent upon and subordinate to the Caesar? These things are also beautifully demonstrated by these four numbers—1, 2, 3, 4—which encompass the universal harmony, as was shown at length in Book 3.

By the **number three**, we understand the military or knightly estate, by which discordant minds are reduced to order and harmony as if by a musical **syncopation**. ### Book X. The Decachord of Nature ###

...to the first order corresponds the mind, or the architectonic <note>Meaning "master-builder" or governing intellect.</note> intellect of the Monarch; to the second order, the reasoning faculty that extends itself into syllogisms. To the third order, the irascible <note>The "spirited" part of the soul associated with courage and anger.</note> faculty; and finally, to the fourth, the concupiscible <note>The faculty of desire or appetite.</note> faculty is suited. Plato demonstrates that the seats of these faculties in the brain, chest, and belly are arranged according to harmonic intervals; to the first he attributes Command; to the second, Counsel; to the third, the military order; and to the fourth, the common people. To these four, the four Cardinal virtues—Justice, Prudence, Fortitude, and Temperance—fit perfectly as the four pillars of the Commonwealth.

Therefore, whatever Prince determines to attune his governance harmonically according to these sayings, he will undoubtedly be said to have attained perpetual happiness, with all dissonances removed. Indeed, this "temperament" <note>In this context, "temperament" refers to the tuning or balancing of different elements to create a stable whole.</note> is nothing other than that harmonic mean acting as a kind of mediatrix between two extremes. Most wise <margin>Comparison of the mean with natural things.</margin> Nature herself is seen to have recognized this, for she inserts certain mediators between every class of things: between earth and volcanic rock, she places clay; between metal and stones, copper-bearing ore; between plants and stones, corals; between animals and plants, Zoophytes <note>term: *Zoophytes* (literally "animal-plants"). Organisms like anemones or corals that were historically thought to be halfway between plants and animals.</note>; between quadrupeds and fish, amphibians; between birds and fish, the flying fish; between humans and beasts, monkeys and sirens <note>In early modern natural history, "sirens" often referred to manatees or certain types of apes thought to resemble humans.</note>; between beasts and Angels, the human being, mortal in body but immortal like the latter; between the Empyrean and elementary Heaven, the starry realm; between the Angelic and elementary nature, man; and finally, between the human, the Angelic, and the Divine, God established Christ as the unique Mediator, a man participating in the Divine nature. Connecting each thing to the next through such means like certain chains, so that the harmonic order of things might be preserved; for if the middle is removed, it is necessary that the beauty of the entire harmony perish.

For here, just as in the human frame, whenever the natural and animal spirit <margin>Examples from medicine.</margin> fails as it decays, and by their agreement the third "vital" spirit is soon affected, or the brain is afflicted by the heart, or the liver or stomach is disturbed by the brain; hence, among physicians consulting on various matters, some cast the cause of the evil on the head, others on the belly, liver, womb, or spleen. Meanwhile, there is a single effect that is multifaceted only because of the sympathy <note>The "sympathy of parts" is an old medical theory that the body's organs are interconnected and feel each other's distress.</note> of the humors and parts. From this, those continuous circles of "fluxions" and exhalations threaten ultimate ruin, unless many medicines are brought together into a unity, and the whole and the individual parts are cared for together. So it is, undoubtedly, in the city: if everyone thinks only himself wise, if he looks out for himself alone, and considers himself to be faring happily once he has placed his private affairs in harbor, he may not notice the destruction coming from the common fate in the distance. For even from an inflamed toe, a fever is suddenly kindled and the principal organ of the heart suffers; from an inflamed eye, the brain is set on fire; and from a defect of the Sun and Moon, the elements are disturbed. Truly, the primary bonds of this kind of agreement are religion itself, the laws of justice, and a supreme moderation in all things according to each person's status or order.

However, the method by which the scattered affairs of citizens are brought back into unity is first through those most <margin>How a dispersed Republic is gathered into one.</margin> common laws of nature; then through the civil and municipal laws that follow them. To these are added the practical applications of Medicine, Jurisprudence, and Theology, following that perpetual connection of souls, body, and fortune—almost common laws and notions implanted in us from our origin, in view of which particular Canons are fashioned, such as the following:

<margin>Practical Rules and Axioms.</margin> *An effect is not removed unless the cause is removed.* *Every act of intemperance and disorder <note>original: *ἀταξία* (ataxia)</note> consists either in too much restriction or too much flow, or in excessive excess or defect.* *Contraries are cured by contraries; likes are preserved by likes.* *Small fires that are neglected often assume great strength, and therefore the beginnings of evils must be met.* *The shameful part must be cut away, lest the healthy part be dragged down.* *Extreme remedies must be applied to extreme diseases.* *Nothing violent lasts.* *Moderate things endure.* *Every sudden change to the contrary is most dangerous.* These and six hundred similar things exist in the monu- <margin>What kind of person a Prince should be.</margin> ments of the Ancients. It is the duty of the Prince to consider these—not just a circumspect Prince, but one established entirely above all personal affection. Like a semi-divine Hero, he should provide for afflicted and disturbed affairs everywhere, above elementary fate and sublunary storms. He himself, placed in tranquility outside the sun-following paths of the year <note>A poetic way of saying he is above the mundane cycles of time and change.</note>, should not establish anything in the city or kingdom out of love for a private good, nor out of hatred for one or another, nor out of a desire for revenge for a slight offense, that departs from the public law of equity or the moderation of clemency.
