<header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

<margin>Various catastrophes introduced on account of dissonance.</margin>
For once an inconsistency is granted, many evils follow; the same principle applies to the end of a matter and those things directed toward that end. As Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a satirist known for his skeptical wit.</note> testifies, hope and fear are the most powerful tyrants, to which almost this entire world is subject, and around which every calamity and the very hinge of every shaken disaster turns. By their impulse, unity itself is dissolved into a multitude, consensus into dissent, and consonances are turned into dissonances. Unspeakable vicissitudes occur in all things, along with many corruptions of laws and judgments; from the pursuit of private gain or convenience, public calamities arise—especially if the disease begins at the head <note>Meaning the ruler or sovereign.</note> or the primary vital organs. Finally, it happens that those once celebrated as victors of all Asia, Europe, or Africa—the Pompeys, Mark Antonys, Sullas, and Neros—were miserably afflicted by internal dissensions and heavily besieged by a domestic enemy; they could not conquer themselves. Suddenly raised and placed as if at the peak of happiness, once they forgot themselves, they fell disgracefully, and faster than they had climbed, they dragged out their lives in darkness and grief. And to conclude at last, I shall set down here a three-fold image of a Republic, such as ought to be observed in a Prince for the preservation of political harmony.

<margin>The composition of states compared with the political world.</margin>
From a King or Prince, as if from a continuous and perennial spring, there ought to flow first Justice joined with Clemency. Second, Fortitude joined with Truth and Prudence. Third, Temperance; these three are, as it were, the primary principles of political harmony. The means, however, are the rewarding of the good, the punishment of the evil, the composition of good things and the removal of evil; and finally, the preservation of the "mean" <note>The "golden mean" or balanced middle ground between extremes.</note>. The end will be the flight from evil, the love of the good, concord and peace, and a balanced abundance that does not exceed its limits. And just as three things are considered in man, by which the whole machine of the microcosm completes its motions, so also in the Republic there is Soul, Spirit, and Body. The Soul of the Republic is represented by common principles, particular reasons, examples, and histories. The Spirit of the Republic consists of natural laws, civil laws, written laws, and customs. Finally, the Body of the Republic consists of the princes subject to the King, the Magistrates, and the People. These are also applied to the Prince, whose power represents the corporeal force, his love toward his subjects the spirit, and his reason or Architectonic <note>original: "intellectus Architectonicus," referring to the governing, master-planning mind.</note> intellect the soul. All these are beautifully presented in the figure below, to be viewed alongside their harmonic differences; and in this same figure, as if in a summary and conclusion, we close our discussion of political music.

# RECORD VIII.
## Harmonic Metaphysics, or Music.
### §. I.
### *Concerning the Composition of the Soul.*

Because the ancient philosophers asserted that the soul was composed of the "same" and the "different" <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where the World Soul is composed of Sameness, Difference, and Being.</note>, they not inappropriately likened it to Number. The matter will be revealed in the number three; for just as

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical exploration of harmony, moving from political structures to the mathematical and geometric composition of the rational soul, drawing heavily on Pythagorean and Platonic thought. # Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature #

<margin>How the composition of the Soul is understood to be made from numbers.</margin>
For the ternary <note>original: "ternarius"; the number three</note> is simple, insofar as it is indivisible, and is not capable of any relaxation or tension <note>musical terms for lowering or raising pitch</note>; yet it is composed of the even and the odd. Indeed, it is not composed of anything except itself, for according to Plato, nothing can be conceived before the number three. If anyone were to conceive of three "unities" before the ternary, those unities would by no means constitute a ternary unless he conceived of them as united; but three unities joined together is properly the ternary. Therefore, it is composed of itself, and because it is composed of itself, it must be composed of the one and the other, of the same and the different, of the even and the odd, and of the divisible and the indivisible. A number composed in this way is conceived as if it were moving itself; and for this reason, the Ancients beautifully compared the rational soul to a number. For the soul is both simple and composite—yet composite in such a way that it does not come from another, but rather (since it exists only by being immediately from GOD, who is simplicity itself) it is a "composite simplicity" flowing from pure simplicity. Thus, just as the soul is a living number composed of the even and the odd, the divisible and the indivisible, so too, insofar as it is life, it can be conceived as a "counting number" <note>original: "numerus numerans"; the active principle of counting as opposed to the number being counted</note> composed of the sensible (or divisible) and the intellectual (or indivisible). From this, the soul gazes upon harmonies within itself; for it measures external harmony by the incorruptible ray of the internal, intellectual <note>original: "noetico"</note> harmony. Since the soul possesses within itself the number that counts all things, it will contain the harmonic proportion of all things within its own beauty. We are speaking here, however, not of mathematical number, but of symbolic and rational number which proceeds from the divine mind; mathematical number is merely a certain image and likeness of this. Just as our mind relates to the divine mind, so the number of our mind relates to the number of the divine mind. But let these things be demonstrated more clearly.

<margin>Which number is understood here.</margin>

<margin>What the first originated principle is.</margin>
It must be understood that there can only be one infinite principle, and this is infinitely simple. However, the "first originated" <note>original: "primum principiatum"; in scholastic philosophy, the first thing created or emanated by the First Cause/God</note>, as philosophers call it, cannot be infinitely simple, nor can it be composed of other parts that make it up; for if those component parts preceded it in nature, it could not be the "first" originated thing. It must be granted, then, that the first originated thing is composite in such a way that it is not made of others, but is composed of itself. It is impossible that anything else could be assigned this kind of composition except number, or the number of our mind. The equilateral triangle places this entire matter beautifully before our eyes, for its ratio and essence cannot be conceived unless three equal lines are composed into a triangle:

<note>A geometric diagram showing three horizontal lines of equal length to the left, labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c'. To the right is an equilateral triangle with vertices labeled 'a' (top), 'b' (bottom-left), and 'c' (bottom-right). The three sides of the triangle are also labeled 'a' (left side), 'b' (right side), and 'c' (bottom side).</note>

For considered separately, as lines a, b, and c are not united, they cannot represent the essence of a triangle. Just as a triangle cannot be conceived except as three equal straight lines united, so too the ternary cannot be conceived except as three unities united. This union effects a certain composite—not of matter and form, but, as was said, a coalescence of the one and the other, the even and the odd, the divisible and the indivisible. The Soul is understood by a not dissimilar reasoning, as will be declared shortly.

<margin>Harmonic and Geometric comparisons.</margin>
Furthermore, when we gaze precisely at unity within a number, we see nothing other than an un-composed composition, or to speak more clearly, a coincidence <note>original Greek: "ὁμόπτωσιν" (homoptōsin); a falling together or structural agreement</note> of simplicity and composition, or of unity and multitude. For when we perceive a "composed unity" in a number, we immediately contemplate a perfect harmony, such as we find in the harmonic unities of the octave, the fifth, and the fourth <note>original: "diapason, diapente, & diateſſaron"</note>. For a harmonic relationship is a unity that cannot be conceived without number. Truly, he who searches more deeply into the relationship of the parts of a whole tone and the octave divided in two <note>An allusion to the difficulty of dividing the octave exactly in half using rational ratios</note> will find that they relate to each other in exactly the same way as the side of a square relates to its diagonal. We will find this number to be simpler than the reasoning of the human mind can reach; for since there is no [rational] proportion there, neither can there be a number—and yet a number cannot be conceived without a relationship, and this number would have to be even and odd at the same time. Who does not see how difficult this is to conceive? We have, therefore, what the first originated thing is and how it is made: number is its type <note>In the sense of a symbolic model or archetype</note>, and it is nothing other than symbolic number. For number is the subject of proportion, proportion is the seat of form, and just as proportion cannot exist without number, so without a fit and congruent proportion of form, form...

# The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance #

<margin>Exemplary unity <note>The perfect, original pattern of oneness in the mind of God.</note> cannot exist without number.</margin>
cannot shine forth. From this, it consequently becomes clear how infinite, exemplary unity cannot shine forth unless it is joined to number, which consists of proportion. For the eternal mind acts in the manner of a Musician, who, in order to bring his concept forth to be perceived by the senses, reduces and adapts many voices into a fitting proportion of harmony; thus it happens that in that harmonic proportion, when it is there as if in its own proper place, it shines forth most sweetly and perfectly. Therefore, in the mind and from the mind, come number and all things; indeed, the plurality of things is nothing other than the "number" of the divine mind. 

<margin>How the divine mind is conceived.</margin>
For from the fact that the divine mind is one, yet understands one thing in one way and another in another, the multitude of all things has arisen; we assert that this multitude is nothing other than a certain intermediate "reason for understanding" within the divine mind.

<margin>How number exists in the mind of the Creator.</margin>
Hence, the first exemplar <note>pattern or model</note> in the mind of the Creator is necessarily number; this is evidenced by the delight and beauty that exists in all things. Truly, beauty consists in proportion, and proportion consists in number. Thus, number is the most fit instrument for investigating wisdom deeply. Since our mind is such a likeness and a perfect image <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of the divine mind, the exemplar of our mind's conceptions can be nothing other than number. For without number, neither discretion, nor assimilation, nor notion, nor measurement can exist. For who could define? Who could distinguish? Who could discern and divide without number? Since one thing is substance, another is quantity, and another is quality, who could comprehend these as distinct without number? Since, therefore, number is the "reason for understanding," nothing at all can be conceived without it. But let us explain how this number is both one and all things.

<margin>How number is one and all things.</margin>
If, therefore, the "one" is in every way nothing but one, how can all things be in it, or how can it be all things? For if all things are in it, the one will be a multitude; if it itself is all things, it will also be a multitude. Therefore, the one will be both one and a multitude; and insofar as it is one, it will produce a multitude within itself, and insofar as that multitude is produced, it will produce itself, and it will be something "principled" <note>an effect or something derived</note> rather than a "principle" <note>the original cause</note>. Or, as the one is the principle, so the multitude is that which is principled; and both the question and the reasoning fall into the same absurdity.

<margin>The solution to the proposed difficulty.</margin>
What, then, is to be said? Or what way is to be found so that the one is only one, and yet likewise is all things? I say, therefore, that all things are not everywhere distinct in their multitude. For since multitude implies number, and every number is necessarily distinct through its individual species and proceeds from its own unity repeatedly folded into itself, every unity will necessarily have respect toward the multitude that follows it, and being derived from the one, it will depend upon the same.

<margin>The One is the apex of the many.</margin>
The "one," however, is a certain apex of the many, just as unity is the apex of numbers.

<margin>"All things" can be taken in three ways.</margin>
But so that these things may be better understood, it must be known that "all things" can be taken in a threefold manner: namely, all things "unitarily," all things "united," and all things "distinct" and thus multiplied. We declare that first way, which is more abstruse, in this manner: In the One, all things exist, but in its own way; just as in another way of its own, all things are in unity; and in a third way proper to it, all things are in a multitude. In the One, I say, all things exist in their own way and—if it is permitted to speak thus—"unitarily" <note>original: "ἑνιαίως" (heniaiōs); in a unified or singular manner</note>, that is, indiscreetly, indistinctly, indivisibly, and as one; so that clearly all things are "onely," such that although they are all things, they are nevertheless "one" rather than "all." For the One exists through itself, by its own nature, and primarily; but it is "all things" insofar as it holds them within itself indistinct and indiscrete in a unitary way, and insofar as it is the cause of all things. Therefore, that first One, upon which all other ones depend, is necessarily either truly one or not truly one. If it is not truly one, it will be either many or nothing; just as this is absurd, so the former must by no means be asserted. Therefore, it will be neither nothing nor many; it will be truly one, and nothing other than one, and simply one—nay, the supreme simplicity and consequently the extreme "absolution" <note>completeness or being set free from all limits</note>. If it is supreme absolution, then it is supreme perfection, indeed the most perfect; if it is the most perfect, then it is the most sufficient; if it is the most sufficient, then it is the best and the supreme good.

<margin>How multitude exists in the One.</margin>
But who does not see this multitude emerging and shining forth in the One through simplicity, absolution, perfection, sufficiency, and the good, as if they were so many attributes of the One, while we descend from the one into the "senary" <note>the number six, representing a completed set of primary attributes</note>? Truly, he who has well understood the preceding points will clearly perceive that this senary, considered in itself, is truly and properly one, and is divided only by our mind. For if anyone should ask us, "What is the One?" we reply immediately, "One." "What is the One?" "Simplicity." "What is the One?" "Absolution." "What is the One?" "Perfection." "What is the One?" "Sufficiency." "What is the One?" "The good"; and vice versa.

Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature.

...so, what is "the Good"? It is the One. What is "Sufficiency"? It is the One; and so it is for the rest. Therefore, these six attributes <note>Likely referring to the six transcendental properties in Scholastic philosophy: Being, One, True, Good, Something, and Thing.</note> are, in our understanding, one within the One, and not many. While those things that exist within the One are only one, they appear as many to us, because we ourselves are many. We are unable to conceive or understand this "One" except under the appearance and name of many things. Therefore, since all things are contained within these six attributes, the One holds all things within itself. Just as unity exists before every multitude, this "unifying unity" is the **uncreated mind** <note>original: "mens increata," referring to the mind of God.</note>, in which all things are one. After the One, however, comes the multitude—that is, the unfolding of the power of that unity. This power is the "entity" of things, the equality of being, and finally the connection of that entity and equality: it is the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "sacrosancta Trias." Kircher is linking the Pythagorean concept of the One to the Christian Trinity.</note>. In no different way, the image of that divine Trinity exists in our own mind; for our mind is likewise a unity which, through the conceivable mind, unifies before every multitude. Yet after that unity, there is every unifying multitude; it is a multitude and plurality that is nothing other than a certain image of the multitude of things, just as our mind is an image of the divine mind. The multitude, however, unfolds the power of the unity of the mind, and this power is the most perfect likeness of entity, equality, and connection.

From this discourse—perhaps longer than was proper—it is clear how, according to the primary pattern, the pattern of the human mind is nothing other than **number**. It is clear how it is composed of the one and the diverse, the even and the odd, and of divisible and indivisible essence. It shows how that same number is a "one" which, beautifully proportioned for the fitness of divine reflection, enfolds every sensible, rational, and intellectual harmony; just as a single string <note>original: "chorda"</note> enfolds every consonance within itself, which can only be unfolded through division.

### §. II. ###

### On the harmony of the mental faculty toward objects. ###

<margin>The mind conforms itself to objects through "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental images or forms of things perceived by the senses.</note>.</margin>
It has now been frequently shown that when one string is struck, it excites another similar to it, even if the second is untouched. Our mind is like a **polychord** <note>A many-stringed instrument.</note> which, by the power of assimilation, brings forth the forms of things from within itself. In sight, it assimilates itself to visible things; in hearing, to audible things; in taste, to things that can be tasted; in smell, to odors; in touch, to things felt; in sense, to sensible things; in imagination, to things imaginable; and in reason, to things rational. For the image exists in the absence of sensible things, just as the sense exists without the discernment and distinction of sensible things. In the presence of sensible forms <note>original: "species"</note>, our mind is carried and excited by the vehicle of the spirit; by the meeting of the forms represented by the objects, it conforms itself entirely to the things through these forms, so that it may make a judgment about the object through assimilation. Whence that vital spirit, animated by the mind, is configured to the likeness of the presented form by the movement of the spirit, not unlike flexible wax shaped by the application of a craftsman’s mold. By a similar reasoning, the mind creates various configurations in the organs according to the various agitation of the spirits and the condition and quality of those organs. <margin>How the mind sees, hears, etc.</margin> In the optic nerve, it is conformed not to the forms of sounds, but of colors; in the ear drum <note>original: "tympano otico sive auditivo"</note>, it is conformed not to the forms of color, but of sounds; and so it goes for the rest. In the "imaginary organ" <note>original: "organo phantastico," the part of the brain then believed to handle mental imagery.</note>, it is configurable to the forms of all sensible things without distinction; but in the "intellectual organ" <note>original: "organo noetico," the seat of higher reasoning.</note>, it is configurable to all sensible things with clarity and distinction. These configurations, since they occur by the medium of bodily spirits, are the assimilations of sensible things. <margin>How the mind abstracts.</margin> After these things, our mind—not as it is immersed in the body which it animates, but as it is a mind capable of being unified with the body—looks toward its own immutability. It creates an assimilation of forms, not as they are in and of themselves, but as it conceives the "whatness" <note>term: quiddity <gloss>the inherent nature or essence of a thing.</gloss></note> of things, using itself as an instrument without any organic spirit. For example, when it conceives a **circle** to be a figure in which all lines drawn from the center to the circumference are equal, it is occupied with a truth that is free from matter. For it is impossible for semi-diameters to be precisely equal in physical matter, much less for a mathematical circle to be described on a material subject. Thus, the circle in the mind is the pattern for the circle that can be drawn on paper. And when the mind makes these assimilations as they are in itself and abstracted from matter, it assimilates itself to those abstract forms. This is no different than two polychords stretched equally, which soon...

# THE GREAT ART OF CONSONANCE AND DISSONANCE
<header>The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance</header>

<margin>A comparison of the abstracting mind with many-stringed instruments.</margin>
...so that whichever string you strike in one, the other corresponding string is necessarily moved in the same way. For if we compare the powers of the soul to different strings—namely, the seven strings of the harp known as the *proslambanomena*, *parhypate*, *lychano*, *mese*, *paramese*, *paranete*, and *nete* <note>original: "hebtachordi... proslambanomenæ videlicet, parhypatę, Lychano, meſę, parameſę, paranetæ, netæ." These are the technical Greek names for the notes in the ancient musical scale, ranging from the lowest to the highest.</note>—these correspond to the various faculties of the body and soul: touch, smell, taste, hearing, sight, imagination, reason, and intellect. Let one of these "many-stringed instruments" represent our internal powers, and the other represent external objects. It is certain that whichever power is stimulated by an object will immediately sound, presenting audible forms to our ears according to the specific degree of that string. 

From this, the lower strings, since they produce duller sounds, fitly correspond to the exterior senses. However, the three higher strings, which produce the most subtle and sharp sounds, beautifully match our interior powers. Thus, tactile qualities move the spirit corresponding to touch to produce sensation. Visual qualities move the spirit hidden within the optic nerve, which—acting as an instrument—is immediately followed by the vital operation of seeing. In the same way, the qualities or forms of things abstracted from matter move the reasoning spirit and the faculty appropriate for performing intellectual operations.

# REGISTER IX.
## Angelic Music.
### §. I.
### On the harmony of the Angelic and human Archetypal intellects in comparison to each other and to the world.

<margin>The Angel as a likeness of the divine Craftsman.</margin>
<margin>A comparison of divine foreknowledge with a conceiving woman.</margin>
God, the Best and Greatest, just as He is from eternity, so from eternity He willed to create all things. These things, however, He did not produce from eternity, but in time. Having sent forth certain principles as the precursors of His creation, He established the **Angelic intellect** as the starting point of His entire creation. For those Angelic intellects are the first and purest offspring of God; they are the foreknowledge of the divine mind of the Creator of all things, and serve as the immaterial **Archetypes** <note>original: "Archetypi." In Kircher’s philosophy, an archetype is a perfect, spiritual blueprint that exists in the mind of God before a physical object is created.</note> and primary patterns of those things which were to be created from matter. 

For God foresaw, foreknew, and conceived all things within the Angels, outside of and before matter, just as a Master Craftsman conceives the entire series and order of future melodies within his mind before playing his instrument. In this, consider that there is a twofold divine foreknowledge of all things to be created. One is **uncreated and eternal**, by which we say God has foreknown from eternity all things that would happen by chance. The other is the **created foreknowledge** of God, which is the first, immaterial, and intelligible work of God. Once this "work" was produced and existed in actuality, we say that all of God's creatures were conceived—even if they did not yet exist physically. Thus, the divine mind gave birth to the first conception and most absolute form of all creatures: namely, the Angelic intellect. 

This is not unlike a woman: first, she conceives simply and in her mind alone that she will have a son from her marriage; second, she conceives in her womb through the help of her husband; and third, she finally brings the mature fetus into the light of the greater world. The woman's first mental and simple foreknowledge of the son is like that first divine and uncreated foreknowledge of all things. The woman’s second foreknowledge and the conception of the son in the womb emulates the second divine foreknowledge. For just as the first conception in the woman’s mind has nothing to do with the son himself and is not a part of the son, so too that first, most ancient preconception of all creatures in the divine mind is not a part of the creatures, nor is it a creature itself. But the second stage, which is the creation of the Angels, pertains to the creatures. For an Angel is a creature, the simplest "act" of all created things. Afterward, just as a woman, after she has conceived a son in her womb, shortly thereafter gives birth to him, and the son is born existing entirely and visibly to the world; so also God, after He...

### BOOK X. THE TEN-STRINGED LUTE OF NATURE.

<margin>A harmonic comparison.</margin>
<margin>Two intellects first emanated from God: the Angelic and the human.</margin>
<margin>How the human and Angelic intellects differ.</margin>
<margin>The angelic intellect acts as the beginning, while the human acts as the end.</margin>
<margin>Various comparisons between the two intellects.</margin>
In the Angel, God conceived all creatures; He then gave birth to them visibly, created them in substance, and fulfilled the design of matter. You will better understand this through a harmonic example: imagine an organ-builder <note>original: "Organædus," a term for one who designs, builds, or plays an organ.</note> who first conceives a most beautiful organ in his mind; second, he brings his concept into physical being; third, he produces the harmony, which is the ultimate goal of his craft. To the first mental concept corresponds God's first conception. The second step corresponds to the second, and the third to the third. Thus, from God—the fountain of all things—two intellects first emanated: the Angelic and the human. The former is pure, separate, and simple; the latter is joined to the body and to matter. The angelic intellect, being made from the start in the full "act" of all things that can be known, knows all things immediately. The human intellect, however, is made at the beginning as a "potential" for all things; it is only through time and effort that it is finally perfected into the actual knowledge of all things. <note>The author uses the Aristotelian terms "Act" and "Potency." An angel starts with a "full hard drive" of knowledge, while a human starts with an "empty drive" that has the potential to be filled.</note> Hence, the Angelic intellect is like an individual point—whole and unified all at once—while the human intellect, which is perfected gradually, is like a line, which is the unfolding and flowing of a point. The angelic intellect therefore differs from the human just as any two opposites do: like act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, beginning and end, the immobile and the mobile, nature and art, or the consonant and the dissonant. Yet, I would not want these opposites to be understood as enemies fighting one another, but rather as things that face each other from opposite sides and turn toward one another. One perfects the other, just as act perfects potency, light perfects darkness, knowledge perfects ignorance, nature perfects art, and the consonant perfects the dissonant. For whatever is present in the angelic intellect from the beginning is present in the human intellect at the end. The Angel is the beginning of God's creation and the most noble Creature, from whom the "line" of created things begins to unfold; Man, however, is the end of God’s creation and the full stop <note>original: "periodus," meaning both a concluding point and a completed cycle.</note> of all creatures, being only "a little lower than the angels." Just as the angelic intellect exists in the "being" and "act" of all things from the start, so too does the human intellect reach this state at its conclusion—the angel is perfected by nature, the man by art. Thus, while there is a great inequality between the two at the start, there is a maximum equality at the end; for the human intellect gains as much through art as the angelic intellect possesses by nature. The angelic intellect is immobile, existing in a single, simple, and indivisible state before and above all things; it is all things in its own being without needing the mental "species" <note>term: "species" — here meaning the mental images or forms of external objects used in the process of thinking.</note> of those things. The human intellect, however, is mobile through all things; by running through the mental images and actions of all things, it eventually becomes all things.

<margin>Both intellects are the boundaries of the entire sensible creation.</margin>
From these points, it is clear that only three things were created by God: the two extremes—the Angelic and the human intellect—and the middle, which is the "sensible creature" or the Macrocosm <note>original: "mundus maior," the great world or universe.</note>. Each of these is a "whole" and an "all." The first extreme, the angelic intellect, is the "being" of all and the universal act of all; the other extreme, the human intellect, is the "possibility" of all and the universal potency of all. Whatever sensible creatures are left between these two intellects are all composed, according to their substance, of both act and potency. Therefore, both intellects are the natural goals and boundaries of all worldly and sensible things. The Angelic is the beginning of every Creature; the human is the conclusion and end of every creature. All things exist in a loftier way in the angelic intellect *before* they have physical being, according to their ideal forms; they exist in the human intellect *after* they have physical being, according to their matter and substance. And just as both extremes are one in the lowest order of things, so too must the middle be one. First, He made the angelic intellect before all; then the middle (the world) containing all things in themselves; and lastly, or after all, He fabricated the human intellect. Both intellects are drawn toward the same object: namely, the Supreme Good, which is the Uncreated Truth, by whose natural light they are illuminated.

Thus, the Angelic intellect proceeds immediately from God through the realm of sensible creatures, and man—having been procreated as man and imbued with the "species" of all things—finally ends in God. You see, therefore, a certain wondrous circle in the creation of all things.

<margin>The angelic intellect is impassible; the human is passible.</margin>
<margin>A comparison of memory with the intellect.</margin>
Furthermore, the angelic intellect is "impassible" <note>term: "impassible" — meaning it cannot be changed, moved, or made to suffer by external forces.</note>, while the human is "passible"—not because of its own nature, but because of memory. It is in the memory that the images of things and intellectual forms are received. As soon as the intellect has captured these from the world and from sensible substances, it entrusts them to the internal storehouse of memory for future use, to be used in the mind's own true turnings and cyclic movements of contemplation and speculation. Indeed, the intellect is like an eye, the memory is like a mirror, and the intellectual "species" is like an image reflecting itself in the mirror...

...they relate to each other. Furthermore, the world, being the place of all things, is naturally prior in time to the intellect's own cognitive faculty as its object. All these things are finally united in GOD in perfect harmony; but these matters will be made much more clear in the discourse that follows.

### Book X. The Decachord of Nature

<margin>The soul becomes all things by understanding.</margin>
...they possess and obtain access to being itself. Therefore, the soul is not a blank slate <note>original: "tabula rasa"</note> void of all notions, but rather, as Proclus testifies, it is a tablet always written upon; it writes upon itself and is filled with writings from the Mind. The mind, or intellect, is a sort of image of that which came before it, revolving within itself—a figure or type made manifest. For if that Mind is all things intellectually, then the soul will be all things in the manner of a living being; and if that Mind is all things as an archetype, the soul will be like its image; and if that Mind is all things in a contracted and unified way, the soul will be so in a divided way. When Plato understood this, he constituted the soul out of all things, divided it according to numbers, bound it back together by analogies and harmonic ratios, and conferred upon it the primary principles that produce figures, moving the circles existing intellectually within it. All mathematical things, therefore, are first in the soul: before numbers, there are numbers moving themselves; before visible figures, there are vital figures; and before things agreed upon or arranged, there are the very ratios of concordances or harmonies.

We can, however, consider a twofold faculty concerning harmonic proportions in this place: first, that which operates through mental discourse, and second, the operative faculty. The mental faculty is again twofold: it is either the *inventive* faculty of the proportions themselves from abstract qualities, or the *recognitive* faculty of chosen proportions in sensible things. Therefore, the faculty that investigates harmonic ratios is the same one that embraces the other sciences and arts—namely, the superior part of the human soul. However, that faculty which notices and recognizes noble proportions from sensible things, or even in other things established outside itself, is a lower faculty of the soul. It directly informs the senses, or is perhaps an even lower faculty—namely, the vital faculty, which neither reasons nor exists only in humans, but also in the irrational soul.

<margin>How the soul knows things presented from without.</margin>
But if this faculty is incapable of reasoning, and cannot grasp the science of harmonic proportions, it is asked: from where does it gain the ability to recognize them when they are presented from the outside? For to "recognize" is to compare an external sensible object with internal ideas and judge it to be fitting. I respond that the ideas or formal ratios of harmonies are present in all those who possess the aforementioned power of recognition; and if they are not received within through reasoning, they instead depend on natural instinct and are born with the being.

<margin>Examples from natural things.</margin>
Just as the number of leaves in a flower is born with the forms of plants, or the proportionate arrangement of colors in feathers, flowers, and birds—an experiment in plants similar to harmonic proportions—so too I would not easily deny to the vegetative faculty in plants its own way of recognizing harmonic proportions latent in its plastic and chromatic power <note>The "plastic power" (virtus plastica) was a traditional term for the formative force in nature that gives shape to living things, while "chromatic power" refers to the ability to produce colors.</note>. Thus it happens that unrefined children, farmers, foreigners, and even wild beasts perceive the sweet harmonies of voices. If you ask where they get this instinct? I would either take refuge in GOD, who forms and presides over all these shapes in bodies as images of Himself according to His mastery, inserting harmonic proportions into the plastic and chromatic power, making them carry these proportions with them just as He Himself has embraced them in His mind from eternity and expressed them in creation.

<margin>The cause why the soul is delighted by harmony.</margin>
Or, what amounts to the same thing, I will cite the kinship indicated above between these souls (even the lower ones) and the circle, according to which they are composed and shaped as a rule and law; along with the circle and its demonstrability, they have also put on the idea of harmonic proportions depending therefrom.

Furthermore, the means used by these lower faculties of the soul to perceive external harmonies are the same ones by which they receive the external objects themselves. If they are sensible, they are perceived by the senses. All of this will be explained most fully, God willing, in the *Hieroglyphic Theology*.

<margin>Imperceptible harmony.</margin>
Specifically, in the faculties of the soul that inform the senses, which themselves—no less than the superior faculty—are engaged in the comparison of certain things, though by instinct rather than discourse. Thus, consonant sounds are distinguished from dissonant ones by the acoustic faculty. In this way, architectural proportions are perceived by the eyes, judged by the power of sight as fitting or unfitting. But if the things themselves in which the harmonic ratio resides are not sensible, but perhaps perceptible by another faculty, those same proportions of things shine back in the soul.

Although in the lower faculties of the soul this perception of harmonies is dull, obscure, and in a way material, hidden as if under a cloud of ignorance: so it is, when seeing—

# The Great Art of Concordance and Discord
### Book X

Sometimes, when seeing something, we do not notice that we see it. Such are those movements and terrors celebrated by the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude; they often discussed "propathai" or first movements of the soul that occur before conscious thought.</note>, which are natural, occurring without deliberation and beyond the reach of the will. This kind of natural affection, whether of love or hatred, is of a truly wondrous nature, as we have discussed at length previously. It occurs when the soul—estimating the goodness or similarity of another soul to itself through the measurement of limbs, the likeness of spirits, and the qualities of voice and temperament—suddenly <margin>Why and from where sudden love arises.</margin> catches fire for that other person. Thus, someone loves another and does not know why, or what specifically they love in them that another person could not provide. 

But a natural philosopher <note>original: "physiologus." In this context, one who studies the hidden laws of nature and the body.</note>, intervening and understanding the latent characters of harmony or disharmony working within, finds in both people a certain similarity or dissimilarity of character. If these characters are dissonant, they will generate natural aversion and strife; if they are consonant, they will produce friendship. Indeed, we must attribute to this the entire "physiognomic instinct," which, although silent and unreasoning <note>original: "mutus & brutus"</note>, is the sole interpreter and arbiter of human affairs. For a person obtains only as much prosperity (naturally speaking) as their face, body proportions, gait, and the movement of their limbs please those in power, creeping into their favor like something hidden, even when no conscious plan is used. As people often testify, they love or hate someone without knowing the cause. Such, I say, is the "sense of proportions without sense" <note>An intuitive perception of mathematical or harmonic balance that operates below the level of conscious awareness.</note> within the lower faculties of the soul. From these things, it is also clear why humans are naturally delighted by music; but since we have dealt with this extensively in the seventh book, we refer the reader there.

## Corollary.

<margin>In the notions of the soul, all things are mixed.</margin>
It is also clear how, according to Plato, all types of things are mixed in the structure of the soul according to a certain ratio. These things are mixed by a *harmonic* ratio, not an *arithmetic* one (otherwise the distribution of said things would be pointless), nor by a merely *geometric* proportion (otherwise there would be such a total equality in the mixture that it could not harmonize with the external diversity of bodies). However, a harmonic ratio, consisting of the similarity of diverse things, makes dissimilar things similar and connects unequals by a certain common equality. To be "blended" is the quality and duty of the soul, both toward itself and toward bodies; whether it acts within itself through a "sameness of intelligence" (if I may put it that way) into which it mixes "otherness," or through a "sameness" born of "otherness." It does the same in imagination and sense. Truly, whoever desires more on the harmonic composition of the soul should read Marsilio Ficino’s <note>A celebrated 15th-century Italian scholar and priest who was the first to translate Plato's complete works into Latin.</note> commentary on Plato, page 1158.

## §. IV.
### Concerning the Tetractys, or the harmonic quaternary of the soul, or the four Virtues.

<margin>An example of mystical arithmetic.</margin>
It is common knowledge that the number four <note>original: "quaternarium numerum"</note> was at all times sacred to the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that numbers were the ultimate reality of the universe.</note> because of the immense secrets of nature hidden within it. Now, therefore, let us see how it exists in God, in Angels, in humans, and in animals. It is established that one, two, three, and four, when joined together, produce ten <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10</note>, the symbol of the entire universe, the goal and limit of all things, which unfolds the natural power of simple unity. From this ten, which is a kind of second unity, the explanation of the square root is reached by an equal fourfold progress: for 10, 20, 30, and 40 joined together constitute 100, the square of the root ten. Likewise, the unity of one hundred, by an equal movement, brings forth one thousand: for 100, 200, 300, and 400 joined together constitute one thousand, which is the cube of the second unity (the ten-root). There are, therefore, by natural influence, no more than 10 numbers, which are bounded by this fourfold progression. Nor does any other variation of repetition occur beyond the thousand (the cube of the ten-root), since the quaternary progression, repeated three times, arises from the decimal order. You have, therefore, in the quaternary of unity, the explanation of the entire number system.

...to contain power. For the general unity is distinguished by four unities, which are arranged here in a fitting order. The first is the most simple; the second is distant from the first by the addition of a zero <note>original: "Zyphræ." The author is describing the progression from 1 to 10 by adding a "cipher."</note> and constitutes the denary root <note>The number 10, viewed as a base or "root" in Pythagorean numerology.</note>; the third denotes the centenary square <note>The number 100 (10 squared).</note>; the fourth, denoting the millenary <note>The number 1000 (10 cubed).</note>, constitutes the cube. In this way, the Mind contemplates its entire entity as distinct in these four unities: in the most simple unity, it considers GOD as the Creator of all; in the root or unity of ten, the intelligence <note>The angelic or purely intellectual realm.</note>; in the square, the contraction of intelligence or the soul; and finally, in the cubic number, which unfolds into volume, it considers the body. All things, however, are God in GOD, intellect in the intelligence, soul in the Soul, and body in the body. Within that first unity, you will behold all the remaining unities, though they are folded together <note>original: "complicatas." Certainly, if anyone <margin>One skilled in mystic arithmetic can penetrate all secrets.</margin> has penetrated this most simple unity alone—having cast aside all multiplicity, so that he proves it to be simple rather than not simple, and one rather than not one—let him know that he has penetrated all secrets. For through this unity, you will see the unity of the mind stripped of all multiplicity, and you will find that its life is not corruptible in its absolute unity, in which it is all things. What else does 1 to 3 denote but the *diapason* with a *diapente* <note>A compound interval of an octave and a perfect fifth (a twelfth).</note>? This represents the other—namely, the human intellect—which is closest to the angelic octave.

# Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature.

<margin>Every number is contained within the decad.</margin>
Therefore, as we have shown extensively above, every number is contained within the decad <note>the number ten</note>, while every progression of numbers is completed by the quaternary <note>the number four</note>; for four times ten makes 40. Hence, we have distributed the entire harmonic schema into 40 circles. In this distribution, we have used the numbers 1, 3, 9, and 27—a most mystical sequence, established by Plato in the *Timaeus* as a symbol of the soul <note>original: "animæ symbolum à Platone in Timæo constituitur"; these numbers are the powers of 3 used by Plato to describe the composition of the World Soul</note>, as will be discussed shortly.

<margin>Explanation of the mystical numbers.</margin>
For these numbers added together constitute 40, a number most fitting for our purpose. For just as 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent the most orderly progression of the universal number—since if you multiply two by itself, you produce 4, and if you add one to 3, the same quaternary results—so there is no more orderly progression toward the quaternary of the decad (namely 40) than 1, 3, 9, and 27. Just as the earlier simple numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 taken together make 10, and this multiplied by 4 constitutes 40, so 1, 3, 9, and 27 joined together constitute 40.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>

First the universe, after this the supreme order, and in the fourth and final place, the supreme choir. You see, consequently, how choir communicates light to choir until the very last; you will also observe how that which is found in the universe and in any specific world is found according to a consistent order. For the decad-unity <note>the number 10</note> signifies intelligence, the hundred-unity <note>100</note> the soul, and the thousand-unit <note>1000</note> the body, as has been said. This exists in one way in the supreme world—according to the sublime, simple, and noble nature of that world—in another way in the middle, and in another way in the lowest, shadowy world. For you will perceive that the lowest part of a superior world coincides in all things with the highest part of the inferior world; for the "sense" of the superior world is simpler than the "intelligence" of the middle world, and the "sense" of the superior order is more perfect than the "intellect" of the one following it.

<margin>All things in all things.</margin>

To these nine-fold triads <note>groups of three</note>, if you add as many units indicated by the three larger circles, you will finally discover the thousand-fold number signified in simple unity by the greatest circle, which surrounds and enfolds all things. You will see how in any world, everything is found; how the same law and constitution of progressions exists in each series of the worlds. For if the first decad of the superior world were as two, the second as three, and the third as four, you would have a perfect progression. The second world, marked by the decad, will keep the same law of progression, as follows: 20, 30, 40; and the third world, marked by the hundred, the same: 200, 300, 400. For if you join these correctly, a mixture of the decad will emerge in each.

# Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...dispositions, they order all things into a perfect harmony.

The duties of this order are threefold: to purge lower beings of their impurities through a certain divine heat; to illuminate the specific knowledge of each being; and finally, to bring both of these to perfection. For all beings, by their very nature, long for the **Highest Good** <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> from which they flowed, and they strive with all their might to turn toward it, so that they may be joined to it and enjoy it as much as possible, while also kindling others to achieve the same. Since they are closest to the Highest Good in essence, power, and action, and are its most immediate participants, they have necessarily been made good themselves. They envy no being and find it necessary to cooperate with all things in goodness through their own benevolence. This is done, as we have said, through a triple action: illuminating, purging, and attracting. Through these same actions, the minds of the first triad <note>The highest ranks of angels: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones</note>, being immediately and continually enlightened by GOD and inflamed by divine fire, are both assisted and impelled by a sweet force toward these works, becoming the primary ministers of divine providence.

<margin>Dominions.</margin>

<margin>Virtues and Powers.</margin>

For it was not fitting for that goodness which transcends all things to create all beings and then leave them to chance, or to allow them to remain alienated and discordant from Himself. Rather, if He were to remain whole and goodness itself, it was necessary that He join all things together at once, so that they might continually depend on Him and be fit to connect back to Him and return to the primary fountain. But this could by no means happen unless the highest, middle, and lowest beings were bound together by certain links, which was most aptly achieved through the love and ministry of these heavenly minds.

Within the perfect knowledge of these matters lies the greatest **Sacrament** of the entire secret of nature; whoever knows this, by adapting consonants to consonants, will know how to perform marvelous effects in the nature of things.

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature <note>original: "Decachordon Naturae"</note>

#### Page 453
**Signature: Zzz 3**

Just as the supreme world abounds in light, so the inferior world abounds in a wealth of darkness; the middle world participates in an equal portion of light and darkness from both, although the upper is not entirely without darkness, nor the lower entirely without light. It is as if light in the lower world, and darkness in the upper, appear in some way absorbed. 

<margin>All things tend toward the One.</margin>
If, therefore, you look more deeply into the diagram <note>original: "schema"</note>, you will discover—through the descent of unity into multiplicity and the return of multiplicity into union—how in the highest Heaven all things that belong to multiplicity proceed into unity itself: namely, the divisible into the indivisible, darkness into light, the composite into the simple, the mortal into the immortal, the changeable into the unchangeable, potentiality into act, the part into the whole, and so on with the rest. You will find the opposite process in the [lower] world. If you investigate these things with a keen mind, you will behold the clearest truths within the greatest yet most obscure light, reaching into the very hidden depths of nature. It is necessary, however, that you conceive of the unity of any particular thing in its perfection, and imagine the quality of darkness according to the intensity of its light. Among the graduations of unities, consider that one to be lesser which possesses more darkness, more multiplicity, more potentiality, and more divisibility; and that one to be greater which possesses more light, more unity, and more of act and indivisibility. For the less a unity exists in act and the more it exists in potentiality, the more subject it is to change. Indeed, a unifying unity is more perfect than a "unifiable" unity, just as the unity of the Soul is more perfect than the unity of the body; for the end of the body's unity is the unity of the soul, upon which the bodily unity depends as if upon its own beginning. Time would fail me if I wished to explain each point more fully. 

Who, however, can sufficiently express in words that admirable order of the celestial choirs, the harmony of beauties, and the concord of blessed minds? That inexplicable and supra-mundane harmony <note>original: "concentum"</note> by which those supreme voices—the sweetest instruments of the unceasing praises of GOD—resound perpetually with the lowest and middle choirs in that great house of eternity?

<margin>Music of the Holy Trinity.</margin>
Where the Leader of the Choir and the Master Architect of Music <note>original: "Archimusurgus"</note> is GOD the Father himself; the incarnate Word, eternal wisdom, is the Son; and the harmonizing <note>original: ἁρμόζουσα (harmozousa)</note> and adapting power of all things acts as the organ-player; where that Spirit of holiness will perpetually animate the organ with the bellows of divine air. Who could express the number of these Musicians? In comparison to them, the sand upon the seashore is nothing. There, a symphony not of three, four, or five, but of innumerable voices will ring out unwearied for eternity.

<margin>Music of the Celestial Fatherland</margin>
There, the "Saints shall rejoice in their beds, the high praises of GOD in their mouths" <note>A reference to Psalm 149:5-6</note>. There, there is no labor in performing musical praises, no fatigue, no satiety; rather, the more they are perceived, the more they fill the soul with a greater desire to perceive them continuously. "How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord. Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee, etc." <note>Psalm 84</note>. Inspired by even a faint whisper of this divine music, certain holy men of GOD, as if Ravished out of themselves, sent a divorce to the love of fleeting things and betook themselves to the solitudes and caves of mountains, so that, separated from the noise of worldly things, they might acquire ears better suited to perceiving this music. 

For if it is true, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>—the instrument of divinity—says, that "eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which GOD hath prepared for them that love him," no one should doubt that the powers of human genius can in no way reach this super-eminent symphony of the celestial choirs. Our ears are deafened by the cataracts <note>original: "catadupas," referring to the deafening waterfalls of the Nile</note> of earthly confusion; but truly, when that day of eternity dawns for us, then the ears of the deaf shall be opened. For as Saint Augustine <note>Diuus Augustinus</note> rightly says, then the souls of the faithful will be immediately animated into the instruments of the living GOD; then the harmony of divine minds will be revealed—not merely Music, but something more excellent than all Music; where there is sweetness and pleasantness, not merely harmonic, but something most sweet beyond all harmony. Thus says Augustine. And let these words regarding Angelic Music suffice; nothing remains, therefore, except that we now say something of the music of the divine essence, which enfolds <note>original: "complicante," a term meaning "folding together" or "encompassing"</note> all the music of worldly choirs.

The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

# REGISTER X.

## On Divine Music, or the Choir of Choirs, which is the Harmony of GOD with All Nature.

### To the Most Illustrious and Noble Lord, Lord Lazarus Henkel, Free Baron of Mount Saint George, etc.

Since I have always known you, Noble Man, to be a supreme admirer of worldly harmony; and being mindful of the benefits which you once conferred upon me in Rome with a generous hand; and inspired by the distinguished grace of your virtue, it has pleased me to dedicate this final Register of the world to your honor. Here you will find what to marvel at and what you truly desire, in which—as if at the final center of all things—you may at last rest eternally, blessed in happiness.

---

# §. I.

## On hierarchical harmony compared to GOD and man.

The Heavenly Father, having fashioned this worldly organ <note>The author uses the "organum" as a metaphor for the universe, suggesting it is a complex instrument played by God.</note>, through His wisdom and by the breath of the Spirit, has opened the registers of the whole worldly instrument described thus far. He has exhibited a harmony—not only perfect in all its measures <note>original: "numeris," referring to both numbers and musical meter</note>, but utterly wonderful and incomprehensible to human minds—both in Himself and in the universe. What this harmony is like, and in what it consists, must now be told.

<margin>How unity accords with multiplicity.</margin>
That the Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the "One" or the indivisible source of all being, a concept central to Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy.</note> is diffused into multiplicity was clearly evident from the preceding pages; but how the nature of unity accords with multiplicity and dwells in it without discord—this is what twists the intellect; this is what presents an obstacle to the fragility of our understanding. You will grant me pardon, O Inaccessible Light hidden in the gloom of eternity, if I, mere smoke and dust, should somewhat presumptuously approach the abyss of your immensity. What the Monad is to mathematicians, we have shown in various places that the Unison <note>original: "vnisonum"</note> is to musicians. And just as the Monad is the fount and origin of all numbers, so is the <term>isophona</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning "equal-sounding." In this context, it refers to the Monad as the source of all perfectly matching tones.</note> monad the source of all harmonies. Therefore, the Monad diffused into multiplicity can in no other way agree except through the harmony of the unity which exists within that multiplicity. 

Hence Plato, imitating Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher who appears as a character in Plato's dialogues; Kircher links Platonic soul-theory to these older roots.</note>, describes the fabric of the soul and the world—as we have shown previously—by taking the Monad and reaching through double, triple, and quadruple proportions as far as 27, which is the cube of the ternary monad <note>3 cubed (3 x 3 x 3 = 27). This mathematical progression was believed to describe the proportions of the World Soul.</note>. For the first and supreme Monad is diffused into the first number, namely the Ternary [Three], as will be taught later; this number squared completes the Novenary [Nine], by which number the orders of separate intellects <note>The "separate intellects" are the nine choirs of angels.</note>, the Heavens, and all elementary things are distributed in the highest harmony. The ternary multiplied again cubically (or multiplied by nine) produces twenty-seven. This number is exceedingly mystical, and although we have explained it more than enough in the preceding diagram, nevertheless, because it is full of divine harmony, we think it should be discussed here at a bit more length. 

There are, therefore, twenty-seven primary kinds of produced things, distinct into three <term>enneads</term> <note>Groups of nine.</note>: the super-celestial, the celestial, and the elementary. Their harmonic concord is seen to be united by God in a certain wonderful connection. For from the Archetype <note>The Divine Mind or original blueprint of creation.</note> to the Angelic sphere or the planetary orbs, and from there to the orb of earthly habitation, that Unity descends, making all things most consonant, so that whatever is in each one likewise responds in the others with the sweetest proportion, through voices sounding with the energy of life. For it is GOD "in whom we live and move and have our being," through the mediation of that Spirit which nourishes from within, and the Mind which moves the mass of fabricated things. This is that true "World Soul" <note>original: "mundi anima"</note> intended by the Platonists, which, by vivifying the members of the world and binding them in harmonic concord, produces the harmonies of the worldly <term>decachord</term> <note>A ten-stringed lute or harp, often used as a symbol for the Ten Commandments or the harmony of the ten spheres of creation.</note>.

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature.

<margin>What Pythagoras felt regarding the order of things.</margin>
...renders them most consonant. Pythagoras, that most skillful seeker of the natural order and concord, was the first to notice this. Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "everything is in everything," a concept Kircher adapts here to describe biological and spiritual affinities.</note> agreed when he contemplated how "anything is in anything"—not indeed that there is a donkey in a fly, or a camel in a worm, but rather that the species of each thing are represented in others through a marvelous affinity. Just as all things live by a single universal life, they are united to one another in a friendly society, held by what one might call "Heracleote links" <note>original: "heracleoticis vinculis." This refers to the "Heracleote stone" or loadstone (magnet), symbolizing the invisible magnetic attractions Kircher believed held the universe together.</note>. From this, finally, that wondrous concord of things is born. The aforementioned Anaxagoras did not fully explain this more hidden secret, but Pythagoras—illuminated by a clearer light and by those who had drawn that spirit from the divine Oracles—delivered it more aptly. He learned first from the Egyptians, and they from the Hebrews.

<margin>How the Prophets knew all things in GOD.</margin>
The Prophets themselves, raised up to the divine symphony—where the forms, archetypes, and models of all things are exhibited with graceful sweetness in a single sound and a single Word—perceived that concord most clearly of all. We, however, being weighed down by the burden of human frailty, cannot perceive this harmony as it is diffused through the very diverse members of this "ten-stringed" world <note>Kircher uses "decachordum" (ten-stringed lyre) as a metaphor for the universe, implying it has ten levels or "strings" of existence.</note>. Instead, we must take up now one tone, then another, collecting them all within the organic system of the mind. Only then can we perceive, with some small sweetness, that harmonic concord of created things with one another and with their Creator. Therefore, it remains for us to explain how that "isophonic" <note>meaning "sounding the same" or in perfect unison</note> Monad of the divinity descends into all things of the worldly ten-stringed lyre to arrange the harmony of nature.

<margin>How uncreated unity spreads itself into multiplicity.</margin>
Not only Christian theologians but also the gentile philosophers recognized the admirable power of the "ternary" <note>The number three</note> flowing from the Monad. Aristotle says at the beginning of his books *On the Heavens*: "We have the ternary number from nature, and we uphold it as a law according to which all things are arranged." Hence, by this number, we are bound to celebrate GOD, the craftsman of all things. For all things, whether spiritual or corporeal, consist of three parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end. This ternary is surely drawn from that ineffable Trinity of the supra-celestial world, from whom are all things, in whom are all things, and through whom are all things, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul (Romans 11:36).</note> testifies. Nature has placed before our eyes very clear signs of those things which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man."

<margin>The Trinity shines in all things.</margin>
For if we believe universal nature to be perfect, we must also confess it to be threefold. In every natural thing, something of the number of the Divine Triad shines forth and is expressed; and since every triple thing is perfect, and we assert that GOD is the craftsman, author, and creator of all, we are necessarily compelled to assert that He is both triple and perfect. For every creature is a "divine something," and as the ancient said, "a particle of the divine breath" <note>original: "divinæ particula auræ," a quote from Horace (Satires 2.2.79) often used to describe the soul.</note>. Every creature, being an image and very near character of the divine goodness, must carry the vestiges of divine perfection and unity. Let us therefore discuss the grades of all nature; let us search the universal nature of things deeply, and we shall gaze with admiration at the traces of this wonderful Trinity impressed upon every single thing.

<margin>The Trinity in Adam. The Trinity in the soul.</margin>
The first production of man began in Adam as a Monad (Unity), which, diffusing itself into a Dyad (Two), produced Eve; from both of them was born Abel, completing the Triad (Three) of human genesis. This same pattern has been preserved in the successive propagation of the human race in the father, mother, and son. Furthermore, the rational soul is one indivisible substance, yet it is triple without being divided: it is fruitful, numerous, and distinct in **intellect**, **memory**, and **will**. The intellect is not the memory, nor the will; the memory is neither the intellect nor the will; the will is neither the intellect nor the memory; yet they are one and the same substance of the soul, distinct by a triple relationship. Again, every soul is triple: **rational**, **sensitive**, and **vegetative**. The intellect is triple: **Divine**, **Angelic**, and **Human**; we call the first the Mind, the second the Intellect proper, and the last Reason.

<margin>The Trinity in a tree.</margin>
A tree is one, joined in its trunk, but distinct in its branches, upon which it brings forth only three things: **leaves**, **flowers**, and **fruit**. There are three intervals of magnitude: **length**, **breadth**, and **depth**, which correspond to the line, the surface, and the body—the common measure of all conceivable bodies. There are three primary and principal units of numbers: the **linear**, **superficial**, and **corporeal** (the tens, the hundreds, and the thousands), flowing from the simplest point or Monad, as we showed in the preceding pages. The tens correspond to the line, the hundreds to the square surface, and the thousands to the cubic body. I could bring forth innumerable examples of this Triad in all grades of being in this place, but since we strive for brevity, we select the choice ones for the purpose of our demonstration.

### §. I. I.

## On the Music of the Triune GOD with the Angelic Orders.

<margin>All things exist in number, weight, and measure.</margin>
God arranged the world through three things: number, weight, and measure, through which all things bear the footprint of the most high Trinity. For they derive their **number** from that supreme Monad <note>original: "monade." In Pythagorean and Neoplatonic thought, the Monad represents the "One" or the indivisible source of all numbers.</note> and the fountain of all numbers; they derive their **weight** from that Wisdom which balances all things; and they derive their **measure** from that Spirit of the Creator who distributes a fitting portion to each. Hence, according to the doctrine of the Magi, three things rule the world: GOD, Mind, and Soul. To GOD properly belongs the Monad or Unity; to Mind or Wisdom belongs order or weight; and to the Soul or Spirit belongs measure and motion. 

The enigmatic pronouncement of Plato to King Dionysius explains this beautifully: *All things are around the King of all; all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all beautiful things.* <margin>Plato's riddle.</margin> For all things are connected around the King by his unity, all things are weighed for his sake, and all are ordered toward him. He, by numbering and proportioning all things, is the cause of all beauty, acting as the efficient, final, governing, and sustaining principle—the beginning, middle, and end of all. As Orpheus also witnesses, all things are from him, all things are toward him, and all things rest established within him. For GOD is a sphere whose center is everywhere (which is the Father through his power), but whose circumference is nowhere (which is the Son or Wisdom through his incomprehensible immensity). The mutual relationship between the center and the circumference, or the radii, signifies the Spirit and reciprocal love.

<margin>Every harmony is completed by three.</margin>
Since, therefore, the first and supreme Monad is triple, the fabric of the universe could not emanate from this triple archetype unless it was also constituted as triple in a threefold order and resonant number. For the most perfect harmony of all must consist of only three voices: the lowest, the middle, and the highest. When united, these form the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason," the musical interval of an octave.</note>, which is composed of the *diapente* <note>original: "diapente," the interval of a perfect fifth.</note> and the *diatessaron* <note>original: "diatessaron," the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>. This is the most perfect of consonances and the first harmony, and it is seen beautifully in these three numbers: 1, 2, 3. 

<margin>Harmony shines forth in 1, 2, 3.</margin>
Here, **1** holds the position of the simple and "equal-sounding" <note>original: "isophonæ."</note> Monad, the origin of all consonances, which belongs to GOD the Father. **2**, related to 1, functions as the octave or *diapason*, and belongs to the Son. **3**, related to 2, represents the perfect fifth or *diapente*, and belongs to the Spirit as the connecting power. Just as the middle voice of the fifth connects the lowest and highest voices into a three-voice harmony, so the Spirit is the bond of the Father and the Son, the beginning and the end, in one incomprehensible harmony. We must now explain how every harmonic concert in Nature is propagated from this ineffable and most fertile harmony of the Trinity.

<margin>How the triad is spread into the multitude.</margin>
Thus, the simple Ternary (the number three) is attributed to the most simple GOD, who exists as the highest and undivided unity, yet is spread into three "hypostases" <note>original: "hypostases," a theological term for the three distinct persons of the Trinity.</note> in a manner ineffable to the human mind. This Ternary, moving outside itself into the "multitude" and being tripled, produces the wondrous "symphonism" of the three Enneads <note>original: "enneadum." An Ennead is a grouping of nine.</note>. This marks the nine Angelic orders, the nine Heavens, and the nine types of elemental nature. All of these are perfected by the Decad (the number ten), not without an admirable mystery, as will be said later. Furthermore, the Ternary when cubed—that is, the Ternary multiplied by its own square (9)—produces the most mysterious number of all, **27**, which is the complement of all enneads and the seedbed of all harmonic proportions.

The first Triad is uncreated. In its second propagation, it spreads itself into the three triads of the intellectual world. <margin>How the angelic orders correspond to the Holy Trinity.</margin> In this way, the **Seraphic order**, being inflamed with love, corresponds to the Spirit (who is the love and the bond of the Father and the Son). The **Cherubic order**, full of Wisdom and Knowledge, corresponds to the supreme Wisdom, the Son. The order of the **Thrones** corresponds to the Father, who, as the Psalmist witnesses, *has set his throne in judgment*, and so through the Son shall judge the world. This is the triad of the perfection and likeness of GOD. 

However, since the Highest Good is diffusive of itself, it produced another triple order through its Triad, so that it might govern lower creatures in a perfect and harmonic order, like a supreme prince and craftsman. The Father, as Lord of all, moderates the entire state of the political world through the order of **Dominations**. Through the order of **Powers**, the Son (to whom all power is given by the Father in Heaven and on earth) administers all things in their due order. Through the order of **Virtues**, which is the "Spirit of the mouth of GOD," comes all their strength; that is, all are led toward true holi— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "sanctitatem" (holiness), continued on the next page.</note>
